I only bought the game because I heard about the upcoming Morrowind expansion, and I was a huge Morriwind fan. I’m not ready to shell out 40 EUR for an expansion that doesn’t actually exist yet, but I wanted to familiarize myself with the base game in the meanwhile.
Like many other players, I had some extremely disappointing and annoying experience with the launcher: it simply stopped after “preparing to install”, without any error message. I had to spend half of my day just to get the game run, which I find completely unacceptable from a big company like Bethesda/Zenimax. (Hint: Starting my system in safe mode with networking did the trick; the launcher was able to proceed.)
Now on to the actual gameplay experience: As a new player, I found the graphics and the atmosphere truly amazing; almost every area I visited so far feels like a piece of art. The voice acting, the sounds, the particles and basically everything else feels polished and well designed. I never had the same feeling in e.g. WOW.
The progression and the adventuring feels a bit boring for me personally though: it seems that there is nothing really interesting to find in the world, it feels very repetitive and completely predictable after only a few hours of playing. I was also unimpressed with the skill tree, it simply seems boring and oversimplified.
Concerning the homestead update and the new home ownership: I was actually quite excited first to get my free apartment, only to find out that you can’t use ANY storage items in your home; you can’t put down e.g. a chest to store your stuff. Really boggles my mind… I can’t see any point in having a home without this feature, but maybe just because I’m such a hoarder.
I really missed the economy in the game… Maybe I’m just clueless how to use it, but I didn’t see any auction house or exchange, only some guild stores which seemed limited and completely uninteresting. In an MMO I’d expect to be able to easily sell and buy items to/from other players. Also, when it comes to buying items from NPC stores… for some reason all NPC traders I found seemed to have the same pointless crap for sale, and everything was grossly overpriced: items with real value of 5 or 10 was selling for 100 or 200 golds, I have no idea why. I didn’t buy a single item during my playtime.
So overall, I find this game very pretty and enchanting, and I’d want to say good things about it, but to be honest I feel like wasting my time whenever I actually play it. I started to write this review wanting to recommend it, but I had to realize that I can’t actually do that with a clear conscience.
To be fair, I’m more into space games and building/survival games generally, so maybe this is why it feels too static for me. So, for players used to complex indie games, or for players who want to hoard and trade… I probably wouldn’t recommend ESO.

Alien Isolation is a true masterpiece of a perfect mix of stealth and horror nicely wrapped up in the skin of my favorite horror movie of all time. As a young kid terrified of the original movie, I always wondered what it would be like to play out a scenario similar to the movie Alien and now I know how scary it really is. The authentic look and feel of the game makes this one of the best games based on a movie that I’ve ever played since Star Wars: Tie Fighter and Goldeneye 007. It’s so good it would be a great sequel to Alien/Aliens if it were made into a movie. I had a few nightmares after playing this and that never happens to me with other games.
The level of detail with the ambience, sounds and music are exactly spot on and faithful to immerse you in the world of Alien. No modern era game hand holding and arrows pointing out exactly where to go or regenerating health. The unpredictable Alien AI is refreshing and there are other enemies you encounter that are also more powerful, hostile and can kill you. Compared to other survival horror games, Alien Isolation easily makes it up to my top three rivaled only by Silent Hill 2 or Fatal Frame. As a stealth game, it is also one of the best right up there with the classic Thief games and in fact, my stealth skills in Thief helped me here.
My main issue is that there are too many hostile humans who shoot first. If you could actually choose to join, leave or kill them with more quests based on who you join, that would add to the game. Also, it seems the Alien is always targeting you and follows you wherever you go, which is unfair but I understand why.
In a generation that has been extremely disappointing so far, this survival horror/stealth gem really outshines them all. I’ll be watching Creative Assembly closely from now on for their next release hopefully another Alien game.

Since this game is currently on sale, I thought I would write a little review. In Alien:Isolation you play as Amanda Ripley in search of her mother. You explore Sevastopol Station looking for the flight recorder of the Nostromo of the first Alien Film. But since it's an Alien game sooner or later things will start going wrong.
First of all, this game is one of my favorite games of the last 5 years. Sega deserve all the respect in the world for making such a game. Especially in times of streamlining. Let alone for having the balls of making a niche game, Sega deservers your purchase. When was the last time you heard of a Triple A horror game?
Now to the actual review. Firstly i would like to point out the atmosphere of the game, which is incredible thick and close to the first Alien movie by Ridley Scott. If you haven't seen it already check it out immediately. I recommend seeing it before playing the game. It will make your experience better, but it is not a must. It captures the spirit of the film effortlessly. Furthermore the game offers one of the best enviromental story telling that i have seen so far. The station kind of reminded of the USG Ishimura of Dead Space, so if you like that kind of look you will  enjoy it too.
Gameplaywise imagen Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but with way better enemy A.I. and also normal enemies. The Alien behaves unpredictable and will keep you on the edge of your seat. It also interacts with normal enemies. The latter being really creepy looking and tough synthetics. They have this mannequin look, which is really freaky. I played it before Amnesia and i could not play it, because it was like playing a worse version of Alien:Isolation.
Storywise the game is ok. But I must say it kept me going till the end.
I heard a lot of compliants of people say this game would be too long. I can see the cirticism, because you might find the gameplay repetitive. But i had lot of fun exploring the Sevastopol Space Station, which kept me going and having fun till the end. Horrorwise it is more stonger at the beging because you learn how to behave when the alien is around, but I still liked it.
I only can highly recommend this game and beg you to buy it. I wanna see a second part so bad and i think it's a shame that Sega sees the game as a finencial fail. Nevertheless in my opinion 50 bucks were well spend in this game. Thank for reading my review, hope you liked it. If you liked it comment me on my Steam Profil page just like many others already have done. If you didnot and want to insult me feel free to do so. K, thx, bye!

Alien Isolation is hands down the greatest atmospheric horror games ever made. The first 5-10 hours of this game is absolutely terrifying thanks to the outstanding work that Creative Assembly put in to keeping the game as true to the films as possible. Despite being in a constant state of anxiety as I played I always had a strong urge to explore the incredible environments.
The game play of Alien Isolation by itself could be described as slow and shallow, but it works so dam well with the atmospheric terror and terrific visual design, that you don’t have time to realize that this is the 100th time you’ve have played the door unlock mini game, as you can hear the alien breathing down your neck. Unfortunately as you start to master the game this dose start to become apparent, luckily this didn’t occur for me until some where into my 2nd play through, and even still this just meant I could finally play with a little more freedom from the terror and finally explore Sevastopol Station.
The game is constantly throwing new challenges at you as you try to survive and excusing one or two chapters of the game where you have to back track, there are always new levels for you to survive. To aid with your chances of survival you have a number of weapons and cartable distractions which you will be either given or have to find as you progress through the game, most of which have their purpose while others can feel abit obsolete. I feel this can come down to play styles and situation than poor design. There is one weapon however that I feel is to overpowered, the
, seeing as it becomes your go to defense for dealing the Alien and the games other dangers. This is kind of balanced by its effectiveness being made worse every time you use it, but I was still able to beat the game never running out of ammo for it. I feel more time without it would have kept the fear factor up a lot longer.
The only real negative of the game form a technical side is the physics. You will occasionally encounter floating objects and boxes that travel faster than the speed of sound when nudged. Surprisingly in a game that works so hard on immersing the player this is easily looked past.
5/5

In the same manner as its predecessor, Bastion, this game is visually stunning despite being locked in an isometric perspective. Transistor draws heavily from the vibrant art nouveau styles of Gustav Klimt and Alphonse Mucha and the Jazzy/Electronic soundtrack resonates beautifully with the painterly visuals (quite literally at times). All of this is reinforced by a compelling narrative and a strategic and satisfying combat system.
Encounters lock you into an area, where you must chain abilities together for maximum effect in order to eliminate your foes. At the beginning, you have limited access to skills and enemies are fairly predictable. However, as you advance through the game (or replays), you can experiment with different combinations of skills which can be used either actively, as an upgrade to another skill, or as a passive ability. Additionally, you can increase the difficulty by selecting certain "Limiters", which do various things like make enemies respawn faster or do more damage. There's a lot of replay value just from the various combinations of skills.
It is, unfortunately, a rather short story. The first playthrough took me about 8 hours. However, the replay feature allows you to continue from the beginning with all of your skills but adjusts the difficulty accordingly.
Art: 10/10 (beautiful)
Music: 10/10 (very good)
Gameplay: 9/10 (minor grievances like things occasionally getting blasted out of bounds or blocked by foreground elements. Combat rewards careful planning, but sometimes you will get ganked nonetheless. Oh, and ♥♥♥♥ those dog guys and the floating Hairpieces)
Story: 8/10 (it ends a bit abruptly and it leaves a lot unexplained. I also have mixed feelings about the sandbox area, since it did occasionally interrupt the narrative to suddenly go to a safe zone to goof around)

Papers, Please is a fun simulation game in which you play as an immigration border patrol agent for a Communist government. You have a book of rules and it is your job to either approve or deny citizens. If there is a discrepancy between the rules and their passport or paperwork, you have to interrogate them. Upon interrorgation, you can detain them (like if they have weapons or forged papers) or let them through. There are some moralistic choices along the way. For instance, one husband has all the correct paperwork, but his wife is next in line with missing paperwork. Do you let her through and risk a citation or deny her because of the rules?
As the game progresses, there are more and more information you have to keep an eye on. Even the tiniest error can glaze over your eyes like mismatched gender and weight on the paperwork. The game may seem "boring and repititive," but that is the point of the game. It's suppposed to simulate a boring, real life job. There is also a secret organization that tries to take down the government and you can choose to participate with them or not. Papers, Please has a great sense of humor with 20 different endings and memorable characters. In order to attain a better apartment for your family as well as food and heat, you have to process people faster and correctly to make more money.
"Glory to Arstotzka!"

Premise: You are a customs officer in a Soviet style world of corruption, dodgy travellers and terrorism. Your job is to check people through customs and earn enough to keep your family alive and well. You do this by checking the paperwork and pick out the discrepencies and decide if they should go through.
Audience: Highly recommend for people who pride themselves on their observation skills and moral standing (latter clearly not necessary).
Gameplay: Good story progression with multiple endings with associated achievements. Characters have medium depth (i.e. you know their names, and get used to their behaviours). Day to Day difficulty increases, especially when situation changes (i.e. policy changes, bombs). Long-term difficulty proves the bigger challenge (i.e. not doing well day to day may end up with family members disappearing later).
Replayability: So so. You'll want to replay from certain days to get different endings but you can do this without restartig whole game and they give a few save options. Replayability for me came from Endless Mode where you compete on the Steam leaderboards.
Drawbacks: Graphics have been deliberately downgraded which gives a bit of distance from some of the really horrible decisions you have to make. Endless Mode could use some expanding.
Conclusion: Worth every cent and highly recommended.

I've grown up with the Sonic series with my first Sonic game being Sonic 3 when I had a Sega Genesis as a child. So as a result, I've seen the highs of the series and lows of the series. (*cough* Sonic Boom *cough*) So, I pre-ordered Forces and got the chance to play it when I got off work the day it released. And to be honest... While it has its GLARING issues, it's really not as terrible as some of the reviews I've read for it say it is.
Story: By far the best aspect of Sonic Forces, because the plot was rather unique. Eggman has finally defeated Sonic with the help of the main antagonist Infinite and manages to take over the world. With Sonic defeated and the world taken over by Eggman, Sonic's friends, with the help of your fan character whom you create (giving me Dragonball Xenoverse vibes in that respect) and your fan character mainly is the catalyst to the plot while Sonic is the protagonist, with the ultimate goal of freeing the world from Eggman's control.
Gameplay: Kind of a mixed bag. One thing I noticed while I play the game is that the game will occasionally chug like an Irishman at the least convenient times, leading to some deaths that really shouldn't have happened. But if the game doesn't chug, overall, it runs pretty smoothly. Unfortunately, the game is VERY, VERY short and easy. I managed to beat the game in three and a half hours. But fortunately, there's oodles and oodles of customization for your character, so there's quite a bit of replayability in that department. One thing that might throw people off is the fact that you now have infinite lives. When you die, the game simply says "Try Again" and has you restart at the last checkpoints. Although... The game does have a system like Phantasy Star Universe where every time you die, it takes away from your score.
Music: As is always with the Sonic series, the music is PHENOMINAL. My favorite track still stands as the Prison Hall theme.
Overall, I generally enjoyed Forces and while I can see where the game gets some of its hate... Like I said before, I do think that the reviewers and the Sonic fandom in general are being a little unfair in their treatment of it.

Sonic Forces is Sonic Generations, but not as good. With Sonic Mania reminding people that 2D Sonic was always good, I had hoped that Sonic Forces would show that games built around the daytime Unleashed stages were also good once you trimmed out the flab. Unfortunately, between Generations and Forces, Sonic has lot a lot of the flair and the little edge (not the Shadow edge) that he had left. 3D Sonic is just not as good in Forces as it was in Generations or Unleashed or Colours, as they have clearly decided to make him a mishmash of his Lost World self and his 'Boost' self. This means he can double jump, which works when the levels are built with it in mind, and doesn't when the game decides to play more like a Boost stage, and drift is removed, but because of how the stages are designed, maybe it wouldn't have any use, which brings me onto another point: the 3D stages are boring and lack a lot of the design quirks present in older 3D Sonic games. Meanwhile on the 2D front, the 2D stages aren't as good as Mania. That is all I can say about the 2D stages, as they feel almost, to be honest, thrown in at the last minute to get fans of the 2D games on board.
Then the there is the Avatar, which doesn't play badly, but does nothing exciting, new or brilliantly either. The Avatar has a ton of clothing options and there are minor gameplay variations between the different species you can select, so it doesn't feel completely pointless, but the stages can't help but feel like 3D Sonic stages with a blaster/flamethrower/whatever instead of a go fast button. Again, it doesn't do anything badly, but it does nothing well, which sums up how I feel about almost everything in this game outside of the graphics. The soundtrack is varied, and there isn't anything bad on here, but I didn't find anything memorable outside of the track that plays when you have the QTE you can fail and the game carries on like nothing happened (it's called Fist Bump I think?).
The story is brilliant, but not for the reasons that the writer probably wanted. Sonic Team managed to throw in so many characters and have them act edgy and never stop talking. Unfortunately, they skipped over fan favourite Big the Cat, and to a lesser degree, Blaze the Cat and <enter your favourite absent character here>. The antagonist, Infinite, is also brilliant, and his backstory, explained in Episode Shadow, is pathetic and only makes the plot seem even more pointlessly over the top and needsly edgy, which sums up the entire plot. It is really hard to take the story seriously with bright colourful characters talking about the edgy horrors of war caused by Eggman, who you can't take seriously due to the hammy nature of the character. The voice acting is still of varying quality, going from Mike Pollock being fun, to good enough, to passable, to grating, to poor and annoying, and the entire story reminds me of the original Titanfall, where the entire plot could be summed up as a cliched radio-drama that plays in the background as you run around and break stuff. Despite that, playing it through I couldn't help but feel too much emphasis had been put on this weak story, whereas in most good Sonic games, the plot takes the back seat to the actual game, here, it is in your face from start to finish.
In short, play every other 3D Sonic game first before you play this if you want more 3D Sonic, and play every other 2D Sonic game before you play this if you want more 2D Sonic, as this game is non-essential. It doesn't do anything stand-out, and feels forgettable, and on that account, I don't recommend this. Platformers on Steam are not a rarity, and there are so many better options out there for you to look into and play first. Even on the Sonic front, although you don't have Colours or Unleashed, you've got other options first. It's not a terrible game, and is far from Sonic 06, but that just makes it even more boring. You can do better, and Sonic Team can do better.

3 years later, sega announced a new game called Sonic Project 2017. Wether or not this game is good depends on who you ask: critics will say it's bad, whereas actually Sonic fans; while admiting that it has a few problems, claim that they had alot of fun with it.
Gameplay:
Again, this is up to opinion. I personally enjoy all 3 gameplay styles, where other people will say that Classic Sonic sucks or that the Avatar sucks and so on. However, I think that Sonic's boost gameplay in this game feels very powerful, feels very fast, and requires you to actually pay attention when using it unlike what some people will tell you, hold down the boost button non-stop will end up killing you, esspecially in the later levels, and the more you die the harder it will be to get a high rank on all the stages. Avatar's gameplay has grown on me over the course of the game, there are plently of weapons (known as "Wispons") to choose from, with every wispon having its own ways of attacking as well as unique perks varying to earning rings from killing enemies, to gaining a boost of speed when you do a stomp. Classic Sonic is considered to be the worst of the 3 styles, and I can understand where those people are coming from, but he isn't completely unplayable, he still has is spin dash, even having his brand new drop dash from Sonic Mania, his levels are great, not too easy and not completely impossible.
Story:
I had very low expectations for the story, which is why the game ended up exceeding my expectations when I ended up finishing the game. All of the characters (excluding Tails unfortunately) are characterized and repesented very well, with the voice acting for each being top notch. Especially Shadow, who many fans previously complained about his new voice actor not being as good as his old, but for this game Shadows VA mananged to pull of Shadows old voice very well and it sounds great. Knuckles in particular stands out as being a very compitent and smart leader, which is a refreshing change compared to his Sonic Boom characterization. Silver isn't super cringey like he has been in previous games, and instead acts very compitent and respectful. There are some good jokes that managed to get some laughs out of me, and I took the story seriously when it wanted to be taken seriously, this is also true for Infinite's character who ended up having excellent voice acting and even some challenging boss fights, which is ALOT more than what i can say for my first impressions from the initial trailers.
Game Time:
While you can go through the whole story in about 3 hours, it is made very clear once you start playing the game that the story isn't even going to take up half your total gametime. The levels where HEAVILY designed with replayablity in mind, such as doing the daily bonuses for score multiplyers to get those S ranks. Getting all 5 Red Star Rings in each level in order for you to play each level AGAIN to get the 5 Number Rings, then doing eaching level A THIRD TIME to get all 5 Silver Moon Rings. Add in the achievments coupled with the fact that many of the stages are very fun to replay in general, and you have yourself a 20-30 hour game.
DLC:
Sega has already stated that all current and future DLC will be free, and that has held true so far. The DLC is all free, and most of it takes less than a minute to install for something that adds harmless extra content to the game.
I definitely reccomend this game, if you are still on the fence about it, get it while its on sale and I assure you it will be worth your time.

Alien Isolation is a true masterpiece of a perfect mix of stealth and horror nicely wrapped up in the skin of my favorite horror movie of all time. As a young kid terrified of the original movie, I always wondered what it would be like to play out a scenario similar to the movie Alien and now I know how scary it really is. The authentic look and feel of the game makes this one of the best games based on a movie that I’ve ever played since Star Wars: Tie Fighter and Goldeneye 007. It’s so good it would be a great sequel to Alien/Aliens if it were made into a movie. I had a few nightmares after playing this and that never happens to me with other games.
The level of detail with the ambience, sounds and music are exactly spot on and faithful to immerse you in the world of Alien. No modern era game hand holding and arrows pointing out exactly where to go or regenerating health. The unpredictable Alien AI is refreshing and there are other enemies you encounter that are also more powerful, hostile and can kill you. Compared to other survival horror games, Alien Isolation easily makes it up to my top three rivaled only by Silent Hill 2 or Fatal Frame. As a stealth game, it is also one of the best right up there with the classic Thief games and in fact, my stealth skills in Thief helped me here.
My main issue is that there are too many hostile humans who shoot first. If you could actually choose to join, leave or kill them with more quests based on who you join, that would add to the game. Also, it seems the Alien is always targeting you and follows you wherever you go, which is unfair but I understand why.
In a generation that has been extremely disappointing so far, this survival horror/stealth gem really outshines them all. I’ll be watching Creative Assembly closely from now on for their next release hopefully another Alien game.

Since this game is currently on sale, I thought I would write a little review. In Alien:Isolation you play as Amanda Ripley in search of her mother. You explore Sevastopol Station looking for the flight recorder of the Nostromo of the first Alien Film. But since it's an Alien game sooner or later things will start going wrong.
First of all, this game is one of my favorite games of the last 5 years. Sega deserve all the respect in the world for making such a game. Especially in times of streamlining. Let alone for having the balls of making a niche game, Sega deservers your purchase. When was the last time you heard of a Triple A horror game?
Now to the actual review. Firstly i would like to point out the atmosphere of the game, which is incredible thick and close to the first Alien movie by Ridley Scott. If you haven't seen it already check it out immediately. I recommend seeing it before playing the game. It will make your experience better, but it is not a must. It captures the spirit of the film effortlessly. Furthermore the game offers one of the best enviromental story telling that i have seen so far. The station kind of reminded of the USG Ishimura of Dead Space, so if you like that kind of look you will  enjoy it too.
Gameplaywise imagen Amnesia: The Dark Descent, but with way better enemy A.I. and also normal enemies. The Alien behaves unpredictable and will keep you on the edge of your seat. It also interacts with normal enemies. The latter being really creepy looking and tough synthetics. They have this mannequin look, which is really freaky. I played it before Amnesia and i could not play it, because it was like playing a worse version of Alien:Isolation.
Storywise the game is ok. But I must say it kept me going till the end.
I heard a lot of compliants of people say this game would be too long. I can see the cirticism, because you might find the gameplay repetitive. But i had lot of fun exploring the Sevastopol Space Station, which kept me going and having fun till the end. Horrorwise it is more stonger at the beging because you learn how to behave when the alien is around, but I still liked it.
I only can highly recommend this game and beg you to buy it. I wanna see a second part so bad and i think it's a shame that Sega sees the game as a finencial fail. Nevertheless in my opinion 50 bucks were well spend in this game. Thank for reading my review, hope you liked it. Alien Isolation is hands down the greatest atmospheric horror games ever made. The first 5-10 hours of this game is absolutely terrifying thanks to the outstanding work that Creative Assembly put in to keeping the game as true to the films as possible. Despite being in a constant state of anxiety as I played I always had a strong urge to explore the incredible environments.
The game play of Alien Isolation by itself could be described as slow and shallow, but it works so dam well with the atmospheric terror and terrific visual design, that you don’t have time to realize that this is the 100th time you’ve have played the door unlock mini game, as you can hear the alien breathing down your neck. Unfortunately as you start to master the game this dose start to become apparent, luckily this didn’t occur for me until some where into my 2nd play through, and even still this just meant I could finally play with a little more freedom from the terror and finally explore Sevastopol Station.
The game is constantly throwing new challenges at you as you try to survive and excusing one or two chapters of the game where you have to back track, there are always new levels for you to survive. To aid with your chances of survival you have a number of weapons and cartable distractions which you will be either given or have to find as you progress through the game, most of which have their purpose while others can feel abit obsolete. I feel this can come down to play styles and situation than poor design. There is one weapon however that I feel is to overpowered, the
, seeing as it becomes your go to defense for dealing the Alien and the games other dangers. This is kind of balanced by its effectiveness being made worse every time you use it, but I was still able to beat the game never running out of ammo for it. I feel more time without it would have kept the fear factor up a lot longer.
The only real negative of the game form a technical side is the physics. You will occasionally encounter floating objects and boxes that travel faster than the speed of sound when nudged. Surprisingly in a game that works so hard on immersing the player this is easily looked past.
5/5

MW2 was the last great game of its franchise. To start off, the story is actually pretty good. It's short, but the characters have good personality and the story was pretty tight, with a fun twist towards the end. Spec Ops is a nice sort of "Challenge" mode, though nothing to get excited over. If you're into challenging your abilities as a FPS gamer, then you'll like it. On to the multiplayer, I believe it's fun. I don't know what it is exactly, but the feel of the gunplay is very nice. I'm a fan of the customization as well as the perks that the game offers to your soldier. The major issue regarding weapons is there are quite a few combos that were left untouched and overpowered, but fortunately most people quietly agree not to use them since they believe them to be cheap. Also, the game has been somewhat of a graveyard and host to hacked lobbies, since Infinity Ward has essentially abandoned it. Despite this, I still recommend the game for its value. Pick it up on sale, and you wont regret it. The game is not completely dead, and from time you time you can get in a multiplayer and have a real good time!

Playing 'How Bad Can I Be' from 'The Lorax' fits all too well when it comes to playing this game, based on my experiences and tastes. ._.
-0-
Joke aside, I can easily recommend this game to anyone that likes building, maintaining, and expanding an ever-hungry machine-of-a-factory. Resource management is definitely noticeable, especially so when the resource nodes you start with eventually run out, prompting expansion to newer territories and establishing secondary bases for resource extraction.
Provided you haven't switched on one option, it isn't gonna be easy all the way, since the local wildlife WILL lash out at you and your factory at some point, or rather, when pollution starts reaching their nests. And like similar mechanics, they will get tougher the more pollution you put out, so it also becomes a bit of a balance act; Optimize production and extractions but suffer heavy attacks from the resulting mass pollution, or try and be (somewhat) green yet take longer to get larger projects done.
Despite the game being in early access, it does take a good while to try and get everything done, especially so if trying to be green and/or get all techs researched. There are mods for this game as well if there are those who are into the mod-making/using scenes, and like always, mods expand the content of the game even more and/or provide fixes for stuff that's currently botched. Can't really think on how often updates are gonna be coming out, but based on what all's present in the game, I am looking forward to seeing what all gets added in later versions.
The multiplayer side of the game...eh, if you're not a fan of portforwarding, I suggest waiting till the current system gets changed to where having to do such isn't required.

since i was told by a friend that he played this game, i decided i might take a look at it. I like Minecraft and Games that are somewhat alike.
First things first, Downloading the game is rather fast ~1gb even with my connection. And the graphics looks neat. But thats about everything good i have to report about this game.
Now, lets take a look at the game. You join, you are naked, and you got no idea what to do. So far nothing bad. But then its possible to rope a player and drag him across the map till he commits suicide or dies due to the lack of water. You cant do anything, but watch yourself getting dragged accross the map. Great Design Choice i might add.
Oh yes, the Map... Its pretty small, there are Servers with 30 slots, 30 Slots means 30 ppl that need resources. Now there are like 10ish Stone Nodes on the whole map, and they are at 3 spots, which are at a pretty small area. Now, you need 30 Stones to make a single stone block of cobblestone. So if you are alone on the Server, you can grab like 1000 stones, which will give you roughly 30 blocks of cobblestone. In itself that doesnt sound too bad, but considering that there are 30 other ppl on the server you might effectively get 1 cobbelstone block per income cycles/spawn cycle. That is, if distributed evenly :D ... yeah IF! being the word here, which leads to the point i made earlier.
What will happen, you are alone and someone is going to rope you and you cant do anything, or 2 ppl will just kill you. That is, if you are not currently dealing with one of the hacking population of this game. considering how many ppl on those servers actually hack it would appear that it is possible to hack the game by simply changing a single property file. Being immortal and having the ability to do whatever you want appears to bore some ppl, so the start to lock up those who try to play without cheating, since there is nothing else for them to do.
Now in addition to this awesome gameplaying, there are situations in which the games will shut down 100%. For example if you disconnect from a server, the game will just crash. This and the fact, that you are never really gone from the server, leads me to believe that you arent really meant to go offline anyways.
You think you read that wrong? NO! You are never going to leave the Server, your Character will remain on the Server for everyone to torture while you dont have a chance to do anything against it. Now you might think that you could build a house/castle to protect yourself against it. Well, let me tell you, that wont help. Chest can be opened by anyone, even tho there is a lock on the chest implying it is actually locked, well you are wrong if you thought your stuff is safe in a chest.
You built a castle with a court? well, too bad someone is just gonna build a tower in front of your wall jump over it and he is in. So you have to have a roof over every room. But, that wont do you any good either, someone will just pick you lock, steal your stuff, lock you up and you are going to start from 0. Okay, you got your house, but there wont be anythign in it except empty boxes. And that house of yours wont do you any good either, as you have just experienced.
oh yeah, and then, there is the tax system, your current king can raise taxes... i witnessed 20% taxes, so everytime you take some wood from a tree, you are going to send 20% of that hard earned stuff to somebody who is just doing nothing, at least there are enough trees arround, so you dont have to worry too much about getting any wood as you'd have to fight for anything else.
Here i am wondering if i missed anything? There are so many bad things about this game, i can barely remember every single detail. I want my money back, this game isnt worth 20€ maybe 5.
almost forgot, the game looks neat, but will lag only quite good hardware. im running an i7 with a gtx 780 and it will lag on high settings. In addition to that, dont even think about running a multi screen setup, the mouse is likely to move out on a screen on which there is no game, so if you click you will be thrown out of the game, and are going to end up in ropes or what so ever :D
I think this coveres the game pretty good. And Argueing Oh its early access might excuse for some flaws and the fact that it will take you about 5-6 hours to build everything the game has to offer.
as you can imagine i do not recommed buying, let alone playing this game. i deeply regret my choice to try it and might reconsider the next time im thinking about buying another game i dont know anything about and yet asks me for 20€. So far ive always been lucky even tho i bought quite a lot of early access games so far.

Papers, Please is a fun simulation game in which you play as an immigration border patrol agent for a Communist government. You have a book of rules and it is your job to either approve or deny citizens. If there is a discrepancy between the rules and their passport or paperwork, you have to interrogate them. Upon interrorgation, you can detain them (like if they have weapons or forged papers) or let them through. There are some moralistic choices along the way. For instance, one husband has all the correct paperwork, but his wife is next in line with missing paperwork. Do you let her through and risk a citation or deny her because of the rules?
As the game progresses, there are more and more information you have to keep an eye on. Even the tiniest error can glaze over your eyes like mismatched gender and weight on the paperwork. The game may seem "boring and repititive," but that is the point of the game. It's suppposed to simulate a boring, real life job. There is also a secret organization that tries to take down the government and you can choose to participate with them or not. Papers, Please has a great sense of humor with 20 different endings and memorable characters. In order to attain a better apartment for your family as well as food and heat, you have to process people faster and correctly to make more money.
"Glory to Arstotzka!"
I <3 oppression!

Premise: You are a customs officer in a Soviet style world of corruption, dodgy travellers and terrorism. Your job is to check people through customs and earn enough to keep your family alive and well. You do this by checking the paperwork and pick out the discrepencies and decide if they should go through.
Audience: Highly recommend for people who pride themselves on their observation skills and moral standing (latter clearly not necessary).
Gameplay: Good story progression with multiple endings with associated achievements. Characters have medium depth (i.e. you know their names, and get used to their behaviours). Day to Day difficulty increases, especially when situation changes (i.e. policy changes, bombs). Long-term difficulty proves the bigger challenge (i.e. not doing well day to day may end up with family members disappearing later).
Replayability: So so. You'll want to replay from certain days to get different endings but you can do this without restartig whole game and they give a few save options. Replayability for me came from Endless Mode where you compete on the Steam leaderboards.
Drawbacks: Graphics have been deliberately downgraded which gives a bit of distance from some of the really horrible decisions you have to make. Endless Mode could use some expanding.
Conclusion: Worth every cent and highly recommended.

ESO Gold top seller in Steam? oh boy some people didn't do their research.
-Graphics are very good, lightning is amazing. Sounds assets are ok.
-Leveling up is meh in ESO, quests are your default run of the mill, fetch/kill quests. At least there are spots where you can grind mobs for xp.
-Collecting stuff like, motifs and achievements is fun, if not a bit grindy at times.
-Level design, costumes, effects are ok, most of the time.
-Dungeons and exploration are mediocre, nothing really interesting or different from what you've propably already seen from an Elder Scrolls game, or any MMO fantasy for that matter.
-Gear system SUCKS so bad. You will have to wear very specific pieces of armor/weapons if you want to get the max out of your gear and aquiring those pieces is VERY grindy, which lowers your enthusiasm for experimentation.
Also no 'transmogrify' here, your character will never look the way you want him to look, despite the myriad of awesome styles of armor the art department has created.
-Also, like the above, Racial unique stats suck, each race is focused on being better on a certain stat. So if you want to focus on stamina for example, a Redguard is far superior when compared to other races and you would be just gimping yourself by picking something else.
-Very, VERY grindy mount upgrade system. It literaly will take you 6 months to fully level up the stats of your horse. And it's not even account based, you have to do that for each character you create. -Unless you spend some extra real money of course-
-Which brings us to the next awful system. DLC. The game is sliced into DLC pieces that cut some serious content from the base game. Some examples: Cyrodill PvP area is DLC, Orsinium province is DLC, Thieves GUild? DLC. Dark Brotherhood? DLC. Imperial race??! DLC!
Why would they make those core content elements into DLC when they already have extra COSMETIC DLC? if you want to "support the devs" (despite you already bought their game, it's not exactly free2play), cosmetic DLC like mounts, pets, costumes etc would be sufficient one would think? Well the devs think like this obviously ---> $$$
This is what made me quit the game in disgust. PVP is simply unplayable.
Firstly, you can only PvP in this huge area in the middle of the map, which you enter through... a menu system, because screw immersion.
Secondly, the map is so damn huge, this makes finding fights almost a quest on itself. Especially when you ride on a low level mount, which you will most certainly do when you first start playing.
But hey you can always spam "LFG" in chat and hopefully get an invite to a larger group, which in this game is known as a Zerg. And more of a fitting name, could not be given to describe what you do in a Zerg. Mindlessly running from point A to point B killing anything you come across. Skill? tactics? strategy? nah this is THE ZERG. This is how EVERYONE plays in ESO PvP and the reason is following:
This game is so damn laggy, the framerate drops SO low and on top of that, there is this weird input lag that no one can explain or fix. In big fights, all these problems get multiplied and you get the feeling that you're playing in a half-baked beta version of the game.
So the only logical solution? Run in Zergs and get kills & assists by the numbers. MEH.
To top that awful PvP system, the devs have created different kinds of PVP campaings. There is one for levels 1-50, one for maxed characters with no champion points, another for maxed characters WITH champion points (here you will discover how much unbalanced the game is), another that lasts 7 days and all of them have 1-3 extra duplicates of themselves!! Way to keep the community separated guys!!
Finally, there are no PvE raids. So if you bought this game thinking you will do some PvP action, then you are screwed.
If it wasn't for the insane lag+framerate drop+input lag in PvP, the game would worth a try, otherwise stay away, this is not playable.

Awhile back I had a very special request from a friend whose disability had progressed to a point where writing is no longer an option: Find a mouse only Sudoku game playable offline.  So when I saw Zen of Sudoku, I picked it up.
When I first booted up, I ran into a problem.  The game booted in Fullscreen Mode and immediately asked for my name.  Without Onscreen Keyboard accessible due to fullscreen mode, I was unable to enter my name.  I needed someone to type in my name before I could move on.
Once my name was entered everything was ok. Options let me change to Windowed Mode which is borderless allowing me to access my desktop easily.  There’s no other accessibility options.  No colorblind options or input configuration are found.
Gameplay so far has been point and click.  To choose what number you would like to enter into the puzzle you can click numbers in a grid & click the one you’d like.  The boxes are kind of small in windowed mode so some precision is needed.  You can correct any mistakes however.  When trying to use the keyboard to choose squares or enter numbers, I had no luck.  So far it seems you need a point & click input but we’ll keep our eye out for any changes.
The game is a peaceful and relaxing.  There’s no timer even on harder difficulties and you can stop at anytime and resume later if you’re feeling fatigued for just need a break.  Audio consists of relaxing sounds but isn’t needed for gameplay.
Zen of Sudoku has been fun so far and will definitely satisfy any sudoku cravings.  We’ll keep checking it out to see if gameplay changes or additional issues pop up, but the first look has easy to play as long as you can point & click.

The riveting sequel to the established military sim franchise, this game offers an intrepid experience in the daily life of Cpl. Ben Kerry, a US marine stuck in on a greek island after being blindsided by the Greek army. This leads to a series of guerilla warefare missions engaging in enemies with a rag-tag group of American-friendly greek forces with a dreamy British leader. You eventually leave your small island to the much bigger island - Altis. Altis is very expansive and covers a wide array of terrain from the salt flats to mountainous regions. It boasts having several large cities and multiple airports. After arriving, you continue your mission with the greeks and the brits. I won't spoil the rest, but you're sure in for a ride.
The real meat of the game is the multiplayer though. Engaging in platoon sized battles between 50 real life people clearing a city against massive hordes of AI is exciting. The combat leaves you awe-struck as bullet modeling and bullet paths have been integrated flawlessly into the hands of the engine. Multiple vehicles, ranging from Main Battle Tanks to Anti-Air Vehicles, are available from the onset and spice any mission up. When you join a large group, it's utterly fantastic the amount of fun you can have. Imagine 50 other players running toward an objective while trying to dodge MG fire. That's the game's experience.

The musical quality of the game is also quite excellent. It goes beyond what you would expect as far as ear candy goes. I also noticed that compared to Bastion, the songs in this game have a more direct message. They're not just catchy, they really fit into the story. If you think the soundtrack for this game is stellar, wait until you hear the humming added in!
Here's a sample:
As far as the story goes, Transistor really runs it deep. There are large gaps in the game that I still don't understand even after completing everything (while reading/listening to all interactables). Alien Isolation is hands down the greatest atmospheric horror games ever made. The first 5-10 hours of this game is absolutely terrifying thanks to the outstanding work that Creative Assembly put in to keeping the game as true to the films as possible. Despite being in a constant state of anxiety as I played I always had a strong urge to explore the incredible environments.
The game play of Alien Isolation by itself could be described as slow and shallow, but it works so dam well with the atmospheric terror and terrific visual design, that you don’t have time to realize that this is the 100th time you’ve have played the door unlock mini game, as you can hear the alien breathing down your neck. Unfortunately as you start to master the game this dose start to become apparent, luckily this didn’t occur for me until some where into my 2nd play through, and even still this just meant I could finally play with a little more freedom from the terror and finally explore Sevastopol Station.
The game is constantly throwing new challenges at you as you try to survive and excusing one or two chapters of the game where you have to back track, there are always new levels for you to survive. To aid with your chances of survival you have a number of weapons and cartable distractions which you will be either given or have to find as you progress through the game, most of which have their purpose while others can feel abit obsolete. I feel this can come down to play styles and situation than poor design. There is one weapon however that I feel is to overpowered, the
, seeing as it becomes your go to defense for dealing the Alien and the games other dangers. This is kind of balanced by its effectiveness being made worse every time you use it, but I was still able to beat the game never running out of ammo for it. I feel more time without it would have kept the fear factor up a lot longer.
The only real negative of the game form a technical side is the physics. You will occasionally encounter floating objects and boxes that travel faster than the speed of sound when nudged. Surprisingly in a game that works so hard on immersing the player this is easily looked past.
5/5

So, what do I think of No More Room in Hell? It's... ok. However, since there isn't a option to recommend it as average I'm going to put it in the negative category. Let's start on something positive before we get into the negative stuff, because why the hell not? For starters, the design of the environments and zombie models are excellent and the sounds are also great, this builds an excellent atmosphere for when you start playing. But then we reach the gameplay... you'll find melee weapons along with guns and ammo that you'll have to use against the zombies. But that's the main problem for me, the attacking. For starters, you don't have a crosshair for when you're holding your gun, this makes it near impossible to properly aim it at a zombie's head and it takes a lot of trial and error until you figure out the aproximate area to point it. Then we get to the attacking, which... you know how in many zombie movies, tv shows or games the zombies are easy to kill? Not the case here. They take so much damage, I need to shoot them in the head about 3 times with the pistol until they die and much of the melee weapons that i've used don't help at all. Now, this along with the lack of crosshair makes it hard enough, but then you need to consider that you run out of ammo pretty damn fast, it it's hard to find more most of the time, which means once it's gone, you're stuck with melee weapons. "But that's ok" I hear you tell me "Because I can use the melee weapons, it can't be that hard? Well, I have to admit, melee weapons like the crowbar do good amounts of damage to the zombies, but that requires you to get close to them, and that results in you getting hit. Half the time you can't get away, and sometimes they even grab you which is a real pain, especially if there's another zombie nearby. Also, if they're in a horde, don't even bother. So, in conclusion, yeah the game can be fun, but it's tedious, excrusiatingly hard and quite annoying at times. I really wanted to like this game, but in the end, the cons are such big problems that it gets a negative review from me.
UPDATE
After playing some more and getting a better feel, I do believe I was wrong to judge the game so quickly. Once you get a proper feel for the controls and learn the mechanics, it becomes quite fun and challanging, especially with friends. I wouldn't say it's fair to compare the game to L4D as many people have. NMRIH is more about stealth and strategy, whereas L4D is more run and gun. Anyway, this game now recieves a positive review from me.

Yes, Sonic Forces has a reasonable audience, despite my overall score of the game in my review. See, Sonic Forces is going to be a hit/miss game: either you're going to love it and will put 20 hours into the game, or you'll hate the one play through and not want to touch the game with a 20 foot pole. For those looking for a game they can dig time into by chasing scores/times, along with finding every collectable and complete challenges for: Sonic Forces is a game for you. Repetition is where Sonic Forces really shines: when you know what issues of sections in levels to avoid, or know how wonky the game can be when you jump at the wrong time. It's presentation, while inconsistent, still delivers in some reasonable visuals and some good sound design in certain levels and playstyles.
Where the game fails is the first playthrough: when you're dealing with all the strange behavior and investigating for the first time. When the game falls off the rails, it completely falls off, with repetitive combat sections as well as physics that can fling your guy into the atmosphere. The story feels like it has been chopped to pieces, with big chunks missing as issues are just resolved with no effort whatsoever. The presentation can flounder at times: The vocal music tracks try WAY too hard to be Escape from the City from Sonic Adventure 2. The games controls take a while to get used to with some of the quick back and forths between different styles, and it still feels clunky all over the place. There's also the issue of length: as 30 levels that take 3 hours to complete, despite replayability, may not be enough for some.
Overall, I still had fun with Sonic Forces. A good amount was laughing at it: but fun is fun none the less. The price tag is what's going to kill it for people: 40 bucks can get you really good games that aren't so specialized.

This, to me, is the most important part of any game as gameplay is ultimately what keeps you coming back to a certain title. And I am sad to say that this game is not one I'll revisit early. The physics engine really screws you over and some of the design choices make you feel like you're fighting the development team 1-on-1.
Sometimes I'd run over a boost pad only to be launched off the level or underneath a stage hazard. There was also an instance where you get boost on a long slide-styled run but if you use it you dash off the stage faster than you can ask for a refund. And the physics don't make it feel any better.
The physics are very weird in this game and don't handle well at all. Characters walk for a short while before speeding up to near-uncontrollable speeds which ruins a lot of the platforming. I've had instances where I was barely reaching a platform with the slow-walk speed jump before jumping completely over it because of the drastic increase in speed. This problem for me was most common for the Classic Sonic stages.
And in a lot of stages you get a sort of scripted cutscene which slows down the pace and takes control away from the player. I've even played some levels where after the initial cutscene I'd run into a little gimmick after which the end of the level was that would leave me wondering just how much of that 1:30 minute level I actually physically played.
5.3/10

As someone who took the time to 100% this game and get every last achievement (and believe me, it took a while and I don't know why I did it), I believe I can now make an objective review of this game.
I would like to start with the positives, mainly to show that this game has some value and merit to it despite having been widely considered a mediocre effort.
Graphically, the game is more than decent. It has good lighting effects, the Avatar character actually blends well into cutscenes instead of innately sticking out from the environment (note you can choose to make it so if you're extravagant enough in your customization choices), and the environments themselves are diverse enough that there's a lot to see without it getting dull, although you may be revisiting certain "regions" from time to time as you advance through the story.
The soundtrack is great. It has that by-now-traditional cheesy rock that's been the norm since Adventure, but it also adds different things into the mix. To note, each of the three playable characters has a "theme" to its music. Sonic has some upbeat electronic that blends and accelerates into his boost mechanic, Classic Sonic has some amazing retro-inspired themes that draw from what sounds like the Genesis soundfont, and the Avatar character has some more common-to-the-series themes, while still adding some freshness in the style of the tune and the lyrics of the song. Together, the graphics and soundtrack are what I would call the highlights here.
The story has its moments. Its main flaw I believe is the it tries to take itself too seriously with characters like Infinite while the heroes, despite being aware of how dire their situation is, continue to quip every other time. This tone shift becomes particularly funny, if very strange, when Sonic's character is thrown into the mix as a full opposite to pretty much every bad situation happening, but, all-in-all, it makes a decent vehicle to keep you travelling from stage to stage, if anything just to see what awkward contrast you'll get to see next in the dialogue.
The highlight this game announced from the get-go is the creation of your own Sonic Original Character (Your Avatar character) to use and control throughout the game, and it is a feature they tried to expand lots upon, with over 700 customization options to unlock, unique perks to each animal species you choose, and different weapons to equip. Looking at the whole spectrum of choices, there's something for everyone, from people who want to make magical girl self-inserts with heterochromia, to anyone who likes making abominations and watching them make any cutscene significantly funnier just by being there.
These are all positives, but after listing them, the good things to mention about this game start to run a little shorter.
The game's level design has some serious flaws that become glaringly obvious as you play through the different stages and that can severly hinder your enjoyment of the game. It is very jarring to pick up a lot of speed on a downward slope only to crash face-first against a row of enemies below that you ran too fast towards and didn't have the time (or traction) to brake so as to avoid them. A number of speed bursts are also followed by precision platforming segments that, unless you knew where there, will result in you falling to your death. The game never seems to settle on whether it wants you to run at top speed or to carefully navigate its different segments and is consitently switching between the two. This, coupled with controls that either react too numbly or with extreme sensitivity to your input and fairly odd physics can result in a lot of frustration, particularly if you're trying to hunt for some of the time-based collectibles or the time trials each stage has.
To follow up on the point of the time trials, the precision and mastery some require in order to complete them is borderline absurd; many times I found myself clearing stages as fast as I could and taking as much shortcuts as possible only to fall mere fractions of a second on the best case, or 5 to 10 seconds on the worst, short of the stage goal. While this did encourage me to be creative about how I manage my speed and the different shortcuts and enemies, it ultimately felt more like a chore than a fun challenge to participate on. This is especially true of the Classic Sonic levels, which I considered the most fun on a regular run, but the most grating to complete time trials on.
The previously-mentioned Avatar customization also suffers partly from this, as a number of what many would call the best or most extravagant or elaborate pieces of gear in the game are only awared for completing time or rank-based objectives on the last stages, by which point they won't really get a chance to be shown except for some gameplay segments. The weapons are not that better-off, either. While they are diverse, no non-boss enemy in the game takes more than 1 hit to defeat, meaning there isn't much point to using them other than for their secondary, exploration-related uses, which are often the way to get to most secrets on the Avatar stages.
Many achievements and challenges are also a really big grind for a game with stages as quick and short as this is; "Ring King" had me play the same stage literally at least 60 times to grind the necessary amount of Rings once I decided to specifically grind for it, since that stage can easily be completed with 999 Rings and the achievement needs 100000. The other 40-50k were the result of over 25 hours of hunting for other challenges. This is easliy the most jarring achievement to get, as well, and the next closest one, maxing out certain awards with each Avatar species, can not be reasonably completed in one or two or even three runs of all stages. I need to point out that I played a total of 32.9 hours, out of which 3 were the story and the rest were grinding for achievements. Make of that what you will in regards to the game's overall lenght compared to the investment it expects.
However, for a single, chill playthrough as my first one was, this game was okay, and many of these flaws don't jump out unless you start repeating levels over and over again (and you will end up doing that if you want to 100% this game...), but, once they do, they can definitely take all the entertainment out of it.
This is, all things considered, a decent game. It's not bad, it's not great. It's not mediocre either, however... It's in a strange point where you can tell a lot of care went into making it, but all these negative factors come together to make it look bad the more you play and experience it.
I recommend this game, -if- you can get it on Sale at one point. Despite not being at a "full" retail price, it it can give you some fun over its 3-hour run, especially if you play it with friends to laugh at the tone shifts and over-the-top interactions some characters have or to make an abomination OC together and set it free into the Sonic World.
Now that I'm finished with it and closing it with this review, I can say I had a lot of entertaining times, a lot of really frustrating moments, and some bizarre in-betweens, but have no reason left to revisit it now whatsoever.

There is a lot wrong with this game right now, for sure. IMC, the developers, or whoever, need to communicate more openly with the community. The negativity is very strong right now, and for good reason. If you guys don't respond to the community and make it known that you KNOW there are big issues plaguing this game and that you want to fix them, people are just going to keep shouting louder. People desparately want this to be the great game they know that it can be.
At the core, I know this is a solid game. I was home from work today and was able to play during a low-traffic time, and it was amazing. I was able to connect everytime I tried, the lag was minimal, and I didn't get booted once. This is why there is a such a strong influx of negativity - because people care about the fate of this game. It sounds silly, but it's true! If the game itself didn't have anything to it, it would just quietly die off. For a bit of perspective for those of your just now checking this game out: When it was still in closed beta testing, it had a 9/10 rating. Scrolling through the recommendations was a sea of thumbs up. We're in an "early access" period now, and the community expects better performance, or at the very least, better communication.
All in all, I'm still recommending this game. If you like the art style, if the gameplay looks appealing, and especially if you were a big RO fan and are looking for a "fresh" spiritual successor, then by all means, buy in. I would strongly suggest you go for the $10 pack, as the two more expensive tiers offer items and incentives that are difficult to make the best use of right now due to the game's performance issues.
If you're reading any of these reviews IMC, please understand that the negativity isn't because we want the game dead. We just honestly want to see it survive, and we want you to show us that you want it to survive, too.
TL;DR: The game itself is great, and has the potential to be awesome. People are lashing out because they understand this, but IMC is not giving us the confidence right now that they're going to see it through and give the game the treatment it deserves.
Oh, and the music is awesome. At least in my opinion.
EDIT: Updating my review to say I quit the game a couple of months ago. I had a fun time, and I still stand by my recommendation - I think if you're interested, it's worth a shot. It might not keep you interested forever, but it's alright.

When you’ve managed to create an unexpectedly great first entry for a franchise, it begs the question: What the hell do you do with the sequel? In the case of Borderlands 2 developer Gearbox has decided to largely stick with what worked the first time around, while implementing a host of tweaks that make it an overall superior game. A few relatively minor complaints aside, Borderlands 2 improves not only the narrative, but almost every major game system. If you’ve been itching for a reason to jump back into the world of Pandora, Borderlands 2 provides a more than ample supply.
The hook of Borderlands 2, the very reason that I found myself thinking about it when I worked or tried to fall asleep, is the loot. Guns, ammo, character skins, grenade mods, class mods -- there’s always something just a bit better, something you so desperately didn’t even know you needed until you found it in Borderlands 2. Just like Diablo or a number of other action RPGs, the hunt for loot becomes intoxicating because of the tiny rush you get each time a rare colored item spills out of a chest or is dropped by a recently slain enemy. Every firefight and intense boss battle becomes all the more rewarding, because, though you might die a few times and want to crush something near you in real life, it suddenly feels like everything is going to be OK when you’re blasting away enemies with a newly looted gun.
Guns really do make up the bulk of the loot, and that’s great because you’re going to spend most of your time in Borderlands 2 staring down a gun sight. No matter the quest, at some point something or someone is getting pounded with lead. Thankfully, snappy shooting and lots of environmental hazards combine with each class’s unique ability to turn every skirmish into a playground. You simply have to decide the best -- or most entertaining -- way to kill everyone.
While many guns operate similarly to one another, the stats and augmentations are just complex enough to create a seemingly endless number of combinations, without being so diverse that they’re hard to understand at a glance. You roll in, you kill anything that looks at you the wrong way, and then you walk around and look at items, utilizing the handy on-screen comparison tools to see if you’ve found something at all better than what you’re already holding. It keeps things from dragging, and drives you rapidly onward in the never-ending quest for loot.
Seeing as how Borderlands 2 takes cues from numerous RPGs, I still find myself disappointed with the lack of visual customization options (Borderlands 2 features the ability to reskin your character, but only with blanket skins that change the look of their body and their head). However, when it comes to class skill customization, Borderlands 2 is heading in the right direction. Like the first game, Borderlands 2’s four classes each have a unique ability. Unlike the original, though, a lot of options have been added to the skill trees to make it possible to create much more diverse builds...at least to a point. No matter what, every Commando will be about using turrets, every Gunzerker about raging out and blasting people with two weapons at once, every Siren about using a stun ability called Phase Lock, and every Assassin about temporarily cloaking and unleashing devastating surprise attacks. But how those abilities and characters function can be tailored to your playstyle (and can be changed over and over again for a negligible fee on a whim). For instance your Assassin might be focused on sniping and avoiding damage, while mine could be tailored to get in close and melee enemies while taking it on the chin. On the surface two people’s takes on a class might seem similar, but the new, more filled out skill trees allow you to create a version of a class that better suits your style.
Trying out skills and then reassigning skill points over and over is important in Borderlands 2, especially when you consider that you can play alone or with up to three other people. Grouping in Borderlands 2 makes the combat feel different; enemies get harder and you can use each class’s power to support your allies. The Commando could toss out a turret, drawing enemy fire while the Assassin closes in and pummels enemies to death, for instance. Since loot is shared you need to pick your partners carefully. Playing with strangers or super aggressive friends means you’ll likely find yourself in a race to see who can grab everything the fastest, and that’s really not all that fun. No matter how you feel about Diablo III, making it so each player only sees their own loot is brilliant design, and it’s a shame Borderlands 2 takes it in a route that means people are competing with one another.
Plot wise, Borderlands 2 is a direct sequel, with a story that picks up shortly after the first. You play one of four new Vault Hunters who’ve come to Pandora to hunt for – you guessed it – vaults. Unfortunately, since the opening of the last vault the planet’s been all but taken over by Hyperion Corporation and its insidious and somewhat charming leader, Handsome Jack. Through a number of events outside of your control, you end up getting wrapped up in a plot to stop Jack, save the world and help out some of the citizens and beloved characters from the first game.
The main story hits on notes you’ve probably encountered in hundreds of other games but, despite being clichéd and more than a little predictable, it’s still far more successful than in the original. Borderlands 2’s campaign narrative actually tells a coherent story, with endearing characters who manage to feel nuanced and real. At times the story can even be touching and heavy, though this is when it starts to feel a bit at odds with Borderlands 2’s overwhelmingly silly sense of humor. Ultimately, though, it’s a yarn worth hearing, one that ropes you in and makes you feel like what you’re doing has purpose – something the original game never really achieved.
The main story’s good, but the best writing in Borderlands 2 comes from the side quests. If you played and enjoyed things like the General Knoxx or Claptrap DLC from the first game, then you’ll be in for a real treat throughout Borderlands 2’s more than 30 hours of game time. Each time the main story starts to slow down, you’re almost always given a number of sidequests to jump into. Mechanically they don’t do anything all that different from typical RPG “kill this” or “collect that” fodder quests, but the writing, presentation, and acting turn them into some of the most memorable content the game has to offer. For instance one mission has you fighting off a “splinter group” of ninja-like bandits who just so happen to live in a sewer, eat pizza and talk like the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles. Another side quest tasks you with collecting body parts for a robot who wants to become human, and his take on humanity, as well as the way he talks, turns into genuine comedy. Not many games manage to make me literally laugh out loud, but Borderlands 2’s mixture of gutter humor and sharp wit did so repeatedly

Papers, Please.
A small game set in the fictional Eastern Bloc country of Arstotzka at the end of 1982. You play as "The Inspector," an immigration officer charged with running the East Grestin Border Checkpoint on the Arstotzkan border with Kolechia, a neighboring nation that was recently at war with Arstotzka. You must check immigrants' papers for discrepencies like incorrect seals, missing papers, wrong issuing cities, and even one case of a hand-made passport. The setting is dreary, the mood bleak and monotonous, and the gameplay a whole heck of a lot of fun.
Papers, Please is not an average game, as evidenced by the rave reviews found across the gaming media. It's not a shooter, like Halo or Counter Strike. It's not an RPG, like Skyrim or Fallout. It's really not a normal simulation, as it has hardly any comparable mechanics to most sims.
Then again, it has elements of all of these. There are scenes of gun and explosive violence, the strain of having to keep your family alive and safe, moral dilemmas when an immigrant is missing papers but gives a touching story, and - of course - the constant clicking and scanning of documents while doing your duty as Arstotzkan Immigration officer.
Personally, I would recommend this game more than once if I could here. Papers, Please isn't for everyone, especially those who rather action-packed games with little thought. However, considering how story has developed in video games over the past forty years, I think these people are growing thinner in numbers.
But, yes. I recommend Papers, Please. In all of it's insane, heart-thumping, emotion wrenching glory. And if you can't afford the full game, Lucas Pope has the original beta available from
.

First and foremost, this game has a little something called "atmosphere" going for it. Everything about the aesthetic, the music, and even the gameplay is carefully crafted to achieve a certain feeling to the game's world, and if that's all you want from a game, then great, pick this up.
However, the gameplay quickly becomes Paper Pusher Simulation 3000, with new gameplay features being little more than another checkbox on your list of tasks. Again, this helps contribute to the game's world brilliantly. However, a couple of things ruin the sense of immersion the game is going for almost as badly as the infamous Conversation Wheel did for Oblivion:
1) Slowing down to appreciate the game's world and feeling are punished. You only receive much-needed money for each case you complete, and each day introduces its own timer. Feel like slowing down and examining each person in the checkpoint throughly, perhaps understanding a bit more of their history or any quandries they may face from being rightfully denied? Want to take time to think over moral choices? OOPS, TOO BAD, YOUR FAMILY IS DEAD BECAUSE YOU DIDN'T HAVE MONEY FOR FOOD. WORK HARDER, SLAVE.
2) You, the player, are meant to be a border inspector, ensuring that no criminals or undesirables enter the country through illegal means. To ensure quality, the player is warned and then fined for mistakes. However, this raises an irritating question: if your employers can instantly detect that the person you waved through has fake papers, why in the name of Odin are they paying you?
However, I will admit that the gameplay is deeply intuitive, and I appreciate that there's no hand-holding tutorial. However, at the end of the day, what I come to a video game for is gameplay. And when the gameplay amounts to cross-referencing data and double-checking statements with few results that the player can see beyond the pocketbook? It grows staler than a "Hammer Time" joke.
In conclusion, I enjoy when games aspire to be art, but if a game sacrifices being fun for the sake of art, then fornicate your art; if I wanted a dull, repetitive job, I'd apply to one or play EVE Online.
