I've only played this game for fifteen hours and I can safely tell you: it's top notch.
You play as the Marked One. An unnamed Stalker that is the lone survivor of a lightning strike that blew up a truck you were sleeping in before it rolled down a clif. You have two objectives: Repay the dept you owe the men who saved your life, and kill someone for some reason. Fortunately, despite having to pay off a dept, you still get paid for the work you do. However the only thing stoping you from going out and doing whatever you want are radiation zones and the excessive number of creatures and Stalkers trying to kill you. A Stalker is a person who resides in the Zone, usually for profit and more often than not hunting for Artifacts. The Zone is the name of Chernobyl after the nuclear disaster in 1986. An Artifact is an object of value that appears along side Anomolies. An Anomoly is a rip in time and space as a result of the nuclear disaster. The Story Telling is top notch.
The combat amounts to trying to score a headshot using the world's jankiest, least accurate weaponry, because enemies will take three entire magazines from bodyshots before finally dying. Unfortunately this is the same for the player, so don't get shot in the head. The only exception is melee attacks which will also kill you instantly. This rule follows no matter what you or the enemy is wearing, exoskeletons are glorified radiation suits. ProTip: Accuracy is the only rating that matters, as anything short of a Sniper Rifle will miss the target at 10 meters. The combat is top notch.
This game takes place in the Zone, which is part of Russia, so you use Rubles. Keep in mind that one Soviet Ruble equates to 0.016 United States Dollars. This means that the most expensive item in the game, the Exoskeleton, is worth 3,120 United States Dollars. I should get me one of those. Problem is that they weren't mass produced because of the sheer cost to make. The Economy in Russia sucks. Trying to make money in this game either comes naturally, or is a giant pain in the rear. The player can only carry 50 kilograms of equipment before being weighed down and only 60 before being immobilized. Only carry what you need, money should only be really be made from Missions and selling Artifacts which usually weigh half a kilogram while being worth 1000 Rubles. Stuffing a corpse with 400 kilograms of gear and dragging it across the entire map is not fun. Most stuff you can buy is hidiously over-priced for what you can actually make anyways. The Virtual Economy in this game is top notch.
This game was released in 2007. The Graphics are top notch.
Ask a question and you'll get the most indirect answers possible, usually just being called a noob. They mostly just talk about mods and how to get them to work properly. The Community is top notch.
The first mod I downloaded made my game crash on start-up. The second mod I downloaded did the exact same thing as the first mod except itstead of crashing my game on start-up it made in-game crashes much more common, a step in the right direction if you ask me. Eventually my game crashed so hard that all 12 of my save files became corrupted and unusuable. The mods for this game are top notch.
I'm glad I've invested 15 hours of my life and 520 Rubles on this game, because it's top notch.

theHunter is an excellent, and beautiful simulation. Much of the negative feedback on here has been about it not truly being "free to play". But I really don't see many completely free games anywhere which have this high level of detail in its gameplay.
The next biggest problem I have seen on here has been "It's too hard, I can't find anything".
Trying to apply a modern first person shooters mentality of "run around as fast as I can and twitch" simply doesn't apply here. theHunter requires patience and precision, and in most ways is completely the opposite of what most people come to expect from a first person shooter. This is a SIMULATOR, not simply a game.
I do think that theHunter is due for a graphical improvement. While it is still beautiful on its highest settings, it is now starting to just lag behind what systems are capable of.  The graphics were impressive for 2009-2010, but I really do feel it is time for a polish up.
All in all, an excellent simulator, and a still beautiful, immersive environment. A 9/10 from me.

So I got together with a couple of mates a couple days ago and we played this game for like 8 hours. I'll give you my opinion of the game.
Textures - 7/10
Textures are reasonable for an open-world game, but could be better.
Scripting/Execution/AI - 7/10
I'll give it descent credit because the AI is kind of detailed, but does glitch occasionally.
3D Models & Art - 8/10
The 3D modellers for this game put a lot of work into the models, which I appreciate as a game developer myself.
Gameplay - ?/10
Your opinion on this game's gameplay is very dependant on your playing style and your style of game. If you play games like Call of Duty or Team Fortress than you probably won't enjoy it all that much, but if you prefer slower-paced games like Minecraft, 7 Days to Die, or like Farming Simulator, you probably will enjoy it lots. But that's just my interpretation. On another note, this game can also be incredibly boring. You could be tracking an animal for three hours and only find their feces. But that's where the slower-paced gamers come into play. If you like to play games with your friends, than I HIGHLY recommend grabbing a couple of friends and getting into a game together. It gets a lot better if you have some friends with you.
Features - 0.5/10
If you've played this game before reading this review than you probably know what I'm talking about. The per month fee that you have to pay to play this game is rediculous. Sure, the game is labeled as free, but in reality all you get is a really, REALLY limited demo of the game. In this demo you get to explore about 5% of the games full map, get one weapon, and you can only hunt a small number of animals. Like one or two. Once you think about it, you end up paying like WAY more for this "free" game than any other game if you are going to play it long-term. It's $15.99 for three months of minimum game features. You can pay more for some more weapons and gear, and EVEN more for what should've been offered with the original copy of the game. And even if you don't want to get into this game long term, you can pay more actual money for face-camos and things like that and you only get about 10 uses for $0.99.
Overall - 2.25/10
This game could have been incredibly succesfull and entertaining if there wasn't some scam of a fee. I understand that they want to make money for their work, but it would have been a better idea to charge maybe $10.00 or $15.00 for the full game. If you like slower-paced games and you wanted to pay $15.00 for 3 months of partial features, or nothing at all for a demo. I do not recommend this game to anybody unless you have a few friends that are willing to pay the fee as well as you.

Alien Isolation beats all games created in the Alien series. We all remember those old Alien games which were so awful that you couldn't play, but this game is truly the opposite of its kin. The story is horrifying with aliens, humans, and killer robots running about a station as you try to survive. Its music and gameplay makes the experience so un-nerving as you wander about this immese game. Alien Isolation will remain one of the great games in horror history as games compete to beat its startling jumpscares and its monsters which lurk in the shadows.
4/5 stars

Following in the footsteps of Amnesia: The Dark Descent, in Alien: Isolation, the player moves through the levels in first person, evading the monster(s) that lurk around on each (in this case, the single Xenomorph). Although you can hold off the Alien using various bits of equipment, you can’t truly fight back in the sense that you can’t kill it. Thus, it becomes a game of avoidance. Coming face to face with the Alien would likely mean death.
You play as Amanda Ripley, daughter of the protagonist of the Alien films, Ellen Ripley, as she ventures to the space station Svestapol on a mission to recover the flight recorder of the Nostromo (from the original film). Plot twist: there is a xenomorph in the space station & no one has the weaponry needed to dispatch of it. The writing in the game is all around solid apart from the character development, which is sub-par. It’s quite understandable though, as you spend the majority of the game alone due to it being a survival horror, & if you look at things through the fourth wall, Ripley turns from an amateur engineer to a hardcore survivor due to you getting better at playing the game.
What makes Alien: Isolation stand out is the fact that the game employs an ‘adaptive, unpredictable’ AI in the Alien creature. The unpredictable part means that no 2 playthroughs will be the same. Unlike most stealth games, the Alien will have no guard pattern you can learn & follow. It’s actions will be dependent on a variety of factors such as how♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off it is & whether or not it has good reason to believe you’re in the area. The adaptive part is 2 fold. It will both adapt mentally to your tactics (learning to check lockers if you frequently hide in them) & physically too (becoming more resistant to fire if you overuse it).
Clocking in at 18-22 hours, Alien puts other single player only AAA games to shame. The pacing was also done to the upmost highest standard, preventing the game from feeling repetitive or draggy. By every definition, Alien: Isolation can be regarded as the video game equivalent of an ‘epic movie’.
The best part however, has to be the art direction + sound design. They’re outstanding. The retro-futuristic world was designed just as it would’ve been in the films. Low-res monitors, analogue tuners, you name it. The sound design is even better. You can hear the Alien crawling through the vents, machines operating & failing, & the creepy voice of the androids amongst it all every now & then.
A complaint I often read in other reviews is that the player is overexposed to the Alien creature. While this may be true for them, encounters with the Alien are 90% due to its AI rather than scripted so this will vary greatly based on how you play & also luck. Personally, I felt the Alien was on screen for the perfect amount of time during the course of the video game with me playing cautiously but not over-the-top ‘inch by inch movement’ cautiously. In the style of Silent Hill, on many occasions, I had a blip on my motion tracker creeping me out without the Alien actually appearing.
I honestly can’t think of a game from 2014 I enjoyed more than Alien: Isolation. The ‘bad’ is mostly things not being as good as they could’ve been.

After completing the game for the first time... dear me, they really put in a lot of effort into building this, did they?
Well, something of a wall of text incoming.
Let me go over the bad first.
-First of all, it's obvious that the game isn't THAT long. A playthrough will probably average at around 7-8 hours, I'd guess.
-There are still some minor bugs, but given that a lot of them were fixed during the first few days post release, by the time you're reading this there will be a lot less.
-The leveling and function(skill) unlocking is a tad... annoying. It can be hard to predict the evolution of your abilities for the first time playing.
-There isn't much enemy diversity, and some enemies towards the end are just plain annoying.
And that's about what I've noticed. I should also note that the game is nearly 100% linear, but that wasn't really a flaw, because the game relies heavily on its strengths to deliver.
-The entire world building is magnificent. Delivery comes from the artwork, from the Narrator (remember that fellow with the rather awesome voice from Bastion? That guy), from the relatively small amounts of text available to you that tell bits and details about the world, from interraction with small bits and locations, and from the fact that they never go too far. You explore, and the game keeps feeding you just enough to keep you interested, and digging for more, while leaving you guessing and wondering.
-There is little that needs to be said about the music and artwork. Both are top notch, and very enjoyable.
-The combat is solid, a mixture of fast paced action combat, and usage of the quite interesting Turn mode, allowing you to string up multiple actions within a short period of time. This ties in with the character progression, and the fact that I've yet to find an ability that's useless. A tad situational at times? Yes, but most of the time, it's never a question of what to take or skip, but how to combine what you have into what you suits you the most. Add in the Limiters(an optional tradeoff that you can switch on and off where you get some penalty in return for extra experience), and the game starts turning rather interesting. I wouldn't mind there being more enemy times, but they're not lacking, not really.
-And last, the story. It is part of the world building, part of the character system, the very beating heart of the entire experience. The world plays into the sense of melancholy and loss, while the music and the very controlls available to you just reinforce it as the protagonist's world crumbles inside and out.
I probably already said too much.
In all honesty, my words don't do the game justice. Yes, it has its flaws. Many perhaps. But in the end, they are a small and trite part of the greater whole, more than easily made up by its strengths. In the end, it's a game that you really should play, if for nothing else, to be richer for the experience of doing so.

The planning mode however might be the more notable thing. Hit space, and the game pauses, giving you a bar of available time units up top, plan out a bunch of stuff, and hit space again, and you execute your stuff in a very short time span.
If you like Supergiant Games' artstyle, a great story that you get to discover bit by fragmented bit and fill in the blanks yourself rather than having it just thrown at your facde, or just would like a beautifully crafted sci-fi world that understands the concept of "show, don't tell" you owe yourself to get this game.

I never thought a sense of grinding dread would be a good thing in a game, but STALKER pulls off its atmosphere like no other game. Chernobyl's "Zone" is a bleak, dangerous land full of adventurers, opportunists, wonders, and mutants. Death is around every corner, and the game can be brutally hard at times. Still, the desire to explore this wasteland and meet the people and factions who call it home hooks you in. The story is nothing amazing, but it does make you want to know more about what's really going on.
Playing the game is like an emotional rollercoaster. You'll be scared when exploring a derelict lab full of God-knows-what, relieved when you make it back safely to a friendly settlement, and happy when you have enough rubles to buy that shiny new gun from a trader.
While technically not a post-apocalyptic game, STALKER has the best wasteland I've ever seen. One needs to be sharp and resourceful to make it in the Zone. Ammo has weight, and the carrying weight is low. You can't lug around twelve different guns and fifty thousand bullets. You pick up what's absolutely needed, maybe a thing or two that you can sell to a trader, and that is it. Sorry RPG-7, but you're not worth dropping a bunch of 5.45x39 ammunition nor medical supplies for.
Knowing when to pick your fights is key, as every engagement has you using valuable ammo and meds, neither of which you seem to have enough of. Even with the best weapons and armor in the game, the Zone can still take your life before you know it.
I would recommend first playing SoC with the Zone Reclamation Project mod which fixes many bugs in the vanilla game. Also, a mod that allows you to repair weapons/armor would be handy. STALKER SoC features unique weapons/armor and item degradation, but no way to repair them in the vanilla game. There's graphics mods as well if the vanilla game looks too dated.
After that, go crazy. STALKER has more total conversion mods than any other game I've seen. It's like a different game every time you play. Also look into the expansions, Clear Sky and Call of Pripyat, which further refine and build upon the experience in this game.

Let's tackle some of the issues players have been having with the game, And some of the misleading reviews, and then let's go on to discuss briefly the actual state of the game as a whole.
People seem to be very upset with the microtransaction system in place, limiting the features of the game.  This is misleading.  The tokens that give your account premium for 30 days are purchasable through the Auction House in game and are extremely affordable currently.

Are they annoying, yes.  Will it cost you money to unlock premium?  Not at all.
I've been playing MMO's long enough to know that stepping into the grind day one is not the wisest decision.  Every night I receive several rewards in game, and problems get fixed.  It happens.  Personally the biggest problems that friends and myself have encountered so far have already been fixed, but there are some issues that absolutely need to be fixed in the near future, and that I have no doubt will be.  Nothing I would consider game breaking.
Side Note : they have also added two new brand new servers for different world locations since release.  Work is getting done.

I'll be blatently clear about this, This area is unfinished, unpolished, and requires a steadily more intense amount of grind, even including an area from 40-60 where there just simply seems to be zero quests, and nothing to help push you through.  Start in Klaipeda.  The storyline is well polished, satisfying, has many more rewards than the Orsha side, and doesn't brick wall you on your quest to level 300 nearly as often.  Do not confuse this with the server also named Orsha,  I am strictly speaking of the starting city options during character select.
1. The client needs to be restarted entirely every few hours, I would say 4 is a nice round number to be safe.  Load times can significantly increase as memory does ableit slowly.
2.
Thankfully it takes a whopping 4 seconds to boot to menu.
3. I get consistantly excellent frames 30-80 during game, and unlike most modern games, your frames do not directly impact the visual appeal or performance of this game in any fundamental way.  It is however extremely noticeable in cities where population can be absurdly high at times.
4.  No matter how hard my internet chokes, burps, deflates, or otherwise acts up, I stay connected to the game and can resume my gameplay without being punished for it. (This may mean a lot to some of you, I thought you should know.)
It's a beautiful, and sometimes brutally charming isometric styled grind em up that wants to be played.  The controller support is excellent, my couch can attest to that, And I don't have to think too much about what I'm doing.  I just like to sit back and explode all the things, and so far I keep getting rewarded for my behaviour and I can appreciate that in a game.  I keep getting these deep Diablo feels, and the game keeps reminding me of its FFT/RO inspirations.
The game is unfinished, put simply.  But I don't seem to mind.  I've been disappointed, engaged, surprised, I've muted the music only to unmute it later, finding that I enjoyed it in the backround.  I've raised a pet by force feeding it silver until it now succesfully headbutts things at the speed of smell.   Ultimately there's a lot I would do to change this game to what I want it to be.  But it's not my game, I'm just here to play it.  And I've been enjoying that so far.
For all my disappointment in it not being the next Tactics Game, It does a lot of things right.  And it keeps it simple, from the gui and large easy to read buttons, to the immediateness of slapping a controller in my palm and booting the game up in just a few seconds.  It's more of a sequal to Maple Story, minus the socialite nonsense.  You just get to look cool, be what you want to be, and kill thousands of monsters.  And that's just what I signed up for.

If you're buying Dark Souls II because it's the sequel to Dark Souls, you're buying it for the wrong reason.  This game is terrible if you think of it as a sequel, but, as it's own game, this game is amazing.  By itself, Dark Souls II is a great fantasy RPG.  It has many elements you won't see in other traditional RPG's, and some elements of the first game translate over.
Unfortunately, the hidden and immersive story of the first game is missing here.  In fact, it seems the writers just threw out ideas that seemed good and stapled them together.  The seamlessness of the world is also gone here; areas don't feel connected like they should and resemble the story of the game, thrown together.  A lot of the bosses feel very similar, and, in fact, there are bosses just copy and pasted from the first game.  However, if this is your first Souls game, or, if you hold it away from Dark Souls and Demon's Souls, the game is excellent.
Pros:
- The game has some decent graphics that can easily be modified by GeDoSaTo
- It has a great replayability factor
- The Difficulty
- Great connectivity to PvP and CoOp
- Great mechanics i.e. Souls that can translate to weapons
- Some epic boss fights
- DLC
- More beginner friendly
Cons:
- DLC
- Difficulty
- Some boss fights feel either cheap or repetitive
- The story seems pieced together a random

Papers Please is a masterpiece in recreating the modern mundaity of work and its dehumanising effects on us in a modern era of targeted workflows and admin jobs. It managed to make me think about what a game can be , what my attitude towards my working life is and the hierarchies of families. The truly incredible thing is it achieved all this while still somehow managing to deliver a game experience that was still a game and most importantly, fun to play.
As a brief setup you play as a border agent processing applications for entry into your fictional eastern European country. You earn money for every applicant you process and you loose money for errors you make in processing.
You are made to care about you finances through a pretty simple set of systems. You have a family and you must feed them, heat them, keep them healthy and put a roof over their heads. It’s chest beating “MAN MUST PROVIDE FOR FAMILY” stuff at its most primal but it works pretty well. So well infact that pretty early on in my playthrough I realised that I had subconsciously cut my mother in law and uncle out of my family. After every days work the money was so tight I would rather save the $5 I had left incase of any issues down the line than to maintain my extended family in the form of the mother in law or uncle.
That is a pretty starling revelation to realise that a game has, without you even realising, made you think about your family hierarchy and who matters most in times of need. It’s a decision I don’t think many of us in the developed world have to make very often but it made me think of those who must have to face similar decisions on a more regular basis.
I have seen it argued that the family aspects of Papers Please don’t work that well as you are given no reason to care for them as they are just a line of text in a menu and you don’t have any real connection to them. I personally found this made the decisions I made in regards to family carry more impact. Family members were being presented as purely positions within a tree rather than characters with personalities that may have given me the basis to change my decisions. Whether that was a genuine design decision or just a function of a small team, it doesn’t really matter. The end result was powerful to me.
Fending for your family is the crux of the overall meta game and it provides plenty of purpose to the nitty gritty of processing applicants through your border but its in this processing that Papers Please really starts to shine.
Papers Please is an absolute masterclass in UI design. Some people will read that statement and think I have gone crazy. In an age of sleek flat UI an initial glance at Papers Please would lead you to think it’s a complete mess. But that’s the point.
I work in a office that focuses solely on the processing of applications. My work day used to comprise of a pile of applications with attached supporting documents that I would then workthrough to deem eligibility for the product we sold.
It was always a complete mess and there was never enough room to see everything you needed to make a decision at once. We then moved to a document scanning system and went paper free. This made desks empty but increased the workflow clutter tenfold. A screen can only show so much info at a time and our system only let you view one page at a time. It was slow, frustrating and you always felt like something was in the way of you seeing the whole picture as just that, a whole.
Papers please simulates this whole feeling perfectly with its UI. Nothing is automated. For you to receive documents you have to manually pick them up from your counter and arrange them on your workspace which is just a small window in your real life monitor. There is never enough room and documents overlap constantly meaning you always struggle to feel truly efficient.
As the days progress and more rules are added to qualify for entry the space just gets less and less and every single additional pressure requires you to manually perform a new action. Not sure on a persons ID? Finger print them, manually hand them the slip, manually check it, manually stamp the passport manually pass them each of their 5 documents one at a time. It sounds like a nightmare but it isn’t and it makes me realise something about our real life working day.
People love a rhythm, we like to see repetition because it confirms we know what is happening. Papers Please shows that even when a task is relatively mundane, as long as it has a certain rhythm and you can feel yourself getting better at it over time, there is enjoyment to be had.
I genuinely started off slightly stressed playing Papers Please. I was constantly worried about cash and if I was processing enough applicants. Given time though I improved and realised I could afford to support my family (minus those tag alongs). Its right about that time when Papers Please starts to show its narrative head and you realise there is slightly more going on here than at first glance.
I won’t ruin specifics as they are some of my favourite moments in the game but you start to see some people at your border control more often than others and each of these people have their own set of requirements from you. It starts off with simple things such as a request to let a wife through (she doesn’t have the right docs) but over time more nefarious requests start to be made that have story consequences for the whole of your nation.
These serve to break up the processing of applications very well and they give the whole game a narrative thread from day one through to the end. They also serve as branching points to give the game around 20 different endings. Ive currently seen about six and there is some good variety in there.
It’s in these character interactions that I started to think about how much a job can dehumanise us. There are people trying to get through my border that will have zero nefarious intent. They simply have a document that is one day out of date. It doesn’t matter though because they never get put through by me. In a real world situation I would probably ruin lives by taking such a hard line approach but the paycheck justifies some pretty inhumane actions in Papers Please. Papers Please made me think about how many people in real jobs will take the same justification home with them every night.
Stylistically Papers Please is also a success. It plays on our preconceptions of eastern Europe in some pretty nice ways. The colour pallet is muted. The music is stereotypical of what we would expect and there is plenty of nationalist imagery. The game over screen even proclaims GLORY TO ARSTOZKA! I’ve never been to eastern Europe so I’ve no idea if any of this hits the nail on the head but it certainly matches our preconceptions of 1980s eastern Europe.
Papers Please is a rare game and a game that could only exist in this modern self publishing world we seem to be in now. It’s a measure of how far gaming has come as a medium that a game that simulates a mundane job can be so high on so many people game of the year lists.
In previous years a risk such as Papers Please would never have been taken. A singular creators vision had nothing but barriers to overcome if they wanted to get to market. This is no longer the case and I hope Papers Please is the first of many games in the coming years that subvert our expectations as to what a game is.
Ultimately, and this is going to sound pretentious, I think Papers Please could prove to be one of the first stepping stones that lets us make strides towards games loosing the tag “game”. The medium can be so much more than the play thing the title “games” suggest and Papers Please proves that.

If you think you've learned all the rules after a few days, think again! This game will make you check, double check, and triple check your decisions, all while upping the difficulty with each day. This game keeps you on your toes, engaged with each passing second. Every second counts; you need to earn enough to support your family, or it's game over. This is one of the reasons why I love this game; the other, because of the recurring characters and many choices 3909 presents us with. For example, would you like to spend a portion of your salary on a booth upgrade, or save it, not knowing if you'll have enough to pay for survival necessities in the future? Do you accept a large bribe, or play it honest?
Your job seems simple enough; admit or deny people into Arstotzka, according to the rules. Are you always going to play by the rules? Maybe you'll bend the rules to save a life, or accidentally admit a wanted criminal.  Apart from the occasional instant recognition of a discrepancy, leading to either denying a person access to Arstotzka, or detaining them, most encounters demand meticulous scrutiny to avoid being penalized with a citation. Every day, the first two are warnings, then the M.O.A start docking your income per mistake.
You can revisit the timeline, and replay any day in the storyline. Will you go for a better score, make a different decision that alters your fate? You can do both. Not to sound clichè, but you don't need to spend blockbuster dollars to get blockbuster quality. If you're looking for a great distraction, get Papers, Please.

I've had very mixed feelings about Just Cause 3. The game does many things right, but also completely fails at other things.
To start off, I love the grapple mechanics. That's basically the main thing about this game. The fact that this game has so many destructible objects means that you can do almost anything with the tethers.
It's a good thing that you have many ways to kill enemies with tethers, because the shooting mechanics absolutely suck. It's bland and uses aim assist, and sometimes even locks on to enemies that I don't even want to hit.
Graphically, this game is also a mixed bag. Yes, the map is gorgeous, and lighting is really nice. However, how poorly optimized this game is basically ruins the experience for me.
Not to mention that this game still feels unfinished. Some glitches are pretty fun, but others plain suck. I remember one time when most of the hitboxes on the map suddenly disappeared, and half the textures were suddenly gone.
Just Cause 3 also gets pretty repetitive after a while. All the settlements that you have to liberate are basically the same: destroy this, destroy that, etc. After doing it 20 times, there's not really any incentive to keep going.
The story is bland and a load of pure
. Honestly, don't even bother. Some of the really cool parts are just cutscenes, and you don't even get to play them.
Finally, there are just some minor gripes that I have with this game, such as the unskippable intro animation and the terrible driving physics.
In conclusion, Just Cause 3 will give you a good 20-30 hours of unpolished, buggy fun. I will reluctantly recommend this game.

I've been thinking for some time that cinema is leaving the spot open for new ways of storytelling. Videogames have tried to take that spot over the years, ofering now a great tool for writers and devs to reach their audience in ways movies can't.
This level of inmersion is often used to put the player in other character's shoes, offering experiences with more or less background. Transistor favours the storytelling in spite of some of this inmersion, making the player an observer, not giving you absolute control, getting carried by the events, giving  you a broader view of what it has to deliver. And what a way to deliver it.
Transistor executes flawlessly everything it attempts. It doesn't offer you the latest in graphics, the best music or the most action-packed gameplay, but it makes sure you enjoy every last bit of it. Don't take me wrong, the hand drawn graphics look gorgeous, the music is great and the gameplay is very, very enjoyable, but it's the way it delivers it to the player, what makes Transistor one of the very best games I've ever played. And I've been around since the 80's.
The game takes all the good things from Bastion, all kinds of influences from our day, and builds a vivid, original world, so full of life and personality it makes everything else look so run-of-the-mill, so old and used. It tells the oldest Story ever told, a Tragedy. But it's the characters, the world they inhabit, the references to our world, the little details, the pauses, the many readings anyone can take from this story... It's more than just a game, just a story. It's an interactive piece of art.
To sum it all up, don't miss this experience if you're looking for something else than quick, mindless fun in a game, because you'll be missing a classic. This game is gonna be high up in the history of videogames, at least as one of those "hidden gems", and will bring you memories (and probably a smile) when you stumble upon it in some years.
Indie games are offering new, fresh, great ideas and masterpieces like Transistor only proves that it's a very good time to be a gamer, enjoy it while it lasts.

A top down, open world sci-fi survival and crafting game, its fairly unique and hard to summarise. It mixes many elements together. You will see bits of top down GTA games, Prison Architect, Minecraft's Tekkit mod, Command and Conquer, SimCity, The Martian and even Starship Troopers.
You are an astronaut crash landed on an alien planet. Your objective is to survive and extract enough natural resources to build a rocket to escape. At the start you dig up some materials by hand, until you have enough to create an automated mine. Then you gradually build up your production to meet your ever growing needs with more mines to extract ore, furnaces to smelt metals, conveyor belts to carry materials around and much, much more. As you raise your tech level you can build fancier machines, but to do this you need more advanced materials and so on.
There are native aliens that are hostile and attack your factory like the swarms of bugs from Starship troopers. You will need walls and turrets to defend from attacks. You will need to research and build armour, weapons and vehicles to go out and destroy hives that have grown to large. But to do this you will need to make sure your factory is processing enough raw materials to make the ammo and components you need.
The upgrade research path is sublimely balanced in the early-mid game. You are not punished for naive research choices while learning the ropes. As you get more adept at the game, it gives you a sense that your choices are having a real strategic impact but steers clear of following a linear formula. It does become a bit less important later on as you just try to get as much researched as possible.
Older systems and materials become obsolete as you move up the tech tree. For instance coal powered furnaces become obsolete as you research electric ones. But your conveyor system is designed to deliver coal to your furnaces. So you have to tweak your system bring it up to date and keep your processed iron flowing to the factories that need it.
For me there are three big reasons to give this a go:
1. There is always something to do. Theres always an assembly line to tweak to give better output, base improvements to make or exploring & combat to carry out. It never gets overwhelming but does give you that "Just one more turn" addictiveness that you get with a Civ game.
2. Freedom. The terrain and resources are procedurally generated so no two factories/bases are the same and multiple styles and approaches work. One big base with mining and assembly all together? sure. Outpost bases each working on one specific resource and delivering its output by train? why not?
3. Its so satisfying. As I said at the start, its easy to pick up, you wont be overwhelmed, you can pick anything up after laying it down so you are free to experiment with layouts and find out how each system or building works. But its hard to master. There are some really complex and smart logistics things you can do in the late game.
Its also got a very fun and capable multiplayer and is fun to play with friends.
You are missing out on a gem if you don't give this a go. 10/10

Allot of this games reviews are based upon the fact that its a "Free to Play" game that requires purchases to do anything.
i will agree on that fact, this game is anything but free, and requires a few bucks to get the most out of it.
HOWEVER, this game is by far the most realistic hunting/sandbox game i have played in years.
The game itself is a work of art, the graphics are amazing and definently make up for the P2P nature of the game.
To add on to the realistic feel they gave the animals in the game abilities to make them seem more realistic, like they can smell, see, and hear you.
Just the feel of hunting in this game is so realistic, the feel sneaking up on your prey wondering if their going to smell, see, or hear you is really suspenseful, and oh so enjoyable.
Now that were past how realistic this game feels, lets get to the part that makes it a game worth spending hours on.
Each time you get a hit *by a hit i mean a bullet/arrow hitting a target* with a type of weapon *example-shotguns, bows, pistols, bla-bla-bla." You gain what i see as XP for that specific action you were doing. Eventually you will gain levels in your weapons and tracking skills granting you very handy abilities like seeing how old a footprint is, or where you hit the animal when you shot at it.
Lets not forget about what the game calls "Hunter Score" each player can increase his "Hunter Score" by completing tasks that are similar to achievments you would see on steam. For example killing a number of a certain kind of animal. Increasing your hunterscore is not only a way to gain bragging rights on your friends it has its perks too, increasing it unlocks other things like more backpack space, and holsters to bring more weapons along your trips.
I myself have spent a few bucks getting everything i could ever want on this game, and im happy about it. SO Putting the fact that this is VERY MUCH a "Pay-to-Play" game behind me. I find this game a very realistic and enjoyable experience whether your hunting alone or with friends. The constant updating and interesting contests/events definently make this game worth paying for.
9/10!

Modern Sonic is something that never been very popular with game review websites. It's always been an acquired taste. This game is no different.
There are moments of frustration, parts of levels that feel a bit clunky. This game is not without fault. I won't argue against that. However, these moments are far outweighted by the positives in my mind, and I'll try my best to explain why.
First I'd like to say that the music is absolutely stunning.
The graphics and visual effects are the best we've ever seen from Sonic, and damn they look good.
The story is one of the best stories in the franchise. It does a really good job at making your custom avatar feel part of the story and developement. You feel important
The avatar customization is great, and the clothing / accessory options are staggering.
I definitely feel like I got my money's worth of enjoyment out of this game at $40. If you get it on sale, its even more worth your money. So if you are on the fence, I suggest you pull the trigger and give it a shot. You just might enjoy it as much as I did.

Pros:
+It's a Sega game, so good music is pretty much a given
+The Avatar levels are really fun, aside from some QTE's in a few levels
+The customization feature is also really good
+The backgrounds look really nice, even on the lowest graphics setting
+The voice acting is pretty good, even if the lines the voice actors were paid to say aren't
+The Classic Sonic stages are alright, they're no Sonic Mania, but they're alright
Cons:
-The story is an absolute mess that leaves several things unexplained and the writing ranges from "tolerable" to "grating" to "not making any sense whatsoever"
-While the Wispons are fun to use, a lot of them are ridiculously overpowered and make combat pretty much pointless
-Modern Sonic's levels are basically just Avatar levels but with the grappling hooks and Wispons replaced with boosting, and, I mean, you can't just introduce me to a better version of an old concept and then force me to go back to the old concept again
-I know I mentioned the story already but I wanna point out a few things that I'm especially upset about:
-Several extremely vital parts of the story are explained either in dialouge, on-screen text, in the tie-in comics that aren't included with the game and you have to go online and find yourself, or just not explained at all
-Classic Sonic has absolutely no reason to be there. He contributes almost nothing to the plot whatsoever
-All three boss fights with Infinite are extremely underwhelming. The first one is pretty much just one of those auto-running levels from Sonic Lost World, the second is you and Infinite in a tiny box with a bunch of robots, and the third is exactly the same as the Metal Sonic boss fight you had earlier in the game
-Speaking of which, Metal Sonic and Zavok are the only bosses you fight besides Eggman or Infinite. You never fight Chaos. Chaos actually pretty much disappears from the story after the first cutscene. How could you lie to me like this, Sonic? I trusted you. I trusted you to bring Chaos back and you lied to me
-The very last phase of the final boss is incredibly dull and repetitive, and the ending is bland and forgettable
-On top of all that, the game just feels rushed. The levels usually last 2-3 minutes at most and a lot of them aren't particularly challenging. This game leaves you wanting more, but not in a good way.
This game presents a lot of good ideas for how to improve the Sonic games, but it doesn't really do anything with them. It's not really a step in the right direction as much as it is sticking your leg out in the right direction but not actually putting your foot down.
I'm putting "yes" only because Steam reviews don't have a "maybe" option. This game is kind of something you have to judge for yourself.

I love Sonic the hedgehog. (Major long time fan here) This game was fun. BUT. This game was medicore and had room for improvement. I thought this game had lots of potential and was severly dissapointed. It's a decent game at best. My friends would think it strange that I would give a Sonic game a bad reveiw. Here are my reasons why without spoiling:
1. Cutscenes are strictly low poly models. (Ex: Garry mod quality) The trailer debut CGI doesn't even make it into an ending like most Sonic games. No awesome CGI ending at all.
2. The story. What story? We finally get a game where Eggman has taken over the world. The writing should have been phenomenal here. But it doesn't even dwelve into Infinite's background or explain much of anything else.
3. The DLC for Shadow was poor. You get 3 levels to play as Shadow the hedgehog. That's it.
4. The music. The first theme of Infinite is catchy but the rest was sub par for a Sonic game. I usually enjoy the music but the ending song was horrible.
5. Barely a game. If you play on Normal you can beat this in about 4 hours or less. I was actually happy it was short for once but there isn't really that much of a game to play.
6. This may not be the games fault but you have to use Big picture mode to make the cutscenes work properly.
7. Wisps need to stay out of the games. They don't have that much impact but I don't the game to stop to slow down and grab a Wisp.
Overall this game doesn't have a lot of content. But thinking on that it may be because it took a lot of time to include customization. Making tons of different clothes can consume a lot of time. But that still doesn't excuse anything. This game should be $20 at most, not $40.
One thing I am thankful for is the option to select voice language so you did great on that part Sega/Sonic Team. I guess I miss the days where the Sonic games had actual stories like Sonic the hedgehog 06, Shadow the Hedgehog, Sonic Riders, Sonic and the Black Knight and Sonic and the Secret Rings.
I don't know if you at Sonic Team or Sega care anymore but I guess I can't blame you if you guys don't. But please keep in mind there are still old fans that are still here with you.

This short simulation game shows that nostalgia and personal association in story telling can make such a simple idea into something great. "emily is away", takes the player on a magically journey back in time to your early teen years to even pubescent days where social networking was nearly non-existent excluding maybe myspace and facebook (more towards 2007) back in the day. For me personally it reminded me of days in chatrooms that needed javascript to load it up, instant messengers like of course AIM, MSN/Live, and ICQ before platforms like Skype, Facetime/iMessage, WhatsUp, and Kakao among many others existed. I'm sure regardless of which medium back then, many of us had a friend similar to Emily which makes it so heart-wrenching at the end knowing things had to end the way it does. And although a happy ending is not what you receive, the realism in the way it ends, make the game that much better even if you are emotionally wrecked by the end. Although the experience in itself, is what you make it up to be. If you find Emily incredibly irritating or don't enjoy textbased adventures/storytelling then this is not the game for you. But if you like being sucker punched and curb stomped in the feels then this is an experience you cannot miss!

Papers Please is a masterpiece in recreating the modern mundaity of work and its dehumanising effects on us in a modern era of targeted workflows and admin jobs. It managed to make me think about what a game can be , what my attitude towards my working life is and the hierarchies of families. The truly incredible thing is it achieved all this while still somehow managing to deliver a game experience that was still a game and most importantly, fun to play.
As a brief setup you play as a border agent processing applications for entry into your fictional eastern European country. You earn money for every applicant you process and you loose money for errors you make in processing.
You are made to care about you finances through a pretty simple set of systems. You have a family and you must feed them, heat them, keep them healthy and put a roof over their heads. It’s chest beating “MAN MUST PROVIDE FOR FAMILY” stuff at its most primal but it works pretty well. So well infact that pretty early on in my playthrough I realised that I had subconsciously cut my mother in law and uncle out of my family. After every days work the money was so tight I would rather save the $5 I had left incase of any issues down the line than to maintain my extended family in the form of the mother in law or uncle.
That is a pretty starling revelation to realise that a game has, without you even realising, made you think about your family hierarchy and who matters most in times of need. It’s a decision I don’t think many of us in the developed world have to make very often but it made me think of those who must have to face similar decisions on a more regular basis.
I have seen it argued that the family aspects of Papers Please don’t work that well as you are given no reason to care for them as they are just a line of text in a menu and you don’t have any real connection to them. I personally found this made the decisions I made in regards to family carry more impact. Family members were being presented as purely positions within a tree rather than characters with personalities that may have given me the basis to change my decisions. Whether that was a genuine design decision or just a function of a small team, it doesn’t really matter. The end result was powerful to me.
Fending for your family is the crux of the overall meta game and it provides plenty of purpose to the nitty gritty of processing applicants through your border but its in this processing that Papers Please really starts to shine.
Papers Please is an absolute masterclass in UI design. Some people will read that statement and think I have gone crazy. In an age of sleek flat UI an initial glance at Papers Please would lead you to think it’s a complete mess. But that’s the point.
I work in a office that focuses solely on the processing of applications. My work day used to comprise of a pile of applications with attached supporting documents that I would then workthrough to deem eligibility for the product we sold.
It was always a complete mess and there was never enough room to see everything you needed to make a decision at once. We then moved to a document scanning system and went paper free. This made desks empty but increased the workflow clutter tenfold. A screen can only show so much info at a time and our system only let you view one page at a time. It was slow, frustrating and you always felt like something was in the way of you seeing the whole picture as just that, a whole.
Papers please simulates this whole feeling perfectly with its UI. Nothing is automated. For you to receive documents you have to manually pick them up from your counter and arrange them on your workspace which is just a small window in your real life monitor. There is never enough room and documents overlap constantly meaning you always struggle to feel truly efficient.
As the days progress and more rules are added to qualify for entry the space just gets less and less and every single additional pressure requires you to manually perform a new action. Not sure on a persons ID? Finger print them, manually hand them the slip, manually check it, manually stamp the passport manually pass them each of their 5 documents one at a time. It sounds like a nightmare but it isn’t and it makes me realise something about our real life working day.
People love a rhythm, we like to see repetition because it confirms we know what is happening. Papers Please shows that even when a task is relatively mundane, as long as it has a certain rhythm and you can feel yourself getting better at it over time, there is enjoyment to be had.
I genuinely started off slightly stressed playing Papers Please. I was constantly worried about cash and if I was processing enough applicants. Given time though I improved and realised I could afford to support my family (minus those tag alongs). Its right about that time when Papers Please starts to show its narrative head and you realise there is slightly more going on here than at first glance.
I won’t ruin specifics as they are some of my favourite moments in the game but you start to see some people at your border control more often than others and each of these people have their own set of requirements from you. It starts off with simple things such as a request to let a wife through (she doesn’t have the right docs) but over time more nefarious requests start to be made that have story consequences for the whole of your nation.
These serve to break up the processing of applications very well and they give the whole game a narrative thread from day one through to the end. They also serve as branching points to give the game around 20 different endings. Ive currently seen about six and there is some good variety in there.
It’s in these character interactions that I started to think about how much a job can dehumanise us. There are people trying to get through my border that will have zero nefarious intent. They simply have a document that is one day out of date. It doesn’t matter though because they never get put through by me. In a real world situation I would probably ruin lives by taking such a hard line approach but the paycheck justifies some pretty inhumane actions in Papers Please. Papers Please made me think about how many people in real jobs will take the same justification home with them every night.
Stylistically Papers Please is also a success. It plays on our preconceptions of eastern Europe in some pretty nice ways. The colour pallet is muted. The music is stereotypical of what we would expect and there is plenty of nationalist imagery. The game over screen even proclaims GLORY TO ARSTOZKA! I’ve never been to eastern Europe so I’ve no idea if any of this hits the nail on the head but it certainly matches our preconceptions of 1980s eastern Europe.
Papers Please is a rare game and a game that could only exist in this modern self publishing world we seem to be in now. It’s a measure of how far gaming has come as a medium that a game that simulates a mundane job can be so high on so many people game of the year lists.
In previous years a risk such as Papers Please would never have been taken. A singular creators vision had nothing but barriers to overcome if they wanted to get to market. This is no longer the case and I hope Papers Please is the first of many games in the coming years that subvert our expectations as to what a game is.
Ultimately, and this is going to sound pretentious, I think Papers Please could prove to be one of the first stepping stones that lets us make strides towards games loosing the tag “game”. The medium can be so much more than the play thing the title “games” suggest and Papers Please proves that.

If you think you've learned all the rules after a few days, think again! This game will make you check, double check, and triple check your decisions, all while upping the difficulty with each day. This game keeps you on your toes, engaged with each passing second. Every second counts; you need to earn enough to support your family, or it's game over. This is one of the reasons why I love this game; the other, because of the recurring characters and many choices 3909 presents us with. For example, would you like to spend a portion of your salary on a booth upgrade, or save it, not knowing if you'll have enough to pay for survival necessities in the future? Do you accept a large bribe, or play it honest?
Your job seems simple enough; admit or deny people into Arstotzka, according to the rules. Are you always going to play by the rules? Maybe you'll bend the rules to save a life, or accidentally admit a wanted criminal.  Apart from the occasional instant recognition of a discrepancy, leading to either denying a person access to Arstotzka, or detaining them, most encounters demand meticulous scrutiny to avoid being penalized with a citation. Every day, the first two are warnings, then the M.O.A start docking your income per mistake.
You can revisit the timeline, and replay any day in the storyline. Will you go for a better score, make a different decision that alters your fate? You can do both. Not to sound clichè, but you don't need to spend blockbuster dollars to get blockbuster quality. If you're looking for a great distraction, get Papers, Please.

A staggeringly astonishing game world, overflowing with detail and care to the source material, with gameplay that won't let you enjoy it. That's what Alien: Isolation is like.
Isolation's gameplay just doesn't work. At all. At least, not for long after it introduces itself. There's the Alien, the Alien is a walking failure condition made of terrifying death, and at first that's freaking amazing and worthy of praise. The thing scares the hell out of you and turns this into an intense hide-under-the-desk simulator, which I mean in the best way possible.
But then the developers ride with the formula of "avoid the Alien" for most of the entire game. When they're not riding that, they're going with weird "avoid the androids" FPS-like gameplay that doesn't really work, either.
You have no idea how much I wanted to just enjoy the atmosphere in a way that balanced out being an authentic Alien experience (which it does do) and being enjoyable (which it doesn't do). Having opportunities to explore the whole space station, everything that it had in it, because I was in love with the stupid thing. But the game doesn't let you. Even on the easiest difficulty, that Alien starts to get on your nerves as much as it frightens you, because once it hears, sees, or freaking smells you, you're done. You're dead. You're reloading your last save. There's no way around it. And it moves randomly in almost completely unpredictable directions for no apparent reason, which doesn't help, because it just makes the Alien look stupid, not in any way goal-oriented or intelligent manner--much less, the "perfect organism" it should be.
Alien: Isolation is a beautiful, top-of-its-class experience at first. It makes you want to yell, "YES. YES. THEY MADE UP FOR COLONIAL MARINES. THEY ACTUALLY SAVED THE FRANCHISE." But the gameplay just doesn't let you enjoy almost any of it due to the random nature of the Alien, its primary gameplay mechanic, and the fact that it's totally unpredictable, but in a way that's frustrating, not thrilling or exciting. The game gets progressively worse as it goes on until it infuriates you, and you might lose interest before you get to its conclusion.

If you have ever played Borderlands you will certainly like the upgrades in this game, the menu system looks sleek, interesting new enemies and plenty of content. There is even more to discover if you get any of the DLC's (and headhunters) and they are all well made with Tiny Tina's Assault on Dragon's Keep as the last DLC, it's probably one of the best DLC's ever in my opinion.
The loot system in this game is very unique if you're new to the series, there's all kinds of different guns, it was very well made in the first game but Borderlands 2 lacks a bit in that department. Lower tier guns become obsolete at higher levels and you'll probably only use legendaries with an occasional unique gun or you'll have a tough time.
The story in this game is kind of generic, but even with little character development you'll still enjoy it a lot, the antagonist has a personality which'll set a nice tone for the game.
Gameplay is very good, different classes with different skill trees and abilities make it a new experience everytime you replay it. Combat is fast-paced unless you don't want it to and boss fights are always interesting, there aren't many bosses but it's a good number if you don't care too much about that. The different playthroughs make for nice difficulty curves, if you ever get stuck somewhere you could try a side-quest for XP or try a different tactic. It's rare to get stuck anywhere though unless it's a unique enemy or boss.
I used to play it on console for about 100 hours but I didn't have any DLC, now I got it on PC with all DLC (excl. headhunters) and have about 50 hours in now.
The PC version is nice in controls and has good settings in case you have a lower-end system. Newer systems might suffer from PhysX though so if you get framedrops you might want to set it to low which turns it off.

The world looks amazing, the music throughout the game absolutely wonderful, and the gameplay solid, deep, varied and interesting. The amount of skills and the possible different combinations that you get are mind boggling, and most have very significant effects on the way you play the game. Combat can be done strategicaly with the Turn mode, or just plain old regular real time action, and are just equally as viable and fun!
Though you are presented with a central plot, much of the lore is tied to the gameplay in an interesting manner and presented in a way that not only allows you the freedom of choosing how much of it you want to read/see/hear, but also adds to the sublime world Supergiant has created. The game has atmosphere, it has character, and it's a testament to how good Supergiant is at building a world, which in my opinion, is second to none.
Despite how different this game is from Supergiant's previous game, Bastion, to compare both games is inevitable. Cloudbank is in most ways busier than the areas surrounding Caelondia, but its aethetics are darker and more muted. The music in Transistor is a bit more synthetic compared to the more instrumental nature of Bastion's music, but is no less wonderful. Gameplay wise, Transistor outperforms Bastion in every which way, offering more options and a more fleshed out combat system. Narrative wise though, it feels like Transistor falls short of Bastion by way of being just slightly less coherant and emotional. But, it is still really well done and stands on its own really well.
My only complaints about the game is how short it is, because I find myself just wanting MORE. While Recursion mode (New Game+) satisfies my desire for more gameplay, I also want more of the story, more of the music, and more of the world. Also, the game sometimes fails to explains the mechanics of its skills properly, leaving you to either figure some things out for yourself or consult a guide.
Should you play this? Absolutely. Definitely do consider buying the soundtrack alongside the game, but do not hesitate to give the music a listen first by way of free streaming courtesy of Supergiant themselves. I only wish the soundtrack had the different variations of all/most of the songs, such as the BGMs with Red humming to them, or the instrumental versions of a few others.
UPDATE: Supergiant has released an extended version of the soundtrack with the aforementioned humming and instrumental verions.

It really nails the feel of being in unknown territory, not sure of what will be around the corner. My time in Cordon, Agroprom, Garbage, and Dark Valley was some of the best time I've had in any game. Lab x-18, is the the high point of this game. The tension in that lab reached unbelievable levels, a tension that sadly was not recreated in later labs and research stations. The game starts to fall apart for me at Lake Yantar. This is the last time you will meet a new type of enemy which are zombies, by the way this is only about halfway through the game meaning for the rest of the game no new enemies will be thrown at you. Lab x-16 had only zombies in it, no horrifying mutants, no tension. The next zone north of the bar, the army camp was semi-enjoyable, sneaking through the bloodsucker village was very tense.  But at this point the game becomes very, very linear. At this point the game becomes a mad dash to the finish, side quests are thrown out the window as you make the mad dash from Red Forest through Pripyat right to the Chernobyl NPP. The end of the game saddens me because it could have been so much better. The last three zones are almost exclusivley fighting Monolith soldiers instead of interesting mutants. The game does make up for this with its multiple endings, which are all very nice. Still for all the faults the end game has I still reccomend it due to its cheap price. After playing this game for a few more hours. I've come to update this review. This game is better IF you can survive for a few hours and get a decent weapon and armor. Since I felt like i was thrown to the wolves with this game, i thought i would share some tips and advice to help new players with the CRAZY difficulty curve. First bit of advice. Where wolf is in the starting town, climb up that ladder and work your way to the ledge to the roof of the house. Run and jump towards the house behind it( you might take a little bit of damage but not a big deal) shoot the crate that is inside the building on the far end for a free merc armor. Secondly some things the game should have told you (or maybe it dead but i was to busy trying not to die to remember seeing it). Hit the 5 key to pull out binoculars. These are useful for spotting enemies and planning an attack. Hit the 6 key to pull out a bolt. throw the bolt at anomolies or to find a safe path to walk. Hit 9 or 0 to switch fire modes, Put your weapons is semi and you can hit your targets easier. N is your nightvision and l is you flashlight. both are useful. As much as it sucks you really should only carry your armor, primary, secondary, and enough ammo to get by. This is still tricky for me since i've found a storming obokan and the l85 (the obokan is a beast of a weapon right now, the l85 has a scope, but ammo is a bit scarce) both are good but there can be only one. your pistols are useful, but only after i found a suppressed pistol.

Dark Souls II is yet another game about undead, but this one is different, and in a lot of good ways, the world created is a charming yet surprisingly deep land of politics and interesting characters all around.
Instead of writing an essay about this i'm going to create a list of Positives and Negatives, I know when you're just looking to see if a game is worth playing you usually don't want to read all that much.
Positives
- The story always seems to be moving forwards and never seems to slow down always introducing new and interesting characters to meet.
- The art style is beautiful, the world in general is extremely bright and colourful and everything is outline with more of a red tone than most games, this helps to differentiate its style from the crowd and really makes it a pleasure to view.
- The characters are all interesting and I always found myself wanting to learn more about them and their origins.
- The relationship between Bearer of the Curse and Lucatiel is great.
Negatives
- The relationship between Bearer of the Curse and Lucatiel might turn off some players.
- The "dying mechanic" is interesting in some areas but it does get rid of some of the tension from certain battles.
- The game ends on an extreme cliffhanger
- Sound was nothing special.
I would recommend Dark Souls II to most people if only because it is extremely short at this stage, it won't take you long to power through the whole game, however if you don't like cliffhangers you should definitely hold off on playing Dark Souls II

Egh, here I go:
Call of Juarez Gunslinger is to me a wildly mediocre game, it's playable and sufficiently enjoyable at times, but for the most part it's frustrating beyond comprehension for all the wrong reasons. And all of those reasons start with the words: "Quick Time Events".
First of all, QTEs are NOT FUN in any regard, and it is beyond my ability to see why developers insist on slamming them into their titles, do they think that a cheap 0.5 second warning followed by a game over screen is a well thought-out game mechanic? No, it's ♥♥♥♥ing not. QTEs are a blight on gaming and they single handedly ruin the experience of CoJG.
Without these rubbish QTEs, Call of Juarez would have been a good game, not great but enough to keep a player invested throughout the experience with it's unique narrative from the point of view of a retired bounty hunter regaling events of his exploits in exchange for free drinks at a saloon. With graphics and dialogue that complement the spagetti western setting Call of Juarez had potential, if only the developers thought out a more original and fun mechanic to keep it from being just another mindless shooter.
The game's duelling mechanic which is supposed to emulate a western quick-draw is in theory innovative, but far from it in practice. Using the mouse to increase the "focus" percentage and the A and D keys to move your hand closer to your gun for "speed" feel far from realistic, instead feeling stiff and difficult to control resulting in a death that leaves the player frustrated and upon victory you feel lucky rather than like you earned it. The controls for duelling are so slippery and stiff one would have better luck trying to bend a brick into a 90 degree angle.
All that said and done, I'm giving in to my stubborn streak and I'm going to buckle down and finish this mothertrucker. Afterwards you can expect to find me either in a bar drinking myself into a rambling delerium or in the local insane asylum as a rambling madman.
And I find it amusing how people are rating this review down because I didn't like this game and listed my reasons why. From now on I'll just thoughtlessly convene to public opinion and brainlessly suck a games proverbial c*ck just to appease people I don't even ♥♥♥♥ing know.

Then, as you progress through the game, you'll eventually get cars that handle really well. I think that the progression was set up in such a manner that I wanted to come back. Overall, I have around 100 hours of play time and I enjoyed them all.

First off I enjoyed the game quite a bit.  Great music, great art, fun class system. There is a lot of grinding to the game and to all the people complaining about camped zones, I have a few tips.  If you are in a heavy populated channel,  change channels and start inviting or requesting invites for a party.  When a party member kills, obtains,  activates a quest item it gives credit to all nearby party members.  I have not had any issue finding the mobs or quest items needed.
The biggest problem and turn off currently is the LAG.  If you have to pickup more than 1 quest you have to change channels and wait for load screens or you end up sitting at the quest person for minutes waiting for server to respond with the NPC dialog box.  This goes the same with most quests that require you to activate items.  The first action on a channel seems lag free and then it goes downhill fast, making constant channel switching the most efficient way to play.   This is garbage and servers need to be updated asap.   Also because some channels are constantly being restarted by the server causing a disconnect when you join a mew one, you can end up back into a waiting queue if you do channel hop so be careful.
TL:DR -  In the current state of things I would not recommend this game due to the shoddy servers.  Please save yourself the trouble and do not start playing on F2p release because you will end up frustrated and disgusted quickly by the server states.  Wait maybe a month or 2 after release and then give it a go.  It is a beautiful game but the lag issues were present in both CB's and its doubtful to be resolved upon f2p release.

This is the best clicker I have found so far.. It's pacing is great. New mechanics are introduced slowly enough that you are never overwhelmed, but fast enough that there's always something to push for. The developers continue to run events and put out new content as players push deeper and deeper into the game.
The number one thing I love is the pricing model. Clicker games are often bogged down with adverts and microtransactions.
There are no advertisements here, nor do I ever feel I have to pay-to-win. There is a one-time "premium" upgrade you can buy, but its reward is not required to advance, and honestly just feels like an opportunity to support the developers, and nothing more. You can also buy rubies, but in 1700+ hours, I've never felt I needed to. They actually get somewhat useless over time, as their bonus is outpaced by other mechanics extremely rapidly.

Es ist jetzt schon eine Weile her das ESO veröffentlich wurde - und trotz das es am Anfang (vor allem wegen monatlichen Zahlungen) massive Kritik bekam, hat sich das Spiel mittlerweile echt "gebessert"!
ESO ist nicht wie jedes andere, typische MMO - Kämpfe sind meiner Meinung nach weitaus dynamischer, so kann man durch geschicktes Bewegen des Charakters Angriffen ausweichen und das Geschehen aktiver als in den meisten anderen MMOs beeinflussen.
Die Story ist klasse, ähnlich wie in anderen Elderscrolls-Spielen wird man mit Infos und Hintergrundgeschichten der Welt nahezu bombadiert - und es gibt an den vielen interessant gestalten Schauplätzen verschiedenste Quests zu meistern!
Die Welt ist die, die man aus Elderscrolls kennt - der Kontinent Tamriel. Dieser ist in 3 in einander überfließende Allianzen geteilt, denen man je nach Rasse vorerst beitritt (später kann dies gewechselt werden, zu Anfang kann es nerfig sein wenn man zB mit Freunden spielt die Rassen aus einem anderen Bündnis spielen wollen). Ich muss nochmal betonen das die Welt von ESO durch ihre immernoch durchaus schöne Grafik, Musik und volle Stimmvertonung für eig. alle NPCs glänzt!
Alles in allem spielt sich das Spiel ähnlich wie eine Onlineversion von Skyrim und macht alleine sowie im Team wirklich Spaß! Fans der Elderscrollsserie und Fantasy/MMO-Fans sowie Hobby-Weltenentdeckern rate ich dringend zum Kauf dieses echt fesselnden MMORPGs!

Dear Emily,

POSSIBLE SPOILERS ALERT.
For me, Emily is Away is a "subjective" form of gameplay. I'll try my best to describe the way how this game works for me.
Emily is Away is a game where it takes on a conversation using old instant messaage system such as AOL or MSN type and uses that system to carry the game.
However the core game structure is actually "Mass Effect" type narrative. The story is presented, you have options to select which route to take with that story.
It's not exactly 1 on 1 with Mass Effect Narrative but we shouldn't focus on that. This game gives you certain options towards the direction of the storyline.
Here's my problems with the game though. Games like these in my honest opinion frustrate me through the decision making process. ME PERSONALLY, have so much weights across variable options in conversations that I personally get frustrated when I'm limited to certain options of this game.
Which doesn't make this game negative by all means, just in my view I have different takes or directions that I want to take.
Games like this provide the options however only so much to provide only so much storyline.
Another thing is the story takes place where you just about to graduate high school and go on to college. With this you talk to Emily along the way, a long holded friend, a lost companion that is with you along your life of a journey.
This game/story is not very long by the way.
I cannot get into the characters of the story, it's just so many variables that I wish I can implement in the game. Such as after the selection of the choice of reply, typing out my own response, etc.
What I do want to take is, even though I tried to bash on the my negative point of view in this game. I sincerely recommend it.
This game actually brings some sort of "feel" back to us whether we care or not it brings some sort of familiarity with life in general of what we go through in a daily basis.
I personally cannot replay the game because of the inputs that I want to put in the game. To me even though I have different choices to choose from in the game I still find the game somewhat linear. Games like this are hard to develop due to so many different variations/elements that could or would happen in game. Pretty much I'm comparing this game to a an actually real life perspective.
All in all. I recommend this game. It's free. Glad I didn't pay for it. Brings that feel of familiary. In the end though, frustrated.
