I'm just gonna be straight to the point with this review. Okay?
First, let's start with the gameplay styles. Sonic Forces takes the same elements from previous titles (Such as Generations, Colors, etc) and strives to fix some of their problems (Not saying the boost formula is bad) in the modern Sonic stages. Classic Sonic's gameplay is about what you'd expect from Generations, except with a few physics problems (Floaty jump, little momentum, etc). And the new custom avatar is a bit similar to modern Sonic, excluding the boost. The homing attack is replaced with the wire attack, which isn't as fast, and you are giving several types of wispons. Each wispon is different, and some even allow for you to go on different pathways within stages. For the last gameplay style you have Tag Team, which is Sonic and your avatar... Think of it as Sonic Heroes, but instead of three characters you have two.
As for level design, modern Sonic stages are 3D and 2D, and are also pretty linear. (Like the previous titles) Classic Sonic is 2D and allows for a couple different pathways, Custom hero is both 3D and 2D, already explained the whole pathway deal above. And finally, for Tag Team, the levels are mostly 3D and again, offer different pathways depending on your wispon, though aside from the wispon they are somewhat linear (Especially Final Judgement).
Storywise, this game has one of the better stories in the series, as it's probably second to Unleashed's story (Which, in my personal opinion, has the best story in the franchise). I don't care to explain it all, as I don't want to spoil you if you do plan on buying this game, but I will explain a little. Eggman defeats Sonic with his new "weapon" and takes over the world within a couple of months. You join the resistance, rescue Sonic from the Death Egg, and fight to take back the world.
And the music... OOOOHHH THE MUSIC! I'm gonna be honest here, this game's music is AMAZING. With the avatar having vocal music in his/her levels, modern Sonic with some non-vocal themes for his levels, and classic Sonic... Well... Okay, his music is actually kinda bad (Especially Green Hill... Eugh). The three vocal themes for this game are great as well, with the theme of Infinite and Fist Bump being all rock and roll and Light of Hope being this beautiful song that can definitely make you cry (Trust me).
Overall, the game is... not the best in the series, but it definitely isn't bad either, it's kinda in between. Though I will say, this game definitely had more potiental, but it's a step in the right direction for the Sonic franchise, after all that Sonic's been through within the past (I'm talking about you, SONIC BOOM!), he definitely needs more games similar to this... Just without classic Sonic, he was really unnecessary here.
I give this game a 7/10, and I recommend you give it a try.
REMEMBER: If you like the game, that's okay. If you hate the game, it's okay. Just don't start a stupid war about it, wether it be in the comments or elsewhere.

'Papers, Please' is a fun puzzle game set around the unlikely theme of a Communist border control post. As the border guard for Arstotzka you are under pressure from the authorities to accurately process entrants according to ever-changing criteria, whilst juggling your meagre salary to keep yourself and your family alive. As your pay is linked to processed entrants, you have to push through as many as possible without making mistakes; mistakes are deducted from your pay. A stream of entrants queues outside your booth, meaning you only have a few seconds to make a decision - yes or no - on each. Will you help through the refugee without papers? Will you take a bribe? Will you help a dissident?
I love the grey, bleak 1984-esque world of Arstotzka and how, as a minor official, you find out about changes through the state newspaper and visitors to your booth. This is a challenging, fun puzzler, with surprisingly deep story writing and I'm really hoping there we'll get a chance to return to Arstotzka in future games from the same developer!

If you told me that an Eastern-European bureaucratic paperwork simulator would be this captivating and addictive, I probably would have said "That's not a game genre, no one would play that".
But it somehow both exists, and is amazing.

I don't know if it's the music, the story or the gameplay. Everything seems to just add up to the atmosphere of this brilliant minimalistic game. Old school gaming with 80's graphics are a plus in this case, but the subtleties of its political and strategical references are so genius that I just keep on playing, no matter how hard it is.

This is a fantastically unique game, that essentially is a fast-paced, highly detailed, border control rpg. You play as a border guard person for the arstotzkan borders, and you are paid quite lowly for this high stress job. while the game might start out nice and easy checking a couple of things, it picks up pace fast, where you will soon find that you have3 or 4 documents to check each with it's own fine list of details to check for. Now if you had the time to check everything at your own pace this would be quite an easy game, but you have a family to take care of, and at 6 o'clock the border closes and you finish up who ever you are attending to and go home.
The plot of this game is very dynamic as in, you make choices, and the choices you make will reward you with money and tokens and sometimes just the feeling of knowing you helped someone in need, while at the same time fining you and causing chaos that cuts the day short, making you miss out on some of the prospective cash you could have earned.
Never the less, this game is intense, rewarding, and has a very good feel to it that makes it so enjoyable to play. It is an experience that is very much worth while, and enjoyable.

Transistor, a cyberpunk themed action RPG made by Supergiant Games is set in a futuristic city called “Cloudbank”. You take the role of “Red”, a young women who gains control of an extraordinary weapon. After a mysterious group nearly kills you, you start your journey, slowly puzzling the story.
The art style, music, and narration create a gorgeous, astonishing and captivating place you want to be part of. Beautifully drawn and rich locations where every step is a pleasure to the eyes, the amazing music by Darren Korb, the fantastic voice acting by Logan Cunningham and the memorable, intriguing characters which grow to your heart are not the only aspects that the game has to offer. The combat is remarkably fun and fresh. While you only have one weapon, there are dozens of "functions" which you collect on your journey through Cloudbank. Those functions act as perks which can be  combined with each other and/or used either aggressively or passively matching your playstyle.
All  in all Transistor is a masterpiece and is probably my favourite indie game. Not only I recommend on buying the game but the gorgeous soundtrack it offers which is absolutely worth it.

A worthy successor to Bastion. You also have the ability to modify one ability with another, gaining the effects of the other ability. Overall, combat is  pretty sweet.
The world, although pretty cool with its programming theme, isn't as vibrant as I hoped it would be. The character backstories you unlock through fighting aren't really all that interesting either, although the main story is still fairly solid.
The ending is good but also rather abrupt. I had hoped for a bit more to it, but it was done well and really I'm only complaining about anything at all because I'd previously played Bastion.

Call of Juarez: Gunslinger... good, bad or ugly?
First, forget everything that CoJ: The Cartel brought you in the CoJ franchise. That previous CoJ was pitiful and a very bad game (still, will buy it once it get utterly cheap one day though) and I'm glad Techland decide to get back into the Wild West with Gunslinger. The game seems to follow a few tidbits of backstory from CoJ: Bound in Blood, as the McCall brothers, aka the protagonists of BiB are mentionned a few times in Gunslinger. Aside from that, if you never played any CoJ, it doesn't matter as in my opinion, this Gunslinger is surely the best CoJ game there is.
PROS:
+Fun gunplay.
+Great voice acting and soundtrack.
+Decent graphics for a budget title (Chrome Engine 5, same as Dead Island).
+Furious pacing, no filler and all killing spree!
+The narrative approach is quite interesting.
CONS:
-Sound-clipping issues at release but were fixed lately from a patch.
-Main campaign is short and very linear (expected for a budget title).
-Frustrating damage indicator.
-Duel mode can be tedious to master.
-Predictable ending.
OVERALL:
For  a Call of Juarez game, I've enjoyed Gunslinger pretty much and I'd even say it is slightly better than Bound in Blood (which that one is a very good CoJ game!).
I recommend Gunslinger especially for a budget title, you can't go wrong with it. For a cheap game, you should give it a chance! Better yet, if you love Wild West games, you'll like Gunslinger pretty much! It is reassuring that Techland is heading in the right direction with Gunslinger and I do hope some continuation follows later on!
RATING:
8.0 / 10

There are a lot of problems with this game. Some are in the publisher's control, some aren't. I'm going to skip the ones that are not in the publisher's control.
1) Progression/Gameplay
A lot of good mmo's in my opinion is like going to a theme park. Can go on whatever rides you want, a guide is going to give you a general direction, but at the end of the day you will have progressed through the theme park doing what you want. This game is like going down a corridor. You HAVE to go through every zone that the game tells you to, in the order they want you to. Now that isn't necessarily a problem, until you realize that even when you follow all the game's instructions, it is almost impossible get to the appropriate zones at the appropriate level. Why? because there are secret quests chains, that are more or less manditory if you don't want to grind, and if you miss these quest chains you won't have enough experience to level up to get to the next level without being underleveled. Now that also isn't a problem until you find out that the spawn rates in this game is extremely low which means that you have to fight other people for mobs to kill. The problem is that this isn't like any other MMO where you tag it and its yours. The person that gets the killing blow in gets the credit (this is also a problem for questing, since everyone is fighting everyone else to get the last hit in). So what you have is, a bunch of people who have finished the quests in the area that are higher level than the people who just began the area, camping mobs that those lower players need for questing because they themselves are too underleveled to progress to the next area.
For example, I've finished every quest I can find and I'm in a level 50 zone, but my character is level 42. This means that I need to go back to a level 40 zone as a level 42 competing against people who are probably level 35 who are trying to finish their quests. They can't finish it because I'm out last hitting them, so they go back to a level 35 zone to try to catch up to 40, etc etc.
2) Lag/Server Issues
This is early access so the problem might be too many people being in the same area at the same time, but there is a huge issue with lag and response from the servers. Sometimes I try to interact with a NPC and  they don't respond until a couple seconds-minutes later. This might be alleviated if they got more servers or if the number of players drop in the areas. This might be the reason as to why the spawn rates are so low as to relieve some pressure off the servers. This is only going to get worse after F2P comes out.
Overall, there are problems in this game mechanically that are totally fixable by the publishers, but whether they will is another story.

The pros and cons have been done to death, so I'm going to attempt a different approach here.
There has been a lot of controversy surrounding this game ever since it went into early founder's access. The rating suddenly plummeted from overwhelmingly positive to mixed, due to the many disgruntled fans who are disappointed by the launch difficulties or other minor problems shared by most other games. Let's clear up some facts:
-Every MMO has troubles with servers, coding, etc. at some point in its lifetime, especially when it first goes live
-The development team has reacted quickly and concisely to all problems that have come up thus far and stability seems to be improving day by day
-Many people seem unable to look past those initial problems to see the great game underneath
Do you generally dislike eastern MMORPGs? Do you not enjoy leveling up different characters simply for the fun of feeling ever stronger? Do you prefer AAA graphics over cartoony/anime style?
Well, you probably won't enjoy Tree of Savior.
If, however, you are open to trying something different, a charming and memorable adventure supported by a great soundtrack and lovingly crafted environments, I suggest you give ToS a shot.
Personally, I am loving every minute of gameplay I can squeeze in, and that's despite the fewer-than-30fps I'm getting on my laptop.
The story is nothing special, but I don't really look for a great story in an action RPG. In my opinion, the game blends together the best parts of Ragnarok Online's general style, exploration and character diversity, with Diablo's action combat and "I-must-have-that-one-item" or "reach-that-one-level" drive into a delicious cocktail of gaming goodness.
Definitely recommended!

I had reviewed this game just over a year ago as I was quite new to it and decided to update my review.
Factorio is a game which is unlike any other i've played for many years. It's quite simply one of the best games I've ever owned, the gameplay is unrivalled in any resource management / building game. The combat is sometimes criticised as basic, but the latest update changes this to make it a lot more challenging, if you want, and the mods available expand combat significantly.
Mainly I want to commend the developers on their commitment to this game and it's community. They are extremely active and listen to feedback / bug reports constantly, always keeping up communication with the players. The community itself is always very friendly in my experience, and the games subreddit is always active with new theories, challenges, builds, mods etc, I strongly reccomend checking out the monthly community map for a fun challenge.
The trailers really do the game justice with showing how a factory grows and some of it's potential, and they don't even cover some of the hundreds of mods available for the game.
The UI isn't perfect, but the developers are really working on it and the game has grown fantasically in the past year i've been playing.
After sinking 350 hours into Factorio, I can't wait to sink another 350, I reccomend this game to everyone and it highly deserves its status as one of the best reviewed games of all time, and especially for an early access game.

This is the best way I can explain this game:
Factorio is like a puzzle. An incredibly fun but challenging puzzle that never makes you feel like you're doing anything wrong; only that you can do it better.
For someone who is obsessed with organization and processes, this game is basically a dream come true.
From the get-go, the wheels in your head will start spinning, and keep on spinning, as you design and build your factory, step by step, piece by piece, until after a few hours when you take a step back and tell yourself "Damn, look at this thing I just made". Then you sit there and watch everything in motion, marveling at the complexity of it all, then you realize that a part of your machine isn't working as well as it should, and a few short hours later, halfway through fixing what your were trying to fix, you realize you only have about one tenth of all the available tech researched, and you need to up production in order to get the next research. Then you add a couple things, then fix some things, then upgrade a few things, and a few more short hours later your factory is twice as big and 10 times more complicated as it was when you first got it up and running. It never ends, and it's great.
Personally, I will admit that I enjoy big budget, ultra detailed games with beautiful visuals and epic storylines, but when it comes down to it, I've already gotten more enjoyment out of this $20, early access "unfinished" game that only takes 512mb of hard drive space than any other game in a long time.

Yes, Stalker SoC is more than worth a buy. The feelings of dread and desperation as you traverse the insecure, almost-open-world will make you yearn for more while simultaneously hopping for it to stop.
It’s Chernobyl. Because, somewhere, it had to be. Be glad it’s here though! Besides the technical issues that you may or may not experience at the hands of SoC, this is a damn fine game that mixes open levels, faction warfare as well as dark, claustrophobic maps. So well is the mixture that you will only take breaks to watch My Little Pony or Adventure Time episodes, in order to calm down a bit.
That’s not to say that it’s all horror, but the horror parts are intense, with mutants invisible, sneaky or able to take control from you altogether. The remaining parts are equal in intensity, with stumbling over faction warfare, random anomalies or stalkers (a.k.a. wanderers) with whom you can talk for the info or kill for the loot.
The world around you is also alive. Nights will see an intensity in animal and mutant activity, while daylight will witness packs of hounds hunting, wild boars migrating from one part of the (large) map to another and so forth. You will also constantly encounter random patrols or couriers, from different factions, the faction itself depending on the level you are in.
But, like I originally said, the game is riddled with bugs. Some from the get-go, some due to the game being out of date. Of course, a title of this caliber will always have a smart fan-base covering it's needs, and there are excellent mods out there, combining graphics upgrades, tweaks and bug fixes all in one.
The only reason I would not recommend getting this is if you already own Call of Pripyat (the 3rd game in the series, that improved much on the formula). If not, SoC is a serious contender to CoP, but ultimately, if you like one, you will want to play both. I recommend starting with this.

I have genuinely no idea why this game is so addicting.
Well, I guess I do. On the surface, it's just another idle/clicker game. Good to have running in the background while you're doing something else, doesn't demand much of your focus, gives you an easy feeling of accomplishment. But there's actually some level of strategy and depth to this one. Instead of only having one way to play through the game - inevitably leading to "buy this many of this upgrade," "copy and paste your save into an optimizer," mindless advancement for advancement's sake - playing using different builds and factions gives different bonuses for different styles of play. More active clicking? Go with a faction aligned for that. Don't even bother opening the game for a week? Go for a build with offline bonuses. There's still the possibility for minmaxing, but it doesn't railroad you into it nearly as much as similar games do.  Reaching goals and getting achievements in the game also actually gives tangible bonuses, making it less "advancement for advancement's sake". And it's free. You can buy in-game bonuses, but it's not shoved in your face at all.
Altogether it's one idle game that I don't mind being addicted to.

Satan is out to destroy the world with his evil forces of mooks and terrorists, and the only people who can stop him are Broforce. This game is a straight-up silly pastiche of 80s/90s era action movie men thrust into a comedic crossover in which everyone’s name is changed to fit the word “Bro”.
As you would expect, everything is way over the top with hilarious levels of patriotism and violence in every level. Your goal is simple: get to the end of the level and kill satan and/or the boss of that stage. Along the way you can rescue captured bros, whom replace your current bro on release. You have a good variety of bros at your disposal and additional bros will become available once you meet certain rescue quotas. This game also features a decent co-op system and can be loads of fun in either local or online multiplayer.
This game does have a few performance issues has been known to sometimes run poorly even on excellent rigs. Adjusting post-processing may alleviate this a little bit but for most of the time you will just have to grin and bear it when the fps drops happen. It also crashed every time I quit the game but I never had any issues with corrupt save data so no big deal there either.
I managed to squeeze 8 hours out of Broforce playing it off and on from when I first picked it up in early access back in 2014. Since then, the game has made leaps and bounds in adding content, characters, and bug fixes and has become somewhat of a success story proving that early access doesn’t always mean “bad game” (granted it did take about 2 years). The game seems to have arrived at its final state so, if you’re wondering about picking it up, any time is a good time to have a bro time.

Papers, Please is yet another example of why the widespread notion that games “should first and foremost just be fun” is not only antiquated, but categorically false. Is a game that’s not “fun” bad? Of course not, we just need to expand our vocabularies a bit. Because Papers, Please simply isn’t fun at all and yet it’s a genuinely good game.
Papers, Please is a bureaucratic simulation game in which the player takes over the role of a customs official of a pseudo Eastern Bloc country at the end of 1982. After a long time, the borders are open once more and it is your job to make sure that the flood of people pouring in have all the necessary documents. Not only that, but you need to make sure that the passports haven’t expired, that the information provided checks out across multiple documents and so on. Rules change regularly due to domestic and international events such as terrorist attacks and disease outbreaks which constantly keeps you on your toes. You will also be provided with bulletins informing you about wanted criminals.
It is as laborious, mundane and monotonous as it sounds. And yet it’s incredibly compelling due to everything around it. You want to do a good job because you get financially penalized for multiple mistakes. Also, the more people you process, the more money you get. And you need that money because your family depends on you for rent, heating and food. But there are desperate people with insufficient or forged documents begging you to let them pass for various reasons. Some people will try to bribe you. Rebel organizations trying to bring down the government will seek your aid. All the while the government will be bearing down on you to do your job in accordance to the strict, but not always fair, rules.
And that’s what’s so brilliant about Papers, Please. You really get a feel of what it’s like, you get into the role and you start to think as if you’re really there and not just playing a game. Why wouldn’t I want to help these guys out? What has my government done for me aside from oppressing and threatening me? But what about my family? What will happen to them? So you juggle all of these thoughts and simply try to do what you feel is best in each particular situation. But there’s simply no way to do everything right, something always has to give.
You go through the story campaign day by day. There are 31 full days to play. To illustrate the many different ways your choices impact the game is the fact that the game has 20 different endings that can occur during various situations within that period. While the game does a really good job to convey its grim and bleak mood, the writing leaves a lot to be desired. Some of the dialogue is just unconvincing and unnatural. Also, for some reason, the game uses a bit of Soviet-esque broken English, but at the same time it uses some silly and very American colloquialisms. Apart from the story mode, there’s also the endless mode which you unlock when you get a certain ending, but by the time that you’ve seen most of what the story has to offer, chances are slim that you’ll be interested in more.
Papers, Please is a brave and wholly original game that deliberately offers mundane gameplay and wraps it up into a surprisingly compelling and profoundly affecting whole.
7 OUT OF 10 (GOOD)

Every day also bears the threat of having the border attacked by suicide bombers and terrorists, at which point you must take up arms and defend yourself and your collegues.

If ever you come across that common question of whether video games truly belong in the world of high art, along with the likes of time-immune paintings, masterpiece films and all-time hit singles, you only need to answer it with Transistor.
To say that Transistor is a work of art is no exaggeration. The beautifully painted art style reminiscent of Supergiant Games' brilliant favourite, Bastion, go hand in hand with the lovely soundtrack by Darren Korb. Ashley Barrett lends her vocals to most of the soundtrack as the protagonist, Red's, singing voice while the gravelly voiced Logan Cunningham returns as Red's companion, a man stuck in a sword. Their story is one of hardship, as they fight a system off in the hopes of getting what was stolen from them back. This good story backs its visuals and audio to make it an attractive package.
The drawback that most see in dedicating a game as art is the common mistake of letting the gameplay slide into abandon. Thankfully, Supergiant Games made sure that the game's mechanics is deep and enjoyful. The combat system is incredibly customizable and allows for versility. I was eager to try out as many combinations as possible to find one that suited my playstyle and I eventually found my favourite life-stealing spamming long shot laser that exploded upon contact. There is an alright amount of enemy variety, especially since enemies gain abilities as you progress through the story.
In short, Transistor is not only brilliant to look at or listen to, its fun to play and has a story worth following. Sounds like the perfect package, right? Now, some have complained that the game is really short and not worth the full retail price. My first playthrough lasted 9 hours, since I took my time to explore both the wonderful science fiction world and the expansive combat options. One should know that the game comes with a New Game + option, known as Recursion where you retain your levels and combat options as you play through the story again. In this mode, the enemies are leveled according to yours to make this second playthrough a tough one. While this NG+ option is there to add to the game's worth, not many would want to play through a second round.
I've been playing this for 15 hours so far and am halfway through my second playthrough, loving it all the same the second time. To me, this is a work of art, one I'll be recommending to many.

The ability system is fun and I find myself wanting a Diablo style game to incorporate a system similar to this because I think it's well done and gives you a lot of customization. The combat is meh, the pacing is meh, the length of the story is very meh and, to me, the ending was meh. I don't know... I was super excited for this game for a LONG time, and can't really say it was worth the 20 dollars. It was a decent experience, but wait until it's on sale. If you're cool with time trials and whatnot, you'll probably get a bit more time out of it than I did. But, for me, when you have a setting this cool and the story is so forced and short, it in no way was very satisfying.

This game surprised me to hell and back. Seriously.
Word of Note: At the time of writing, I have not beaten the game. This "Review" is more of a "First Impressions" than a proper review, so please keep in mind that the game may have a few more surprises down the line that may completely change the gameplay or atleast alter it drastically! Review will be updated accordingly after I beat the game if anything new pops up.
*I also won't summarize the Premise of the Game's Story as the game itself starts you out completely in the Blank and shows you what happened.

Visual-wise, pretty dang amazing, albeit a few scaling issues with buildings and such. This game is the epitome of low-poly modeling and hand painted textures. The enemy models and landscapes are very simple looking as far as modeling goes, but the assets/textures used on everything gives the world life even if the places are deserted, it invokes a tone of lonelyness and helps you figure out somewhat, what exactly happened that there's not a single soul around. When Red moves around and drags the Transistor (Sword) it leaves a trail on the ground that disappears shortly after, but helps mark direction, additionally, some moves can leave holes in the ground depending, and won't disappear until it's replaced by the same "break' textures elsewhere. Enemies themselves are presented as robotic creatures and are reminiscent of Kingdom Heart's Nobodies in that same way - as creatures sent to hunt your player character, but are mindless in nature.
The Soundtrack is also quite a treat! Boasting pretty impressive Lyrical compositions that gives it a bit of a Noire feeling and are pretty well varied. Additionally, Red can hum alongside any given track, effectively making a sort of "remix" to that particular song. Soundwork is also pretty well done, the Transistor does it's charging noises, it clings and clangs when slamed unto the ground, there's a subtle noise for steps, for the trail the sword leaves and enemies make their odd creature like noises when they're going after you. Voices are also excellently done. Red doesn't speak, but you can hear her sing in some flashbacks, the Transistor also serves as a sort of narrator to help divulge neat little extras. Something the game does, that I really dig, is that the way he speaks to Red, sort of feels like he's talking to the player aswell, giving it a 4th wall kinda feeling. It's all amazing.
The game also fares pretty well, if a little slow and methodical. This is the part that may make or break the game for a lot of people, for sure. Red moves VERY slow, it's done on purpose though, as areas in general are subdivided via "zones" and they aren't very large in scale either. The game's Battle Structuring is simple, but feels a tad linear in execution (atleast at the start) where enemies ambush you in certain parts of a Zone but won't respawn after a battle ends and you walk back into the area.
Combat is where the gameplay really shines. The battles play out sort of like Crisis Core, once you enter combat mode, you're trapped inside the zone until enemies are defeated. Enemies will be mercilessly going after you, and you have just the one Health Bar to tide you over the entire battle, if your health bar depletes, you will lose a "Function" instead of dying.
During combat, your attacks depend solely on the Functions you have picked out and set up. Each function, obtained either through finding people that died or leveling has multiple functions. This gives the game a LOT of depth as far as building your character goes. You have 4 main slots to assign a Function too, and those slots have 2 extra slots that you can assign more functions to to power up that function - * * * example: You can have a function that shoots out grenade like particles in an area, you have another function that, by itself, creates a bomb in place that needs to be self detonated, however, you can add that function to the previously mentioned function to add, let's say explosive attributes which come via the way of damage buffs, range buffs, etc * * * You can continously build more and more powerful functions to use to kill your foes, move faster, avoid attacks while dealing damage, etc, there's I believe, TONS of ways to build the character you want and fight the way you want.
When fighting, the Combat Areas have little grey squares, these serve as your main method of avoiding attacks. You can destroy these squares yourself or the enemy can. During Major Boss battles, this is very important to keep track of, as bosses can deal a TON of damage and are very patternized. You also have the "Turn" Command, which freezes the entire battle field and let's you plan out attacks ahead of time, this can also be used to avoid attacks. The Turn command works via a queing system - Imagine you have a time slider and you're editing it with the stuff you want Red to do, wether it is move away or closer to an enemy, use specific Functions to continously attack an enemy, avoid an enemy, or both. It is, however, not 100% accurate, as while you're in turn mode you continously set Red to Attack the enemy in a specific area, but the enemy CAN still move when combat resumes and avoid your attacks, thus giving the combat a ton of strategic aspects to it. Turn mode is balanced due to the way you're forced to wait until the turn slider returns to normal, when you deplete the Turn Bar, you CANNOT attack or use any function, so keep that in mind always, and don't use Turn Mode haphazardly as it can leave you VERY vulnerable after usage.

The game is, for its price tag, short and merely functional for its parts. The level design tends towards flash over substance. For the first run, there are some exciting moments but they give way to shallow spectacle very quickly. If we were still in the era of physical game rentals, this game would be prime Blockbuster bait.
It's playable, and arguably it's easier to appreciate what level design there actually is once you start trying to hunt down the collectibles, but it just doesn't excite the way Sonic Mania did. I would recommend this easily for much younger fans, as the difficulty and structure (short levels, infinite lives) are a much better fit for inexperienced gamers.
Lets face it. Sonic gets a bad rap. However, this game is good. Is it great? No, but it's good. Generations and colors was good as well. It's not sonic mania, but it doesn't have to be.

The game is, overall, decent. It's no Generations, but I found the game pretty fun the first time around. The story is considerably more "edgy" than Sonic games of late, which led to many ironically funny moments. The soundtrack is great, haven't been able to stop listening to it since the game came out, especially the vocal Avatar tracks. One of my favourite things about the game is the ability to, finally, play as Shadow the Hedgehog, not just in his 3 DLC levels, but in some Modern Sonic levels, too.
The level design is probably one of the games biggest pitfalls. I didn't mind it in my first playthrough, but going back and trying to get all the collectibles and S-ranks, I noticed that most of the levels were very short and simplistic. "Boost-to-win" has never been a more appropriate term for Modern Sonic's levels. There are some segments where you can just sit back and hold down the boost button, with little other input required. And then, before you know it, the level's over. The Avatar levels are the most interesting, as you can play as your own custom character, which you can equip with different "Wispons", giving you certain powers that will help you in various ways throughout the levels. As for Classic Sonic... Come on. Why is he even here?
Wow, that review went on longer than I expected. Unlike the game. Which is pretty short, even for a Sonic game.
I'd probably give this a 7/10. Not bad, but not what I expected from apparently 4 years of development.

Although the game has been released as early access, the gameplay and experience does not feel like a finished product. I'll start with the positives before explaining the negatives. The core themes and graphics of the game are absolutely stunning such that it gives a great fantasy MMO experience. This combined with the stunning sound and music, really does immerse you into Tree of Savior's world perils. In the first hour of jumping in, the artwork and the graphics really emphasise the capacity and potential of what a great game this will be. With over 60 different classes to play and a complex class system which allows a variety of builds, you can be a unique character in a beautiful fantasy world. The level cap is also enormous, being at 600, which definitely shines as a MMO grinder with a long-term future and goal. Class skills and gameplay has been thought out and the combat system does feel fluid to the extent of how a 2.5D game should feel.
However, the game falls flat after an hour or two of gameplay, where buggy quests, an extensive lack of game features, poor lag and frequent disconnections have riddled the game to be a nightmare in itself. The game in itself is very linear and can likened to be sitting on a straight rollercoaster at a theme park. It seems that the developers have just made many maps, pieced them together and thrown one or two NPC's in each one to give quests. Furthermore, there are only two main 'cities' in the game which are your starting cities and the entire game's NPC vendors are situated in the two areas. Nowhere else in the entire game do you find any other vendors or non-quest related NPC's. This makes exploration poor and lacking for a person who loves to explore every inch of a map. Additionally, if you are a non-paying player who chooses not to purchase tokens(equivalent of buying 30day VIP status), then you will be unable to perform a wide range of basic game functions. A few of these functions includes trading and sending items/currency to other players, not being able to use shared storage between your characters and only being allowed to list one item on the Auction House at a time with a higher tax rate. However, it is not to say that you cannot purchase these 'tokens' on the Auction House given you are commited and dedicated grinder.
The problems do not end at game design but also to the management of the game. Poor planning to this 'early release' can be seen in the troubles every player are having in completing quests, where server overloads are forcing players to wait 5-10minutes when talking to each NPC. At the time of this review, half of the channels are not working and it disconnects the players from the server entirely. It has been a few days and there is yet to be an update from the developers on the situation of this issue. Furthermore, there are many stories of character being 'stuck' on these disconnected servers and as such, players are stuck unabling to play. You'll be ripping out your hair more than the enjoyment of the game.
I would strongly recommend new players to holdout from playing this game until there are further updates which fixes alot of the problems and issues this Tree of Savior has.

This game sounds terrible on paper (no pun intended); you are an inspector for a border of a communist country that is now just reopening its borders for the first time in years and it's your job to make sure that EVERY SINGLE bit of information lines up with EVERY SINGLE document of EVERY SINGLE person. Sounds like the kind of job your cousin complains about at family reunions.
But then you actually start getting enveloped in your duty as a citizen of Arstotzka.
Do you let the woman without the proper papers go through after her husband who went just before her? Do you turn away the ambassador because of his country of origin? Do you take the bribes or report your findings to the M.O.A.? Do you trust the masked figures? Will there be another terrorist attack today? If the day is cut short, can you make rent? Are you willing to kill an innocent for what you believe is right?
All of these questions an more race through your strained mind as the clock ticks the day away as you pour over document after document for discrepancies, all the while knowing that while processing more people gets your family much-needed money, failure to detect even the SLIGHTEST fault will result in penalty...and that penalty could mean the difference between saving the life of a loved one down to buying a present for your son's birthday.
There are 20 different endings in all, each varying from living happily with your family, to getting executed on suspension of aiding extremists. There are also secret achievements for performing certain tasks that may or may not contradict what your handy-dandy rulebook might say. All I can say is:
Glory to Arstotzka.

Rome II is an excellent game for multiplayer battles.  The graphics are amazing and the sight of seeing large scale armies face off against eachother is amazing.  I would strongly recommend the game for multiplayer battles.  Not a fan of the campaign, but the game is worth it for the battles.
For a balanced review I have to see there are two significant problems associated with the multiplayer that hopefully the developer will fix in future games.  First, the games can often be quite laggy.  The game does not indicate the ping of each player nor the system performance for each player.  That leaves one guessing as to which player is causing the lag.  Unforunately people play when their computer cannot handle the requirements to play the game smoothly and this lags everyone.  This can be very frustrating.  Second, there are a few little glitches in the game.  The most annoying glitch is that each player for a multiplayer match must check to "start battle."  When all players have checked start battle, the game begins.  Problem is, you check the start battle, then your "start battle" gets broken after another player overspends.  Then you need to hit start battle again.  Often times there is an idiot or two that keeps overspending.  Then finally all is done but someone's start battle got broken and he has now gone to the restroom to take a leak.  Because of this glitch, it can take quite awhile for the game to begin.  This would be a deal-killer for most any other game, but the battles are so well done that it can still be worth the wait.

Transistor is Supergiant's followup game to Bastion, and they, in my eyes, confirm they are not a one-trick wonder. With far my rpg gameplay than its predecessor, including the turn() system, wherein you pause the game to set up your attacks. Every ability works synergistically, meaning you can come up with your own combinations for the gameply style you like, with everything from basic power attacks to summoning a cyber-punk dog to fight for you.
The story is on a different scale than Bastion, centering around a single city instead of two nations, but is nonetheless satisfying. It is not as rich as Bastion's, but if you liked Bastion's story, you will like this one too. The art style is as fantastic as ever, and the music brings you into the world with the first song. If you liked Bastion, check this out, and if you didn't, it's different enough that you might still look into it.
It's also worth noting, that it's a short game. I beat it in about six hours, and I am no speed player. I enjoyed it, and I appreciate that it didn't drag on. It includes a new game plus mode, so there is plenty of time to unlock new abilities, use different combinations, and keep moving on with the game.

Another great installment published by Supergiant Games. Overall really well made in both thee visual and gameplay designs. The combat is extremely fluid and well thought out, and the story is stunning as always. 11/10. Replay value: High.

There's a TL;DR at the end of this essay for those who don't want to bother.
Supergiant Games has created a masterpiece. Transistor is artistic, challenging, engaging, interesting, unique, and very very moving in a lot of ways. I'm finding it difficult to accurately describe how amazing an experience this game was without giving anything away. The story is incredibly well written, with likable, interesting characters, and a helluva unpredictable twist at the end. Complimenting the story very well is the art and soundtrack. Everything is beautifully drawn and animated, and the soundtrack is absolutely stunning. Together, the art and music do a fantastic job of giving life and personality to the main character, who is otherwise mute - something that is all too common in videogames, but is handled very well in Transistor.
Transistor's combat mechanics are also remarkable. They manage to turn what would otherwise be your regular hack'n'slash into a genuinely cerebral experience through their queuing mechanic. Because of the difficulty, combat requires a level of strategy and skill that most games do not require, forcing you to actually think about what you plan to do, and then challenging you to execute it in the most efficient way possible. (speaking of difficulty, transistors difficulty system is also really interesting; though it's the same as Bastion's more or less)
I only have one major complaint: Transistor is short. With limited replay value and only seven hours or so of gameplay, Transistor is a fast, powerful, but sadly short-lived experience. This is somewhat cured by the recursion function that you receive at the end of the game, but it's still not a lot. I understand why it's as short as it is, but I wish that Supergiant Games had created some sort of side quests that could develop the world and certain characters (the Transistor itself, for example) even further. Often, I found myself asking questions about the history of the world, and unfortunately Transistor provides few answers.
Despite these complaints though, Transistor is a game that gives me hope for the industry. In my opinion, it shows that videogames have the potential to be an incredibly valid medium to tell a deep, powerful story, while allowing the player to interact with the world that has been created for them - something neither a book nor a movie can really accomplish. Transistor takes for advantage of the potential of videogames, and tells the best story I've experienced in a long time. I would recommend this game to anybody and everybody.

Borderlands 2 Review
What is Borderlands 2
Borderlands 2 is a FPS (First Person Shooter) that takes place on an alien planet called Pandora. Pandora is a ruthless unforgiving world consisting of bandits, rivaling companies fighting over a resource called eredium, mutants, and alien wildlife that’s only seeks to kill you and your friends. Though not all is death and pain on Pandora.
In borderlands 2 there a great deal of features and unique skills you can utilize to change your style of gameplay and experience throughout the game.
Pros
When playing borderland there are six characters the player can chose to experience the game from. Each character has three skill trees with 11 different skills each tree, making for 33 individual skills to choose from. Depending on what tree you chose your style of gameplay varies from each character.
For ex. The Psycho is a melee based character whose special ability relies on heavy close combat with the enemies. And in contrast to Zero an assassin who uses long ranged weapons to deal damage from afar.
Some of the Psycho’s skill trees, Bloodlust and hell born have similar gameplays. Bloodlust allows for buffs on enemy kills while hell born relies on a chance to catch on fire to gain damage boosts, the ability to heal from catching aflame, and a unique ability that lets the psycho to breathe fire.
Zero’s two trees, sniping and bloodshed have completely different stiles of gameplay where one relies on ranged weapons while the other tree provides boosts to melee stealth ability.
Story and quests
The main story starts off with the player chosen character navigating through a glacier with a small robot. The glacier is used as a prologue or an introduction area to allow the player to learn the controls and prepare them for the main game. It offers small side quests and lets the player go at their own pace. In the prologue following the main quest is difficult without doing side quest to level up the character.
One of the first side quest you obtain is to clean a grave yard of alien monsters called bullymong. In this quest the player is rewarded with cash and experience. Experience levels the character up making them stronger so that they can complete the main story quests.
Another side quest at the beginning is to obtain bullymong fur by meleeing the alien brutes to death. After the fur is collected you receive an option, you can give the fur to your trusty robot companion or sir hammerlock the one who give you the quest in the first place. Depending on who you chose out of hammerlock or your robot you can receive either a new sniper or a new shotgun.
Graphics and gameplay
Borderlands 2’s graphics are different in their own creative way from other games.
The game looks like it was taken right out of a comic book. It has the features and 3d look of an FPS but its developers chose not to make the graphics look realistic. Instead they aimed to replicate the look of something animated on purpose.
Each individual weapons along with their abilities, ammo's, stats and look are randomly generated. This also applies to the gear that can be found through the game as well.
All Pandorian monsters have their own individual abilities making each encounter challenging and interesting.
Pandora is an open world where you can chose your path, vehicles are available to hasten your travel over your journey between quests.
Con
Rarely Minor bugs occur when venturing into the wasteland. Usually these don’t change or affect gameplay. These unusual occurrences often happen in multiplayer and can provide a laugh when playing with friends.
For instance in one case when playing online during a cut scene a characters head made an abnormal 180 degrees turn for 5 seconds until snapping back into place in an instant.
Conclusion
This concludes my borderlands 2 review. As displayed above the pros outweigh the cons for this game. Personally its one of my all-time favorite 4 player online FPS’s to play with friends.
Single player alone for the story and comedy is worth buying this game. You’ll be laughing nonstop with your friends while shooting down your foes in the face. I hope this review will help you decide (or not) to buy this game.

Aaaah, Borderlands. After so many hours spent playing this game, I should finally write a review or Tiny Tina will blow up my house.
I have so many thoughts about this game, and I am not even sure if I will manage to tell everything.
The most important thing I want to tell you: If you are playing this game for the first time,
Even if that means searching for someone in Steam community. It's literally the only one and the biggest con of the game. Trust me. You are not used to how this game really works, to fight bosses at the beginning, you are not used to get a second wind while dying, you won't just understand how to fight to not die every 2 seconds and not to ragequit after so many attempts. After you'll get used to the mechanics, so probably after first full playthrough, everything is fine and doing this solo won't be so scary anymore.
I must say, that Borderlands 2 is the first game since forever, which got me so much into itself, and its fandom. I just love everything about it. Main story is really catchy, if I can call it like that, and if we'll add some side quests and all the recordings we can randomly find while going through the Pandora, we'll receive huge, detailed plot, where every playable character, every NPC and every boss has its own, unique story.
What makes this game so special is variety of weapons available. Just take a look.
- Weapons don't require particular class to be used;
- Some of the weapons have "red text", which is most of the time some kind of reference quote, and always means that weapon has it's special trait, made just to that one weapon;

- All the elementals makes the gameplay more diverse, because you have to think what kind of weapon will be the most efficient to fight each kind of enemy.

All these reasons are enough to prove that BL2 is gorgeous, but let's add even more! First let me say that I feel like I must have missed the point of this game completely. If you are a fan of the series, then by all means truste the number of positive reviews out there. But if you intend to buy this without any knowledge of the franchise, then you might want to read on.
After this necessary preamble...
I bought the game with friends to play in co-op and that is the only way I have played the game: playing with friends make it bearable but on my own I could not stant the tedious repetitive tasks. I felt like I was playing a first-person shooter mixed with Diablo 3 (make what you want of this comment).
The game has its funny moments, especially with some dialogues, but for the rest I felt like I was spending most of my time checking weapon stats in order to decide what to discard and what to keep in my limited capacity inventory.
I did not understand the point of the hundreds of chests scattered everywhere, other than to trick the compulsive side of gamers to open them all. You do open them all, only to be disappointed.
Money seems to have no real in-game value. Eridium is a much rarer currency and the only thing that you will find yourself caring about. At some point even min-maxing your weapons feels more like an accountant job than a fun task and you end up thinking: "meh, whatever, this will do, I cannot be bothered to check the specs of the others".
In terms of story, I completed the game and I feel like no part of it was particularly memorable. Sure, it has quirky characters but other than that, all battles merge in a single blur. There are supposed to be "sad" moments but it is hard to care for any character so you just shrug and keep going.
About the gameplay, I clearly recall myself yawning with boredom while clearing yet another map: normal enemies are more an inconvenience than anything. The bosses are (sometimes) more fun but still not challenging. On harder levels they become tougher, not smarter, so you just have to spend 10 more minutes shooting at them while avoiding their attacks.
And speaking of clearing maps: the fact that enemies re-spawn as soon as you leave an area felt like a cheap way to increase the longevity of the game. The only result is that it makes you wonder: "can I be bothered to go back now or shall I try to optimize the quests?". You know, the kind of decisions you make in real life while deciding whether you should pick up the milk before or after taking the kids to school. In a game, I would like something more exciting.
As I said, I was probably not the kind of target this game so take this review with that in mind.

I beat Alien Isolation recently.  Funny thing is, I kept thinking I was near the end and when I first thought I was almost done, I was only about 1/2 way through the game.  If you can get past it being sometimes extremely stressful to play, it feels very well done.  The character you play is down to earth, and not a super hero by any means.  She can kill other humans but she can also die very easily.  It sorta keeps you on your toes and makes you think about how to approach a situation.  Other small things along that same line are that you can run, but maybe you shouldn't because its noisy.

They seem to really want to tie it to the 80s movies right down to the fact that there is 80s technology in the game.  I suppose its seems nonsensical now, but it was kinda a nice touch to see things like tape recorders and boomboxes around the game, since that's what you'd have seen in the movie.  Visually appealing too, in that most of the rooms feel like a space station would be (sometimes cramped hallways and rooms) and not big and wide open.  Though there are certainly those open spaces too.  Speaking of visuals, the game makes excellent use of film grain effects, lighting, textures, and shaders, and other 3D effects are just really nice looking but without being over the top.
The audio is great.  Music is tense and it seems to change depending on just how "in danger" you are.  Lots of ambient sounds, clanging, sparks, that sort of thing to creep you out.  Firing up certain systems in the game produces a whir that just "sounds right".  A sort of aural ecstasy.  The alien really stomps around rooms and using those audio cues is a part of how you determine if its safe to move.
There are weapons in the game but most of the time you are relying on crafting items instead of the weapons.  Mainly because you don't get most of them until later.  That and the items actually help you with the alien and the weapons don't.  Speaking of crafting, there is certainly a decent amount of things to make.  It's not an RPG lite even, but you do find a blueprint here and there that tells you how to make a new item.  Once you learn something, you can make it over and over again as long as you have the materials.  You don't even need to remember the materials, the game simply shows them to you and you click on them to apply them to the recipe, then you hit a "click here to build" button to craft the item.
Finally, the game play is a mix of exploration, hide and go seek, and a little bit of fighting.  With the alien its certainly more hiding and baiting it with things.  I found later in the game that even flares work well for bait.  I wish I had known that early on as I basically never used flares.  Your motion tracker helps you locate the alien, people and androids.  The motion tracker also has a small bar or compass to help you move in the right direction.  I'd say most of the game I had no issue figuring out where to go, but I did have to reference an online guide 2 or 3 times to figure out sections of the game. So, there is some thought to be put into what to do.  Again, usually its very clear.  But once or twice I knew where an objective was but I couldn't figure out how to get to it until I checked a guide.  It's been ages since I've had to read a guide so you can decide if that bothers you or not.
There was one tense moment in the game that was initially thrilling, that later became tedious as I actually knew what to do and simply couldn't get from point A to point B.  So that was slightly frustrating.  A time or two it felt almost "too hard".  In the end though, just really giving it some thought and very carefully saving at every save point I could get to, and I was able to get to the end.  You also learn that you actually can "hide" from the alien almost in plain site.  Sometimes simply sitting under a table works, essentially as long as it doesn't have line of sight on you, you're fine.  Oh and if it doesn't hear you.

I give it 9.5/10.  Only due to the fact that I had to reference a guide a few times and got stuck on one part for a good while (probably died 20+ times in an area) and felt it was a bit overly hard at that one spot.  Absolutely phenomenal game.

I had it pre-ordered via Steam, without seen a trailer, without having read news about it. So the surprise was bigger when I started the game. Call of Juarez Gunslinger is a game whose price is in no relationship to the product, much too low in my opinion. This game is great, hope the developers have been sufficiently rewarded. Can not say more ... everything else you have to find out by yourself.

Call Of Juarez Gunslinger is an action packed first person shooter, set in the Wild West. It has big shootouts, duels, famous outlaws, you name it. Everything you would want from a game with a theme like this.
The story is told as a tale, so occasionally the story will rewind or change on the fly in order to adjust bits of the story. It's well integrated and it's a fun way to keep the story fresh. Now, this game is all about shooting so it's important that this part works well. Thankfully, it does.
The shooting aspect is tight and the reward system behind it is solid as well. Killing enemies will reward you with XP and if you kill enemies fast enough you'll build up a combo meter that will reward you with even more experience. There's also a focus key that will slow the game down so you can kill enemies more easily.
The skill trees are diverse (for a shooter, so don't expect any skills that don't belong here) and allow you to mix things up fairly well.
Graphically the game looks awesome. It has a realistic look with what looks like a little bit of cel shading in it.
For a downloadable game Gunslinger is pretty long. It took me roughly 8 hours to complete the story. After that, you can start a new game with New Game Plus.
If you have no interest in starting over again, there's always the Duel and Arcade modes.
Duel will have you duel (duh) against all of the enemy bosses from the story, with only 5 lives, and Arcade will put in your several levels of the game with cleverly placed enemies. The goal there is to kill enemies as fast as you can while building up your combo meter. A fun, very fun, challenge. In fact, I think I had more fun with the Arcade mode than the Story mode but that's because the Arcade mode is fast paced and allows for replayabilty, even if a level is only a few minutes long. Collecting 3 stars on all levels should take you a long time.
Gunslinger managed to truly impress me. But then again, I was already looking forward to playing this as there really aren't enough games around like this (I count The Club as one of them, more or less). It's now one of my favorite games of this year. I hope it does well enough to give us a possible sequel... downloadable or retail.

After beating the game (main story anyway, haven't gotten around to Shadow yet), I can say with full confidence that... well, it's pretty good. I mean, I absolutely LOVED the game. In fact, this game's actually kinda gotten me back into Sonic, but that's besides the point.
The game isn't perfect. Far from it. The jumping can be kinda weird, movement takes some getting used to, and the game's framerate has a tendency to slow at certain points, though not to the point where it's unplayable. While I enjoyed the game all the way through, I wasn't that big of a fan of the Classic Sonic stages. They weren't bad, not in my opinion, just not as good. Also, Classic Sonic plays kinda weird, and honestly, didn't really need to be there... but it's okay, because he gave Tails meaning again, so that makes up for it! I think.
I also feel like there were a couple missed opportunities, and those were a letdown. Like, certain characters just getting their butts handed to them in, like, one hit, in a cutscene. That was disappointing.
The bosses were just okay in my opinion. Nothing special, just okay. I did like fighting Infinite, at least, mostly. 2/3 of Infinite was good, I'll say that.
Now, everything else, I really enjoyed. The story is cheesy and stupid, but the game thrives in it. There isn't really a point where the game tries to take it too seriously, which is good. This isn't Sonic 06. The story is fun, and that's what matters, I think.
The gameplay, aside from what I previously mentioned, is a bit unpolished, but still fun. It's a bit of a step back from Sonic Generations, and I miss being able to perform tricks in midair, but... I liked it. There were a handful of levels that felt like they were boost-to-win, and there were others that has platforming that was a bit unfair? Or maybe I just suck. Either way, it's good.
The soundtrack, like almost every other Sonic game, is FANTASTIC. It's absolutely fantastic, and I love it. Well, okay. There were a few tracks I wasn't a fan of, like... everything else was amazing.
Can I just mention how great the voice-acting in this game is? Because it's really great. All the voice actors sound really invested in their characters.
Character creation is really fun! My only complaint is that the bear looks kinda weird.
My final complaint is that the game is, overall, pretty easy. Unless you're like me, and are trying to get through every single stage without taking a hit, the game is a breeze.
Not perfect, but definitely enjoyable and a definite step in the right direction. If you hate Sonic, you're going to hate the game. If you're coming here expecting Mania, you're not going to get Mania. If you're not either of those, you'll probably enjoy the game. Maybe not as much as I did, but still. Objectively, it's passable.
ALSO I JUST REMEMBERED
I haven't had any crashes, but I think that's because I was playing on Big Screen Mode (which can be accessed via the little gamepade icon by the top right), because when I was playing without it, I got major audio and framerate issues. Haven't tested it, but I think that's the case.

Transistor is an RPG by the creators of Bastion. Similarly to their previous game, the art, story, and sound design are all fantastic. The combat is a weird hybrid between real-time and turn-based that will probably be hit-or-miss with most people. The robust skill system was incredible and is probably one of Transistor's best features.
The combat is different than most other games. You can move and attack in real time, but you'll find it difficult to survive without using the Turn() feature. Turn() pauses the game and allows you to plan out your next few movements and attacks. The planned actions will then be executed very quickly, without the enemies being able to attack or move. Turn() then goes on cooldown for a few seconds and most of your skill won't be usable. This creates a turn-like tempo in the the fights where you attack with Turn() and then play defensively when it's on cooldown.  The combat takes a little getting used to and won't be for everyone, but it really works well with the skill system.
The skill system is one of the games best features. I didn't unlock all of the skill on the first playthough, but there are at least 16 of them. Each skill can be used in 3 ways.
1. Active Skill: The skills you use in combat. You get 4 active skill slots.
2. Augementation: Each active slot has two augmentation slots which alter the effect of the active skill.
3. Passive Skill: Each skill has a different passive effect when placed in one of the 4 passive slots.
Although this seems to be overly complex, you only start with a couple skills, the 4 active slots, and an augmentation slot for each of them. You gain additional skills and slots when you level up so the game does a good job of easing you into the skill system. Furthermore, the game does an excellent job of pushing you to experiement and try new skill combinations. I had a lot of fun experimenting with the skills and trying to find effective combinations.
In conclusion, Transistor is a great game. If you liked Bastion, or are a fan of turn based RPGs, you should get this game. If you're unsure that you'll like the combat, you should look at a couple gameplay videos, but try not to spoil the story for yourself.

PROS:

TIPS:
* I found that this game ran smoother in "Windowed Fullscreen" than in "Fullscreen". Your mileage may differ.
* Also, be aware that you can and should adjust the FOV and Film Grain Effect to your liking. They are located within the settings menu.
Alien: Isolation blends horror, exploration and puzzle solving better than most games.
Include the amazing sound design and lighting effects and this game is a masterpiece.
The jump scares are plentiful and the story is fairly immersive. The visuals are modeled beautifully to reflect the retro feel of the first film.
The only negative point that I can make about the game is its slight repedetiveness.
That said, Alien: Isolation is a must buy for any horror enthusiast.
One of my favorite games of all time.

I'll start with something very important: This game has a horribly slow, downright boring start. Very little happens in the first two missions and you spend far too long trying to figure out what to do thanks to a complete lack of direction.
Then things get good.
Alien: Isolation is a flawed gem, but a gem nonetheless: It chronicles the experiences of Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley's daughter, when she and her crew get locked inside the Sevastopol station with the xenomorph. From then on, it's basically a stealth game: Complete the missions without the alien finding you or suffer the consequences.
While the game was criticized for its difficulty, I didn't find it too hard or too easy - there were only two missions (Missions 5 and 10, I'm looking at you) that I deemed truly difficult or borderline frustrating, with the rest being for the most part manageable, with a few easy ones for variety. The game luckily doesn't overuse its main enemy, instead having whole sections where your enemies are humans or robots, all the while telling you the story of what happened aboard the station, why the alien is there, and why there are weird things (Other than a horrible, unkillable monster from outer space) happening in the station.
I really liked it. It's a slow game, it's nothing like a shooter (so if you're looking for one stay away), and the setting lends itself perfectly for a horror game, making you jump a few times during its length. I must recommend it, considering it's one of the two stealth games I've loved the most (The other one being, of course, Dishonored). If you like stealth/horror games, don't miss this one (Although the DLC is highly redundant, so feel free to skip it).
PS: If you suffer from motion/simulation sickness as I do, there's an XML hack that allows you to set the FOV up to 100. That, along with spending most of the game crouched (Which you'll do anyway, because otherwise the friendly Xenomorph gets you) to minimize the head-bobbing you can't get rid of worked for me to not get sick.

After finishing the game, you get the option to play through again on a harder, extreme difficulty. I started this difficulty, handling it like I had the previous difficulties. Turns out the alien can show up before the official alien reveal cutscene.

While I haven't completed the game yet, I can safely say that this game is absolutely amazing. great experience overall, only enhanced by the above average use of sound. Each chapter has its own feel of terror to it, and you end up revisiting a few areas in the game. You can then unlock more of the area by the new weapons and tools you have unlocked. I'll go over some individual mechanics of this game for this review:
While the alien AI is extraordinary and it learns more about your distractions, sometimes he can be frustratingly blind. As for the human and android AI, it's not the best. It's still nothing too bad though, as the Alien really feels smart when he double checks an area or comes from different entrances every time he hears a sound. In short, 7/10
Use of sound is good. The way the alien footsteps sound like is terrifying and has scared me more than when I'm hiding from it. Speaking of sound, the music isn't too shabby either, but nothing over the top either. There's no large choirs, which to me always seems annoying in horror games.
Weapons are very effective against humans and it takes quite a lot of shots to kill androids. But the alien does not fear your weapons. Don't try to shoot him, it's basically suicide. There are a few weapons that stun the alien briefly. H
owever. He also learns from this though, so don't use them too much early game.
Visuals look great, I play on the lowest settings and my game looks great, there's no visual bugs at all for me and it doesn't take that much for a modern computer to run this game with high graphics.
In a certain chapter you'll encounter a bug with some NPC's and objectives not loading. It's quite the spoiler saying exactly what chapter, so if you want to, look it up. The only thing I'll say is that it has to do with androids, maybe that'll help looking it up. A simple fix for this is apparently putting your settings to the lowest.
While it is one of my favourite all time games, there's certainly an amount of faults. But those faults do not outweigh the positives at all, and it's definitely a great game, one of the best horrors. It has a reasonable amount of times when it's on discount, so just watch the game if you're low on budget.

Transistor is an action RPG made by the same guys who made the magnificent title: Bastion. It was just released yesterday and it's available now on PS4, Xbox One and Steam. And while it certainly resembles Bastion a lot, it is a very different masterpiece altogether.
As far as plot goes, the story is told in a fashion very reminiscent of its predecessor, only this time around, cut-scenes are more frequent and since they are comprised of amazing art and genius portrayal it becomes a delight to witness every single one of them. To put it bluntly and spoiler free, you assume the role of Red, a former high class member of the Cloudbank society who's now on the run after a tragic event. The only thing to keep you company is a very sci-fi looking great sword that can speak, and oh boy does it sound sexy as hell.
The game's visuals are stunning and its art style is outstandingly charming and colorful, it also does not sacrifice the slightest shred of complexity and seriousness where it is needed, and it is needed a lot, trust me. A soundtrack just as beautiful and varied as in Bastion accompanies you throughout your journey and often interacts with the way you traverse the city and battle your way through waves of evil technological monsters spawned by a phenomenon called "The Process".
It is often difficult to praise a game's design as well as its aesthetics and soundtrack when it looks and sounds as beautifully as Transistor does but it undoubtedly surpasses the latter. Transistor's strongest suit is it's refined gameplay, and here's why:
Where as Bastion felt as if it was catered to a western audience, Transistor is heavily motivated to please the complicated strategist palette of the JRPG audience. Dozens if not hundreds of more numeric, priority focused and postinioning tactics plague Transistor's combat system, and that's a good thing. Instead of being chained to an optimal dps model, you are given multiple choices when it's time to address your encounters. Be it through sheer fortitude, stealthy obliteration, multiple target barrages, ally recruitment subterfuge or even kiting methods. Virtually any wave can and should be addressed differently than the last and the amount of substantial change is chosen by you!
To better portray it all: You have 4 abilities that you can map to four buttons, but every ability can be turned into a passive for you, or an upgrade for another ability. The way you use these is just like you would in any action RPG game by pressing the button, duh. You also have a technique called "Turn" which stops time and allows you to program and deliver a sequence of abilities and movements in order to turn the tide of battle, dodge an obviously fatal blow or deliver the final one yourself.
Ultimately a story with an astonishing setting, compelling lore and characters, wonderful soundtrack and sound design, intricate strategic combat that doesn't sacrifice flow or immersion and rewards the player for learning its ropes all the while respecting his or her intelligence, cool boss battles and a nice amount of extra content. This is what makes Transistor a game very well worth it's price tag and a title you must have. Whether you're into action RPGs or not, give it a go. I promise you, you wont regret it.

First off, excuse my possible stunned review, because I just beat my first playthrough. I couldn't have asked for anything better from Supergiant. After playing through Bastion, I knew that I would have to get this game as soon as possible. The art, as well as soundtrack, is what sold me right off the bat. I'm very into games that have breathtaking visuals. Darren Korb sells the soundtrack again, however this one is more ambient and flowy. The gameplay is very unique, with turn planning and strategies being your main combat. After playing for about 5-10 minutes, you get the hang of it right away. (Personally, I recommend using a controller, rather than your standard keyboard/mouse. But that's just me.) The boss fights are challenging, but not frustrating. (You can turn on the limiters to increase difficulty!) The story is beautifully done, although you definitely need to pay close attention. I suggest either turning on subtitles, just to make sure you don't miss anything. I felt as if the story definitely left it open so that the player can question the universe and everything in it. It's well worth reading through each character's story and unlocking them to find out more. The characters are so diverse, especially with relationships, race, gender.
Needless to say, I had goosebumps. I was not expecting the end of the story to go as it did, because it's nowhere near what happened in Bastion. That doesn't change the fact that it's absolutely phenomenal. The work that this company has put into the game really shows, and it's worth your money, in my opinion. The money for time spent is great as well. It took me about 12 hours to complete my first playthrough, and that includes taking in all the sights, areas, and character stories. Overall, the game is super refreshing, visually stunning, and absolutely enjoyable.
(Also, props to the tech support team for responding to my email super duper quickly, even at 2am EST! They got me right back into the game.)

Supergiant Games know how to craft an exceptional experience from top to bottom, start to finish. Amazing art, amazing music, amazing world-building and some of the most unique and enjoyable combat/loadout systems you can get in a game like this. The combat centers around a sword, the Transistor, which you can attach functions to and you can also slot 2 other functions into those functions and you can also slot functions in as passive abilities. Any function can be used for any of the three types of abilities which means there are a ton of combinations.
You will also be made to experiment with different combinations as the functions are tied into your health. If you deplete your lifebar, one of your functions "overloads" and becomes unusable for a couple of save points which makes you take them out and try new combinations. A wonderful way to keep the combat fresh, IMO.
I haven't even gotten into how the Turn() system works, either. Combat is basically part turn-based and part real-time and using both systems is very fluid and enjoyable. I'd recommend looking up a video to see it in action if you haven't already.
And one final thing, I've heard a lot of silly low-ball numbers for this game's length, as low as 4-6 hours. That's a joke. Maybe if you blitz through without reading any dialog/profiles, without reading any terminals or doing any of the backdoor stuff and just running from start to finish, maybe 6 hours is possible but for me 6 hours only got me past the second boss. There is plenty of gameplay here for $20.
10/10, must-play.
