Early Access Review (pre f2p):
Klapedia and Orsha are located on US East Coast.
Klapedia is a mess and is horrendously over-populated.
Orsha, apparently, is being avoided like the plague since it has been deemed as the (un)official South American server.
The EU and SEA servers are currently hosted in USE, but will be relocated to their respective regions next month or so.
For the love of goodness, if you're in Oceania join the SEA server, it's 1000% more playable than the US servers, dungeon queues actually pop and there is little to no problems with population.
Game itself:
It is similar to Ragnarok Online, if you enjoyed that, you'll enjoy this. It's the type of game where you can form parties on the fly and just grind your way to levels if you don't feel like questing.
Pros:
+Artstyle & Music
+Extensive Class system
+Can customise stat points (yes you can be a str-based healer if you want... whether that is viable though...)
+Costume/Hat collecting
+Satisfying core gameplay/party play
+Not bound to the trinity (can be pure DPS/Heal/Support/Tank or a combination of)
Cons:
-Servers (US ones at least) are a MESS at the moment.
-One part of their Token (their sub system) System is controversial, gives you exp boost, improved movement speed, more market listing space, , THE ABILITY TO TRADE. Granted, I don't really care much about trading but some might consider that core to their experience, especially with party play and other small QoL things.
-RMT/Bot spammers are rampant. Though blocking rmt is an easy 2-click process. Someone from the community has even developed an app that can automatically filter out shouts that include things in your blacklist but it's in a grey area when it comes to the terms of service.
I like it overall and I think it has potential, if the devs can salvage the disastrous launch and bring it to a stable condition, it certainly has the potential to be a good game. Time will tell if this is the case though.

As of this review, I have spent nearly 50 hours playing this game, and nearly 100% completed it. So what's my opinion on Sonic Forces?
The game is decent. It's good, but it could be better. There was potential, but it hasn't been fully fleshed out yet, but it's a fun game! Visually its beautiful, the graphics are top notch (not as beautiful as Unleashed, but still pretty to look at), and runs very well at 60fps, with very little framedrops (could be just my laptop, not the game itself). Soundtrack is amazing, as it always have been within Sonic games. Voice acting is superb and all the voice actors did a great job. Story is decent and an improvement from past Sonic games, with its return use of dark elements like in Sonic Adventure 2 and Unleashed, but still keeping some of its goofy-ness from Colours and Lost World. The use of creating your own character is a cool and fun feature of the game and I think it was a great move by SEGA and Sonic Team to do that.
Having said positive things, it does have its flaws and issues, which does bring the game down a bit. Firstly, the physics are a bit off. Comparing it to Generations, the three gameplay styles have all the same physics issues, and Classic Sonic suffers from it the most. Classic Sonic's jump feels a lot more heavy than he did in Generations and Mania, although his spindash is not as OP as it was in Generations, but he does have the Drop Dash from Sonic Mania, which adds a new and unique way to play as Classic Sonic in a Modern Sonic game. All three characters (Modern Sonic, Classic Sonic, Avatar) have crazy acceleration which can put you off when you want to time your jump correctly, or to avoid getting hit by enemies. It can screw you over when doing basic platforming. Secondly, the stages are really short, which Modern Sonic suffers the most, since we are basically boosting through the stages in around 1min30 to under 2mins. Modern Sonic and your Avatar/OC take most of the number of stages while Classic Sonic has only 6 stages, plus 1 boss fight (not including Final Boss) out of 30 stages, which makes him seem less important.
People say its a short game, which I can agree on, however it is longer than Generations, regarding story wise and number of levels. Still a lot better than Sonic Lost World. The story has it ups and downs. Personally, Classic Sonic was only involved to be a tie-in to Sonic Mania, which makes sense marketing wise and potentially good for a plot, but really for this story, he really didn't need to be involved, which is also supported by the number of stages he has in the game.
If you are new to the Sonic franchise and Forces is your first game, it will take you about 4-5 hours to complete the story, but for those who have played Sonic games in the past (Unleashed, Colours, Generations, etc), it will take you about 3-4 hours to complete the story. The Episode Shadow DLC adds around 20mins of gameplay and acting as a prequel to Sonic Forces. It's cool to be able to officially play as Shadow (without using mods) for the first time since Sonic 06 (not including any of the Riders games and the Black Knight game), however I wished he had at least 5 stages, instead of 3 to add more to the game and give more of a backstory, but at least you can do through Modern Sonic stages with Shadow, adding more of replayability. If you enjoyed Generations, then you'll have some fun playing Forces, and give Forces a go.

Once in a while one can come across a game that is so immersive, deep, and vast that it raises the bar for great games. In this regard, Dark Souls 2 (and indeed the original Dark Souls) is in a league of its own. With its incredibly challenging and unforgiving gameplay, subtle storytelling, and fascinating environments, Dark Souls 2 is one of the best (if not THE best) games I've ever played, despite its flaws. If you haven't already, I could recommend starting with Dark Souls 1, but that is not at all necessary to enjoy DS2 to its fullest.
What's good about it:
-
. There's no hand-holding to be had here. You're thrown into a brutal world where even the lowliest of enemies can send you back to pre-school if you don't pay attention. The game is always challening, but hardly ever unfair. You lose, cry, swear, and probably rip your hair out because you're just not good enough yet. When you fail, you get back up and try again and again until you win, and when you do, you'll feel like the Best Player of Video Games Ever ™.
-
. The combat mechanics make for some of the most incredibly exhilarating battles I've ever fought in a game. The wide variety of weapons and their respective play styles has something to offer for everyone. Remember that Fashion Souls is the best Souls.
-
. Or rather, the lack thereof. Nobody tells you where to go or what to do, and the actual story isn't delivered like we're used to. Instead, the world around you and the items you find will tell you the story. With a keen eye for details you'll be able to figure out the purpose of certain locations, characters, and items.
-
. The concept of Phantoms being summoned to your world seamlessly as you explore the world is incredibly clever. You can at any time (outside of some safe zones) be invaded by another player in the form of a Dark Spirit, or summon another player to help you as a Phantom or Shade. There are other ways to be summoned/summon as well, which will at times leave you wondering if you just fought a player or an NPC.
-
.
What's questionable:
-
. You can only be matched with people in your own tier, decided by the total amount of souls your character has acquired, whereas in Dark Souls 1 character were matched by their level. The system in DS2 seems like a step backwards. However, this will reportedly be fixed in the upcoming SotFS update.
-
. DS2 introduced a new stat, Agility, that determines the amount of invicibility frames your character gets when rolling and dodging, and the speed at which you can raise your shield. To get to the same amount of invicibility frames as in DS1, you have to dump a few levels into Adaptability, or the doding will feel very off if you're used to DS1. I can imagine that this was introduced to give agile characters an advantage, but it feels like a strange stat dump.
-
are simply inferior to playing with a controller. That said, they're a lot better than they were in DS1.
Dark Souls 2 in my opinion even better than Dark Souls 1, which is saying quite a lot, considering that Dark Souls is (was) my favourite game ever. Truly a worthy sequel. Do yourself a favour, play this game, and git gud.

Dark, dreary, and brutally unforgiving, this RPG is one of the few in recent memory that is truly difficult no matter how you play it.  Dark Souls 2 has next to no tutuorial and no guidance as to where you should go and in what order.  If you have someone holding your hand through it, or an online guide to follow, it may not be incredibly frustrating.
This game is the first RPG in recent memory that actually gives you the option to play it offline.  This has its own caveats however, and in a moment I will explain why.  First you must know that when you die, you drop all of your currently accrued  "souls" (currency for everything in-game from repairing to leveling) and must run back to where you died in order to get them back.  If you can't make it that far, and die again - you have lost all of those original souls.  On top of that, you are now "hollow", and have reduced life in increasing increments each time you die.
The positive aspect for being online is that you can get an item that allows you to write a symbol on the floor, which allows players in that area to summon you to them as a "phantom" and to fight with them.  In this state, you cannot loot items from chests and you cannot interact with levers or doorways, but as you help the other player you begin to gain back your humanity.  Once you fulfill your duty, you are teleported back to your own world, a human again - your hollowed state cured.
The negative aspect for being online (at least, it's a negative in my eyes) is that you can at almost any point be invaded by another player of your relative level for the soul purpose of surprise PvP.  Often times, these players know what they are doing and, for the PvP-inexperienced or super-casuals such as myself, only serve as an annoying and stressful death.  This is why I opt to play in offline mode much of the time.
Still, Dark Souls 2 is an engaging and clearly challenging game.  One I would prefer to play with friends, but still play on my own (very, very slowly).  If you enjoy a true challenge and don't mind a steep learning curve, this is a game you should consider.

When I first bough this game, I thought it would play out exactly like the other Elder Scrolls game, notably Skyrim. I found out soon that it is not the case. Sure you could make some arguments that there are indeed similarities but overall, the game is far different from any Elder Scrolls game I ever played.
You have to remember that this is primarily a MMO game with a Elder Scrolls skin on it. So don't get too trigger happy and buy this game just from looking at the screenshots and brief gameplay on YouTube. (I'm guilty of this)
As for the game itself, I was initially underwhelmed with the limitations it bought upon having played the other games from the franchise but the game grows on me as time passes. There are so many things you could do from 4 person dungeon raids, trials, PVP or even lay back and play it casually like a Single Player game.
The system that it has built upon is really fleshed out. There is a layer of depth and sense of progression to it and for the most part it feels rewarding to get to the max level or the best gear. The community are also very noob friendly. I have noticed that people were willing to help out others even with the most minial tasks. And mind you, this isn't a one time experience, I've seen countless people help others during my travels around. If anyhting, the community is the best part of the game frankly.
The quests are not too shabby either but they are not perfect. Most of the time you'll find yourself skipping through the dialogues just to get to the end because it is kind of boring and predictible, moreover, your actions doesn't affect the outcome. There are some couple of good quests scattered around the world but they suck mostly.
Overall, I would recommend this game for those who are a fan of the Elder Scrolls franchise and like MMOs but don't mind the quirky bits and differences from other games in the franchise.

I'll start with something very important: This game has a horribly slow, downright boring start. Very little happens in the first two missions and you spend far too long trying to figure out what to do thanks to a complete lack of direction.
Then things get good.
Alien: Isolation is a flawed gem, but a gem nonetheless: It chronicles the experiences of Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley's daughter, when she and her crew get locked inside the Sevastopol station with the xenomorph. From then on, it's basically a stealth game: Complete the missions without the alien finding you or suffer the consequences.
While the game was criticized for its difficulty, I didn't find it too hard or too easy - there were only two missions (Missions 5 and 10, I'm looking at you) that I deemed truly difficult or borderline frustrating, with the rest being for the most part manageable, with a few easy ones for variety. The game luckily doesn't overuse its main enemy, instead having whole sections where your enemies are humans or robots, all the while telling you the story of what happened aboard the station, why the alien is there, and why there are weird things (Other than a horrible, unkillable monster from outer space) happening in the station.
I really liked it. It's a slow game, it's nothing like a shooter (so if you're looking for one stay away), and the setting lends itself perfectly for a horror game, making you jump a few times during its length. I must recommend it, considering it's one of the two stealth games I've loved the most (The other one being, of course, Dishonored). If you like stealth/horror games, don't miss this one (Although the DLC is highly redundant, so feel free to skip it).
PS: If you suffer from motion/simulation sickness as I do, there's an XML hack that allows you to set the FOV up to 100. That, along with spending most of the game crouched (Which you'll do anyway, because otherwise the friendly Xenomorph gets you) to minimize the head-bobbing you can't get rid of worked for me to not get sick.

After finishing the game, you get the option to play through again on a harder, extreme difficulty. I started this difficulty, handling it like I had the previous difficulties. Turns out the alien can show up before the official alien reveal cutscene.

Early Access Review:
I understand that this game is still underdevelopment and that many changes will be coming later. This review is based on the game up to this point.
First off, don't believe the videos. The do show what the game looks like but only in a perfect world yes you build large castles with your friends. Defend them against your enemies. Try to take over the world, yada, yada yada. In reality you will log in and die immediately. Then you will re-spawn and then die immediately. You will do this several times and then get frustrated and quit the game. So why am I recommending this game? The problem isn't with the game, but with pure lack of respect from other players ( though the game does provoke it in some ways, see below ). The only way I have found this game enjoyable is by creating my own private server and playing with my friends.
Private Servers:
This is the only way to play and have fun in my opinion. The nice thing is that it was really easy to set up a private server. The developers thought that through pretty well. With a private server you don't have much control over the server it self other than setting a few things like a server name, password, message of the day, etc. One thing I would like to see is to allow us to change the day / night cycle times ( they seem a bit short ). Also it seems, like a bit much to have to wipe the server every update.
The World / Items:
The world unfortunately is very small in comparison to most survival games I have been playing. The resources are very limited and clustered. So you will find yourself running around a lot to find a little. Unfortunately right now there is only a small selection of items that can be crafted and used in the game right now. However, this is expanding as the updates come in. Some of the items are a bit twisted for my tastes, but as you will find in the Official servers you will be tortured often with different devices.....not my cup of tea.
Building:
I love the building in this game. It reminds me a bit of MineCraft in the fact your are dealing with blocks on a grid. However, unlike several other survival games you are not limited by the terrain height changes. You don't have to worry about if you have find a flat spot to make a house, just build up a foundation to make a flat area.
All in all the game is very fun and has a ton of potential, but as stated above you will more than likely want to play on a private server.

'Papers, Please' deserves its reputation for excellence. I played it first in Beta, and had already clocked up hours of play before the final product arrived on Steam. Most games give the player power - over a gun, or a car, or a team of small and aggressive monsters - but few provide the sort of authority that comes with the 'thunk' of a rubber stamp at the Arstoktzka border checkpoint. How the player uses that authority is at the heart of the game, and poses some difficult questions about freedom of choice, human rights, individual responsibility and collective security. Do you take a bribe to feed your family? Put your neck on the line to reunite someone else's? Detain a minor offender for a healthy kickback? The choices don't seem as clear-cut when you're sitting in that box, and that's the genius of the game: the choices become important. Out of very basic mechanics comes a believable world, and it's absolutely beautiful in all its depressing, overbearing glory.
You may find yourself regretting your actions, or quietly justifying them to yourself. You may frighten yourself with the ease with which you can have a person marched away, saving yourself the paperwork of processing them and earning a little pocket money to boot. By the latter half of the story, turning an applicant away over a slight clerical error saves a hell of a lot of checking, and they might hate you for it but you've got a deadline and mouths to feed. And besides, it can't be as bad as the terrifying 'rat-tat-tat' of a printed warning, and maybe a hefty fine. Personally, I was shocked to discover that I was developing nationalistic prejudices towards fictional people. (It's always the bloody Kolechians, isn't it?)
It's tough, it's complex, and while it may not be perfect, 'Papers, Please' deserves all the praise it recieves, and I can't reccomend it too highly.

Grinding doesn't work all that well, quests give the most exp, and when you're out of quests and exp cards, you're basically stuck grinding.

Trading, training two attributes at a time instead of one, or doing dungeons three times a day instead of two, requires you to have a token. Those cost $18 and last 30 days. So you can't trade with other players unless both of you have tokens... fake subscriptions.
Do not play Tree of Savior. IMC is a failure of a company.

The Call of Juarez series has always had a place in my heart (excluding Cartel; as that was horse crap); esspecially due to my strong love for Spaghetti westerns.
Gunslinger is the latest (at this time) installment and it does a Kick♥♥♥♥♥job of bringing back what we loved about the series AND goes above and beyond.
The Combat is incredibly fast paced and you never really get a chance to chill out before a new hoard of Bullet loving badies rock up to take your slugs. There is something very satasfying about the way the Bullets EXPLODE from your gun and rip your enemies to shreds; you just feel like such a bad♥♥♥♥♥
The story is Okay, but the way it is presented, in a sort of Popup book/Flash back representation is fantastic! You'll find yourself fight a battle and then all of a sudden the Narrator will remember something else about the faithful events and those new features will spring into the scene.
The Achievements are fairly so-so, standard Collectables and a few cool ones (shoot a bird during a dual and still kill your opponent), but nothing ground breaking.
All in all Gunslinger smashes into my top 5 GOTY lists for 2013 easily, It's kick♥♥♥♥♥ brutal and entertaining... Absolutely worth the ~$20 AUD

Lot's of games aim to make an interesting story and a great game. Gunslinger easily delivers on fun with fast paced shootouts, a skill tree based leveling sytem and dodging death as bullets whiz right past your head in slow motion. However, Call of Juarez Gunslinger tells the story in the form of a saloon story. Taking advantage of how dime novels of the time used to exaggerate stories to make them more exciting, and at times even rewinding the level completely and even having to correct mistakes in the story. Each level is short, great, and feels full of action despite many levels only having around 50 enemies. Top it off with a dirt cheap price tag and this is one call that you do not want to leave hanging.

Dark, dreary, and brutally unforgiving, this RPG is one of the few in recent memory that is truly difficult no matter how you play it.  Dark Souls 2 has next to no tutuorial and no guidance as to where you should go and in what order.  If you have someone holding your hand through it, or an online guide to follow, it may not be incredibly frustrating.
This game is the first RPG in recent memory that actually gives you the option to play it offline.  This has its own caveats however, and in a moment I will explain why.  First you must know that when you die, you drop all of your currently accrued  "souls" (currency for everything in-game from repairing to leveling) and must run back to where you died in order to get them back.  If you can't make it that far, and die again - you have lost all of those original souls.  On top of that, you are now "hollow", and have reduced life in increasing increments each time you die.
The positive aspect for being online is that you can get an item that allows you to write a symbol on the floor, which allows players in that area to summon you to them as a "phantom" and to fight with them.  In this state, you cannot loot items from chests and you cannot interact with levers or doorways, but as you help the other player you begin to gain back your humanity.  Once you fulfill your duty, you are teleported back to your own world, a human again - your hollowed state cured.
The negative aspect for being online (at least, it's a negative in my eyes) is that you can at almost any point be invaded by another player of your relative level for the soul purpose of surprise PvP.  Often times, these players know what they are doing and, for the PvP-inexperienced or super-casuals such as myself, only serve as an annoying and stressful death.  This is why I opt to play in offline mode much of the time.
Still, Dark Souls 2 is an engaging and clearly challenging game.  One I would prefer to play with friends, but still play on my own (very, very slowly).  If you enjoy a true challenge and don't mind a steep learning curve, this is a game you should consider.

So, first off, I loved this game. Really beautiful, really well done, spot-on job, Supergiant does not disappoint. However, it has the unenviable task of having to walk in the footsteps of Bastion, arguably one of the greatest indie games of all time, in which context it falls somewhat short on one or two fronts.
But first the positives:
The style this game exudes is excellent. It's completely different than Bastion, but easily on par in terms of quality. The visuals, the music, the framing, everything just flows together to form a really unique and strong atmospheric experience. But that's all something you'd expect if you've played Bastion. And it delievers, if not exceeds, on those expectations.
One of my favorite things about the game is not what is in it, but what is markedly NOT in it. That is: tutorials, long-winded cutscenes, exposition out of nowhere, etc etc. So many tropes that make up your expected fantasy adventure game are absent from this, and it plays it so well. In terms of gameplay, the game just throws you right into the system, with little explanation, and exploration of your powers quickly makes it apparent that the game rewards experimentation. In terms of setting and story, everything is fluid, very little is directly told to you, and you are often left to piece things together. Both of these things in tandem make the entire experience of progression feel very natural and rewarding.
The combat system is super fun and diverse, allowing countless combinations of abilities and upgrades, and it is just a joy to play.
However, one aspect of the game which I feel could have been much better is the story. It wasn't BAD, don't get me wrong, it's interesting and in some ways moving, but by the end of the game I didn't really feel any connection to the main character. Or any of the characters really, with the possible exception of the narrator. But it's a shame because there are so many places they could have taken the story that would have been a lot more fulfilling and interesting than what they chose to do.
Overall though, highly enjoyable game, I know I'm going to jump right back in for new game +. If you liked Bastion, you'll love it. Or even if you're in the market for a fresh, unique cyberpunk action-RPG, give it a go.

PROS:
1. When everything is working as it should, the combat is extremely satisfying, especially for us gore lovers. Want to lop off your opponents head? How's about their arms and legs? Even after all that is said and done, anything that they were carrying is now yours for the taking! ( The friends that I do play with have told me this game's combat is similar to that of Chivalry's, so if you like that I'm sure you'll enjoy this )
2. I'm not one for long drawn out executions, but if you are, this game has just about every tool you'll need to make your enemies wish they'd never messed with you! Once you've captured your opponent, you'll have a list of humiliation/torture/execution devices to chose from. From the gallows to the guillotine, you name it, they've got it.
3. Perhaps you want to play some music before battle or just insure that everyone knows of your presence. If so, you should go and craft yourself a long horn, and maybe even a drum or two. That'll keep em on their feet!
4. Although I'm not much into roleplay, you'd have to be blind to not see the amount of potential this game has for it. If you're into rp, you'll find an abundance of community servers just for you.
5. The character creator is incredibly goofy. ( Which isn't a bad thing in this case ) From the tallest, skinniest, big chin...iest person you've ever seen. To the most pregnant, hulkiest, shortest guy you'll never meet. You can really make just about whatever kind of character you want.
CONS:
1. The video shown may include large scale ffa combat, but you'd be hard pressed to find a single situation that doesn't involve a 10v1. ( Unless you're with friends )
2. The combat itself is incredibly inconsistant, especially with the hardcore desync issues that are still present within the game. Even in servers where my ping is below 10, it can get pretty bad. It's basically, "Whoever is laggier wins". ( And that's after all of the updates leading up to version 10 )
3. Despite the recent efforts from Code}{atch to stop cheaters from ruining the game, they can still be found in just about every server you join. That being said, there have been several instances of people being banned for using modified dll's.
4. The engine isn't the greatest. ( Or rather; they're use of the engine isn't the greatest ) You'll find people double jumping and sometimes triple jumping directly over your walls. From boosting onto another person's head, to making siege workshops and hopping clean over a 15 block high wall. ( Even if they're within your crest's borders )
5. Fighting anywhere near your opponents base is almost always fruitless. If you do any significant amount of damage to them, they'll simply run into their base and instantly close the door behind them. ( Sometimes having two or more doors in order to trap you inside ) Most recently people have been excluding doors from their builds entirely. Simply removing their own blocks to enter/exit the base, then replacing them.
6. The building mechanics can be and most often are, abused. Have a trebuchet and want to tear down someone's walls? Too bad, they can rebuild everything you've destroyed faster than you can reload. ( Unless you have several people helping you. Even then it's tedious ) Lest you have an unimaginable amount of ammo for your trebuchet, good luck making any progress.
7. This game is riddled with performance issues at the moment. Code}{atch has been releasing updates to try and fix that, so hopefully this shouldn't be a problem in the future.
TLDR;
If you can't tolerate the sometimes inconsistant combat, bad and occasionally horrible mechanics,
"hackers"/cheaters, several glitches present in each update ( Often seen in Early Access games ), and in most cases a terrible community ( Based on which server you join ), I'd stay away from this game until it's had some time to progress.
Keep in mind; this review is based on the current state of the game ( Version 10 ) and things are bound to change in the future!

This is a shockingly good game. Shocking because in something so simple, you get great pathos and good comedy, and great mechanics. More than that, you get an uncanny sense of immersion into this poor guy's life, and a glimpse into all these other  lives. Weirdly lifelike lives. Unsettlingly meaningful, meaningless little lives. Bits of this game will likely haunt your dreams for a while.
And then you find out that just one guy made this. I recently played Ryse Son of Rome, which was gloriously beautiful and all, but it was as shallow as a puddle in the Sahara compared to this, and that was a couple of hundred people working for years.
There's some real talent at play here. You'll kick yourself eventually, if you don't at least taste test this game.

Words can not express. Papers, Please is a silently harrowing tale. This game represents everything that is oh so wonderful about indie gaming. A game that defies all convention and staggers the player to the very core. Very few big-budget games could ever hope to achieve the kind of nail-biting, psychological thrill that Papers, Please provides. It's terrifying, engaging, and chills on a level that has never been seen before. This game deserves our support; and if you value games as an art form, you'll give it nothing less.

I've only played this a little so far (4-5 "days" in the game), but it is really addictive.  Each day adds complexity to your job as immigration officer at the border of some ficticious cold-war era country.  The feeling is sad, totalitarian, hopeless.  You're lucky to have this job, and your family has been put up in one of the ritzier concrete apartment blocks, where I'm sure there's only three rats instead of the normal ten.  As the days progress and the government allows more entry with more fluidly changing requirements, you have to ensure that the documentation people present adds up.  Names need to match, documents must be issued from the right place, do they have the right ticket, is it stamped and dated properly, etc.  It's a seriously messed up brain game for adults!  Oh you'll laugh your backsides off at some of the comments the people make, like trying to bribe you with tickets to the strip club.  For the price of a cup or two of coffee, this is totally worth a few hours of your time if not many more.

Ok, so a simple explanation for all the negative reviews is that the lag and connectivity issues make for a pretty hit or miss experience. However, even with moderate lag and constantly relogging I've been enjoying myself. I understand that the server is under tremendous load due to the popularity of this game and the hype leading up to it. Coupled with the fact that everyone has shunned one of the servers because they fear a toxic community after the Brazillian members claimed that server as their own. Which has caused everyone else to flock to the one remaining NA server, and what does that cause? Lag and connectivity issues.
There are a few other things that are being pointed out such as the trading and auction system being restricted and less than what we expect from most MMO's now a days, on the one hand I agree it's pretty bunk, but on the other hand I think it's better than what Blizzard did with D3 when they wanted to get away from gold sellers after creating a mess for themselves.
As far as asthetic, gameplay, and OST this game is top notch IMHO. There is a plethora of classes and items, an immense number of zones, and I think 500 levels of content. It's a big undertaking and while I think IMC could do better in handling these things, it's only been out ~2 weeks and that's early access. So I am hopeful that these things get addressed, and if they don't then it was a potentially great game gone to waste.

Servers go down almost daily, entering dungeons, switching channels, and traveling between maps cause crashes and disconnections. Every item on the market, including cash items worth ~$18 each, all disappeared into thin air. Talking to NPCs or other quest objects, pressing the button for a regular auto attack, switching equipment, leveling stats or skills, and changing key binds can all be delayed for minutes at a time due to lag.
"Premium" status confers such benefits as:
Enabling direct trade with other players, excluding in-game currency, where items permanently lose upgrade potential when exchanged.
The ability to list more than 1 item on the market at a time, which also reduces upgrade potential, and not losing 30% of the sale price to tax. You still have to wait 48 hours to retrieve your earnings, however.
Increased character movement speed.
Account-wide storage access.
3 global dungeon runs per day, rather than 2, as well as an extra chance to re-roll boss loot.
The cash shop includes an item that adds a random amount of random stats randomly between certain values to otherwise cosmetic accessories, set at a price point where free players cannot afford even one per day (nor any amount of time). They can drop one at a time at an extremely low rate from bosses, typically found at the end of limited dungeon runs, to somewhat assuage free players.
Exclusive to the international release, the price of certain cash items have been increased, the rate at which players accumulate free cash points has been lowered, the total number of dungeon runs for all players has been reduced, defeating certain bosses grant smaller rewards, some items can no longer be found as loot, several skills have been nerfed compared to the Korean version of the game, and now players' account names must be unique across all servers rather than only exclusive within their own persistent world.
Chat is flooded with RMT bots, which still displays in a marquee at the top of the screen, even while blocked, and is not cleared from the chat window unless these features are disabled entirely. Even when hidden, the spam continues to be processed by the client which results in a surprisingly hefty performance hit. More interestingly, the network traffic for chat is sent in plain text, where the timestamp of messages can be altered, causing artificially "later" messages to be forcibly scrolled to every time a newer message arrives underneath.
Character customiazation options are barebones, offering 12 hair styles of a fixed color as the only aesthetic change available to players besides their starting class (so no skin or eye color swatches, either). The styles range individually from light to dark, but there is as of yet no way to mix and match between the default styles and colors, not even via the cash shop. A limited set of colors are available as rewards from per-character achievements, and several exclusive styles can be purchased with real money, but it is far from an exhaustive list of all possible combinations. You may never be able to have blonde/brunette/red hair in your preferred style unless it was always that color to begin with.
At least it isn't RO2.

Great game. While it's not quite as strategically deep as DOTA or League (at least until 2018 when they completely overhaul the Conquest map), it provides MOBA gameplay with a much more engaging movement and combat system. The over-the-shoulder perspective makes the game a lot more immersive and adds other elements of gameplay. You can't see what's around the corner, you can't see what's behind you without turning around... so movement and positioning is a lot more difficult since you can't see what's going on everywhere at once. And of course, moving with WASD just feels so good. There are also a bunch of different game modes, so if you don't want the slow paced farming or you just wanna frag, you can do that too.
The business model is pretty solid. You start out with 5 gods permanently unlocked, one from each class (Warrior - Guan Yu, Assassin - Thor, Hunter - Neith, Guardian - Ymir, Mage - Ra). And there is constantly a free god rotation that changes every week or two, so if you never unlock another god, you'll always have 10 playable. Sometimes an extra god or two will be on rotation, and occasionally they will do a free god weekend where every god is playable. Additional gods can be purchased for in-game currency (Favor) - which while levelling your account level you can probably unlock about 2 per week. Once you get to level 30 and no longer receive level-up bonuses, you can get about 1 new god per week from the free currency. For $30 (sometimes on sale for $15-20) you can permanently unlock all gods that will ever be released. Gods are pretty well balanced and most of the free ones are considered in a good tier, so it's not exactly pay-to-win either.
Money can be spent to purchase Gems (in-game currency to buy premium stuff), and you can also get up to 50 gems per week just by logging in daily and collecting the reward (for a point of reference, it's about 400 gems for an average skin). They will also occasionally have gem events where you can earn gems over a weekend by playing games. With gems you can buy Voice Packs (so the voice-over quick chat will have your character's voice instead of the default voice), Skins, etc.
Pro League is quite competitive and well-run, good broadcast. Decent payouts for players, though because it's a much smaller scene than most other games (e.g. CSGO, LOL, DOTA...) they are struggling to keep big orgs invested in it. Most of the orgs now are newer orgs such as NRG, Luminosity, etc. We've lost the support of some big names like Envyus and Cloud 9.
Playerbase is spread a little thin. In off-peak hours the matchmaking can be pretty bad because the game prioritizes short queues over good matches. So if you're not playing ranked, prepare to have new players and high-ranked players in the same casual games if you're a night-owl. While having a lot of game modes has its perks (something for everyone), it also means each individual game mode has fewer players.
Servers aren't the best. Many issues with routing, particularly for the EU and South American (LATAM/BR) servers. Sometimes people will unexplainably have 200+ ping even though they normally get like 50 ping to the server. The server provider in general seems to not have very robust infrastructure, as ping increases a bit as the game progresses (e.g. load into match with 70 ping, you'll probably have 90 ping 10 minutes into it). NA server location isn't good - it's in either Atlanta, Georgia or Virginia (people have said Virginia, but my hop test showed Atlanta, so I'm not 100% sure). So west coasters and mid-westers will have 100+ ping.
Account security needs improvement. 2FA implementation took them years to add, and is still in beta and some people have been locked out of their own accounts (it's buggy). You can change e-mail on an account if you know the password, without having to confirm ownerhsip with security questions.
Match replays need improvement. Only custom games and high-rank ranked games (diamond-masters) are recorded, so you can't watch back your games outside of that to try to improve. Additionally, when a new patch comes out, all games from the patch before are no longer viewable.
UI updates are really bad and infrequent. One of the game modes (Siege) has been borderline dead for like a year because of a UI update that made it not visible on the game mode page unless you scroll down (which it's not obvious that you can do so), so many people don't know it exists or don't think to queue for it. Minimalistic HUD for in-game has been teased for years now, and the files are there (you can occasionally see it very briefly upon loading in before it updates) but hasn't been actually released yet. The spectator interface has gotten worse (for the pro league mainly) with its update. etc.
Pros:
- Fun gameplay
- Fair business model
- Good competitive scene
- Lots of game modes
Cons:
- Account security isn't good
- Servers have issues and are rarely acknowledged
- Poor match replay system
- Playerbase isn't great in off-peak hours
- UI updates rarely happen, and thats sort of a good thing because they often make things worse

TLDR
The experience is a mixture of hypnotic atmosphere and frustrating interruptions from the game mechanics.
The worst thing about Alien the Isolation is the alien.
This game is beautifully true to the movies. The music, effects, art direction and story are all shown with such care that it's like playing a hypothetical extended cut of the movie Alien. Unfortunately, that means there is an intense amount of overlap with the key beats of the original movie, to the point that it felt borderline plagiaristic.
It's plainly fanservice. That's ok. That's fun.
There was only one instance where I felt the story, straightforward as it was, fell flat, and that was Amanda's reaction to

The pace was especially rough early on. You have very few tools for dealing with the alien itself at that point. It's an incredibly frustrating period of time, especially if you are a fan of more walking-sim fare of horror games (Amnesia, SOMA) combined with frequent loading screen tips emphasizing that you play as stealthy as possible.
The learning experience was riddled with frequent deaths and hitting those save points. The game rarely, if ever, autosaves. The alien became less horrific and more an annoying obstacle.
When you finally get more weapons, especially the flamethrower, the atmosphere becomes faux-AlienS. You're able to deal with your invulnerable stalker and chase it off. The sense is more adversarial against a sworn enemy than always hiding from it.
Hiding. Hiding is boring, but it's central to the game. Used against the other enemies you encounter, you ambush them. It's rewarding and fun. Hiding is a way to preserve your critically low resources and tools, cobbled together through crafting. You're exchanging time, minutes every time you hide + medkits from choking damage, to preserve your ability to directly fight.
That is part of why the early game is more frustrating, and less scary, when such time and effort follow a death tied to a manual save. I will say though, the manual save did make me take the threats seriously, if only so I could feel the relief of updating my save and feeling free to recklessly experiment, die, and optimize my way forward.
You'll love the idea of this game, but be frustrated until you get the flamethrower, allowing you a reasonable way to explore the oppressive industrial decor of the space station Sevastopol.
It's too good at locating you. It's invulnerable. It's oppressively persistent. It's overused in the game.
The way to get past the alien is primarily by distracting it, but difficult to do competently when you are a stranger to unfamiliar halls.
The alien will drain your limited supplies as you experiment with ways to get it off your trail so you can advance the story through its many interactive minigames (cutting open doors, hacking interfaces). Usually when the alien spots you and charges you, it's a death sentence.
This means hiding. You're going to be hiding a whole hell of a lot, and that feels like time wasted. This is where my sense that the alien is overused comes in. Hiding is so central to advancing past the alien that you're going to be exposed to it for hours at a time from waiting for it to leave, and that amount of exposing the alien so constantly diminishes it as a horrific creature, and more as an adversaray to be bested.
That isn't a huge mistake. It still follows the arc of Alien and *then* Aliens, the sequel, but a point people love to make about Isolation is that it's like the first movie... but it isn't. There's a massive amount of action and direct combat in the game that blends the emotional arc of both films.

The second half of the game became such a grind, such a chore to do, that it killed my enjoyment for it completely. The worst part is I don't see *why* the developer studio felt the need to drag the game on for around 3 to 4 hours, constantly use cutscenes to set your finish line another ten miles away every time you get to it. The game didn't suceed in scarying me, it suceeded in frustrating me. I took full advantage of the crafting system to build items to avoid as many encounters as possible, and so will you when you play this, because this is not a game that will make you feel like you've enjoyed playing it once you see the credits roll. My personal suggestion is watch its story online if you're that curious, and pass this title.

A truly superb action RPG. This game positively oozes style. It's a treat to play. The battle system is solid - mixing real-time action with turn-based strategy as you freeze time to queue actions to be completed in rapid succession. Every ability you gain may be used in three ways - as an attack/ability, as an augmentation to another attack/ability, or as a passive boon to your character. Further, if you wish to gain levels faster (or feel that the game is getting too easy for you), you can pick up "upgrades" that will increase the difficulty (and experience gained) in various ways.
My only complaint about Transistor is that it was all over too soon. The game won't take you much longer than a double-feature at the theater to complete the first time 'round. That said, every minute was enjoyable, and just like Bastion before it, Transistor adds some replayability as you continue to progress in levels (and enemy difficulty) as you play through again and again.
I give this game 5 out of 5 stars. It excels in every area. I only wish that there were more of it.

I usually trudge through a game's actual gameplay to get it over with, but Transistor's gameplay was so enjoyable and solid that I found myself playing through the entire game again the very next day. The deep customization of your abilities with the various Functions(), the blend of real time frantic play with the powerful frozen planning of Turn(), and difficulty scaling done right make all the game extremely enjoyable to play. There are unbelievably powerful ability combos in the game, but you're always facing enemies that can meet the challenge. If you're not, then there's still the combat modifiers and restrictions you can add.
Story-wise, the world is significantly more sparse and spare than Supergiant's previous title, Bastion, but it seems to be an intentional choice: a bit of mystery allows for varied interpretations and a long narrative shelf life, which is what I think they were going for in this game. I think they leaned a little too far in the direction of limiting information, but the game doesn't suffer for it too much. I think the endgame buildup and final fight were excellently executed and they are going to be a favorite among the games I've played.

Ah, well. Transistor. Where to start eh? First off I'll say I'll try not to spoil specific plot points, but I will be talking about the story in loose terms, as well as enemy encounters. Little of it should spoil anything for you.
Lets get the positives out of the way first: The game looks gorgeous. It is scenery porn from start to end. The combat is competent and the upgrade system is interesting with a lot of choice. Your two main characters, Red and the Transistor are well written and the relationship between them is both incredibly heartwarming and heartwrenching in equal measure and they've certainly outdone themselves in that respect. You will believe a woman can love a sword.
The combat encounters, in the first third of the game at least, are fun, varied and - surprisingly - are equally possible using both the real-time combat mode and the planning mode (called 'Turn()' in game). The story is set up quite well here, you're goals are clear and the scene is set as the world collapses around you due to "The Process" that is turning everything into blank white tiles. While you never encounter another person during this part, the flavour terminals you interact with give you a real sense that this is all happening around you and you're not 'late to the party' or folowing in the wake like other games. Everything from the combat scenarios, the bosses and the action set pieces are all well done, enjoyable and very memorable.
Once you get into the second third they started to get a wee bitty lazy in my opinion. You traverse back through the levels you'd been through, but they've started to fall to the Process more and more - this still looks gorgeous. However, rather than give you new challenges they recycle the same enemies (though with some new abilities) and the same bosses. It gets mixed up a little bit but it's still very easy.
The final third is even worse. The enemy dubbed 'Man' is introduced and becomes the only enemy type you fight. No reason is given for this plot wise either, they just stopped putting in other enemy types. You could say that 'Man' is the final evolution of 'The Process' that was spawning them - but only if you wanted to sound like you're writing for your Art Degree. Whatever the reasons there are 4 types of 'Man' with the same basic attack (spawning a weak but deadly minion) but a different buff (like speed, or HP regen, or stealth or... actually I don't know what the fourth one is). You're not going to beat them without liberal use of Turn() either.
It got boring. Quickly.
Story wise, in the final third, it started to flag and waver. None the questions set up in the first two thirds were ever resolved, never even hinted at. I'm all for enigma and intregue, but this is taking the cake. The final boss felt like it was at the mid-way point and it did a very poor job of building the opponent up or foreshadowing what would happen. It was just "Yep, we're here. I have to kill you now", and while it didn't quite come out of nowhere the setting for it certainly did.
The ending did not have the emotional impact it was clearly going for either as it was never built up properly. It was a complete anti-climax and there was no feeling of pay-off for completing the game.
Of course, this is where we compare it to Bastion (And, if you've not played it, go play it. It'd been 3 years. I'm going to spoil it here). I loved Bastion and I loved its ending. You had a choice at the end of Bastion. It was a cleverly presented moral choice that essentially broke down to "Get the good ending" or "Play New Game+", but was smartly written and engaging. In Transistor there was no choice, unless you count the screen at the end basically saying "Quit game" or "Play New Game+". For Bastion it merged the ending to the new game + in a wonderfully meta way that I really appreciated. It gave it a nice warm send-off, and knowing that the 'good' ending really way the good one, and that the other one was a stable time loop appealed to the physics geek in me.
Transistor had none of this. In a game based in a world that might as well be entirely inside a computer; I had expected some kind of smart twist at the end that reflected the nature of the world in which it was set. Nothing.
From start to finish, Bastions pacing was spot on. You collected bits of the monument in part 1, in part 2 you had the conflict and the search kicked up a notch, and in the final third you had the twist, and suddenly you had clarity of perspective and the whole game you'd experienced before changed into something new.
Transistor had none of this. It started strong, story wise, then never picked up any steam, it ended on a damp note and I'm really disapointed in it.
If you want a story, the game does not deliver. If you want to see a unique relationship pan out this has it in spades. All the little moments stuck into this game between Red and the Transistor are excellent, though most seem to be limited to the first third and if anything the only thing the games ending does is resolve that particular thread.
Then there's the lore outside the main story. Bastion had the whole world of Ceylondia, the gods, the wilds, the wall, all this rich landscape that hinted at what the world was once and what terrible force ripped it to pieces. None of which was really central to the main plot, but provided a great deal of join-the-dots kind of lore where you could fill it in yourself with what you thought. It hinted, sometimes strongly, sometimes not, and painted a beautiful world that let your imagination run riot. Transistor does not do this. It's a cyberpunk world ruled by fashionistas, artists and celebrities with the power to create whatever they dream and it all goes wrong. And that's about as deep as it goes.
Bastion was a story of the world it was set in. Transistor is a story about the people who inhabit it. Unfortunately - outside of Red and the Transistor - they're not fleshed out enough to be cared about.
The game also has a soundtrack. Well, it's good, but it doesn't seem to stand out in the way the Bastion sound track did. You've got 'We all Become' that plays over the end, and in the trailers, but on the whole it's a much more subdued affair. I was also quite disappointed that none of the tracks, like Zia or Zulf's themes from Bastion, added anything to the lore of the game. 'We all become' is really just a reflection of the ending in my opinion.
The soundtrack in Transistor is just 'there', it's not as deeply engrained as Bastions was, although it is just as good to listen to (so if you're into that kind of thing buy the version that includes the soundtrack like I did).
Would I recommend this game? Yes. Once it's on sale. Sorry, your lacklustre final third makes it just not worth the asking price.

A little while back, on a lark, I deciced to give the indie game "Papers, Please" a try.  The concept looked interesting, so I figured it was worth a shot.
In my mind, I think of it as the "Checkpoint Charlie Simulator".  :)
The game takes place in a fictitious, mid-80's Eastern Bloc-ish region of the world where your homeland of Arstotska has finally gotten around to opening its borders with Kolechia after a long bitter war.  You play an unnamed citizen who has won the labor lottery and been assigned as the checkpoint inspector of those entrance points.  Your family is "generously" housed in a Class-8 dwelling (snerk).
The graphics are old school (purposefully so, I'm guessing), but it doesn't detract from the details, which is good because the game is all about details.
From the time you punch in to the time the checkpoint counter is shuttered, you deal with a never ending stream of people attempting to cross the border into Arstotska.  It is up to you to grant or deny access based on their paperwork and the policies to be enforced, as determined by the Ministry of Admissions (MoA) at the start of each day.
The first day is simple -- you are instructed to permit all Arstotskan citizens to cross and deny everyone else.  Each country has a distinct passport cover that you'll soon recognize and it is easy to automatically stamp DENY on any that aren't Arstotska.  For Arstotska passports, you have to spend a few more moments making sure that it isn't expired, the photos match, and the issuing city is valid.
Yeah, seriously, someone made a government desk job into a game.  :)  So having said that, why on earth would anyone bother playing something like this past the first 5 minutes?  After all, we've all seen the soul-crushed individuals who work at the DMV and post office...why would we want to play a simulator on that sort of drudgery?  :)
Well, for one thing, there is actually a storyline.  Your perspective never changes -- you'll spend the game basically working in your booth, looking out at the snaking line of hopeful immigrants and visitors, the armed soldiers keeping watch, and of course the interior of the booth itself.  However, things happen around you.  There are terrorist attacks, internal unrest, new edicts from the MoA in response to these events, and these all affect you and your work.  And this is where it gets interesting.
You see, you have a family to support.  You get paid $5 for each person you successfully process.  If you're REALLY efficient, you can process maybe up to 15 people per game day (time moves very quickly, the booth clock spins like a stopwatch -- each "day" lasts maybe 5-10 minutes of real life time).   Improper handling of applicants (either unwarranted denials or incorrect admissions) result in a citation.  You get 2-3 free mistakes, and then each subsequent citation that day will dock $5 off your pay.  The money you make goes towards paying rent, heat, food, and medicine for your family at the end of each day.
The rent will rise, family members will get sick and need medicine, and the ever expanding rules from the MoA make it harder for you to quickly process applicants.  You must always pay rent...but you can opt NOT to spend money on food, or heat, or medicine if you have to.  Of course, if you do that, your family members (and it looks like you have a wife, son, uncle, and MIL) will start to suffer or even die.
As the game progresses and the entry rules become more complex, you will get additional options in your booth -- you can interrogate people on discrepancies in their paperwork (some are kind of funny, like a bald fat man trying to pass through with a passport listing his gender as "F" -- really??), you can have them searched for weapons or contraband, you can even in some cases have them detained by the soldiers, depending on how suspicious the discrepancy is.
Some times they'll offer you bribes.  Given how close to the wire you are in expenses, it can get awfully tempting, especially if your son is about to die from his illness because you can't afford medicine and you have "free" citations left for that day.
Some times you have to make a moral decision -- like a woman who slips you a note with her passport saying that the man in line after her is trafficking her to a brothel and asks for your help.  If his papers are in order, do you deny him entry anyway (and earn a citation)?  Let him through because it's not your concern?  Spend precious time finding a way to detain him?
You start recognizing certain characters (most are randomly generated, but story-based events have recurring characters) and if you're smart, you'll start piecing together clues that something's up.  When the time comes, what will your big decision be?
It turns out that this game actually has multiple endings.  On my first try, I took too long at my work, didn't make enough money, spent too long interrogating some people, had my uncle die of illness because I couldn't afford the medicine, went into debt, and promptly got sent to jail for debt delinquency.  An ignominious end.  Well, at least they didn't shoot me (that's a possible ending, too, apparently, for a number of end game scenarios :)
There is also an "Easy Mode" that grants you a $20 crutch for each day.  That helps A LOT, though you can still♥♥♥♥♥♥it away if you don't earn enough during the day to cover your expenses.
Reading back through this review, I can see it is still hard to convey why I find the game fun.  Well, maybe fun isn't exactly the right word for it.  To be fair, it's not un-fun.  It is challenging.  For now I find it rather compelling, too.  It's an odd mix of feeling like you are welding a lot of power (people will beg you to let them go rather than being detained...etc) versus feeling powerless at the same time  (every time I stamp my decision, I tense in anticipation of hearing that damned citation being printed because I missed some detail!), and just general curiosity of how the story will unfold.
It could be that part of the appeal is that back in the 80s, I remember watching Cold War Era spy movies where the characters have to bluff or sneak their way past border crossings and checkpoints, and wondering what life is like for the indifferent (or suspicious) clerk on the other side of the window.  I guess now I have a better idea.  :)

TL;DR version - don't bother with this game. It's another cash-grab title that will become a ghost town in 1 year.
Here is a long list of problems with Tree of Savior:
1) You can't trade with other players. You read it right! You can't trade at all. The only way to trade with your friend, is if both of you purchase a 18$ token that allows trading for 30 days. And it has a limit of 30 trades per month! Sharing items to your alt character also decreases the trade count by 1.
2) You can't trade silver in a direct trade, even if you have Token. If your guildmate needs to borrow 100k silver really quickly to buy something from auction house, too bad you can't do him a favor!
3) You can only put 1 item in the auction house, the item takes a random time between 30 minutes and 2 hours to appear on the market, after you sell it there's 30% tax, and you need to wait over 2 days to retrieve silver from the market! If you have a token, you can put up 5 items at a time and the tax is reduced to 10%. There is another limitation to the market - the price at which you try to sell your item is adjusted by the system and there's nothing you can do about it.
4) IMC (game developer and publisher) did all of the trade/market restrictions supposedly to fight the RMT traders (goldsellers). It did absolutely nothing. Goldsellers are still littering the game. The real reason behind those changes was to force players to spend 18$ a month on a token.
5) As a result of the above, the market is a joke. If you enjoy a healthy marketplace, that's not what you'll find here. Playing the market to earn money is barely profitable because of the market's flaws. The market is bugged and can be exploited by malicious players.
6) You can't create a guild until you have reached rank 7, which is nearly the level cap of 280. For the whole game you can't be in a guild.
7) This game destroys the social aspects of interacting with other players. I'll make a short list:
a) When you make a party, you expect to be able to choose basic loot options. Not in this game. You can only choose Round Robin, Random or Pick-Up. If you play with random people, you can't trust them enough to have pick-up option enabled, because one of them will most likely steal all the loot. There is no class-restriction when looting, no dice-roll system, no greed/need system, no bid system like in B&S. Pray to RNJesus that you get the drops that you need.
b) When you're leveling with a friend, you can't trade without a Token. Even if you buy that, you will be restricted to 30 trades per month. You'll run out of this limit in a week of playing together.
c) Market has so many limitations, it destroys the idea of healthy and vibrant economy. In this game, you'll think twice before putting anything on sale.
d) All the leveling/questing is easily soloable. An MMORPG is supposed to be a multiplayer game, where people feel the need to party up to clear the hard content. Here, the only times you'll need a party is for dungeons or for grinding spots that are heavily contested for.
e) The mob population is too small, there are not enough mobs for everyone on the map. There are not enough channels to accomodate all people. The spawn timer is between 2-5 minutes for almost all mobs! So 80% of the time, instead of fighting, you'll be running around trying to find mobs to kill.
f) Dungeons have a limit entry of 2 times per day. And this limit entry is shared between all dungeons. So, if you do dungeon A 2 times today, you can't enter dungeon B or C. If you have a token, that's 3 entries per day.
g) You can't queue to a dungeon if you're in a party. If you enter a dungeon in a pre-made party, you only get 450% exp bonus. If you queue solo, you get 600% bonus. You either go with people you know and get punished for that, or you queue with random people who probably have no idea how to play.
f) Same thing with PvP - you can't queue if you made a premade party. Want to play PvP together with a friend? Sorry, you can't.
8) The game is, not very advanced in terms of graphical effects and shouldn't be very demanding on your PC. At least in theory. You'll need a high-end PC to enjoy a framerate exceeding 50 fps.
9) You will be getting random screen stuttering all the time. If you play in a party, sound begins to stutter when 5 people are hitting one boss at the same time. It's painful to hear.
10) Dungeons give way too much exp. Consequently, many players will just do their daily runs and log off because grinding on the fields isn't very efficient exp-wise.
11) The issues with lag/latency/server instability are very bad. I've played many MMORPG in the past, some of them right from day 1, but never experienced something like this. On the first day, the only way to login was to select a server, click "Enter" button, then patiently wait for 2-3 minutes to log in. If during that time, you clicked "Enter" button again, you are put right at the end of the queue. There was no way of figuring it out that you're supposed to wait patiently for 2-3 minutes to log in. Most players would just assume that the login is broken and keep clicking on the "Enter" button every few seconds.
If you managed to log in, there were queues everywhere, that could take up to 2 hours or more. It persisted for more than 2 days. The lag during combat was tolerable. But, the lag manifests if you want to talk to NPCs or use an item. You can't even pick-up drops from mobs instantly, it takes over 10 seconds for them to be picked up. When walking around, you will be randomly teleported back because of the server issues.
12) There is little to none communication with IMC or their Staff. They don't respond to people constantly complaining about the problems I mention in this review. Some of those problems have existed in the game since the first closed beta, but still weren't fixed. Some of the quests, mobs and NPCs are bugged since over 6 months ago, and guess what? It's never been fixed.
13) The game is tending towards being a cash-grab product. You are blocked from basic functions like trading with other players if you don't pay. In KR, you need to spend TP (real-cash currency) to list items in the auction house. Buying a hair costume costs 20$. You can't trade items between your main and alts unless you have a Token. There is already P2W item in the shop that gives random stat bonuses to accessories, and this game was just recently released. Despite the players' reaction in KR and overseas, they will probably keep bringing more P2W items in the future.
14) The cash shop is a big joke. First of all, there is no global chat in this game. The only way is if you use a megaphone, which costs TP to buy. You get 5 free TP to use each day, and one megaphone costs 1-2 TP, so you can use some for free. But it's not nearly enough if you're a market person, and you will be forced to spend real money just to communicate with players.
There are not enough cosmetic items in the shop, and they're way overpriced. If you're a Wizard, there's only one costume you can buy. Costumes are class-restricted. There are only 6 costumes in total right now. The hair costumes are overpriced, and it costs way more to buy a female hair than male hair, which is a ridiculous cash grab.

I really want to recommend this game (This is supposed to be the actual 'successor' to Ragnarok Online, which I played back in early 2000), but in it's current state, I really can't recommend it.
1.  Lag.  The lag is awful and I don't think it'll get any better once the game gets out of the 'month early access'.  It'll only get worse.  Not to mention when I played earlier, channels were crashing, leaving a lot of players to go to 3 channels.  I ended up logging out because getting any quests done was next to impossible.
2.  F2P players are at a disadvantage.  You can't do trades unless you have the 'subscription' aka token active.  Like really????  Trading is a basic feature in nearly every mmo!  Account wide storage is also behind this wall, which can be a real pain if you're playing more than 2 classes.  You get extra speed too, which is useful, but this could be a problem in PvP down the line.
3.  Shoutting gold spam.  Every night I come on, I have to block the wall of gold spam.  It wouldn't be bad if the chat wouldn't lag the game.  ~_~  At this point, just turn shouts off.
4.  Quests are boring.  Very generic quests, but how many ways can you make kill -insert mob here- interesting?  Also, make sure you cover every base on a map, quest NPCs are not marked, so you have to watch for a npc anc click on them to see if it's a quest.  Can miss out on exp because you're not combing every corner of the map.
5.  Research is a must.  Before you play, I would highly suggest you goggle the game and see what builds are recommended.  Granted, there's a skill/stat reset, but you might save yourself money/time by doing some research yourself.
6.  Some bugs.  I came across 2 quests I could not complete.  Both of them, I could not interact with the object I needed to interact with.
7.  Combat is rather boring.  As a cleric, I lay down heal, lure monsters in to attack them, and if the monsters are 'floaty', I have to bash it to death with my mace.  Rinse and repeat.  I'm hoping there's more involved at later levels, but so far, I'm not impressed.
The good about this game?  It's a very pretty looking game and the music is there.  But as they say, graphics cannot save mediorc gameplay.
Could this be a good game?  Yeah, with some polish, it could very well be a good mmo.  But in it's current state?  I don't see myself playing it long term.  I might use as much as I can on the token I used and just move on to something else if nothing comes.

The guns are randomly generated by any enemy that drops it (which is pretty much every enemy, given that each gun has a droprate of sorts), and there are a TON of copies of the same gun that can turn the gun upside-down. Even if it's the LITTLEST change in the name, it still gives the gun a different setting.
Challenge? Bring it!: It's expected from an RPG to bring challenge. You have a leveling system. ...That's kinda obvious, right? If not: It determines your strength and survival. So don't rush through the story, and grab some friends to speed-up the leveling. Otherwise, you're gonna take a long time leveling. Yup. :/
WHO'S THE BOSS NOW?!?!: Good lord, the bosses can be INSANE! ...I mean, OK, in my opinion, some of the bosses are mini-bosses or tutorial bosses. These include pretty much the first three bosses (Knuckle Dragger, Boom and his brother Bewm and Captain Flint). But HOLY ♥♥♥♥, you are wrong when you think you were done with the final boss! There are Raid Bosses, and as per usual with raid bosses, you're going to need some friends. But what if I told you...that when friends join your game, that the game itself gets more difficult too? PLUS, you get an extremely higher chance of finding epic loot from enemies with friends tagging along your adventure!
*panting* Jeezus, I've been talking a lot about the game...alright, better sum it up with the weapons again.
The guns (and items) can get ♥♥♥♥ing INSANE! ESPECIALLY the legendaries (or some other guns)! They have their special stats in a red-flavor-text, which sometimes is a reference! For example, we have (this list is by the names of the guns):
Hellfire: An SMG that burns your target into crisps...in SECONDS!
Florentine (DLC restricted): An SMG that fires Slag (lowers target's armor) and Shock (deals extra damage to shields)!
Conference Call: A shotgun whos shots SPLIT into the right and left directions, basically creating a moving crossfire!
Pitchfork: A sniper rifle that shoots 5 bullets in a vertical line! And the barrel looks like it can shoot only 1!
Butcher (DLC restricted): A shotgun that fires rapidly with an automatic trigger! The fun part? It slightly regens ammo in your magazine as long as you hold the trigger down!
Gunerang (Maybe DLC restricted, Idunno): Before I can tell more about it, I shoud probably tell about Tediore, the company that made the pistol.
Basically, Tediore makes guns that act like grenades when you reload. The more bullets are left in the mag, the more damage the reload does.
OK, now the Gunerang. It returns to you when you reload it...which is gonna hurt, I can promise you that.
Infinity: A pistol with 1 bullet in the chamber....AND IT NEVER RUNS OUT!!!
The Sham: A shield with the highest chance to absord bullets (those types of shields return those bullets to your ammo capacity)!
The Bane: A blue-rated SMG that is OP!-Yet it is annoying since it screams out of its lungs, and it slows you down to a super slow crawl. ..But it's pretty powerfull. x3
And that's all I can remember. But there's SO much more, and no weapon is EVER the same!
TL:DR=I fangasm too much about this game, alright? I'll just give it a PERSONAL 10/10. OK? It's my thought about it. No need to♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants and scream at me.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Shadow of Chernobyl is a post-apocalyptic open world classic game with a cult following. Even though it was released in 2007 it has a very mod-friendly engine and the best fan base ever. After 10 years of existence, the game is still alive and well thanks to a great fan/mod community dedicated to it. As the game is kind of ancient today, it is recommended to play it through some mods (which make the game look extremely contemporary). It remains one of the most atmospheric games ever made, and many mods that enhance the game graphically (and in various different ways) only boost the game's largest strength - the open world, weapons arsenal, funny glitches (the game wouldn't be the same without some ridiculous vanilla game bugs/cheeky dialogues, of which many are fixed in mods unfortunately). My personal favorite is the Autumn Aurora 2.1 mod.
Out of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. trilogy, Shadow of Chernobyl remains a fan favorite, mainly due to it's story, locations, and mystery being in the Zone for the first time. The story is not revolutionary, but there are a few twists, and a reveal at the end is not underwhelming - it is a very interesting concept, that doesn't leave all question answered, nor does it raise questions that challenge logic behind the plot.
