After beating Broforce for the second time since I bought it maybe a year ago, I'm ready to review this thing. Spoiler free.
I'll be dividing this review into 3 sections: Pros, Notes, and Cons. Pros are what people could generally agree would be good for what this game wants to be, Notes are things that people may like or dislike based on preference, and Cons are what people would generally agree are bad in a game. Most of the reviews here are jokes or memes, so I'm gonna give a real one. Let's get right into it while I'm still pumped up by the ending of this game!
Pros:
- AWESOME, Dynamic Gameplay! : The controls are smooth and once you get used to them, it plays like a dream. The cast of bros and enemies are diverse enough to keep you wanting more interaction with them throughout the game. The destructable terrain makes leaping away from exploding enemies, throwing them over a ledge into enemies below, or blasting holes in walls and pulping everyone on the other side all the more satisfying. The carefully placed explosive barrels and tanks also create some extremely epic chain explosions, and some crazy and HILARIOUS chain reactions can happen naturally that the developers didn't even script in there. Finally, if things are about to get crazy, you can high-five your fellow bro at any time to get a few moments of slow motion!
- It started in Early Access, and actually escaped it! Not only that, but it escaped it in a state so awesome that no one could have expected it after all the other games that failed through EA. I must admit that I pirated a really early version of the game, but I enjoyed it so much that I felt guilty for stealing it and bought it (I never pirated again, by the way). When I got the full version, I was expecting some extra levels similar to the ones early in the game, and that's about it. However, what I got was a much more polished game, WAY more levels, and a complete 80's - 90's action movie story with no depth at all, featuring generic terrorists, explosions for no real reason, blood, destruction, and American arrogance and stereotypes on steroids! The developers knew that the formula from early on in the game would get old, too, so they kick it up a few notches toward the middle by COMPLETELY changing the threat, and build it up toward a massive grand ending that could not be any more epic even if they
.
- FULL CONTROLLER SUPPORT!!! WITH VIBRATIONS!!!! : I rarely use controllers to play games on my PC (actually I never do unless I'm playing a local multiplayer game with my brother), but after playing this locally with him, and feeling the vibration support, I haven't played without one since. After you get used to it, I'd say it plays even better with a controller.
- The graphics are amazing, and this is a game I could point to for excellence in graphics in the indie genre. This game is also solid proof that a game doesn't need to have modern graphics to have good graphics. From the pixel art in-game, to the drawings on the cut scenes, the art in this game looks so great that I forget I'm looking at pixel art. On top of that, they threw in some post-processing effects so you're not just staring at sprites the whole game. On top of that, there are subtle things like trees shaking in the background from explosions or bullets flying past them that make the game's universe solid and believable. The animations and the way they make things look like they're 3D/rotating makes this art some of the best I've seen in all games with a pixel art style. Period. That's saying something, because I own a lot of games with pixel art.
- The sounds are clear, well mixed, and are always appropriate for whatever's happening in the game. Apparently, they hired a professional sound designer to remaster some of the sounds in the game awhile back, and the quality shows.
- ALL THE MULTIPLAYER AND GAMEMODES YOU COULD EVER WANT. Local, Online, and Online + Local. You can play several gamemodes including the campaign all with up to 4 players. Just playing singleplayer can be crazy, and two can be complete chaos, so I can only imagine what a 4-player experience is like... I think I played it once but I don't remember it. Must've blacked out lol.
- This game is more than just a dumb mindless action game. It's clear how much effort and attention was put into this game to make a full experience.
- More "HOLY ****!!!!" moments (ranging from things created by the developers to experiences that just happened as I was playing) than I could put in an entire seperate review without exceeding the character limit. I'd advise you not to look at IGN's reviews or too many other reviews on Steam. Just dive in head-first with some buddies.
- Even if you don't like some of the content, or you've completed it all, the developers have given you the very level editor they've used to make their levels directly in-game (hooray for not having to be forced to visit the developers' website...). I don't know how easy it is to use, but it should be alright considering how many maps and campaigns are being made all the time. (EDIT: I have used the editor since the time of writing this review and it is solid, and relatively easy to learn and use.) Once you open up the level maker, you can make a few and assemble them into a campaign, or download other people's creations from the workshop from directly in-game!
- WORKSHOP SUPPORT!!!
Notes:
- Levels can sometimes be very challenging, and you might be restarting a lot to the point of desperation. So there IS challenge in this game, but it begins toward the middle.
- Levels can be incredibly short. Like... from 1 - 3 minutes short with a single player, so again, I can only imagine what it's like with 4 players.
- Loading times can be kind of long, say, maybe 30 seconds to a minute. However, to be honest I don't have a gaming computer, so you guys out there with powerful rigs should be fine. As a trade-off they load a bunch of levels at once (every level in the game's "zones") so the transition between them is almost instant. This can be based on preference I guess. Some people like to have the wait divided evenly, but I enjoy sacrificing some time before so my immersion isn't disturbed too much between levels.
Cons:
- If you've made it this far without purchasing the game, I'm disappointed in you. THERE ARE NO CONS UNLESS YOU COUNT THE ONE BUG I EXPERIENCED ONCE BUT NEVER SAW AGAIN. PURCHASE THIS GAME!!!
The Verdict:
Broforce is a fresh experience with great graphics, audio, and gameplay. More than just a dumb 90's action movie style game, Broforce is an example of AAA quality from an Indie team of developers. Its campaign is great, and with several other modes, a built-in level editor, and full workshop support, there's more than enough here to keep you coming back for more.

Okay, I just want to make something very clear before I put various long sections containing different opinions compared to different games and different styles, etc. I don't really play this game incredibly often, but when I do, I generally play 3-4 hours at a time before calling it quits. I know it say's I only have 0.1 hrs on record, but the steam version of the game did not work for some reason so I had to download it directly from the Hi-Rez Studios Website. I'd say I have about 200ish hours invested in the game, as well as a fair amount of money.
For a TL:DR of whole post, see Sect. 6 at the end.
Here is a quick table of contents, as I'll have several sections in this review. There will be a short TL;DR at the beginning of the long sections.
Sect. 1 : First Impressions and Progression
Sect. 2 : MOBA Comparison
Sect. 3 : RPG Comparison
Sect. 4 : Graphics/Environment/Sound/Etc.
Sect. 5 : Gameplay / Balance
Sect. 6 : Overall Rating
Section 1: First Impressions and Progression
TL;DR - First impressions were okay, the PvE was very fun and immersive, however the transition to PvP wasn't very good (possible matchmaking flaws). The prices of gods aren't proportioned to their difficulty, making it difficult for players new to Smite or new to MOBAs.
When I first played Smite roughly 2-3 years ago, I was coming out of my first year in MOBA games, specifically League of Legends. I had become a MOBA fan over that time, and also really enjoyed playing MMORPGs such as World of Warcraft  and Elsword. Naturally, when I saw there was an RPG-view MOBA, I was totally psyched. I went into the game, and the initial impressions were good. The graphics and sounds were great, even on my mediocre-ish PC (I have since upgraded, and this game looks/sounds amazing, but more on that later). The PvE run at the very beginning of the game was definately fun, exciting, new, and immersive. In League, I was just rolling with the punches, but when I transitioned to Smite, I felt like I had a whole new level of gameplay I had to think about due to opaque vertical surroundings. Overall, the PvE at the beginning was great. However, unlike League, the transition to PvP was just cruel and unusual punishment. I'm not sure if the smite smurfing community is big or not, but it certainly did feel like it was. League takes a while to get used to. Not necessarily because of a skill curve but more because of a knowledge and champion (character) curve. It probably took me a good 25 hours (roughly 40-50 matches) of league before I got the hang of things. Smite, however, took at least double that. Past all of that, however, the progression was alright. I feel like the match rewards are a lot smaller than they should be. In league (sorry for drying out this comparison) it takes anywhere between 10-80 games to get enough of the free in-game currency to buy a champion. The reason this gap is so large is because of the price of the champions. In general, the easier ones are cheaper, and the harder ones are more expensive. This is done so newer players arent forced to overcome a huge skill curve when they first start playing. Smite, however, seems to have their difficulty spectrum sprinkled throughout the price curves. This is somewhat remedied by the rent system, but not to the extent it needs to be. At least 60% of the Gods with any appeal to novices and newbies alike are located in the upper half of the price range, which means you have to either overcome a huge skill curve to expand your playable god pool or play the free to play and starter gods nonstop until you can purchase the more expensive gods. This being said however, it is a hell of a lot easier to pick a God in smite and spam them until your a god (haha XD) at them than it is in league, and the time it takes to adapt to harder gods isn't too long for veteran MOBA players. I'd say that this game isn't very appealing to players new to the concept of MOBAs, but if you have experience in games like League or DOTA, this game has an okay tutorial and progression system. As a side note, if you are a veteran to Overwatch-esque FPS games, you will find it incredibly easy to transition to this game.
Section 2 : MOBA Comparison
The transition from other classic MOBA games like League and DOTA can be quite difficult, but if youre a veteran to these games, it is a bit easier to transition from your starting pool of gods to a larger one. Also, the skill curve is very rewarding. Becoming very good at Gods like Nu Wa can be compared to having mastery of champions like LeBlanc or Lee Sin in League.
Section 3 : RPG Comparison
One of the main reasons I started this game was because of the RPG view. Surprisingly, I found my affinity of World of Warcraft quite helpful to transition into this game. Fast reaction times, skill/cooldown management, and combo knowledge all go a long way to becoming a veteran Smite player and having an enjoyable experience.
Section 4 : Graphics, Environment, and Sound (etc...)
TL;DR - Good graphics on low quality, STUNNING graphics when on high quality. Good sound effects, slightly annoying music.
The graphics on this game were pretty good for my PC specs at the time I started. My computer only had 4gb of DDR3 RAM, so needless to say, I had to run this game on low graphics. Even on the low setting however, the game quality was still impressive. When I upgraded to a custom-built gaming PC with an Nvidia GTX 740 GeForce (2gb RAM) graphics card and 16gb of DDR4 RAM, I was able to run this game at 80 FPS on max graphics, and I can tell you, this game is BEAUTIFUL. The environment has an uncanny amount of detail that I can only compare to the likes of console RPGs like Skyrim and Fallout. It was truly stunning to look at. It was so stunning that I almost couldn't focus on the match. The sound is pretty good. The music gets kind of annoying after a while. personally, I prefer to mute the game music and play my own. The sound effects however are another story. I have fairly expensive studio headphones that I use on a day-to-day basis, as I play and record instrumental music. The quality of the sound effects is very good, and even has some surround-sound effects for higher-end listening devices. Overall, very good graphics and sound.
Section 5 : Gameplay & Balance
TL;DR - Typical MOBA Balance. Certain gods counter others, but skill counters all gods.
The TL;DR says it all. The one area in which I feel SMITE heavily surpasses league is in the balance department. Hi-Rez Studios is very good about not making changes to Gods that already exist in order to provoke "meta" changes. Not to mention, there is never one certain meta that 100% dominates another. Right now in late season 6 of League of Legends, bruiser (tank/damage hybrid) solo laners are completely dominant. No jungle, mid, carry, or support champion could ever change that unless they had their stats adjusted by Riot. The same cannot be said for league, however, as I feel there is no one type of champion that flat out dominates all others. This makes mastering a certain type of god extremely rewarding, because they don't have extra barriers to overcome in oder to become relevant. Like I said in the TL;DR, certain gods kind of counter others, considering both players are exactly even in skill. However, a good player can counter any god on any god.
Section 6 : Overall Rating
Rating : 8.5 / 10
Overall, I highly reccomend this game to any veteran to the MOBA genre or overwatch-esque games. The skill curve is very fun and rewarding. However I would not reccommend this game if you are new to MOBA games, as it can take a long time to adjust to the nature of this specific game. I would also recommend having a mouse with extra buttons, because having skills on 1-4 can lag reaction times. Good game, just not for everyone.

This game has had pretty mixed reception, most Sonic fans tend to like it but most critics have been quite harsh. To me, this seems to have been due to people expecting Generations 2 and were just put off by anything else that isn't that. Sonic Forces is not Generations 2, if anything it feels more like Generations combined with Lost World. It's different but it works.
The custom avatar aspect was something I never really cared for, that is until I played the game. I spent a lot mroe time than I thought I would with the avatars in this game. It was a feature that I planned on trying to ignore but ended up spending quite a bit of time with customising my various avatars.
While some dismiss the story and label the new antagonist "edgy" I felt it was quite good. It's not an amazing story and is pretty typical for a Sonic game but I like Infinite and how the Phantom Ruby ties in to Sonic Mania's story too.
The graphics are great, there are some really cool cinematic moments and the environemnts are full of detail. The music does really well to complement the style of the game, 'Fist Bump' is a song that you can't help but sing along to as you double boost with Sonic. There are plenty of other great songs in the game, the Classic Sonic stage music had its moments but I wouldn't consider them the best songs in the game.
The Classic Sonic levels in general felt like a let down to me. While you do have Mania's drop dash, you don't have that same sense of speed and control. Classic Sonic feels heavy and doesn't maintain his momentum, some platforming over small gaps can be difficult as the controls don't feel very tight. While I didn't hate the Classic Sonic levels, they would have to be my least favourite levels in the game.
The Modern Sonic levels are by far my favourite ones in the game. The lack of drifting is disappointing but the same sense of speed from past boost Sonic games is here. Some levels will transition between 2D and 3D which I feel worked pretty well and added some extra variation to the levels; although perhaps less 2D would have been better. Avatar levels tend to have a similar layout to Modern Sonic levels but feature a variety of wisps that can be used to access new paths to find rings or collectibles.
While there have been many complaints that the levels and the game itself is too short, it offers enough replayability to give you your money's worth. Completing missions (including daily missions), competing on the leaderboards, collecting the collectible items (red star rings, number rings, silver moon rings) and testing out your avatar's wispons/clothing. I have replayed the levels many times now and still have quite a few things left to complete (at the time of writing this review I have 24.6 hours in the game).
It's not a perfect game but I don't feel the harsh critical reception it has received is deserved. It's overall a really enjoyable experience that still has plenty more challenges to offer me.

Okay, here comes a "Mania-hype-free" / neutral, short review of Sonic Forces.
IMPORTANT: I will rate this on a 1-100 scale
but instead really does just mean mediocre.
Keep that in mind.
It's definitely a damn pretty game, and while the locales' aestehtics are largely (not entirely) reused from older games, there's no denying they look really good. The screen can get a bit
busy at times with them pretty effects though, which keeps me from giving an even higher rating in this category.
A mixed bag. In terms of music, the game is a sort of wild mix of great tracks and pretty mediocre ones, with enjoyable voice acting and good sound effects - hence why this lands right in the middle between 50 and 100.
Just a flat "good" here with nothing special to say about it. Nothing spectacular, but it keeps you entertained along the way.
There have been longer Sonic games with more variety, yes, but Forces is by no means bad in this regard. Let's say it checks a box - it provides enough content to satisfy, but doesn't go above and beyond in this regard.
This is the one that I imagine will have people split between giving my review a shrug-nod or saying I'm full of sh*t. I admit, due to what I was used to from Generations, I had some trouble getting used to the increased floatiness of Modern Sonic and the Avatar, and the increased heaviness of Classic Sonic. And yes, it's definitely not without issues - some levels are a bit too simple in design, and specifically the Avatar can feel too floaty in 2D segments.
But overall, after getting past that and getting used to the way this game handles and plays, and leaving aside any comparisons to Generations or "hype residue" from Mania, I find myself definitely enjoying this game.
The more I play the game and get over my habits from Generations, the more I find myself warming up to it, and the more do I find that a lot of what I originally deemed "problematic" is actually just my Generations habits netting me hits and deaths.
Thus, I adjusted the category score to 80 to reflect my changed opinion.
While there are levels that can feel a bit "flat", I did notice while playing that there are actually many levels with plenty of alternative paths that I just straight-up didn't notice at first. And trying these out, and also trying out all the various equippable attack moves and special abilities for the Avatar, makes sure to check a box here. Again, not as replayable as some past Sonic games (particularly 3 & Knuckles, Generations and Mania, which are nigh endlessly replayable), but completely fine.
The overall result leaves me giving this game a
77 - which, for the record, means
And that, I feel, is the most accurate statement one can make about this game, and sadly also what hurts this game the most - it's not outstanding, but it's not one of the bad ones either. It's simply a fun, good Sonic game.
But considering the expectations set due to it going back to Generations' gameplay style and due to Sonic Mania being so otherworldly amazing, "just being good" probably hurts this game more than "being bad" would have.
People expected this to be for 3D Sonic what Sonic Mania (a game I'd wholeheartedly give a 97/100) became to 2D Sonic - but instead of a game like that to celebrate, or a really bad game to be angry at, they got a game that's "just good", giving way to a sense of disappointment.
And while I
go in with such expectations and thus find myself enjoying the game a lot, uninhibited... I can at least understand how some other people feel, and where these really bad, sour reviews come from.
Because, as we all know, being disappointed can feel far worse than being angry.
So to those who had really high expectations and wanna just hate this game -
And those who appreciate it for what it is and are angry at the bad reviews -

But there seems to be a portion of players who do experience issues, so I suggest googling around a bit for that before buying.

(Before I start, I'm going to mention level names here, but aside from that, it should be spoiler free.)
This game is one of those that the longer you look at it, there's more to like, and also more to dislike.
At first glance, a lot of the levels are rather linear and you can pretty much finish them by going full speed ahead into the course. After watching a few YouTube videos though, I'm actually quite surprised how intricate some of them get - I had no idea about being able to slide under a number of platforms in modern Sonic's Network Junction stage which opens up whole new avenues of paths, nor did I realise how wide Mortar Canyon can get with its diverging path, not to mention how sheer fun these can be to try and speedrun. Metropolitan Highway is equally both stunning and downright fun, though aside from the first section, seems to be rather single path.
Some of them are still fairly linear, but usually these are the traditional tutorial levels, your Stage 1s and the like. They tend to have a few paths, but often they're not terribly deep, so you more or less end up doing a largely similar run. Their main problem always tends to be one thing, and it's a pretty big thing... automation.
In removing some of Sonic's moves (such as his drift), the Forces team instead throw him into some slightly annoying automated sections that remove control from you - if you're boosting through the stage, these are pretty obvious, since the boost doesn't even continue through these sections... and they really ruin the experience. There's tons of gameplay outside of these sections, but because of how frequent they can be in some stages, it can begin to feel like you're just watching Sonic or the Avatar play the game themselves.
Speaking of, the Avatar is actually a really cool addition. Cosmetic items are a great way to offer players some challenges to do in order to unlock them, and they're genuinely pretty fun to play, when done right. Their stages can suffer from a lot of the same problems Sonic's does - the hookshot is a cool mechanic, but often feels to pad out the experience by twirling around objects at a mediocre speed, rather than offer a path for those without the Wispon for another optional, often quicker (or higher score generating) path.
Tag-Team stages put the Avatar and modern Sonic together, and depending on the stage, these can either be really cool or interesting (Null Space), or feeling like they wasted an interesting stretch of gameplay (Arsenal Pyramid). Often, this helps remedy the feeling of Sonic's movesets being stripped down, as it gives you the ability to use the Avatar's hookshot and Wispons. Arsenal Pyramid could have had some interesting multiple paths to ascend the pyramid itself before phase two of the stage, which I largely have no real major qualms with other than it definitely favours certain Wispons and offers no alternative for others. I also wish there were more jumps like the first one in this stage in the game, where you can choose to hookshot out and swapping to the Avatar, or stick with modern Sonic in the lead with a lower path.
Which... this game seems to leave you feeling a lot. There's a bunch of mechanics that just seem to exist once and are never touched on again. For example, Avatar has a single stage in which wall jumping is used, and modders have found Sonic has this ability too, except with nowhere to use it. Sonic's slide is used in two stages, with his wallrun being used on a final path at the end of Lost Valley. If we count Episode Shadow, Shadow's multi-hit homing attack is only used on two of those stages, and never turns up in the stages he can play of the main game. There was a real opportunity to let Shadow have a unique move that offered alternate pathways in the main stages, but... nope.
I should talk some about Classic Sonic too, but he feels so tertiary to the experience (and honestly, also a bit awkward and broken to play) that it's hardly worth talking much about him. His stages are... okay. They're not wholly bad, but not great, either. There's a couple of neat sections, such as a reimagined Chemical Plant stage in 3D, but the way he moves and controls just feels off. Modern Sonic and the Avatar never really have a point in which they feel to control badly, just automated, but Classic definitely got the short end of the stick here. All he does is tie this game in with Mania, but really, they could have left him out and had the story still revolve around the Phantom Ruby, and all would still have been fine.
The sum total of all these gameplay comments make it feel like a really good building block for what *could* make a great Sonic game. It's a lot of steps in the right direction, but there's just no room for the player to utilise any of the potential within it, which is frustrating in and of itself. The removal of some of Sonic's moves and the automation that replaced it add to this feeling of what could have happened, and while we do have some stages that feel great to play after going through them a few times and learning them, should that be something to celebrate? Surely, a stage that feels great on the first run, then can be appreciated further on subsequent ones, would be much better than stages we outright learn to enjoy.
Gameplay aside, there's a decent story. I quite like the more Sunday morning cartoon vibe from this, it suits Sonic better than the grim and underacted type the Adventure games did, but I do feel that some corners were cut to make it fit around the limited number of stages. There's a whole piece of soundtrack that's heard for a grand total of five seconds in the Red Gate Bridge stage, fighting for time to air between a QTE and a boss fight, for example, which only makes me think that there was originally going to be a full stage fitted around these sections. The story is told between cutscenes and in-game radio calls, which are pretty well written and delivered quite nicely. (Don't worry, you can turn off the radio in the options menu if you'd like to experience the stages without the plot happening there, too.)
All in all, it's a *weird* game. I personally enjoyed this thoroughly - I've gotten plenty of time out of the collectibles and just general running through the stages again to experience them... but I can't deny that this feels like a half-baked product. Single-use features and a frustrating feeling of loss of control seep through a portion of the stages, but the ones that tickle that itch for frenetic and varied gameplay can really make this game shine. It's just a pity they're somewhat hidden.

I want to start by saying that though I only have a few hours logged on this version, I played the Xbox One version extensively upon release, so I do have a lot of experience with this title.  I also want to say that I am a huge fan of both Alien and Aliens, and that because of my fandom, I held this game to incredibly high standards.
Alien:  Isolation is amazing.  This is by far the best Alien game ever made, which sadly, isn't saying much.  I remember being nine years old watching my much older brother playing Resident Evil 2.  I remember the fear that game put into me through use of the atmosphere, the environment, and the enemies themselves.  This is the first game in all of those years that has not only replicated that fear, but trounced it.
You are Amanda Ripley, Ellen Ripley's daughter.  Your mother has been missing for years and you are given hope when the flight recorder of the missing Nostromo is found being held on the Sevastapool, a space station set for dismantling.  Naturally our protagonist heads off to the Sevastapool in an attempt to finally find some closure on what happened to her mother.
The game is terrifying.  That can not be understated.  The Sevastapool itself is menacing, and from the first moments of Ripley's arrival it is obvious that there is more going on than a mere decommission.  The environment breeds in you a sense of dread, the eerie silence broken up only partially by bumps and bangs, the music ramping up during moments of tension.  Before the titular antagonist is even introduced you find the tension ramping.  When playing this game I feel like my nerves are on fire.  Everything about the game is created to instill this sense of dread, and it does so perfectly.  As Ripley you are no soldier, you aren't trained to fight, and this shows when wielding a gun, her hands shaking as she points it.  Not to mention that firearms are practically useless against anything other than humans, the weakest threat, and that using them inevitably brings the Alien down upon you.
Ah, the Alien.  That ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ scares the crap out of me.  Just knowing that he's around causes me to shake almost uncontrollably, my hands sweating as I grip the controller.  He's intelligent, try the same trick against him too many times and he'll figure it out, he's fast...There is no running from him.  He sees you and it's over.  And he's invincible...Watch your revolver harmlessly ping right off him.  The Alien is absolutely terrifying, but he's not alone.  The Worker Joes are scary, in their own way.  They calmly walk towards you, telling you that everything will be alright as they pummel your skull into pieces, even after you've poured an ungodly amount of ammunition into them.  Even worse?  The Worker Joes ignore the Alien, and it ignores them.  It's like the Sevastapool itself has risen up against you.
The plot is pretty good, though it drags itself out a big, and the atmosphere is amazingly true to the world that Ridley Scott created with the original movie. S.T.A.L.K.E.R - Fantastically broken.
IF YOU ONLY LIKE LINEAR/COHERENT GAMES IGNORE THIS REVIEW
S.T.A.L.K.E.R Shadow of Chernobyl is an openworld FPS-RPG very loosely based off the book Roadside Picnic by Boris and Arkady Strugatsky (good book). It tells the story of a stalker with amnesia dubbed the Nameless One on a quest to find a man known as Strelok.
I first played S.T.A.L.K.E.R in 2010. I was at a tip shop, saw a copy for 1 dollar and bought it.
I'm sad to say that I COMPLETELY missed the point of the game and hated it. I found it sluggish, bland, weird and too hard. A few years later I saw it on sale here and thought why the hell not, I'll give it a spin for five bucks, and absolutely adored it. This game still looks really good for 2007, definately better that -ugh- Fallout 3 due to its high-res textures and impressive draw distance.
THE GOOD
The randomness of the world is something praised and criticised simultaneously, but I tend to see it as a part of the appeal of this game as it lets you feel like your engagement, achievement and path are forged by you. There is a path to an objective but the path is filled with other interaction, not just Fallout 4-style fetchquests and pop-pop gun battles, though those are sadly common in sidequests. The NPCs interact with each other in interesting ways such as playing guitar at campfires, banter and passing vodka back and forth, and some of my fondest moments in S.T.A.L.K.E.R have been spent cowering around a campfire in the pitch-black night listening to mutants howl and distant gunfire from bandits. It's fantastic when stuff like this happens, and because of its random nature these times feel priceless.
THE BAD
Hoo boy, the bad. You might be surprised to hear this after my bloated paragraph of praise but holy sh!t is this game lackluster. The radiation of Chernobyl seems to have completely altered time and space in the exclusion zone because enemies while living or dead will fly into space or sink through the floor. At one point a soldier fell through the ground while alive and as I tried to see where he had gone he shot out, catapulting me into the sky, where I promptly fell to my death. Due to sh!t like this and the crushing higher difficulties S.T.A.L.K.E.R's most important key is F5. A good example of this is when you have to cross under the broken bridge to get to Garbage, and a crowd of soldiers are in your way. This section literally requires you to quicksave after every kill, as do most fights throughout the game. The more difficult mutants like
hand your♥♥♥♥♥to you on a silver platter early on, and bandits can turn shotguns into Dragunovs for no clear reason.
TL;DR
This game is REALLY GOOD, but is plagued with issues that bring down what could be an almost perfect horror/action FPS-RPG. If you can stand some issues at the beginning and like challenging games by all means buy it, but if those issues sound unbearable to you give it a miss.

Ahem, sorry.  Sacrifice is an exceptional RTS with a fun and entertaining story.  Each level you choose a god to work for.  Your wizard gets spells and units from that god that are yours to keep, so each playthrough can yield different units/spells based on your choices.  As you progress some gods will become offended and stop offering you work.
Your wizard is active on the battlefield along with your units.  Units are summoned with souls.  When friendly units die their souls can be easily recaptured by their wizard, or converted to a hostile wizard with some effort.  This caps the total number of units and makes each fight a potential boon or loss to your pool of souls.  There are a couple structures that can be built for the purpose of generating mana, defense, and movement.  These can only be placed at certain locations and require units if using for defense.
All-in-all, this is still one of the best, most unique games I've played.

So I have played ~10 hours as a "Guest", or a free player. I have not spent a cent on the game.
Here is another review I posted on the official forums, that does have some pictures:
To sum everything up...
- They are beautiful. The animation of the various animals are gorgeous. The swaying grass, the lighting, the fog, is all amazing. It looks very very good.  9/10
- The ambient sounds are great. The rushing of the wind, the brush crunching under your feet, and the breathing of your hunter after running. I do have a small gripe with animal calls. While most of the time they are directionally accurate, sometimes they aren't. And while the volume level to help distance is most of the time accurate, sometimes I will hear a call that sounds off in the distance and the animal actually isn't that far. 7/10
- Fun. I thought the whole concept of the "HunterMate" and chasing around red hemispheres would make things too easy. Wrong. It is still a challenge. This simply helps bridge the gap between the realism of spotting tracks, and the limited ability to see them in a video game on a monitor. I enjoy the active pursuit. I know there are options of using scents, lures, feeders, stands if you prefer a more passive hunting experience.  9/10
Now- for the biggest complaint I see. The pay model.
1- The game is definitely not "pay to win". The only way you can win in this game is to win competitions or score the seasons largest game on the leaderboards. As a guest, I can hunt 100% free Mule Deer and Cottontail Rabbit. These scores do count for competitive leaderboard scores. What spending money allows you to do is use different gear (that isn't going to make it any easier to hunt- just a different experience, or actually makes it tougher like a bow) and compete to hunt other animal types.
2. The game is free to play. 100% free. You can login and hunt on any of the reserves from any lodge at any time. The only animals you can shoot however are Mule Deer and Cottontail Rabbit. But guess what? You can still track and spot every animal in the game. Just because you don't own a hunting license for that species doesn't mean you can't see them. You can still level up your spotting and tracking skill for every animal in the game.
So why buy a membership?
If you want to hunt with a specific weapon type other than a bolt action rifle. Hanguns, bows, shotguns (actually- you can buy a shotgun I believe using the ingame currency you acquire by doing missions), etc.
If you want to hunt different game. If you want to specifically hunt waterfowl, bear, moose, etc then you have to pay. You can either pay specifically to hunt that animal or you can buy a membership that covers all species.
If you want to use a tree stand, tent for loading at a campsite, feeders, etc. These options do require you to pay. Since I have not paid, I can't speak to them. But I have no problem loading in early in the morning and then walking to a deer stand and waiting paitiently for a deer. You also have a call that can help lure them so you do get that.
This game is 100% not pay to win, and it is 100% not pay to play.
You can play, right now, for free. And enjoy doing it.

A disgustingly bad business model on an otherwise fantastic game..
**UPDATE!!**
I just wanted to say that I recently gave the game another go and apparently they've added a free rotation to what kinds of animals you can hunt, kind of like different FTP games like League of Legends have a free character rotation that cycles week to week on what you're allowed to use, or in this case hunt. THIS IS A STEP IN THE RIGHT DIRECTION! It certainly does not turn the game completely around, but it's a start. I'll give credit where credit is due, but the problems that were always there still remain. The problem with this free rotation is that.. if your basic free ammo or gun can't hunt that specie.. then it's pretty much useless to you. You still have to buy the correct gun and the correct ammo to be allowed to hunt it. I'm not going to change any of my review beyond this part here, as I believe it's important to maintain records like this. Some info may be slightly out of date, however. Just keep that in mind.
OLD REVIEW:
It's such a shame when you come across a fantastic game that's ruined by one of the worst payment models in any game you've ever seen. TheHunter is one of those games. What can you do for free, you ask? Well, you can hunt Mule Deer. That's it. That's all you can do. Shoot Mule Deer with one gun, one type of ammo. The default stuff you start with is all you get. It says you can also hunt Cottontail Rabbits, ah but the catch is you need to buy the correct gun to use in order to be allowed to hunt it. So, Rabbits aren't even free either.
Can you earn enough to eventually buy another gun? Only one other gun is available for purchase using the game's earned currency (called gm$). Every other gun must be bought using real world money (called em$). And that's not all.
Want the privilege to be able to hunt something else? You need to buy licenses. Doesn't sound so bad, does it? Well, they come in 1 day, 7 day, and 28 day variants. Yup, that's right. They expire. So you have to buy them multiple times to continue hunting what you want. Buy a 1 day license but then get called in to work? Congrats! You've just wasted your money! You CAN buy these with gm$, but the costs are so high that you'll be farming Mule Deer for weeks in order to finally be able to experience something else.
Oh but hold on. It's not like each kill you make earns you gm$. Hah! You wish! Nope. The only way to earn gm$ is to complete "missions" which range from tracking certain animals, spotting certain animals, and harvesting certain animals, among other similar tasks. Doesn't sound so bad, does it? Well, they typically reward only 100 gm$ for each mission, and your shotgun costs 6300 gm$, a typical 1 day license costs anywhere between 1800 - 2400 gm$. For ONE DAY, for ONE SPECIE. Let that sink in.
Would I recommend this game? Based on its business model at the time of writing? NO WAY. Stay FAR away from this cash-grab game, unless you enjoy having them grab at your pockets the moment you try their game.
Also, NEVER EVER EVER DO ANY OF THE 3RD PARTY STUFF THEY ASK YOU TO DO. You can do things like surveys, downloads, watch videos, etc. to earn some em$ (that's right, paid currency). But most of these third party "offers" infect your computer with all sorts of malware, and most of them don't end up forking over the em$ at the end. You'll be turned away from most surveys because you "aren't the target consumer". For instance, when I answered that I was a white male on a survey, I was immediately declined and turned away, reward not given.
If the payment model is improved? I would recommend this game in a heartbeat. It's fun to play, all the shady practices considered. I just wish they had gone about their payment model better than this garbage. Oh well, someone else will come along and do it right eventually.

GOOD:
Sonic forces has one of the strongest soundtracks of any sonic game I have ever played.  It's no Crush40 but man is it catchy! Honestly more than anything what makes me want to go back post story completion and keep playing it is the amazing music.  Ontop of that loot in this game is aquired through completing missions, there are no microtransactions for anything in this game which is a breath of fresh air.  The main selling point for this game is the character creator and it does not dissapoint! The best looking gear is locked behind the hardest missions, meaning there is a very real feeling of going from Zero to Hero as you play.  Though you look absolutly rediculous in the beginning stick with the game and by the time you've beaten it you'll love how your avatar looks!  Infinate also make an astounding Sonic villian.  Though he wouldn't work very well in any other francise.
BAD:
As previously stated, Infinate's pure unfiltered edge makes him a good Sonic villian, but he comes off as extremely cartoony and both he and Eggman are impossible to take seriously.  The Avatar levels are extremely clunky, and momentum is a massive issue in this game which is where most of the damage to its overall score comes from (it is a Sonic game after all).  There is also a really big issue on the Modern Sonic levels where the first several levels encourage using Boost at every opportunity, with some levels being clearable without needing to press any buttons other than your boost, but the later levels punish this severly, and the shift occurs with absolutly no warning.  Every level feels way shorter than it should be, and the hardest levels in the game aren't hard just very VERY annoying...
BULLSH*T:
WHY IS THERE NO CHAO GARDEN?! CUSTOM CHARACTERS TAKING CARE OF CHAO, THAT BY ITSELF WOULD HAVE BEEN WORTH THE PRICE!
In the end this is a game strictly for Sonic fans.  I recommend it to them exclusivly, if you're not a fan of the series this wont get you into it.  Sonic Adventures 1&2 will continue to be the apex of 3D Sonic in my eyes, but this is definetly a strong 2nd place contender.

Transistor is a very stylized and fun game with very interesting game mechanics as far as story goes you play a red a singer who was attacked by this group call the camarada or something like that for some reason which the game never really goes into detail about. Anyway her lover scarifaces himself to protect her and ends up inside of the sword (the transistor) and now you have to stop the group. For the most of the game you have use of only 4 abilities but you will get more as the game goes on and you can switch these abilites out with each other at access points. The ones you don't use can be used to augment the ones you do use by either added more range, a dot, life steal, etc. you can also increase how hard the game is by using limiters to make the enemies stronger but they will reward you with more experince. However i found that doing this wasn't all that needed as the enemies you fight vary greatly and work will together to try and stop you offering a pretty good challenge and one could see that a lot of effect when into the design of all the enemies especially the bosses. the game's turn system is also a lot of fun basically you can stop time and plan out you actions once you choose to unfreeze it your moves are carried out with great speed however doing this does put all abilities on a cd so it balances out. I only had three things i didn't really like about this game the first was the fact that i wish they had of explained things a little better for the story. After beating the game i still was a little hazy on why Red was attacked was she trying to tell people what the camarada were planning, just what are the processes ( the enemies you fight in the game) the game just left to many questions to ask at the end also i'm not sure why but for some reason the game freezes up on me for a couply of secs every now and then it returns to normal i'm sure this will be fix but it is a little werid. the last thing i didn't like about this game was i felt it was a little short now don't get me wrong i wasn't expecting a 50 hour game for $20, and it does have a new game+ mode along with challenges but it would of been nicer if they had of made it a little longer in order to tell the player more about what the hell was going on now its no where near as bad as mgs 5 ground zeros but it would of been nicer to have a little bit more play time. as for my final verdit i think this game is worth picking up however if the idea of a 5 hour game doesn't sit well with your wallet then maybe wait for a price drop or a sell.

Finished the game today after 3 gaming sessions and here is my review, as spoiler free as possible:
Story 9/10
Like in Bastion you are thrown into the middle of the events without much clue about whats happening. The story starts with a high tempo, then it just kinda threads water but finishes big. The ending is by far the best part and the only part that really had me emotionally invested. Don't give up if the story telling is too slow tho, its well worth finishing.
Characters 6/10
Its pretty hard to relate to the two main characters as you don't know or understand much of their relationship until later in the game (or at least I didnt). The main character is kinda void of a personality as well so she never really becomes relatable. The 2nd lead character is interesting though.
Narration 7/10
This might be colored by the fact that I loved the Bastion narration and this was just different, but in my opinion its not nearly as good. The story isnt told from an all-knowing story teller that explains everything we need to know, instead we follow a one-sided conversation that flows thru the entire game. This leads to the narration leading to a lot more questions and can be a little confusing.
Gameplay 7/10
Nothing amazing. The gameplay is kind of a live action / turn based hybrid which is pretty interesting, but all abilitys had a pretty big wind up and just felt generally clunky. I spend pretty much all my fighting dodging enemys until my turn-based ability came off cooldown.
Replayability 7/10
The gameplay certainly doesn't warrant a second playthrough but the New Game+ format is always fun. The story also throws you right in the middle of the events so a 2nd playthrough will make you pick up and understand a lot of things differently.
Overall 9/10
Even though the game leaves much to be desired, especially in the gameplay department, its the story that is the focus of the game and in the end its the story that is the reason why I played it. Even though the story progresses slowly it leads up to an amazing ending. Its not the most original story ever told (though the setting is pretty damn unique), but its effective. I strongly recommend this game if you play RPGs for the story.

From the creative geniuses at Supergiant Games comes Transistor, a birds-eye sci-fi RPG with a strategic twist in its gameplay functions that creates a gaming experience that is both refreshing and unique in today's video game market.
The first thing the player will notice in the game is the art-style and narrative reminiscent of Bastion; stylized environments, characters and enemies that can be instantly recognized and a story that is unveiled in little pieces through the smooth tones of the games narrator, who is actually the talking sword you're using throughout the game. Which creates a much more atmospheric effect than Bastion as the narrator is sharing in your experience instead of outlining what happens as you play.
Transistor's story is difficult to percieve at the beginning, but as the player progresses and pays attention to the narrative and ques from the world one can piece it together over time.
For the gameplay, Transistor is similar to Bastion in the birds-eye view controls and sporadic groups of enemies that have different strengths and weaknesses that you must approach in a careful manner or else you risk exposing yourself to more damage than needed. However, that is where the similarities between the two games end. Transistor uses a "Turn()" function that allows the player to pause combat in order to plan out their movements and attacks, then executing them in rapid succession, Turn() is mildly similar to the VATS system in Fallout 3, but much more unique and reactive than simply "clik on whurr u wanna shewt and hope u dunt miss". Turn() is useful for allowing yourself to punch a hole through enemy defences or to allow yourself some breathing room. However the drawback that must be taken into consideration is the short cooldown after Turn() ends, during which you are completely vulnerable as you cannot attack until the cooldown duration ends. Turn() gives players endless possibilities when combined with the notable selection of specific attacks that you are given access to, which can range from a simple energy blast to a quick dash, and even summoning a friendly unit to help you in combat (which can also be controlled during Turn()). One thing that makes the combat fast-paced and reactive are the "cells" dropped by all enemies when killed. Cells have a roughly 10 second cooldown timer when dropped, and if aren't picked up before the duration ends the enemy you just killed will respawn with full health, which in my opinion makes the combat much more dynamic and fast paced.
Another point of interest in the combat system is the power selection and upgrade system. The player gathers a good selection of abilities throughout the game, but you can only equip four at a time. Never fear, because you can take the other abilities you gathered and use them to upgrade the abilities you currently have equipped to create powerful combinations. The only thing keeping you from upgrading yourself to over-powered proportions and keeping the gameplay balanced is the memory, which will require consideration while upgrading.
Finally, instead of chugging down health regenerating items in combat like in Bastion, the player instead needs to be absolutely mindful of their current health. When your health is depleted you will automatically enter an "Emergency Turn()" that gives you the chance to eliminate the immediate threat. But once you execute the Turn() you still only have one hitpoint left, and if you get hit again during the cooldown you will return to full health but one of your abilites will be "overloaded" and cannot be used until you reach an "access point" (which not only act as save points but also are the only places where you can equip and upgrade your abilities). Esentially your abilities act as your lives, and the more you "die" at a certain area, the more difficult that area will become.
To summarize, Transistor is in my opinion much more fun than Bastion and a game I thoroughly enjoy playing. I honestly recommend Transistor to all who are reading this review.

Very quickly going up to one of my favourite games this year, Transistor is everything I could have wanted from a Supergiant Games title.
The combat is fluid and tactical and can be played in both a real-time hack-and-slash type affair or using the tactical Turn() mechanic similar to that of V.A.T.S. in the Fallout series.
The storyline is an unsurprising ride of emotion and characterisation. The character of Transistor provides a similar commentary to Rucks in Bastion but on a much more personal level.
I can't recommend this title enough, well done Supergiant and thank you for such a great title.

I really enjoyed playing Factorio, and will most likely continue to play it for some time. In general, sandbox games and other types that require you to be really creative haven’t been the most fun for me, including even Minecraft, but I seem to really enjoy the more complex and challenging types. Infinifactory is another one that I enjoyed a lot, and even though it was more a puzzle game than sandbox, it still involved creating well optimized factories and conveyor belts.
While the game is very fun and can easily last me hundreds of hours, it just feels like there’s untapped potential. This is mainly because there are no goals, except to just constantly refine how you create a factory. It even feels like an RTS at times, since there are enemies and you can make a variety of military items, but combat isn’t complex at all. While the base game wouldn’t really work, it would be nice to see a modified game mode where multiple players/AI build a base/factory more focused on combat stuff, and it plays out like an RTS would normally.

This is my favourite game of all time, and it's not just a nostalgic feeling, I still play with this masterpiece. It has a magical athmosphere you cannot find elsewhere, the story, the characters are so well written that I know nearly all quests by heart, yet I still replay them 'just one more time' when I get the mood for it.
The story is about a banished wizard, who enters a new realm of magical floating islands that are controlled by five gods, who constantly fight each other for justice, dominance or just fun. All gods control a sphere of natural energies which are earth, fire, air, life and death. You can choose one patron god on every level to do quests for them, and in return you get new spells to cast and creatures to summon from the chosen god's sphere. Keep in mind though, that if you serve the dark powers, you will soon lose the favor of the benelovent gods and vice versa, so choosing sides has limits according to your previous choices. All the gods have an interesting character that can always surprise you, as the good guys can become quite warlike, the bad guys may become just scared, the smart guys can act foolish and the simple guys quite resourceful, so everything and everyone turns out to be quite different than as they seemed at first.
The creatures in game are colourful and interesting, the spells you can control are ok first, but become quite powerful as you get more power, in the end you may summon volcanoes or tornadoes, or even death itself, depending on who you serve. The islands look like paradise or hell, depending on which god has control over them. On every stage every wizard get an altar, which serve as a base for them. Mana fountains are scattered across the island you play on, which can be occupied to get mana from it. The key element of gameplay however is the resource called 'soul', the more you have, the more powerful army you can summon. Yes, by using souls, you can summon creatures to fight, who will serve you until they die. If a creature falls, you can collect its soul again, but if the creature served another wizard before, you must sacrifice it on your altar first to get its soul, which means the enemy has a chance to prevent it. The key to victory is to desecrate the enemy wizard's altar: you may sacrifice one of your own creatures there, and if the enemy wizard dies during the ritual, you win. Oh yes, death is not permanent in the game until your altar stands, as you may easily resurrect yourself at a mana source.
To sum up things, gameplay is quite dinamic and fast, there are no slow base building elements, you just get a few mana sources, then you summon creatures, and the enemy is already upon you. This game mechanic is actually quite fun - even if it seems a bit difficult at first - it mixes roleplaying and tactical elements in a way no other game does. Voices and music are also amazing, graphics are still ok, and it is a big pro, considering that this game was published in 2000.
To cut things short, if you like decent old fantasy games that were made with devotion and enthusiasm, you must try out this one, but beware, once you get the feeling, you will never be able to stop playing it.

The first STALKER game, and the one that kicked off an amazing franchise. SOC is quite rough, but well worth playing through.
SOC is a fairly non-linear FPS with light RPG elements. RPG elements are mostly in the form of an inventory system and NPCs to converse with. Character progression is purely in the form of equipment, as you progress through the game you will find better weapons, outfits and artifacts (radioactive items that grant small defensive bonuses). There are plenty of side quests, mostly taking the form of repetitive fetch quests, but sometimes more complex.
What really sets the STALKER series apart from most games is the amazing atmosphere. The game has an extremely bleak and depressing atmosphere. The game is set in the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, and contains many real world locations that the developers painstakingly researched.
SOC has an extremely active modding community, I would highly recommend skipping the highly publicised "Complete" mod and instead playing with ZRP for your first playthrough. After a first playthrough with ZRP it might be worth trying out the Oblivion Lost or AMK mods, which make quite drastic changes to the gameplay.

This game has a lot going for it, and it's not often I get to say that of a Sonic game. Forces has a great story that's littered with goodies spanning all of Sonic's canon, including slight nods to the Archie Adventure Series. The story and narrative are delivered in a very pointed way to tell a darker, grittier, more action oriented story, and their depiction of a global conflict on (Mobius?) isn't too far off from what I would have expected from the SATam Cartoons or the comics.
The fact that the game rewards you for progression should be a major selling point these days. While the character creator doesn't have a ton of options, they make up for it in accessories. Every task rewards you with ways to customize your character and all without a single Lootbox or Microtranscation in sight.
I picked it up because I watched a reviewer state that the first level could be completed with less than 20 button presses, and my bullsh*t meter went off immediately. I've not been very lenient with Sonic over the last 15 years, but Mania and Forces are a pair of Sonic games that do well to show that it's never too late to fix a mistake. While I hold very little hope that SEGA has finally learned their lesson, I can safely say that I've enjoyed Sonic Forces so far and I look forward to finishing it. If you're looking for something that tells a serious Sonic story, without taking itself -tooooo- seriously, then give it a go. It's certainly not '06, and that's only the 2nd time I've been able to say that without sarcasm.

Once upon a time, Reign of Kings was a very promising game. After realising that they couldn't optimise their game or prevent hacking, the developers made a series of game breaking design choices that completely killed the game. It is now dead with a peak of 100 players a day, if that.
Combat is horrendous. It is possible to make your hitboxes miniscule by reducing every slider in the character creation screen, rendering you a 3' tall stick insect. If you make yourself pitch black it is very difficult to be seen in the dark. What this causes is a load of 3' tall anorexic coloured gentlemen trying to hit each other on an incredibly laggy, poorly optimised server/game. This was bad enough back in the day but after the addition of spears, the hitbox of which is about 4x that of said gentlemen, the game is virtually unplayable and definitely not fun.
The only thing the developers needed to do was prevent hacking, optimise their game, and release sporadic content updates that didn't break the game. Instead, they did nothing while hackers helped them kill their game. Instead of optimising the game or providing 'low' graphics settings, each update became more intensive, somehow. Instead of fun content we got game-breaking changes like base immunity which detracted from the dog-eat-dog nature of the medieval sandbox that players loved (and sometimes hated), but was nonetheless always thrilling.
The game was broken, people got bored of losing their work to hackers, laggy fights devoid of any skill or cognition what-so-ever, and design choices that detracted from what made the game great and left everyone who loved it incredibly frustrated.
I don't think the developers are scammers, I think they're probably just incompetent. I hope one day someone makes a similar medieval sandbox that actually delivers on its promises instead of making a mess and dodging the mop.

Finished the game today after 3 gaming sessions and here is my review, as spoiler free as possible:
Story 9/10
Like in Bastion you are thrown into the middle of the events without much clue about whats happening. The story starts with a high tempo, then it just kinda threads water but finishes big. The ending is by far the best part and the only part that really had me emotionally invested. Don't give up if the story telling is too slow tho, its well worth finishing.
Characters 6/10
Its pretty hard to relate to the two main characters as you don't know or understand much of their relationship until later in the game (or at least I didnt). The main character is kinda void of a personality as well so she never really becomes relatable. The 2nd lead character is interesting though.
Narration 7/10
This might be colored by the fact that I loved the Bastion narration and this was just different, but in my opinion its not nearly as good. The story isnt told from an all-knowing story teller that explains everything we need to know, instead we follow a one-sided conversation that flows thru the entire game. This leads to the narration leading to a lot more questions and can be a little confusing.
Gameplay 7/10
Nothing amazing. The gameplay is kind of a live action / turn based hybrid which is pretty interesting, but all abilitys had a pretty big wind up and just felt generally clunky. I spend pretty much all my fighting dodging enemys until my turn-based ability came off cooldown.
Replayability 7/10
The gameplay certainly doesn't warrant a second playthrough but the New Game+ format is always fun. The story also throws you right in the middle of the events so a 2nd playthrough will make you pick up and understand a lot of things differently.
Overall 9/10
Even though the game leaves much to be desired, especially in the gameplay department, its the story that is the focus of the game and in the end its the story that is the reason why I played it. Even though the story progresses slowly it leads up to an amazing ending. Its not the most original story ever told (though the setting is pretty damn unique), but its effective. I strongly recommend this game if you play RPGs for the story.

From the creative geniuses at Supergiant Games comes Transistor, a birds-eye sci-fi RPG with a strategic twist in its gameplay functions that creates a gaming experience that is both refreshing and unique in today's video game market.
The first thing the player will notice in the game is the art-style and narrative reminiscent of Bastion; stylized environments, characters and enemies that can be instantly recognized and a story that is unveiled in little pieces through the smooth tones of the games narrator, who is actually the talking sword you're using throughout the game. Which creates a much more atmospheric effect than Bastion as the narrator is sharing in your experience instead of outlining what happens as you play.
Transistor's story is difficult to percieve at the beginning, but as the player progresses and pays attention to the narrative and ques from the world one can piece it together over time.
For the gameplay, Transistor is similar to Bastion in the birds-eye view controls and sporadic groups of enemies that have different strengths and weaknesses that you must approach in a careful manner or else you risk exposing yourself to more damage than needed. However, that is where the similarities between the two games end. Transistor uses a "Turn()" function that allows the player to pause combat in order to plan out their movements and attacks, then executing them in rapid succession, Turn() is mildly similar to the VATS system in Fallout 3, but much more unique and reactive than simply "clik on whurr u wanna shewt and hope u dunt miss". Turn() is useful for allowing yourself to punch a hole through enemy defences or to allow yourself some breathing room. However the drawback that must be taken into consideration is the short cooldown after Turn() ends, during which you are completely vulnerable as you cannot attack until the cooldown duration ends. Turn() gives players endless possibilities when combined with the notable selection of specific attacks that you are given access to, which can range from a simple energy blast to a quick dash, and even summoning a friendly unit to help you in combat (which can also be controlled during Turn()). One thing that makes the combat fast-paced and reactive are the "cells" dropped by all enemies when killed. Cells have a roughly 10 second cooldown timer when dropped, and if aren't picked up before the duration ends the enemy you just killed will respawn with full health, which in my opinion makes the combat much more dynamic and fast paced.
Another point of interest in the combat system is the power selection and upgrade system. The player gathers a good selection of abilities throughout the game, but you can only equip four at a time. Never fear, because you can take the other abilities you gathered and use them to upgrade the abilities you currently have equipped to create powerful combinations. The only thing keeping you from upgrading yourself to over-powered proportions and keeping the gameplay balanced is the memory, which will require consideration while upgrading.
Finally, instead of chugging down health regenerating items in combat like in Bastion, the player instead needs to be absolutely mindful of their current health. When your health is depleted you will automatically enter an "Emergency Turn()" that gives you the chance to eliminate the immediate threat. But once you execute the Turn() you still only have one hitpoint left, and if you get hit again during the cooldown you will return to full health but one of your abilites will be "overloaded" and cannot be used until you reach an "access point" (which not only act as save points but also are the only places where you can equip and upgrade your abilities). Esentially your abilities act as your lives, and the more you "die" at a certain area, the more difficult that area will become.
To summarize, Transistor is in my opinion much more fun than Bastion and a game I thoroughly enjoy playing. I honestly recommend Transistor to all who are reading this review.

Very quickly going up to one of my favourite games this year, Transistor is everything I could have wanted from a Supergiant Games title.
The combat is fluid and tactical and can be played in both a real-time hack-and-slash type affair or using the tactical Turn() mechanic similar to that of V.A.T.S. in the Fallout series.

This game made me relive my childhood fears of the night and darkness. To think I wanted to hate this game during the first 30 minutes of it as it looked like the game was going to be another "epic" movie cinematic experience. I'm so glad I continued to play!
As a child I used to have nightmares about the Alien constantly for years. Ever since I saw Alien and Aliens on laser disc in the mid 90's as a small boy I was both terrified and strangly drawn to the Alien. To this day, the Alien is my favorite creature and Alien/Aliens ranks among my favorite movies ever made. This game re-captures the fears I had as a child and it's rare to be immersed in a large budget modern video game. The last game modern game I was immersed in was Dark Souls 1. Onto the review!
Gameplay: This game is a stealth game with survival/scavenger elements. This game reminds me of Thief 1 and 2 in design, where combat is greatly discouraged  (often impossible in Alien) and most of the tools the player aquires compliments the stealth gameplay. What's really fun about the stealth in this game is the depth masked by simplicity. You avoid three enemies in this game. Humans, who have long ranged weaponry or do not attack at all. Androids, who are your basic stealth enemy guard types with very simple behavoirs. Lastly, the Alien, who I will go into detail about. These three enemie types are easy and simple to deal with when you only have to deal with their type alone, but when the three start to intermingle the game becomes complex and so many choices open up on how to deal with the situations.
Most of the gameplay is centered around a cat and mouse game with the Alien, your main adversary of the game. It's an invulnerable killing machine who is fast, hard to see, and extremely hard to predict. Much of the stealth vs. the Alien comes from playing hide and go seek with the player as the hider. At first this sounds boring, just waiting for the Alien to finally do something than patrol/hunt around your location but thanks to the amazing Alien design both visually and audibly these moments are almost always tense. The Alien does not have set patterns it will follow, which keeps the game fresh and scary throughout the entire playthrough.
One aspect of the game which might turn off potential players is how slow the player character is at doing actions. Even taking a look at a computer screen takes about 4 or 5 seconds, and you can still die while doing it. I understand why these animations are long and are also in real time, it's to create fear and tension throughout the game. This also falls under the area where this game is actually punishing. Save points are spread out pretty far and death is something that you will get used to, no matter how much you don't want it to happen. One mistake is death in this game, literally.
Video: These days any game with a budget looks good. What's impressive about this game is the lighting, specifically the darks. Dark areas are pitch black, none of that dark blue nonsense. It's both realistic and frightening. The animations for the Alien are the best animations yet aside from the suits in Alien and Aliens. This game's visuals have a grim and realistic look, which complements its dark atmosphere.
Audio: This is another area this game excells at. Every sound effect works, all of them. Opening a menu, crafting, footsteps,  power generators turning on, weapon fire, you name it. They're all pleasant to listen to, and I've even made some into "text tones".
The androids must have hundreds of unique dialogues that express their stealth "mode" or "behavior", and they're all creepy. Impressive.
The Alien sound design is the best part of the audio. Not only does it have its terrifying hissing and growl noises to freak the player out, it also has very well made sound queues that add to the gameplay. Every unique action the Alien does has a unique sound effect associated with it, which allows the player to see what the Alien is doing even without actually looking at the Alien it self. Crawling through vents, stomping around the floors, getting ready to exit the vents, etc. which is exactly what a stealth game needs to great and what a horror game needs to be scary.
Overall this game is a pleasant suprise. It's one of those unique modern video games that trys something familiar (stealth) with a lot of original gameplay mechanics (mostly the Alien it self) to support it. It feels like a product of love instead of potential wealth. Play this game, you won't regret it.
