Where do I even begin?
In short: 5.5/10, just bland game.
Please read with an open mind :)
First, the Positives:
1. Music
Sure, Fist Bump (the main theme) can get a little repetitive, but the overall music was great, most of them compliments the level they were in, and the boss battle themes are spot on. Was kinda hoping Modern Sonic's stages music would put more emphasis on the guitars & rock genre feel, or orchestra like in Unleashed. Most of them are EDM inspired (for me anyway), I don't enjoy them as much as previous games' music, still great though.
2. The darker tone of the game
A (kinda) post-apocalyptic earth/mobius? Sign me up! Unlike many titles before, the overall atmosphere makes you take Eggman seriously. Plus, the creation of the background (or lore, if you prefer) was pretty good, and kinda 'Forces' you to wonder what kind of **** that Eggman has done, like when Infinite shows up with Chaos, Shadow, Metal, & Zavok. That is, before the game was released (Note: this is the premise, not the story execution).
3. Re-appearance from the most of the cast
The Sonic franchise has a lot of characters, was glad to see most of the characters are coming back and contribute within the game, although most of them are limited in few cutscenes and radio chatter, the idea itself was appreciated.
4. Custom character (Minor spoiler)
I play a lot of RPGs, and I seriously liked the customization (mostly). I liked how the character changes from the start to the end, too bad that the Avatar offer almost no dialogue. The Avatar leaves a lot to be desired, but since this was a first in a Sonic game, I can give it a pass.
5. Voice acting
The cast really does credit to their respective characters. While I do not know this is because of the directing or the VA themselves, they've done a really good job. For example: Knuckles is now serious and calmer, they do not butcher his character into a complete dumbass, but yeah, it still shows sometimes (It's fine to make Knuckles clumsy or naive at times, partly because of his isolation). Shadow, he's no longer a forced-to-be edgy character, now he's like a straight-to-the-point agent who does what needs to be done. Amy's voice is now feels more mature while keeping that "cutesy" feel. Overall, they've done a solid job.
Now for the serious (negative) parts:
1. Story execution (SPOILER!!!)
Really, the developers put many story crucial elements in dialogue boxes? on the WORLD MAP which is inaccessible apart from DELETING YOUR CURRENT SAVE? I do not mind if they put it on the levels. Heck, a longer cutscene is better. Next, they say that Sonic is supposed to be KIA in the first minutes, and that Tails has gone bonkers. While I do like the grim reality of the first cutscene, they ruined it when in the VERY NEXT dialogue box that SONIC IS ALIVE. Don't get me wrong, I know Sonic is alive, but the developers ruined the dread feel of losing a hero and a friend that is established in the first scene. That would be a great build-up in the next 2 to 4 levels of finding out that Sonic is indeed alive, and in addition help Tails come to his senses. FYI, for someone who has "Lost it", Tails seems fine, he even tried to repair Omega, which for some reason already destroyed (I'll come back to that later). For Sonic, who supposed to be tortured by Eggman, HE ACTS LIKE NOTHING HAS HAPPENED. Seriously, six months of torture would do crazy ****tor ANYONE, and I know this will never going to happen, but how the hell Eggman DID NOT KILL HIM? HE HAD SONIC FOR 6 MONTHS! For the other characters, we really never got a chance on how they got into the resistance. For some like Chaotix & Team Dark, they have no conflicting background that keep them from joining, but for Silver's cause, how does he get here? He's from the future, and why he was in the resistance in the first place? As for Knuckles, does someone watches the Master Emerald for him? and no, this was not explained in the game, and a good story should not rely on outside source to clarify plot holes. In addition: Omega was destroyed prior to the start of the game. While it was explained in Episode Shadow what exactly happened, nobody took care of Omega for 1 + 6 months! Missed potential, but not major. And did everyone forget about the chaos emeralds? Even with the phantom ruby seems to be more powerful than the emeralds, it would greatly help to have one emerald. Oh, and the phantom ruby got beat by three base form heroes, so much for the 'invurnerable ruby'. Whoa, this one was longer than I expected, maybe a little nitpicky, but whatever.
2. Controls
Why does Sonic (both Classic & Modern) feels sluggish when it comes to Jumping? I feel like I should've landed on the platform while I missed a teeny bit, It's like the character feels heavier than usual. Somehow I got the feeling they shoe-horned Classic Sonic into Forces, he feels dragged the entire game. The irony is, Shadow, while not free of the control problems, is the best character to play with. He does not drag much, his momentum were better, and he can just smash enemies better than Sonic. Lost potential: The avatar cannot switch wispons on the go. Just give the character at least three wispons that can be equipped and switched, it makes finding red star rings a chore, you cannot just find them all in one go. Worst of all, the double-jump. Sluggish & no reach. Hell, the bad jumping mechanic can be easily avoided if they used the air-dash rather than the useless double jump.
3. Level length
Too short. One to two minutes for at least for 3/4 of the entire game, painfully easy, too. Generations, while also short, at least you have to spend three to four minutes for each level (not counting speed runs). Plus, there's a lot of bonus in Generations, not so much in Forces. Unleashed day stages also have the longer length. Forces, for $40-50 or €30-40, it's too much if you ask me.
4. Level designs.
You can say one area can have many levels, like the classic games, that's fine. But, If most level looks almost exactly the same, then what's the point of having 30 levels? The most major letdown was "Null-Space". Why name the level "Null-Space" when you're actually in it only for about 10 to 20 seconds? Furthermore, the levels seems like they must be visited by every character available.
5. Wasted characters
I'm not talking about the allies, it's the enemies. I mean, why even bother putting Chaos on the teasers if we NEVER interacts with him in the actual game. Zavok & Metal, we still fight them, but Chaos? No, he got beat by Classic in a cutscene. Shadow, the fake one, kicked out by the real Shadow, Silver-style. Wasted potential boss fights with Fake Chaos & Shadow. And why Metal does not have a "VS" tag on the world map?. On a lesser note: I kinda wish the allied characters like the Chaotix or Silver, appear in some stages. We only heard them doing things on the radio. Plus, did everyone forget that Tails CAN fight? It would not hurt to show other characters doing stuff, right?
6. Un-appealing segments
Like the double boost, just leave the controller and you'll be fine. At least with the boost, you gotta control where you are going, double-boost? Mash away and just leave it. QTEs? meh, does not really care for it. Grinding? Use the drill wisp and you can just skip past those grinding segments. S.O.S missions? just another replay for the same levels, no actual replay value.
7. No save slots & extra menu.
Generations also have this issue (save slot), there's alot you can miss (DIALOGUE BOXES: plot points!) that you cannot view later. While extras may not seem too important, it would be a nice incentive to find collectibles, and I miss the music player.
Minor nitpicks:
- No Infinite's face in the DLC? (It's in the comics)
- Where's G.U.N and other humans? They didn't care?
NOTE: I am NOT saying Forces is a bad game, just.. bland at best. It can be fun, sometimes. Probably best to wait for the price to drop before buying.

Like many users, I downloaded the game, and it was buggy as hell. The cutscenes were running at 10fps and it was unplayable.  Lucky for me, "Big Picture" mode solved almost all problems. I say "almost" because Classic Sonic stages still had a little bit of choppiness, but it was still very much playable, and the cutscenes were fine.
After that annoying start, played it, beat main storyline with the Bird Avatar (my little Cinder, he's so cute!).  So what do I think of the game?
I enjoyed it. A lot! Sure the "running on rails" style gameplay isn't my favorite by any stretch (give me SA1 Sonic style anyday) but really, it wasn't all that bad. The levels are short, and I for one am very -thankful- for that. Some older Sonic games had ridiculous level lengths, while these are short and sweet, sub 3 minutes per level if you don't die. That's a good level length to me. I like speed running Sonic, because that's what Sonic is about, speed, not slogging through levels.
Out of the 3 playable characters, I liked playing as Avatar best, then Modern, the Classic (sadly classic lost points due to it being the only stages that had bad lag for some reason...). The Wispons were a neat gimmick, though some of them were terrible to use and figure out how to use. I stuck with the flamethrower myself, I liked watching things burn.
I -adored- the music.  Oh my YES I want that soundtrack! All of it was good... though, maybe take my tastes with a grain of salt, I love Sonic R's lyrical soundtrack too.
Storyline was interesting, just the right amount of cornball "taking ourselves too seriously" to have fun with it. I very much loved the characters personality tweaks, like putting Knuckles in charge, I am SO tired of seeing him played off as a doofus (looking at you, Boom). Though, I do think Twilight Sparkle might want a word with Sonic for stealing her shtick. He'd make a great "Prince of Friendship"!
So what didn't I like? Well, at times the controls were a bit unresponsive, and I found myself dying in the same spots over and over occasionally, due to no real fault of my own, as the character would just come flying off a ledge or a rail and plummet into a pit.  Enough times it was comically annoying, but not right out frustrating. The final bosses were a bit of a letdown too. I was hoping for something a little more epic, and it kinda missed the boat there.
Overall, the game is pretty easy. At no time did I find myself getting frustrated or overly annoyed. It was a fun little romp, and I do think it's one I'll keep picking at to collect all the goodies. I recommend giving it a try, it may not be totally "worth all the hype", but to me, I really liked it for what it was, just some good Sonic fun.

• The music is top notch. Fits the exotic climate in an unconventional fantasy theme.
• The voiceacting is outstanding.
• The gameplay: you summon an army that follows your lead and you get to cast spectacular spells that can even affect the terrain. You're after enemy wizard's altars.
• The combat: put amidst the chaos and madness you strive to eliminate the enemy forces while avoiding massive tornadoes, volcanos, eruptions and other insanities. You have to keep up with conjuring units as your army falls, but that takes time and you definitely want to be an asset with the powerful magic you wield.

I don't see why people get so upset about game still in development. Especially from a new publisher, as IMC never published any game on such scale before.
Literally ANY publisher existing in the world had same if not more problems with their games. And sometimes it wasn't even that their game was early in development. They failed to prevent problems for games where solutions already exist or at least are easy to make because problems already are known (recent examples - AA and BnS western releases).
The only argument could be made that I paid for early access. But, strictly speaking. It is still a CBT phase and not stable state of the game. We are playing on a test servers even (helloe EU servers situated in NA). Why create problem if you willingly jump into game which is still trying to get better? Having problems is great, because it gives IMC chance to fix them. If you realistically think about whole "I paid argument", people literally pay 500$ for games with much more problems, or even pay thousands for games which aren't even playable yet. Yet here were are. Paying at the minimum 7$ (in some steam regions) to get early access. And still unhappy with great game over some usual stuff.
Like I said. No game ever escaped these problems we are facing. If you really think you are entitled to get problem free experience for 7$-50$ at objectively CBT phase, you should think twice. Its delusional. In real world it never happens, and not because developers and publishers are bad. Mostly it happens because problems aren't easy to solve with how things are in our world.
Be patient with what you love. Don't expect to finish game in the first few days of early access, take it slowly and help IMC with constructive criticism instead of angry words.
TL;DR :: It's fun enough to spend cash as you are willing to pay in MMO, but let me remind you that everything is still not in a 'good' shape. It's not even 1 week since the release of early access.

Overall I enjoy playing this game, but it needs a lot of love and work from IMC in its current state to make it playable and sustainable at that. The game is beautiful, the music great, intricate and interesting class system, and it certainly has a nostalgic feel to it for old players of RO. However there at many issues currently that marr it and I'm generally concerned with how it will play come F2P in April. There are constant issues with server lag and connectivity issues (as of this moment the commaderfail debacle). The devs have removed basic mmo functions that must be purchased to be accessed (trading, basic use of market without heavy heavy limitations). Some tweaks are also needed for things like respawn rates and what not.
In summation the game is fun and very enjoyable when its working. However, IMC really needs to step in and put in the time to fix the issues and redo some of the current limitations and features that make some systems feel archaic or incredibly restrictive. I wish there was a neutral rating, but in just looking at the game and what it offers, i recommend. From a dev standpoint and design choices implemented i do not until something changes.

Capture the flag may be one of the oldest, most basic premises for a game ever, but it is a classic that can be easily reinvigorated with a fresh design and a few modifications. Oh My Godheads by developer Titutitech and publisher Square Enix Collective is a multiplayer combat game that is loosely based off of capture the flag, and it succeeds in keeping it engaging and fun by changing up the rules and impressing with its colorful, sharp style. With a few tweaks in gameplay, it has a bright future ahead.
First of all, this game innovates gameplay by adding an extra dimension: instead of capturing an inanimate flag, you try to hold onto a living, breathing head of a god. When preparing for battle, you can pick the location of the battle from a huge range of destinations, such as the Aztec Pyramids or Greek temples; this, is turn, determines which gods and goddesses you can choose from for the Godhead. For example, Greece includes the Lightening God Zeus, and Mexico includes the Aztec god Tezcatlipoca. Every deity possesses special powers that can help or hinder the player holding it, and this is often the determining factor of who wins the round. Obviously, then, it is imperative to quickly assess whether the Godhead can help or hinder you, and then use or avoid its powers in order to beat your competition. An extra element is when someone succeeds in carrying the Godhead to the altar of their team, after which they have the chance to “honor the gods” by killing the other player under a time limit. From experience, I can say that the creative new elements that Oh My Godheads applies to a basic game premise brings a whole new dimension of playing enjoyment.
Another aspect of the game that impressed me was the graphics. These days, especially with the rise of Millennial gamers, appearance and “aesthetics” count for more and more. Oh My Godheads hits the nail squarely on the head (no pun intended) with its uniquely vibrant and textured game design. The characters you can choose from are not only various races and ethnicities, but also include different animals and creatures. The graphic style renders their appearance adorable but also fierce, and to indicate which color team they fight on, they sport different accessories and skins. The battleground stages are also visually stimulating, and the layout and color scheme changes with every location. Finally, each Godhead has its own individual style, and the visual effects that erupt when the Godhead utilizes its special powers is stunning. More than just fun gameplay, Oh My Godheads is a treat for the eyes.
The one critique I would make is the limited game controls. To begin, there is only multiplayer gameplay, and you can only play with other people by using the same laptop, not other people connected to the online server. Also, the second player controls are mostly on the number pad, which is not included on a lot of laptops. This severely reduces the number of people who can play Oh My Godheads. Some solutions to this may be including a single player version that lets you fight computer-generated enemies, or changing the controls of the second player to keys that appear on more laptops. Besides that, though, Oh My Godheads is a rollicking joy ride of fresh challenges and visually appealing design that has the potential for enormous popularity.

Utterly cracking game! first played at EGX17 and had to buy it the second we got home. i rate it 10/7

+ The gameplay is pretty fun. There are multiple game modes, but the main ones involve picking up the "Godhead" and either keeping it away from the enemy team or scoring it by bringing it to the goal (capture the flag). Meanwhile you fight with the enemy players with a variety of attacks and special abilities.
+ Each Godhead has a unique trait. For example one of them explodes when held for too long, while another is heavy so it's better if you throw / roll it. I think these add variety, and I hope they continue to add more Godhead types in the future.
+ Visually the game looks fantastic! Each map / arena is very pleasing to the eye with vibrant colors and a great style that is perfect for the game.
+ There's currently 7 maps which all have a unique settings. Some have their own environmental hazards like the Volcano level with platforms that raise and lower which really adds to the game. ( Although I do hope more maps get added in the future to prevent repetiveness)
+ Great soundtrack
- Currently, you can only select 1 type of Godhead to play with in each game. I think the game would be far more exciting if the Godhead was randomized each round to add some variety.
- Some maps have poor spawns for certain game modes. For example in the two deathmatch modes "Headhunters" and "Last Man Standing" some maps have you spawn literally right next to another player which results in instant spawn killing. I suggest they fix the spawn locations.

This CTF style game is on par with games like Gangbeasts and Sausage Sports Club in terms of graphics and gameplay. Frantic and constantly changing, the one thing I do think this game is missing is 5-12 player multiplayer, and ideally 3 and 4 team maps/gamemodes. This game is a great start for an Early Access game, having waited for a better maturity before release, so you won't feel burned or incomplete on this one!
While there is not a specific tutorial mode, the trials mode does a good  job prepping you for MP gameplay, although jump attacks are difficult to execute. The built in FPS counter is a nice touch, and the only time the game suffers lag is on the trial with 16+ enemies, which is only specific to a trial mode round, and not to regular gameplay. Playing far enough through trial mode unlocks a regular flag for normal CTF gameplay.
With the godheads, each one greatly changes the dynamic of gameplay, with some being helpful, others hurtful, and a few others both helpful and hurtful to the holder and surrounding players. Ones like Zeus help kill other players, while ones like Gaia impair movement. I would not nornally reccomend using Gaia on maps with lots of movement/jumping, especially with changing goals, as that could prove very frustrating.
The gameplay is fresh with each map, which is very unique with different layouts and mechanics. For example, the treasure room has boulders that can crush players, while the Greek City has 4 potential goal locations that alternate positions.
The creation of individual profiles for achievement and stat tracking is a little bit confusing, but the built in AI mechanics and multiple game modes is great for adding further customizations to gameplay either individually or with other players. This game though is of course best suited for party gameplay, especially with 4 players. You be default have a rb-attack that throws a pie at other players, although as the trials demonstrate, these can be deflected back with enough skill.
Overall, I think this is a strong buy even for an Early Access game, and like Gangbeasts and Sausage Sports Club, I bet that there will be many more content updates in the future. The developers have been working on this game for approx. 3 years and are very responsive on Facebook, which is also great!

I just beat this game and here is why you should buy it.
Good:
- Very good engaging story
- Superb music
- Beautiful artstyle, especially during the cutscenes.
- Combat system is like nothing you've seen before, with the choice of switching between real-time and a planning mode, without either feeling superior.
- Very deep upgrade system that let's you play like you want to play.
- Has a New Game+ mode called Recursion that randomizes enemy encounters, so you can replay it with added difficulty if you feel like it.
- Has a 'limiter'-system that allows you to change the difficulty on the fly with various different debuffs/buffs to you and the enemies respectively. Adding difficulty this way gives bonus exp.
- Has checkpoints that allow you to change your loadout almost every 2-3 minutes.
Bad/not as good:
- Took me 4 hours to beat, could have been a little longer, but wasn't needed. It provided the necessary closure.
- The gameplay is mostly just moving from fight to fight. You walk a (mostly) pre-determined path and once every 2 or 3 minutes you fight something. Not sure what they could have done to make this better though, since I found the combat system really enjoyable.
- Some of the lore is locked behind your combat abilities, and this lore is unlocked by using the abilities as just a normal ability, as an upgrade to an existing ability, or as a passive bonus. I understand that this is done to make you explore different ability-combinations and to try out all of the different combinations, but I found it annoying that I had to change away from my favorite loadout if I wanted the complete story.

The hook of Borderlands 2, the very reason that I found myself thinking about it when I worked or tried to fall asleep, is the loot. Guns, ammo, character skins, grenade mods, class mods -- there’s always something just a bit better, something you so desperately didn’t even know you needed until you found it in Borderlands 2. Just like Diablo or a number of other action RPGs, the hunt for loot becomes intoxicating because of the tiny rush you get each time a rare colored item spills out of a chest or is dropped by a recently slain enemy. Every firefight and intense boss battle becomes all the more rewarding, because, though you might die a few times and want to crush something near you in real life, it suddenly feels like everything is going to be OK when you’re blasting away enemies with a newly looted gun.
Guns really do make up the bulk of the loot, and that’s great because you’re going to spend most of your time in Borderlands 2 staring down a gun sight. No matter the quest, at some point something or someone is getting pounded with lead. Thankfully, snappy shooting and lots of environmental hazards combine with each class’s unique ability to turn every skirmish into a playground. You simply have to decide the best -- or most entertaining -- way to kill everyone.

Sacrifice is one of the defining titles of Shiny Entertainment, with all its pros and cons. By now it has become a classic.
You are a wizard serving one (or more) of five gods through events that will lead to the eventual destruction of their world. To help them you have two abilities: Spells and Summons.
Spells are what you expect, buffs, heals, damage, aoe... on later levels you can demolish the landscape and kill entire armies. Summons  give you access to a wide variety of different creatures, different for each god, some of which have cool abilities and none are looking generic.
It is important to point out that is game is controlled like a third person RPG. The camera is fixed on your wizard and can be zoomed out, but not controlled individually. This takes some time getting used to since Sacrifice is, at its core, an RTS-Game.
Once you get used to the mechanics you can admire the awesome style, good writing and general good story.

This game holds up surprisingly well - still looks decent even on a widescreen monitor, which is more than what can be said about a lot of games from the same era or even a few years later. The units and characters all have a very distinct look (although several models are re-used for a few different units), it's not all cookie-cutter humanoids everywhere like in most RTS you can see. It's definitely very refreshing.
The gameplay is great and very innovative, still feels pretty unique as there's not been any kind of sequel or competitor since then (Brutal Legend has some similarities, but the atmosphere is so different you cannot compare the two). One small "bad" thing about the soul mechanic is that every mission basically has a negative difficulty curve : you must beat back the enemy assault with your small initial force, and as you convert some of their souls each subsequent fight becomes easier. Doesn't prevent the game from being very fun to play.
The storyline is also pretty interesting, and the fact that you can choose a different god for (almost) every mission makes for good replayability - the campaign lasts 10 missions and 9 of those are different for each god, so that's a total of 45 different maps and scenarios to play through if you want to be torough (which I definitely recommend). The first missions seem to have almost no impact because they're minor (so even if you're not the one doing X, it will still happen) but as you progress in the story there's definitely major differences between, say, a Charnel playthrough versus a James one.
Cheap, often on sale (4,99€ as I'm writing this) and very enjoyable, there's really no reason to not get this if you remotely enjoy the RTS genre.

You set off building and automating your entire process from top to bottom as your knowledge grows so does your base and its complexities. The game introduces new and ever exciting machines to help you achieve your goals but at a pace that isn’t overwhelming. The sheer number of ways one can build and automate a level allows for a great reply value.
Pros:
-	The city building part of this game is amazing and quite a change from most games in this genre, concentrating more on the industrial side of things more than any other I’ve seen.
-	Allows the player free roam over the map to build and grow however they see fit.
-	The sheer number of technologies at your disposal make for a ever complex set of bases at your fingertips
Cons:
-	The enemies are nothing more than mindless drones that attack in waves every so often allowing you to ignore them almost completely once you get your defense set up.
-	The story line, all be it not bad, doesn’t really add anything to the game or the level as they are pretty much all they same, build and defeat and repeat.
In conclusion, Factorio is a very fun industry builder game that allows you automate your entire work force from the ground up however you see fit, allowing countless hours of enjoyment to be had and a great deal of replayable value. 3.5 Out of 5

"Papers, Please" is an amazing game. It is charming, thought-provoking, and tests your powers of observation to the limit. You will fall in love with some characters, hate others, and maybe even hate yourself a little when it comes to moral dilemmas.
When a woman without proper documentation begs you to let her in so she can see her son, do you deny her? When you think of your own young son at home, do you feel for this woman and let her in? But that could mean a dock in pay, and the risk that you may not be able to feed your own family. What about the guy who is smuggling harmless medicine across the border? And what do you do when a friend of your boss tries to illegally enter, and threatens your job if you don't let her in? Do you put your foot down because rules are rules, or do you back down so your boss doesn't fire you?
Gameplay-wise, you are literally checking paperwork to ensure that people's passports and other documentation are all in order. It starts off simple and increases in complexity. Oh, and the rules change pretty much every day. Work quickly, get people through your line fast so you have enough money to pay your rent, feed your family and keep the heat running through the harsh winter. Oh, but don't go so fast that you get sloppy, because mistakes cost you -- literally. Less wages for you, you inaccurate speedster.
I know, it sounds weird and kind of boring and a bit like work, but it's incredibly engaging. If you're a good worker in the storyline, you can unlock the endless modes. There are three endless game modes: Timed (process as many people in a set amount of time), Perfection (game over at your first error), and Endurance (keep playing until your points balance goes negative). I really like the Perfection game mode. That's saying something when you can take away the story elements and the gameplay still stands as entertaining by itself.
"Papers, Please" is not really a puzzle game. It is not really a simulator. It's not really an RPG. It's something else entirely, and it's awesome.

Tree of Savior is an MMO created by Mr. Hakkyu Kim.
This man is responsible for the single best online experience ever created: Ragnarok Online.
I'll explain the genius in his design philosophy:
While most MMOs focus on online play for end game content, the approach to player interaction is mechanized, automated. You'll queue up for some dungeon and quest, in a game like WoW, and you'll find a dungeon. In it, there'll be players you won't speak a single word to, and they'll do their job like mindless bots. In Tree of Savior and Ragnarok Online, the approach to player interaction attempts to be organic:
For example, Players are encouraged to buff one another, or to roam maps and make friends with the people they find while journeying. The simple act of being a priest and walking around low level zones in Ragnarok Online, giving players Bless and Agi Up made you interact with new players in an interesting, fun way. You felt overpowered, satisfying your fantasy. They felt rewarded and wanted, satisfying their newfound curiosity.
WoW is balanced, which means low level content is not meant to be skipped by having a higher level player's help. In Ragnarok, you can donate a small quantity of 5 million to a newbie and watch them jump with joy.
Tree of Savior borrows much from that philosophy, although some of the modern MMO needs have made it a bit more streamlined. Shops are placed all over the city, and you're encouraged to window shop, picking favourite shop owners and growing accostumed to their presence.
There are queues in the game, but you still need to physically move to the map and meet the players you'll be queuing with anyway, and you're encouraged to talk out the strategy of the dungeon beforehand, as there are no clear cut roles for players. You're there to do your class' job, but there are no tank/healer/dps requirements. You can beat a boss by dodging and damaging it in diverse, fun ways. In fact, there are more than 60 classes currently available for players to mix and match from.
The guild vs guild battles have also been slightly streamlined, but the fact the game boasts a small(3000ish per server) community means guild leaders and famous guild members are known, and having your dream of being internet famous realized is just a few grinds away.
The game also has no clear cut metagame, as there are few and far between people willing to make any guides at all, and those are all wrong: The real good players keep it to themselves to gain advantages in GvG wars. Your theorycrafting is rewarded with good results.
Grinding is still part of the game, but until very late in the endgame, completely optional. You'll be leveling by questing and doing dungeons with friends, and partying up actually increases your experience intake, as opposed to RO's system. You'll also never lose EXP for dying, reducing frustration.
The game's spread out over 330 levels(so far), which means players get to enjoy the pleasure if seeing that level up popup multiple times, as well as changing classes 7 times(for a total of 8 classes per character). You'll never get bored of your character's rotation, as you'll be learning new tricks every few levels, changing your entire playstyle. Your old skills will still be useful, of course, and synergy is encouraged.
TL;DR Try this out. You might like it, you might not. I do. A lot. I've been playing it since launch and 0 regrets.

While this game may have a few shortcomings that will leave you asking, "Why the heck can't I..." that's really the only bad thing I have to say about it.
Even though it has its own story that fits in nicely between 'Alien' & 'Aliens,' it feels like a film adaptation, and in this case, that isn't a bad thing. If you're going for authenticity, this may be the best game based on a film franchise ever. Instead of taking a raw action approach like so many other games based in this universe, the devs opted to recreate the terror of the original film: Alone in space, with weapons that at best can briefly deter the beast, and at worst, tick it off. Staying alive is about outsmarting the alien by sneaking around (Newt-style) and improvising, rather than trying to kill it. Ridley Scott should be proud of how scary this game can get if you're willing to let it immerse you. A few good fights are interspersed to keep the experience fresh, and the occasional space-walks provide some breathtaking imagery.
This might not be your cup of tea if you're looking for an FPS. But if you've ever wanted to find out what it would feel like to be a character in 'Alien,' look no further. This is it. Turn off the lights in the room, put on your best headphones, and try to survive.

Recommended: Not just content to rely on a vivid aesthetic or the same powerful narration of it's predecessor Bastion, Transistor takes Supergiant's style and art into a much deeper and thoroughly-enjoyable game.
Full review is too long for Steam, and includes images, so take a read here:
Incredible game. Supergiant made bastion. This is just as incredible. Their games are probably the best example for the arguement that games are art.

A word of warning - If you are looking for a casual hack & slash experience similar to Bastion or the likes of Diablo stay away from this game. It will save hearing you whine about how complicated or confusing Transistor is.
This game, much like its predecessor Bastion, is a genuine work of art. I cannot convey just how amazing the artwork, music and narration is in these games, you must truly experience that for yourself.
Transistor has stepped it up in terms of gameplay since Bastion. You really have to think and strategize every encounter you face and this can be done through an intuitive 'Plan' mode. This game is brutal and punishing; one mistake can lead to having one of the Transistor's (your primary weapon) abilities overload and become unusable until the next checkpoint. This can really make things hard for you. I have seen this being cited as a negative factor but I believe it only adds more to the emphasis on strategy that this game demands of you.
In terms of story we are met again with a sort of distant, abstract plot which falls together throughout the course of the game. Some people seem to have found this a turn off, most likely the kinds of people who expect every video game or film to explain itself to them without rousing any sense of personal contemplation. Transistor has a deep and compelling storyline which you will uncover as you play, adding to the list of reasons for you to push forward. It is nice to still see some intelligent storytelling present in modern gaming.
All things being said I have found Transistor to be well worth the money paid for it. For all you Steam junkies out there achievements are present. It may not be the longest game in recent history but who cares? It is short and sweet and I would rather play 4-5 hours of an amazing video game than 30-40 hours of another mediocre crowd-pleaser.

I honestly don’t know why people seem to♥♥♥♥♥♥on this game so much. Well, I am fully aware of the problems but I think most reviews exaggerated them. I’d say this one is at least as competent as colours and generations. I was initially reluctant to buy this game since I had heard it was really bad and short for the price but now I regret waiting a few days. By the end of the game I was 100% invested in the story. I love how self aware and dark(?) it tried to be, it felt a lot like a Saturday morning cartoon or something, except better than the actual sonic Saturday morning cartoons. The modern sonic and classic sonic levels were about as good as generations and I really didn’t have a problem with them being short at all, if anything it made for a really tight feeling game with little to no filler, which is something that sonic games fall into a lot where generations had the filler missions that no one ever mentions. The amount of cutscenes and talking was refreshing too, this is the first time in ages where we’ve had a large cast of the characters all interacting with each other, I think heroes might’ve been the last one to do so but I’m not certain.

And of course, the OC. This was the main reason I was interested in Forces. At first the creation system is extremely shallow, but you unlock more pieces of clothing, fur patterns, weapons ect for your character the more you play, which is a very good way of getting players to come back for more and it doesn’t even take very long to unlock a satisfying amount of these items. Knowing the way 2017 has been, they could have very easily made these items microtransactions or lootboxes, but nope, you unlock them just by playing and you unlock them very quickly, just like the good old PS2 days. The gameplay for the “Rookie” as the characters call him/her in the cutscenes is very enjoyable too. I was expecting it to be slow and boring but the characters grapple hook and “Wispons” were very fun to use and experiment with and actually felt quick and responsive.
But yeah, In all honesty Sonic Forces might just be my favourite Sonic game now. I know that’s a controversial statement especially since it was released right after mania but at the very least it’s by far my favourite of the modern sonic games.

The old review is below. I will not remove it but I change my recommendation for the game, now that it's come back from the dead and it's been supported again with Empire Devided and seemingly more to come. I still think there are quite a few problems in Rome 2, but the main reason for my previous "Not recommended" review was that the game stopped receiving support. Now that this is not the case, I certainly recommend this game to anyone interested.
***
I'll start this by saying I really like the TW series, I own all TW games and DLCs, plus some CA games that I bought mainly to support the studio. Generally I don't play many other games on Steam.
Rome 2 was the first TW I was hyped for and wanted to get on release. It is just too diverse, too big not to be entertaining.
Seeing the buggy mess it was on release I decided to wait a bit and give CA the chance to fix the game.
Which *spoilers* they never did.
Now, as someone who enjoys playing even the original Shogun I am not one for graphics. I really liked how they went with all games since Empire and goddamn, Medieval 2 still looks great in field battles. But I couldn't care less about the looks. I fell in love with the game mechanics, they clicked right in place with me and I spent numerous hours trying to get to understand them, both ingame and in real life. That's how you know a great video game - you get to constantly think of it when you are not playing it.
Learning Shogun 2 took me quite some time and I won't win a competition for knowing the game. There are still new things I discover every now and then. They all fall right into spot, close the cycle and it just feels great to come up to the next revelation.
This is, unfortunately, not the case with Rome II.
Rome II introduced some new things which are great. Like the army stances.
So why on Earth does the Fortify stance say "boosts reinforcement range by +50%" and does not do it?
This is the case with so many faction bonuses, personal traits and retainers, skills, etc, that it's mindblowing.
When playing games I like to be on fair terms. Get helthpack -> health goes up. Critical strike on enemy -> 50% more damage. Things like this. Things we're used to take for granted.
Rome II does a really poor job of explaining its mechanics. There are tutorial videos, but they are somehow obsolete as the game received 17 patches, the last one with major core changes. I had to play Attila to understand the whole party politics thing.
Rome II is big and diverse. And this is a curse more than a blessing. There are so many little things missing, not working or just straight-forward overlooked by the developers, that I won't bother listing them all. Just go to the official support forum and check the Single Player Campaign support page.
Fairly said, I think Rome II did not ever make it out of beta.
The reason for this review is that CA stopped supporting the game. A game I paid and bought all dlcs for. A game I really wanted to like. The last patch fixed (arguably) some things, but not merely enough. And that is not even considering all the technical and graphical bugs, which are not a subject of this review. For a moment there I thought they are on the right way, but they just abandoned the game. The game with my favorite time period, that was supposed to revolutionize the TW franchise as the core mechanics weren't changed since Empire. Well, I'm sorry for being mad, but I am. As a user, as a customer. False data, false advertisment and false promises. Thanks CA, I'll gladly pirate your♥♥♥♥♥♥from now on and not buy a single title. Unless Rome II is fixed that is.
***
PROS:
+ Looks great. Some folks may argue here, but for me the game running on Ultra is gorgeous.
+ One of the biggest maps in TW games. Meaning a lot of factions, traits, bonuses, variety in general.
+ There are some great historical campaigns in addition to the main game that make the title's worth.
+ New mechanics and even controls to make the TW experience more up-to-date.
CONS:
- A bit buggy even after all the patches. Soldier groups will shout different units' lines. No anti-aliasing; water reflection is broken. Some really ugly textures. There's a lot more to that list.
- Unfinished mechanics that clearly can be fun but are not even a factor to work with.
- Some clearly broken gameplay elements. Bonuses not given though they should be. Traits acting on the opposite. Sometimes your generals will get bad (or good) traits with no apparent reason.
- Too much DLCs, some arguably not worth their money.
- Continious lack of support for some of the major elements and problems this game has.
- Looks like some of the best ideas for Rome II didn't make it in the game and we were sold Attila instead. Which is fine, but everyone can see that Rome II needs some Attila in it.

I'm on day 8 of the head start release now, I log in and I get a good 5-10 minutes worth of gold farmer spam in shouts (you have to spend real money currency to buy items per shout, like Maple Story) before anything else shows up and by the time I block them all another one shows up.  There's no players talking, I try to zone out of the main city and I get an error message that says "CommanderLoadFail" and it boots me to the login screen.  I spend a few more minutes trying to get back in and every character I try to log in gets the same error message and boot to the login.  Really now, this is just unacceptable for a game that's been out a year over seas.
The game has potential but I'll be surprised if it ever gets there.  They would have to change some really basic things to make the game decent.  An example is they have a double fail system for trading items.  Items have a stat called "potential" which drops every time you trade it and when the item is out of potential it is unusable.  And on top of that you have to pay a monthly subscription to be able to trade and you're limited to 30 trades a month.  So you're literally paying about 50c(USD) per trade and whoever you trade with is also paying that 50c and if you trade the item more than like 4-5 times it just dies and can't be used anymore.  Sure you can sell items over the market (auction house, exchange, ect) and "trade" them that way but the item still loses potential and whoever sells it loses 30% (10% for a sub) of the sell price to the market and the potential STILL goes down.
Oh and you have to pay monthly to use the shared stash and you have to pay in game currency every time you transfer an item in or out of your stash which again..... ridiculous.  So yeah, it's a fun game but the outright idiotic "features" will soon weigh in to be more than the fun.  I really can't recommend until some major changes are made.

"Arstotzka so great, passport not required. Right?"
Wrong! Well, most of the time. It depends. Those are the rules, but sometimes the rules need to be broken. Maybe for moral reasons. Maybe because you just slipped me a bribe to stamp "APPROVED" on your passport.
"Papers, Please" is an amazing game. It is charming, thought-provoking, and tests your powers of observation to the limit. You will fall in love with some characters, hate others, and maybe even hate yourself a little when it comes to moral dilemmas.
When a woman without proper documentation begs you to let her in so she can see her son, do you deny her? When you think of your own young son at home, do you feel for this woman and let her in? But that could mean a dock in pay, and the risk that you may not be able to feed your own family. What about the guy who is smuggling harmless medicine across the border? And what do you do when a friend of your boss tries to illegally enter, and threatens your job if you don't let her in? Do you put your foot down because rules are rules, or do you back down so your boss doesn't fire you?
Gameplay-wise, you are literally checking paperwork to ensure that people's passports and other documentation are all in order. It starts off simple and increases in complexity. Oh, and the rules change pretty much every day. Work quickly, get people through your line fast so you have enough money to pay your rent, feed your family and keep the heat running through the harsh winter. Oh, but don't go so fast that you get sloppy, because mistakes cost you -- literally. Less wages for you, you inaccurate speedster.
I know, it sounds weird and kind of boring and a bit like work, but it's incredibly engaging. If you're a good worker in the storyline, you can unlock the endless modes. There are three endless game modes: Timed (process as many people in a set amount of time), Perfection (game over at your first error), and Endurance (keep playing until your points balance goes negative). I really like the Perfection game mode. That's saying something when you can take away the story elements and the gameplay still stands as entertaining by itself.
"Papers, Please" is not really a puzzle game. It is not really a simulator. It's not really an RPG. It's something else entirely, and it's awesome.

So I'm new to playing this game on Steam, but I've played it for a long time now over many saves, and I felt I needed to recommend it when I learned it was on here.
Realm Grinder is one of the many contemporary games that came from the out-of-nowhere craze of cookie clicker among casual gamers and obsessive people alike- though it had next to no substance, it was formulated just well enough to pull people in and become a topic of discussion. It's worth noting that cookie clicker was a 100% perfect formula but with no actual game attached, which is a fascinating concept, albeit a little hollow feeling after a while.
Now if you take that idea and actually attach a game, you'd end up with something like Realm Grinder, which is my favorite game in the "cookie clicker ripoff" genre by far. It has more emergent gameplay than I've ever seen in a game like this, and hundreds of hours in you're still unearthing new features, unlocking new ways to play, and making decisions you've never made before. It's an insanely well paced game- the main loop of the game after a certain point in time is to reset your progress after you've made it far enough, but carrying some benefits to your next playthrough- and there are a lot of different layers of resetting to the point where you've just done 100 resets to do 1 reset to get closer to your next reset. It sounds grueling, but each time you reset it gets faster and there's some new fun upgrade to get or some weird achievement to grind for, and it's just really really well directed.
So happy that I found this game and the Clicker Game Genre! Watch those numbers rise, plan new strategies to maximise efficiency on the go, the mind is delighted! Purrr~~~

Awesomeness ~ play this game

GENERAL
What's really weird about this game is the  fact that it doesn't have a main menu - it just drops you right into the game. You have different profiles, but the game automatically saves and reloads where you last saved whenever you start the game.The game has a slow start at first, though you quickly pick up extra Functions and add more versatility to your playstyle.
FUNCTIONS(abilities):
You get quite a few Functions; some you get via story, others via levelling up. Since you can equip every Function in an active, upgrade or passive slot, you have quite a few combinations available; though most functions have the same effect on almost every function, it can change your playstyle considerably. This comes to show later into the game, when you need to plan more carefully or else you die like a ♥♥♥♥♥, like I did. But instead of losing the game the second you lose your HP, you keep losing functions until you've lost all you have - survive the fight, and you'll take 2 save points to recover the ones you lost. Through this feature I changed my build and learned to appreciate Functions I never used. However, even at the final level, it feels like you are rather limited in the amount of Functions you get; You have 4 Active slots; you can unlock a total of 2 Upgrade slots for each as well as 4 passive slots. I've never managed to fill all the slots up.
What I really miss here is a proper dodge function. You have a Function that takes care of it, but it has a long after-cast delay that you cannot really rely on it for anything other than Turn()
Oh, that's another thing I haven't mentioned. Welp, you can plan your moves and attacks in a strategic mode. The problem? You're virtually useless for a few seconds afterwards, unless you have a survival ability or upgrade an attack function with the dash Function. Forgot its name.
GRAPHICS:
The visuals are stunning and flow quite well most of the time. My main complaint is that the character model seems to move a bit awkwardly. Then there are also cutscenes which are supposed to reveal crucial events of the story, that are shown simply as a still image with parts that are barely moving. So that's a letdown; especially when they're coupled with the Trailer music. You'd think it'd be epic or more action packed, only to get a very slow moving image.
MUSIC:
The music is amazing; though the tower song seems a bit too repetitive for my taste.
STORY:
Story is nice overall, though I'd say everything escalates all too quickly. You're dropped into the game and only later learn the circumstances surrounding you obtaining the Transistor; which is fine. What I do not like is that you fight just about two bosses and you're already retracing your steps back to the beginning and get to the finale. Supergiant Games' previous title had a lot more levels full of small things that enriched the story, and boss-like instances when it came to that. Here the environment does not really complete the story that well, aside from the terminals, which are quite heart-breaking towards the end. Bastion would take different turns, too, not just "Start at point A, reach point B, go back to point A; visit point C. VOILA! You beat the game." I was seriously hoping the game would have been a bit longer than Bastion and that the story would be more fleshed out, but nope. Though it feels quite rushed, it's still enjoyable nonetheless.
PERFORMANCE ISSUES:
I have a PC that's well above the requirements yet I experience quite a few bugs and random freezes. Hopefully they'll fix this in a future patch.
FINAL VERDICT:
It's a good game. Personally I'd give it a 7 or 8 out of 10. Had it been just a little longer story-wise and a bit more fleshed out, it would've been amazing and well worth the price. Right now, it just feels like I did not get quite what I paid for. Sure, good for casual fun, but didn't really touch me as much as Bastion did. Maybe wait till it's on sale?

I love the first Dark Souls. I love it so much that I recompleted it on my PC. Dark Souls II is different though. Part of it is that I'm going to have to rebuy the game in a couple of months. Which makes me feel so much better about doing the preorder on it last year. The other thing is that the setting is no where near as interesting as the first game. Everything connected in Dark Souls I. I could look in the distance and know that eventually I would get to that point and explore it. Everything in Dark Souls II isn't connected in anything coming close to a sensical way. Seriously, I went up a windmill and came out in an active lava flow. The game mechanics in this one are cool, especially dual wielding, but with everything other part of the game lacking the charm the first one had it just feels fake and rushed. Hopefully the final version I need to repay for is going to be better, but if the setting is still so bad I really wonder if I would bother.
The complaints aside I did enjoy the game though. I liked it better than Demon's Souls. I spent quite a lot of time exploring all the nooks and crannies and pulling as much as I could out of the game.
My least favorite part, aside from the setting, though was interaction with other players. When it was good it was great! When it was bad though it was enough to make me want to put the game aside and not pick it up again. I really want to 100% this game, but I just don't think I have it in me to go through the covenants on this one.
If you're thinking about getting this get it cheap, or just wait for the shiny new version to come out in a couple of months. If you're fine with how it is now it's definitely still Dark Souls, all be it a lesser version, so you'll still find enjoyment in it. If you want something better though it you might want to just buy the original and play that until the fancy version of DSII comes out.

Tl;dr: Gameplay is engaging, graphics are pretty, controls are intuitive, PvP is an option, and support is amazing. 10/10 would recommend.
So from what I can tell, this is meant to be the MVP (minimum viable product) for what they (the developers, producers, etc.) envision as the fully fleshed out game. With that in mind, I am wholly enamored with what the developers are creating here. I will address the good, the bad, and the not so pretty, both in game and out.
Let's start with gameplay. The controls are fairly intuitive if you've ever played a horse game for the PC before. Reminiscent of the Lets Ride franchise, but with beautiful scenery which allows you to move about fluidly and comfortably, this game takes me back to my early adolescent years without being more of the same. It doesn't feel heavily nostalgic, because everything here feels so fresh and new. There is an effortlessness that comes through to me as a player when my horse is galloping along, responding easily to my cues with no major rendering issues to interrupt my immersion.
On to shows, at present, players have three main options for showing: a player can run timed trials by oneself, compete against other players in a Ranked Match, or enter the Weekly Showdown with many other players. Weekly showdowns cost skill tickets, which are accrued during normal play when a player levels. One can compete in Agility and Show Jumping courses. One can also choose to ride around the paddock and practice one's jumping and maneuvering one's horse in general. A player will need to level one's horse and tack (don't ask me why tack affects stats) before one will have a reasonably easy time of showing. I confess I am not an avid gamer, but I do have a reasonable amount of experience with horse games in particular, and I found the early game controls to be a but slow and heavy. I acutally had to slow my horse to make some of the turns required to successfully take a jump, which I suppose is accurate to real life courses, but it makes it difficult to complete certain courses in the time alotted.
When you're done showing and you horse is tuckered out, you can head to the stable and give him or her a good grooming. You can also use the game currency, coins, to hire a stablehand to do the job for you if you're not so into the work part of owning a horse. You run through cleaning your big baby from top to bottom, and the actions are fully animated. The ragdoll physics used to keep your tool in contact with the horse could use some refining (sometimes your brush will just spin uncontrollably at random), but UI does a good enough job conveying the idea.
Now, this is about as good a place as I can think of to mention the one flaw in the graphics: That horse's tail looks so awkward it isn't even funny. Regardless of your graphics settings, it has an absurdly low poly count and moves about as freely as as a stick. The horse itself moves beautifully, and the mane is well drawn, though entirely stationary. Aside from these issues, I found nothing lacking. I typically choose the highest quality settings, which allows trees to sway in the breeze. There are also tufts of overgrown grass scattered about the otherwise packed, dusty earth. I find very few issues with framerate and lag at this quality setting.
On to customization: upon loading into the game you are met with a tutorial. Immediately after which you are prompted to choose your rider and design your horse. The options for horse color are mostly true to life (however, you can choose a red mane and tail on a black horse), and you can also select the gender and name of your horse. You can also choose your tack and apparel through the store.
At this time, currency is earned by showing or by riding through the paddock for an excessive length of time. Either way, the only time a player sees a real increase in the old bank account is by leveling up. This is probably my largest complaint about the game: I am not a fan of any game which makes you pay to win. In order to purchase better tack ( in a timely fashion) than that with which one begins, purchasing more coins is a necessary evil.
So why would anyone play this if it costs money to really go anywhere? Well, I would argue that it is possible to accomplish the same things these purchases would give a player if one spent enough time in the game to earn it. Also, I had an encounter with support, and this is where I discovered my enjoyment for this game. The support staff was friendly and helpful, but more importantly, they addressed my concern in a way that showed me politely that the mistake was mine and that they were still willing to meet my suggestions for resolution regardless of fault. Let me put it another way: I paid for something. I made an assumption about what I was buying which did not line up with what I actually paid for. I was annoyed. I wrote them an email expressing my dissatisfaction. They told me what I actually bought. Then offered a refund anyway. They were courteous, they did not have an attitude of assigning blame, and they offered to use my solution for resolution, even though they did nothing to warrant it.
For this alone, I will be declining said refund, and I will be a paying player of their game. The reason is simple: any game with PvP options costs money in servers, in domain name, in support, and so on. This game is still in development as far as I can tell, and that staff also has to get paid. Moreover, if this is what a partial product looks like, I wait with great anticipation for the finished product. Finally, they understand the value of a single player. I have never been treated with such dignity by support in all my life. I am an IT person by trade, and I will be supporting this so long as I am able.

I wish steam had a neutral recommendation option, because I can't give this game a positive review in its current state.  I do personally find it enjoyable, but then I also don't compete against other players unless I get a quest to do so.  However, even though I personally enjoy the gameplay aspect, it does have some pretty significant drawbacks.
Let me start with the things I do enjoy.  I love that grooming is included as something that you either have to do yourself or pay to have someone else do for you.  If you're like me and not interested in paying, grooming after each competition or ride makes it easy to keep your horse clean.  I also like that, as in real life, if I don't get a clear round there's a reason why, and it's always because I screwed up somehow.  Practice does make perfect.
However, this game is very grindy.  This is a Facebook-type MMO, and it really, really shows.  Want to upgrade your tack?  Buy coins.  Want to upgrade your clothes?  Buy coins.  Don't want to buy coins?  Sorry, you only get 25 coins per completed course, even for high level courses or no fault rounds.  Want to level up your horse?  You only get 100 xp per completed course, unless you buy enough coins to buy a book.   You can subscribe, for $10.00 a month, but the perks just don't feel worth it to me.  Oh - and the horses' manes and tails look very plastic, not realistic at all.
Bottom line: If you've played Facebook-style games before and are looking for a semi-decent horse game, this game fits that bill.  However, in its current state, I don't find it worth paying real money to play it.  I probably wouldn't have started playing it at all if I hadn't had problems installing the latest Star Stable update.  This game is an acceptable stopgap solution for me, but if you want a non-Facebook style horse MMO with an actual storyline, this isn't the game for you.

Despite the graphics lacking in some places such as the horse coats (although the scenery is fabulous), this has to be one of the better horse games I've played. It's one of the few games that doesn't make me mad and rage quit because I know that anything that goes wrong is /always/ my fault. It's very much like real horse riding in that sense, because there is always a rational reason why you didn't get your new highscore, or why you keep knocking that pole. It's because you don't time your strides, you don't hit the right take-off point. Your horse swerved? Don't approach the jump at an angle. You can't match the striding between a jump? Slow your gallop, or lengthen it according to the amount of strides needed. Granted, it lacks realism in many ways, but I have to admit that I've been hooked since I first got it. I appreciate how the hit-boxes actually match the object they represent, and I love how the galloping animation mirrors when you change direction to alter the lead leg - little things like this come together to make a really great game. It's just a shame there aren't many players to compete against online at one time.

ESO is a fun and rewarding experience for a casual PVE player, like myself. The lore is what one would expect from an Elder Scrolls game and it is extremely gratifying to see many of the areas not seen in the main series of Elder Scrolls receive much needed atttention. Character customization is excellent and though it can hold your hands at times the game does offer sufficient challenge as you progress through the levels.  The biggest issue that I have with the game is the ability to use abilities (more acurately the lack there of).  Most MMOs offer ability bars with anywhere from 10-15 slots on each bar. In ESO you only receive 5 (plus a limited sixth slot for your ultimately ability). This gets somewhat better when you hit level fifteen as at that time you gain access to a secondary weapon slot and an additional 5 slot ability bar. However this still does not allow for adequate usage of the skills that you will undoubtedly accumulate in your adventures. This in combination with  the reletively recent One Tamriel expansion (which effectively made leveling irrelevant for most of the PvE game as I can do nearly as much damage with a level 7 character as a max level character) makes it difficultfor me to recommend for anyone looking for more than "Skyrim with friends". Some of these issues may be addressed in the recent Morrowind expansion however I have been unable to log in since downloading the expansion. In summary, it is a good albeit flawed MMO.

I think people are getting caught up by this game's looks, instead of focusing on the game itself. It's got a lot of issues.
- The leveling system is broken. Monsters have massive HP bars and give very little experience when killed, which turns leveling up into a massive chore.  The game keeps giving the player these XP scrolls for some reason, instead of bumping up the XP you get from killing monsters, which is the whole point of a game like this.
- No PvP mode. Seriously? PvP was a huge part of the late game in Ragnarok Online and it's baffling to me how it's nowhere to be seen in ToS.
- Lack of Gear Customization. The card system in Ragnarok Online was awesome and it had a lot of depth. In ToS, you only have these boring gems that have no depth to them whatsoever.
- The developers LOVE to toot their own horns, saying how deep the class system in this game, and how many classes there are, when in reality, the class system in ToS is not even half as deep as the class system in Ragnarok Online. Quality, not quantity is what I always say.
- The Boss Fights are BORING and repetitive. Do you guys remember how awesome it was to fight an MVP in Ragnarok Online? How badass they looked and how they could one-shot your character if you weren't careful? ToS's bosses have more in common with Diablo 3's than Ragnarok's bosses.
- Lack of an Attack Speed counter/stat. This is more of a personal opinion, but it really bums me out how you can't really measure or change your attack speed in the game.
- The controls are terrible. When your Korean MMO controls best on an Xbox 360 pad, you know you got problems. The Mouse controls are buggy as all hell and the Keyboard controls are just not fun to mess around with. I just don't get why they didn't stick with Ragnarok Online's control scheme? You shouldn't have to play a PC MMO with an Xbox 360 pad.
There's a reason why people still play Ragnarok Online 11 years after it came out. That game has depth, it knows how to keep the player engaged, it has an awesome PvP mode, group events, Guilds actually mean something and above all, it's fun to play. Tree of Savior looks better and that's pretty much it. I'm absolutely devastaded by how this game turned out, but I'm not gonna be deceived by its familiar code of paint like a lot of people did. I'd recommend you to give it at shot when it becomes free in April, but it's definitely not worth your money at this point.

This is easily the best Aliens game I have ever played.  That may not necessarily be speaking high praise, but it was a good game.  The tension was nice; the xenomorph is basically an unstoppable beast that you always need to avoid.  Humans are more of an annoyance than any type of threat.

I am very cautious about games I buy.  I usually have a "dollar an hour" game rule, because I can't exactly dump money into games.  Because of this philosophy I have waited to get this game since it came out, until it was on sale.
That said, I am also a "scardy-cat" and don't do well with horror or thriller games.  Then, why did I continue playing Alien: Isolation instead of returning it?  Because it is a phenomenal game.
Not only does Alien capture the feel of the original, and what others have described as "lo-fi" 70s style Sci Fi, it captures the feeling of a space station in disorder and decay, that is inhabited by an invincible creature meant only to kill; the perfect predator.
The game looks fantastic, captures an authentic feel, and has very few graphical errors or other blemishes that take you out of the moment.  The story was very well done, although, I do feel in some places it was lacking background for main characters that was referenced, but never discussed, in the game.
Overall I give this game 5 stars, and I believe it is worth its full price, though I picked it up on sale.  If there is to be a sequel, I will pay full price for it, as I believe excellence should be rewarded.

I can't reccomend this game.
First, the game has a great soundtrack and artstyle.  Great atmosphere.  That's about all the good I can say about Transistor
The story is vague.  Very vague.  So vague that I can't follow along with anything.  A sword is speaking to the voiceless "Red" who seems to only show any personality through art pieces.  You learn about other characters through skills after having found them in a dying state.  You get a snippet of dialogue about the character and a view lines of text.  So basically, it feels like tidbits of lore, but the plot doesn't go anywhere for quite a while.  I like mystery and stories where you figure things out only until the end, but this...it's just so empty and vague with little to no motivation.
The gameplay boils down to walking down corridors with the occasional alternate "dead end" path leading to more short tid bits of the sword speaking to you about the spot, or a communication hub.  Thus you learn short bits about the characters previous life, but little to no exploration of the actual world.  It's basically running from Save Point- Enemy Fight- Story bit, Repeat.  Also, while roaming the levels you will see "flashes" of other players playing the game.  Well, so I hear.  I don't think the game ever really tells you that.  But apparently, this is what causes the 3-4 stall/freezes you will also run into in the game for such a pointless feature. They could have just made that client side, because in other games it actually has a purpose (Dark Souls).
Besides that, the combat.  What a mess.  What we have here is a blend of turn-based and action.  Sounds cool, and I actually could see it working.  But it doesn't here.  You will spend your time in turn based because that is where the most damage and safest way to be is.  The downfall is that this game does a horrendous job of telling you what you need to do and giving you decent feedback.  Now, when you go into turn based mode, the world will phase out and stop.  The game shows you arcs of the moves you choose and also shows just how much HP will be taken off or if the enemy will evade/block it.  The fact is, this system is highly inaccurate.  I've chosen AoE moves, and it clearly shows my AoE should hit 3 of the targets because they are highlighted.  Guess what?  One didn't get hit, even though he was highlighted.  In another instance, I qued up three attack moves and that turn based system said that enemy would die, and after executing, it did not die.  Why give me misleading information?
Now, perhaps I missed something.  I don't see how though.  Although, the game does a bad job of teaching the player how to play.  Oh yes, I enjoy learning things on my own.  I don't like to be hand held and have a tutorial for every little thing.  This though...The UI for assigning skills and such is not very self explanatory, combat is a mess, and when you die, you lose a skill until you reach the checkpoint after next and get full hp to finish the battle (Usually I just hit retry, because a. I don't like losing a skill and b. I don't like being held by the hand.  I find it an insult to just replinish my hp to full automatically so I can defeat the already beaten down enemies).  Which can hinder you badly, especially if you have limiters on.  All lmiiters do is enhance the enemies, giving you more exp for the difficulty boost.
All in all, I found it more frustrating than I did enjoyable.  Shame though.  I hate seeing games with great music and art style have cumbersume design and messy gameplay.

Another great game by Supergiant Games, though very different from their first, Bastion.
The combat in Transistor involves a highly flexible ability system that lets you mix and match your abilities to create new abilities that play out in real time combat with some turn based elements. The combat constantly makes players choose when the optimal time to use their slotted abilities are, and when to use the planning mode (a mode that freezes enemies while you queue up and then execute some abilities before the enemies get to move again) as using abilities or planning mode can put things on cool down and make you vulnerable for follow up.
However the combat does start a bit slow as you only start with a couple abilities and unlock both more abilities and more upgrade slots (the slots that let you combine abilities) as you go, so it starts slow but picks up fast as you go along. Similarly enemies are very easy at the start and most players will find fights fairly easy till most of the upgraded late game enemies start showing up. If those still aren't enough for you, you can activate "Limiters" which are optional and make the game even harder (such as spawning more enemies and make them do 2x damage).
The story is very good and personally I enjoyed it even more than Bastion, though it is done very differently. Where Bastion gave the player a lot of knowledge, including knowledge the players character wouldn't know, and all but held the players hand through the story, Transistor gives you story through the eyes of it's characters, and it's up to the player to gain an understanding of what is going on in the story through the information their character is given throughout the game. This gives the story greater depth and immersion, but can also make the story more difficult for some people to understand or for those who skip through a lot of the dialogue. If you want to know everything about the in-game world then you might not enjoy the story of Transistor, however if you like to see a story from the view of a character present at the time and immersion that can bring, then you will probably find the story of Transistor amazing.
Finally the length of the game runs about 5-6 hours. There is NG+ (and I hear NG++, though I haven't quite gotten there yet) and you can get further upgrades for playing NG+ so if you enjoy the gameplay there is some incentive to play past the ending of the story (you can get a couple hours of gameplay just trying out different ability loadouts with the amount of combinations available), though if you only want the game for story then there isn't much incentive for multiple play throughs unless you want to revisit the story.
In summary the game is simply amazing. Both the combat and the story have a lot of depth to them. Though players who want the story spelled out for them or more twitch based combat may want to consider looking elsewhere. For those coming from Bastion know that this game is great as well but it is also VERY different, so don't expect Bastion 2.0 in a sci-fi setting, both the gameplay and story are done in a very different fashion so be sure to keep that in mind if you decide to pick it up.

An interesting game with a poetic ending.
I played this game for roughly 40 minutes. Probably less for you, if you don't get distracted like I did. Essentially, you play as some guy with the hots for your friend emily, and you act out 5 different conversations from 2001-2005. It's set like an old AIM messenger. What icon you choose matters. What name you choose matters. What you say to Emily and what you do all alter the journey towards the destination. If you don't want spoilers, quit reading and play for like 30 minutes.
Like I mentioned, I played the game for roughly 40 minutes. The other 20 minutes of my playtime was keeping the game open as I desperately searched for any inclination of another ending. In the end, your character fails. You and Emily have drifted apart. It's over, no matter what you do or say. You're reduced to erasing important things and rewriting trivial chit chat until there's nothing to talk about. It's sad.
I used to hate games without a good ending. However, this game is more designed to cut a slice of life instead of providing a fantasy. It presents a very real situation and ends with a very real ending. It connects with the average player more than the references, icons, and callbacks do. At worst, it's a cliche "the one who got away" scenario. However, it's strongest attribute is that the scenario presented is so real, more so than your Hallmark movie. Would I pay money for this game? No. However, it's a brief and poetic experience, and I'd recommend it if you're somebody who can see the beauty in failure. Or someone who needs to see the beauty in failure.
