First of all: I certainly had fun with this game. It offers enough for dozens of hours, which for that price is really good.
Factorio is best described as "Minecraft in 2d, where redstone is used in the first hour of gametime". Why?
Factorio is based on the urge to optimize a production system. Transport belts, robotic arms and rails are waiting for you to arrange them most efficiently on a basically infinitly big map. You can mine resources by hand, too, but that's hard work easily automatable. But as the resources aren't infinitely available, you'll have to expand and/or find another place to build a base.
The only real enemy are aliens that attack you more often as you create more pollution, thus if your base gets bigger. However, the isometric perspective and the poor combat system isn't worth bothering imho, for you can easily defend your base with some turrets.
So what's the content: Some items/resources, refine them, get something out of it. Mainly science points to get new technologies. If you like the combat (I don't), you can also go and fight aliens (consisting of walking around and holding space, it's really not great).
And that's the problem I have with this game: Most of the items are utterly useless and/or serve one simple cause: Science. After grinding science, you can get a rocket silo to start a satellite that lets your fleet know where to pick you up (or something).
I'd really like to say that is game was great, but it isn't. The point of doing it all isn't evident, and while you can set the map to many properties (whether you can deplete resources, how big the map shall be and many more), I don't seem to get the point of this game. It's moddable and it's still in early access, and it runs smoothly, so technically it's better than ok and it can still be expanded, but it seems to me rather like a modding platform than a full-grown game.
I can't see the idea behind it. Is the point to rush the rocket silo as fast as possible? Is it to be creative? Is it to murder everything?
Minecraft offers a 3rd dimension. In small spaces it's still tidious, but try doing something in factorio. You need so much space for most production chains that you start asking yourself how you can even keep the overview (you can't).
The worst things by far (imho) are the trains. They're very prominently placed, yet automating them is a pain. I've played 100h+ of Simutrans (great game btw, take a look, it's free), where the main goal is to make train lines and I've never had any problems. Here, it's a mess. Pathfinding of the trains is ridiculous, the signals do more or less, what they want and building rails is a pain in the a** as soon as you try to go through a forest. Same goes for cars: I've never had to cross distances a) long enough and b) without these [omitted] trees. As soon as you bump into them, the car gets to a full stop - and because you can't see♥♥♥♥♥♥because of the isometric perspective, you'll bump into them a whole lot -> I rarely use cars.
Against aliens, I've destroyed most of their bases by basecrawling into them - the handguns aren't good enough and using tanks requires huge production lines and supplies of fuel and ammo - basecrawling with laser turrets does only require fairly cheap turrets and really cheap electricity poles.
*Sigh*
What should I say? It's not a bad game, but compared to minecraft, it's not enough of a game yet. It feels flat. The whole science stuff's only purpose is to stretch the game as you want to see it all, but nothing more. In multiplayer, it might be fun to have multiple bases, but even then it doesn't offer enough. Minecraft's redstone isn't minecraft's main part, but it exends the game to build huge fortresses. Here, the "redstone" (or technology in general) is the main part, but it's not enough to make for a full game.
I can't say what would make it better, but I'm sure that with more macro- and less micromanaging (cutting trees one by one isn't fun), it could be better. Maybe with real armies, it could be better. Maybe with things that make it worth exploring, it could be better.
But as it is, I can't really recommend this game. Minecraft offers so much more for roughly the same price, and if you want to be creative, this game isn't for you really: The optimal ways of doing things are too narrow.
It's simply not enough content: You're supposed to imagine your own content, your own story, your own plans.
Maybe it just needs some more work.
TL:DR:
+ Engineering
+ Sandbox
+ Optimization-Addiction
+ Better-than-average engine
- Train systems broken
- Not enough content
- Basically afk-able for half of the time
- No 3rd dimension (for a game of this kind, this really would have been nice if you have WASD controls)
I'd really the way the devs are working on this, and I'm happy to see a game that's actually not scamming with it's "Early Access"-title. However, we see a game that's not really a game yet (or just extremly simple), and even though I'd like to assume the devs continue expanding this game A WHOLE LOT (for it needs it), I can't help doubting it - Early Access still leaves paths open.
Conclusion:
At this point, I can't recommend this game and it's certainly not worth the hype, but it looks promising. If you're already familiar with these build-up games and have seen to many of them already, you'll get bored pretty quickly.
If you like these kinds of games, give Factorio a try - it's not a bad game.
But if you just saw the good reviews or the mainly positive Steam reviews, keep in mind that Factorio offers close to nothing contentwise - and I doubt that Factorio will be sellable at a much higher price than 20 bucks even in the future, so you should consider waiting for the final game to come out and read some reviews then.

The biggest complaint I have right now, other than the lag which was expected, is the lack of information and recognition by the company. At least let us know that you're working on the servers and you are aware of the problem right now. This way we're not sitting in limbo wondering when and if the servers are coming up.
IMC needs to work better on informing the community of what is going on and "TBD" like situations. I also agree with some and disagree with some of the things listed in this post.
I agree the trade limitation should be lifted from the premium players, but still be restricted for the free to play. If you don't want to support the game then I don't think you can rightfully complain about not being able to trade as a F2P user. Other games out there, like WoW, give 'trial' periods where you have limitations so why is this one so  different from other MMO's? Support the game and have your limitations lifted.
Gold sellers will always be a problem in MMO's. An idea I had to solve some of the smega spam is make them 11 for 10TP. However, this would only solve the problem for the gold spammers and now punish users who generally don't abuse smega's. The smega spam noticebly created heavy server lag.
I'm unsure the reasoning for why it would take 48 hours to receive your silver from the Marketplace. As a premium player this is kind of frustrating. Once you start selling items consistently the money doesn't stop flowing if you're a very active player. A shorter wait time on this would be a nice quality of life change to the game.
As for quests & cutscene's yes the developers need to start ironing out the kinks in this game. The current state of the game, when online, isn't unplayable. It's frustrating yes, but this is early access and some issues from iCBT still exists which is quite a let down.
Overall I think this game has great potential. The game is still young, yes this isn't iCBT, and moving forward will take time. If nothing is done in a timely manner I will consider quitting, unfortunately.
tl;dr - IMC has work to do and some things to consider.

Sacrifice is a beautiful, incredible, rich, and dangerously addicting game. The world oozes personality and its unique, almost alien charm will keep you coming back just to see what just might pop up next. With an all star voice cast a full decade before its likes could be considered the norm and gameplay unique but intuitive and natural, Sacrifice is a Real Time Strategy game like none other. Seeing it on Steam is like a dream come true, a truly innovative masterpiece of a game on the gold standard of online distribution services.
However, and it pains me to say this, you had best save your money. Sacrifice came out in the year 2000, and some systems may struggle to run it. I know mine did, and even now I experience crashes while loading the levels of this game. What's more, Steam's dashboard does not get along with Sacrifice, causing all manner of bugs and glitches whenever I bring it up. This review is to the game itself, however, and I would certainly advise more people to pick up Sacrifice, as it is a one of a kind experience, but it is not one currently optomized for Steam. I would advise those who enjoy this game to continue playing it and to share it and their experiences with others, and that those who have not played this game to try it and see for themselves just how amazing it is. I would also say that, in order for the consumers to truly get their money's worth, people look into updating Sacrifice, at least to the point where it can function within Steam.

Sacrifice is a bit hard to describe. It's an older game so don't expect much from the graphics. Sacrifice is an army-focused spell-casting game. You play as a wizard that summons creatures to create an army and fight other wizards. Your character comes from a dying world to a new world with five gods. Your wizard introduces himself, and starts selecting which of the god's quests he wants to complete.
What makes this game neat is that you can only choose 1 of the 5 quests, which makes that god like you more and the others dislike you, and the storyline spirals out from there. The same overarching storyline applies, but how you go about completing it and the way the story is told changes slightly depending on which god(s) you help. The five gods go from "Good" (Persephone) to "Evil" (Charnel), and it doesn't matter which one(s) you choose to do quests for. Besides the storyline shifting slightly, the god(s) you choose to assist will give you summon creatures and spells from their domain. For example, Persephone will give you healing spells that the other gods do not have, as well as Druids and Rangers, creatures only granted by Persephone. The game has a ton of re-playability because of the many combinations of choices you can make yielding entirely unique arsenals of creatures and spells for every playthrough.
I highly recommend this game as a unique experience for gamers, even if "army-based strategy RPG" doesn't sound that appealing to you.

Edit: And with a little bit of effort I finished all the achievements for the game with 3 playthroughs of the game - still playing with friends to help them progress through which remains enjoyable even after all the playtime.
When I first began this game, the common tale was that it was the "easiest" of the Souls series and that it just wasn't the same.  Looking back - I think it's just the shared mechanics in the games that make people say each one is the easiest because you've become a veteran of the series.  The increase in the number of bonfires may have made the experience slightly less frustrating but there were plenty of deaths and surprises to make up for it.
Now for the actual game's specifics.  Presentation is well done - each area feels unique albeit a bit dark at times but thematic areas definitely bring a rich atmosphere.  The boss entrance cinematics give you just a bit of time to absorb how awesome the boss is before you rush in and begin swinging.
The gameplay is well done - responsive and there doesn't really feel like there is a dump stat (Arguably VIT and equipment load is with the new linear scaling of equipment load with fewer break points than before) and progressing through the game legitimately shows you as a player getting better at the game.  Deaths and mechanics all seem fair after the initial set back of not knowing how to deal with it - but if I had to have a complaint about gameplay it would come down to multiplayer.  The multiplayer experience is great in the Souls games and invasions and covenants feed into this BUT the biggest drawback to the experience is hit detection in multiplayer even on the best of connections and machines.  I've had many cheap victories alongside those defeats where people are rolling or blocking or dodging and the game doesn't register hitboxes correctly.  Peer to Peer connections for multiplayer allows a nimber roguetype jumping around to get blasted by the slowest spell in the game which was clearly dodged. Rarely both machines seem to be running in sync and the experience works but more often than not it's frustrating rather than fun.
Sound / Music isn't too special outside of very few boss battles but there are enough audible queues that help you which promotes not blasting your own music while playing (atmospheric I suppose).
I still highly recommend this title to any who have never played a Souls game before and want the challenge that the game brings, you should probably take a gander at how the PvP/Multiplayer system works unless you really want to play the game offline (which is perfectly fesible) or avoid and research and just let the blows surprise you as they come (because that experience is priceless).

Absolutely wonderful. The art and music comes together wonderfully, the story is engrossing and the darker atmosphere is a nice change from Bastion. Combat consists of a hybrid hack n slash/strategy system, by using the turn() function to temporarily slow time and plan out your attack. Difficulty is scaled fairly well, challenging but not too hard (If you're struggling, use void() to buff your attack power, and if you'd prefer a challenge then enable some limiters). Make sure to check out all the OVC terminals, as Red uses them to communicate with the Transistor and Camerati. If you skip past them all, you'll miss a vast majority of the character development. Game also includes "Recurse" (aka new game plus) which allows you to replay the game while carrying over all unlocked skills, levels and limiters. In short, it's a masterpiece. If you buy a single indie game this year, make it this one.

If you have any respect for the visual and musical arts, you should buy this game.  It's beautiful.  You've probably heard that ad noseum, but it's true.
What's more, the combat and story are also good.  Though you do need to approach it with the right mindset.  As far as the combat goes, you really should use the optional "limiters" to increase the strategic depth of the fights.  That's when the combat system really shines.  Essentially the game starts on the easiest difficulty and gives you the option to make it harder at a faster rate when you gain levels.  Though if the main story leaves you wanting a little more fulfillment, the side challenges are fantastic and make great use of the combat.
As for the story, it's much more along the lines of a sci-fi short story than Bastion was, though it still has their very distinct method of narrative progression.  While it certainly shares a significant amount of the narrative structure from Bastion, it... This is kinda hard to explain, but it seems to me that Transistor is driven more by themes and ideas, whereas Bastion was driven more by relational emotion (emotion of relationships?).  That's not to say Transistor doesn't have a strong theme of relationship, it very much does, but it's quieter.  It stirs in the backdrop.  Once the big event has done its course, its brought in to the forefront as if the character is saying, "My only intention was ever this.  All else was coincidental, to me."
I've seen some reviews that said the ending was not very emtionally satisfying, but I think that's because (and this may be somewhat spoilerish, but should actually enhance your experience) the main character's goals are different from what the player might be tricked into thinking her goal is.
So yeah, I like it.

With a low price tag for a big title release, and a LOT of unlockable stuff, as well as some free DLC, Sonic forces is a good buy for someone with a love of the series. For new comers? Eh. It's janky, too fast at times, and admittedly they force you to play as other characters you might not want to be. Nothing really new there for complaints. Hecking fun customization though and some meeeeeaty feeling weapons (like the lovable cube). Story wise? Pretty much your standard fair, but with a nice throw back to the old comics and story roots with a resistance against the mechanical hordes of a tubby mustachioed mecha hitler.
If you have a huge nostalgia boner for those old Sonic era days and you want your multicoloured, awkward, bow tie wearing, custom character to come to life, this is the buy for you.

The game does have some flaws, such as the levels being shorter than they could've been and the gameplay can feel clunky at times. The story also doesn't feel like it was completed and I think there was a lot of potential for levels they could've added or expanded on, but overall I enjoyed playing the game. It might not be the best game out there, but you can definitely have some fun playing it.

"And when I'm playing Modern Sonic's 2D sections, I just wish I was playing as Classic Sonic, which means I just wish I was playing Mania.'
And he replied:

Buy Mania
Buy Generations
Get two better games for the same price.

Sonic Forces is not a perfect game; in fact, it has several very concrete flaws. Then again, which Sonic game doesn't? I thoroughly enjoyed the game despite its issues, if only for the visual spectacle and character moments. Oh, and the character creator. That stuff's very addicting to me.
1 out of the 30 levels it good, what went wrong???

Wispons seemed like a good idea until you unlock the "void" wispon, which not only destroys all enemies, but also grabs all nearby rings, resulting in big points for an easy S-rank. They could do with balancing that somehow. Overall, if you're a Sonic fan, you'll like it. If you feel like it's very little to do with Mania then, well... it's supposed to be.

Borderlands 2 is unexplainably fun to me; the act of violently murdering people shouldn't be this fun. But the randomly generated content, the pure gameplay itself, and the execution shows the great game for what it is. Maybe you shouldn't trust the company, but certainly trust this game to give you a very enjoyable time.

Despite a disgusting middle-eastern stereotype carried over from the first, Borderlands 2 is bigger and better in every way. Bigger maps, longer campaign, a more refined loot system and a bevy of quality DLC. My only real complaints would be the constant backtracking, radio messages overlapping each other, the tedious and glitchy inventory system, and *Stalkers*. Most obnoxious enemy ever designed.
Oh, and the screaming. There is far too much screaming in this game.
Still, if you liked the first, this is a must-buy. Per usual, the shooting mechanics gel perfectly. I loved playing as Zero but Maya eventually won me over with her invaluable Phase Lock skill. Some of the vistas here are truly breathtaking; you always feel like you are traversing a real, expansive, alien world. I don't know why some people decry the cartoony, cell-shaded graphics; they are an under-used and under-stated art form. There are loads of secrets and easter-eggs to discover, and while the humor is quite juvenile, I couldn't help but smirk.
Oh, and the most important improvement over the original? YOU CAN BOOT PEOPLE. No longer will you have to worry about foreigners joining your game, immediately bringing up their inventory screen and idling as children and angry grandmothers scream and bicker in the background.
8 out of 10, would throw a birthday party for an autistic robot in a back alley again.

While this game was a travesty when it released, (forcibly, might I add, by SEGA), they have culminated their efforts into this final release, titled "Emperor Edition".  This final release is just as good as, if not better than, any of the other releases in the Total War lineup.  With the very first integration of both Land and Sea battles at the same time, and the inclusion of naval invasions for the first time in this series' history, you have a very experimental, very enjoyable, tactical strategy simulation at your disposal.
The scope of the game is astounding, stretching from Great Britain all the way to far east Asia Minor.  The game pits you against all kinds of different obstacles, ranging from pikemen, legionaries, to chariots, and to elephants.  While it does have plenty of unit variety, it doesn't dissappoint with the AI either, so even if you're stuck in the same region and fighting the same armies, the AI will actually try to beat you instead of just going through the same routines, meaning you will not always fight armies that use the same tactics and strategies against you.  Indeed, you will find that the AI will experiment in trying to expose you and draw you out, sometimes successfully, sometimes unsuccussfully.  the main point being, this game does not rely on it's large swathe of units in order to entertain, as it has the tactical capability to back up the gameplay.
The AI can get a little troubled during sieges, but that has been present in every total war, but it seems to be working best this time around, as the AI actually uses its siege equipment, instead of just staring at you like in Medieval 2.
The tech tree is fully expanded and very interesting, along with improved diplomacy, economy management, government management, and army management.  Battles provide new options for defense, such as laying traps, and with the new vision mechanic, you really can never be too careful, as the AI can easily hide itself, out of your view, and surprise you with a counter attack from over a hill.
It's hard to describe every aspect of this game without going on and on.  This was clearly the game that they meant to release originally, and had they, it would've been recieved much better than it was.

When I first began this game, the common tale was that it was the "easiest" of the Souls series and that it just wasn't the same.  Looking back - I think it's just the shared mechanics in the games that make people say each one is the easiest because you've become a veteran of the series.  The increase in the number of bonfires may have made the experience slightly less frustrating but there were plenty of deaths and surprises to make up for it.
Now for the actual game's specifics.  Presentation is well done - each area feels unique albeit a bit dark at times but thematic areas definitely bring a rich atmosphere.  The boss entrance cinematics give you just a bit of time to absorb how awesome the boss is before you rush in and begin swinging.
The gameplay is well done - responsive and there doesn't really feel like there is a dump stat (Arguably VIT and equipment load is with the new linear scaling of equipment load with fewer break points than before) and progressing through the game legitimately shows you as a player getting better at the game.  Deaths and mechanics all seem fair after the initial set back of not knowing how to deal with it - but if I had to have a complaint about gameplay it would come down to multiplayer.  The multiplayer experience is great in the Souls games and invasions and covenants feed into this BUT the biggest drawback to the experience is hit detection in multiplayer even on the best of connections and machines.  I've had many cheap victories alongside those defeats where people are rolling or blocking or dodging and the game doesn't register hitboxes correctly.  Peer to Peer connections for multiplayer allows a nimber roguetype jumping around to get blasted by the slowest spell in the game which was clearly dodged. Rarely both machines seem to be running in sync and the experience works but more often than not it's frustrating rather than fun.
Sound / Music isn't too special outside of very few boss battles but there are enough audible queues that help you which promotes not blasting your own music while playing (atmospheric I suppose).
I still highly recommend this title to any who have never played a Souls game before and want the challenge that the game brings, you should probably take a gander at how the PvP/Multiplayer system works unless you really want to play the game offline (which is perfectly fesible) or avoid and research and just let the blows surprise you as they come (because that experience is priceless).

Sacrafice is a great game.  If there's ever been a "overlooked game that deserves a sequal" it's this one.
The graphics actually hold up still, they were absolutely the top of the line at the time is likely why.  The only thing that bugged me in a recent replaythrough about them was ingame there isn't lipsync.  That said, the gods themselves have prerendered animation that looks great still.
Recognize the protagonist's voice?  Yeah, he's the guy who did the voice of the warrior in the first Diablo and Aldaris in Starcraft.  Yeah, he's badass.  Also one of the gods is voiced by TIm Curry.
Something a lot of people might overlook is the world has some incredible lore put into it.  It feels like it might be a game out of a long standing fantasy book series, but it's not.  The game is also home home to one of the biggest plot twists in gaming.
If it has any faults, its that the difficulty is a bit uneven.  Some levels are stupid hard, some don't challenge you at all.  The RTS elements have some faults, I personally find it hard to do all the actions they set out to have.  It's generally easier to jsut have all your creatures guard you and sweep the field than it is to strategically move units around the map.  Things are a bit too fast paced for advanced strategy and it want to be near your units to collect their souls when they die too.
That said, tenattaten, 10/10, best game, best game.

Finally, another 3d Sonic game. And I have pros and cons to show what this game is. This game is amazing. A lot of people complain about this game being 2d/too linear. Personally, I don't mind the 2d, and yes, sections of levels can seem linear. However, it for some reason feels cool, I guess to run in a straight path while going fast. The custom character is an amazing feature, which I at first thought was dumb, but now I realize it's amazing. Your character's Wispon (weapons) are all unique, and you will find yourself changing Wispons amoung your avatar. I feel like Sonic Team also improved on the Classic Sonic gameplay, even though I thought it was pretty good in Generations. With the addition of the dropdash, a move from Sonic Mania, Classic Sonic can go fsater/gain momentum faster. The spindash is still in the game, but I find myself using the dropdash a lot more.
Overall:
Pros:
-Great soundtrack
-Great story (for the most part)
-Good voice acting
-Amazing gameplay
-Good balances between Stages (except maybe there could've been a few more Classic Sonic levels. I know not a lot of people like Classic Sonic stages, but this is just my opinion)
-Good variety of outfits/Wispons for your Avatar.
-TONS OF REPLAY VALUE, whether it's getting S ranks or getting the collectibles in stages.
Cons:
-I loved the story, but the end seemed a bit rushed, along with the game being about 3.5-4.5 hours, I wish it were longer.
- Not a lot of Classic Sonic Levels, which can be a good thing for those against Classic Sonic, but since I didn't mind him, I wish there were more levels of his playstyle.
-There is a duplicate of a boss, marked as a separate boss, wasting a level spot.
-(Not sure if this is a con, because it can work either way, but there are unlimited lives, making the game seem easy, however, it can be a good thing, too because it can cause less rageful moments).
Overall Score: 9.5/10

The hook of Borderlands 2, the very reason that I found myself thinking about it when I worked or tried to fall asleep, is the loot. Guns, ammo, character skins, grenade mods, class mods -- there’s always something just a bit better, something you so desperately didn’t even know you needed until you found it in Borderlands 2. Just like Diablo or a number of other action RPGs, the hunt for loot becomes intoxicating because of the tiny rush you get each time a rare colored item spills out of a chest or is dropped by a recently slain enemy. Every firefight and intense boss battle becomes all the more rewarding, because, though you might die a few times and want to crush something near you in real life, it suddenly feels like everything is going to be OK when you’re blasting away enemies with a newly looted gun.
Guns really do make up the bulk of the loot, and that’s great because you’re going to spend most of your time in Borderlands 2 staring down a gun sight. No matter the quest, at some point something or someone is getting pounded with lead. Thankfully, snappy shooting and lots of environmental hazards combine with each class’s unique ability to turn every skirmish into a playground. You simply have to decide the best -- or most entertaining -- way to kill everyone.

As a preface, I would like to state that SuperGiant's previous game, 'Bastion,' is one of my favourite games of all time. If I present an obvious bias or compare the two games on unfair grounds, then I appologise in advance.
First let us discuss what Transistor does right. The gameplay presented is the same isometric world navigation that was apparant in Bastion, the major difference being its approach to combat. It abandons the hectic run-and-gun/hammer skirmishes of the former and instead takes a far more intelligent plan and execute method. The player can temporarily pause time and plan out their battle strategy before hitting the pause button again and watching it play out at lightning speeds. The numerous variaties of enemies and the layouts of the battlefields provide ample chances to scratch that 'General Chessmaster' itch. The massive amount of weapons (called 'functions()') alsoadd to the tactical depth of this game. Each weapon can be equiped in one of four wepon slots, where it functions normally, firing lasers, dropping bombs etc. Each weapon may also be assigned to either a passive slot, providing you a powerful, perk-like bonus, or to an upgrade slot, in which one weapon buffs the other (LASERS THAT ALSO DROP BOMBS!?). The amount of combinations is truely staggering and will be greatly apprieciated by gamers who like a more intelligent approach to their combat (myself included).
Next the art style. Although the more charming cartoon-like character proportions from Bastion are gone in favor of a more realistic-(ish) art style, the vibrant colours and tones make a glorious return. The mood and the tone of various scenes are masterfully enchanced by use of reccuring temperatures and unique art assets. The forboding height of Coudbank City, as presented soon after the beggining of the game, is alleviated by the cool yellow and blue lighting, giving it a more distant, lonesome feeling, to give one example.
And the soundtrack, oh my, the soundtrack. I was so thrilled to hear that Darren Korb would be returning and boy does he deliver in the audio department. Echoing guitar riffs and droning synthesizers, alongside beautifully melancholic vocals do wonders to nail the sad, lonely cyberpunk feel that is so greatly apprieciated by big nerds such as myself. Particular standouts for me are 'In Circles,' 'Forecast' and 'The Spine.'
And now to cover what I personally was let down by. The story. WAIT! Allow me to expand. (No spoilers don't fret!) The characters themselves are very nicely portrayed, with excellent moments of individual characterisation, but I took issue with the game's plot, its over-arching story. You are dropped right into the world with zero idea of who these characters are, where you are, or what the hell is going on in general. 'But that happened in Bastion too!' I hear you shout. Yes you woke up in a floating bed in Bastion with zero understanding of what was happening, but this created a sense of wonder as the game's  plot was quickly given to you, (The world blew up, but the Bastion can fix it) and as you progressed the world, characters and other various story flavor was gradually revealed to you in satisfying amounts from level to level. And most importantly by the game's end all questions had been answered. This is not the case with Transistor. Although it does a good job with the aforementioned characterisation and also with the same story flavor being drip fed to you, major components of the the plot are flat out not explained, which frustrated me greatly as it gave me difficulty in understanding vital things such as character motivations. These questions are also not addressed, or at least not in any way a near satisfactory level, by the games end. The final boss in particular was very confusing for me, the fight itself comes out of nowhere and takes place in a very strange location and I found myself thinking 'WHAT THE HELL IS HAPPENING? WHY ARE WE FIGHTING NOW? WHERE-WHA-BUT I DIDN'T.........' and soon after the fight the game ends. The ending itself is rather emotional, but I couldn't get into the mood the game wanted me to due to my extreme frustration and confusuion owing to the fact that the credits were rolling and my questions had not been answered. Now I'm not some fool who only enjoys simple by-the-numbers stories, I understand that not all questions need to be answered, but jesus christ SOME would have been nice. Thematically , the game is not as strong as Bastion. It is clearly attempting to make commentary on topics such as the irrelevance of an individual in a system, and the fickleness of the general public but it falls flat if suitable context is not provided.
To summerise: Wonderfully cereberal combat with powerfull art and sound direction that is only let down by its adequately explained story. Or maybe I'm just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.

My time played on record only shows single player activity, as STEAM separates the two (single and multiplayer).  My total time played in Multiplayer is 970 hours.
Update: Now that the game is infested with hackers, I can no longer recommend it.  It isn't a rare to end up in a hacked lobby which will do anything from deranking you to altering your unlocks to changing settings in your mp config file.  Playing the game requires keeping backups of all your stats and MP files.  More information about this can be found in the forums, so if you are considering the game at this point, be sure to inform yourself about all of the serious issues affecting it.  It may not be worth the hassle.
Is the game playable and fun? Sure. And in some instances, when you find a good host and players who want to have an enjoyable time without noob tubes, commando, or other nonsense, it can be really fun. But just beware, it's infested with hacked lobbies, people running exploits, and a less than respectable community. If you can stomach all that, you can find fun in it.
*Original Review:
Quick pacing and nonstop action keeps you moving forward to the inevitable end game of the single player at around a 5 to 8 hour completion time. This is good if you are looking to jump into playing an hour or so at a time as each chapter of the campaign is relatively short. The action on display is compelling and the thrilling score, outstanding militaristic dialogue, and visceral imagery keep things constantly engaging. The story, as epically scaled as it may be, is a little too contrived. Modern Warfare 2 decides to up the ante with a full scale invasion of the United States. The U.S. is under siege and the stakes are high.  It is unfortunate then that the reasoning behind the whole ordeal, while tragic, is somewhat farfetched. The multiplayer is excellent, yes, with superb shooter mechanics and fluid gameplay.  It is also somewhat rage inducing.  Prepare to be noob tubed to kingdom come. That aside, it is fast and great fun.

Core gameplay here is fun, but overall the game is lazy, and its kinda dissapointing. The boss fights are copy/pasted
so its kinda annoying considering how sonic team knows they're in a bad situation and need to put a lot of effort into the game.
The Avatar segments are a lot better than i expected, they are fun and add a nice bit of variety to the game.
Classic Sonic Segments are dissapointing, he has is speed limited extremely slow for some reason and the only way to get past this is to spin dash/drop dash.
Modern sonic still follows the "Boost2Win" formula of past games, but its harder to get your boost gauge up now because its only filled with wisps and enemies and not rings. so you can find yourself slowing down to do platforming sections and its a nice change of pace.  The Inclusion of the Lost World Double jump is annoying, it's an addition we diddnt need, and should be reverted back to the Homing Attack, There were many times where i was jumping a gap and went to homing attack to make it, but isntead double jumped and died was insane. Why however, Modern sonic STILL has 2D segments when Classic Sonic is in the game (Who only exists for 2D gameplay) was baffling in Generations, and its still baffling now.
The story is layed out really well, the ability to go straight back to older stages is great, and the way you play stages is one of the best layouts i have seen in a sonic game. The charector variety though is a bit strange, you play One short Modern Sonic stage, then you play 2 Avatar stages, then a Classic Sonic Stage, before playing as Modern Sonic again, and then its a short, dumb downed boss fight
then you go back to more avatar stages. so thats a bit frustrating.
But the worst thing overall for me is that two of the "Box Art Bossess" (Shadow and Chaos) you dont even fight. Shadow you get given an explaination, but it still would have been nice to fight him, they even threw away the perfect oppourtunity to have a throwback to SA2 and fight Shadow in the Jungle area, and recreate that fight, which would have played on nostalgia, and made a lot of fans happy.
Then we have the Chaos Boss Fight...Which never happens, Chaos himself, totally dissapears, hes there at the very beginning of the game
and then he dissapears until the very end of the game
and thats the only two times you see Chaos! And he was a poster boss for the game! Again showing us how lazy Sonic Team got with this game.
Bosses are dissporpotionate also, Metal sonic is 8 times bigger than Sonic in the fight, and they do exactly the same thing later with the infinite fight. (the one thats copy/pasted from the Metal Fight) so that again shows the lack of polish that was shown with the game.

With all that said, its the age old story of sonic games "Needs More Polish" but its a step in the right direction at the very least.  Personally im enjoying the gameplay, but i enjoyed Unleashed and Generations Gameplay too, The storyline is a bit short and it doesnt even take long to 100% (Ive done it in about 12 hours) But if you liked "Boost2Win" Games, you'll enjoy this.

Sonic Forces is quite a trivial matter when it comes to what was expected and what I got. There are many arguments you can make for this game good or bad. For example, the avatar character aspect of the game was very well worked on and the customizability of your avatar is great but the execution of how the cosmetics and weapons the character gets was less than favorable. Forces is honestly not that bad of a game when you sift out the superficial, but it shows something potentially dire that is becoming much clearer to me as someone who has seen Sonic evolve through the years.
What the game excels at is providing a very beautiful looking landscape, backdrop, and stages, discarding the fact that most stages were re-used. Plant life was abundant and detailed, metal surfaces could be rusted or look shined and polished, the death egg itself looked very bright and electronically complicated in a good way. Also, as an example, seeing that globe like power core of sorts at the end of Classic Sonic's stage helped capture the scope of the death egg as a space station built for war. As mentioned previously, another good aspect of the game is the avatar character customization. There was an abundance of cosmetics available as well as many specific parts of the character that you could work with. The cosmetics also range from out of the box ideas that would appeal to many different people with accessories like backpacks, a camera, or even themed shirts for each of the major characters. Looking over everything else I can be safe to say that the game itself has had a general improvement compared to previous titles
What I see lacking with the game is most importantly the consistency of the plot and the things that seem left alone that honestly need an answer to them. There is a large amount of moments that left more questions than answers and to avoid spoilers I won't mention a specific instance. And, there were moments that were cop outs where a cutscene would have done better. Classic Sonic has a strange momentum vibe with his physics as well as the speed shoe use seems extremely short. Modern Sonic seems to have the most improvement to me in control compared to other boosting Sonic moments in earlier games. The character wispons are large in variety but that also applies to the balance they have between to each other.
What I am afraid to wonder is if some or a majority Sonic Team have become incredibly fatigued with the process of making Sonic in general, but I like to think that this game was better or a step towards the right directions with Sonic. The most troubling thing I found with Forces is that in the end, I feel like the 'Buddy' really did not have a choice when it came to him/her fading out of the plot in the end. Probably because, the plot had to have continuity and have the character fade back into the populous. But, this among other things in the game destroys the remaining immersion that the player who put the time into this avatar and feel touched or included with the Sonic Universe with.
The final verdict from me though is that I can say I really enjoyed Sonic Forces in the end, the game did better than I expected but, I can note that it was a shorter experience. I got my money’s worth and I do hope to see what both the modding community and potential is for official DLC that may show up for Forces in the future. While this game was a travesty when it released, (forcibly, might I add, by SEGA), they have culminated their efforts into this final release, titled "Emperor Edition".  This final release is just as good as, if not better than, any of the other releases in the Total War lineup.  With the very first integration of both Land and Sea battles at the same time, and the inclusion of naval invasions for the first time in this series' history, you have a very experimental, very enjoyable, tactical strategy simulation at your disposal.
The scope of the game is astounding, stretching from Great Britain all the way to far east Asia Minor.  The game pits you against all kinds of different obstacles, ranging from pikemen, legionaries, to chariots, and to elephants.  While it does have plenty of unit variety, it doesn't dissappoint with the AI either, so even if you're stuck in the same region and fighting the same armies, the AI will actually try to beat you instead of just going through the same routines, meaning you will not always fight armies that use the same tactics and strategies against you.  Indeed, you will find that the AI will experiment in trying to expose you and draw you out, sometimes successfully, sometimes unsuccussfully.  the main point being, this game does not rely on it's large swathe of units in order to entertain, as it has the tactical capability to back up the gameplay.
The AI can get a little troubled during sieges, but that has been present in every total war, but it seems to be working best this time around, as the AI actually uses its siege equipment, instead of just staring at you like in Medieval 2.
The tech tree is fully expanded and very interesting, along with improved diplomacy, economy management, government management, and army management.  Battles provide new options for defense, such as laying traps, and with the new vision mechanic, you really can never be too careful, as the AI can easily hide itself, out of your view, and surprise you with a counter attack from over a hill.
It's hard to describe every aspect of this game without going on and on.  This was clearly the game that they meant to release originally, and had they, it would've been recieved much better than it was.

Factorio sets you upon an alien world, crash landing with only a few resources to start you on your way you quickly find the world around you to be hostile but not completely without its charm. You set off building and automating your entire process from top to bottom as your knowledge grows so does your base and its complexities. The game introduces new and ever exciting machines to help you achieve your goals but at a pace that isn’t overwhelming. The sheer number of ways one can build and automate a level allows for a great reply value.
Pros:
-	The city building part of this game is amazing and quite a change from most games in this genre, concentrating more on the industrial side of things more than any other I’ve seen.
-	Allows the player free roam over the map to build and grow however they see fit.
-	The sheer number of technologies at your disposal make for a ever complex set of bases at your fingertips
Cons:
-	The enemies are nothing more than mindless drones that attack in waves every so often allowing you to ignore them almost completely once you get your defense set up.
-	The story line, all be it not bad, doesn’t really add anything to the game or the level as they are pretty much all they same, build and defeat and repeat.
In conclusion, Factorio is a very fun industry builder game that allows you automate your entire work force from the ground up however you see fit, allowing countless hours of enjoyment to be had and a great deal of replayable value. 3.5 Out of 5

To this day this game remains the standard I compare adventure and survival games to, especially in the open-world non-linear category. Other reviews will use the term "ahead of its time" and in many ways they are right, but the term I wish to emphasize is "Masterpiece".
I don't know how I came across this game, I think my bestie told me to check it out sometime back in 2006/7; after finally acquiring it, putting a few hours in, I realized that I have been feeling something I hadn't felt since my Freshman year roommate presented me with Fallout 2 back in 2000. (Yes I've played Bethesda's Fallout games, yes they are enjoyable, well-made and recommended, but the bottom line is that I compare FO3/FO4 to Stalker, and Stalker did it better, end of argument).
I have played it a total of 7 times since 2007, meticulously finishing all the unique side quests and story-lines, and on a number of occasions, playing one of the overhaul project mods that add tons of content and fix the vanilla issues I remember suffering through playing back in 2007. Yes, I suffered from the stupid decision to release the game before it was completed, but it is so good I went ahead and played it any ways! There were many frustration moments back then, and I learned valuable lessons about Hard Saves and questing management, so if you haven't played the game, I envy you, because you will get to enjoy this Masterpiece after it has ages splendidly.
I'll start with the Cons:
-You shouldn't play the Vanilla, not when excellent overhaul mod projects exist. The game has been patched by the original development team but there are still some bugs that can be really annoying.
-This game will test your limits, both in patience and resilience, mirroring in a way the plight of the protagonist. There will be moments when you jump scared, and others when you jump screaming in rage.
-This is an FPS game, so shooting is mostly how you solve your problems. The trick to thinking outside the box is how to circumvent your problem so you won't have to shoot in the first place (or shoot a lot less)! Don't expect much from the dialogue resolution options nor expect high levels of stealth options in missions, but sneaking around can both be useful and rewarding!
Pros:
-Immersive, beautiful and haunting. It's not a huge world, which allows you to truly bond with each location as many locations will be revisited so many times as you quest and adventure on.
-Strong story-line, lore and voice casting. Just the right amount of Sci-Fi-Realism fusion.
-A user-friendly interface and control system that doesn't concern itself with console 'peasants' (Sorry Bethesda, but your UI needs serious remodeling, it's the main reason I stopped playing your games)
-Great gun action, great thriller moments, heart-pounding narrow-escapes. Gun handling feels authentic, combat is exhilarating.
-The game ages like fine wine, with texture mods and 1080p support you won't believe this is an 8 years old game coming from the Ukraine.
I'm tired, and hungry, go play the game if you haven't, you'd be a fool not to!

A big step up from iRO imo, and that's saying a lot cos that was my first childhood MMORPG. The detail is gorgeous as it is immersive, the combat much more dynamic and interesting, classes completely customizable, character costumes as opposed to currently class only appearance, sprites are reminiscent of iRO with new and improved hairstyles and achievement unlocked dye options, and of course collectible kawaii headgear. I've seen complaints about the lack of customization, like hair colour and the various styles aren't enough, but I personally think it's great that the devs focused on the seemingly endless options of class and skill customization rather than eye colour or different faces. Stand out by being great at or finding your combination of skills ffs. Nobody is going to care if you have bunny ears and pink hair or a special outfit if you can't even hold your own past lvl 30.
The next thing I'm seeing is the complaints about gold sellers, whichever course I would have to agree with. However, every game has bots and gold sellers especially upon release. We have to remember that the game is technically still in beta. We have to have faith that by true release, the GMs will be in better supply and have more tools and a system set in place to tackle this problem. Until then, just turn shout chat off as I have, tab back in when you need something, use the block feature at your disposal, and instead focus on the game and have fun sans shout chat until then.
That's my singular complaint about this game though- everything else is wonderful. I'm starting to see a pattern with the cry babies that were already complaining before the game was released that are the same ones complaining now about completely irrelevant things. This is a beta. Yes you bought the game, but along with in-game perks, you bought early open access. Hang in there, dry your tears, have mommy make you some pizza rolls, and just wait for the devs to catch up and fix the issues. Creating, coding, marketing, and releasing a game is hard work. The devs obviously care and have heeded the fanbase's advice so far, and I'm sure they'll continue to do so.

Don't make my mistake. Don't buy this game. Get Mania instead if you haven't already.
The good, the bad, the ugly.
First, the good:
Uhhhhhh....
-Sonic Team made a game without Dimps.
There, there's the good.
Now, the bad:
-Denuvo
-Controls respond incorrectly
-Homing attack sees all, knows all, doesn't care that you're not in a position to homing-attack an enemy and are trying to double jump onto a platform.
-ALMOST NO GAMEPLAY CONTENT. You have 30 stages total that actually matter. 6 of these are boss battles. These stages are played in 7 zones. This wouldn't be so bad except they're all bad. I'll explain in the ugly.
-There are 6 side-mission stages, or "secret stages", but they're horrible and they only exist to unlock more wispons. Otherwise, all you have is Burst.
-There are missions encouraging you to replay the stages and do certain things, which would otherwise be good, but these are just to get more DeviantArt clothes.
The ugly:
-Episode Shadow. 3 stages, crappy prequel story for DeviantArt villain, and barely even frigging PLAYABLE. You know that homing attack glitch I mentioned above? Try that with Phantom Ruby bullet hell.
-Mania Sonic gameplay in Forces is horribad beyond belief. HOW DO YOU MESS THIS UP, SEGA? You had Sonic Mania to look at and say "Yeah, our Classic Sonic gameplay should be like this. Get on it, team." It's slippery, the acceleration is glitchy, and SO MANY THINGS GO WRONG! Not to mention 2D mode does NOT support the d-pad. I know the d-pad on Xbox controllers isn't the best, but you really need it here, where platforming accuracy is a must. It's not just Classic Sonic either. They're all slippery, and I suspect Classic Sonic is just playing Modern in 2D mode with Spindash enabled and Double Jump, Homing Attack, and Boost disabled.
-With a Shadow the Hedgehog's Potty Mouth rating of E-10, why can't Sonic swear? I hear a lot of characters, actually, NOTICEABLY holding back their language, but every time I hear Roger say "butt" it sounds like he's being warned not to swear WHILE HE'S RECORDING. It's rated E10 for Edgies 10 And Up. Roger, you can swear in E10-rated games.
-Infinite. Nuff said.
-Sections that take control away penalize you for the scripted gameplay falling off the stage.
-Water slide frequently removes the ONE AXIS of control you actually have during the slide, causing a death.
-It gets hard to tell when you have control and when you don't. It's like if you had an expensive yuppie car and turned on its driver assist to get properly parked, it said "Take your prissy hands off the wheel, child, I'll handle it" and then it just runs you into oncoming traffic and stops controlling itself. But in Forces' case, you didn't have a choice to do it manually.

Ultimately, it's not an awful game, but it's not good either.
Coming off the heels of "Sonic Mania" (aka Sega literally gave Sonic fans the ability to make their own Sonic game) and Nintendo putting out "Super Mario Odyssey" really didn't help frame Sonic Team in a good light.
There just seemed to be a lack of focus and missed potential everywhere. Overall control wasn't as tight as Colors, Unleashed and Generations (still the best 3D Sonics of this decade). You had to be five miles away to homing attack. Far weaker level design had boost sections that sent you off the stage or didn't come with helpful signalling. Weapons were weak or broken with little in-between. Characters unceremoniously exited stage left or didn't even have proper boss fights, and there was never enough time to get attached to anything. Finally Classic Sonic had no real reason to be there and shaved off some needed time in the oven. It's a mess, but it's not an unplayable mess. The low points don't crash the game or have auto-run sections that rocket you off a cliff. Okay, not a good standard to hold to, but Sonic's been far worse.
Though there's one completely-subjective high point to Forces, and that's the main idea that was lost in the muddle, your own Sonic OC. If you can dial back to your inner cringe-worthy 13 year old and throw away the notion of having to look cool like some Faker, you can enjoy its criminally short playtime with full childhood whimsy. Because let's be honest, what teen DIDN'T have his or her OC be this total badass who saved Mobius from an ultimate evil in a dark and serious fanfic?
That's when what fun there can be had kicks in. The game looks and sounds gorgeous, and while your avatar is limited (wish it took a page from big MMOs) there's so many different outfits you can design. I spun around in my chair thinking, "What else can I make? What other cool, cute, or edgy furry can my imagination crank out?". Run some missions, and marvel at the haul of gear. "Geez I wish I could share this with other players!" (Another missed opportunity) When I stepped back, I realized I was 13 again and loving it. Each new creation had a dark and angsty backstory, a god among furries dominating the laughable enemies in rich landscapes to the tune of cheesy toe-tappers. You know how all those lame Buzzfeed-tier content aggregates always like to call to the "good old days"? Well, forget some trite shotglasses featuring the Kanto Pokemon starters, we're going raw childhood, the good, the bad, and the ugly. "Sonic Forces" lets you tap into that in an authentic way Unilad, WatchMojo, and co could never hope to achieve even if it fails to stick the landing.
Well, if only this could have been more. Maybe get it if it's on sale and/or you're really sold on the Avatar. If I were to grade it, I'd say C-.

Surprised as I was, after many years of keeping an eye out for a decent Hunting game, one comes along that I can not stop playing. It seems to be designed for hunters; as the attention to detail and customs are kept alive in this stunning open world hunting sim experience.
(+) My positive thoughts first.
The game simply pulls you back-in time and again, this is mainly due to the sense of freedom acheived with very large open landscapes were you can freely explore.
The feel of the experience is well balanced, tracking can be both hard and easy after walking a mile you might not see an animal, yet the anticipation of maybe seeing more is what makes a hunt and that final meeting when it comes.
Sounds, weather, lighting are all stunning in these huge environments, with steam riseing after a heavy downpoor for example. I stood still in the forest to count the sounds I could hear and came to about 12 seperate sounds; birds, insects, wind in the trees, twigs breaking, a distant call of a deer etc etc etc, yet together it was just right for that area. a little further and the sounds keep your senses hightened. The tracking system is clever and you start with all you need.
The equipment rely feels of the quality it should and there are lots to choose from.
Plenty of new content including a new bio, were you can climb a mountain, yes the game can go that far.
You can do missions freely or hunt with friends, were you go and what you see is up to you alone.
You can try the game free of charge and get a low powered rifle, bow, tracker, Deer caller and binoculars etc to start with, yet you are limited to shooting the Mule deer found on a not so little island. There are loads of missions for the many types of animals you might find and with a little story behind each one.
(-)
One or two catches to be aware of! You will want more; the large animals, the bears etc Yet it costs to branch out in this game and everything costs money. I found you can expect to pay a total of 27 Euro for 6 months fun, that includes a better rifle and a tent. Yet they will try to get more money from you with all the extra equipment you might not need, so watch your money; as I found out  that buying large equipment CAN NOT BE USED/PLACED in a MP game with a freind! There is no warning for this and after seeing your freind use a "Treepod" you will want one too... so only when you try to deploy it, is when you are told you can not. Crazy right. Complaints will not get you very far, yet I was told that they were looking into this without a "Time-frame" for it as yet.
The other HUGE disapointment is that you will have to buy your bullets, YES you heard right. The company is pritty tight, they have set a price on stupid items like the ammo and wind detectors, even having special types of ammo and even charge for .22 air riflr pellets = 35 ems as there called.
So what does this game cost? You ask!
After you try the free experience, you might want more like me, this is what you can expect it to cost and why using in-game money called ems translated to Euro:
a/ 6 month sign up =  18.99 Euro  1 year = 35 Euro. Yet they do have a 3 month = 10 Euro to try.
b/ A decent rifle for most animals 450 ems - 100 ems = 4 Euro
c/ A tent, yes you will need one, the areas are HUGE and a tent can be a spawn point as well as an equipment point 550 ems = 4 Euro. The problem is that you might need more than one later on, due to the many fine places.

So, before I even go into any variation of explanation / input, it should be noted that this game has no angle of PvE. At all. If you intend to play this game alone, in a non-competitive manner or simply want to build castles in a medieval sandbox game, look elsewhere. This game and everything about it is, well, competition. If you cannot deal with loss, whether you had opportunity to deter it or not, don't bother. Fair warning given.
---
Combat: Simplified / not as polished, Chivalry-like combat with a limb and parts health limitation. That said, I'm not complaining. Blocking, countering and general combat is simple and easy to grasp. Gear makes a pretty decent difference but a skilled player can and will easily out do a person with superior gear.
Map: It's actually perfect, for now. The resource nodes for important materials are in locations that actually demand eventual conflict. The map itself actually looks pretty damn good and the map's size isn't anything that I personally can complain about. Players should have no problems establishing castles or hovels around the map.
General Gameplay: As I said with the paragraph above, it's all competitive play. People will screw you over and given the opportunity, you can, should and probably will do the same. Don't come into the game expecting to be untouchable and don't come into the game alone. These things considered, it's a really entertaining game to play with friends. A few bugs do exist here and there but, it's Alpha. The hell do you expect?
- It should be noted that they've begun arming admin staff with methods of effectively removing players that are using hacked clients. If you are genuinely having issues with hackers and the sort, I suggest NOT playing on official servers. Instead, look into a community server with generally active and competent admin staff.

One of the best games of all time. Many of you will skim over this because you've never heard of it, because none of your friends play it or because of its sparse store page. You shouldn't.
Sacrifice offers the best mix of tactical depth and ease of learning I have ever seen in a strategy game. You play as a wizard standing down on the field where everything happens. Any units you summon are summoned directly next to you, buildings are created only by you standing next to them (for up to 10 seconds for the largest buildings), and orders are given based on what you can personally see. This makes for a much more immersive and easy-to-grasp gameplay than most other strategy games out there where you may be queuing up orders, units and buildings; might be zoomed far enough out  to be disconnected from the world but not far enough out to see any useful distance.
Furthermore, the wizards you can choose from in multiplayer (you always play as Eldred in the fully-voiced campaign) are all equal. That is, everyone you might play against has access to the exact same spells and units as you. Or rather they have access to the same choices: your spell and unit lists are fully customizable offering a massive amount of variation possible. You could have ranged units that damage over time, can go invisible, can track enemies etc. Or you could pick units based on style if you prefer and do just fine: disease-ridden monsters, aloof mythical creatures, rangers, soldiers, constructs...
This customisation is in the campaign too but in a much more organic style so that you won't have to worry about choosing units based on no previous experience. Every level of the game has 5 alternatives (one for each of the gods) and each god will try to convince you the help them for each mission. You can decide who to help on a mission-by-mission basis, picking the most interesting or beneficial mission for you. You can become unwaveringly loyal to a particular god (or a certain alliance between 2 or more gods) and only server them. Or you can decide completely randomly if you like. Every mission you take increases your pool of spells or units equally, with units and spells granted by the god you choose to work for. You can also pick up heroes along the way who will be loyal to you (unless you do something completely against their nature) and will follow you in future missions until they die or you lose their trust. Every mission you choose (and don't choose) affects future levels to varying degrees. By making a god's defence stronger you protect their territory that another god or being was after and would've been able to use in future levels. Discovering something allows the god you discovered it for use that information in future battles. Capturing a village, building, character, area etc. will give the benefits of that asset to your god (whether that be a new factory, new allies, a weakness in another god or a number of other boons). This all leads to your character and the world evolving organically in a way that's not always obvious but always makes sense. By the end of your fifth mission you'll have access to a wide variety of spells and units (and perhaps a hero or two) and certain gods will have grown or diminished in power noticeably.
All of the spells are breathtaking. From the bog-standard heal and speed-up spells you begin with which create a pleasant glow/melody and a cool-looking trail effect respectively. To the more extreme spells granted later on including tornados, volcanos, earthquakes, death-incarnate and many more. In addition, most of these spells can be cast within a couple of seconds and without stopping. This allows you to run amidst your army healing, speeding up and buffing who you need, sniping an important enemy unit (or a bunch of them) and then hiding behind your own units again within a very short period of time. A lot of these spells (and some units) scare the landscape permanently too. This makes places where small skirmishes and large battles have occurred very obvious, even after 5, 10 or 60 minutes. Scorch marks, blood stains, unnatural bumps or dips in the earth, sometimes even the earth itself has gone.
The penultimate thing will mention (even though there is so much more I could say) is that the humour in this game is incredible from start-to-finish. From the gods (voiced by Brad Garrett, Kevin Michael  Richardson, Castulo Guerra, Jennifer Hale and Tim Curry) to the units (every one of which with the sole exception of the manahor (an armless, mana-dispensing bunny) has a half-dozen lines if you enjoy clicking on a unit repeatedly long enough for it to yell at you to get lost) to the wizards. This game has so much personality and not in an annoying way.  The humor interlaces with the rest of the game beautifully instead of being forced like in so many other games.
Lastly, this game is worth your money and time without question. Without exaggeration I have played through the campaign seven times with a vastly different playthrough and experience each time: once following each of the gods wholeheartedly, once working for all of the gods and keeping them all as friendly with me as possible for as long as possible and once attempting to keep a pair of gods powerful and friendly with each other until the end.
At £7 it's worth it easily, at half-price (as it is at the time of this review) I can't recommend it more to everyone I know. Get it, it's awesome.
-Edit- There isn't much more I can say about this game before I nominate it. It's great, get it now.

DISCLAIMER: The recommendation for this game comes from having used the Zone Reclamation Project mod to alter much of the way the way the game handles accuracy. I've found some settings that allow me to enjoy the game without turning it into some kind of a run-and-gun fest. The original review can still be found below.
The man who helped save my life asks a favor of me; find one of his boys. He went missing with some important information, but one of the men in town might know where he is. In town, I'm given a worn pistol and told that he's being held hostage in a nearby car park, and that some allies are on a hill nearby. Rather than risking a full-frontal assault on the place, I decide to ghost my way in there, see if I can't clear the place out on my own.
I slip into the compound and make my way along the outside of an old brick building. Through a hole in the wall I can see the moving light of a burning fire. Peeking around the corner, I see a bandit seated less than three feet away from me. Dropping into a crouch, I level my weapon, taking aim at the back of his head. I squeeze the trigger. The pistol rocks back from the recoil, and the sound echoes loudly.
And nothing happens.
Actually, that's inaccurate. Something did happen: the bandit calmly stood up, turned to face me, and used his shotgun to turn my head into a fine red paste.
A friend of mine told me that S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl was entirely playable with the latest patches and absolutely zero mods. After today's experience, I'm honestly starting to doubt that. I get that trying to take out the bandits in the first mission on your own is tough. I get that the starting pistol you're given is possibly the worst weapon in the entire game. And I understand that the beginning of this game is fairly brutal in itself, but for a game that totes "realistic combat mechanics," having a point-blank headshot do nothing is beyond ridiculous.
EDIT: Enjoying this game takes some time, primarily in the form of finding which mods (or lack thereof) that make the experience enjoyable for you. I recommend buying it (and maybe its sequels) on discount during one of the twice-yearly Steam Sales, maybe in some sort of a bundle.

Would I completely recommend this game? It depends if you want to support a diverse gaming industry. I find that when games try to give the player more control over what goes from seeming complicated to simple in a small amount of time that the learning curve is an easy one, but makes the gameplay all the better. I'm a big fan of RTS games that allow for individual FPS control (think starcraft but you could control a single marine, or a pyro, and when you die you become the guy next to him). This wasn't exactly the case, but doesn't meant I can appraise the game for what it is.
Sacrifice's storyline itself is good. In fact it's great that I won't talk about it because if your really into story telling of four gods duking it out waging wars with one another and you being the catalyst, you might like this. The gameplay itself I like for the reason the game designers had the intentions of making a FPS RTS game, they tried pushing boundaries. This game back in the day may have been phenominal, but today the gameplay leaves me to hunger for a bit more. You are a sorcerer of sorts able to casts spells to build certain buildings (mana places or soul collecting places for troops) and build units around those buildings and replenish your mana faster. Over the course of the game you come across units and similar buildings to yours, which of course you have to attack commanding your units or by your magic. Different units allow for different purposes. Mana horns I learned early on that you need them to replenish mana in the field (after dying several times... probably should have read a tutorial but ain't nobody got time for one longer than a minute)! The control scheme as well I find is easy. The only thing I would really like if they allowed you to zoom out furhter on the character.
I will give this game a .9 instead of a .7 due to it trying to break more boundaries. I find games like this allow gaming to go beyond graphics, but start looking at gameplay again (be it single player, coop, or multiplayer. They all have their own joy to offer).
RATING : 7.6/10

Dark, hard and unforgiving.
What could be material for a title of a porn video are actually the three words that most people associate with the DARK SOULS series. DARK SOULS™ II, as the second entry of the series, makes no difference to that concept.
___The Story:__________________________________
The game takes place in the kingdom of Drangleic. You're an undead, bearer of a curse. And you're out to seek healing in these lands from said curse.
That's it. The game doesn't really explain more to the story. But that is what makes up the DARK SOULS franchise.
Who you are in this game and what actually happens while you play and the background of these events aren't directly told to you by the game. But you rather have to find it out yourself. By the dialog you can have with the certainly negligible amount of NPCs in the game, or by simply reading item descriptions that all bear fragments of the game's lore.
While the lore is certainly interesting, it is tedious to find out everything all by yourself if you're not that much into it. Luckily other people on the internet took their time and effort to present the lore in form of reddit posts or Youtube videos.
Admittedly though the story was, for me, never the driving force that kept me playing, although I like the style in which the story is presented.
___The Gameplay:__________________________________
While probably the trademark of this game is its the gameplay.
It is true that, in comparison to other genre contemporaries, the DARK SOULS series got a rather unwelcoming approach to gameplay, it is far from being neither unfair nor impossible.
And when I say unwelcoming, I mean it.
The moment you start the game, as good as nothing gets explained to you by the game.
Because DARK SOULS never explains anything to you, it rather lets you find out stuff by yourself. Which means that certain gameplay approaches might not even be slightly hinted to you, but the game leaves enough room for you to explore it and find it out yourself.
Furthermore, every enemy in this game has its own way of how it is ought to be approached. Every enemy got its own characteristics and move sets and it is on your own to find these things out in order to adapt to the enemies' behavior in order to take them down most effectively.
For example: You're stuck at a boss and have no idea what to do in order to defeat it. The game won't explain sh!t. Don't expect it. You're left in the dark. But what do now? The only option is to TRY AGAIN and LEARN!
The boss is always kicking your @ss and you don't know why? Find out why! Find out what make the boss kick your butt and try to avoid certain moves and attacks that made you die beforehand, counter these and kick some @ss yourself!
This whole process of dying and learning is crucial to the game! It is what makes the DARK SOULS series stand out so much. When you're making your first experiences with this franchise you might as well find it very hard, maybe sometimes even unfair.
But it's not.
You can beat anything in this game with enough patience to learn from your mistakes. Which undoubtly involves a lot of dying that this game is infamous for. But it's part of the experience and you'll learn that it's no reason to let yourself down, because the joy you get out of the results of this whole learning process is precious and the reason while fans of the series love these games so much!
It is quite fascinating how all the frustration that you get when failing at the same boss over and over turns into joy and motivation to keep on playing right after you beat exactly that boss enemy!
___The Graphic & Sound Design:__________________________________
Additionally notable are the looks and sounds of the game.
For the former point counts the saying "looks aren't everything".
Don't get me wrong, DARK SOULS™ II is by no means ugly, but it's certainly no Witcher 3 as well.
Although the graphics themselves are not top notch, the design and tone of the game convey the overall atmosphere of the world of DARK SOULS really well and though I said the graphics aren't top, the graphic designers still managed to design the world that good that you'll probably still catch yourself seing certain landscapes and thinking "Wow!" (leaving Aldia's Keep towards Dragon Aerie had such moment for example).
This gets furthermore supported by the game's gorgous music. While the overall music design is very fitting to the gameplay it essentially helps creating the overall atmosphere of the game and makes every boss fight all the more intimidating!
___Conclusion & last words:__________________________________
In conclusion, DARK SOULS™ II is a very enjoyable game and was my entry to the DARK SOULS series.
Just don't expect the game to be a casual gaming experience.
Because it's not.
This game is clearly targeted towards a rather core-gaming oriented audience, towards players that like to put more time and effort into playing a game but in exchange gather a more enjoyable experience out of it.
That means this game is therefore  not a relaxing game due to its challenging nature, this is something to keep in mind.
While playing DARK SOULS, you'll see yourself sitting in front of the screen all tense and focused.
If you're searching for a light-hearted gaming experience for relaxing after a long day of work you're probably better off searching somewhere else.
But if this sounds fitting to your taste, then I highly recommend you to play this game.
