Surprised as I was, after many years of keeping an eye out for a decent Hunting game, one comes along that I can not stop playing. It seems to be designed for hunters; as the attention to detail and customs are kept alive in this stunning open world hunting sim experience.
(+) My positive thoughts first.
The game simply pulls you back-in time and again, this is mainly due to the sense of freedom acheived with very large open landscapes were you can freely explore.
The feel of the experience is well balanced, tracking can be both hard and easy after walking a mile you might not see an animal, yet the anticipation of maybe seeing more is what makes a hunt and that final meeting when it comes.
Sounds, weather, lighting are all stunning in these huge environments, with steam riseing after a heavy downpoor for example. I stood still in the forest to count the sounds I could hear and came to about 12 seperate sounds; birds, insects, wind in the trees, twigs breaking, a distant call of a deer etc etc etc, yet together it was just right for that area. a little further and the sounds keep your senses hightened. The tracking system is clever and you start with all you need.
The equipment rely feels of the quality it should and there are lots to choose from.
Plenty of new content including a new bio, were you can climb a mountain, yes the game can go that far.
You can do missions freely or hunt with friends, were you go and what you see is up to you alone.
You can try the game free of charge and get a low powered rifle, bow, tracker, Deer caller and binoculars etc to start with, yet you are limited to shooting the Mule deer found on a not so little island. There are loads of missions for the many types of animals you might find and with a little story behind each one.
(-)
One or two catches to be aware of! You will want more; the large animals, the bears etc Yet it costs to branch out in this game and everything costs money. I found you can expect to pay a total of 27 Euro for 6 months fun, that includes a better rifle and a tent. Yet they will try to get more money from you with all the extra equipment you might not need, so watch your money; as I found out  that buying large equipment CAN NOT BE USED/PLACED in a MP game with a freind! There is no warning for this and after seeing your freind use a "Treepod" you will want one too... so only when you try to deploy it, is when you are told you can not. Crazy right. Complaints will not get you very far, yet I was told that they were looking into this without a "Time-frame" for it as yet.
The other HUGE disapointment is that you will have to buy your bullets, YES you heard right. The company is pritty tight, they have set a price on stupid items like the ammo and wind detectors, even having special types of ammo and even charge for .22 air riflr pellets = 35 ems as there called.
So what does this game cost? You ask!
After you try the free experience, you might want more like me, this is what you can expect it to cost and why using in-game money called ems translated to Euro:
a/ 6 month sign up =  18.99 Euro  1 year = 35 Euro. Yet they do have a 3 month = 10 Euro to try.
b/ A decent rifle for most animals 450 ems - 100 ems = 4 Euro
c/ A tent, yes you will need one, the areas are HUGE and a tent can be a spawn point as well as an equipment point 550 ems = 4 Euro. The problem is that you might need more than one later on, due to the many fine places.
I spent;
6 months 18.99 Euro
A very good 9.3x62 1780 D FL Bolt Action 3.99 Euro
A happy camper tent 3.99 Euro
_____________________
Total = 27 Euro

Awesome game if you like the idea of a hunting simulator all about tracking and ambushing, and you are willing to put a little time or money in.
By default, you can only hunt mule deer, in one reserve, with one gun, with one type of ammo.  Contrary to many reviews, the .243 is a decent weapon for taking down deer (IF YOU ACTUALLY HIT THE VITALS LIKE YOU ARE SUPPOSED TO), and the 4x scope is typically enough to make medium range shots.
However, the contention in most reviews is about monetization, and I do not blame them.  Calling it "pay to win", however, is ridiculous; there is no winning, its a simulator.  All guns are locked behind a store by default, which can be purchased with a currency you buy with real money.  There is one shotgun you can get with the free mission-earned currency, but earning this weapon (and the ammo for it) can be a chore, as it requires doing all of the mule deer mission line, and a bit of excess.
There is an alternative to purchasing the game currency (Em$) in the "Earn Em$" feature, which can not be accessed through the Steam client version.  Simply log in to
to access this.  This will allow you to complete certain offers in exchange for Em$, including filling out surveys.  As long as you keep an extremely critical eye on the offers you take, you can earn all the Em$ you need to purchase new gear and licenses through this service, however doing so is particularly time consuming and tedious.
If you find that you are having a blast hunting mule deer, and are willing to purchase a subscription and/or Em$, you can look forward to quite a fun time taking down all sorts of creatures.  Take it for what it is and you may enjoy it: a serious hunting simulator with a somewhat flawed monetization system.  Not the best game of the ages when it comes to costs, but I haven't seen a comparable hunting game yet, so sometimes you take what you can get.

This game's AMAZING!
I won't be spoiling anything either, because it's really best to dive in blind.
The story is a much darker than usual one, resembling the SatAM cartoon the most. And I really, REALLY love it for that.
Gameplay is with classic Sonic, modern Sonic and your Avatar Character and as someone who played both the original Genesis games and more modern Sonic games, I am very happy to see both of them in.
The Avatar levels were my personal favorite though, since even despite rather limited options at the start of your creation process, you unlock a load of attire, from sunglasses, to hair tufts to flippers, so you can truely put together quite a good looking character (or a funny one, if that's how you roll!)
It also made, me at least, feel very involved in the whole thing. It just gives it a bit of a personal touch and I really like that. And the gameplay is also fun, as it can vary, depending on both the weapon you choose for them and your skill level.
I played through the main story in 5 hours, still have the Shadow Episode in front of me (which should be enjoyed after the main game) and I see a ton of replayability in this and do not regret spending money on this.
There is just so much still to collect, so many S ranks still to gain and so much avatar attire to find. That, and I maybe take up speedrunning it, just for the fun of it.
The music also gets you really hyped up and the amount of detail that went into the level designs, the backgrounds, the things that happen throughout the levels shows as well. The dialouges were hilarious, the characters written at their best and Infinite was actually pretty intimidating at points.
In short: If you like both classic and modern Sonic and generally enjoy Sonic game storylines (though again, this one's a bit darker, but still absolutely enjoyable), you will most likely enjoy this entry too. Just be that kid again that used to play Sonic Adventure at every waking moment and enjoy Sonic for what it is.

As someone who has played the vast majority of games in the visibly inconsistent yet successful sonic franchise, I can say that while this game isn't the best game in the catalog, it isn't the worst either. It sits in the middle with games that are just average. But this isn't necessarily a bad thing as this game is an example of Sega's gained knowledge from their mistakes and the hopes for them to start a new line of games to save the franchise are anything but absent.
Sonic Forces isn't a game for all fans of the franchise, but it is a highly reccomended game for casual gamers and those who enjoyed the rendition of the boost formula more built up from Colors than Generations or Unleashed. The game is extremely linear and feels as if it is on autopilot during a lot of the more speedy sections, but it still manages to keep fairly things active and fast paced with precise jumps and mild trial and error that the game plays off of. Where having a good memory of where to use certain abilites or make certain types of movements rewards you with speed and allows you to maintain a good amount of rings for a better score overall.
However, this game could use a physics tweak or two to lighten up the characters and their movements. Jumps sometimes feel heavy and can be overshot with ease if you don't adapt to the physics well enough. Characters also get sudden bursts of speed which can be disorienting and awkward when trying to get through some platforming sections. Even if it is doable, I still believe Sega should at least make a few slight tweaks to the physics and take away some of the weight behind each character's movement at high speeds.
The level design keeps your physics and mind, but the platforms and hazards are placed in odd ways that can work against the player a bit too well. Which can lead to some frustrating platforming sections which will be satisfying to accomplish, but feel like a hassle intially. I guess Dr.Eggman really meant business this time! But try to keep in mind that there's no shame in restarting and having another go at a jump or obstacle you can't quite ovecome yet. Practice makes perfect, and it's vital if you want to adapt to this game's physics and learn how to play around them. Your memory of the level's layout will be your greatest strength in the long run. Especially in stages with sudden, startling gimmicks such as the auto scrolling section in Iron Gauntlet or the swiftly moving platforms in Metropolitian Highway.
This game has 3 different styles of play that are all fun on their own, but have their fair share of minor issues as well.
Let's start off with the star of the show; Your Avatar. This character controls more akin to Modern Sonic, but with a few extra features to keep it fresh and interesting. Taking the old concept of weapons in Sonic games from Shadow The Hedgehog(A game that is really hit-or-miss in the community, but heavily flawed in community's collective opinion.), Sega gives us Wispons. Unique weapons that inherit different abilities and offensive or defensive attributes that give the game plenty of replay value as the Wisps did in 2010's Sonic Colors.
The weapons have their different uses, but you'll find yourself using more offensive wispons for bosses and levels that require lots of hard offense. Wispons like the Cube and Drill wispon revolve around hard offense and high damage output for quick sweeps of enemies in a level. Being fairly difficult to use as a result. While more easy weapons like Burst, Lightning, or Hover are more defensive and ranged. Usually put to work at the press, or holding of a key. They deal less damage to bosses, but they are easy to use and ideal for players who still need to get a grasp of the game's physics and control scheme. They also have various builds with various properties that can be unlocked through missions to make them more fitted to one's play style. Allowing one to use their favorite Wispon even if they feel that it isn't very helpful at first.
In terms of Mobility, the Avatar is primarily focused on 360 degree movement and has arguably the most 3D of the three playstyles with a lot of their levels being focused on a wisp gimmick for speedruns, a brief puzzle and/or platforming section, or a messy horde battle with ambushes by surrounding robots. While this is fine and dandy, this leaves the avatar feeling a bit unfinished. With one thing always hanging too far over the other with not much balance between the three. It leaves more to be desired. One will be left using their wispon too less, or too much depending on their level choice. There could have been a lot more done, and it's dissapointing to see that Sega didn't notice this during development.
Modern Sonic is next. And he's just as you remember him from Sonic Colors and Generations. His boost, air boost, stomp, slide, and homing attack make a return, but his drift is strangely absent. It wouldn't have been utilized very well with the game's more linear design, but it would have been a nice touch for more risky parts of the game that force you to take speed management into consideration. His stages are rather short and primarily focus on bursting your way through a stage as fast as possible. But he's only ever a true challenge during bonus stages and stage 22 where percise platforming is truly required.
A lot of his stages can be cleared within under 4 minutes, but they can be stretched on and replayed with various missions and time challenges that give unlockable cosmetics for the avatar character. He is mediocre at best, but those who enjoyed the boost formula have nothing to worry about in terms of how he controls. He's just as you remember him in Colors. Similarly to the avatar, Modern Sonic feels unfinished and leaves more to be desired. He seems to take two things into consideration and always leave one of the three out. Still entertaining, but he could definitely use some work. And I don't see this working out in future games with the overall fatigue it gives off from more frustrating areas such as stage 22.
Classic Sonic feels just as he did in Generations, but with improved physics. He has the most fun handful of levels in the game as he focuses on hard platforming and speedy percision with a mix of creativity. His levels are a lot less linear. Featuring multiple pathways and encouraging a bit of exploration while keeping a firm grasp on the speed aspect. He controls very well, but suffers from the minor weight issues of the other two characters. The Addition of the drop dash makes him feel more advanced and fast paced. Allowing you to regain lost momentum in a snap and keeping the flow going.
While he isn't as snappy and responsive as he was in Mania, everything is still as entertaining and tight as it needs to be. With skillfull, memory based platforming being key to success. The length of each stage may be intimidating at first, but once you understand the level layout, you'll find yourself going back to redo levels just to see how skillfully you can jump through them and blaze past your own times for better records.
Overall, I give this game a 6.5/10. It is a damn good time and has enough content to fill in for the $40 spent on it with over 11+ hours of gameplay to offer for completionists and speedrunners. But it's flaws hold it back from being great and among those of the best recent experiences of Sonic to date. It was slightly dissapointing. But not bad to a point of deserving ridicule and universal hate. Sega did a good job with the presentation and overall aesthetic of the game. And it's story, while extremely cheezy, is entertaining and well-written as well. Good job, Sega! Sonic had a good year!

So, Sonic Forces.. To start out, if you don't want to read a not very long, but kinda medium length review, score-wise, I'd say this game is about.. A 7/10. Average. Not bad by any means, but also not a masterpiece.
That being said, I enjoyed playing Sonic Forces. Most, if not all of Modern Sonic's stages were pretty damn fun, and I also enjoyed a majority of the Custom Heroes stages. I like the music for both of these types of stages, espically the Custom Heroes ones. It was cool to here vocal tracks in actual stages. Reminds me of SA2. Customizing and messing around with the custom heroes looks, and whatnot is also pretty fun.
Now, for the less enjoyable part of this game, which is Classic Sonic. From the beginning Classic Sonic is forced into this without needed to be anywhere near it. Honestly the only reason I think they did the whole Sonic Mania prequel thing to bring Classic over was to attract that Classic Sonic 2-D loving crowd. As for his gameplay, he seems really slow, and his levels are defintely the most bland, and boring, and I don't see myself ever replaying them other to collect red medals, and attempt at S ranks for 100% completion. Oh, and the music for some of his stages are just awful, and in other stages, "Eh.", at best.
As for overall problems with the game, I'd say the biggest issue, is in fact the controls. In some spots the game controls really weird, and fidgety. The lack of a drift for Modern Sonic, is really missed here as well, escpecially on one particular stage, where boosting thru a turn can send you off the stage.
However, this game visual-wise does look pretty damn amazing. Defintely the best looking Sonic game in my opinion. I enjoyed Modern Sonic, and Custom Heroes music, and most of their stages, and being able to play as Shadow is pretty cool as well. As far as story goes, I enjoyed this one, as cheesy as it is.
Sonic Forces, doesn't reshape the Sonic series, or take it like, 10 steps back. It's an average game, a good game even. I just really hope that Sonic Team, and SEGA get it together with the next one. The visuals/graphics are amazing, and there's plenty of good ideas here that just need to be executed better.

My friend lich and I wanted to play multiplayer, and we couldn't because of the lack of steam intergration(Shift + tab to join games) so we had to use a third party application called Evolve( I recommend it, it made setting up a server in factorio and many other games very simple.) Once that was all done, we made our first multiplayer, and we said "F**k it, we are setting biter hive density to max!" And it was oh, so fun.
After about a hour in the game of getting our stuff destroyed constantly, we decided "Hey factorio has a great modding community, lets get some warfare mods to make this more fun!" So we browsed around and found High tech laser weaponry, Better tanks, aircraft, and much more.
Once we had gotten these mods(Which were so simple to install and work in multiplayer without any hassel!) We had started to gradually push back the never ending sea of Giant cockroach monsters, we established 4 layers of walls, and even a couple of "Outposts" Dedicated to producing steel and one town had a man made resource deposit(using the mod Mining tools -- The high pressure water injector) And we made a large "Research town" So we could rapidly move towards the end-game.
We soon realized that the biters seem to becoming back, and in greater numbers( Like that crappy reference?) and thats when i noticed a very cool feature, the evolution factor. Meaning that if you are violent like us and expand rapidly, you will be killed quickly on.

All in all, I love this game so much, and its even better with multiplayer, and even better with mods! I highly recommend it to anybody who wants to just play a game for hours on end without even noticing it!

To start, the only reason I'm not recommending this game is due to the incredible amount of hacking currently going on in the game. Most servers are plagued by this issue, but if you join an empty server, you might be able to play without having to deal with this problem. If you decide to go ahead and buy this game, YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED.
Having said that, this game is really well made, and offers a lot of entertainment. The developers have taken all the best ideas of Rust and implemented them into RoK (Reign of Kings). The creative building style is very much like Minecraft and players can do a lot of intersting things with the items and building blocks currently available. There is no traditional level system, which takes away a lot of the grinding issues, however with the most recent update, many items have had their building costs increased, which adds a bit of a grind to the game.
The king gameplay mechanic is really well thought out and adds an interesting dynamic to gameplay. The king can tax the citizens and gain a portion of whatever resource players are collecting, which can be used to create defenses around the throne. However, if the king taxes players too much, they will revolt and overthrow the king.
All-in-all, the game is really interesting, especially in a roleplaying envoriment or with friends. Hackers are ruining the game now, so I don't think I'll be playing a ton of it until RoK implements VAC or another anti-cheat program. The game would also be a lot better if a vote kick/ban system was implemented to allow players to kick hackers from the game immidiately.

At first I thought this game was overly difficult due to people killing you on sight and farming fresh spawns.  Once I figured out the basic survival tactics of this game (being sneaky) and figured out the map I found this to be a fantastic and challenging survival/RPG/crafting game with good graphics, fantastic artwork, great gameplay and decent performance (for alpha).  Once you find a server with a good community and you figure out the VOIP this game has some real potential.  Then the hackers hit me.  They spawn in, fly around and litterally bomb all of your work to the ground.  This ruins everything about this game.  But if you can find a hacker free server its a good time until they arrive and it appears that the developers will probably fix this issue.  As a result, I have to recomend this game as it is reasonably cheap, has incredible potential, and will likely turn out to be a really fun time.  If you don't was to risk spending your money on something hackers will ruin then wait until the issue is resolved.  It may just be a few weeks before the hacker issue is a moot point.  As of writing this review this game is in very early alpha stage.

The outstanding voice-over work includes Tim Curry (Stratos), Tony Jay (Mithras), Paul Eiding (Eldred), and Brad Garrett (James), among others. The script they are given to work with is pretty good, too; the five squabbling gods are full of character. It's hard to pick your favorite.
Imagine Brütal Legend actually had some depth to its units and you have Sacrifice in a nut-shell. What units you get depend on which god you decide to follow for that particular mission, allowing you to mix and match units and spells for the first half of the game, allowing for a different experience each time you play through the story. There’s something to be said about the way Papers, Please comes at you. It isn’t inviting, or necessarily fun, but not unpleasant. It’s an unapologetic reminder that as an essential part of some grand machine you are one that is easily replaced. And as dull as skimming through documents seems, the layers of tension create an experience so unnerving I couldn’t help but feel like a citizen in the dying days of some corrupt communist regime. Very few games have shown what such a dehumanizing role can feel like. And though the bleakness might be an acquired taste, Papers, Please tests you in a way games rarely do.

I played this game a while back when it was first available for download before it moved to Facebook (which I played, too, but quickly abandoned due to its p2w leanings) and now Steam. I loved the original version of the game; back then it was fun and challenging and although many of those components did transfer over from its earlier predecessor it seems like it retained more of its Facebook flaws than it did the greatness of its first version. With recent updates the company producing this game is shooting for quick cash by pricing in-game upgrades WAY above the rate at which in-game currency is collected. Not only that but levelling has turned into a nightmare -- I can completely understand making those higher levels a little more challenging, but only gaining 100xp every time you complete a course when needing 21,000+ in order to level up is maddening and not so easy for people who don't have that sort of time to spend on a game that, honestly, offers so little at this point. Asidde from those aspects I do enjoy this game - I have since I orignally discovered it so many years ago. I would suggest to the developers, though, that they make gaining XP and currency easier, take away the "pay for currency" gimmicks, and instead focus on making money through a meaningful subscription - such as attractive "add ons" for those who do decide to invest in the game in order to help it grow. Maybe, rather than reaching for funds by limiting a players ability to earn currency in-game, they should focus on "premium" aspects that someone would be interested in paying for (possibly like the ability to own multiple horses, etc.) -- I know this game is a bit of a fledgling (again) but there are better ideas out there to help get it off the ground other than pure frustration for the people who are playing it at this point.

No More Room In Hell is a FPS survival horror game similar to the style of the Left 4 Dead franchise, but without any special zombies.
*Skip to bottom if you just want basic pros and cons*
One of the biggest problems I have with this game is the fact that it can take up to ten minutes to get into a server while you have to spectate, and once you finally get in (and die) you have a pretty good chance of going through that same waiting cycle. At first, I thought this game was really cool in the fact that it was a nice looking FPS game. What I later found is that many of the maps just seem to be very dull and dreary, and not in the way a game like this is supposed to be dull and dreary. The community is also one that is sometimes a problem, where half the time you have kids screaming at you because you took a weapon, or you just can't understand anybody, whether it be a different language or bad mic quality (not a problem, more of an inconvenience).
In the end, if you have friends to play with, maybe it won't hurt to check this game out. But if you're playing on your own, then honestly I would say just go buy Left 4 Dead 2 (you're welcome Valve). This game honestly just puts me in a dreary mood whenever I play it, while I should be excited about killing♥♥♥♥♥♥ which is the primary reason why I'm now avoiding this game like the plague. The game isn't terrible, but it's not exactly good, which is why I just can't recommend this game.

I should probably begin by saying I have a weakness for idle games. The allure of always progressing and the goal of that next unlockable is appealing to me. I can't describe properly why that's the case. I've played many idle games. Clicker heroes, adventure capitalist, soda dungeon, the cookie game, time clickers and more.
Realm Grinder is the best by an absolute mile.
Does it do anything different to the other games listed? Not really, no. You're still clicking on things to make things happen until you reach a point of allowing the game to be self sufficient and left alone until you want to update it and get bigger numbers. What Realm Grinder does differently to the other games is include a gigantic amount of depth. You're not simply trying to reach the biggest possible numbers. Instead you are trying to reach goal after goal after goal. And everytime you think you've reached the limit, the game adds even more goals.
You start off with six factions, three good and three evil. They each have their own unique playstyle and game impacting spells. One is focused on you the player clicking and rewards you for being active. Another focuses on spells and increases mana regeneration and decreases spell costs. Another rewards you for playing for long periods, including exponentionally increasing offline bonuses.
With each soft reset you unlock new perks. Eventually you unlock neutral factions, which (temporarily) are an absolutely enormous shift in power. The previous factions suddenly seem a joke in comparison. But wait, there's more. Eventually you unlock challenges, rewarding powerful passive bonuses. But to unlock these bonuses, you have to complete the challenges on the vanilla classes. But wait, there's more. Eventually you unlock Mercenaries, enabling you to choose perks from every available faction and combine them into an extremely powerful unit. The best of all 9 worlds are available, giving you the choice of whether to massively boost spell production, production bonus or a hybrid.
But wait, there's more! After enough time with mercs and enough soft resets, you unlock bonus sub factions for the vanilla classes. These sub factions increase the power of vanilla classes to ridiculous levels and make them completely viable again. But wait, there's even more. Soon enough you unlock research, allowing for passive bonuses for the faction you are playing as. But similar to challenges, you need to match a criteria to unlock them. You also only have a limited amount of options initially. Each soft reset slowly adds more and more options, each increasing in power. You only have a limited amount of options to choose from, but there is also a lot of freedom. I've neglected to talk about trophies, which play a huge role.
Trophies are gained through specific criteria. They are similar to challenges, but the rewards are available to every faction at all times, rather than the faction specific challenge rewards. These trophies incentivise you to reach goals, rather than reach numbers. For example, one of the most powerful rewards comes from a challenge that requires you to reach a mana regeneration that is higher than your maximum mana. This involves picking an appropriate faction, picking appropriate bonuses and being very careful about not buying bonuses you  instinctually  would normally choose. Some are quite simple, some require a lot of time and patience and some require precise actions to unlock.
There's a lot I haven't mentioned. Bloodlines. Monthly events. Excavations. A spell casting micro management system. And remember the sub factions I mentioned earlier? Remember the stupidly powerful neutral factions? Eventually you unlock a sub faction for the neutral factions (took me about 750 hours). But even then there's more to do. Now I have challenges for this sub faction. I have more research to unlock. I still have trophies to earn. And I know that way into the distance I'll unlock mercenary specific research making them relevant again.
Simply put, this is a game that has kept my attention for over 750 hours (which doesn't include the time spent in my browser before it launched on Steam) and I still come back for more. But most importantly, I enjoy it. I've had days where I've been so engrossed by new content unlocks (looking at you Dwarven Elf builds) that I've spent all my spare gaming time which I'd ordinarily use to play a regular game and instead spent it all focused on Realm Grinder.
If you enjoy idle games and are prepared to handle the complexity required, then you will absolutely adore this game. And to my Steam friends who have to put up with seeing Realm Grinder in my currently playing all the time, Sorry, not Sorry!

I recommend this game to a select few, but honestly it's an iffy game to say the least.
Let me explain.
Sonic Forces is one of those games where Sonic Team throws a lot of darts on the board to see what works, and in doing this, creates a mediocre product that really doesn't fully satisfy every type of fan they were aiming for. Like a Jack of all trades, but master of none. So let's break it down piece by piece:
[Classic Sonic] - by far he's considered one of the worst additions to this game, only shoehorned in to appease to Mania fans and appeal to Nostalgia. I agree with this, and it's such a pain because honestly 3D Sonic games should stick to 3D and 2D Sonic games should stick to 2D. You already have a masterpiece in 2D thanks to the Mania team, so let the Mania team handle future 2D games and stop putting Classic Sonic in 3D games and 2D sections in 3D games. Classic Sonic is somehow worse in this game than in Generations due to him feeling like a heavy brick with iffy physics. There are times in the game where Sonic slows you down no matter what you do, and this is experienced mostly in the loops and even surprisingly some stages DOWNHILL! yes you read correctly! there are sometimes in the game where you go downhill, even in ball form, and somehow don't move as fast as you would any other time. I'll stop before I get too frustrated and we'll move on to the main Sonic in a 3D game.
[Modern Sonic] - his gameplay style feels better than Classic Sonic's, but not by much which is quite surprising. The boost formula is back, and seems to be more balanced as you don't refill it using rings, but only with Wisps and by beating down enemies. He seems to work out fine for the most part, but my issue is with the physics, which sometimes has you flying off the the screen and falling to your death. It seems Sonic Team was aware of this issue, and decided to make parts of the game force-hold your hand through twists and turns in order to keep you in the middle and alive. People aren't really happy with this, and I don't blame them, because it makes you feel restricted to simply holding down the boost button to win. In the end Modern Sonic isn't as problematic as Classic, and plays decently enough that I found enjoyment in it, but there was a few moments I called BS. With that said let's jump into the final character in this review...YOU!
[Custom Hero] - by far the ONLY reason I really wanted to buy this game. Sonic Team has finally allowed fans of Sonic to create their own custom hero to join the ranks of the Sonic universe and interact with your favorite heroes, and how was this handled? quite poorly in my honest opinion, but not completely terrible. The custom hero's gameplay style is similar to that of Modern Sonic, without spin dashing around. To remedy this, and make the custom hero a unique character, the developers gave the hero "Wispons", which are weapons powered by Wisps. You have some unique ones with unique abilities like a flamethrower, a drill, an electric whip, etc. My main issue with this gameplay style is the physics (noticing a trend here?) which might have been a bug in the game, but there were times where my custom hero would zip faster than super sonic on steroids and I could not for the life of me control him. It only happened in a few stages so it wasn't a complete clusterf*** but it happened enough to make it in this review.
Aside from the gameplay, the main draw for me with the custom hero was by customizing them with the features we were given. I can understand it not being so great since it's their first time with custom characters in a Sonic game, but they could have done so much better. The options are so limited that each animal race you could choose from only changed the head and tail of the hero, otherwise they just all looked like they came from that online mmo Toon Town you used to see commercials of as a kid. The clothing options however are a mixed bag of decent to bad in my opinion. Decent in that you can actually get some cool pieces of clothing from original stuff, holiday stuff, to character specific clothing, but the problem with this for me was the lack of ability to color these clothing pieces, and instead you only unlock 3 color variants of the gear you get (for example there's 3 shadow shoes with one being the original color, one being green, and the other purple). All in all I give Sonic Team a pass for this because I always wanted to play as a custom character in the Sonic universe, and it's their first time doing this type of thing so they have room for improvement. I suggest in future 3D Sonic titles that the Custom Hero returns and you're given a lot more customization options like body types, more eye/mouth/head styles, and a lot more clothing with the ability to just color them ourselves.
There is also Tag Team stages where Sonic and the Custom Hero team up, but you already know how they play so not much to say except I'm glad this was added for those fans who wanted to play as an OC and team up with their favorite blue blur.
[Story] - the story for Sonic Forces is decent/mediocre, but so poorly written it's a damn mess. I won't go into detail with this, except with a few examples so early in the game they don't matter much. One big problem I have is how the pacing is. In the first 10 or so minutes of the game Sonic is defeated, presumed dead by his team with Tails (losing it), and then discovered to actually be alive but "tortured" and you are tasked with saving him. You eventually see Tails and he seems perfectly fine, and you eventually see Sonic and he's perfectly fine (even cracking jokes) regardless of being supposedly "tortured". Infinite is our new baddy and his design is really cool and so are his powers and voice, but that's all taken away when you find out how stupid his backstory is and how little he matters in the overall plot of the story. In the end the story will most definetly be told through comics in a better way, but in this game it was just annoying to spot the inconsistencies.
[Music] - the music is good, and some tracks from classic are decent when they could have been better. Honestly not much to say really you should know Sonic music in a 3D game by now.
[Gameplay] - Stages are short and some levels are poorly designed with some enemies that just stand there just waiting to be killed. The best levels are later down the line in the game, but that's not good considering you should be hooking people up from the beginning. Also their addiction to constantly throwing nostalgia everywhere is getting old really fast. Enough with Green Hill ALREADY!
In the end Sonic Forces isn't GREAT and it isn't TERRIBLE. It's just "okay" and that's frustrating for me as well as other Sonic fans who are used to "okay" games or bad games from Sonic Team when we haven't had a hit in a long time. Mania gave us hope for Forces, but unfortunately it wasn't what I was looking for. I only recommend the game if you want to create your own character and team up with Sonic for some decent fun, cool looking cutscenes, and support Sonic Team. Hell even Sonic Team made it a point to create a survey for us to fill out, so hopefully they are truly listening to the fans this time and I beg you to fill out the form yourself if you've ended up buying the game. I'll link it here to make it easier:
Hope you enjoy Sonic Forces if you bought it, and if you're on the fence all I can say is don't expect greatness. There's a reason the game costs as much as it does. I personally liked Forces, but just wish it could have been more.
P.S. - Sonic Team if you're reading this I hope the Custom Hero is here to stay for future Sonic games. Maybe even consider doing a Sonic Adventure 3 game with the custom hero and incorporate all the good feedback Sonic Adventure 1 & 2 received.

Coming from a long-time, dedicated fan of the series, who even thoroughly enjoyed Unleashed:
Sonic Forces is a complete and utter disappointment. It has almost no redeeming qualities, feels completely unfinished and misdirected, and serves no other purpose than to allow SEGA to metaphorically slap us in the face once again. It gives Sonic '06 a run for its money, for sure.
I could write a book about how bad this game is. The entire time I was playing, I was just drudging on to get it over with. It was by no means enjoyable. Anyone who says otherwise is either willfully defying what "everybody else is saying" with no grounds to do so, has never played a Sonic game before, or is otherwise completely unqualified to judge this game due to lack of taste or an eye for good game design. This game is bad, and that's that.
I'll keep this review spoiler-free, not that it really matters with their being such little story.
- Classic Sonic DOES NOT belong in this game. He has no influence on the story, and was tacked on for no apparent reason. His levels are even more terrible than the rest of the game, and he controls like hot garbage (yes, worse than Generations).
- There are **far too many** 2D sections littered throughout the game. And no, I'm not referring to Classic Sonic's sections. The "modern" sections seriously shouldn't have had any 2D sections, yet they make up 40% of those levels.
- The levels are as poorly designed as they are short. Couple that with slippery controls that feel like they were almost intentionally broken, and you'll find yourself frustrated faster than the speed of sound.
- There's almost no original story or writing in this game. The majority of the game is all clichés.
- The bosses are a joke. Even the final boss.
- Wisps? Seriously? They were cool in Colors and all, very much so, but they need to stop appearing in games. Let them go home.
- I won't go as far as to say the Avatar has no place in this game, but it was very poorly executed, and in the game's current state, it would be be better if the Avatar was gone entirely.
- The Avatar + Sonic stages are just as poorly designed as the rest of the game, and are pretty pointless. I feel the game as a whole would have been better if they just gave Sonic a grappling hook, removed the Avatar and Classic Sonic, and left it at that.
- The game had THREE level designers, and two of them have never worked on a Sonic game before. The one that *did* work on a Sonic game before can only credit their experience to Sonic Lost World, which was definitely not the series' strong point. It goes without saying that their lack of experience clearly shows. There's no variety, and what little "level design" remaining (if you can call it that) is just garbage.
- Most of the game feels like one giant recycling bin. The levels, characters, and concepts are recycled from either older Sonic games, or previous levels. Nothing feels polished or original. Also, get used to Green Hill Zone. You'll be seeing it a lot. No, I'm not kidding.
- There are way too many instances where the game literally plays itself - there are many "autopilot" sections that you rarely have any control over. When you DO have control, it's just "Button Mash - The Video Game." It shouldn't be this way.
- Almost all of the crucial story points are told by text and voice overs. That's right, SEGA even managed to screw up cutscenes.
- What little story we get is completely rushed, and lacks any sort of impact or meaningful buildup. It's just sad (though, if it's any consolation, the voice acting was well done).
- "Episode Shadow" is too short, and all of the exposition here would have been better suited for the main story. The level elements are pretty much just recycled from the main story as well, not to mention being just as poorly designed. They should have called it "Chapter Shadow."
- It took SEGA about 4 years to churn out this garbage. I'm really not looking forward to waiting that long for SEGA to redeem themselves, and I'm certainly not looking forward to being disappointed yet again after all that time. Disappointment is inevitable, to be sure.
There's plenty more, but I don't feel like dwelling on this anymore. I can quite confidently say that I have absolutely no desire to play nor think about this game ever again. After I post this review, I'm done. I will try my best to pretend that Forces never happened.
SEGA has successfully trashed this series yet another time. What more is there to say? There were a lot of cool concepts here that SEGA will never be able to use again, because they ran this game to the ground. To me, that's the most disappointing part of this game - we will never see a proper "Eggman wins" game ever again.
Now if you'll excuse me, I need to go wash out the sour taste in my mouth by playing Sonic Heroes.

Although it's a short game without a lot of content, this is a pretty fun game, and is one of Sonic's best 3D/Modern games in years. It has both its pros and cons:
Pros:
1. It has a pretty good storyline! It's much like Sonic Mania's--simple and straightforward while still being engaging and leaving a lot to the imagination (in a good way). To me, the serious tone is much more engaging than the goofy, lighthearted stories of Lost World or Colors. I can forgive more of the tired inclusion of Green Hill and Chemical Plant for now because of the way the story was written.The inclusion of Sonic's friends is also a welcome change and only enhances the experience for me (with the exclusion of Classic Sonic, who added nothing to the storyline and subtracted from the experience.)
2. The inclusion of the avatar character is another welcome change in the series, and I have had a ton of fun with it so far, even if it may not matter to some. If you're someone who likes to make Sonic OCs or just customize things in general, there are a lot of parts to win from completing stages or doing simple missions, and it's fairly easy to win them, as well. You can also create up to 15 avatars after you've completed the story campaign. Having a color palette for one item instead of making multiple, different colored items would have made things much more organized, too.
3. The in-game music is FANTASTIC! It's the best OST in a Sonic game that I've heard in a while and it rivals Sonic Mania's awesome soundtrack (and it succeeds it, in my opinion). It has a Liquid DnB sound and, with Naofumi Hataya (the co-composer of Sonic CD's OST) and Tomoya Ohtani as the brainchildren behind the soundtrack, it's no wonder it's spectacular!
4. The game is visually stunning, and the level designs and boss battles are inspired and creative.I haven't seen any graphical errors or have experienced any glitches while playing. The Hedgehog 2 Engine is pretty solid.
Cons:
1. What everyone says is true; the controls are really weird in this game and only favor fast-paced gameplay. Sonic will not hone in on enemies unless he's facing in their direction, and when you're at a full stop, you lose all momentum and it makes doing tight platforming a frustrating experience, especially in stages 20 and 25.
2. The game, and the levels in it, are way too short! Just when you're starting to have fun and getting the hang of things, the level ends. While there are 30 levels total (including boss stages, but not including secret or extra stages), I expected more for $40; I feel like the levels would have been perfect being twice as long.
3.  There's a lack of content and not a whole lot of replayability. The story mode can be beaten within 2-4 hours if playing all in one sitting, and the game is quite easy to get through on Normal mode. The greatest incentive there is to keep turning the game back on (for me) are the Daily Challenge bonuses, which help you get S-ranks in order to help you collect more custom parts for your avatar. I would have liked to have seen more content--whatever that may have been, like a 2-player mode (or vs. mode), a time-trial mode, a series of Special stages, or even a longer story to play through (More levels in Episode Shadow, for instance).
[THIS NEXT POINT BELOW CONTAINS SPOILERS]
4. Classic Sonic's inclusion. I feel so strongly about this that I had to make it its own point. I know that this game kinda ties in with Mania as two anniversary titles or whatever, but including him was a poor decision that does nothing but mock Sonic's heritage instead of paying tribute to it. The Classic Sonic stages were uninspired and forgettable, and his inclusion in the story was entirely inconsequential to the plot and final outcome.
Lastly, he is just the odd-Sonic-out, incapable and unable compared to the cooler Modern Sonic that everyone in-game is clamoring for. He's just the "other Sonic", or as Tails puts it, "they need a Sonic, ANY Sonic". It's just sad and frustrating to see him devalued and dumbed down like this when Whitehead, Headcanon and Pagoda did such a wonderful job of capturing the essence of what made Sonic so cool in the past. The difference is staggering, and I pray that Sonic Team doesn't try their hand in recreating the magic of the past anymore, because they simply do not understand what made him so great.
Although it seems like I've complained about more things than I've praised, I really do recommend trying this game out. I feel like this game would have been more worth its value at $30-$35 instead of $40, but it's still not too bad of a price point, (especially since the Shadow DLC on day one made it all the more worth it). Any Sonic fan will enjoy it, and I think that gamers new to Sonic or unfamiliar with his games will also be able to enjoy it, too.

This game takes everything you love about Sonic Generations and completely ruins it. Modern Sonic and the Avatar are really slippery and hard to do precise platforming with, and it abruptly puts you in places where you have to do precise platforming so often you just fly off the platforms and die before being able to try it.
The Infinite battle with the Avatar is simply horrendous as you slip and slide everywhere and it's hard to ignore his attacks. You just have to get lucky.
Classic Sonic also controls like crap. He is slow and his jumping is really floaty and makes no sense for the speed he is going. He is also not fast enough to go up a hill at full speed. You have to spindash everytime you get to one of those little slope things that you had no problem with in Generations.
Modern Sonic is also way more linear this time and his level design is just kinda bland, and they are over in like one minute. The levels are not long at all in this game. Also, Sonic's new double jump is horrible. Not technically new, as it is returning from Colors, but whereas the Colors one is actually useful, this one is not useful at all and often times ends up messing up your jumps than helping you out. They really should have just kept that side dash thing when you pressed X again from Generations.
It's a shame Sonic Team messed it up. All they had to do was literally use the exact same gameplay from Generations and make it longer with a bigger story, but they failed to do that simple task.
This game is really not worth the $40, but if you want to get it, get it when it's on sale. It's not horrible, it's just a disappointment.

First of all, this game has serious issues. Upon starting a new game, all that appeared was a blank box that took up 1/4 of my screen, with desktop in the background. Only, the game itself occupied that desktop space (while crashing), so I could not close it without restarting Comp. It happened again and again and after hours of research, I finally found the right ini settings that I had to delete and tweak just to first play the game.
It played well for a while after that, and then went back to doing the same thing. Now I am stuck with it and changing the resolution doesnt work. The only way I can play this game now, is in windowed mode.
The game itself though is wonderful. I tried the Fallout series for the first time and was greatly dissapointed. It was bland, and the setting was god awful for a post-apocalyptic theme. The lore was impossible to remember and it had severe lack of player motivation.
But then I tried S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and my thirst was quentched. Despite not being able to create a character and name them, the game still gives a great FarCry-esque roleplaying experience, in an open world covered in radiated forests and territories ruled by diverse factions.
The game world is very limiting in terms of exploration, but that is easily changed with the use of mods. Exploring the Russio-Ukrainian lands it sets you in offers an immersive and unique experience, and keeps you interacting with the people and the environment. The Skyrim and FarCry-like feeling of delving deep into dangerous territory, getting into a firefight with a group of bandits or monsters to save a friend, knowing that you can walk away and explore at any time. It lets you know that YOU are still in control, and grants a great amount of freedom with this. The graphics are amazing for a 2007 game, and its age allows beautiful FPS and a variety of PC's to handle it.
If you like exploring the grey and rainy forest in an open, diverse, post-apocalyptic world, this game is for you.
Be prepared for launch issues though, which do set the game back a lot.

So after some time with the game, getting to know its in's and out's, I'm changing up my review to reflect on some things I find lacking with the game's design.
TLDR version: With a heavy heart I give this game a 7.5 out of 10. While the atmosphere, soundtrack, voice work and overall idea of the game are top notch, there are some conflicting designs within the game that are just too glaring to let slide. The good news, the game could make a small patch TOMORROW if they cared to, that would fix these issues and bump the game up to a 10/10 in a heartbeat.
First issue. I dont lke the idea that when you die, you lose skills. What this translates to in game is if I die, I pause the game and hit "retry" immediately. It would be nice if there was a toggle in the options menu to make this the norm. This is more a nitpick which doesn't bring the game's score down, but still a minor inconvenience.
Second: I'm not a fan of one of the "limiters" being a removal of "memory" for putting more skills in. The game should get harder as you as a player find more tools and cominations to meet that challenge. Indeed the rise in difficulty should be an impetous for the player to put more and more things together to overcome thsoe challenges. When a challenge is, "Hey, you now get less tools to work with, k?" then what happens is very degenerative gameplay where the metagame now shifts to: "Find the most memory efficient set of skills to break the game mechanics for this fight." The answer to said question 9.9 times out of 10 is, "Perma stun, always perma stun". Remove the limiter and replace it with something more interesting. Fix this and the game is an 8 out of 10.
Third: If the second weren't bad enough on its own, a new limiter called "Permanence" pops up. Firstly, a warning that it stays in effect EVEN WHEN TOGGLED OFF would be awesome, just awesome. But now consider the following 3 things: The fights in this game change drastically to the point that what "breaks the game" for one fight is utterly useless for another. Due to my second issue, you have terrible memory and thus only have access to one cookie cutter build at a time. In new game plus, overloaded skills stay overloaded for ? time, and uninstalling a skill to change builds uninstalls a skill. What? Giving the limiter a warning would bump you up to an 8.5.
Also consider that you now get "copies of skills" in NG+ which can fundamentally alter your builds. To make use of them, you have to uninstall skills to make room evven without a memory shortage. The entire way this game is designed is just not consistent with the idea of permanent skills, at least not unless you're max level and have enough memory to make a well balanced build. Maybe make it a thing for a challenge mode or something? This change wouldn't effect rating, since I could always attempt to turn off my "must play game on hardest mode OCD" and just turn it on at the end of the game, but it would be nice nonetheless.
Fourth: Your entire NG+ system is broken. So here' my current situation in game currently. I deleted all my skills just to see how many the game would let me delete. Turns out I can't delete less than 3. The 3 I hafve are useless and thus can't progress past the fight I'm on. The "Reset progress" option doesn't start me at the beginning of NG+ with all my skills, it starts me back at the beginning of the entire original playthrough. How about no? Your design philosophy was to be respectful of player's time, and most of the game thus far has been. This, however, is a huge oversight. As far as making the game remember what skills you started out with after the last boss fight, how about we make that irrelevant. Just when enterring NG+ for the first time and every subsequent time via restarts, make the "Prepare yourself!" message pop up so you can pick your skills and get moving. There, problem solved. Fix this, and even if you FIXED NOTHING ELSE, I'd bump this game up to a 9.5 out of 10.
Other than these large gripes, my main general gripe is that most attacks are too slow outside of Turn(). More or less half of my skills get relegated to "upgrade or passive" status because they're more of a liability to use in harder battles than anything else. Some general TLC for attack animations for some skills would go a long way.

Okay, so from what I've gathered from reading the reviews I have seen TONS of negative feedback due to either not being similar to Just Cause 2/ JC2 being better, or it not running well on their PC even though it's a monster. I purchased the game with the DLC pack for 20$ on sale expecting to encounter the lag issues as well and end up refunding it before the 2 hour mark. My experience is as follows:
-Anything higher than medium on the graphics lags the game really hard.
-The first few seconds of starting the game lags a little.
-The game clears up after a little and is fine to play for the rest of the time, no crashes.
As for the gameplay:
-I played JC 2, and honestly, I grew pretty bored with it after 10 or so hours (Sorry it was a great game, but I got to the party a little late, and it was a little less than what I expected it to be). On the otherhand, I'm having a blast (literally) in this game. The explosions are massive, the game is pretty for what it is, I like the wingsuit and such.
-Keep in mind I haven't played this much, so I haven't gotten to the so called "grindfest" of unlocking all of the upgrades, but I am genuinely enjoying what I have available to me.
-The cars. Everyone is complaining about how they drive. From what it feels like, the cars are nowhere near realistic, but I actually quite enjoy the way that they drive. Shoot me for having an unpopular opinion, but the handling doesn't feel as hard as people are saying it is. I was able to drive pretty well after messing around for 10 or so minutes. But to each their own I guess.
-The explosions. Hooooly cow they are good. The way that the sphere tanks and the gas stations explode is awesome. Being able to drop a couple of bombs and see what is essentially a nuke go off is great. In addition, when you drive the cars, you can nudge a car off the road and watch them explode, I had quite a fun time seeing how many cars I could hit off before I blew up myself.
-The gunfights. Yes, you are a bullet-sponge, what did you expect? The fights are pretty redundant, but being able to use the grapple to throw people is fun. I quite like the gameplay with the fighting, though the AI is a little on the dumb side. As a sidenote, the addition of highlighting the enemies when you are at very low health is really nice and unique for the games I play.
-The movement. This is where the game shines. The movement is brilliant in every way. The idea that you can see a mountain, grapple hook up it using you parachute, then proceed to wingsuit down it, except with anything in the map is a great feeling. It feels smooth, and is probably the signature part of the game.
The map. The map is bloody HUGE. OfficalNerdCubed has a challenge video of him using his grapple, jetpack, and parachute in order to FLY across the map that takes twenty minutes long. About the time that it takes to walk across Fallout 4's map. Now if you try to WALK the map, it will likely take hours for you to do. For a scale on things, GTA V's maps excluding North Yankton is approximately 130 square miles. Just Cause 3 triples that number with an approximate 400 square miles. In addition, the map is beautiful, and packed with things to blow up and goats to throw off of cliffs.
TLDR; I would completely recommend buying this on sale if you like games that you can mess around and blow stuff up in. Buy it, see if you can get it to run on your computer. If it doesn't, just make sure you don't go over 2 hours so you can refund it. The game is hilariously fun, and I feel that the main issue that the developers need to fix is the optimization.

If you liked Just Cause 2, I think that this is a better, far more fun and fluid, and tighter/more polished/more focused version of it. There's more satisfying destruction, the new engine means movement, combat, destruction and traversal is far more fun (ESPECIALLY considering the wingsuit), the multiple tether and unlimited rocket booster explosives was an excellent and very fun choice by Avalanche, and the challenges and collectibles bring out my 100% completion instinct in a most beautiful way. A common criticism I've heard is that locking more fun gear behind being good at the challenges isn't fun - in my experience, I want to do well in the challenges just for my own satisfaction (especially wingsuit courses, getting those perfect scores and aiming your trajectory correctly is bliss), and gear upgrades are of course a sweet incentive. Ultimately I think it's a wonderfully fun experience, not to mention beautiful (though taxing on older graphics cards - my GTX 670 with an i5 4th gen has to run it at 720p all low settings to maintain a stable 60fps, but even then the world still looks beautiful and I barely notice it since the game is so engrossing). Try it out if you liked JC2, and you can always return before 2 hours of play time - if you're not sold in the first 2 hours, you probably won't like the rest.

A pretty polished 2D shoot'em up platformer like the Metal Slug series. Parody of USA bros delivering freedom via firepower. You play as a bunch of action star bros in (mostly) left-to-right stages and shoot anything that gets in your way. You die in one hit but there are plenty of extra life/character crates and you have more than enough firepower to easily clear the way.
For me, the best thing about the game is that you frequently unlock new characters as you collect extra life crates. There is a good amount of variety in the characters' weapons and abilities so you never know who you'll be playing as next (and you always respawn as someone new).
There's no real story so the theme started getting stale for me partway through the campaign. However, eventually it shifted to aliens and then hell. The final extra level was fun and the alternate ending was nice.
Other thoughts:
Worth a try for Metal Slug fans and a look for anyone who likes platforming with overwhelming firepower.

You start off figuring out how to build a few things.
Then you find better and more efficient layouts.
Then you research stuff that allows you to build new things.
Those new things take either a new resource, or a lot more of the resources you have.
So you figure out even more efficient designs to try.
Then you find a bottleneck in your production.
So you figure out an even more efficient design.
Then aliens attack (unless you turn on peaceful mode).
So you you have to beef up your defenses.
Then you need a resource that's far away.
Do you build a train system? Do you use robots? Do you start a new base?
This game is all about finding the most efficient way to adapt to your ever changing needs.
The more you play, the more you learn, and the better your designs become.
And it's so fun!!

I wanted to write an amazing review for this amazing game, but I can't, so I found some words that I couldn't agree with more:
Show’s over, building games. It’s time to go home.
Seriously: I can’t think where there is left to go after Factorio [official site]. It pushes the concept of resource-management to such an extreme that anything that does anything less risks seeming underwhelming, while anything which tries to go further could well be overwhelming. We’re talking dozens of conveyor belts, hundreds of robotic arms, thousands of chunks of ore, and constructions quite possibly in the millions. It’s a remarkable thing. A ridiculous thing. My first instinct, when I saw screenshots, was to run into a corner and mutter rude things about how Kids Today eschew artfulness in favour of absurd excess, but I couldn’t have been more wrong. Factorio is both impressively artful and as accessible as most games with only a fraction of a percent of its moving parts.
It’s early access, although outside of an arguably crude UI you probably wouldn’t know it. I mentioned moving parts early, and not only are there bloody thousands of ’em, they all seem remarkably well-balanced too. There is absolutely nothing to stop you pulling a generous clump of hours from Factorio in its present form, and at no point could you realistically argue that it felt unfinished.
GOOD GAME

I played this game years ago, before it went to facebook due to funding issues.
Back then it had Cross country, Dressage, Agility/Obstacle and Show Jumping. It wasn't free to play. When it went to face book they dumbed it down considerably, to the point that I wouldn't touch it. Now that the history lesson is out of the way...
The revision seems solid. It's still missing Dressage (Thank god, that was so boring) and Cross country (Very sad) but it has the Show jumping and obstacle courses. As well as almost all the old horse colorations, even if you can't mix and match your own anymore they still gave us most of the combinations. (I got my old horse back, for instance)
The game does take a little skill to master. Horses do lead changes (correctly, might I add) and they jump fluidly. You have to master your aim and allow your horse to line up it's strides for the jump. If you keep adjusting you will lead change and hit it. The game also allows for you to do hard turns, which is as rare in a horse game as correct lead changes or stride-length. You can lengthen or shorten your own stride as well, which is important depending on how close together the jumps are or how wide they are.
I'm not used to the skill point and leveling system but I guess it adds incentive, especially if they don't intend to keep the game afloat with vanity items alone. Since they revised the system in october I am finding myself more tempted to play longer and possibly purchase a sub.
A player can level up thier items the same way they level thier horse and each peice of clothing or tack has it's own stats so you can mix and match what you think you need. It is possible to get through the game without paying a dime, but it will take some dedication and time. It's good to remember though that support breeds development.
Speaking of horses and breeding. There is none of that in this game. You get one horse and only one. I do not know at the time of this review if you can change it with an item so choose your steed with care. And remember to groom it often, (arrowkeys make grooming and hoof cleaning easier) as it will get quite dirty. :P
I adore this game and always have, I am very nitpicky about my horse games as well and while simple, RCC is a quality game for what it is attempting to achive. Especially for being almost 10 years old and dug up from the digital grave twice now.

I should probably begin by saying I have a weakness for idle games. The allure of always progressing and the goal of that next unlockable is appealing to me. I can't describe properly why that's the case. I've played many idle games. Clicker heroes, adventure capitalist, soda dungeon, the cookie game, time clickers and more.
Realm Grinder is the best by an absolute mile.
Does it do anything different to the other games listed? Not really, no. You're still clicking on things to make things happen until you reach a point of allowing the game to be self sufficient and left alone until you want to update it and get bigger numbers. What Realm Grinder does differently to the other games is include a gigantic amount of depth. You're not simply trying to reach the biggest possible numbers. Instead you are trying to reach goal after goal after goal. And everytime you think you've reached the limit, the game adds even more goals.
You start off with six factions, three good and three evil. They each have their own unique playstyle and game impacting spells. One is focused on you the player clicking and rewards you for being active. Another focuses on spells and increases mana regeneration and decreases spell costs. Another rewards you for playing for long periods, including exponentionally increasing offline bonuses.
With each soft reset you unlock new perks. Eventually you unlock neutral factions, which (temporarily) are an absolutely enormous shift in power. The previous factions suddenly seem a joke in comparison. But wait, there's more. Eventually you unlock challenges, rewarding powerful passive bonuses. But to unlock these bonuses, you have to complete the challenges on the vanilla classes. But wait, there's more. Eventually you unlock Mercenaries, enabling you to choose perks from every available faction and combine them into an extremely powerful unit. The best of all 9 worlds are available, giving you the choice of whether to massively boost spell production, production bonus or a hybrid.
But wait, there's more! After enough time with mercs and enough soft resets, you unlock bonus sub factions for the vanilla classes. These sub factions increase the power of vanilla classes to ridiculous levels and make them completely viable again. But wait, there's even more. Soon enough you unlock research, allowing for passive bonuses for the faction you are playing as. But similar to challenges, you need to match a criteria to unlock them. You also only have a limited amount of options initially. Each soft reset slowly adds more and more options, each increasing in power. You only have a limited amount of options to choose from, but there is also a lot of freedom. I've neglected to talk about trophies, which play a huge role.
Trophies are gained through specific criteria. They are similar to challenges, but the rewards are available to every faction at all times, rather than the faction specific challenge rewards. These trophies incentivise you to reach goals, rather than reach numbers. For example, one of the most powerful rewards comes from a challenge that requires you to reach a mana regeneration that is higher than your maximum mana. This involves picking an appropriate faction, picking appropriate bonuses and being very careful about not buying bonuses you  instinctually  would normally choose. Some are quite simple, some require a lot of time and patience and some require precise actions to unlock.
There's a lot I haven't mentioned. Bloodlines. Monthly events. Excavations. A spell casting micro management system. And remember the sub factions I mentioned earlier? Remember the stupidly powerful neutral factions? Eventually you unlock a sub faction for the neutral factions (took me about 750 hours). But even then there's more to do. Now I have challenges for this sub faction. I have more research to unlock. I still have trophies to earn. And I know that way into the distance I'll unlock mercenary specific research making them relevant again.
Simply put, this is a game that has kept my attention for over 750 hours (which doesn't include the time spent in my browser before it launched on Steam) and I still come back for more. But most importantly, I enjoy it. I've had days where I've been so engrossed by new content unlocks (looking at you Dwarven Elf builds) that I've spent all my spare gaming time which I'd ordinarily use to play a regular game and instead spent it all focused on Realm Grinder.
If you enjoy idle games and are prepared to handle the complexity required, then you will absolutely adore this game. And to my Steam friends who have to put up with seeing Realm Grinder in my currently playing all the time, Sorry, not Sorry!

NOTE: THIS REVIEW CONTAINS SOME SPOILERS FOR THE GAME. I WARNED YOU.
I am going to start by saying that Sonic Forces is not a bad game, although it is not a great one either. I am going to list the cons first and then the pros so we can end things on a lighter tone.
CONS:
- Level design: easily one of the worst parts about the game. Classic Sonic's level design is okay, but 50% of Modern Sonic's level design is straight lines with hordes of enemies and groups of boost wisps. Custom Hero's level design is slightly better, but not by much. Too much rail-grinding.
- Physics: don't know what happened with this one, but a lot of times after landing on the ground, if you happen to slightly be pressing forward when you land, you go flying forward and many times off of a platform into the abyss. This makes 2d and the occassional 3d platforming levels especially gruesome. Specific levels include the Tag Team Green Hill level and Modern Sonic's Metropolis level.
- Story execution: Infinite has almost no backstory, a tiny piece of which is revealed in Episode Shadow. Classic Sonic has no reason for being there. The four villains are not integrated into the main plot whatsoever and show up for about 2 minutes each. Chaos and Shadow are not even boss fights at all.
- Boss fights: most are extremely weak, besides a few other exceptions such as the final boss. Two of the bosses are literally copy and paste, and several boss fights involve mashing the homing attack button to win.
- Classic Sonic: again, no reason to be there. Just for a tie-in with Sonic Mania and no story significance.
- For some reason, in order to run correctly on Steam, you need to be in Big Picture Mode? (as of 11/12/2017)
PROS:
- Visual presentation: amazing artwork, especially in full 1080p. Environments are quite varied and interesting. Easily the best looking Sonic game to date.
- Music: extremely good for the most part. Classic Sonic's music isn't terrible, but it clashes with the rest of the soundtrack. Custom Hero's themes are especially great.
- Custom Hero: in my opinion, the best play-style in the game. Ingenious integration of wisps from previous games, combined with the outstanding music make for a great experience. Tons of customizable assets to make your own OC.
- Shadow: Episode Shadow may be short, but you can play as Shadow in almost any Modern Sonic stage, which is just plain awesome.
- Replayability: multiple collectibles and short levels allow for returned visits to most stages to be quite fun. The amount of different paths in stages, although minimal, allow for some different experiences with the same stage.
Overall, Sonic Forces is really a game made for hardcore Sonic fans. Newcomers may enjoy the Custom Hero, but that's about it. Fans who only played the Adventure games may be tempted to come back with Forces, but they will be surely disappointed. Forces manages to be a decent game with broken physics and dull level design. Mania is much more worth your time, and its half the price. I only recommend this game to hardcore Sonic fans who absolutely need more boost-to-win gameplay with a slight CHANGE OF PACE.

Oh boy, where do I start...
I have been a diehard Sonic fan for years. Not a bad one, I just followed up on all the big releases (no comics or ds ports or anything). So I've seeen amost every aspect in terms of Sonic's core "gameplay".
Here's what I found....
It's only good if there is a sense of SPEED. Pretty generic, I know, but you would be suprised at the number of slow sonic games out there. But speed enough isn't alone. It needs to NOT BE SCRIPTED. Sonic adventure 2 and Sonic colors are two excellent examples. While drastically different, they both had a sense of speed that you could control, with the older games relying on game breaking physics too (pretty funny, but controllable). Honestly, the game isn't as bad as everyone claims it is. It might not be the Sonic Team's magnum opus, but it's a pretty solid game that's enjoyable to play.
PROS:
+ Beautiful graphics
+ Fun, if sometimes infuriating, level design
+ Character writing and voice acting has improved substantially since Boom (Shadow no longer sounds like he has a 12 pack a day habit!)
+ Fairly robust and entertaining character creator
+ Callbacks to older games in Episode Shadow! Result screen posing from '06, jumping pose from Heroes, music remixes from ShTH and SA2... lots of nostalgia, really makes the whole episode feel like a love letter to the fans.
CONS
- The character rigging feels like a large step backwards from Unleashed, with mouth syncing being much more generalized and rarely matching dialogue. Stiffer animations feel like the team focused more on texture quality than proper rigging and mocap.
- Floaty and inconsistent controls. Platforming is often hit or miss and can be very frustrating in later precision-oriented levels.
- The story feels a bit forced and pointless at times, with a lot of useful plot points either glossed over or ignored altogether. :(
- Level length. It's hard for a Sonic game to hit the sweet spot for level length between the 15-minute Unleashed levels and the 2-minute Forces levels, though, so I don't really hold much of a grudge for that.
- Every pair of glasses floats six inches in front of your avatar's face. Every single pair.
All said, however, the game is genuinely fun and has a lot of replay value to get all the avatar clothing and weapons. Weapon variety is awesome, species bonuses make it interesting to replay with new avatars, and it's really genuinely fun to see all the effort everyone's put into their avatars with the rental mechanic. I'd give it a 7-7.5/10.

I'm wrapping it up; stages could be longer, physics could be better (Generations' were fine, don't why they rewrote the physics), story is interesting, graphics and stage design are totally stunning just as the soundtrack is.
