This game gets to be fairly intense once you get a couple weeks into the storyline. One of my favorite things about it is that it requires both precision and speed, but no real dexterity; the precision required is entirely mental. (Though a quick mouse hand certainly helps a lot—there's an awful lot of clicking and dragging in Papers Please.) Good spatial reasoning is also helpful; a lot of people complain about there not being enough room on the screen for all the documents, but at no point did I fail to find a configuration which allowed me to compare all required documents simultaneously, with the rules a single click away. (And my keys in plain sight & easy reach!)
I made it about 2/3 of the way through the game without a citation before discovering (by looking at a wiki, for another detail) that you're allowed 2 "free" citations every day, and that (aside from impacting your income) they have no effect on which endings you can get or which achievements you can earn—there's no achievement for getting through the game without any citations!
On the morality side, though the tendency is to perceive Arstotzka as a totalitarian dictatorship, or at least to have a corrupt government, I noticed no such facts explicitly in evidence within the game. Certainly they are harsh, and through the tiny window we are given we can see little more than impenetrable bureaucracy which often institutes ineffective or unfair policies (usually with the best intentions clearly in mind), but I don't know whether they are democratic or what the country's economic status is beyond my own family. On the other hand, most of the government seems to function with startling efficiency; when news breaks one evening & new documents need to be issued, they are designed, printed, filled out, stamped, and in the hands of at least dozens (probably hundreds, from the looks of that line!) of people
before 6AM the next morning; this applies to documents issued by both Arstotzka and all its other neighbors. Rule books are updated. Permits are issued. At one point, in the time between the morning paper hitting newsstands and me reaching my desk at 6AM, some sort of computerized stamping machine was developed and deployed which keyed into the voice transcription system and created custom stamps for every denied visa—a task which would take months-to-years in the modern age, and this is in 1982; the technical prowess of the Astotzkan is not to be denied. Arstotzka has advanced medicine, develops ground-breaking surgeries, offers affordable healthcare, and appears to have one of the best job markets in the region.
Before you decide to join the side of the terrorists, consider carefully the (in-game) reality of Arstotzka.

Okay, so from what I've gathered from reading the reviews I have seen TONS of negative feedback due to either not being similar to Just Cause 2/ JC2 being better, or it not running well on their PC even though it's a monster. I purchased the game with the DLC pack for 20$ on sale expecting to encounter the lag issues as well and end up refunding it before the 2 hour mark. My experience is as follows:
-Anything higher than medium on the graphics lags the game really hard.
-The first few seconds of starting the game lags a little.
-The game clears up after a little and is fine to play for the rest of the time, no crashes.
As for the gameplay:
-I played JC 2, and honestly, I grew pretty bored with it after 10 or so hours (Sorry it was a great game, but I got to the party a little late, and it was a little less than what I expected it to be). On the otherhand, I'm having a blast (literally) in this game. The explosions are massive, the game is pretty for what it is, I like the wingsuit and such.
-Keep in mind I haven't played this much, so I haven't gotten to the so called "grindfest" of unlocking all of the upgrades, but I am genuinely enjoying what I have available to me.
-The cars. Everyone is complaining about how they drive. From what it feels like, the cars are nowhere near realistic, but I actually quite enjoy the way that they drive. Shoot me for having an unpopular opinion, but the handling doesn't feel as hard as people are saying it is. I was able to drive pretty well after messing around for 10 or so minutes. But to each their own I guess.
-The explosions. Hooooly cow they are good. The way that the sphere tanks and the gas stations explode is awesome. Being able to drop a couple of bombs and see what is essentially a nuke go off is great. In addition, when you drive the cars, you can nudge a car off the road and watch them explode, I had quite a fun time seeing how many cars I could hit off before I blew up myself.
-The gunfights. Yes, you are a bullet-sponge, what did you expect? The fights are pretty redundant, but being able to use the grapple to throw people is fun. I quite like the gameplay with the fighting, though the AI is a little on the dumb side. As a sidenote, the addition of highlighting the enemies when you are at very low health is really nice and unique for the games I play.
-The movement. This is where the game shines. The movement is brilliant in every way. The idea that you can see a mountain, grapple hook up it using you parachute, then proceed to wingsuit down it, except with anything in the map is a great feeling. It feels smooth, and is probably the signature part of the game.
The map. The map is bloody HUGE. OfficalNerdCubed has a challenge video of him using his grapple, jetpack, and parachute in order to FLY across the map that takes twenty minutes long. About the time that it takes to walk across Fallout 4's map. Now if you try to WALK the map, it will likely take hours for you to do. For a scale on things, GTA V's maps excluding North Yankton is approximately 130 square miles. Just Cause 3 triples that number with an approximate 400 square miles. In addition, the map is beautiful, and packed with things to blow up and goats to throw off of cliffs.
TLDR; I would completely recommend buying this on sale if you like games that you can mess around and blow stuff up in. Buy it, see if you can get it to run on your computer. If it doesn't, just make sure you don't go over 2 hours so you can refund it. The game is hilariously fun, and I feel that the main issue that the developers need to fix is the optimization.

If you liked Just Cause 2, I think that this is a better, far more fun and fluid, and tighter/more polished/more focused version of it. There's more satisfying destruction, the new engine means movement, combat, destruction and traversal is far more fun (ESPECIALLY considering the wingsuit), the multiple tether and unlimited rocket booster explosives was an excellent and very fun choice by Avalanche, and the challenges and collectibles bring out my 100% completion instinct in a most beautiful way. A common criticism I've heard is that locking more fun gear behind being good at the challenges isn't fun - in my experience, I want to do well in the challenges just for my own satisfaction (especially wingsuit courses, getting those perfect scores and aiming your trajectory correctly is bliss), and gear upgrades are of course a sweet incentive. Ultimately I think it's a wonderfully fun experience, not to mention beautiful (though taxing on older graphics cards - my GTX 670 with an i5 4th gen has to run it at 720p all low settings to maintain a stable 60fps, but even then the world still looks beautiful and I barely notice it since the game is so engrossing). Try it out if you liked JC2, and you can always return before 2 hours of play time - if you're not sold in the first 2 hours, you probably won't like the rest.

First of all, this game has serious issues. Upon starting a new game, all that appeared was a blank box that took up 1/4 of my screen, with desktop in the background. Only, the game itself occupied that desktop space (while crashing), so I could not close it without restarting Comp. It happened again and again and after hours of research, I finally found the right ini settings that I had to delete and tweak just to first play the game.
It played well for a while after that, and then went back to doing the same thing. Now I am stuck with it and changing the resolution doesnt work. The only way I can play this game now, is in windowed mode.
The game itself though is wonderful. I tried the Fallout series for the first time and was greatly dissapointed. It was bland, and the setting was god awful for a post-apocalyptic theme. The lore was impossible to remember and it had severe lack of player motivation.
But then I tried S.T.A.L.K.E.R. and my thirst was quentched. Despite not being able to create a character and name them, the game still gives a great FarCry-esque roleplaying experience, in an open world covered in radiated forests and territories ruled by diverse factions.
The game world is very limiting in terms of exploration, but that is easily changed with the use of mods. Exploring the Russio-Ukrainian lands it sets you in offers an immersive and unique experience, and keeps you interacting with the people and the environment. The Skyrim and FarCry-like feeling of delving deep into dangerous territory, getting into a firefight with a group of bandits or monsters to save a friend, knowing that you can walk away and explore at any time. It lets you know that YOU are still in control, and grants a great amount of freedom with this. The graphics are amazing for a 2007 game, and its age allows beautiful FPS and a variety of PC's to handle it.
If you like exploring the grey and rainy forest in an open, diverse, post-apocalyptic world, this game is for you.
Be prepared for launch issues though, which do set the game back a lot.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is probably the most overrated game I've ever played. It's broken, unfinished, untested, unbalanced, and hard for all the wrong reasons. The last few hours of this game, a one way trip to a giant uninteractive level 10x the size of any before it, are laughably attrocious. When you get to pripyat, you'll notice it's already bigger than the entire game preceding it, unfortunately, unlike the rest of the game it's completely uninteractive and just filled with enemies. There's nothing to do but walk from one side to the other. Chernobyl itself is even worse. The entire rest of the game map would fit inside of Chernobyl, including pripyat which its even larger than. It's entirely empty, and you only need to walk through about 1/100th of it. About halfway through, a timer kicks in literally forcing you not to look around because they didn't finish the level. Fantastic. You can explore more of the facility in the best ending, but in total you can only explore the middle, top left corner and bottom right corners of the chernobyl map.
Fans of this game will sell it as some genre-defining and perfect FPS-RPG, but I've played genre-defining and perfect FPS-RPGs, and this ain't one of them. The inventory management and artifact system doesn't hold up to System Shock. The role-playing doesn't hold up to Deus Ex. Gunplay is notably weaker than other realistic military shooters on PC, and guns are laughably innacurate. The endurance/food system is annoying, poorly thought out, and clearly an afterthought. This game's primary lasting influence is on the survival genre. Unfortunately, the game's survival experience is also laughably phoned in compared to later games in the genre, though I will give it credit for being an early attempt. That said, I don't really consider a game with a segmented 1-road south-to-north game map a true open-world survival game, and honestly think the survival aspects get in the way of an otherwise decent FPS-RPG experience.
This is the general problem with Stalker. While its defenders swear that there's a great game under all the technical problems, the game is inherently flawed from a design perspective. A handful of levels, particularly late game, are outright awful. This doesn't mean its not good, but it holds it back from being the masterpiece that it is often claimed to be.
This game is replete with some of the ♥♥♥♥♥iest, outdated mechanics I've ever seen in a modern game. Cover is worthless. Guns are completely innaccurate. Enemy accuracy varies ABSURDLY. Sometimes enemies will miss you from 10 feet away while you loot corpses taking no damage, other times getting within an enemies range at all will cause them to auto-hitscan whichever part of your body takes the most damage. I have a 200% health artifact, and I still occasionally go from full health to dead in less than an 1/8th of a second. Even 5 400% artifacts will not correct this, as all items that raise health raise bullet damage by 10% as well. On Master difficulty, where accuracy for enemies is at its highest, you'll still occasionally survive out in the open fights with 3+ late game enemies, to later be murded in less than a second by someone with an AK.
Every single enemy encounter plays out exactly the same. You are tasked with going to an abandoned building and killing everyone. Often times, the AI will cause enemies to hide from you so well and for so long that you will believe they are simply spawning behind you. This will never stop happening. Oh, by the way, I hope you like radiation, because the devs used it to make sure every area has exactly one entrance and exit. In the early game, this is achieved via light radiation and your lack of a stalker suit. Late game, radiation is so heavy you'll need to stand around and wait for your health to respawn at times unless you literally grinded 10+ hypos and science medkits each. If you thought you'd get some emergent deus ex and Wolfenstein: New Order style choice in your raiding of buildings, its here, but only occasionally. Don't bother logically clearing rooms either, you will clear entire buildings, go outside to loot corpses for ammo, and be greeted with enemies running after you and instantly killing you having decided to run away from you until your back was turned. This happens particularly often in Pripyat and Chernobyl, which seem to literally spawn with 100s and 1000s of enemies respectively. I find myself saving more often in this game than I do even in DOS RPGs where spiders lurk behind every corner and wait to crit you to death. In those games, at least the spiders kill you slowly enough that you can heal. To be effective in stalker you will need to learn to apply medkits, hypos, and energy drinks via menu while running from things. Often.
Making progress in this game is a matter of saving mid-fight constantly. If you even attempt to fight 3-5 troops without saving, you're making a huge mistake, because one of them will find a way to stand behind a bush his AI doesn't account for that you and the radar can't see through and slowly kill you from a mile away.
This game has aspects I like, and I see why it's a cult game, but this is not a game everyone should play, nor is anyone missing out on anything if they choose not to play it. These are simple open-world mechanics that are done better, and less frustratingly, in even the oldest games in the genre such as Elder Scrolls Arena and Daggerfall. This is not some Dark Souls style "Hard, Broken and Frustrating, but also important to game design" game. In Dark Souls I can't walk off the map by simply drinking lots of estus the way I can abuse science medkits to do so here. Stalker is a callback to older, better games, in a period when not a lot were coming out. While this makes it good by the standards of the day, it can't compare to the best shooters of the late 90s or even now, and I find that a lot of the praise is solely there because, hey, at least it's not as boring as Gears of War.

Overall this game amazed me in many ways and dissapointed me as well. I do applaud this game however for being unique and being able to hold up almost a decade after it was made. It appeals essentially to everyone who are fans of action, FPS, adventure, horror, and RPG games. So if there is one aspect of the game you don't like there are other things you can dwell on to enjoy. The game had a few bugs, some of which I don't know if it was my own personal computer at fault or if it was the game's. It kept crashing a few times but other than that the bug were just weird glitches that didn't hurt the game but kind of ruined the immersion. The graphics are ok in my opnion, I know that this game came out in 2007 but the graphics didn't age too well. However, the modding community can help you there and get you what ever you need to make this game as pretty as you want. The CGI cut scenes were pretty cool as they were ominous and motivated me to progress in the story, and the graphics that were used in them looked pretty cool (even by today's standards), but it is a shame that they only make up about 1% of the game. The enviornment itself amazed me for the first few hours. It really compelled me to exlpore it all and level up. However the later parts of the game throw this concept out the window during the parts you REALLY want to explore. Not to spoil anything but the town of Pripyat and the Nuclear power plant occur later in the game and there is only one major mission for each section and that is it, which kind of sucks because everyone in the game talks about how awesome it is! Staying in those areas is a death sentence and it is such  shame because if the developers didn't push you to the ending and let you have fun in those areas then the second half of the game could have been really fun. (Try to imagine it like when you were a kid and your mom took you to the groccery store and you really wanted to hang out by candy and toy isle but your mom pushed you past it for only a small moment before you took you to the other parts of the store you really didn't want to hang around) wierd anaology but that is the only thing I can compare it to. RPG fans will be kind of disapointed as there isn't much emphasize on leveling up your character and taking time to make sure that they are a one man army. The side quests only matter in the first 1/3 of the game but after that they are pointless unless you want some extra cash. Try to imagine the game in 3 parts
Part 1-exploring, having a good time and leveling up (really fun part)
Part 2-going to really spooky areas and learning more about the story (horror fans will love this part, side quests don't matter anymore, only the main quests do)
Part 3-rushing into warzones and trying to survive the areas you really wanted to explore since the beggining of the game (nothing matters anymore other than survivng and getting to the ending as quickly as possible)
One aspect I would like to mention is the diffuctly, if you never played this game before I recomend it to be on easy (espeically in the later parts of the game). There are some parts where the game will hold your hand and other parts where it will push you down and and kick you repeatly. My words of advice are YOU CAN NEVER HAVE TOO MUCH AMMO
Not to spoil the ending, but it was kind of dissapointing  (All the good endings that is). The bad endings were a little more rewarding because your character gets everything they wanted for a breif moment and it feels alright with you because you just don't give a damn anymore. The good ending is really tidious to obtain and the game sends you on this weird travel thing where you just keep asking yourself "why am I doing this?"
Overall good game with many flaws, but would still recomend.

My experience with Tree of Savior so far has been a rollercoaster of emotions ranging between love and frustration to the point of wanting to delete my character.
+ The gameplay is very enjoyable for what it is, a little unchallenging maybe, but fun.
+ The game has a wide range of customizability of character. Even so much that it is overwhelming at glance. You are presented with 4 base class options, each of which can further evolve into more specialized variants, tallying up to a total of 80 available classes.
+ Amazing artstyle, amazing OST.
- In it's current state the game runs very badly at times. VERY badly.
- Many bugged quests, so far I've run into two MAIN STORY quests that prevented me from progressing because they were broken.
- Gold sellers are running rampant in-game to the point where you have to completely disable the global chat channel to not have your chatbox filled by messages from Zskdfjgklh and friends at all times.
- Trading is completely locked behind a paywall in a game advertised as "free to play". F2p players have access to the market but are restricted to selling a single item at a time.
- You're only allowed to enter dungeons twice a day. Not twice per dungeon, but two dungeons per day overall.
- Premium status gives benefits such as permanent increased movement speed, +20% experience gained from combat and increased maximum buff count.
- The game doesn't do a good job of educating you about how building a character works. Leveling the wrong stat or picking the wrong class can "ruin" your character permanently very easily. Upon realization you either have to remake or redesign your character, or play with a gimped character.
I will most likely continue the game but I would not recommend it as the experience is very frustrating most of the time. Regardless I feel like there is a gem hidden in this pile of dirt, and if IMC manages to fix all or at least most of the issues causing tension in the playerbase the game has potential to be great.

Realm Grinder is a clicker game from Divine Games, published by Kongregate, released earlier in 2017. I saw this for free on the Steam store and decided to give it a go; it reminded me of games like Guild Quest, a game I have enjoyed quite a bit before. I was quite surprised at how much I actually enjoyed this.
Realm Grinder does a very good job of bringing strategy into clicker games, where as many clicker games are very much a bit of a struggle to know what to upgrade, what to buy, what skills to unlock, etc. The achievements themselves are also very good to aim for in order to give yourself a strategy for the game you’re playing at the moment, and it all links together really well.
This is actually a really fun game if you enjoy strategy, progress, and challenging yourself to do the best you can with different routes. That’s another fun thing about it – there’s two routes you can take – you can be a good King or an evil King, and which route you take changes what you can unlock and what you can buy for your kingdom. It’s a lot of fun with a lot to discover throughout the game, and if you like strategy, I would definitely recommend this one. This might be a game I actually keep after completing it.
Definitely give this one a try.

This game gets to be fairly intense once you get a couple weeks into the storyline. One of my favorite things about it is that it requires both precision and speed, but no real dexterity; the precision required is entirely mental. (Though a quick mouse hand certainly helps a lot—there's an awful lot of clicking and dragging in Papers Please.) Good spatial reasoning is also helpful; a lot of people complain about there not being enough room on the screen for all the documents, but at no point did I fail to find a configuration which allowed me to compare all required documents simultaneously, with the rules a single click away. (And my keys in plain sight & easy reach!)
I made it about 2/3 of the way through the game without a citation before discovering (by looking at a wiki, for another detail) that you're allowed 2 "free" citations every day, and that (aside from impacting your income) they have no effect on which endings you can get or which achievements you can earn—there's no achievement for getting through the game without any citations!
On the morality side, though the tendency is to perceive Arstotzka as a totalitarian dictatorship, or at least to have a corrupt government, I noticed no such facts explicitly in evidence within the game. Certainly they are harsh, and through the tiny window we are given we can see little more than impenetrable bureaucracy which often institutes ineffective or unfair policies (usually with the best intentions clearly in mind), but I don't know whether they are democratic or what the country's economic status is beyond my own family. On the other hand, most of the government seems to function with startling efficiency; when news breaks one evening & new documents need to be issued, they are designed, printed, filled out, stamped, and in the hands of at least dozens (probably hundreds, from the looks of that line!) of people
before 6AM the next morning; this applies to documents issued by both Arstotzka and all its other neighbors. Rule books are updated. Permits are issued. At one point, in the time between the morning paper hitting newsstands and me reaching my desk at 6AM, some sort of computerized stamping machine was developed and deployed which keyed into the voice transcription system and created custom stamps for every denied visa—a task which would take months-to-years in the modern age, and this is in 1982; the technical prowess of the Astotzkan is not to be denied. Arstotzka has advanced medicine, develops ground-breaking surgeries, offers affordable healthcare, and appears to have one of the best job markets in the region.
Before you decide to join the side of the terrorists, consider carefully the (in-game) reality of Arstotzka.

This game is certainly very different, but it is a masterpiece. You play as a man working at the border checkpoint of a fictional country  called Arstortzka. You check passports, documents, permits, etc. of anyone trying to enter Arstortzka. This might sound boring, but it's actually very fun. Once you get into the game, it offers a lot of variety. You don't just check paperwork in this game. You can also test fingerprints, search for concealed weapons, detain suspicious individuals, or even shoot terrorists with a tranquilizer. Despite being 14 years old this game has aged very well. The fact that the world and the creatures look like something designed by Hieronymus Bosch is part of the reason why this game still looks unique and interesting. But the voice acting is also very well done. In fact if you look up the IMDB page with the voice cast of this game it reads like a who's who of voice acting. If you've been watching cartoons or playing games in the past fifteen years there's a good chance you've heard their voices many, many times. Tim Curry is probably the most well known, but veteran voice actors like Tony Jay and Michael Bell (Legacy of Kain), Tara Strong (Harley Quinn in recent Batman games and cartoons), Dwight Schultz (Murdock on the A-team and Luitenant Barclay on several Star Trek shows), Frank Welker (Megatron in the movies and the cartoon series) and Rob Paulsen (Yakko from Animaniacs, Stanley Ipkiss from Mask) are just a few of the actors that deliver the voices heard throughout the game.
The game is also a lot of fun to play. It's a real time strategy game where you are a wizard who has been driven from his own universe and is now a drifting mercenary for hire. Each level you can choose one of five gods to work for and this god will grant you two of their minions to summon and spells to cast. This makes for great replayability because all the minions have different strengths and weaknesses. Because some of these gods hate each other working for one god will make other gods dislike you. So if you choose the same god several times some of the other gods won't be available.
Once you start a level you'll need manna to cast spells and souls to cast creatures. Each level is a tug of war between you and several other wizards who are all trying to grab as many souls and as many mana fountains as they can. Only by destroying the altar of an enemy wizard you can really vanquish him from the area. This makes for some frantic gameplay where the tide of battle can suddenly take a change for the worst.
Shiny also infused the game with their unique sense of humor. For instance each time you cast a spell you'll hear your wizard shout out some magic words. Some of these sound a lot like "klatuu barada nikto" a command used in the classic scifi movie "The Day the Earth Stood Still" (1951) which is often referenced in games and movies (like in Evil Dead 3 where Bruce Campbell has to use these words as a spell to calm down the Necronomicon). But there's also a spell which will summon a huge cow which will crash down like a meteorite and create a large crater. One of the gods (Stratos) has a head painted on a balloon comming out of a bottle of helium and James (the god of earth) looks a lot like earthworm Jim.
After a while most battles will feel similar because the basic strategy never changes. But there's an interesting story being told in between the levels and the constant addition of new spells and creatures helps to keep things fresh. The game got rave reviews but didn't sell well. So back then I bought it cheap and had a lot of fun playing it.

This is a game that SEGA spent a lot of time hyping up, and does it live up to their hype? Not even close.
I'll start with the positives: the game CAN be fun and it does have a few cool stages.
Now we get into the negatives.
Control: All the characters either feel really floaty or really stiff in terms of controls, and this is mostly evident in 2D sections. Often I found myself either overshooting a jump when I jumped from quite a distance away and several instances of bad braking which would send me down to a lower path or to my death. This happened a lot with Classic Sonic and the Avatar specifically, who had 2D sections more often than Modern Sonic did.
Stages: Most of these stages, if not all of them, can be completed in under two minutes when not trying to speedrun them. And most of them also have highly linear setups, excluding some Classic Sonic stage and one Tag Team stage. Most other side paths were just five second detours to get Red Rings before setting you back on the main path, and with Modern Sonic this could often be cheesed via the Boost. I would accept this stage length if it was how fast you could do it for speedrunning, but a lot of the "fast" challenge times can be achieved fairly casually. Avatar stages, however, are the worst offenders of stage design. The difficulty of these stages depends almost entirely on your Wispon of choice, and 90% of the time you're going to be using Burst or Lightning since they have the best shortcuts, and with Stage 25 the Hover Wispon allows you to effectively ignore the entire stage. Wispons should only produce shortcuts to get you through parts of a stage, they shouldn't allow you to literally skip the entire thing.
Bosses: Rehashes or very simple fights. There's no real difficulty to any of these fights unless you're new to Sonic games, and even then the only one that could potentially be hard is the final boss, and even that's a stretch. Also Stage 27 is a literal clone of a boss you previously faced, that's not something most people will let slide in a game with only seven bosses.
The Avatar: This gets a section on its own because it's the game's selling point. To me, the Avatar is the most fun to play as when the stage design doesn't allow me to skip whole stages. That being said, with the seven playable races available it's kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ that only one of them (Wolf) is actually useful to a decent player. The rest of them either have abilities that only benefit you if you're screwing up or abilities that don't seem to do anything in the long run. I played as a bird before beating the main story, and let me tell you that double jump they advertise is hardcore bait because of how low the jump height is for it. There are SOME uses for it where it can outshine other races, but ultimately I'd recommend going Wolf if you care mostly about getting points. The Wispons are fairly balanced on the combat side besides Void, but you don't get that one until post-game so it's not much to talk about. If I had to make recommendations, spend most of your time using Burst, Lightning, or Hover for combat and mobility, as they also have the best Wisp Powers for most stages. That being said, watching people speedrun stages using the Drill Wispon is fun as hell to watch considering charging it fully sends you a fairly far distance at lightspeed.
Red Rings: Due to the short stages, the placement of these outside of Classic Sonic Stages gets really infuriating really fast. Hell, in two Modern Sonic stages I've played I've seen pairs of these placed right next to each other, and in Stage 8 I managed to have both of them on screen at the same time. Whoever was in charge of hiding these things must've been frustrated because this speaks volumes for how few places they had to hide these.
Music: Lots of synth music and some electric guitar. Not the best soundtrack in my book to be honest, though some of it is admittedly catchy.
Overall: This game is not Modern Sonic's big break, in fact I'd say this game is a step backwards from Generations in almost every way. The level design is overall worse, the boss fights are much less of a spectacle than most fights in Generations, and it just doesn't seem to play as smoothly. Also for the PC version, to view cutscenes properly you have to play in Big Picture, or you get a lot of static in the sound and the cutscenes play at around 20FPS, not to mention it dislikes AMD cards. I do have fun with this game despite its flaws, much like Shadow the Hedgehog, but also like that game I would not in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. If you're a diehard Sonic fan you'll probably enjoy it, but if you're trying to get into the series, go play Sonic Mania instead and skip this travesty. You'll save $20 and effectively get more out of your purchase!

Transistor and the Studio's previous title Bastion, have some similarities. I may refer to Bastion for some notes, however to avoid confusing those who haven't played Bastion, I will refrain from mentioning it if possible.
+ Absolutely fantastic art style, which can be seen in the environments, as well as enemy designs and your own character.
+ Beautiful soundtrack, still listening to it now. Most of the songs (if not all of them) have been uploaded to Supergiant's official youtube page to listen to.
+ Narration has plenty of dialogue for optional parts of the game, as well as lines during combat.
+ Planning takes the center stage in combat. Transistor mode allows you to stop time, to set out some orders and execute them.
+ 10+ abilities you can select from, all with interesting combinations to try out.
+ NG+ brings stronger enemies and some new lines of dialogue to your second playthrough
- The game is pretty short, I only got about 8 hours from the first playthrough.
- Not the most challenging game, but it
become difficult if you add in 'limiters' in the form of extra difficulty options.
- Frequent freezing if you've been playing for a few hours at a time, including during combat. I've heard of crashes, but haven't experienced them myself yet.
+/- PC controls are pretty good, but may require you to get adjusted.
+/- Story leaves a lot to personal interpretation, while some solid conclusion is given, some may not be content with what is there.
Now for the details.
This is a bit touchy, as I feel most of the story is really revealed in the second half of the game, or at the end, so I won't go into to much detail. At the start of the game, you're introduced as, Red a famous singer who has lost her voice and her friend to a strange group of individuals. Your friend's mind is thrown into a sword, the Transistor, which is the only weapon you'll use through the entire Journey. You begin following the only trail you have, seeking answers. Why you? What is their end goal? What is happening to the city? As your progress, you'll get your answers, and you'll watch as the world around you changes. Will you be truly satisfied with these answers though?
This is mostly subjective I suppose. However the art style present feels unique, or at least like a mix of other influencing styles. The blend of realistic environments with this strange cyber-esque world creates a very surreal feeling to the world, which is only further added to by the art style. Enemies encountered called 'processes' are very machine like in nature.
The soundtrack is an interesting mix of genres, with Darren Korb's personal spin on all of them. Individual songs vary quite a bit. Some songs are very dramatic vocal heavy pieces, that will have you just gushing over the singer's fantastic voice. Other's will get you deeply rooted into the atmosphere, providing a great backdrop for walking around the interesting enviroments. There is of course, good combat music as well. I'm still listening to the sound track, as I write this review actually.
This is where the mention of Bastion has to come in. Bastion (as most of you likely know) had a great narration system, which had an interesting personality narrate your actions throughout the game, highlighting key moments. Transistor uses the same voice actor, for a slightly different system. Instead the narrator, is an actual character, or rather your sword. That's right your sword talks to you throughout the game. He will comment on specific spots and regions, his thoughts and opinions. Sarcastic remarks are thrown around as well occasionally. In combat he will make comments based on your actions, such as when you execute a turn, or if you lose too much health.
While this is personal taste, I find this style of 'narration' much more interesting than Bastion's narration. In Bastion, it seemed as if he was just telling the story of the protagonist, maybe even to someone else. In Transistor, he plays a character, he frequently talks to Red, not some ambiguous audience. This adds some personality to both Red and the Transistor. As he spoke throughout the game I grew an attachment to him, and a level of appreciation. Red and the Transistor also seem to grow together throughout the game, even if they are only small subtle ques. I suppose this is a bit hard to convey though, as Red can't speak.
The gameplay is relatively simple at first, you have four abilities at your disposal, that can be activated with the right click and aimed with the mouse. You move with ASWD or left mouse click. It gets a little more interesting when the Transistor mode is brought in. Transistor mode allows you to stop time to move and use your abilites to plan your attack, and then execute it. Then of course, there's a cooldown between turns. This is probably the meat of the combat, more options besides your four abilites will open up to be used in interesting ways.
Your four abilities have one initial modifier slot. These modifier slots obviously modify the ability, using other abilites. For example, Crash can be modified with Jaunt to be usable inbetween turns. Or you can combine Ping with Crash to proc mini-stuns on your target. Eventually you can unlock two modifier slots for your abilities which will introduce more options. Such as a Crash that splits into three projectiles and explodes on impact. Keep in mind there are about 10 abilities, so the combinations can get a bit crazy. This however, makes it all the more fun.
It's a fantastic game with plenty to offer in terms of execution and style, but it feels lacking in the amount of content it has to deliver. It may be a normal length singleplayer game (by today's standards), it still doesn't offer a large quantity. However the quality debatably makes up for the short length. For some, this will leave a lasting impression, an experience you won't forget. One that has such a unique combat system, combined with a beautiful soundtrack, art style, and presentation. If you don't care for that stuff however, this game might not be your sort of thing. Don't expect an open world sandbox experience.

-Shallow RPG elements, leaves a lot to be desired.
-Looting is not exciting or varied.
-Factions are left in the background. Can't pick sides, you just shoot the bad ones and help the good ones.
-The occasional bug and glitch.
-One or two sidequests might break.
The positives far outweight the negatives though. Shadow of Chernobyl is still a very unique and enjoyable game. A true gem of PC gaming. The kind you just need to play yourself to understand how this flawed game is actually a great open-world adventure experience.

Haven't encountered any bugs on the first three hours of playthrough and that's a good thing. The graphics are pretty and questing has been pretty good so far. I got a mount right out of the gate for the gold edition with no sub so that's pretty cool. Don't expect Skyrim as an MMO in here though.
Mage type class seems less diverse then what it was in Skyrim. I loved playing a pure caster in Skyrim and playing with lightning, fire, ice, etc. Here I can't seem to play that way so far which kind of turns me off to playing a caster. Also picking a caster class had me start out with a discarded great sword which really didn't sit well with me.
Since I liked melee better in Oblivion then Skyrim I figured I'd give that a go and started a dual weilding assassin type character. That seemed to go much better on the initial play through. Still got the great sword at the start but I discarded that for more appropriate dual dagger weapons. Not near as disappointing as the caster was starting out and on my initial impression.
This game has a built in UI for installing and managing add/ons. This puts it years ahead out of the gate for where World of Warcraft is when it comes to add/on managing. I don't remember seeing anything like that in WoW before baked in to the game itself like that.
The UI is decent, not as touchy feely tablet like as Skyrim was and that's a good thing. Takes a little getting used to though out of the box for me. Unlike SWTOR and WoW it seemed there was a slightly increased learning curve to finding things.
So far the combat has been good for me when fighting bad guys. Slid easier in to that because it feels like Elder Scrolls combat. The crafting system seems a tad overwhelming at first. I couldn't find any trainers and soon realized out of the gate you know all the profession and can harvest and such. Just no recipies to make anything right off.
The game is pretty good out of the box. I'd recommend giving it a try.
Finally, this game NEEDS a Linux version.

When you read about what Papers, Please is about, it probably sounded like the most boring, dumbest game out there. But it's actually quite the opposite. I took a leap of faith when I decided to purchase Papers, Please. It's a game I heard great things from but never really appealed to me when I saw some footage of the game. When the game won the Community Voter's Choice during the Steam Holiday Sale I decided to see if my $5 would be a good investment for something new. I'm happy to report that Papers, Please not only impressed me, but turned out to be one of the most addictive and intelligent games I've ever played. Papers, Please is a game that puts you in the role of a border patrol agent. Your task is to take passports from many incoming immigrants and citizens and either allow or deny them access to the dictatorship that is Arstotzka. The people you meet all have varied personalities and some are more patient than others. The game challenges you as you constantly have to review information for any discrepancies that you may find. This may result in invalid gender, issuing city, or an false identity. Even more so is many of your clients will come to you and beg for entry or bribe you so they can access the country  and not delay their plans. Your role is to ofcourse, make money. You have to survive but also take care of your family which consists of your son, mother-in-law, uncle, and wife. These people can get sick, hungry or cold. You'll have to balance your money and choose whether to feed your family, turn on the heat, or give your sick family member medicine before they die.  There is also a conspiracy theory going on deep within the city. Some people you meet will be secret agents, government officials, or members from a dark old organization. This game will challenge your moral standpoint as you'll have to decide whether you can trust someone or whether the person who's supposed to be someone, really is that person. The game will take up more time than you'd expect but will constantly challenge you and pull you into it's well crafted gameplay. Papers, Please is truly a game that you'll get value out of. It will make you question your morals and make you feel the emotional weight of your every decision.

"In this world nothing can be said to be certain, except death and taxes." - Benjamin Franklin
When DLC was first introduced to the world, people were afraid of it becoming too out of control, which it has, and while its hard for most free-to-play games to survive in the market these days, a game based entirely off of DLC is something that you can be sure will die off quickly.
Enter theHunter, where the base game is free and features a miles-long island for you to explore, a shooting range, and nothing else.
The game's economy is based in the real world and funded by buying DLC packs. Here you need hunting licenses just to hunt animals or defend yourself from an attacking one and for that you need to spend real world money. An exorbitant amount I dare say. That means paying real money to hunt virtual animals. While the guns themselves do come at a cost, that could be understood from a DLC perspective. It would make better sense to charge $15 outright and have the first DLC be the game. The devs have assumed that you're interested and will pay for the privilege to shoot something. Allow me to make a suggestion to you, the reader: play the Cabella's Dangerous Hunts series instead, they offer a better and more exciting experience, and if you buy the game used, a cheaper one. How theHunter has managed to remain online this long without offering anything for free is a total mystery.
The graphics are on par with the last generation of games and hold up really well if you have a computer that's a few years old. The island atmosphere and landscape are well done and the animal models look good. There's no guessing as to what you're trying to shoot. This is about the only saving grace that this little bit of game has to offer.
I know I'm being unfair but since this game is labeled as "free-to-play" and only features the engine itself, the DLC being something outside of the initial package means that all you're allowed to do is shoot a couple of guns at the shooting range which makes this whole thing merely a tech demo. Its in bad taste to say something is free but offer nothing. If I wanted to go hunting I know people who will take me along on a trip and it will be a more fulfilling experience. Cheaper too.
Death and taxes are the only certain things in life, so I can safely say that I'll die before I'm taxed by a video game.

10 hours into my second restart and the depth of this game is just astounding.  It starts easy with just making iron plates and copper plates and turning them into iron gears so you can get red bottles (science).  <<Hey, I got an assembly factory, this isn't too hard.>>  Green bottles, okay so now belts and inserters, no problem, just got to start making green circuit boards.  So how do I get my copper cables?  Hey, underground belts solve everything!!!  I need what to build blue bottles!?!  How in the heck do I mass produce smart inserters?  Where in the hell do I get plastic?  Why are my factories not making red boards?  Of course because there aren't any green boards.  Why is that stupid factory stealing all the green boards to make inserters that I don't need???  Blue circuit boards?!? You got to be kidding me.
So yes, it is an incredibly in depth strategy game you have to think how you are going to route parts to the right parts in the right quantities and not over-produce what you don't need at the time.  I have just started using smart inserters to split conveyors and fill chests.  Trains seem incredibly useful to move lots of stuff as you expand outwards to grab distant resources (so yeah, there is a train simulator built into the game also).  I haven't even touched logical circuits and just starting to get robots researched (construction, logistic and combat).  And then there are cars and tanks to play with plus rocket launchers!
One thing I especially like is that your factory is meant to be torn down multiple times and rebuilt.  You don't lose any resources and you can carry so much stuff.  So in other games when I would get into a tough spot because of the learning curve, just restart and apply what you learned.  In this one, I'm taking time to see how to reroute things and make things more efficient.  This also especially helps when you realize that you've trapped yourself in your pipe maze trying to route your fluids from your refinery to your first chemical plant that supplies the second plant.
And the developers are very active at this point even though this game runs very smooth and is really polished at this point.  Just purchased the game early this week and it updated immediately followed by another update 2 days later then a flash bug fix (internet was out that night so wouldn't launch without the update :-(.  ) So it looks like the sky is the limit for the game at this point (as if building a rocket and satellite doesn't take enough resources sounds like the next end game update is a space platform {maybe with a death laser to kill all the spitter nests ;-)  })
Only drawback of the game so far is that no help and in game documentation is sparse.  I was wondering what I needed to research to build blue bottles and searched through the tech tree to find the needed tech.  After 10 minutes of searching realized had unlocked the tech an hour before but still couldn't remember what it took to build them (because you have to build fast inserters then smart inserters).  Then it took forever to figure out how to build engines because you don't have the option to hand build them so you have to put down a factory to see the recipe.  I am sure a help guide will be implemented soon otherwise the wiki and the forums are invaluable.

Score: 6/10 (weak recommend)
TL;DR: A short game with a lot of missed opportunities that sadly is worse than Sonic Generations, with downgraded, clunky controls, a lackluster storyline and cringy "teenage-core" music, but a game that nonetheless provides a decent amount of fun.
Expectations: If you are a Sonic fan, you'll probably enjoy this game. Expect a worse version of Sonic Generations.
Pros:
+ Beautiful level designs
+ Unlocked framerate
+ Rich avatar customization options
Cons:
- Terrible controls that are a step backwards compared to Generations
- Uninspiring story that missed a lot of opportunities
- Bad, cringe-worthy music (this comes from a Sonic fan who loves SEGA music) that was clearly composed for edgy teenagers
- Game can be completed in ~3 hours
REVIEW:
I'm a long time fan of Sonic Games, who was around when the first Sonic the Hedgehog game was released on the Sega Mega Drive. Admittedly, Sonic's 3D games are a hit and miss, with some very good ones (Sonic Adventure, Sonic Colors, Sonic Generations), some pretty bad ones (Sonic 2006, Sonic Boom) and ones that are in between (Sonic Lost World). After Sonic Generations was released, all I was hoping for was another game with the same engine, with even better levels and gameplay.
After watching the first gameplay trailer for Sonic Forces, my hopes were high. The level design looked great, with a lot of details and rich backgrounds. Unfortunately the more videos I watched, I became more and more unsure about what this game will be like. I was hoping that, perhaps like in Sonic Unleashed, there will be parts to the game that are boring and tedious, and parts of the game will be fun like modern Sonic's boost gameplay.
So eventhough my expectation were low, I was still dissapointed to discover that the controls in Forces are worse than in Generations, a simplified version it seems that don't respond as well. This meant that even the boost-based modern Sonic segments of the game weren't as good as I hoped.
Then, the music. I am a huge fan of the music in Sonic the Hedgehog series, but this... The music is clearly controversial. I am completely aware that there are a lot of people who praise the music, but to me it's just cheesy, cringeworthy, lazy, "edgy" music designed for "cool teenagers" who get wet when they hear a cliche dubstep synth. This was definitely another dissapointing aspect of the game.
The story was weird. Generation's storyline was trivial and simple, yet it worked for the purposes of the game. What happens here is that we have a story that tries to be deep, but never really goes deep. We suddenly hear about some resistance soldiers, and captains speaking on their behalf. Who are they? How do these soliders look like? How does the fighting look like? We only get to see the "fighters" towards the end of the game, and that scene is simply hillariously bad - colourful, simplistic looking animals holding Wispons (weapons used in this particular Sonic universe). The story simply is trying way to hard, ending up being way too shallow.
The gameplay is... it's fun actually. Ignoring the bad controls, and frustrating moments caused by them, I did enjoy playing most of the levels. The ability to customise your avatar is not too bad, adds variety to the game. There are plenty of options that allow you to create many different types of characters.
Overall, I am dissapointed. I wish they kept the same controls and physics as in Sonic Generations. I wish the story was more detailed, wasn't as lazy, and went deeper. I wish the music wasn't this bad. But, at the end of the day, I did have fun.
So I'm torn here. I think a 6/10 is a fair score, and because it is above 5, I am "recommending" this game. If you're unsure whether you want to buy it now, wait for a discount.

TL;DR: It's not very good. It's pretty much a streamlined and more automated version of Generations with a playable OC and cheezy but entertaining cutscenes. Only get it if you really liked Generations, and probably wait for a sale.
Okay, first of all, I actually liked the story a lot, at least for the most part. Just like SA2's story, it's not really that good, but it's quite entertaining. How it mentions Sonic getting tortured, how Knuckles talks about the horrors of war, and how Infinite is a total edgelord makes the story pretty funny in an unintended way. It just takes itself very seriously. My avatar character looking really silly may have helped it too.
I enjoyed the dialogue itself too, despite, it being written in a way similar to Lost World's. Sonic still cranks up some chili dog jokes, but it's never as obnoxious as "BALDY MCNOSEHAIR XD" from Colors and Lost World. The voice acting is overall pretty good too, especially for Infinite and Shadow. I don't really like the way Amy sounds for some reason though. It's also a bit weird to have Knuckles very serious, especially after getting used to seeing him as an idiot in Sonic Boom. As for the animations, they aren't very good, but none of them were bad enough to ruin the experience at least.
My only big problems with the story are how Tails' personality contradicts with his entire story arc in Sonic Adventure, and the ending. Like, in this game Tails always depends on Sonic. It's like he can't do anything on his own, other than being the smart guy in the team. Sure, he guides Classic Sonic for most of the game, but he doesn't do anything alone. Heck even at the start he cries for help from Sonic, twice. As for the ending, it's just very underwhelming. Infinite just kinda disappears, then we fight with Eggman and bam, done. All this "friendship" talk doesn't really help either.

As for the gameplay, well, it's not very good. The main problem with it is the level design. The 3D sections feel like there isn't any thought put into them, they only rely on automation and cool looking cutscenes so you don't really do much in them most of the time. Compared to Generations it's a HUGE downgrade.  2D sections are a bit better as they have some decent platforming with some interesting gimmicks, but I'd also consider them a downgrade.
But there's a bigger problem with the level design, all the levels are way too simple and short, especially at the start of the game. Just hold up, occasionally boost or use your weapon for the avatar, and jump. And the difficulty never really increases, so there isn't even a proper difficulty curve, excluding the bosses. The level design does get a bit more complex near the end of the game, but they never reach the level of the level design complexity in Generations and Unleashed, and I wouldn't even call the level design in these games complex.
At least the levels are somewhat fun to speedrun.
Other than Modern Sonic you can also play as the Avatar. It's just Modern Sonic without boost and with a weapon. The game gives you a lot of choices for weapons, And each weapon is based on Wisps that appeared in previous Sonic games. Unfortunately all of them kinda suck compared to the one the game gives you at the start of the game, so you have no reason to change your weapons other than to collect the red rings. Your character also has a grappling hook, but it's mostly used to make the gameplay even more automated lol.

The controls are also a downgrade. 3D sections control alright, but the 2D sections? Ooh boy. Let's say that I think Sonic 4 Episode 1 controls better than this game's Classic Sonic. Yeah, I went that far. It isn't unplayable levels of bad, but even if this was a fangame I would complain.
Oh yeah, I totally forgot about Classic Sonic. He's in the game too but they totally messed him up. The level design of his levels is a MASSIVE downgrade from Generations and especially Mania. It's far worse than the downgrade Modern Sonic's 3D sections got. But thankfully the levels are still playable and kiiinda enjoyable.

I can say that the graphics are the best part of this game. I think Generations was a better looking game overall, but I still like the look of this game overall. like for an example, I really like Modern Sonic's model in this game, it looks really nice, possibly even better than Sonic's model in the previous games. I like some of the effects too, like that sliding effect and Sonic's jumpball. The lighting is pretty good as well, and a lot of the stages look very pleasing to the eyes, especially the space, metropolis, and destroyed city levels. There are some graphical glitches though, like the main platform turning to black in Zavok's boss fight for a few frames sometimes.
The game also freezes while loading a lot. That really sucks as I had to reopen the game at least 20 times because of that. I'm not joking.

But the best part of the game is the character editor. It's really fun to mess with. I've always liked this kind of stuff in games, though, so if you're not into character customization stuff then it might not be for you.

So even though I didn't found this game very good I kinda enjoyed it, so I'd suggest getting it on a sale only if you really liked Generations, and even in that case get ready to be disappointed.

I've just finished this, and for the 4.4 hours it took, I genuinely enjoyed this. I have not played a Sonic game in a very long time now since the last time I played Sonic CD, and I have to say... coming back to a game like this was just absolutely amazing. Yes, I had my gripes here and there with it, but in no way does it deserve to get bashed on the way it does. Whether it was because of crash bugs on release (which Sega was quick to fix), or because of elitist players of previous Sonic games comparing it to older entries, I thoroughly enjoyed this. Want to know the secret of how I enjoyed it?
I came into this game with no expectations, or comparisons whatsoever. I took the game for what it was. And by that, I mean what it was ON ITS OWN. Not what it was COMPARED TO THE OTHER GAMES. And to be honest, it was a good game on its own! I enjoyed it, despite some issues here and there, and I wish more people did.
The Character/Avatar Creation was a truly great decision. A lot of people, myself included, have had their little Sonic OCs because it's just so easy to make Sonic OCs (and I'm NOT talking about cheap and uninspired DeviantArt recolors). So this was a real nice thing, to be able to make your own character and fight alongside your iconic favorite characters. The Avatar stages were fun as well! So nice to see that a character doesn't need to have superhuman speed, strength or smarts to measure up to the likes of those who have!
The Modern Sonic stages were, naturally, filled with hype and speed, and I was absolutely enjoying myself when I blast through enemies with the Burst Dash, and Homing Attack from foe to foe with rapid succession. The ONLY gripe I have with this are the Classic Sonic stages. Honestly, I myself see no point in bringing in Classic Sonic in this. It worked for Generations because that was literally the plot of the whole game, but here it just felt out of place. And his stages were slow, clunky, and sorta unbearable for me. But other than that, no other complaints for the other parts!
So for me, with the Avatar Creator, the stage designs, the story, the music (the FRICKIN' MUSIC) all being pleasant to me, and rounding up into an honest and decent game, I give this a 8/10. Definitely recommend this if you just go into it and enjoy it for what it is, and don't try to compare it to other games in the franchise.

Bad stuff (the main two for me):
First, the energy/aciton point depletion rate.
You have an initial maximum of 100 points, which are consumed at a rate of 4 points per jump and 1 point every few seconds of running or standing within the paddock (even while paused).
These points are restored while resting (on the main menu) at a rate of 1 point every 35 seconds, which works out to 100 points in an hour.
This means you can play for about 5-10 minutes every hour.
In fairness, you can upgrade certain clothing items to offset this, increasing the rate of recharge to 1 point every 17ish seconds and a max of 200 points.  But the amount of currency to upgrade the items needed is ridculous.
Second, the currency rewards are pitiful.
There are two kinds of courses, jumping and agility.  Either way, if you knock stuff over, you incure penalties.
Once you complete the course, you receive 100 coins, 5 diamonds and 100 xp (after gaining 9 levels, these rates have remained unchanged).
These rewards are unaffected by how well you ran the course, which means you could knock everything over and still get the maximum reward.
To put these numbers in perspective, an apple that restores 100 energy costs 400 diamonds.
The most basic of the upgrades mentioned above costs 5000 coins and 500 diamonds.
To get this much currency, you would have to run 50 courses.
In the end, to play this game, you will either be paying lots of money or spending a lot of time waiting to recharge your horse so you can grind your way through a few minutes of play.

Transistor and the Studio's previous title Bastion, have some similarities. I may refer to Bastion for some notes, however to avoid confusing those who haven't played Bastion, I will refrain from mentioning it if possible.
+ Absolutely fantastic art style, which can be seen in the environments, as well as enemy designs and your own character.
+ Beautiful soundtrack, still listening to it now. Most of the songs (if not all of them) have been uploaded to Supergiant's official youtube page to listen to.
+ Narration has plenty of dialogue for optional parts of the game, as well as lines during combat.
+ Planning takes the center stage in combat. Transistor mode allows you to stop time, to set out some orders and execute them.
+ 10+ abilities you can select from, all with interesting combinations to try out.
+ NG+ brings stronger enemies and some new lines of dialogue to your second playthrough
- The game is pretty short, I only got about 8 hours from the first playthrough.
- Not the most challenging game, but it
become difficult if you add in 'limiters' in the form of extra difficulty options.
- Frequent freezing if you've been playing for a few hours at a time, including during combat. I've heard of crashes, but haven't experienced them myself yet.
+/- PC controls are pretty good, but may require you to get adjusted.
+/- Story leaves a lot to personal interpretation, while some solid conclusion is given, some may not be content with what is there.
Now for the details.
This is a bit touchy, as I feel most of the story is really revealed in the second half of the game, or at the end, so I won't go into to much detail. At the start of the game, you're introduced as, Red a famous singer who has lost her voice and her friend to a strange group of individuals. Your friend's mind is thrown into a sword, the Transistor, which is the only weapon you'll use through the entire Journey. You begin following the only trail you have, seeking answers. Why you? What is their end goal? What is happening to the city? As your progress, you'll get your answers, and you'll watch as the world around you changes. Will you be truly satisfied with these answers though?
This is mostly subjective I suppose. However the art style present feels unique, or at least like a mix of other influencing styles. The blend of realistic environments with this strange cyber-esque world creates a very surreal feeling to the world, which is only further added to by the art style. Enemies encountered called 'processes' are very machine like in nature.
The soundtrack is an interesting mix of genres, with Darren Korb's personal spin on all of them. Individual songs vary quite a bit. Some songs are very dramatic vocal heavy pieces, that will have you just gushing over the singer's fantastic voice. Other's will get you deeply rooted into the atmosphere, providing a great backdrop for walking around the interesting enviroments. There is of course, good combat music as well. I'm still listening to the sound track, as I write this review actually.
This is where the mention of Bastion has to come in. Bastion (as most of you likely know) had a great narration system, which had an interesting personality narrate your actions throughout the game, highlighting key moments. Transistor uses the same voice actor, for a slightly different system. Instead the narrator, is an actual character, or rather your sword. That's right your sword talks to you throughout the game. He will comment on specific spots and regions, his thoughts and opinions. Sarcastic remarks are thrown around as well occasionally. In combat he will make comments based on your actions, such as when you execute a turn, or if you lose too much health.
While this is personal taste, I find this style of 'narration' much more interesting than Bastion's narration. In Bastion, it seemed as if he was just telling the story of the protagonist, maybe even to someone else. In Transistor, he plays a character, he frequently talks to Red, not some ambiguous audience. This adds some personality to both Red and the Transistor. As he spoke throughout the game I grew an attachment to him, and a level of appreciation. Red and the Transistor also seem to grow together throughout the game, even if they are only small subtle ques. I suppose this is a bit hard to convey though, as Red can't speak.
The gameplay is relatively simple at first, you have four abilities at your disposal, that can be activated with the right click and aimed with the mouse. You move with ASWD or left mouse click. It gets a little more interesting when the Transistor mode is brought in. Transistor mode allows you to stop time to move and use your abilites to plan your attack, and then execute it. Then of course, there's a cooldown between turns. This is probably the meat of the combat, more options besides your four abilites will open up to be used in interesting ways.
Your four abilities have one initial modifier slot. These modifier slots obviously modify the ability, using other abilites. For example, Crash can be modified with Jaunt to be usable inbetween turns. Or you can combine Ping with Crash to proc mini-stuns on your target. Eventually you can unlock two modifier slots for your abilities which will introduce more options. Such as a Crash that splits into three projectiles and explodes on impact. Keep in mind there are about 10 abilities, so the combinations can get a bit crazy. This however, makes it all the more fun.
It's a fantastic game with plenty to offer in terms of execution and style, but it feels lacking in the amount of content it has to deliver. It may be a normal length singleplayer game (by today's standards), it still doesn't offer a large quantity. However the quality debatably makes up for the short length. For some, this will leave a lasting impression, an experience you won't forget. One that has such a unique combat system, combined with a beautiful soundtrack, art style, and presentation. If you don't care for that stuff however, this game might not be your sort of thing. Don't expect an open world sandbox experience.

A friend summed this game up in a passing comment once, he called it "Reign of Rust" and for the most part in its current form that is exactly what it is. Now Rust is a fine game, you may be thinking being likened to it is no bad thing but I found for me at least it had no real long term playability. RoR in its current form generally will encourage the worst in most players, what I mean by that is going around killing other players and wrecking their accomplishments. It is standard practice for most survival open world games, which is easy to understand because without a story or objectives there's little for players to really do.
RoK has some pretty major balance issues for instance the trebuchet which can be loaded with 1000's of ammunition in a single shot which will just melt any wall you choose to build giving nothing you build any real longevity/durability and all the armour just feels wrong for instance I don't think in any reality someone with a wooden club should be able to kill someone else in head to toe steel plate armour
But in spite of all that I did enjoy the majority of my 100 hours, due heavily to the fact that the server I mainly played was populated with generally nice people who liked abit of role play, now I generally felt a little uncomfortable with the whole RP thing but over time I came to really appreciate  it , it adds colour to an otherwise kill people, build/wreck stuff experience, RoK just added a two ingredients a guild system and throne, then in this framework the server created a town, guilds with mutual defence agreements a sudo police force and a church with daily services.
I am in conclusion hopeful about this games future development, although unless you know of a server with top notch admins i would wait to see if the problems are being resolved before buying, hacker issues have been well documented  bad game balance etc all are issues which are fixable and if the developers concentrate on how players can better work together by further developing the guild system having other objectives to rally around like separate taxable regions and making it so new to server players cant just kill anyone or wreck stuff within a couple of hours RoK may be a game you could play week in week out instead of being something you get bored of within a week

This fantastic Action-RTS hybrid (which amazingly was released in 2000) is a spiritual predecessor to Brutal Legend, but as far as the RTS mechanics go it plays more like a faster, more furious Warcraft III, another game it preceded by a fair amount. It's built on the tried-and-true Melee/Ranged/Flyer triangular counter system and focuses on a central unit, the wizard, which gains experience levels and new spells as the match or mission progresses.
There are no goldmines or forests to exploit, however, the only resources on the field are manafounts, which, once built upon, can relay mana to you and your army. To build units, you use souls, which are painstakingly converted from heathens, including enemy military units. Since you're feeding on your enemy, you can either chip away at the enemy army in a passive game of zoning and area denial, cut down his mana supply by harrassing his manaliths, or you can just strike at the jugular and attempt to kill the wizard in a battle royale, severely reducing the potential of his units if successful. Despite the strategic simplicity of the game, all RTS playstyles are accounted for.
Sacrifice is a third-person view game centered on the player, not top-down view like a traditional RTS. The camera is notorious for not zooming out a lot - the wizard is advised to seek high ground so he may properly command his forces. Control groups help a ton. The interface is extensive and highly-customizable, but it'll probably take a lot of playing before you're making use of all the shortcuts.
There's an all-star cast of voice actors and they're all in their element here. The soundtrack is memorable and no game element seems odd or out of place, as bizarre and surreal as the game world is. The grotesque monsters, the meaty ground, the strange plants and structures, the whole aesthetic of the game comes together so well.
If I had to criticize one thing about the game, I'd have to criticize its competitive value. The game is better-suited for tournaments than many RTS but there are a lot of random elements that plague the player, particularly the random nature of melee attack damage and certain endgame spells and units. Speaking of the endgame, the final levels of the campaign and the credits seem a bit rushed in comparison to the tons of love given the early missions.
No matter what you're looking for in a classic game, I'm pretty certain you'll find it here. You cannot truly experience this game on the first playthrough. The lore is deep, the gameplay is deep, and the crevasses between the floating islands that make up the world are deep. If a flier is shot down over the abyss, his soul is lost forever. ;_;7

Even if you max out your stats you can lose miserably to other players (or NPCs) at far lower levels than yourself. Dark Souls places a heavy emphasis on your skill as a player more than anything else, and that's what I love most about it.
I wouldn't say there is a story so much as there is lore. You have a goal, but you aren't really pushed to it by any means. Rather, you are pretty much left to yourself to do as you see fit, and there is lore behind everything you do or see for you to study or ignore. Occasionally the lack of direction could be frustrating ("Where do I go next?!") but mostly it was freeing. It's just you, your weapons, and the enemy.
For me the most rewarding things were the feeling of finally defeating a difficult boss, getting that weapon I'd been aiming for, beating the game on harder and harder difficulties, doing well in PvP (optional)...It can be brutal but it's one of the best games I've played.

The Elder Scrolls® Online: Tamriel Unlimited™ - short TESO is often mistaken for an MMORPG. Which it is not.
TESO is an RPG with social elements. Since the Tamrial One update the whole world scales with yourself - everything is available from the start, and everything is always on par with you. The whole game can - besides group dungeons and raids - be finished solo.
There are, however, a lot of social sides. Crafting, Guilds, Guild Markets, soon to be implemented housing, all this plays a big role. Grouping up to beat a world boss or running dungeons with friends improves the game a lot.
Leaving aside the mistake above, the game is simply great! Questing is a lot of fun and quite varied, you will have hundreds of hours to spend if you want to finish everything. THe dungeons are challenging, the crafting system is very nice and the endgame is incredibly varied! There is not "best" equipement to get, what you need soley depends on your build and what you aim to be. The incredibly high amount of skill points allows skilling more than just one "role".
If there is any downside to be found, it's most probably the crown shop. Selling crafting motifs, mounts, pets, exp scrolls, style items [...] really takes away something. Your best choice is to get the DLC's you want in a sale and skip the rest of the things.
(comparison: the game in gold edition in a sale - 20€. 1 Crafting motif - 40€)

When you read about what Papers, Please is about, it probably sounded like the most boring, dumbest game out there. But it's actually quite the opposite. Yes, it sounds boring, but after a while you get addicted to the gameplay. Should I let this person in because he hasn't seen his son in three years, but his passport is a fake? Should I take the bribe so I can pay for my familly to not starve? The choices you make affect the outcome of the game. And, there's actually a storyline to the game that is very interesting and choice-affected, but I won't give anything away. Papers, Please isn't only a simulator, it's a dang right amazing and beautiful one.
And P.S., the soundtrack and the graphics just fit so amazingly with the russian-inspired country.

I took a leap of faith when I decided to purchase Papers, Please. It's a game I heard great things from but never really appealed to me when I saw some footage of the game. When the game won the Community Voter's Choice during the Steam Holiday Sale I decided to see if my $5 would be a good investment for something new. I'm happy to report that Papers, Please not only impressed me, but turned out to be one of the most addictive and intelligent games I've ever played. Papers, Please is a game that puts you in the role of a border patrol agent. Your task is to take passports from many incoming immigrants and citizens and either allow or deny them access to the dictatorship that is Arstotzka. The people you meet all have varied personalities and some are more patient than others. The game challenges you as you constantly have to review information for any discrepancies that you may find. This may result in invalid gender, issuing city, or an false identity. Even more so is many of your clients will come to you and beg for entry or bribe you so they can access the country  and not delay their plans. Your role is to ofcourse, make money. You have to survive but also take care of your family which consists of your son, mother-in-law, uncle, and wife. These people can get sick, hungry or cold. You'll have to balance your money and choose whether to feed your family, turn on the heat, or give your sick family member medicine before they die.  There is also a conspiracy theory going on deep within the city. Some people you meet will be secret agents, government officials, or members from a dark old organization. This game will challenge your moral standpoint as you'll have to decide whether you can trust someone or whether the person who's supposed to be someone, really is that person. The game will take up more time than you'd expect but will constantly challenge you and pull you into it's well crafted gameplay. Papers, Please is truly a game that you'll get value out of. It will make you question your morals and make you feel the emotional weight of your every decision.
