While Rome 2's now imfamous launch was attrocious, in its current state, the game is one of the best of the Total War series, and a shining example of a RTS.
1. Campaign: As always, Rome 2's campaign is a mix of turn based strategical management on the campaign map, and real time battles. For the most part, the AI does a good job managing their cities and armies. They don't make foolish mistakes, they defend their cities, and they attack any vulnerabilities left by the player. The UI is fine, but the lack of branching skill trees for generals can be annoying. The removal of family trees is another annoyance as you feel no attachment to your faction's characters. One place where Rome 2 shines, however, is its variety. There are dozens of faction to chose from, exact numbers based on DLC, all of which have interesting units, traits, and challenge levels.
2. Battles: Once again, we see the return of CA's battle AI. While it is not totally imcopetent, it consistently makes moronic mistakes. It will engage your pikemen head on, charge cavalry into the front of heavy infantry, and often attack with no real tact. However, the battles are still fun. Troops are easy to control and the battle UI is slick and customizable. Sure, when a cav unit inexplicably gets stuck on one lonely spearman it can ♥♥♥♥ you the hell off, but it never detracts from the overall expirience.
3. Multiplayer: Due to the variety of factions, Rome 2's multiplayer shines. Each faction is fun to play as and offers different stregnths and weaknesses. The added bonus of phasing out the battle AI is just the icing on the cake. However, technical issues still at times hinder the multiplayer, as you will often expirience severe lag and will occasionally be dropped from the game.
4. Graphics: As one of the best optimized PC games out there in its current state, Rome 2 has no issue delivering both stellar graphics (in-battles and on the campaign map) and smooth framerates.
5. DLC offerings: While the 'Wrath of Sparta' DLC fell short, and I still have yet to see the point of 'Blood and Gore,' Rome 2 still has some fine offerings for DLC. Some packs will add fun new factions, and others will offer new, full legnth historical camapign scenarios to be played out on customized maps. Without a doubt, 'Hannibal at the Gates' and Caesar in Gaul' stand out from the pack as superd additions to the game and engrosing windows into some of the most fascinating wars in antique history.
Without a doubt, Rome 2 stands out as one of the most extensive and deep offerings in the RTS genre. It is a stellar game and in its current condition, and it is the best Total War game to date.

I used to play this before it came to early access on steam, and the developers delayed this as long as they could to smooth over all the things that people might be more critical of so that they would avoid the usual gripe of early access games. These devs do weekly news updates and regular patch fixes etc.
This game is going to disappoint anyone who is looking for an easy game or some sort of terraria clone. This is a niche game. You're expected to be pretty engaged to enjoy this game. The positive reviews this game has gotten does not mean its for everyone.
This game expects you to be interested in managing resources, willing to learn quickly or gradually depending on how you set your map up. There's some weak expectation of programming logic in this game as well. So if you're completely uninterested in learning about logic, or manipulating logic, etc. This game will be incredibly boring to you, or if you choose to ignore this, it can get boring a lot faster once you exhaust all technology you can make with or without mods. It is not required to learn anything about this to play normally however, it's just another thing you can do.
This game is not a pure strategy game. This game is removed from the usual strategy expectation, although I would say it's more analysis based than strategy. You're a one man lone engineer. You create intricate systems to manage your resources and make materials to research with, there are infinite ways resources can be managed, a lot of youtubers out there like to adhere to some general guideline for how you set up your factory. But, this is not something that people who are new to the game should watch. If you want to have fun playing this game, you need to experience it with no outside influences. Play the tutorial, play the campaigns, then play your own freeplay map.
Don't be surprised if it's hard to get into, it's a niche game, and it grows on you.

I think this is a good game to start with if you've never played boost formula sonic games before. Its very forgiving, and will constantly give you the feeling of going reaaaaally fast most of the time.
Modern sonic stages are very beautiful to look at, and the music for each stage fits it remarkably well. The boost itself has improved since generations, and Sonic can finally walk around in a 3D space without flying off the stage from the slightest touch. However, the 2D platforming sections feel a bit stiff and you often gain and lose momentum seemingly out of the blue.
But by far the biggest issue is that the modern sonic stages are way too short. By the time I found myself really getting into a stage, it would end. Luckily, most of the stages have multiple pathways to take, and since there is no life system, you can restart as much as you want if you see another pathway you'd like to take.
The Avatar stages are honestly my favorite in the game. They're pretty fast most of the time, but the platforming is better than the modern sonic stages (especially in 2D). You have a lot more variety on what you can do in them as well. The different wispons allow you to either blast through levels as quick as possible or to explore the area for collectibles. It takes a little bit to get the hang of, but once I did, I found myself replaying avatar stages the most! (They're very fun to speed run!) Also, if you're a fan of jpop or EDM, the avatar stage themes are just for you. I'm a sucker for corny pump up music, and these levels do not disappoint.
The customizing system leaves a bit to be desired with different hair styles (especially regarding the hedgehogs), but theres more than enough options to create all kinds of outfits. This is by far my favorite feature of the game. If you love character customization, I can almost guarentee you'll like the avatar feature.
As for Classic Sonic's stages...they're there I guess. It's definitely a downgrade level-design wise from generations. Of course, these stages are also quite short, and theres not very many of them so they really dont add or take away to the experience. They're forgetful, but if you liked classic sonic's gameplay in generations, you'll probably enjoy these.
Now, I won't dwell on the story because I could go on and on. But I will admit the main reason I was looking forward to this game was the story as I'm a fan of the more serious sonic stories. This story really didn't feel like the serious all-out war Sega was pushing it as. Sonic is constantly cracking jokes, and the plot moves veeeery quick, giving little time for things to set in at all. It seemed like a conflict would arise only to be immediately solved in the very next scene. The concepts introduced could have made for a phenomenal story, but in the end it's it feels like Colors or Lost World if they were in gritty realistic settings instead of fun fantasy worlds. I guess it makes sense that a quick game with quick levels would have a quick story. I feel like if they had slowed the pacing down, and maybe developed plot points instead of throwing stuff in for fanservice, this story could have rivaled that of Adventure 2 and Unleashed. Not to say the story is bad though. Its a step in the right direction, and its a lot better than any other sonic game plot within the past 7 years.
Another thing the game does well is the earlier boss fights. Its just a shame that theres so few of them, and the later ones feel somehwat lackluster. But for the first few ones, I often find myself replaying them--something I hardly ever do when playing Sonic games. But like a lot of stuff in this game, the fun boss fights are over far too quickly.
Overall, Sonic forces is fairly nonoffensive and good fun if youre looking to just go fast without nonsense and goof around making your own character. If you liked Generations, you'll probably have fun with Forces. And if you haven't played a boost sonic game, I dont't think this is a bad one to start with by any means.

A spectacle speedrunner geared towards completionists. The game is separated into 3 gameplay modes tied to a respective character and while fun it often suffers from a lack of difficulty at any level. But solid presentation can help you overlook easy and often shallow gameplay.
With “Classic” gameplay you play as Classic Sonic, if you played any of the early Sonic titles or played generation you might be familiar with this type of gameplay. The main focus here is platforming, and can be considered to have the most diverse paths of the 3 characters to get from the beginning to the end of the level.
Next is “Boost” gameplay with Modern Sonic, this is gameplay more associated with recent Sonic games where the focus is generally to get from the beginning of the level to the end as rapidly as possible. This can easily be considered the weakest link of the 3 types of gameplay (though it is not without it's moments) with levels usually being straight forward and generally failing to take advantage of Modern Sonic's speed as previous titles did outside of unobstructed lengths of level that provide no actual challenge.
The main draw of Sonic Forces is the new gameplay associated with the new avatar character (henceforth referred to as “Original the Character” because it amuses me). While far more interesting than Modern Sonic it does suffer from some of the same problems. Original the Character can be equipped with different items to traverse the level but levels rarely take advantage of Original's equipment with most levels playing exactly the same regardless of equipped item. Most completionist goals are focused on this character as all in-game rewards are tied to items or cosmetics for Original.
There is levels featuring both Original and Sonic but add nothing but “boost” to Original's move set.
In the end Sonic Forces is not a bad game; it simply is too easy, simple, and linear. I hope we see more of Original the Character in later games (or DLC) that greatly expands their gameplay and focuses more on them rather than splitting gameplay between 3 characters.

Just as Bastion was my choice for #1 best game of 2011, I will venture to claim that Transistor will be that for 2014. It's early in the year,5/21/14, but it has already outdone every game released this year.

The people who made Bastion blew me away again with Transistor. Between the beautifully painted art style and the moving soundtrack, I was already interested in this game before I ever got a chance to play. Now that i've gotten my hands on it I can honestly say the combat is fairly unique (in my experience) and is an interesting alteration in the hack-and-slash genre. It's fun to run around and button mash attacks (which are all customizable, yes- there are loadouts you can make!) but when it gets tough you can (and should) stop time and plan out your moves in advance. Definitely buy it a try if you liked Bastion or if you want a deviation from mainstream game genres. If not, try it out anyway.
This game is on a totally different level to Bastion. If Bastion was the refined and artistically aware smash 'em up, then Transistor is the refined and artistically crafted strategy RPG game.

Everyone’s going to downvote me to hell and back but I’m going to give you all my honest opinion. Transistor is a massive disappointment and ultimately a  rather mediocre game. Bastion is one of my favorite games and that’s why I pre-ordered this game the day I was first able to. Now I'm really starting to think Bastion was just a fluke by Supergiant, because this game is way under par. The combat is a slog, it’s either a real pain or a total cakewalk. Losing abilities when you die is a real dumb idea and if you screw up enough can leave the game unwinnable. The combat has some interesting ideas, but it just ends up being boring and it feels a bit more complex that it needed to be.
Unlike Bastion which had likable characters and an interesting and well-written story, Transistor has cardboard cutouts for characters that the game expects you to really care for and a plot that tries to appear deep and layered when it’s really just convoluted and vapid. I love a really good story driven game with likable characters, that’s why I loved Bastion so much, but Transistor utterly fails at this. I felt nothing for the characters and didn't care about what was going on, the exact opposite of Bastion. There is no sympathetic and morally gray antagonists like the Ura and Zulf, but instead we got a bunch of janitors that cause every problem in the game because they are bunch of incompetent buffoons. They're neither threatening nor interesting.  Attempts at character and charm just feel artificial and forced, the game just tells you the characters’ relationships instead of showing you.  Red and the sword's being chief example, you never really get a good understanding about either them and Red being a mute really doesn't help matters any. The plot is filled with holes and never adequately explained, as stated before the whole game wouldn't have happened if the Camarata weren't all braindead. The ending also makes Red comes across as really selfish and unlikable because of it. Finally, the Transistor’s narration just seems forced and it lacks a lot of the charm and character that Rucks had. Most of his dialogue is also pretty pointless and doesn't illustrate the world and characters nearly as well Rucks did.
The only good things about Transistor is the aesthetic and the soundtrack. Both are real quality stuff but they are wasted on everything else. Overall this game seems like had an extremely troubled development because there’s so much potential that gets utterly squandered. What we get is a hollow facsimile of Bastion with little of the heart. I say don’t buy the game, (If you really, really want to though just get it when its a lot cheaper) just buy the soundtrack and/or play Bastion again. I’m probably not buying anymore of Supergiant’s games if this is what they’re going to be like from now on, it’s a real shame.

This is one of the best games I have ever played. Unique mixture of RPG/RTS/TPS, which doesn't feel like almost any other game. You are a wizard, who comes to a new world and is being offered to serve multiple gods, totally 5 of them, which one you will pick is your choice and each of them has its own distinguishable personality + the voice acting is just excellent! With names like Tim Curry, Brad Garrett and Jennifer Hale.
The gameplay self revolves around collecting souls that enables you to create your own units and capturing manaliths that gives you mana regeneration to cast spells and summon creatures. The objectives vary in campaign, but is mostly  focused on defeating enemy Sorcerer by desecrating their altars (casting Desecrate spell on own unit and killing enemy sorcerer), since if you only kill them, then they can ressurect.
Every time you choose to play mission in campaign, you have to pick which god you are going to side with, which grants you either specific creature/spell of that god or both, meaning each god has 9 Creatures and 9 Spells that you can combine. Some creatures and spells have similar concepts, but each has specific visuals and/or twist, which provides huge variety and replayability, although I personally think Pyro is the most powerful one.
The campaign also provides interesting story with some quite nice twists, it's indeed not the anything extremely extrodinary, but I still like the story regardless. The best part is that you can side with different gods with each gameplay, thus playing from different point of view, making it look like multiple different storylines. Every god has also specific personality, based off elements. Nature/Life + Ground/Rocks/Earth + Air/Ice + Fire/Machines/Technology + Death/Decay.
The graphics looks quite good for it's time (2000!), especially thanks to the character designs I've talked about earlier, but Sacrifice was also one of first games to use anti-aliasing, terrain change and other advanced technologies, which actually makes it feel more like 2004-2006 game, which is quite an extrodinary achievement, so kudos to developers.
Still, despite being accepted extremely well by critics and being called one of the best games of the year, the game didn't sell well. It probably was due to many factors, but one of the main ones would be that it was quite performance depending game and only top PC setups of its time could run it propetly, making it sort of Crysis of its time, thus the actual market for the game quite tiny and the Shiny (company that developed Sacrifice) ended up in huge losses and never recovered, which is personally kind of ironic, since I consider this one of best games ever made to this day.
In conclusion, Sacrifice is worth not only playing, but also replaying. It is one of most unique games that works flawlessly, the designs looks amazing and characters are extremely memorable, with great writing and voice acting, it is a gem that we should treasure, not only for its quality, but also for the efford it took everyone to make it. The developers put everything they had into this game and I only wish they had opportunities to make more great games. So buy and play this game, because it actually has, I dare to say it, soul!

Be it a frantic murderball trying to stomp everything around you or carefully sending packs of troops to flank your opponent's manaliths, there are many stratagies that can work for you.
A great formation system allows you to keep your ranged troops behind while your melee takes the brunt of the enemy forces, but beware! Friendly fire is always on, so your ranged troops might hit some of your own!
The storyline has one ending but multiple paths you can pursue, with some missions being incredibly challenging while others are a breeze to go through so expect some variation if you choose to be the vassal of different gods in your playthroughs.
My only complaint about this game is that there is no sequel or remake.

This older title (2000) has a unique style of RTS game-play (resource gathering--collecting souls and building--summoning minions) and the game-play feels similar to some games of the MOBA genre, e.g. Smite. The single player campaign has hours of replay because each missions is selected from pool of five choices that result in different selections, which either lock or unlock missions based on player decisions.  Although the Steam Store doesn't show multiplayer available for this game it is and multiplayer is one of the best parts of the game!
In Sacrifice multiplayer you can choose one of the preset casters that correspond with the gods in the single player campaign: fire mage, earth mage, necromancer, air mage, life mage or you can complete the single player campaign and use your custom mage (each level in single player grants a new spell and those spells differ based on which god you serve).
Sacrifice was ahead of its time. If you can get past the graphics, you'll love the game-play and the single player storyline.

Stalker has been considered by many a post-apocalyptic first person shooter game. But it isn't, your in a Cordon zone of the Chernobyl area that has been abandon since April of 1986 due to NPP4 catastrophic failure rendering the environment hazardous to live in. Yes, the place dose exists for real, all locations are based on real locations in the real zone. Life is still going on everyday for the people out side of the zone. The Stalker game series is inspired off the book "Roadside Picnic", which is a short science fiction novel written by Arkady and Boris Strugatsky in 1971. More information on this book is available on a wiki, and the book is also available in English now.  The game is a open world exploration as well as mission directive, Remember that.
Shadow Of Chernobyl is the first release of the stalker game series, not only is it less buggy, but the most mod friendly. I been in this zone since the first release of the dvd 1.0 in 2007. Back when modders were just starting out the great mega big mods that change the game story such as AMK, Inferno, Oblivion Lost, and Priboy came along pioneering the way to the mods of today. Matter in fact, some of the modders works can be found even in Clear Sky's dbase files like AMK is listed, some of the team even has scripts in it.
Here your in the Cordon off Zone in which has become a prison. You can get in, but you can't get out. There is trading with traders, and different factions that may or may not care for you. Many dangerous anomalies to contend with, and artifact to collect and sell for money. Have to watch out for the areas that are radioactive still. One of the things to remember is question everyone and trust no one. Being skeptical with a gut feeling at times is better than a fire fight, When in this game it is important. It also in this game you have 3 alternate ending, pending on how or what you do will decide the end of your fate..
It works on win7 64 bit, you may want to check in the forums. There has been complaints pending Operating systems causing issues with the game. The stalker community out of many I have seen is the most helpful there. It seems every stalker dose what they can to help you. And a good community like that is a nice thing to have.

Truly unique among games - Papers, Please appeals to your powers of perception, as well as personal ethics. I can scarcely mention anything that hasn't already been said in every other review. This game is about choices, the choice to protect yourself, your fellow man, your family. Are you a good worker, a good citizen, or a good person? Is the distinction relevant?
This game is detail oriented, and the faster you learn the rules at the beginning of each work day, the faster you can decide what's more important- to do your job well and protect yourself (and by proxy, your family), or to help those who pass through your check point.
My guess is, if you enjoy the gameplay enough, you'll want to play through a few different times and your ethics will become more malleable over time. It's thought provoking stuff, which is a hallmark of good art.

While Rome 2's now imfamous launch was attrocious, in its current state, the game is one of the best of the Total War series, and a shining example of a RTS.
1. Campaign: As always, Rome 2's campaign is a mix of turn based strategical management on the campaign map, and real time battles. For the most part, the AI does a good job managing their cities and armies. They don't make foolish mistakes, they defend their cities, and they attack any vulnerabilities left by the player. The UI is fine, but the lack of branching skill trees for generals can be annoying. The removal of family trees is another annoyance as you feel no attachment to your faction's characters. One place where Rome 2 shines, however, is its variety. There are dozens of faction to chose from, exact numbers based on DLC, all of which have interesting units, traits, and challenge levels.
2. Battles: Once again, we see the return of CA's battle AI. While it is not totally imcopetent, it consistently makes moronic mistakes. It will engage your pikemen head on, charge cavalry into the front of heavy infantry, and often attack with no real tact. However, the battles are still fun. Troops are easy to control and the battle UI is slick and customizable. Sure, when a cav unit inexplicably gets stuck on one lonely spearman it can ♥♥♥♥ you the hell off, but it never detracts from the overall expirience.
3. Multiplayer: Due to the variety of factions, Rome 2's multiplayer shines. Each faction is fun to play as and offers different stregnths and weaknesses. The added bonus of phasing out the battle AI is just the icing on the cake. However, technical issues still at times hinder the multiplayer, as you will often expirience severe lag and will occasionally be dropped from the game.
4. Graphics: As one of the best optimized PC games out there in its current state, Rome 2 has no issue delivering both stellar graphics (in-battles and on the campaign map) and smooth framerates.
5. DLC offerings: While the 'Wrath of Sparta' DLC fell short, and I still have yet to see the point of 'Blood and Gore,' Rome 2 still has some fine offerings for DLC. Some packs will add fun new factions, and others will offer new, full legnth historical camapign scenarios to be played out on customized maps. Without a doubt, 'Hannibal at the Gates' and Caesar in Gaul' stand out from the pack as superd additions to the game and engrosing windows into some of the most fascinating wars in antique history.
Without a doubt, Rome 2 stands out as one of the most extensive and deep offerings in the RTS genre. It is a stellar game and in its current condition, and it is the best Total War game to date.

This is absolutely one of those games you're definitely going to know whether or not you'll like, within the first 30 minutes to an hour. There's so much content here and it's incredibly deep, yet I've barely even began to scratch the surface.
That being said, it's definitely an acquired taste. One of which I'm incredibly happy to see exists, because for what little I've seen of this game, it's both fascinating and addictive.
That being said, it can be incredibly overwhelming at first. In fact, I'm still incredibly overwhelmed. I'm sure this is something that could be addressed as development progresses and things, the UI especially, is more polished, but with a game of this nature, being overwhelmed is almost a compliment in it of itself. It's a signal of just how deep the game is.

You start off figuring out how to build a few things.
Then you find better and more efficient layouts.
Then you research stuff that allows you to build new things.
Those new things take either a new resource, or a lot more of the resources you have.
So you figure out even more efficient designs to try.
Then you find a bottleneck in your production.
So you figure out an even more efficient design.
Then aliens attack (unless you turn on peaceful mode).
So you you have to beef up your defenses.
Then you need a resource that's far away.
Do you build a train system? Do you use robots? Do you start a new base?
This game is all about finding the most efficient way to adapt to your ever changing needs.
The more you play, the more you learn, and the better your designs become.
And it's so fun!!

I wanted to write an amazing review for this amazing game, but I can't, so I found some words that I couldn't agree with more:
Show’s over, building games. It’s time to go home.
Seriously: I can’t think where there is left to go after Factorio [official site]. It pushes the concept of resource-management to such an extreme that anything that does anything less risks seeming underwhelming, while anything which tries to go further could well be overwhelming. We’re talking dozens of conveyor belts, hundreds of robotic arms, thousands of chunks of ore, and constructions quite possibly in the millions. It’s a remarkable thing. A ridiculous thing. My first instinct, when I saw screenshots, was to run into a corner and mutter rude things about how Kids Today eschew artfulness in favour of absurd excess, but I couldn’t have been more wrong. Factorio is both impressively artful and as accessible as most games with only a fraction of a percent of its moving parts.
It’s early access, although outside of an arguably crude UI you probably wouldn’t know it. I mentioned moving parts early, and not only are there bloody thousands of ’em, they all seem remarkably well-balanced too. There is absolutely nothing to stop you pulling a generous clump of hours from Factorio in its present form, and at no point could you realistically argue that it felt unfinished.

This has gotta be the most complex "idle" game I have ever touched.
I was a huge fan of Clicker Heroes and a few other notable titles in the idle game genre, but unfortunately they pale very much in comparison to Realm Grinder. The biggest difference between this and all others is the huge factor of every single action you take in the game influences everything. Cast more spells--you get mana regeneration/spell oriented upgrades. Buy a lot of buildings--you get stuff based on the amount of buildings you have. Do something really interesting, like cast a spell named after a period of time in the day during the opposite time frame in real life--you unlock an upgrade directly related to the act.
And, instead of just two resources/upgrades you get for soft resets, you get FOUR resources to work with, one being a soft reset mechanic and then you get ANOTHER soft reset upgrade. All of these are easily obtainable without being spoonfed to you. Sounds a little contradictory, but if you play long enough, you will see what I mean.
The reason I put quotes around the word idle earlier was because of how the game is able to switch between active and inactive playstyles. You can literally pick one from the other. If you play all the factions to the "end" of their regular upgrades, you unlock passives you can use no matter who you choose later. The game infinitely rewards you in every single choice/action you will ever make in it. Feel like playing for an hour or so? You can do that. Gonna be gone for a few days and still want to reap some benefits? There's a faction for that.
The list goes on, and it is absolutely wonderful how much work was put into this. I am looking forward to more from this game.
(My only gripe is that there is NO SOUND and it freaked me out when I first started playing)

Honestly, this was much better than I expected. In fact along with Sonic Mania, SEGA have been pretty fanservice-y with us as of late, makes you wish *this* was their so-called 'Year of Sonic'. Better late than never though eh?
Sonic Forces takes a different turn from previous entries by returning to the 'boost' formula that was absent in Lost World and... some other game which doesn't need mention. Many will welcome its return while others will roll their eyes; to be honest I think a lot of Sonic fans minds will be already made up on this game. However I would implore all of them, and non-fans for that matter, to give this game a look. As I said, it's much better than what you'd expect. Plus it's fun, which never hurts either.
The plot of the game is probably the biggest change in recent Sonic titles; we are back to 'serious' plots now. The new villain, Infinite, is so gloriously edgy (especially in the Shadow missions which give him a bit of backstory; which is almost Metal Gear Solid levels of ridiculous), he cackles and broods even more than Shadow ever did. It's amazing he never says 'Nothing personell kid' frankly. Despite this, it never goes *too* far like Shadow, nor does it take itself way too seriously like 06. The game manages to both feel self-aware, but plays itself straight at the same time, it's hard to describe. However I will say I had good chuckle at the melodrama and there were a couple of moments where I was surprised with where they went. It's also rather nice to see Sonic's friends back, and taking more active roles (though I still don't know why Silver is there).
Graphics and presentation are decent, nowhere near as good as Unleashed, but not terrible. There are some really nice looking stages but also some fairly barren ones. Voice acting is pretty good all-around.
Of course, the gameplay is why we're here, and I will warn you that this game is somewhat short. If you ignore the side-missions you could probably beat it in less than 3 hours. However the real meat and bones for me when it comes to Sonic games is replaying the levels, to beat my own score and to get 100% completion. Fortunately, there is a lot of that on offer here, which along with the relatively cheap price makes it easier to recommend.
There are three styles of gameplay, four if you include the Tag stages, Sonic, Classic Sonic, and the Avatar stages. Now much has been made about the Avatar, at the start of the game you are given some super-basic options, basically sending the guy or gal out naked except for some gloves and a basic Wispon (Wisps are back, whether you like it or not). However there are a lot of unlockable pieces of kit to customise your character, and while I normally pour scorn on 'Original Characters' I won't lie, I had a bit of fun trying to remake Manic the Hedgehog from Sonic Underground (unsuccessfully, but maybe the right hairpiece will come up). The Avatar plays in the same manner to Modern Sonic, sans the boost ability, they do however have the wispon, a variety of which are available and give you certain abilities which does offer a fair bit of replay value. Classic Sonic is classic Sonic except he can do the drop dash from Mania. In terms of control for the most part it's pretty good, though Classic does take a little getting used to (in short, the physics are not the same as the Megadrive ones), but he could easily not be in this game. Tag combines Sonic and the Avatar together and it's probably the best fun overall. Level design is fairly short, some levels being only a couple of minutes long, however there are a few branching pathways, though nowhere near the same amount as Generations.
Which brings us to the final bit, is it as good as Gens? Sadly, no, it does feel like a step back in many ways when it comes to the level design, which is a shame. However while there are shortcomings there was nothing really frustrating on offer here, my only real point of criticism is that the game is too easy, though that does overlook the whole 100% aspect mentioned earlier. In which case there is a lot of gameplay on offer here as you try different routes and perfect your timing in order to get all those Red Rings or up your score to S-Rank.
Overall, I'd give it a 6.5/10; I had fun playing it, but it's not great. If you're a fan of 'boost' Sonic games then give it a go. If future Sonic games were this workmanlike the franchise would be in a better place (nary a glitch to be found), but more oopmh is needed in order to win back the gaming audience (though Mania has instilled lots of good will and this game, while nothing special, isn't another crash and burn which is helpful). The Avatar is actually really fun to play as and customise, and you will surely find ironic or unironic enjoyment from the latter. HOPEFULLY Sonic Team can build on the what they've done here, however knowing Sonic Team they'll probably make a Shadow FPS game or just try and copy Mario Odyssey. Also, *never* put classic Sonic in a modern Sonic game again ST, it's just not working, give that to the Mania people and concerntrate on *Modern* Sonic's gameplay and level design!

I personally really enjoyed this game. I do understand some of the criticism it's getting. This game is definitely not for everyone. There are so many different Sonic fans with different opinions on which Sonic games are the best (Classic, Adventure, or Modern/Boost) and it is impossible to please the entire fanbase with a single game because of this. I didn't become a Sonic fan until late 2009 so I personally enjoy the Modern games the most, but still find enjoyment in the Classic and Adventure games.
It's been a long time since we've had a Sonic game with a serious and in-depht story. I think the last game that had one with Sonic Unleashed, which I hope gets ported on to Steam soon. I was also happy to see Sonic's friends returning to take part in the story, even more so than in Sonic Generations, one of them being Silver the Hedgehog who I love. Sadly, Blaze the Cat is not in this game. It's also been a while since we've had music with vocals in a Sonic game, including a vocal theme, and let me just say that I am NOT dissapointed in the soundtrack. There are a lot of great songs, some better than others. I think my favorites include the main theme: Fist Bump, Theme of Infinite, Space Port, the Final Boss music (last phase), and The Light of Hope.
Way before Sonic Forces was a thing, I thought of SEGA making a Sonic game where you can play as your own customized character and go on missions with Sonic and his friends (at the time I was thinking of some online game similar to Cartoon Networks Fusion Fall). Sonic Forces has now made this a reality. This is a great idea considering that a good amount of the Sonic fanbase has been making Sonic OCs for the longest time and SEGA wants to appeal to those fans. I personally don't have any Sonic OCs, but have thought of what I myself would look like as a Sonic character along with characters from other franchises. And now, they can all be somewhat playable thanks to the Avatar Creator in this game.
The gameplay of this game is where most of the criticism comes in. In my opinion, it wasn't too bad, but it could have been better. There were a lot of times where I would fall due to jumping to far or not jumping far enough, especially in the later levels. But overtime, I got used to the controls and was able to play through. The levels are pretty short (about the length of Sonic Colors levels) and there is a lot of places that are revisited during the playthrough (eg. Green Hill, Chemical Plant, City, etc...). To me, this makes sense because unlike Sonic Mania, the gameplay is completely story driven, given that you have to tasks to help take back the world from Eggman along with ingame dialogue. However, because the levels are short, they don't have as much replay value as the levels in other Sonic games have, such as Mania and Generations. This is, of course, if you just want to play the levels for the levels themselves.
HOWEVER, if your like me, a completionist, and want to try to get every single Steam achievement in the game, then there is a lot of replay value. You have a lot of challenge missions that you can complete in order to unlock more outfits and accessories for your Avatar. These missions include getting S ranks in every stage, completing certain stages within a certain time limit, completing secret and extra stages, and performing certain actions like the Air Boost in a Modern Sonic stage. There are also Red Star Rings to collect in every stage (not including the boss stages) and once you've collected those, there are also Number Rings and Silver Moon Rings to collect. However, now that I have collected all of the achievements, I will admit that I don't have a big desire to pick this game up again unless it's for the avatar creater. But then again, I'm like that with ALL games.
I definitely recommend this game, but not to everyone. If you like Sonic the Hedgehog, enjoy the Modern Boost gameplay, and enjoy unlocking lots of content and working to recieve all of the game's achievements, then I HIGHLY recomend you try this game. If you prefer the simple but fun Classic games or the games from the Adventure era or if you don't care for Sonic, then this game might not be for you. If you're somewhere in the middle and are unsure of whether or not this game is for you, I recommend checking it out when it's on sale at the very least. There's a chance that you'll like it and also a chance that you won't, but you'll never know until you experience the game for yourself.

The Elder Scrolls® Online: Tamriel Unlimited™ - short TESO is often mistaken for an MMORPG. Which it is not.
TESO is an RPG with social elements. Since the Tamrial One update the whole world scales with yourself - everything is available from the start, and everything is always on par with you. The whole game can - besides group dungeons and raids - be finished solo.
There are, however, a lot of social sides. Crafting, Guilds, Guild Markets, soon to be implemented housing, all this plays a big role. Grouping up to beat a world boss or running dungeons with friends improves the game a lot.
Leaving aside the mistake above, the game is simply great! Questing is a lot of fun and quite varied, you will have hundreds of hours to spend if you want to finish everything. THe dungeons are challenging, the crafting system is very nice and the endgame is incredibly varied! There is not "best" equipement to get, what you need soley depends on your build and what you aim to be. The incredibly high amount of skill points allows skilling more than just one "role".
If there is any downside to be found, it's most probably the crown shop. Selling crafting motifs, mounts, pets, exp scrolls, style items [...] really takes away something. Your best choice is to get the DLC's you want in a sale and skip the rest of the things.
(comparison: the game in gold edition in a sale - 20€. 1 Crafting motif - 40€)
They even introduced case gambling recently... as if there werent enough of those on steam allready.
The cashgrabbing part doesn't mean i don't like the game. It's just the shadow that keeps disturbing the fun every now and then.
Overall, highly recommended. One-time-pay RPG with Social elements and hundreds of hours to spend on - really worth your money.

Still an utterly fantastic and unique game though.

Supergiant Games aren't taking the route of perfecting a certain genre of games, but rather perfecting a unique approach to a game. Like Bastion, the story is told in a non-conventional way, player choice for combat style (weapons/loadouts/dynamic difficulty) is paramount, and the art direction is breathtaking.
Unlike Bastion's fast-paced arcadey shmup-style combat, the combat in Transistor almost feels like a cross between DOTA (this game is obviously influenced by one of Greg and Amir's favorite games) and Shadowrun Returns, XCOM, or similar turnbased strategy games. Most combat can be played either as real-time or turnbased with seamless switching between the two. It makes Transistor an entirely different genre than Bastion even though the presentation is so similar.
So why won't I recommend this game?
Well, it's difficult to make things so black and white as YES/NO. I really, really love the artstyle. The audio/visual aesthetic alone might be worth the price of $20 or more, BUT you've still got the game on top of that.
I'm not saying that the game is all that bad... but it's just not good enough for the price of admission.
Let's start with the story. Like Bastion, the story is told to the player in bite-sized chunks from a singular narrator. Unfortunately, the story just isn't told very well. Not enough is ever given to the player to know what is ever going on. The question "why" will pick away at any given turn, and many things are simply not explained. (Oh and that ending, I'll be the first in line to read why that ending made any sense whatsoever because I'm lost)
In Bastion, many things about the world were unexplained or left unanswered. Here, Transistor tries a similar approach, but often just seems ambiguous and complicated for the sake of being ambiguous and complicated. The characters will drop hints left and right but not directly tell the player much of anything about anything. In Bastion, there were many one liners that were snarky, witty, poigniant, and, most of all, relevant. In Transistor the characters make several of these one-liners that have exactly none of these attributes.
It also doesn't help that all of the characters in the game seem to have taken morphine before trying to talk to you. Seriously, if the character has something to say there's absolutely know reason that they cannot just say it without all the pausing and repeated words. There's only one time that it makes sense for a character to be slower in his speech, but that's another can of worms. I'll spare you the rant, just know that there's about two hours of dialogue in the game that's actually just dead air.
Now for the actual gameplay. At first, I played Transistor heavily turn-based. It's what made sense to me, and the real-time elements felt clunky. About halfway through, though, I began to realize the DOTA influence, changed the keybindings to match, and found that the real-time combat was far easier that what I had been doing.
At the end of the day, however, the combat still feels weak. I didn't feel like I had enough mobility in either play-style. The Jaunt() is good, but is most useful in a fully real-time strategy and still not fast enough to feel like I can get out of tough situations, nevermind just walking out of them. Hammering escape/retry became a staple for me at the end.
Fortunately, there's a save-point after nearly every fight where you can fully regain your health. Unfortunately this ends up being every minute or so.
Fights are small and quick. I can see this as an advantage for the player, but really it makes them feel like fights have no consequence. Sure there's an "overload" system whereby if the player takes too much damage, then they will lose a Function. But if the savepoint was literally two-seconds before the fight, then why would I not just restart the fight?
That's not mentioning the bugs where I've launched enemies out-of-bounds and therefore unable to stop them from respawning... Or where you can exploit the upgrade system... Or how the final battle is just an exercise in frustration and avoiding tossing your keyboard through the monitor (0/10, will not fight again)... but I'll spare you.
Finally there's the exploration. Walking around, there are many places that the player can click on and learn a little more about the environment or the story or whatever. There are also places that will transport the player to somewhere else and they will be unable to return. There is no differentiation between the two. It's far too easy to mistake a gateway for a senic overlook and find that content will now be missed. There are too many times where the player must approach a hotspot with trepidation of whether they will be forced into the next area or would be better to keep exploring.
The "backdoor" areas are nice in theory. They allow for a break of sorts, but really have nothing to do with anything and just grind the story to a halt (which is already difficult to keep track of). They're an interesting idea, but just take far too much from the story.
And there you have it in a nutshell. It's an interesting idea.
Transistor is full of interesting ideas. It's got, really, one of the best presentations ever made, but the execution just doesn't quite hit the mark. It's a $30 game aesthetically, but only a $10 game, maybe, to play.
See you in the country.

Even though Supergiant's previous hit, Bastion, ranks in my favorite games of all time, I have to admit that, going into Transistor, I was extremely wary of its combat. Generally I'm not a fan of interjecting RPG elements into a real-time gameplay environment(Fallout 3 and New Vegas being perfect examples of how to do this entirely wrong). I am very pleased to say that my concerns were unfounded.
The combat is designed in such a way that you can't rely entirely on one strategy. Being able to pause the game and queue up actions(referred to as Turn() ) while enemies can't react seems like it would be overpowered, but the game is designed in such a way that you're quite vulnerable outside of Turn(), necessitating its use. On the other hand, many enemies, especially later in the game, have ways of countering your offense even while you're in the relative safety of Turn(), so you need to keep on your toes.
Like in Bastion, how you play the game is highly customizable and dependent on what abilities you have equipped. The fact that every ability can also be applied as a modifier to other abilities or as a passive benefit to Red gives you incredible variety in your tactics. Another returning feature is the ability to add gameplay modifiers to make the game more difficult, so you can find a level that you're comfortable with.
The visuals, sound design, and writing are, of course, superb(and arguably the best reasons to play the game), but are better experienced firsthand than described.
If you're on the fence about Transistor, like I was, take the plunge and support this awesome developer.

This Game got me good. Even though it's almost ancient (It was released in 2000), it has really awesome thoughts put into it. The idea of this game is fantastic, yet it's a bit hard, since you only have that 3rd person perspective with sort of crappy camera adjustments. However, it sure is a Game worth playing: Magic in this game is something I'd considder *REAL Magic*, I haven't seen any game with that sort of magic concept such as in Sacrifice, since it's really affects the environment or is 'realisticly' big. A summoned Tornado, for example, is roughly the game characters size multiplied by 255. It's fantastic to look at that. Furthermore, the Game itself has gigantic potential. I personally hope for a improved remake of this game.
Pro vs Cons:
+Great replay value as mentioned everywhere; Due to the campaign.
+Great Concept and Ideas.
+Unique Troops. And I've seen lots.
+Awesome Spellcasting. By far the most awesome part in the whole game.
+Differences between races/elements is good.
+Entertaining, as you can influence the slightest flow of battle.
~Challenging. My longest battle till now was 'round 12 Minutes of non-stop summoning/spelling stuffs.
~Amass of Species: There is enough for everything, but there could be "more". More Maps for skirmishes, maybe levelable summons, things like that. Maybe even a skill-tree for your wizard.
- Camera Angles: Can often disturb the scenery, also there's only 3rd Person, as far as I have played.
- Ressource-Management: There could be some sort of other way to gain Souls; Since if you lose an important battle, you basically lose the match, as you lose all your gathered souls to your enemy, except if you were agile enough to gather them during battle.

Truly unique among games - Papers, Please appeals to your powers of perception, as well as personal ethics. I can scarcely mention anything that hasn't already been said in every other review. This game is about choices, the choice to protect yourself, your fellow man, your family. Are you a good worker, a good citizen, or a good person? Is the distinction relevant?
This game is detail oriented, and the faster you learn the rules at the beginning of each work day, the faster you can decide what's more important- to do your job well and protect yourself (and by proxy, your family), or to help those who pass through your check point.
My guess is, if you enjoy the gameplay enough, you'll want to play through a few different times and your ethics will become more malleable over time. It's thought provoking stuff, which is a hallmark of good art.

Coming from someone with a lot of game play experience in the Total War scene, unfortunately none of the games seem to incorporate the best qualities all in to one single game. I have played every single one that has been released and honestly, have spent more time playing Rome I, and Medieval II than any of the newer ones. I looked forward to Rome II so much, but, just didn't feel that the game was done justice. I would still give it 7.5/10 or somewhere around there and suggest that people try the game before they buy. I would give that advice to any one about any game to be honest. I'm picky when it comes to video games but something about the Total War series has always captivated me. Love the strategy aspect of the games more so than I do the actual battles. The battles seem to be what a LOT of people have the most issue with, but I think that is absurd. This is a STRATEGY based game. If you want to just blow through battles or kill people then play GTA or Elder Scrolls. I'm sorry if some people find the concept difficult or don't enjoy what seems to be the real reason behind these games. However, this does fall on you heavily. Read the descriptions, reviews, and consumer posts before criticizing the game just based off of battles. I have more experience playing this series than any one that I have seen make a post so far, but I could be wrong on that considering I haven't read through the 1000s of reviews. So if you're looking to buy this game, I would encourage you to play Rome I before purchasing Rome II. If you like Rome I, then you will enjoy Rome II. Also I have probably tenfold the gameplay on Rome I and Medieval II combined and you can take it to the bank when I tell you this, if you like those two, then you will enjoy Rome II.

First off, as many of you have probably heard, launch of this game was rather terrible:
Yes, there are many issues in regards to this game about its server(s) (for Klaipeda at least).  However, the developers, IMC Games are actively working to fix those problems:
This, along with other patches, shows that they are listening to the player's complaints in order to improve the player's experience(s) with the game and thus allows them to be worthy of praise.
Now then, onwards to the game itself.  The gameplay is rather simple.  You run around and you kill mobs and sometimes bosses and you get stronger and fight stronger mobs and bosses.  Yes, it is repetitive and some people may not enjoy this type of gameplay.  There involves alot of "grinding" in this game so for those that are rather appalled by such this game may not indeed be for you. I mean, it is  fun to gather several mobs in one location and kill them all at once; watching them explode into tiny little bits.  So yes, game is fun (at least for me that is...).

All in all, this game definately is a gem hidden inside a rock.  I believe that it is fun and think that you too can enjoy it if you at least give this game a try.  Perhaps not now during exclusive founder's access but when it is released for public free-to-play.  By then, most of the problems that is currently going on should be fixed (hopefully, but judging by how things are progressing then hopes are rather high currently).

Even though Supergiant's previous hit, Bastion, ranks in my favorite games of all time, I have to admit that, going into Transistor, I was extremely wary of its combat. Generally I'm not a fan of interjecting RPG elements into a real-time gameplay environment(Fallout 3 and New Vegas being perfect examples of how to do this entirely wrong). I am very pleased to say that my concerns were unfounded.
The combat is designed in such a way that you can't rely entirely on one strategy. Being able to pause the game and queue up actions(referred to as Turn() ) while enemies can't react seems like it would be overpowered, but the game is designed in such a way that you're quite vulnerable outside of Turn(), necessitating its use. On the other hand, many enemies, especially later in the game, have ways of countering your offense even while you're in the relative safety of Turn(), so you need to keep on your toes.
Like in Bastion, how you play the game is highly customizable and dependent on what abilities you have equipped. The fact that every ability can also be applied as a modifier to other abilities or as a passive benefit to Red gives you incredible variety in your tactics. Another returning feature is the ability to add gameplay modifiers to make the game more difficult, so you can find a level that you're comfortable with.
The visuals, sound design, and writing are, of course, superb(and arguably the best reasons to play the game), but are better experienced firsthand than described.
If you're on the fence about Transistor, like I was, take the plunge and support this awesome developer.

I remember when this game was a buy to play title back in 2009 onwards. I also remember when they made the game free to play and that's pretty much when things started to go down I think. It was truly fun, I won't lie, but the lack of income led to the game's downfall. They switched to Facebook which in my opinion ruined the game. Now, we are here, on Steam and as many have mentioned the game is a classic pay to win facebook game which is a great shame.
The game itself is okay. If you love horses, like show jumping or simply want to have a fun past time activity it's a good game, and it's free. You can own a horse that you can customize with a big number of different coats and patterns, main and tail colors, etc. You can buy new tack and new gear in the shop or upgrade what you already have to increase your stats. There's a ton of different courses where you can compete in ranked matches, alone, championships and so on. You have a paddock where you can run around and practice, collect small gifts of exp and coins/diamonds. When you level up you can assign points to different stats of your horse. At the end of the day you horse will need to be groomed and you can sit down and create your own courses for others to use.
Well, that's pretty much it actually. And it's not as fun as it may seem. Or at least it's not as fun as it used to be. You no longer have dressage, or cross country (it was in the original game). The graphics seem far worse than the old game was (most likely because they put it on facebook). And to top it all off the game is a money sinkhole. You are required to buy a premium account (subscription) + buy diamonds which are necessary for you to upgrade your items to keep up with other people, and to buy items from the shop which will allow you to have a proper amount of action points which are needed to play and which run out ridiculously fast. Not to mention other small perks which cost diamonds. If you want to play this game casually I guess you can, but if you want to be at all competitive or spend more time playing this, you will have to cough up a lot of cash. The worst thing is that it's not worth it, cause the game doesn't seem to be getting any updates to it's gameplay or graphics. You'll get bored really fast.
Despite the fact that I am marginally enjoying this game, I cannot really recommend it. At least not to serious players or those who are not extreme horse fans. You have to pay too much simply to play. Having action points (a.k.a. energy) to play is something that only facebook games should have, not proper computer games that you post here on Steam. If you are a hard core horse fan, give it a shot, because it's free. It's a nice little thing to pass the time. Your action points will not even last for anything longer. If not, then look for something else. If you are willing to pay for a sub, go play Star Stable.
Update: I counted the amount of time you have to play with your avaiable action points when they are 100% full. It took me between 5 and 8 min to run out of them. Maybe less.

TESO is an RPG with social elements. Since the Tamrial One update the whole world scales with yourself - everything is available from the start, and everything is always on par with you. The whole game can - besides group dungeons and raids - be finished solo.
There are, however, a lot of social sides. Crafting, Guilds, Guild Markets, soon to be implemented housing, all this plays a big role. Grouping up to beat a world boss or running dungeons with friends improves the game a lot.
Leaving aside the mistake above, the game is simply great! Questing is a lot of fun and quite varied, you will have hundreds of hours to spend if you want to finish everything. THe dungeons are challenging, the crafting system is very nice and the endgame is incredibly varied! There is not "best" equipement to get, what you need soley depends on your build and what you aim to be. The incredibly high amount of skill points allows skilling more than just one "role".
If there is any downside to be found, it's most probably the crown shop. Selling crafting motifs, mounts, pets, exp scrolls, style items [...] really takes away something. Your best choice is to get the DLC's you want in a sale and skip the rest of the things.
(comparison: the game in gold edition in a sale - 20€. 1 Crafting motif - 40€)
They even introduced case gambling recently... as if there werent enough of those on steam allready.
The cashgrabbing part doesn't mean i don't like the game. It's just the shadow that keeps disturbing the fun every now and then.
Overall, highly recommended. One-time-pay RPG with Social elements and hundreds of hours to spend on - really worth your money.

Elder Scrolls Online: 10/10
Where to start....I know. This game to start off is not the Elder Scrolls experience one would be used to (havock physics, single player, Morrowind, Oblivion, Skyrim, etc.). It is a MMO but, with the rich, humourus, deeply lore friendly environment of the elder scrolls universe.  In fact, many of the mechanics present in lets say Skyrim is still available in ESO. For example, one can be a thief, an assassin, a mage, or a warrior. I believe the two most exciting aspects of ESO would have to be one, despite the class you choose as with your first character, you are NOT bound to the aspects of that class. For example, one could potentially pick to be a sorcerer for their class. At first one would think that, " Oh, I'd have to have light armor or staff with my character at all times." NOPE! You can specialize in dual wielding, two hander, or whatever skill line you choose for your weapon while spitting lightning bolts out of your hands! Well, something like that anyway. What I'm trying to say is that one can be whatever they want to be in ESO. Wanna be a Destruction Staff wielding badass with a class of NIght Blade? Or how bout a two handed axe wielder who just so happens to also have serious skills with sorcery as well? ESO lets you build your way. The next aspect I EXTREMELY enjoyed about ESO is the questing and exploration of ESO. Remember when you were playing Skyrim and saw that cave and wondered what is was only to find out is was full of vampires trying to suck the life out of ya? Or how about just exploring an elder scrolls world lead to rewards and sweet side quests? ESO uses this aspect to its full potential. When I'am traveling through, lets say, Auridon(High Elf territory) I randomly was exploring locales of the island when a random event triggered, which spawned Daedra who were sent to kill me! Or this one time I was jumped by a group of bandits! But remember, these are all random events like in other Elder Scrolls experiences! I even stumbled upon a cave that led me to a shrine of Mehrunes Dagon, which prompted swarming Daedra. The questing and story telling of ESO is something written very well and I thoroughly enjoyed due one, it was just plain fun and two, learning more and more about lore is awesome.
Let me wrap this up, if you want an online Elder Scrolls experience which is fun and rewarding, get ESO. And add me!

Taking place in a fictional Communist-state (very similar to the USSR of yesteryear), you're forced to use your powers of deduction to verify if people crossing the border into your country are valid residents -- then things get a little fuzzy.
There's something both addicting and terribly sad about this title.  The lines begin to blur as you realize that the rules you're following are causing genuine hardship on others. Need I mention that you'll be sent to prison (and your family will be thrown out to the streets) if you fail to do your job right? A stellar 'art meets adventure' experience.

is a fantastic indie game set in the fictional dystopian country Arstotzka, which is reminiscent of the USSR. Your character has been selected to work at a border check stop allowing or denying people from entering the country. Sometimes, you must stop criminals or terrorists, other times you must choose to allow or deny people in need of sanctuary. All in all, this is a fantastic game with compelling mechanics and style.

Bureaucracy at its finest, "Papers, Please" puts you in the shoes of a border crossing inspector. Players verify documents and must determine whether the poor souls in line deserve entry into the great nation of Arstotzka.
It starts out simply enough, with only the passport to inspect, but the game steadily ups the ante, adding new documents and clever ways to fool you into allowing entry. Eventually, as society collapses around you, players even get the opportunity to take down impatient applicants who attempt to cross the border prematurely.
Take bribes, serve justice, detain smugglers, scan crossdressers, deny your family food, heat or medicine... could you ask for anything more of a game?
I can't stop, won't stop.

Although the premise is relatively simple, the game design, both artistically and functionally, is so clever that I cannot help but be drawn into my alternate life as a border control officer in Glorious Arstotzka. As I shuffle immigration documents around my desk I feel like a cold-blooded bureaucrat, who narrows his eyes as he glances across your information, sniffs knowlingly and loudly stamps your papers, deciding your fate. Will you be allowed through, or will you be sent away?
Insanely addicting despite the simplicity in nature and repetition, this came is incredibably fun. I wish it were longer. Don't let the graphics fool you, this is a top quality game

A surprisingly "simple" game that is very good at what it tries to do: place you in the role of an overwhelmed, low-class worker in a dystopian society, fighting to get through the rules and regulations that each new day brings in order to feed their family.
As I said, the game is very simple at the heart of it. You check passports and answer the yes or no question of whether you allow someone into your country or not. But right away the game starts ramping up in difficulty. You have so many variables to check with a person's identity, their looks, birthdays and passport codes, cities and countries and insignias that need to match. And that's only within the first few days.
Pretty soon you are hit with immigration passes, work passes, forgeries and bribes, terrorists that can end your entire day's work if they're allowed through, among a number of other things. I'm only a third of the way through the days and I have so many things to keep track of, I'm swamped. And that's just what the game is going for.
Is this a game full of action and adventure? Not really. Is it full of exploration and excitement? Well, not really in the traditional sense. Is it worth playing? Certainly.
I didn't know what to expect from the beginning, and although the game is spent sitting in a window overlooking immigrants and civilians, frivolously examining passports and documents looking for faults, stamping acceptances and denials, it is still very interesting. I'm nowhere near done, but it does seem to be building towards something that I don't want to say, as it may give expectations away.
But go and play this game. Give it a chance.

I spent a lot of time being skeptical of this game. I was worried about Classic Sonic's inclusion, as it indicated that they were going to ride the success of Generations and not try any new ideas. I was concerned that Forces was going to "just be another Boost Engine game", as I've never been super into those games. I think Generations is a good game and I enjoy it, but I generally prefer the older 3D sonic titles to the Boost Engine games. They feel a lot less like platformer games to me and almost akin to racing games, everything happens so fast and there's little time to really enjoy the stages, in my opinion. These games are still good, (with the exception of Unleashed, lol) but my point is that I wasn't really excited for Another Boost Game. Generations had 2D stages that I enjoyed quite a bit and I felt like it did a much better job bringing back the "platformer" aspect and it's the Boost Engine game I liked the most until Forces.
Forces absolutely exceeded my expectations in almost every way, and although it's not perfect or the greatest Sonic game of all time, I think it seriously is worth playing. The graphics and setting are both fantastic to me, the storyline is ridiculous and stupid and I loved the hell out of it, the three different gameplay styles all felt great and I never felt like "oh great, another of these levels interrupting the levels I actually WANT to play", I even loved all the Classic Sonic levels and thought his inclusion in the game was actually clever and cool. This game is officially a tie-in with Mania, which rules.
The soundtrack is one of the best in the series, for sure. I can't get most of these songs out of my head, it's insane how good it all sounds.
There are still issues, as with pretty much all Sonic games, sometimes you may find yourself boosting off of a path, into a sudden death, but the omission of lives takes pretty much all the frustration out of that so I never found it being too bothersome. This game has a lot of "Boosty" parts where you're basically just speeding through helpless enemies until you reach the end of the part of the level but it never really bothered me in this game like it bothered me in previous Boost Engine entries in the series. It's weird, I dunno how to describe it. It feels a lot more satisfying in this game for some reason. The levels are also all quite short as well but I didn't find this to be too bad. A handful of times I felt like I wanted more from the stages by the time they reached their end but absolutely none of them overstay their welcome, a sin I feel is far greater in games like this.
I didn't find this game to be too short, either, it's about as long as other Sonic games, I beat it in about 5-6 hours. I'm still replaying a lot of levels and doing missions and secret levels and stuff, I'm not really finding it to be lacking in the content department. There are a lot of things to unlock and do and it's all really fun to spend time doing.
The character creator aspect of the game is a lot more fun than I was expecting, also! There are so many clothes and style options, and their part in the story feels in-place and very welcome. The storyline in general was also quite to my liking, I very much loved seeing so many of my favorite characters return and have important roles.
Bottom line, this is honestly, in my opinion, a triumph and I hope Sonic Team and SEGA don't ditch 3D Sonic games in favor of just retroesque 2D platformers. I love Mania a whole bunch but 3D Sonic games have always been my absolute favorite. This game is fun and memorable as hell and worth playing. Definitely consider picking it up if you're even slightly interested. I know it's been getting a lot of negative press and I'm honestly dumbfounded as to how, unless people are just dissapointed that this isn't exactly like Mania.
Again, please consider picking this one up. It's struck a chord with me that I wasn't expecting it to at all, and for that I wanted to say my piece on it. It's great. I love it. Best Boost Engine game so far, in my honest opinion.

I'll try to keep things as spoiler free as possible.
The short version: The game is definitely good and is on the right path, but there's some things that weren't executed right or a lot of wasted potential. I'd give it a 7.5/10. Reminder to keep your expectations low, otherwise it'll ruin the game for you.
The long version: I definitely have had fun with this game and personally liked it a bit more than Mania (mainly cause I prefer modern Sonic over classic). But however, it's not perfect and definitely has flaws.
The Modern stages are an absolute blast to play and are NOT as linear as people like to say. In terms of linearity, it's definitely a step above Colors for the most part and can even get as many pathways as Generations at times. However, as sweet as Modern Sonic is, his stages are way too short if you're just playing to blaze right through them as normally. It's definitely longer when you're collectible hunting though. Not to mention his control felt stiff for a bit, especially coming from Generations, and not to mention the weird acceleration and heavyness of his jump. However, you'll get used to it pretty quickly. Though I will admit, there were times where even if I was used to it, the control would act up.
The Avatar is definitely the best part of the game, and the one that had the most effort put into. There's a lot of customization options and the wispons are fun to use, not to mention the different species' abilities make for some great replayability. The Avatar also controls the best out of all the playable characters. Though there was like one level I absolutely hated, for the most part I loved the game.
The tag team stages are super fun, and the best part is, it's entirely in 3d! Not a single 2d section in sight and it has lots of alternate pathways later on. Plus, the double boost is just an absolute blast to use.
Admittedly, the worst part about Forces is Classic Sonic, and was my least favorite part of the game. There wasn't much story importance given to him...he's just THERE. Plus, his control is just plain weird, especially considering they already got it right before in Generations. The only thing they really improved upon from Generations is that pressing down and rolling actually gives you higher speed now. The oddest part I found about Classic's gameplay was that stupid speed cap they brought back from Sonic 1. One question: why?
Graphically, the game is absolutely beautiful! This is some of the best art direction I've seen from a Sonic game since Unleashed. Plus, the music, as always, is totally kickass. Especially given that all the Avatar stages have vocals in them, and Classic's songs actually sound like a Genesis game instead of those dumb Cash Cash dubstep remixes from Generations (not dissing them, I love them too but c'mon).
The story was alright, but as always when Sonic Team themselves writes it, I feel like they could've done more. Eggman taking over the world and actually winning is a great concept, but it's not much if you don't do anything with it or develop it properly. It's weird too because Unleashed had a great story, and that was internally written.
Overall, the game is good but flawed. Is it another Generations? No. Sonic Team's rookies they got from restructuring could never replicate what the Generations team did. But is it better than the recent crap we got like Lost World and Boom? Oh hell yes. And the inclusion of Shadow as a playable character and having his own FREE story based DLC is great.
I'd say it's worth a buy if you really like Sonic games or character customization. But just remember to not have high expectations of the game. I didn't and that made it all the more better for me.

I have thoroughly enjoyed rome 2, but at the same time this could have been so much better. I never played rome 1 or medieval to death and maybe that explains why i'm not constantly feeling cheated at the game just blatantly not being as good as those. Everything is beautifully presented on the map, the icons and the buildings etc, but this games problems are not interface related.
For starters, the warface engine used in the battles destroys the experience in battle. Infact the only fun i have in these anymore is either A) Using my OP units or B) performing basic battle tactics....almost all of which are enough to outmanouevre the♥♥♥♥♥♥AI.
Combat is completely broken. The engine insists on having men perform 'kill moves' in completely scripted stab then withdraw scenes.....instead of just stabbing the ♥♥♥♥ing guy infront of you to death quickly and efficiently. The roman and barbarian, eastern and hellenic units all fight thus in the same basic way- the only way to break the deadlock in the later stages of the campaign on VH or legendary ( After you've butchered you're way through the customaryshockingly bad start faction surrounding your home province ) is to get more and more OP Units which eventually spoil all the fun of combat in the first place. With no family trees, you're practically invited to use a 4 turn per year mod in order to get better invested in their life and victories....but all this does is make them massively overpowered, twice i fought large scale battles outside alexandria against full stacks of egyptians and both their commanders were level 10. This from a faction that hadnt actually gained another full province in the first 90 turns....they just sat in their homeland accruing tarits and getting more and more unbalanced.
The building system is poorly explained at the start ( not helped by the terrible encyclopaedia system) and the whole system of commerce/politics not really explained. My seleucid campaign was eventually ruined/spoiled after i conquered an african tribes final city in about turn 10. this conatined one of their own factional military buildings.....yet somehow allowed me to recruit silver shield swordsmen and royal cataphracts - massively OP late game units.
Agents are totally overpowered. As a consequence i now find myself agent spamming on every save i do....simply because they are broken on this game. DO NOT USE 4 turns per and then use agents. The spies ability to 'poison provisions' in an enemy army- sometimes killing as many as 400-500 men, and the champions 'raid' ability ( inflicting damage to every building in a town or city) are just some of the highlights. By the end of the game they are more powerful than standing armies.
The online unfortunately loses the avatar conquest features from shogun 2, which i personally enjoyed. Yes the try -  harding some people were willing to go to just to level up a smidge more was just unenjoyable, but i still felt the game benefitted. Online battles are still fun, but ( in a similar way to medieval 2 and particularly shogun 2) are often decided by whoevers overpowered units perform better in the long run. In the hands of a competent ( slightly evil ) player the syrian armoured elephant is capable of such destruction as to be utterly ridiculous. This made all the more galling ofcourse by the fact thet whenever the ai has control of them they seldom get 25 kills.....
Ultimately this game is not as good as rome 1 in alomst all comparable things. Shogun got a bit of a free ride because of its beautiful presentation-though the combat was still broken, though this game was robbed of that because of the state of the ai and presentation at launch.
I dont want to give it any kind of rating as i hate scores but at the end of the day if you are new to TW you should not be playing this first when rome 1 and medieval 2 exist, unless you're a graphical manic like me.

The expansions to this game , caesar in gaul and hannibal are very good, adding interesting new factions and different settings obviously...but would have benefitted from some napoleon esque scripting in their layout- rome for example are 9 times out 10 hammered in CIG by all the ten-a-penny barbarian factions, spoiling the expansion a tad.
