Sacrifice offers a nice variation on the usual, top down real-time strategy game. I don't usually play RTS games, resource races and clicking contests. So far Sacrifice avoids those pitfalls with emphasis on unit choice, formation, and position...you know...strategy.
Sacrifice also doesn't require every decision to be made at blazing speed, which is nice, so you can take a moment to regroup, spawn some things, re-position, and re-engage. This softening of the real-time aspect also makes the game more enjoyable.
This is probably a little too casual for the hardcore RTS types, and the old-school nature of it limits the graphics, storyline, and unit choices, but its a cool game and for $2 you can't ask for much more.

I've been a supporter for this game since a couple of years back, before it went up on steam. A couple of years back I followed a rumor on a forum and go to see the trailer, and then for about 18 hours I literally could not stop thinking about this game.
I just HAD to try it. I couldn't really afford it at the time, but I HAD to.
So I bought it anyway.
I then emerged from my apartment about a week later, having run out of food and thus being forced to stop playing.
This game takes all the best parts from survival games and sim games alike (most heavily transport tycoon) and turns them into pure crack cocaine.
Every time you build something your mind starts working on future plans on where to go next, and even before you've halfway managed to construct that you realize there's a better way to do it, and THEN after you've finally put all those elaborate plans into action and built your factory the way you wanted it and give it a look-over...
...you realize it's some sort of mechanical spaghetti monster from space, having landed on the planest nose first and splattered conveyor belts in a hadhazard pattern that literally makes no sense at all.
Except it does. Or rather, it DID while you were bulding it. You know exactly what each part of this overly complicated machine does and how it works, but with that last tech you just researched you realize you'll have to somehow pull this whole thing apart to fit the new stuff in, and you realize that it might actually be easier to just do it all over again.
So, you start over from the beginning, thinking that THIS time you'll anticipate all the pitfalls and make the machine perfect.
Even after restarting for the 12:th time you'll STILL come back for more, mind brimming with ideas on how to improve your next design.
And as you've finally put your best end-all, new and improved, iterated and perfected factory design into practice, you just quietly sit there and soak in the poetic sights of your latest creation. A new spaghetti of conveyers transporting goods in weird loops and excessive workarounds that only it's creator could love.
And what a thing of beauty, it is.

Galcon Fusion is a micro-RTS, where you take over planets with ships and eventually conquer your opponents' forces.
I'll start off with the good. This is a simple game that's very easy to learn, and the simplicity of the graphics really helps. The battles are won or lost purely by numbers: troops will kill eachother one-for-one. As a result, battles come down to who can produce troops the quickest, and that will be the player with the most planets. It can lead to some interesting strategies... I had a three-way game where I held the most planets while being bombarded by the full might of the other players. Keeping my planets was a back-and-forth struggle, because I had to retake my planets within seconds or die a quick death, eventualy getting the smallest advantage that I could use to take one more planet.
Now, for the bad. The levels are randomly generated, which adds some diversity, but is often unfair. While there are many game modes, they still boil down to the same basic gameplay, and it gets repetitve (with added frustration from bad maps). And the controls are terrible on a PC. I played this on a tablet, and it was a little better, but I yelled at my computer a few times when I couldn't do what I wanted. This game requires quick thinking and rapid movement. It requires what StarCraft players would call "good micro strategy". Moving from one planet to another with clicking is fine, but dragging was unreliable (required to move troops to an allied planet). Multi-selecting planets is really useful, but double-clicking and box-dragging were both unreliable as well. It really sucks when you know what you want the game to do, but the game refuses to do it.
Also, the sound is slightly annoying.
Overall, This game is a fun diversion for a few hours, and not much more. I probably wouldn't pay over a dollar for this. There are plenty of games of similar quality on Kongregate (though I don't think those have multiplayer).

So I didn't know much about this game before I played it, as I wanted to keep most of it blind to me. I can honestly say that while this isn't the BEST Sonic game out there, it was honestly a satisfying experience to play it.
Could I have asked for more? Absolutely, but I also could've asked for less.
(SPOILER WARNING DOWN BELOW!)
Pros:
-Amazing Graphics. Best out of the series so far.
-Upbeat Soundtrack for Modern and Avatar Levels. While not songs I would listen to all the time, I liked hearing them in the game.
-Easy to handle controls. I gave the controllers to a friend who had never played Sonic before, and besides not knowing which button is where, they had no problem playing the game.
-The Avatar. For the first time ever we get to make our own character in the game, and for being 50% of the whole experience, it was great.
-Short and Simple. The game doesn't drag on for too long, and the story was very easy to follow. Especially if you had played Sonic Mania first.
Cons:
-Short and Simple. While it may be a good thing for the game, it can also be a bad thing, as the game can be beaten in around 3 hours, or less if you don't play around with the Avatar Outfits, or go for the Special Missions.
-Lack of story. The story felt extremely rushed, and it left a few plotholes such as who Infinite is, and what exactly the Phantom Ruby does, as sometimes it seems like it makes you travel in time, but other times it seems like it makes you travel through dimensions. It's never fully clear other than that they call it "Virtual Reality", and no the Episode Shadow DLC doesn't do much to help, other than to make Infinite seem more angsty than what he already was.
-Classic Sonic. While he was fun and cute to play as in Sonic Generations, he was not fun in this game. His levels were always the lowpoint of my experience, and he barely had any involvement with the story. His music were also the worst in the entire game, and were worse than the music he had in Generations.
-Lack of Boss Battles. The game in total has 7 bosses, which isn't that much for a Modern Sonic Game. It also doesn't help that two bosses are just reskins of two other bosses that were fought earlier. You also don't get to fight Chaos or Shadow, which Shadow I can understand, but they had the perfect opportunity for another Chaos Boss Fight, with maybe even a new Perfect Chaos fight. Instead we get a lame fight against Zavok, An okay Chase fight with Metal Sonic, and the rest are just Infinite and Eggman. The best boss in the game was honestly the first Infinite Boss Fight, which was only the 2nd boss in the entire game. I think that goes to show how uninteresting these bosses were.
-Episode Shadow. I mean... the levels were cool, the music were nice remixes, and it was nice to play as Shadow again... but it literally explained NOTHING as to what Shadow did in the story, and why he was gone until Park Avenue. I may have gotten it as a Free Pre-Order bonus, but it really didn't do anything to fix the story up in any way.
In the end, it's not a perfect game, but none of the Sonic Games are. Sonic Mania had its flaws, and so do the old Classic Trilogy. No Sonic game is perfect, but Sonic Forces is not a bad game.
If you want to get in to the Sonic Series, but don't know where to start. I would recommend Sonic Forces as a starting point for the Modern part of the Series, It's easy to learn the controls, The game is not as complicated as the other Modern games (Unleashed, Colors, and Generations), and it's great for people who love Character Creators.
Sonic Forces gets a 6.5/10 from me. Not the worst I've played, but not the best. It's above mediocre, but I still recommend it.

Disclaimer: If you're expecting Sonic Generations/Mania or S3+K good, it's not here.
That said, Forces is probably my favorite "offbeat" Sonic game. The original character/Wispon system is probably the most original and compelling part of this game, once you understand what you're doing with them; and this is what gives the stages a lot of nonlinearity. The ability to recruit "Rental Heroes" (instead of reequipping your own all the time) allows you to explore the stages in a variety of ways, and the way "SOS" missions pop up on the world hub as a result of other players' actions is a cool feature that isn't immedately evident to early players.
Modern Sonic levels play a lot like in Generations, but about 1/4-1/3 of the length of a Generations/Colors stage. The ability to play them as Shadow doesn't change much except cosmetics and... most importantly... it turns off the plot dialogue so you can just play the effing game. There are team-up levels between Modern Sonic and your character that... are basically Sonic Levels that apply your Wispon powers to them, kind of neat but probably the least polished and most weird to control, especially at first.
Classic Sonic stages appear - usually after a combo of Modern Sonic and your OC, and before the team-up stages, to fight the most notorious of enemies - monotony. His appearance is really just to bring some variety to the game, and to tie it's mythos to Sonic Mania's (it's kind of a time-warp sequel of sorts?). In no way does Classic Sonic levels tie into your original character or the SOS system, which makes it feel a bit disjointed from the rest of the experience - but that doesn't mean it isn't fun, either.
The only thing that really hurts the experience overall is the lack of variety in the level's themes. There's Green Hill, Chemical Plant, Death Egg, Casino Forest, and a couple of cityscape levels; and not with the iconic kinds of soundtracks you'd expect from them. There's some good new tracks for sure; but there's also a few that just feel plurped out.
A decent experience through and through, though.

This is definitely a very fine example of "Early Access Game".
Pro's:
- Amazing kingship/guilds features, Definitely something not seen in a lot of games.
- Yields a lot of gameplay time, has a lot to do.
- The map is fairly large, and has a lot of places to build.
- Players cannot logout to avoid death, their character just goes to "sleep".
- Servers are pretty configurable; Different ranks & permissions, and different customization for each rank.
Con's / Known bugs:
- It can almost automatically be assumed that any public server will have a hacker on it.
- Basically all processing is run clientside, making it easily hackable.
- Items are known to randomly disappear.
- Sometimes opening cage doors can crush you and kill you.
- Things have a very short hit radius. You basically have to be close enough to be glitching into trees/rocks to collect them.
- You swim like you're carrying a mountain on your shoulders (which sometimes you may be?)
- Torches / Lanterns will show that they can burn with wood, but will actually only accept oil.
- Chests don't show the correct holding space (IE; Iron Chests say 20, but holds 24.)
- Players are only banned from a server until it gets restarted [Bug].
- Players are IP-Banned, so VPN users or users with a Dynamic-IP can easily rejoin. (Probably should be banned via Steam ID.)
Suggestions:
- Fix Bugs ASAP
- Some sort of Anti-Cheat for servers
- More advanced permissions for kingship/etc for more RPG-Based servers
- Skills (?)
Overall it's a great game, and I hope one day to change to a positive review.

Papers, Please is described as a “A Dystopian Document Thriller", which introduces the general setting but doesn't tell me much at all about how the game plays. Basically you are a new worker at a border checkpoint, responsible for maintaining security for your nation within the small role you have. At first you are just checking for minor discrepancies for incoming foreigners and returning natives, allowing those in who check out and turning those away who don't have everything in line. Meanwhile, you have a small family to bring home your wages to, making sure to keep on top of rent and heat and food so that they can at least survive in a not-ideal situation. The game is segmented into days over the course of a month, allowing for bite-size play sessions, and each serves as a savepoint from which you can retry in case you don't care for a certain outcome.
However, for each day that passes, the layers of complexity multiply, at first slowly and then the gameplay becomes increasingly more complex as the month heads towards its conclusion. While the first and most obvious way this manifests itself is the degree to which you have to use the information (documents) available to identify good and bad immigrants, the underlying "dystopian" going-ons come further and further into the light until the game's sudden conclusion, which highly varies depending on your in-game decisions. Throughout the month you'll have to make moral judgments about whether to aid people who earnestly require you to bend the rules, or whether to take no nonsense and abide to the letter of the law while forsaking the goodwill (and generous bribes) of those you figuratively crush under your unrelenting bureaucratic boots. The end result is a lot of decision making, in which the right answer is not immediately obvious. It does allow you to roleplay to some degree, whether you make decisions as you yourself would, or whether you shoot for the fewest citations possible, or getting away with as many bribes as possible. Needless to say, the game suits itself to many, many replays.
It's quite astonishing how quickly and strongly this game sucked me in. "Just one more day" became quite the excuse to keep playing regardless of how late it got or whether I originally intended to do something else. Before I knew it I had a couple family members sitting in front of the monitor, lending their eyeballs to double check what I might have missed

Have you ever played Brutal Legend? If yes, have you heard of Sacrifice? Assuming not, Sacrifice IS one of the first and the best Action RTS hybrid titles out there, so BL's gameplay is hardly all that "innovative" (though still fun). Fun fact: Tim Curry starred in both of those games. You don't know who Tim Curry is? Go sit in the corner, you're on timeout.
Sacrifice is an incredibly bizzare and twisted game. Probably the weirdest I've ever played, aside from American McGee's Alice and The Path. The game sounds fantastic, has got a very memorable soundtrack and the voice acting is simply superb. The world and the creatures that inhabit it are quite strange, but unique and beautiful in their own way. The graphics are pretty outdated in this one though and it's something that may be difficult to overlook, especially if you're having a hard time getting engrossed into the game.
The gameplay is something that takes time to get used to and playing the (rather comprehensive and enjoyable) tutorial is a must here. As previously mentioned, it's a third person squad based game where you make formations out of your units, cast spells to aid them in battle and complete various map objectives. Whatever units and spells you acquire vastly depends on the deities you choose as the story progresses, thus making the game replayable due to the large amount of combinations that can be created.
Last but not least, game has the same oddball sense of humor you might find in titles like Earthworm Jim. Considering that Earthworm Jim was the first successful creation of (now defunct) Shiny Ent. along with Sacrifice that followed a few years later, it's not all that surprising.
This game is really, horribly underrated. But at the same time, it's not for everyone. If you enjoy the hybrid gameplay of games like Brutal Legend, Overlord or Natural Selection (to name a few, but those three are on Steam), you might as well give Sacrifice a chance.

This game, as I see it, is THE MOST boiled-down RTS ever. You have a color. Planets generate ships depending on size. Ships attack and defend 1:1. Deplete a planet of enemy ships and it's yours. This sounds simple, but it plays out in frantically-paced battles where you have to micromanage planet-by-planet, while overarching resource-management also affects outcomes and turns of fate.
A round takes about ten minutes to play, so it's easy to get in a casual round. Unfortunately the server browser leaves a lot to be desired so sometimes you spend another 5 minutes looking for a game that hasn't started and isn't empty. There are still a number of regular players although there tend to be few populated servers to choose from.
Still, when this goes on sale, it is worth picking up just to witness the simple, elegant strategies that unfold when you remove all the crazy additional variables that most RTS games introduce. Galcon Fusion doesn't reinvent the genre, but it streamlines it better than anything else I've played. It's also available on a bunch of different platforms, so yay Galcon.
Buy it! And one protip: don't immediately attack someone with all your ships when a round starts! You might survive long enough to enjoy it!

The start of the bleak ex-bloc survival shooter. STALKER SoC is an example of a systems-heavy open world FPS, that does an amazing job of demonstrating the broader potential within the genre. The mix of exploration, survival, hostile environment, and warring factions, makes for a much more compelling setting than any standard military or tactical shooter. The story of SoC is particularly strong, despite leaning on an amnesiac opening, and with multiple endings, you'll at least want to keep a few save files on hand. Travel and exploration are both dangerous and rewarding. Managing your inventory is a challenge, requiring mastery in itself. If you go into Stalker expecting to be an RPG-style pack mule, you'll be disappointed. For all that it does so well, and the ways in which it innovates, I don't feel that the game as released is truly "complete". While I'd recommend playing it in vanilla, for your first run through (and you'll probably want a second), I can't recommend "Oblivion Lost" too highly, when it comes to revisiting the game. Previously empty areas of the map are filled, new creatures introduced, and others taken to a superior state. If you ever wondered how the "Psuedodog" got its name, you'll figure that out pretty quick, in a playthrough of Oblivion Lost. If you're a fan of the FPS genre, this is a must for you to experience. The Zone is not for the feint of heart, but it is a pivotal stop for FPS fans.

"Proper story's supposed to start at the beginning. Ain't so simple with this one."
That was the first line said in Supergiant Games' debut RPG, Bastion. While the line was definitely fitting for the story of said game, I'd say that it's even more fitting for Transistor, the indie company's sophomore release.
Transistor starts off with the protagonist, a famous singer named Red, standing over the silhouette of a man who had been impaled by a USB-stick sort of thing known as the Transistor. There is no information as to what lead up to this moment- the game starts here.
For the next hour or two of my time in-game, I was constantly trying to imagine what exactly had happened. The game had me lost- in a good way. Transistor's story is, in some senses of the word, all over the place. But it was never too difficult to follow. I've yet to beat the game myself, but with the progress I've made, I'm definitely willing to say that it has one of the best stories out of any game I've played this year.
And where there's a good story, Transistor also brings more good things. A lot of good things, really.
For starters, the soundtrack is beautiful. Ashley Barrett, also known as Zia in Bastion, makes her return as the voice for Red- and the songs that she sings are better than ever. From the low humming that plays whenever you're in the Planning phase of combat, to the entirety of The Spine, Barrett is back, and better than ever.
Speaking of the "Planning phase of combat," Transistor brings about a new combat system that has been done before, but never quite as well-implemented as it was in Transistor. You can play the game like it's Diablo, sure- but this is incredibly dangerous, difficult, and most of the time, uneffective. The game also features a Planning phase, in which the character is able to move freely about in a frozen world, planning their movements and attacks. Very turn-based in style. Along with this unique combat system, Transistor features countless upgrades, many difficulty mutators in the style of the Shrine from Bastion, and the ability to string attacks together for devastating results.
All in all, I may be a bit biased towards Transistor, as Bastion is arguably one of the best games I've ever played, but I without a doubt recommend this game. The $20 pricetag stirred me up a bit at first, but I can guarantee that it was worth it. Transistor is definitely an unforgettable experience that I cannot recommend you to buy enough.
And while you're at it, buy Bastion. You won't regret it.

This is the kind of game that sets standards for how other games should be made. The artistic direction and design are top of their class, and shine as a beacon for all the messes that have been coming out on Steam lately, barely deserving the $5 price they ask. This game is worth every penny, as is the soundtrack if you decide to pick it up.
On the art side, we all knew from the trailers that it was looking great, and in game it lives up to that expectation. The game makes clever use of paralax and shifting 2d layers to create a breathing world that makes the art pop. The attention to detail in the visuals is superb, from the sword that Red carries to little subtle glows that bring your attention to exactly where the game wants you to look. And where you look is equally amazing, shifting from close and intimate characters, to panning wide landscapes that take you into the world of Cloudbank. Gorgeous.
On the design side, I must admit that coming into this game I scoffed initially at the time stopping mechanic, thinking it would make the game too easy and make you just want to spam the time stop and repeat the same damaging moves. I was wrong. The ability design is superb, each with tradeoffs that make some more useful in time stopped mode and some more useful in real time. It lets you set up damaging combos with your abilities that you have to plan carefully to get the most value. Being able to combine abilities (or functions) together to make variations on the abilties opens up a kind of freeform that gives the game deep tacticals that you can make suit your playstyle. The enemies are designed in ways that make you think carefully about when to enter the time stop, what the best way to finish the time stop is, and how you will position yourself for the next time stop. It also does a great job with its pacing of some "show don't tell" game design. You'll see the mechanics you need and the difficultly will ramp up to where you will need to take advantage of what you've learned in previous battles. And the bosses... challenging and great fun putting it all together.
I enjoy the bonus challenge events in this game even more that I did in Bastion. With this one, rather than it being a wave after wave horde mode, each door in the challenge area leads to a challenge where you have to consider a specific piece of the game in greater depth. It allows me to experience pieces of the game that I don't think I otherwise would have tried out on my own.
In short, of all the indie games that you buy that end up just sitting in your Steam library unplayed, this will not be one of them. Find time to play it, and you will be rewarded with one of the clearly best games of 2014.

This is THE best indie game I've ever played. Supergiant Games deserves all the credit for creating such a perfect, moody atmosphere. I personally love the steampunk choice of setting. It breathes life into Cloudbank, the city in which the game takes place. The voice acting is top notch, which comes as no surprise considering everyone from the Bastion development team has returned. The music is fantastic and easily surpasses Bastion's very solid soundtrack.
The gameplay is varied and reminiscient of Diablo and other ARPG's with the exception of a unique turn-based system. The combat is constantly evolving, even into New Game + as you unlock new ablilites and experiment how each build can be used to defeat enemy. Supergiant's effort pays off in ensuring each build is viable to beat the game. It gives the player a beautiful canvass to experiment within. You simply can't beat the art direction of Transistor. It's second to none in my opinion.
My only gripe is the variety of enemies. Given the setting of this game, it would have been nice to see a lot more variety within the enemy combatants, but I never felt the combat became monotonous because of this (as I have read in other reviews).
In short, this game is well worth 20 dollars. If you are a fan of the steampunk setting, I'm sure you'll find this to be very fulfilling. It can't be matched in terms of narrative, setting, acting, style... Just give it a go.

Very highly recommended to fans of Alien, or survival horror. Or to anyone in general -- you can turn down the difficulty to experience the story if you're not a fan of restarting at checkpoints occassionally, but I would recommend playing it on HARD for maximum tension, even though it's a real ♥♥♥♥♥ when you get hunted down close to a save point after 20 minutes of careful sneaking.
The game emphasizes stealth and tricks to evade enemies rather than direct combat. Where many games rely on cheap jump scares (Dead Space, even though I do enjoy that game), this game will create genuine scares (along with some good ol' BOO moments for good measure) -- a feeling of real dread (hearing the xenomorph snarling, thumping around the vents, the sound of it slithering down out of the vents, the stamping of its feet).
Well paced action/story/frights with some fun throwbacks.
Art style/music/gameplay is all very on point.
edit: I need to add more to this review now, after reading "professional reviews for the game" (IGN's 5.9/10 lmfao, are you kidding me).
This game is masterfully done, in all categories. If you want a near perfect experience of the Alien world, this game nails it.
Some reviewers criticize it for being too long, which is a clearly indication of their lack of taste/understanding/maturity.  A) Do not try to binge this game in one sitting, it is long. Enjoy it. B) Do not try to force your way through the game, you will die. You are not Team America World Police here to defeat the xenomorph with your bare fists... It will eat you.
Backtracking? I hardly noticed it. You go through the ship, and revisit certain areas, but it may as well be new places since circumstances/goal/direction are all different. With different tools you open different paths.
C) Spacewalking is too slow? I disagree, I love the experience of pretending to be in outer space. These parts are few.
D) Too repetitive? The alien's AI is fantastic, I didn't get bored once --> Refer to point A.
All in all, this is a masterful game. So tense, yet fun. The feeling of successfully escaping, or just barely avoiding death (smashing a facehugger last second with your wrench as a twitch response as it's ready to pounce).
Is the game perfect, of course not, I'm sure we all would have our "what I would do" -- and that goes for ANY title. It is a work of art, which I can OBJECTIVELY tell you is amazing. Their love for the Alien series is matched by their talent as software engineers, and they do the series so much justice... much like how Batman Arkham Asylum/City did to use one outside comparison.
It is not a game I wll be replaying soon, but for all the best reasons. It is intense, frightening, exciting and will demand a lot of your time and focus. But by those reasons, it is a game I would recommend to anyone and will remember fondly.
Would be awesome if these devs would take the helm for a future title that does Aliens justice -- since Colonial Marines was such a collosal failure.

An excellent piece of social commentary on the dangers of unfettered capitalism and greed. Upon landing on a pristine alien world, you, a lone human survivor, will proceed to devastate the local plant life and loot the bounty of unclaimed resources for your own personal comfort and survival. The swath of pollution left in your wake is merely a side-effect of your own sweat and blood, and it matters not that the local wildlife takes offense to it; it is your duty as an entrepreneur to kill them and their children, raze their homes to the ground, and steal their possessions all in the name of your own personal goal: To return to space and do the same thing over on another planet.
Oh, and it's also a game about automation.
Facetiousness aside; Factorio is what would happen if you made a game out of the industrial mods from Minecraft, and it is fantastic. It speaks to the inner programmer in everyone - you need to be the right amount of lazy, as you need to be lazy enough to want to automate all of the work, but not so lazy that you never actually get around to doing so. It scales to your progress through the Pollution mechanic, which attracts more and tougher enemies. The world gen has plenty of flexibility to alter the challenge posed without an explicit difficulty setting. The tutorial does a great job of teaching you how to play and the possibilities are practically limitless for how you can configure your factories. Not to mention that you can always turn to mods for new experiences. Highly recommended.

This game is going to disappoint anyone who is looking for an easy game or some sort of terraria clone. This is a niche game. You're expected to be pretty engaged to enjoy this game. The positive reviews this game has gotten does not mean its for everyone.
This game expects you to be interested in managing resources, willing to learn quickly or gradually depending on how you set your map up. There's some weak expectation of programming logic in this game as well. So if you're completely uninterested in learning about logic, or manipulating logic, etc. This game will be incredibly boring to you, or if you choose to ignore this, it can get boring a lot faster once you exhaust all technology you can make with or without mods. It is not required to learn anything about this to play normally however, it's just another thing you can do.
This game is not a pure strategy game. This game is removed from the usual strategy expectation, although I would say it's more analysis based than strategy. You're a one man lone engineer. You create intricate systems to manage your resources and make materials to research with, there are infinite ways resources can be managed, a lot of youtubers out there like to adhere to some general guideline for how you set up your factory. But, this is not something that people who are new to the game should watch. If you want to have fun playing this game, you need to experience it with no outside influences. Play the tutorial, play the campaigns, then play your own freeplay map.
Don't be surprised if it's hard to get into, it's a niche game, and it grows on you.
I personally rate this game 9.5/10; It's got great atmosphere and creativity, It's great for people who like technical games and setting their own objectives, and just in general enjoying their freetime doing something interesting, etc.

Flaws List:
1. Hackers galore: There are soooo many hackers in this game. It's less of a survival game and more build enough stuff till you can♥♥♥♥♥♥over everyone else game.

(Make sure to shove sharp stones up your bum because thats the only way to kill yourself when you are trapped) I am okay with these guys they make the game more annoying but they are not actually doing much to destroy the game for other players. They are annoying but they do add a bit of a thrill to the game. It is the other style of greifers that do that really destroy the game.
2B. Base destroyers: These guys come onto the server at off ours (when there are few people) and go around with siege weapon and completely destroy peoples base when they have no way to defend themselves. So when you log back after sealing up your huge castle of a fort that you and your guild spent 10+ hours building you find yourself on the beach naked and when you go back to your castle all you find that your base is all gone after they broke through ur walls, destroyed your crest, replaced it with their own and then went on their way taking every last block you worked so hard collecting.
2C. Greifer kings who generally work in a guild of 5+ and then set the taxes at 20% and then go around the map being like the other 2 types.
3. The combat system: The combat system is a bit wonky. Because of how poorly this game is opitimized you will be hit by lag spikes and frame drops during fights. This means that what you think should be a direct hit is a complete miss or what you think is a good dodge is you running right into the guys swing. Then there is the fact that if you are in steel armor using a 2 handed weapon you move and attack so slowly that a naked guy can just run around you and kill you with a weak weapon. He will just run behind you as you wind up your swings and kill you if he is even semi competent (as can be used by you to take down armored guys with 2 handed weapons) This needs fixed because whats the point getting armor unless you are in a large brawl where you just swing randomly hitting whatever moves. 1v1 it is more of a detrement than a help.
4. Server resets (100% wipes to the almost 1 an hour you get because of dupers): The first one while expected because this is an early access game is also the more annoying of the 2. About once or twice a week you will log on to the game and find that you need to remake your character. That also means that everything you have done on that server has been wiped and you are back to square one. Meaning if you are the type of person who spends tons of time farming to build big forts you are SOL. The second one is also a pain because it doesn't actually tell you when the server resets so you may be mining materials for 10 minutes only to realize when you go back to open a door or your chest that you can't because of the crash. Then when you log back in (if your server is not full making you wait spam trying to connect) you find out that not only did you not get anything you collected in the 10 minutes you were playing on the crash server but also everything from 10 minutes before that because thats the point it reset to.
TLDR: I would give this game a 0/10 because of hackers and the fact it seems to favor greifers over people playing to build cool forts and have interesting battles instead of 5v1. If you are a hacker or greifer though this game gets a 10/10 you will love it because of how easy the game is to exploit. If the developer gets rid of the hackers this game would probably be a 5/10 and if they balance the game so the greifers can't just destroy peoples bases while they are logged off and they lowered the number of server wipes to like once every 2 weeks or once a month I would give this game an 8 our of 10. A wizard fleeing from a land torn asunder, his past tinted a bloody red, finds succour in a land on the eve of war. A pawn of the gods, or chaos itself? Or perhaps no pawn at all...
Imagine a world without the internet. Imagine being alone in a room with a computer, and no internet, for several hours a day. Perhaps some of you don't need to imagine, perhaps some of you still live a life away from the madness of the net, able to sequester yourself in an insular paradise. Well, if that is the case, or perhaps you need to forget the world for a few hours and a lifetime, I honestly have to recommend Sacrifice.
I bought this game back in 2002, the first year of uni, and I have to say for about 4-6 hours of every day - before I met up with my friends, this was my world. I suppose I should have been a better student, studied more and achieved better grades. But it's very rare to be able to look *back* at a time, and say while it mightn't have been the best use of the time, you don't regret it. This game was that much fun.
Later on it was joined by staples such as Wizardry 8 and fps's i'm sure we've all played, but even throughout the next two years of my life, it still earnt its place on the shelf. It's just...an amazing game. It is still beautiful, the insane character models defying time, the gameplay still challenging and sometimes even frustrating, the spells still awesome, the gods still scheming and the action as frantic as ever.
I have yet to play a game that really catches up to Sacrifice. Like a lot of great innovative games, at the time it just didn't get to its audience. Like your system shocks or deus ex's, where decades have passed before they've been emulated and resurrected, Sacrifice fits into a niche that is hard to define. You play like a field marshall, summoning troops to your side even as you dodge incoming fire and fury, and your objective is often simply to conquer, to destroy, to cleanse. But the path to that goal is often turf-war, sneak attacks, flanking, trap-setting and straight bull-dozing through your enemies. It's a wild and wonderful ride, with an atmosphere that pulls you in almost from the first moment.
I can't recommend it enough.

Realm Grinder is a free game but tucked away inside are a bunch of micro-transations. These aren't forced or intrusive, so I'm fairly neutral on their existance. -Personally, I think the Modern style has been the best its ever been, I think Modern Sonic controls fine, and has really improved upon previous titles.
-The Avatar gameplay is new to the Sonic Franchise, and I think it hit the mark quite well, it could definitely use some work, but overall I can see this return in future titles, and I really hope it does.
-Classic is really hit or miss, I initially didn't enjoy the classic gameplay, but it did grow on me.
Story:
The story is fine, whatever.
, could do with some improvements, but who cares though? Unless its a story driven game, E.G. Telltale's library, story should never be the focus in developing a game, or the deciding factor in buying a game.
Graphics:
Sonic Forces offers graphics and visuals that are absolutely stunning, definitely the best the series has ever seen, I actually didn't even know I was playing on the low settings until about an hour in.
Stability:
Aside from a few hiccups on the PC port, that were fixed relatively quick, Sonic Forces is very stable possibly the most stable 3D Sonic game in the series, you dont fall through the floor, you dont spaz out in place, and the framerate was quite consistent for me at least.
Overall Design:
Now, this is a tricky subject, complaints towards the level design or how the physics are broken (except the latter, I dont see how the physics are broken, I never once had an issue), but level design is a valid complaint at face value, but if you look deeper, things might be a bit clearer, lemme explain.
-Sonic Forces uses a brand new way of presenting the game cinematically, this results in fancy camera angles, at the cost of automated parts of levels and Quick Time Events (QTE), now normally, I would be against this, and even at first I was slightly let down by it. But after playing the post game for a while, I noticed that the short levels and automation at certain parts might've been nescessary. This game has a lot to unlock, and if you want to unlock all of it, you need to complete a massive amount of the game in order to do it, ranging from beating the level, beating it with an S rank, beating it within a certain time frame etc. The game requires you to replay a lot of the levels in order to unlock everything, keeping things simple in my mind is a great way to achieve it, it brings a nice balance between replayability and enjoyment, it definitely could be improved upon, but with newbies at the helm, I think they did a fine job.
Overall, I think Sonic Forces is great,I think its the best 3D Sonic has ever been, it has its problems, like any other game, but I still managed to have great fun with it, plus, its a AAA game that's been marked down from the general AAA price, So I recommend getting it, and if you're skeptical but curious, get it on sale.

The game overall was fun, though nowhere near perfect. There were times I got bored, or others when I felt frustrated. The story isn't really much to talk about, but for what it is, it is interesting enough to keep the ball rolling. Customization of your avatar took a bit to get interesting, but it was fun once you get it going. I do recommend this game, but not with a lot of merit.
The mechanics of playing the game were relatively solid, though sometimes inconsistant or outright working against you. Controlling the avatar and modern Sonic is probably the best and most consistant. While they do have unique attributes and abilities, switching between the both of them will never be too confusing. Switching play to Classic Sonic on the other hand is a pain, but not because of poor controls; the controls for these segments are solid, fluid, and easy to get the hang of just as the games from way back. The problem in lies that his momentum, controls, and playstyle are so vastly different from the other too that it's jarring until you adjust, which again isn't that difficult, just annoying.
The pain most inlies with playing as modern Sonic though. His high speed works against the homing attack and ironically the boost ability on occassion. When doing the homing attack, all momentum is lost and it can be difficult to regain speed, and depending on the level design could mean death. The boost is a problem because it can lead to you vastly overshooting a landing, running into a wall and killing momentum, launching you into an unseen hazard, and a few other issues. The issue with the boost though seems more to come from level design, though, which I will discuss later.
Playing as your avatar is the probably the best out of the three, overall. They move just slow enough that your abilities don't stop your movement to the point of no recovery, yet fast enough to speed through the environment (when possible). The moveset changes based on your Wispon and can open up a lot of different play styles as well as paths on levels. However they do accelerate the slowest, so if you find yourself on/in a hazard that causes damage on contact, don't expect to get out of it unless it's small.
The one big consistant problem that you will see, especially when using a controller, is that sidestepping on the rails or on on foot is miserable. The game tells you to do this either by pointing the stick left or right, or by using the left and right bumpers on the controller. The bumpers don't register quickly, so if you need to sidestep twice in quick succession, you won't. Doing so with the stick is so rediculously sensitive that you'd end up doing it twice, maybe even thrice. All this makes dodging hazards difficult and tedious.
Another issue is that the homing attack has to be "aimed" now, as in it only works for targets in front of the character. Now this can be nice in that you don't accidentally go for something behind you and ruin your flow. This can also be a problem since there could be two lines of targets and sometimes you might not be facing the one that you'd like to go to. The targetting is also extremely inconsistent, even the enemies your ARE facing won't get targetted and you'd end up jumping and not doing anything. It's rarely a life or death problem, but geez it's irritating.
Dear lord, this is awful. So before I start, let me ramble. A lot of people say the Sonic games are about speed and momentum. I say that's not the case now, and it never has been. The games have always been about flow. Being able to smoothing go through the entire level, not necessarily with consistant speed, but with consistant movement.
The levels in this game work almost consistantly against you when trying to maintain flow. If there is platforming, they are spaced inconsistantly so that you can't judge your required speed on the fly. While going top speed on one jump might be good, the very next platform will be too close, meaning you'd have to stop entirely to make the proper jump. And no, you can't just slow down and make the jump, you do have to stop entirely because the platform you landed on is too short for you too keep moving. Other times, perhaps there is an enemy standing somewhere on far way platforms. You use your homing attack as modern Sonic or the Avatar to destroy it, but now you lost all momentum and the platform is still a bit away. The Avatar likely won't make it, and Sonic probably won't either since controlling him midair is nigh impossible. Even playing as Classic Sonic, the levels are problems because the levels don't seem to be designed for him either and the only improvement he has above the others is that jumping on an enemy doesn't entirely kill your forward momentum.
What hurts the most is that in parts where you get the best flow (with any character) it's left to "cutscenes". No skill, no control, and in some cases you don't even get a quick time even. Nothing. You just watch the player character go about with you sitting at the controller, not doing anything and not feeling accomplished.
Did I say momentum enough in this review? I don't think I have...
The initial customization is nice, but limited. You don't get a lot of options and you're character will come out looking bland. Even after the first handfuls of unlocks, it's not great. It does start to get interesting about half way in though once you start to get gear that match nicely together. It's fun trying to get just the right costume for your personality.
As with pretty much any Sonic game, everything is usually made quite beautifully. The backgrounds were wonderful to look at and the tracks were fun to watch zoom by, given you could actually keep the flow going. There is the occassional oddity in design where something might be out of place or just bland to look at, but overall it's nice.
The graphics are nice, they get the job done. Aliasing is oddly inconsistant, sometimes appearing for no reason. For most people, this won't be an issue, but to others it might be. I don't know. Framerate does tend to drop every now and then, but weirdly enough not where you expect it. You could be in the center of a Metropolis stage or perhaps in a particularly noisy boss fight or in-engine cutsene and get a smooth 60 frames. However, when you seem to have sheer nothingness on screen, then BAM!! It drops! Never by too much, but it's just weird.
Also, in the sidescrolling segments, the camera will stutter to keep up with the player. Doesn't happen all the time, but when it does, dear lord you might lose your momentum from how jarring it is.
What happened to the old guys, Crush40? Did Sega end a contract with them? Or do they just not sound the same anymore? Either way, the use of lyrics in the music was way too much and sometimes interferred with dialogue, or more often then not, just didn't fit with the moment. And the lyrics themselves? Well.... They felt way to literal. Heck, they could have been musically narrating exactly what I was doing and it'd probably feel exactly the same as what it is now.
Sound effects were weird. They were either so loud that it detached itself from the environment, or so quiet that it had no punch. Minor problem, but is noticable.
It's a sonic game, don't expect art. Expect an adventure. But wait... where is the adventure? I didn't feel like I was turning the tides to a losing battle, just an upbeat "Hey we're always winning, even when we're losing" kind of battle. And we probably could have gone a few more levels without modern Sonic. It would have added more to the "We've lost all hope" feeling. That and Classic Sonic, while fun, was completely unnecesarry. That's just my opinion, though.
Even with it's cheese, though, it did keep things moving along and relevant. So yeah. Not much here.

OK, now i previously had a review written for this (and the other ones), but am going to pull a mulligan here.  When i wrote the reviews for the stalker series i based them off the Complete Mod.  Well, now i'm going to do one based off the vanilla experience.  In case anyone reads this VERY soon after publishing this, if you read the other stalker reviews before i've edited them, disregard them because they will be based on the Complete Mod.
So, where do i begin?  Oh yeah, the bugs.  For any new gamers playing this game....it's buggy as hell.  Thank God for mods.  This was the last of the 3 stalker games i played on vanilla because i heard so many bad things about the vanilla experience.  Let me just say this.....i REALLY wish i had played the vanilla game first before the mods, because you truly get a glimpse of just how difficult and demanding of focus this game is/demands.
It took me 5 years after release to buy this game because i kept seeing the letters R, P, and G.  Those 3 letters are a turn off to me because when i think of RPGs i think of relentless inventory management, grinding of situations to level up, and MILLIONS of side quests that make for a overlong experience thats full of filler....and more filler.  These 3 games managed to be FPS's with RPG ELEMENTS.  As i've learned while playing many of these types of games....this is what i like.  I like RPG elements.  Just not RPGs.  There is no filler here.  Sure, you have side quests to do, some of which pertain to the story, some don't.  Usually they take a matter of 5-10 minutes, so doing the numerous side quests doesn't feel like a drag.  And as far as the inventory management is concerned, you can only hold 50kg of weight, so you might have to drop something to make room for another.  However, this notion has a little bonus that i personally enjoy.....YOU ARE EXPOSED while accessing your inventory.  Nothing quite like checking to see how much ammo or money you have in the middle of a field when out of nowhere a bloodsucker comes and starts clawing at your face.....love it.
Now, on to more pressing matters.  First of all, story.  While i didn't do alot of research regarding the Chernobyl Nuclear meltdown in 1986, i did have knowledge of it happening.  What this game (and franchise for that matter) did, was open my eyes to the destructive wonder the zone has created.  An environment such as this is presented with this haunting, grimm, terrifying beauty.  It's hard stating that because of the real lives lost and the vacancy of a city of 50,000 people, but a real world event presented in a video game has managed to propel me to researching the city of Pripyat and the events of the meltdown.  Never before has a video game world captivated me so much.  Groups of people known as Stalkers travel to the zone for mysterious artifacts that provide a fortune.  Yet, even in a time of destruction humans cant seem to unite, and instead branch off into different factions.  Ever wonder why our world if this way?  Check out the story of Metro Last Light.....you'll see a glimmer of hope.  Anyway, you venture through the zone gearing up to battle other stalkers and mutants to reach the heart of the zone...The Nuclear Power Plant.  Wont spoil anymore.
The sound design is some of the best i've ever heard in any game. Never before had i played a game that made me jump out of my seat.  When you're walking through a corridor in an eroded lab with virtually no light and no ammo with a gun thats 10 bullets away from breaking in half, and the only sound you hear is either the growl of a controller or a pipe creaking, you're ready to take 2 steps back.  Such is life in the underground labs.
The artifacts provide an RPG element to the table that is the equivelent to supernatural powers.  They provide you with powers such as protection from anomalies, claw attacks, or added bullet protection.
Last but not least, the gameplay.  Now, my personal tastes of a sandbox game with no filler aside, this game has a decent length time.  A completionist run can be accomplished in about 25-30 hours, which i personally believe is a perfect length.  There is some inventory management, but with the realtime aspect, you wont be spending much time sifting through.  Your guns erode with use, meaning the accuracy is affected with extensive use and they can even jam.  Always make sure you carry a couple guns with you at all times.  Your armor also diminishes after taking some punches, which again, cause the protection to lessen.  As you lose armor, bullets and anomalies will do more damage to you.  Thankfully, with all the artifacts spread across the zone, money isn't an issue, so buying a new armor suit shouldn't be a problem.  But the biggest thing for new players reading this to know is, once you get about 3/4 the way through the game, there's no turning back.  You might not know when that moment is exactly, so be sure you're equipped for ANY situation.  This game is quite difficult, but there's a bit of a difficulty spike in the last 1/4 of the game.
It's one of those games that's oldschool, in the regard that it doesn't hold your hand.  Gamers are spoiled today by having everything spoon fed to them.  This game?  Not al all.  There is basically no tutorial and a steep learning curve.  If you ask me, it works well because it trains you to be on your toes.....and you need to be to finish this beast on the hardest skill level (which is where you should play it).  It's gritty, it's relentless, and it may cause some rage in the many deaths you may have, but somehow manages to be so rewarding at the same time.  Fantastic game, with even more potential if not for annoying bugs and a better optimized engine.

Don't let the hour counter fool you, I've spent probably a dozen or more hours in the game offline when my cable went out. I played so much STALKER during those few days. I highly recommend using one or two "quality-of-life" mods if you purchase this game.
STALKER is an open world RPG and survival shooter. And something about STALKER really hits the spot for me sometimes; something about the level design and weight of gameplay. There's something wonderfully satisfying about defeating some of these seemingly insurmountable odds.
In STALKER, you die fast. Really fast. Gunfights are tense and invigorating because of this. And if it's not the people with guns trying to kill you, it'll definitely be the mutants. Your resources are limited. So is your carrying space. So is the durability of your weapons and armor. It's as much about survival as it is about twitchy action shooting. I said this game was an RPG, but it presents it in an interesting way. Sure, there are sidequests and what have you, but you never actually level up. Your weapons and armor get better, but you don't. You also get these little "Artifacts", which are special items which give you mysterious benefits when put on your belt.
One complaint, other than some of the jankiness when played Vanilla, would be it's poor end game. The game just kinda feels like it stops, and suddenly becomes a super straight forward chug to the end. It just does not feel as open as it did before.. Then the ending comes (asuming you get one of the unhidden endings), and it feels pretty unsatisfying. And what's worse is you suddenly get a few of these awesome weapons near the end, but you barely get to play with them, or do any fun infiltration like occured in the earlier parts of the game. It's a shame, really.
I enjoyed this game, anyway. Play it if you want! I don't give a hoot.

This is THE best indie game I've ever played. Supergiant Games deserves all the credit for creating such a perfect, moody atmosphere. I personally love the steampunk choice of setting. It breathes life into Cloudbank, the city in which the game takes place. The voice acting is top notch, which comes as no surprise considering everyone from the Bastion development team has returned. The music is fantastic and easily surpasses Bastion's very solid soundtrack.
The gameplay is varied and reminiscient of Diablo and other ARPG's with the exception of a unique turn-based system. The combat is constantly evolving, even into New Game + as you unlock new ablilites and experiment how each build can be used to defeat enemy. Supergiant's effort pays off in ensuring each build is viable to beat the game. It gives the player a beautiful canvass to experiment within. You simply can't beat the art direction of Transistor. It's second to none in my opinion.
My only gripe is the variety of enemies. Given the setting of this game, it would have been nice to see a lot more variety within the enemy combatants, but I never felt the combat became monotonous because of this (as I have read in other reviews).
In short, this game is well worth 20 dollars. If you are a fan of the steampunk setting, I'm sure you'll find this to be very fulfilling. It can't be matched in terms of narrative, setting, acting, style... Just give it a go.

Transistor is the latest game released by Supergiant Games, creators of the wildly successful sleeper hit, Bastion. I'm sure a lot of you have played it and expect similar things, which is both a pro and a con in this game.
Graphically, the game is amazing as expected; Lush colours and architecture help build the world you play in, almost as effectively as Bastion. The only gripe was that there was little variation between stages and areas. Granted it was all set in one city, but It could of done something.
The Game runs acceptably, although I have had occaisional frame drops and one crash near the end of the game. Other users have also reported this and it hadn't happened to Bastion before, so I hope SGG fix this.
Gameplay is definately the strongest factor in this game. While taking some conventions, It also adds nifty and refreshing takes on combat. All the upgrades for the transistor can be abilities, ability upgrades or even passives for your player, making it completely interchangable and personal. Do you want an ability that lets you rapidly fire pulse rounds? or do you want it to speed up your abilities? Its a clear step up from the run-of-the-mill, although satisfying combat of Bastion. Enemies are relentless, and theres plenty of variation between them (although you'll have to play in NG+ to really see variation). The "Turn()" aspect of the combat is definately something that defines the game. It ended up keeping me on my toes, while finding a way to exploit it for massive damage. Theres a palmful of side gameplay including challenge trials that let you unlock songs to play from the incredible soundtrack, as well as the mentioned New Game Plus that lets you continue your levelling, as it is not possible to get all upgrades, abilities and difficulty multipliers in the game in one play.
Now, storywise, it is definately up for debate. The setting is great, a number of characters are great, but the game felt too short to build enough of the world around you. Bastion had you scouring the land, experiening every biome and location in the world. Thick swamps, icy fortresses and deserted mines made you interact with the story a lot more. Transistor,  although somewhat with reason, only has its objective in hand; To find out what happened and stop those who did it. Theres not really any time to stop and smell the roses. Although there were nice terminals scattered around the game which gave me a nice representation of the city, it wouldn't of been as good as seeing it first hand. No sideline objectives, no detours. It was definately something that made me feel like something was missing. In addition to that, Supergiant seems to have taken a rather safe approach the the story in general. A lot of things echo from Bastion. Logan cunningham, as good as he was, didn't feel like he connected to the story. The personalities in the game were also a missed chance, espescially the antagonists, who don't have enough time to introduce themselves. Although beautiful, the world of transistor missed a chance at something wonderful.
If Bastion had an amazing story and setting, but mildly disappointing gameplay, Transistor is the opposite of that. And with planned support, DLC and possible online features, it's definately something to look at, just not for more than what Bastion is worth (Never pay more than $20 for a video game).
Graphics - 8.5
Sound - 9
Gameplay - 9
Story - 7.5
Overall - 8.5/10

Transistor is a beautifully writen and designed world with a soundtrack to match.  The gameplay is fast paced while balanced with the "turn()" mechanic allowing you to pause the world and plan out your next set of moves as they play out in a second or two of game time.  There are enough twists and turns in the story and mechanic to keep combat fresh and the backstory is revealed as you mix and match various moves and combos, encoraging experimentation.
All in all I highly reccomend it.
There are a few cons to be away of however.
The first is that as of now the game is a little buggy with the occasional hiccups, but so far I've seen nothing that has caused me to die or loose progress.
Another issue is its length.  Your $20 will net you roughly 7 hours for your first play through.  While this is a fair trade in my opinion, you still got more for Basition's $15.
This last issue aggrivates me as someone who shares a computer with his partner.  The game offers no support for multiple saves as Bastion did.  Beyond that, there seems to be no option to start the game over from scratch once you've beaten it.  In order to give my partner a chance to play the game I had to uninstall and reinstall the game, permanently destroying my playthough.  I can only view this design as a way to try and force partners to buy the game twice and is an affont to the concept of social gaming for the sake of nickle and diming their customer.

I'm unsure where this feeling came from, but considering the sale I figured I had to finally try it out. I'm glad I did.
Papers, Please is described as a “A Dystopian Document Thriller", which introduces the general setting but doesn't tell me much at all about how the game plays. Basically you are a new worker at a border checkpoint, responsible for maintaining security for your nation within the small role you have. At first you are just checking for minor discrepancies for incoming foreigners and returning natives, allowing those in who check out and turning those away who don't have everything in line. Meanwhile, you have a small family to bring home your wages to, making sure to keep on top of rent and heat and food so that they can at least survive in a not-ideal situation. The game is segmented into days over the course of a month, allowing for bite-size play sessions, and each serves as a savepoint from which you can retry in case you don't care for a certain outcome.
However, for each day that passes, the layers of complexity multiply, at first slowly and then the gameplay becomes increasingly more complex as the month heads towards its conclusion. While the first and most obvious way this manifests itself is the degree to which you have to use the information (documents) available to identify good and bad immigrants, the underlying "dystopian" going-ons come further and further into the light until the game's sudden conclusion, which highly varies depending on your in-game decisions. Throughout the month you'll have to make moral judgments about whether to aid people who earnestly require you to bend the rules, or whether to take no nonsense and abide to the letter of the law while forsaking the goodwill (and generous bribes) of those you figuratively crush under your unrelenting bureaucratic boots. The end result is a lot of decision making, in which the right answer is not immediately obvious. It does allow you to roleplay to some degree, whether you make decisions as you yourself would, or whether you shoot for the fewest citations possible, or getting away with as many bribes as possible. Needless to say, the game suits itself to many, many replays.
It's quite astonishing how quickly and strongly this game sucked me in. "Just one more day" became quite the excuse to keep playing regardless of how late it got or whether I originally intended to do something else. Before I knew it I had a couple family members sitting in front of the monitor, lending their eyeballs to double check what I might have missed

If you read any list of "games that should have sold a lot better than they did" then it is likely that Sacrifice will be somewhere on it. This is a game that was ahead of its time in several aspects - player choice, voice acting and simple gameplay.
Sacrifice is something of a cross between a strategy game and an action-RPG. You control a wizard, and you can summon troops, cast spells and summon buildings across the map. This sounds like pretty standard fare, but the context of the single player campaign is what brings it to the next level; there are five competing gods, any of whom you can side with from mission to mission. The spell(s) and creature(s) you unlock depends upon which god you sided with on each mission, and is permanent for that playthrough. Of course, do enough to♥♥♥♥♥♥off a specific god and they will no longer be prepared to deal with you, and towards the latter stages of the campaign you are forced to lock-in your final choice anyway, as events reach their climax. I mentioned voice acting, and the gods in Sacrifice are the main source - my personal favourite - Charnel, the god of death - has some cracking lines and jibes at the others.
In this day and age, Sacrifice is going to be a bit dated - hell it came out in the year 2000, but for a few quid this is really one of those hidden gems from gaming history.
P.S my playtime on Steam is pretty low because I bought the original CD version back when it came out.

Don't let the hour counter fool you, I've spent probably a dozen or more hours in the game offline when my cable went out. I played so much STALKER during those few days. I highly recommend using one or two "quality-of-life" mods if you purchase this game.
STALKER is an open world RPG and survival shooter. And something about STALKER really hits the spot for me sometimes; something about the level design and weight of gameplay. There's something wonderfully satisfying about defeating some of these seemingly insurmountable odds.
In STALKER, you die fast. Really fast. Gunfights are tense and invigorating because of this. And if it's not the people with guns trying to kill you, it'll definitely be the mutants. Your resources are limited. So is your carrying space. So is the durability of your weapons and armor. It's as much about survival as it is about twitchy action shooting. I said this game was an RPG, but it presents it in an interesting way. Sure, there are sidequests and what have you, but you never actually level up. Your weapons and armor get better, but you don't. You also get these little "Artifacts", which are special items which give you mysterious benefits when put on your belt.
One complaint, other than some of the jankiness when played Vanilla, would be it's poor end game. The game just kinda feels like it stops, and suddenly becomes a super straight forward chug to the end. It just does not feel as open as it did before.. Then the ending comes (asuming you get one of the unhidden endings), and it feels pretty unsatisfying. And what's worse is you suddenly get a few of these awesome weapons near the end, but you barely get to play with them, or do any fun infiltration like occured in the earlier parts of the game. It's a shame, really.
I enjoyed this game, anyway. Play it if you want! I don't give a hoot.

This is THE best indie game I've ever played. Supergiant Games deserves all the credit for creating such a perfect, moody atmosphere. I personally love the steampunk choice of setting. It breathes life into Cloudbank, the city in which the game takes place. The voice acting is top notch, which comes as no surprise considering everyone from the Bastion development team has returned. The music is fantastic and easily surpasses Bastion's very solid soundtrack.
The gameplay is varied and reminiscient of Diablo and other ARPG's with the exception of a unique turn-based system. The combat is constantly evolving, even into New Game + as you unlock new ablilites and experiment how each build can be used to defeat enemy. Supergiant's effort pays off in ensuring each build is viable to beat the game. It gives the player a beautiful canvass to experiment within. You simply can't beat the art direction of Transistor. It's second to none in my opinion.
My only gripe is the variety of enemies. Given the setting of this game, it would have been nice to see a lot more variety within the enemy combatants, but I never felt the combat became monotonous because of this (as I have read in other reviews).
In short, this game is well worth 20 dollars. If you are a fan of the steampunk setting, I'm sure you'll find this to be very fulfilling. It can't be matched in terms of narrative, setting, acting, style... Just give it a go.

Transistor is the latest game released by Supergiant Games, creators of the wildly successful sleeper hit, Bastion. I'm sure a lot of you have played it and expect similar things, which is both a pro and a con in this game.
Graphically, the game is amazing as expected; Lush colours and architecture help build the world you play in, almost as effectively as Bastion. The only gripe was that there was little variation between stages and areas. Granted it was all set in one city, but It could of done something.
The Game runs acceptably, although I have had occaisional frame drops and one crash near the end of the game. Other users have also reported this and it hadn't happened to Bastion before, so I hope SGG fix this.
Gameplay is definately the strongest factor in this game. While taking some conventions, It also adds nifty and refreshing takes on combat. All the upgrades for the transistor can be abilities, ability upgrades or even passives for your player, making it completely interchangable and personal. Do you want an ability that lets you rapidly fire pulse rounds? or do you want it to speed up your abilities? Its a clear step up from the run-of-the-mill, although satisfying combat of Bastion. Enemies are relentless, and theres plenty of variation between them (although you'll have to play in NG+ to really see variation). The "Turn()" aspect of the combat is definately something that defines the game. It ended up keeping me on my toes, while finding a way to exploit it for massive damage. Theres a palmful of side gameplay including challenge trials that let you unlock songs to play from the incredible soundtrack, as well as the mentioned New Game Plus that lets you continue your levelling, as it is not possible to get all upgrades, abilities and difficulty multipliers in the game in one play.
Now, storywise, it is definately up for debate. The setting is great, a number of characters are great, but the game felt too short to build enough of the world around you. Bastion had you scouring the land, experiening every biome and location in the world. Thick swamps, icy fortresses and deserted mines made you interact with the story a lot more. Transistor,  although somewhat with reason, only has its objective in hand; To find out what happened and stop those who did it. Theres not really any time to stop and smell the roses. Although there were nice terminals scattered around the game which gave me a nice representation of the city, it wouldn't of been as good as seeing it first hand. No sideline objectives, no detours. It was definately something that made me feel like something was missing. In addition to that, Supergiant seems to have taken a rather safe approach the the story in general. A lot of things echo from Bastion. Logan cunningham, as good as he was, didn't feel like he connected to the story. The personalities in the game were also a missed chance, espescially the antagonists, who don't have enough time to introduce themselves. Although beautiful, the world of transistor missed a chance at something wonderful.
If Bastion had an amazing story and setting, but mildly disappointing gameplay, Transistor is the opposite of that. And with planned support, DLC and possible online features, it's definately something to look at, just not for more than what Bastion is worth (Never pay more than $20 for a video game).

Transistor is a beautifully writen and designed world with a soundtrack to match.  The gameplay is fast paced while balanced with the "turn()" mechanic allowing you to pause the world and plan out your next set of moves as they play out in a second or two of game time.  There are enough twists and turns in the story and mechanic to keep combat fresh and the backstory is revealed as you mix and match various moves and combos, encoraging experimentation.
All in all I highly reccomend it.
There are a few cons to be away of however.
The first is that as of now the game is a little buggy with the occasional hiccups, but so far I've seen nothing that has caused me to die or loose progress.
Another issue is its length.  Your $20 will net you roughly 7 hours for your first play through.  While this is a fair trade in my opinion, you still got more for Basition's $15.
This last issue aggrivates me as someone who shares a computer with his partner.  The game offers no support for multiple saves as Bastion did.  Beyond that, there seems to be no option to start the game over from scratch once you've beaten it.  In order to give my partner a chance to play the game I had to uninstall and reinstall the game, permanently destroying my playthough.  I can only view this design as a way to try and force partners to buy the game twice and is an affont to the concept of social gaming for the sake of nickle and diming their customer.

The Just Cause games aren't really ripe for deep analysis, because at the core Just Cause is really just about blowing crap up - just cause. Just Cause 1 was a completely forgettable anecdote, Just Cause 2 was an accidental cult phenomenon fueled by the hilariously janky multiplayer addon and the $2 steam sale price tag, and Just Cause 3 is the incidentally forgettable conclusion to a strange trilogy.
It feels like Square Enix missed what made JC2 so damn fun. This isn't a terrible game, not by any means, but it just is not a good one either. I've had a lot of fun playing JC3, but all of my enjoyment has been seasoned by intense moments of frustration.
The controls will randomy behave in unexpected ways. For example, you can usually count on Rico's ability to grapple on to a helicopter - except, once every so often, Rico will somehow fail to grapple on to the helicopter and will instead send himself flying through the blades which causes him to ragdoll and fall to the ground at an awkward speed. Driving was not the best in JC2, but JC3 feels like you're controlling a shopping cart with bad wheels. Cars will decide to flip themselves over if you turn too sharp, and if you try to correct yourself you just might end up flipping yourself the other way. The wingsuit, while fun, controls like hot garbage sieved cheesecloth.
I've found myself dying randomly to things that seem unavoidable. On my first attempt of an early mission, Rico was riding in the back of a truck and trying to keep enemies from destroying it. Suddenly, Rico was flung from the truck at a high speed in the opposite direction as a ragdoll, which prevented me from recovering until I came to a complete stop. While flying through the air, the hitscan helicopters that were tracking the truck kept their sites on me, shooting me to a pulp. I didn't do anything to start this, I couldn't do anything to recover in the middle of it, and in the end I was just frustrated about how unenjoyable that whole sequence was. Another mission required me to lose heat before meeting up with a character - I drove and grappled and parachuted all over the damn place but I just could not shake the enemy. I tried to grapple on to a helicopter, but Rico instead flung himself through the helicopter blades, and when I tried to pull my parachute to regain air control I somehow opened it upside down, causing Rico to flutter all over the place while my health was chipped away by the other helicopters. After dying and reloading, I spawned with 0 heat, which allowed me to casually make my way over to the checkpoint.
If you really enjoyed JC2 and got hours of fun out of the random wanton destruction, goofy physics, grappling jook, and other certified-janky fun, you will probably enjoy JC3 for what it is. In some aspects, it is uniformly better than JC2, and the moments when those shine through are great. In many other ways, though, JC3 is the logical conclusion to the unexpected success of JC2. JC2 just barely missed being a bad game and managed to nurture cult success via the occasional cheap Steam sale. JC3 just barely misses being a good game.
This is yet another game where I wish I could give it a middle score - I don't necessarily recommend this game, but I don't necessarily think it's a terrible game that you should skip. I err on the side of positivity in this case, because JC3 has enough moments that make me laugh out loud at the absurdity.

I enjoy the game. If you liked Ragnarok Online, you will like this game. However, let me say something about the pay-to-win complains.
The game is F2P. If trading wasn't behind a paywall, people could spam new accounts to bot and transfer items, thus destroying the economy anyway. Further, Elder Scrolls Online has an even more restricted economy than TOS, and that game is doing just fine.
The only thing remotely pay to win are these scrolls that you can use to enchant accessory headgear with up to 3 random stats. However, in practice, the stats don't really come out to matter much - e.g., you can enchant and get 400 HP extra, but your base health late game will be 20,000-35,000+ anyway.
So overall, while P2W is bad, so is making exaggerated claims about the level of P2W in this game. Game is fine, there is no P2W, you will enjoy it
