An excellent piece of social commentary on the dangers of unfettered capitalism and greed. Upon landing on a pristine alien world, you, a lone human survivor, will proceed to devastate the local plant life and loot the bounty of unclaimed resources for your own personal comfort and survival. The swath of pollution left in your wake is merely a side-effect of your own sweat and blood, and it matters not that the local wildlife takes offense to it; it is your duty as an entrepreneur to kill them and their children, raze their homes to the ground, and steal their possessions all in the name of your own personal goal: To return to space and do the same thing over on another planet.
Oh, and it's also a game about automation.
Facetiousness aside; Factorio is what would happen if you made a game out of the industrial mods from Minecraft, and it is fantastic. It speaks to the inner programmer in everyone - you need to be the right amount of lazy, as you need to be lazy enough to want to automate all of the work, but not so lazy that you never actually get around to doing so. It scales to your progress through the Pollution mechanic, which attracts more and tougher enemies. The world gen has plenty of flexibility to alter the challenge posed without an explicit difficulty setting. The tutorial does a great job of teaching you how to play and the possibilities are practically limitless for how you can configure your factories. Not to mention that you can always turn to mods for new experiences. Highly recommended.

Though it may look retro and simplistic the gameplay can get pretty complex in this space RTS. In Galcon Fusion you control a fleet that you most use to conquer all of the planets while your opponent does the same. Its a great game for the money, and with its many different game modes to choose from Ii will keep you coming back for more.

Space triangle warfare in a neat and entertaining package.
If things like plot, build orders and unit counters are your favourite things in RTS games, you might want to check out a different game.
There is one unit in Galcon Fusion: the space triangle. It defeats its enemies by crashing headfirst into them. For as long as you control a planet, it makes more space triangles. You can then use these to get more planets. Which, in turn, allows you to have more space triangles.
Sometimes, there are other players pitting their space triangles against yours. Standard protocol in those situations is to engage in space triangle warfare. Some other times, there are also allies who help you crush the enemy space triangles with their own.
So, just like bullets, you keep throwing space triangles at the enemy until it is no longer able to throw his own back at you.
Space Triangle Warfare.

I held off buying this game for almost two years hoping that the bugs at launch would be fixed. The game runs stable, but the AI is still terrible. Nothing new from a Total War game, but I'm very disappointed that the core mechanics are fundamentally broken.
I disagree that the game is "dumbed down". Towns are streamlined, but the minor province/capital system works really well  and makes more sense than every province having a town the size of Rome like in the previous game. You no longer need ships to embark/disembark units, but navies now disembark their own units to patrol the coasts or help out in a siege against a coastal city.
Many of the added features just don't make any sense to me. There's an intrigue system involving control of the senate with small events that pop up ala CK2 that can affect your family's influence and power. I have no idea what any of it means.The first major complaint I have is there's no family tree to give you an idea who you family is. If your family head dies, they are replaced by... someone. The second complaint is I have no idea what the influence does. If I make my family member a general, I lose influence? If I adopt someone into my family, I lose influence? Why do I even need influence if I control all of Rome's armies and cities?  Rome 1's solution of splitting Rome into 3 allied factions the dissolve into civil war wasn't perfect but it was much more intuitive and  a lot more fun.
The city happiness system has been made much harder. I think what they were trying to do here was prevent steamrolling entire countries with a couple full armies.  Once you conquer a province, you need to keep you army around until you culture eclipses that of your conquered foe and put down any rebellions that pop up. On paper I like this, but I feel like the math is ♥♥♥♥ed up because a rebellion popped up nearly every other turn in the same province (or slave rebellion). I don't know if I built the wrong buildings, but I spent nearly 10 years running back and forth between the same cities in Northern Italy putting down rebellions turn after turn. Something isn't right there.
Overall, I don't understand why Rome 2 turned out how it did. Shogun 2 and it's expansions were probably the most polished games in the entire series, yet the sequel feels unfinished.

530 hours later, here's my thoughts:
The Grand Campaign does its job moderately well, but it is a bit lackluster in comparison to the previous Total War titles. For instance, the AI's more incompetent that ever, which surprises me considering CE boasted of having a larger budget and would feature improved AI for Rome 2. Family trees are also removed, the Roman Senate's nearly non-existent, you can't change your capital, and just a lot of details like that are missing. The mods in the Steam Workshop can be spectacular though, adding some much-needed substance.
The Augustus Campaign to Rome 2 is like what Barbarian Invasion was to Rome 1; it's a solid addition with some improvements here and there. Although it feels a bit emotionless and the AI's still a mixed bag, I had a blast playing as each Roman party. People may not find it as gripping if they haven't seen HBO's Rome (OR just aren't familiar with the politics of the time).
Can't comment on the other expansions or multiplayer though, as I haven't partaken in them. What I can briefly comment on is co-op campaigns. Aside from the occasional lag and crash, I can't really complain about it. The hard part is finding someone who's willing to invest a chunk of time into it with you. Haven't played Shogun 2 co-op in a while, but friends say that Rome's co-op feels a  lot slower, as you can't manage anything on the campaign map once you have ended your turn.
All-in-all, I recommend the game, especially if your computer can handle it on high graphics settings.

I never knew the interactive story telling potential of bureaucracy till I played Papers, Please. Nor indeed, the fun.

I was very intrigued by the concept of the game, seeing as I had never played anything even remotely comparable before. Papers, please truly is a unique experience - alas - not an enjoyable one for me.
The biggest problem I had with this game was the core gameplay, the paper checking. As you progress, the game grows more complex as it challenges you to review more and more information in the same amount of time. You'll be granted new ways to check up on and process people, and sometimes characters will slip you unexpected offers/bribes/etc. with their passports. However, most of what you do is just that: checking papers for matching data. That is not fun. It's... paperwork.
While for other people, this activity might take a backseat to the other facets of the game, I couldn't bring myself to sit through this bland, monotonous grind just to experience what else the game might have to offer. If you've ever had to work a really boring job and felt like it was the wrong decision to take it in the first place, you should know what I'm talking about. Maybe the creators of the game wanted you to feel bored and disengaged. Perhaps they wanted to use the game as a medium to recreate this feeling of working a horrible job. If they did: kudos, mission accomplished. But I can't help but feel like this may have worked better as a choose-your-own-adventure book, where you would have gotten to the story bits faster and wouldn't have had to drown yourself in repetitiveness in-between these parts. The game managed to make me quit because it was too boring. That can hardly be its intention.
Something else that bothered me is the visual style of the game. Although I consider myself a fan of pixelated graphics, I feel like Papers, please could have profited from more detailed character models. If the face of the people whose life depends on you is almost expressionless, you will have a hard time mustering up the empathy needed to feel anything toward these characters - no matter what happens to them. The often monosyllabic dialogue or the mumbling voices don't really alleviate this problem. Even if the creator's plan was to create an impersonal, dystopian setting, the human interactions at least should feel a bit more personal. Otherwise it'll just keep people from immersing themselves in the game.
I did not complete any of the game's branching paths. So naturally my review can cover only parts of the game. Although there seemed to be interesting stuff going on story-wise... after the eighth (in-game) day of stamping papers I just didn't want to anymore. I recommend this only if you do not mind enduring depressingly dull gameplay for the sake of narrative.

Realm Grinder is an Idle/clicker game developed by Divine Games and Published by Kongregate. Thump'in good one I'd wager.
A Guild member of mine caught me playing Clicker Heroes and he said "You should play Realm Grinder!" So I looked it up, and said "well... it's not on steam, If I wanted to just play an idle game I'd go back to cookie clicker".
Actually Realm Grinder seems like it was partially inspired by cookie clicker! I did Excavate a "Chocolate Cookie" with the text reading: "Found in a wasteland made of cakes and sweets, snatched from the hands of an old woman".
If that's not a cookie clicker reference I don't know what is.
As you might expect, Realm Grinder is grindy, clicky, and afk-idle-y. Belive it or not, this was probably one of the more fun AFK idle games I've played
The thing that sticks out to me is the CHOICES you can make in the game. Yes, you read that right; there are choices to make in an idle game!
Really early on you can choose between leading your realm in two distict ways: Good Kingdom, or Evil Kingdom. And then you can allie with 1 of 3 factions within the Good or Evil Kingdom. Then once your game slows down you "Abdicate", reset the game, get some gems which'll make your next run go farther... and do it allll again.
So yeah, that might not win people over when described like this, but each faction you allie with will change how you play the game!
If you choose to be good, and then side with the Angel's, Magic spells will cost less, last longer, and the max mana will increase! Or you can choose Evil, side with the undead, leave the game offline for a day or two, come back and get stuff.
There are thousands of unlockables/trophies, and so far just when I hit a point where I think "okay... I've been stuck on this part for a week now", something new happens to keep me invested.
Realm Grinder will always be an idle afk clicker... but if that's what you're looking for, this one is quite solid and even has tons of tiny aesthetics to keep you invested for hundreds of hours to come.
...See you all in Sakura Clicker when I've grown tired of this one.

Realm Grinder is a clicker game which means is has no end and its all about numbers.
Theres a lot of clicker games out there and many of them satisfy your urge for progression, growth, success and complexity but none of em do it as well as REAL GRINDER. This game is simply awesome. It manages to keep your interest up where other clicker games lose themselves in an eternal griding loop. Realm Grinder instead manages to offer more and more stuff and become more and more complex the higher you manage to get your count up.
Of course you ll have buildings (substitute with heroes/whatever) to get you up a few notches and the well-known soft-reset mechanic is as well presented as in other games.
The first "hooker" is the faction select. You ll have access to 6 different factions at the start. 3 good and 3 evil factions. Once selected you can tap into faction specic buildings and abilities which make changing factions interesting and keeping you busy while exploring each factions posssibilities. Thats not all tho, once you progress far enough into the game you ll be faced by "challenges" which allow you to unlock neutral factions as well which give you completely different playstyles.
Once you unlock and master all neutral factions you ll have access to the "Mercenary" quest which allows you to mix and match faction abilities, spells and skills to your lueasure enabling you to create your "own" factions that fit you perfectly.
But thats not all. Apart from the "soft" resets known as "Abdications" you ll eventually get access to reincarnations which represent a different layer of resets offering yet more powerful bonuses and even here you ll encounter more stuff thats new the higher you get.
Challenges, trophies, bloodlines, heritages etc etc. There really is no end to content that will keep you enthralled and entertained long after games like Hero clicker become boring. I already pumped more then 100 hours into this game and I realize I only really scratched the surface of whatever is has to offer. At the time of writing this review I unlocked "Reincarnation 7" and it allowed me completely new combinations glueing me once more in front of the screen and I know from research that there is even more stuff to discover and master.
Many people wonder what the fascionation is about clicker games but if you are a fan of the genre then this is definately a "must-have". I give it an unreserved 10/10 and am looking forward to countless hours of optimization heading my way :)
I consider "Clicker Hero" an entry title into this genre, I linked my review about that as well to give you an idea what to expect but really.....Realm Grinder is so much better.....

An amazingly animated, detailed, and entertaining Art Nouveau world to be immersed in. The unique battle system compensates for an otherwise linear game; and the exceptional art & music production makes this an undervalued interactive art piece.
Technical Notes: --Some people are having lagging & freeze issues on Steam, the developers are working on a patch. For myself, offline mode will play it seamlessly. However, this means no steam achievements or accurate game time log.--
Issues have been fixed and runs as-is. Enjoy!

-Gameplay-
The mechanics of Transistor are solid in most regards. Functions (attack abilities) work like you'd think they would, attacks feel solid, and upgrades are both visible and have a noticeable effect on your combat style - nothing you do feels like it's pointless, really, it's satisfying and interesting to know that you can try out any combination of your functions with the assurance that they'll work - and every combination feels unique. Even if you have a favorite function, there'll be situations in which you - willingly! - will switch styles in order to counter a new threat; that the game not only provides viable alternatives, but makes every combination fun to use is great.
Complaints, though, include the standard difficulty of using a WASD setup in an isometric game, though the difficulty is minor. Additionally, the complexity of the function system, in regards to the interlocking upgrades and effects, can be overwhelming, especially at the start of the game when a half dozen abilities are being unlocked at once, though familiarity eventually does come with playtime.
-Storytelling-
Transistor is "narrated" by Mr. Nobody aka That Guy in the Sword aka Logan friggin' Cunningham. For those not in the know, he's the guy who narrated Bastion. Just like its stylistic predecessor, Transistor delivers on intriguing, well-written narration, even though the circumstances and tone of the narrator is completely alien from Bastion's style. There's just no complaining on this front.
Aside from that, the world of Bastion is a good blend of mystery and discovery. You can uncover a lot of the backstory and details of the world through various efforts of exploration and unlocks, anything from finding computer terminals scattered about the levels to using your functions in new ways.
-Bugs-
Hoo, boy. As much as I've enjoyed the game so far, the sheer number of bugs, both major and minor, has really put a damper on things, to the point that I've set the game aside until a patch comes out. From crashing on start, to crashing on moving in a certain way, to the screen going black and requiring me to alt-tab any time I transition scenes, to the game locking up when I try to change around my functions, to... well, you get the point. The game-crasher bugs are fairly rare, but they always hit when least convenient, and there are a plethora of minor bugs (such as the aforementioned "black screen, requires alt-tab") that just break the immersion on a regular basis.
-Recommendation-
Buy it, see how it runs on your machine (maybe you're one of the magic few who doesn't get the bugs as often), and then wait for a patch. It's a fun game, it's an interesting game, but currently it's an unpolished game.

I feel that Transistor as a game was cut or rushed out. There are cutscenes and area's in the trailer of the game that you do_not_see in the actual game itself. The Cameratta are not very fleshed out as to what exactly they are hoping to achieve or how they set about doing so. They have a generic goal of creating a static reality because they don't like change and create the process to stop this.  The game allows you to piece together your own conclusions with what sparse plot information it gives you but it leaves glaring holes in the overall story. You go through the game hearing about other citizens disappearing but then you never see any of them alive. The few you do see are dead and you absorb them. That stops happening pretty quickly.
The process has a sort of obsession with red shown with the Camera-like enemy taking pictures of reds poster and the theater incident where cluckers are shown in the seats. Yet this is never elaborated on. It feels like "The Process" as an enemy were to be so much more but were cut down in the last second decision to be simply "The Antagonist." The evolving form of The Process is shown in the later enemies more human appearance and seemed to be a precusor to a revelation in the making about this enemy. Or when you enter into the Dark Lady Nursery.
Another thing is how did the Process became what it is, which is not explained, simply shrugged off with a "I gave the Process to a guy for a second and then he screwed it up." Or when you find the first of the Cameratta but they have been somehow turned into a Process being which is never ever explained.
There are several places that are mentioned in the game but never seen, the country is refered almost constantly yet what it actually is, is unclear in what was a digital utopia. The other place that was refered to was "Underground", where the process came from as it has the cube like spawner enemy which the Transistor mentions is bringing them up from below. This game feels like it had a lot of missed potential.
Then we come to the Deus Ex Machina ending. The "Cradle" of the Transistor which when used will destroy or contain all of the Process. You want reasons to why this happened? No, ♥♥♥♥ you, no reasons for you. This happens because plot. This and the fact that for some reason it creates another Transistor sword which the last remaining person other than you has and you have to kill them to get out of the random plane of existence you've been teleport to.
Summary: If you are looking for the sequel to Bastions great storyline and narrative you won't find it here, if you are story nut
I advise you pass this game on. But if you want a game with a great soundtrack, good visuals, and entertaining gameplay you've found your game.

Sonic Forces. The game I was worried about at first because it didn't look appealing to me at all.
Honestly, I thought it was just going to be another generations clone, but its far from that.
Forces is great, honestly. In a lot of aspects. Is it up the with Sonic Adventure, and Sonic Adventure 2? No. Not really. But it's there with Colors and Unleashed for sure. There are tons of great aspects of this game and i'll get into those.
FIrst off, the story is on par with the Adventure series for my favorite. It's enjoyable. Seeing the world in ruin and restoring everything with the resistance. All the characters together here is very, very refreshing.
The soundtrack is fantastic. Classic levels are really a hit and a miss. But that's not a shocker there. (Music wise)
Classic Sonic gameplay is also...Really a hit and a miss. If you want Classic Sonic gameplay that's ((GOOD)). Please go to Mania, 1, 2, 3&K, CD, etc. You get the idea. It's not BAD in Forces. But it certainly isn't the best or the greatest. Mediocre is probably the correct wording.
The modern music if you could call it that(?) (Music with Sonic and your custom character) is just complete amazing. Sonic Team outdid themselves with a good soundtrack that i'll be listening to along with the Adventure series. It's really catchy. The fact that lyrics are back in songs makes things even more better. I'm a sucker for it.
Gameplay wise. I can see why people call it 'straight line simulator with button pushing' and such. I get it.
But in the end, it's still an enjoyable experience, especially rail riding and homing attacking badniks one after another with Sonic, plus all the custom abilities and attributes of your custom character, now onto that.
The custom character and their abilites species wise and weapon choice wise really freshen things up and I think that's a great additon they did for the game. Especially weapon perks. It keeps you wanting to play and even maybe change up your species and start a new game, and use new weapons or the same weapons, that have different perks. You can pretty much become really strong with a stacked perk weapon.
The daily missions keep things fresh as well, and secret levels are like mini games. Those are pretty entertaining to do and find on the map.
Overall. This game is great. It's a good start for SEGA and Sonic Team again. It's like any other Sonic game. If you're a Sonic fan. You'll enjoy it. I can't say you'll LOVE it. But you'll enjoy it. It's worth a buy.

Sonic Forces confuses me. Everything I know and understand about game design points to Forces being mediocre, at best. I agree with the majority of the common criticisms, levels are too basic, linear and short, as is the game as a whole, controls aren't the worst they've ever been but they're a step back from previous games, and (at least up until the last couple levels) the game is very easy.
And yet its the most goddamn fun I think I've ever had with a Sonic game, and I'm not exactly sure why.
I'm not even much of a Sonic fan, its the franchise that got me into gaming way back when with Sonic 2, but after that Rayman was my platforming series of choice, and going back to those Genesis games I find them way too frustrating to be that much fun. Out of the 3D games in the series I've played (Adventure 2, Heroes,  Generations) I've had some enjoyment but nothings been particularly amazing.
But Forces just made me smile in a way videogames rarely do, and again I'm not entirely sure why.
It may be the avatar aspect. I've always been drawn to games that put a heavy focus on a character creator as a selling point, and the one in forces starts off pretty basic and barebones but actually opens up into something quite wide and varied with the ammount of items you can unlock for it.
It may be the story, something about a surprisngly grim, if predictable, tale being played out by colourful cartoon characters is strangely endearing, even if it is tonally confused.
Maybe levels being easy, linear rollercoasters is actually a positive for me, a thrill ride I can just sit back and enjoy without putting much thought into what I'm doing.
I dunno, what matters is I enjoyed my time with the game and I'm glad I decided to get it on a whim.
If your still unsure about getting the game, best to wait for a sale, at least 30% off might make it more worthwhile to you, or maybe, like me, just take the plunge, go in with no expectations and see what you come out thinking.

530 hours later, here's my thoughts:
The Grand Campaign does its job moderately well, but it is a bit lackluster in comparison to the previous Total War titles. For instance, the AI's more incompetent that ever, which surprises me considering CE boasted of having a larger budget and would feature improved AI for Rome 2. Family trees are also removed, the Roman Senate's nearly non-existent, you can't change your capital, and just a lot of details like that are missing. The mods in the Steam Workshop can be spectacular though, adding some much-needed substance.
The Augustus Campaign to Rome 2 is like what Barbarian Invasion was to Rome 1; it's a solid addition with some improvements here and there. Although it feels a bit emotionless and the AI's still a mixed bag, I had a blast playing as each Roman party. People may not find it as gripping if they haven't seen HBO's Rome (OR just aren't familiar with the politics of the time).
Can't comment on the other expansions or multiplayer though, as I haven't partaken in them. What I can briefly comment on is co-op campaigns. Aside from the occasional lag and crash, I can't really complain about it. The hard part is finding someone who's willing to invest a chunk of time into it with you. Haven't played Shogun 2 co-op in a while, but friends say that Rome's co-op feels a  lot slower, as you can't manage anything on the campaign map once you have ended your turn.
All-in-all, I recommend the game, especially if your computer can handle it on high graphics settings.

Tied with Deus Ex as my most favorite game ever. Sacrifice is an action/strategy hybrid game where you play a wizard who fights for the favor of 5 gods (who constantly fight among themselves). Summon creatures, issue them orders, buff them with defensive spells or cast offensive spells to destroy enemies. Claim the souls of your fallen foes in order to summon more units for your own army, then push your enemy back to their altar, and sacrifice a minion to destroy it, banishing the enemy wizard from the world and preventing them from respawning.
Fight for the gods:
Persephone, godess of nature, order and healing,
James, god of earth, stone and peace,
Stratos, god of air, cold and knowledge,
Pyro, god of fire, chaos and industry, or
Charnel, god of death, plague and suffering.
Stick with one god to get all their toys or build an army of mixed units from certain combinations of gods to exploit their unique advantages. This game has a large, branching campaign and great multiplayer.

This game for the record is very challenging. For first time players I highly recommend you read a survival guide before playing to get a better understanding of what to do. I had to restart after I got to a point and had ran out of bandages and first aid and bled to death.
The good
+Atmosphere is great.
+Very challenging
+Does not hold your hand at all
+Unique story concept (though kind of vague you learn more about the world as you talk with people and do quests.)
+Survival horror aspect
+Unique monsters
+Realistic bleeding requiring bandages
+7 Different endings
+Insanely good AI enemies most of the time especially soldiers almost never miss you when they shoot and often know where you are.
The Bad
- The quest designs are flawed in this game because certain quests require you to pass through a certain area as a checkpoint even if you manage to find an alternate route out, so in order to advance in a quest you need to go where they want you to go.
-The UI is kind of lacking there are a few hot keys but not enough
- Story is kind of vague, it is a pseudo sci-fi game your main character survives and is in search of a nemesis of his.
- There are factions but they have minimal impact on the game since you can't really join any of them
- Lots of walking unless you download the Stalker Complete mod which allows you to fast travel to transition points on each map, this feature can be a good and a bad thing because it can cheapen the experience of the game if you aren't careful.
All in all I enjoyed this game but IMO this game could have been a much better game had they taken some of the concepts further. As an FPS it is good and very challenging. Overall I would give this game a 7/10, entertaining with potential.
Would I recommend it? This game is best suited for FPS enthusiasts looking for a challenge where there is a survival aspect and a unique sci-fi setting.

As the word of a new and promising kingdom beyond the land of Lordran came upon me,
I decided to peer upon its dominion myself to contemplate whether my quest for the Sun may be favorable on these foreign grounds. But as I proceeded to advance through the barren wastelands of Drangleic, all I ever encountered was hostility and bitterness. After defeating her and collecting her soul i took the throne for myself, supposing there was any further meaning to it.

The gates of the throne room closed in on me, leaving me alone in the darkness, but hence my unyielding willpower i managed to overcome this dreadful trap and made my escape.
Now everything that is left for me to do is call out to you, ambitious adventurer:
Pay no mind to those misleading voices telling you to proceed!
For all you will find is sorrow and despair.

Tree of Savior is a fun game but has too many flaws to make it enjoyable in the long term.
Pros:
-Great class customization
-Great OST
-Can be played using a controller, or keyboard + mouse

Cons:
-Server problems like lag.
-Game is infested with bots and spammers. Now granted, the developers has done a great job at controlling bots and spammers during early access but at the end of the day, you can't really beat botters. This problem would only further continue come F2P.
-Mob density and low spawn rates. IMC may fix this issue in the future, but several areas of the game has horrendous spawn rates. This makes finishing quests a chore and rather unfun as you would most likely be waiting for 5 mins to kill one specfic mob.

An amazingly animated, detailed, and entertaining Art Nouveau world to be immersed in. The unique battle system compensates for an otherwise linear game; and the exceptional art & music production makes this an undervalued interactive art piece.
Technical Notes: --Some people are having lagging & freeze issues on Steam, the developers are working on a patch. For myself, offline mode will play it seamlessly. However, this means no steam achievements or accurate game time log.--
Issues have been fixed and runs as-is. Enjoy!

-Gameplay-
The mechanics of Transistor are solid in most regards. Functions (attack abilities) work like you'd think they would, attacks feel solid, and upgrades are both visible and have a noticeable effect on your combat style - nothing you do feels like it's pointless, really, it's satisfying and interesting to know that you can try out any combination of your functions with the assurance that they'll work - and every combination feels unique. Even if you have a favorite function, there'll be situations in which you - willingly! - will switch styles in order to counter a new threat; that the game not only provides viable alternatives, but makes every combination fun to use is great.
Complaints, though, include the standard difficulty of using a WASD setup in an isometric game, though the difficulty is minor. Additionally, the complexity of the function system, in regards to the interlocking upgrades and effects, can be overwhelming, especially at the start of the game when a half dozen abilities are being unlocked at once, though familiarity eventually does come with playtime.
-Storytelling-
Transistor is "narrated" by Mr. Nobody aka That Guy in the Sword aka Logan friggin' Cunningham. For those not in the know, he's the guy who narrated Bastion. Just like its stylistic predecessor, Transistor delivers on intriguing, well-written narration, even though the circumstances and tone of the narrator is completely alien from Bastion's style. There's just no complaining on this front.
Aside from that, the world of Bastion is a good blend of mystery and discovery. You can uncover a lot of the backstory and details of the world through various efforts of exploration and unlocks, anything from finding computer terminals scattered about the levels to using your functions in new ways.
-Bugs-
Hoo, boy. As much as I've enjoyed the game so far, the sheer number of bugs, both major and minor, has really put a damper on things, to the point that I've set the game aside until a patch comes out. From crashing on start, to crashing on moving in a certain way, to the screen going black and requiring me to alt-tab any time I transition scenes, to the game locking up when I try to change around my functions, to... well, you get the point. The game-crasher bugs are fairly rare, but they always hit when least convenient, and there are a plethora of minor bugs (such as the aforementioned "black screen, requires alt-tab") that just break the immersion on a regular basis.
-Recommendation-
Buy it, see how it runs on your machine (maybe you're one of the magic few who doesn't get the bugs as often), and then wait for a patch. It's a fun game, it's an interesting game, but currently it's an unpolished game.

This game met the expectations beset by Bastion: better combat, the same great narration we have come to expect from the likes of Logan Cunningham, the amazing music provided by Ashely Barrett and Darren Korb, and a high-calliber story to boot.
But, comparisons invited need adressing:
-The story is different, but not in a bad way, because it is an entirely different story: Bastion was more of a world-focused, mini-epic, and Transistor is closer to a film noir. It is more of a personal journey of the titular character Red, and the voice trapped in the Transistor. I still feel that there are some themes(especially towards the end) that seem a bit similar to Bastion, but on the whole, it is a different story. It is still great, especially if you can enjoy something nuanced.
-The combat is a bit heavy to begin with, but it is a joy to experiment with. It is built in such a way that you can employ any strategy you wish to, without making the game too easy or too hard: I often found myself using Jaunt(a dodge/dash move) as my primary damage output, and I wasn't punished for it, which is nice. I still think that whilst its preferrable to utilise the Turn() mechanic, it is entirely possible to use only the real time part of the combat. There are enough cooldown modifying abilities that you could unleash entire barrages at the enemy without having to go into Turn().
Aside from that, well the music is a bit more cyber-punk, as goes with the setting, but it did satisfy me more than Bastion's soundtrack. However, that is due to my own preferences in music. The art style is still as gorgeous as it was before, and the enemy design and variation are also pretty good.
Overall, it is definitely worth your time: it improved in Bastion in its gameplay, the story is brilliant, and everything else is of the same(if not greater) standard than the studio's previous title. It is well worth the asking price, because it is that damn good.

From the organic ways of Bastion, from the bush and jungle, from levels created by tiles floating up beneath you, we get Transistor. Where the style has evolved into a futuristic, neon-lit, already built level. The world does no longer face the problem of falling apart, but instead it is losing it's style. “The Process”---the equivalent of “The Calamity” in Bastion---covers the creativity made from humans, with a grayscaled and blocky veneer, which seems detrimental to this particular game, where style is easily the highpoint of the experience. The music this time around leaves the closeness of acoustic guitar picking(except for the beach soundtrack) and goes for a more distant, electronic and futuristic atmosphere. Distorted electric guitars and heavy bass lines accorded with ambiance make Transistor a sonically sound experience. The story is very reminiscent of Bastion, but yet completely different. Transistors style and sound design, as with Bastion, perfectly accompanied each other. At points I felt like the levels were specifically made with the soundtrack in mind, because it was so eerily well thought out.
We start of as Red, a singer that lost her voice(it found its way to the soundtrack, though). Standing above a man with a sword in his chest. This sword can talk to us, and also play the roll as narrator. Why only this man can speak through the weapon is unknown to me, since the player ingest other fallen men and women and gain powers through this procedure, but not their voices as with the first body. At this point of the game we don't know who this man is or why we should follow his advice or directions, but it's a game, so we do it anyway. We progress through the levels and gradually begin to understand the situation, “The Process” was a failed experiment from “The Camerata” and the city is conveniently told to evacuate, so we can have that barren emptiness that is so effective when it comes to atmosphere. And The Process is what haunts us throughout the game. As we try to get to the bottom of what happened.
The vagueness and convolution of the story straddles the line of being annoyingly vague and mysterious and intriguing. Where at some points I feel the story would be better told if you knew some of the things you are told in the end. That would make everything feel more natural. In this mysteriousness, the story was overshadowed by the stylistic choices and obligatory gameplay sections. It's unfortunate when Transistor could have been both if they just dropped any pretensions of being deeper and having more substance than there really was. When you get to the end of this two hour game, things will be rather clear, but you will also feel like there should be more, where there are hints and ways the story could have gone that were never shut down or explored in a satisfying way. Despite it not feeling as fulfilling as it seemed to have the potential for, it was enjoyable and the game easily grabbed you and kept you interested up until the end.
The gameplay seems to be a rather contentious subject. I for one, sort of liked it. You could play it like in Bastion, hack and slash, designing your “build” for this purpose. Or you could go a more tactical way, as with a controller I thought would be more suiting. And it was! Although the combat often boiled down to using your tactical slow down time mechanism, killing one foe to then run around, trying not to die until the cooldown ran out, I really enjoyed it. There was tension in that way of playing, trying to just avoid getting hit, spamming RT. While some abilities seemed useless to me, most of them were used at some point due to the fact that you lose an ability when you lose all your health. This was a clever way of making the player use all the different devices, but it's equally as dumb when you have you remake your whole build every time you “die”. The frustration of having to go in to the these access points and try to manage your attacks when half of the things you want to use are unusable somewhat breaks immersion. See Transistor tries to squeeze in a whole bunch of different attacks and combinations into, what was for me, a two hour experience. Perhaps if the game was longer and had more uses for some of the attacks, this wouldn't be so jarring and above all boring. However, when you had the attacks you wanted, with the combinations and everything, the gameplay was a lot of fun. Beautiful colors emitted from every blow, cool sound design and every attack felt more or less powerful, but alas, that didn't mean they were.
All in all it's neat parcel. Well worth it for the creativity. The clumsiness of some decisions didn't come close to ruining the experience whatsoever. So it's a worthy successor to Bastion, and it will probably stay in the same place in my mind as Bastion. As a memory of a stylistically and sonically amazing experience, while the gameplay and storytelling will surely fade out of the collective memory, sooner or later.

I never knew the interactive story telling potential of bureaucracy till I played Papers, Please. Nor indeed, the fun.

I was very intrigued by the concept of the game, seeing as I had never played anything even remotely comparable before. Papers, please truly is a unique experience - alas - not an enjoyable one for me.
The biggest problem I had with this game was the core gameplay, the paper checking. As you progress, the game grows more complex as it challenges you to review more and more information in the same amount of time. You'll be granted new ways to check up on and process people, and sometimes characters will slip you unexpected offers/bribes/etc. with their passports. However, most of what you do is just that: checking papers for matching data. That is not fun. It's... paperwork.
While for other people, this activity might take a backseat to the other facets of the game, I couldn't bring myself to sit through this bland, monotonous grind just to experience what else the game might have to offer. If you've ever had to work a really boring job and felt like it was the wrong decision to take it in the first place, you should know what I'm talking about. Maybe the creators of the game wanted you to feel bored and disengaged. Perhaps they wanted to use the game as a medium to recreate this feeling of working a horrible job. If they did: kudos, mission accomplished. But I can't help but feel like this may have worked better as a choose-your-own-adventure book, where you would have gotten to the story bits faster and wouldn't have had to drown yourself in repetitiveness in-between these parts. The game managed to make me quit because it was too boring. That can hardly be its intention.
Something else that bothered me is the visual style of the game. Although I consider myself a fan of pixelated graphics, I feel like Papers, please could have profited from more detailed character models. If the face of the people whose life depends on you is almost expressionless, you will have a hard time mustering up the empathy needed to feel anything toward these characters - no matter what happens to them. The often monosyllabic dialogue or the mumbling voices don't really alleviate this problem. Even if the creator's plan was to create an impersonal, dystopian setting, the human interactions at least should feel a bit more personal. Otherwise it'll just keep people from immersing themselves in the game.
I did not complete any of the game's branching paths. So naturally my review can cover only parts of the game. Although there seemed to be interesting stuff going on story-wise... after the eighth (in-game) day of stamping papers I just didn't want to anymore. I recommend this only if you do not mind enduring depressingly dull gameplay for the sake of narrative.

While awaiting Sonic Forces, a whole host of questions occupied my mind: How could this game possibly hope to compete to the hype of Mania? Why was Classic Sonic shoehorned into another Boost formula game—is Sonic Team that desperate to pad their games? Could the OCs add something different to Sonic other than cringy avatars? Is this somewhat like the Sonic SATAM cartoon with your OC? Lastly, who on earth is this game marketed towards? Young kids? Casual audiences who like Sonic? Die-hard fans with a host of OCs? The answer to all these questions is simply this: Uh… Yes.
Now the more pertinent question is, “Is Forces worth $40?” Absolutely not! In terms of raw gameplay, it fails spectacularly to understand why Sonic fans play their games. You would get more value from Sonic Mania and Generations, two games that Forces attempts to stand as a sequel. Or, if you want to support solely the fanbase that knows what makes Sonic great to play, go buy Sonic Mania and Spark: The Electric Jester (the creator of Sonic Before/After the Sequel’s original game) for the same price. If this is the case for Forces, then why on earth do I still recommend the title if it is without a doubt a worse game? That’s a more difficult answer.
Not since my revisit with Sonic Lost World has a Sonic game put me into an uncomfortable position of asking myself, “Do I like this game?” Tentatively, the answer to that question is yes.
This is not because Forces improves the Boost formula, especially not in its level design. Everything mechanically about this game is the worst of the Boost formula. It has a broken ranking system that can be S ranked simply from daily challenge boosts with zero rings and some deaths; its mostly linear, short levels for both Modern and Classic Sonic offering few side-paths, if any, with a few decent levels that never matches the quality of Generations; and there is so much reuse of assets from Generations and even Forces that it wouldn’t surprise me that this game has cut-content. (For example, Chaos, who is teased from the beginning, never gets his own boss fight, yet we get one with Zorvik from Lost World.) In order to coerce the player to replay these levels, the game uses the lure of cosmetics in-game—which is admittedly my favorite inclusion—as well as the Red Rings to unlock more “stages” and the Moon and Sun medals for bragging rights. Every minute wasted on these stages could have been added to the main game to make it more effective.
If there is only one saving grace about its gameplay, it never reaches the pits of other Sonic games and there are moments where it does reach the peak of other titles. Out of all the three/four gameplay styles, the one that works the best is the Avatar because his Wispons and grappling hook allows for what passes as traditional Sonic level design the most effectively. Classic Sonic is more of an afterthought as he has no impact on the narrative or gameplay, and I would have preferred those levels given to the Avatar to let the player get more out of the experience than an even more botched Classic Sonic than Generations. Modern Sonic controls largely the same with two key omissions; he cannot drift into a ball nor does his speed work the same as his boost is limited to obtaining Wisps, which only feels as a way to make the game not seem shorter than it is. The somewhat fourth section that could have used more levels is the tag-team sections where you control as both Sonic and the Avatar, alternating depending on whether you are boosting, shooting your Wispon or grappling. This last style is the most underappreciate version that could have further made the game centered around the one character that saves it, YOU.
However, what makes this game work when all odds are that it shouldn’t is that there is a level of emotional attachment and spectacle that makes this mediocre game enjoyable. The story itself is admittedly so serious it’s hilarious. It’s mainly because of how tone-deaf the storytelling is. It begins where Sonic is tortured for six months as a POW only to make quips after his release; Tails goes AWOL because Sonic is gone; and Commander Knuckles says, “This is WAR, Vector.” This set-up where the side characters could have taken more prominent roles like Sonic SATAM is squandered along with many other ideas of Forces. What surprised me the most was how effective the Avatar’s journey was to support the whole game as the most derided feature of the game is its saving grace.
Sonic is no stranger in building emotional connections. Everything about his design, the level of detail of his character and his levels, adds more ways for the audience to connect with a cartoon. This game even goes back to Sonic Adventure 1 with how the Avatar is an RPG foundation for a Sonic game. Somehow, the Avatar with a simple backstory allows players to further connect with Sonic as they develop their OC. This is often used effectively in the small tag-team sections or cutscenes that make good use of blatant fanboy moments worth the journey. On top of this building tool, the absolute spectacle sells itself over its shallow gameplay. Had the game been nothing more than the Avatar stages and Sonic Tag-Team stages, the game would have been more brilliant with its pathos than it has any right to be.
Now here is the paradox of Sonic Forces: If a game can make you emotionally enjoy it to connect with a character’s journey yet the gameplay falls flat on its face, does that make the game effective? Did the Avatar serve its purpose and work, or is that manipulation to excuse the shortcomings of a game either too rushed out or with signs of cut-content? Honestly, I do not know whether to say it’s enough to excuse the game. It’s enough of an enjoyable romp that it would be worth replaying it in the future, but the price point and the underwhelming quality of its gameplay give me reasons to pause.
Ultimately, what bothers me the most of Forces is what it thinks will incentivize players to keep playing has more time and effort put into its systems than the levels themselves. Once you have maxed out one character’s progression in six to seven hours, the game expects you to make six more OCs to unlock everything. Anyone who has enjoyed Modern or Classic Sonic knows that it’s the levels themselves that warrant replayability, not the rank systems and completionists journeys themselves. The only thing I can hope for is that with Forces, in all that it succeeds, inspires modders to take the Avatar concept further as well as it results in the Boost formula dying because it was too costly of a return to overemphasize speed with alternative ways to make up for its poor quality of levels.
No amount of cosmetics, marketing and other bandages can fix what appears to be an inefficient design that Sonic Team/SEGA does not believe in if they constantly have to find new avenues to make up for it, even if they have to stoop as low as Deviant Art, and that alone says a whole lot more than any one review.

Let me preface this review with the score, 9/10, one of the best horror games I have ever played. I just got it on steam, but I have played through numerous times on both PS3 and PS4. This is more than a game. This is an experience. If you are looking to run and gun and blow aliens away, stick to colonial marines (actually don't, it's terrible).
I love the horror genre. And Alien:Isolation hits the nail on the head. I also love the Alien franchise. This is one of the most involving and immersive games around.  . Traversing the tense and claustrophobic corridors of Sevastapol Station is tense and even when you aren't in immediate danger, the sense of dread rarely subsides. The graphics and lighting are superb, really selling the environment, and the style is incredibly true to the 1979 masterpiece. The game mechanics are a little much at first, and can be overwhelming (particularly the crafting system), but once you better understand it, it ends up being a joy to use. The fact that the game is still ongoing when you are saving, and the save points are few and far between, really make you value your life, and feel like you are fighting for it.
The character design is fantastic, especially the aliens, but the facehuggers, androids and human NPCs are also stellar. The androids are actually terrifying in their own right, but fighting them can be annoying, and often running is the way to go.
One of this game's strongest points is the audio design. The ship itself feels alive, with mechanical sounds, machines turning on, the PA system going off etc, and the sound of a nearby vent popping open will make you  crap your pants. The ambient noise and music is also very good. The stomping of the alien, the "tut tut tut" of the androids, the conversations between NPCs, all absolutely brilliant.
You cannot defeat the alien, just run, hide, or temporarily fight him off. This was an excellent choice, and reallya dds to the suspense. Really, I could go all day, but the point is this: If you love horror games, buy this game. if you love aliens, DEFINITELY buy this game. It can be a bit slow, but instead of being bored, when it's slow I feel relieved. You are rarely safe here, so when you are, you cherish it. The biggest issue I have with this game is the amount of back tracking you do,  but with the environment being as rich and beautiful as it is, it is a small price to pay.  Really, this is among the best horror games out there, right at the top with The Last of Us and Resident Evil 4, and while not as action packed, is certainly the scariest of the bunch. Again, 9/10.

This is very much a step down for the Creative Assembly compared to earlier Total War games. The campaign UI really does do a poor job conveying information, often hiding the information you want in metrics that are misleading. The diplomacy system is wretched, as rather than being able to freely specify an amount, you are required to give in incriments of 10% of your treasury. When trying to get AI powers to sign trade treaties, its rather odd to offer them several thousand gold because you can't offer them a few hunderd.
On the battlefield, the combat is more of a grind. Even when flanked or encircled, units will stick around for a disconcerting length of time. Naval combat is not an improvement over Shogun 2, and the tactic seems to be, "Get artillery ships, win." Battle is just not as fun as in past games.
On the campaign map, the province system is rather clunky. Having multiple areas connected to a capital really makes things problematic from a strategic sense, since it makes far more sense to go all or nothing, and take an entire province, than settle for a portion of it. Additionally, the objectives given in the single-player game, while historic, force the player to play the game in a way that might not be fun for them.
In short, Rome II has shaken my faith in the Creative Assembly as a quality development studio.

For those of you who love fps and horror with forboding atmospheres, then this game is worth a play.
This game puts you in the shoes of a mysterious person who has lost his memory with only a single task written on his PDA "Kill Strelok", but he doesn't know who Strelok is or why you are tasked with killing him. So now you must explore "The Zone" around Chernobyl and find out the truth.
If you like, there are plenty of side quests to keep you busy and earn money to buy stuff from traders.
The game is an open world enviroment around the Chernobyl Power Station, where you will find hostile bandit groups, various S.t.a.l.k.e.r factions, dangerous anomalies, man-eating mutants and heavy radiation pockets. To survive, you will need to loot for food, ammo and better weapons which you can get from fallen enemies and stashes found in ruined buildings. The game has a variety of weapons to fight your foes (rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, etc), but don't carry too much as this will slow you down or even preventing you from moving at all.
There is also a multiplayer mode where there are some interesting game modes to choose from.
The S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series is known to have occational in-game glitches but this isn't a constant problem and I haven't found any game-breaking ones. Something I found a bit disappointing with the game is that there is no after-story, free-roaming mode which you would nomally find in any open-world game. So be sure to save a copy of your game before going to the finale.
Over all, although glitches can happen sometimes, this won't effect your experience. This game will have you engaged in an interesting story-line and keep you busy with side quests and muliplayer modes.

This game met the expectations beset by Bastion: better combat, the same great narration we have come to expect from the likes of Logan Cunningham, the amazing music provided by Ashely Barrett and Darren Korb, and a high-calliber story to boot.
But, comparisons invited need adressing:
-The story is different, but not in a bad way, because it is an entirely different story: Bastion was more of a world-focused, mini-epic, and Transistor is closer to a film noir. It is more of a personal journey of the titular character Red, and the voice trapped in the Transistor. I still feel that there are some themes(especially towards the end) that seem a bit similar to Bastion, but on the whole, it is a different story. It is still great, especially if you can enjoy something nuanced.
-The combat is a bit heavy to begin with, but it is a joy to experiment with. It is built in such a way that you can employ any strategy you wish to, without making the game too easy or too hard: I often found myself using Jaunt(a dodge/dash move) as my primary damage output, and I wasn't punished for it, which is nice. I still think that whilst its preferrable to utilise the Turn() mechanic, it is entirely possible to use only the real time part of the combat. There are enough cooldown modifying abilities that you could unleash entire barrages at the enemy without having to go into Turn().
Aside from that, well the music is a bit more cyber-punk, as goes with the setting, but it did satisfy me more than Bastion's soundtrack. However, that is due to my own preferences in music. The art style is still as gorgeous as it was before, and the enemy design and variation are also pretty good.
Overall, it is definitely worth your time: it improved in Bastion in its gameplay, the story is brilliant, and everything else is of the same(if not greater) standard than the studio's previous title. It is well worth the asking price, because it is that damn good.

From the organic ways of Bastion, from the bush and jungle, from levels created by tiles floating up beneath you, we get Transistor. Where the style has evolved into a futuristic, neon-lit, already built level. The world does no longer face the problem of falling apart, but instead it is losing it's style. “The Process”---the equivalent of “The Calamity” in Bastion---covers the creativity made from humans, with a grayscaled and blocky veneer, which seems detrimental to this particular game, where style is easily the highpoint of the experience. The music this time around leaves the closeness of acoustic guitar picking(except for the beach soundtrack) and goes for a more distant, electronic and futuristic atmosphere. Distorted electric guitars and heavy bass lines accorded with ambiance make Transistor a sonically sound experience. The story is very reminiscent of Bastion, but yet completely different. Transistors style and sound design, as with Bastion, perfectly accompanied each other. At points I felt like the levels were specifically made with the soundtrack in mind, because it was so eerily well thought out.
We start of as Red, a singer that lost her voice(it found its way to the soundtrack, though). Standing above a man with a sword in his chest. This sword can talk to us, and also play the roll as narrator. Why only this man can speak through the weapon is unknown to me, since the player ingest other fallen men and women and gain powers through this procedure, but not their voices as with the first body. At this point of the game we don't know who this man is or why we should follow his advice or directions, but it's a game, so we do it anyway. We progress through the levels and gradually begin to understand the situation, “The Process” was a failed experiment from “The Camerata” and the city is conveniently told to evacuate, so we can have that barren emptiness that is so effective when it comes to atmosphere. And The Process is what haunts us throughout the game. As we try to get to the bottom of what happened.
The vagueness and convolution of the story straddles the line of being annoyingly vague and mysterious and intriguing. Where at some points I feel the story would be better told if you knew some of the things you are told in the end. That would make everything feel more natural. In this mysteriousness, the story was overshadowed by the stylistic choices and obligatory gameplay sections. It's unfortunate when Transistor could have been both if they just dropped any pretensions of being deeper and having more substance than there really was. When you get to the end of this two hour game, things will be rather clear, but you will also feel like there should be more, where there are hints and ways the story could have gone that were never shut down or explored in a satisfying way. Despite it not feeling as fulfilling as it seemed to have the potential for, it was enjoyable and the game easily grabbed you and kept you interested up until the end.
The gameplay seems to be a rather contentious subject. I for one, sort of liked it. You could play it like in Bastion, hack and slash, designing your “build” for this purpose. Or you could go a more tactical way, as with a controller I thought would be more suiting. And it was! Although the combat often boiled down to using your tactical slow down time mechanism, killing one foe to then run around, trying not to die until the cooldown ran out, I really enjoyed it. There was tension in that way of playing, trying to just avoid getting hit, spamming RT. While some abilities seemed useless to me, most of them were used at some point due to the fact that you lose an ability when you lose all your health. This was a clever way of making the player use all the different devices, but it's equally as dumb when you have you remake your whole build every time you “die”. The frustration of having to go in to the these access points and try to manage your attacks when half of the things you want to use are unusable somewhat breaks immersion. See Transistor tries to squeeze in a whole bunch of different attacks and combinations into, what was for me, a two hour experience. Perhaps if the game was longer and had more uses for some of the attacks, this wouldn't be so jarring and above all boring. However, when you had the attacks you wanted, with the combinations and everything, the gameplay was a lot of fun. Beautiful colors emitted from every blow, cool sound design and every attack felt more or less powerful, but alas, that didn't mean they were.
All in all it's neat parcel. Well worth it for the creativity. The clumsiness of some decisions didn't come close to ruining the experience whatsoever. So it's a worthy successor to Bastion, and it will probably stay in the same place in my mind as Bastion. As a memory of a stylistically and sonically amazing experience, while the gameplay and storytelling will surely fade out of the collective memory, sooner or later.
Other than a few hiccups that the game has (Lag, freezing for a few seconds, etc., which can be solved by playing in Offline Mode), the game is great!

Absolutely gorgeous and the gameplay is an incredible mix of action with strategy. The story falls a bit on the short side, but some additional challenges add quite a bit of content, and the New Game Plus mode has scaling enemies and lets you progress further, which still should remain fairly enjoyable.
What it did though, it did amazingly. The narrative, just like Bastion, is really well done and adds a lot to how you view the world around you and immerse yourself in the game. The characters presented, although few, are very charming and leave you wanting to know more about them, which for some of them you can get some backstory by inspecting their functions through access points, but most of the major characters kind of go without explaining much about themselves.
A couple things end up lacking - The game teases the Transistor being used for outside of battle purposes with a very simple and short puzzle right at the beginning, however that is really the single out of battle use it gets. Very few bosses, although very challenging ones. And the story leaves a few plotholes hanging, although for most part you can fill them yourself.
Despite those few issues and its brevity, it's an absolutely amazing and beautiful game that is well worth your time and money, if you're into action/strategy and story-driven games. And even if you aren't, to be honest.

Ok, Im as qualified as it gets to writing a review on this game. "Oh really, you are a big expert on this idle game," you think.
Yes, yes I am. Iv played this game since it was first plopped on Kongregate back in the golden age of idle games. The game you see here is absolutely nothing like what it was those beginning days.
There once was no beautiful scenery of a growing kingdom in pleasent pixelated sprites.
There was once a time where there were no Dragons, a time with no ascentions, no research, no reincartantions, no mercenaries, no Dwarves or Drow, no major Neutral Factions, and not even the excavations. Oh lord, who remember the days before Autocasting.
I was there when this game was just AdCap with even crappier graphics and interface, and the only special gimmick was the RPG like alignment system. Just Good and Evil. Just Angels, Demons, Fairies, Goblins, Undead, and Elves.
But slowly over the years it took the foundation it laid and expanded adding more faction play styles. Reincarnations, the more potent form of a soft reset was added because of growing pains. Mercs were added for customized powerhouse play styles (wanna increase your reset currency by factors of 1 million percent in 15 minutes, you can). The Devs are as passionate about this game as its players. When rumors of the neutral prestige faction started we all decided it must be a faction starting with the letter 'D' just like the Drow and Dwarves. There are strategy guides and well crafted builds for late game progression.
The game grew so fast that it dwarfed AdCap, which occured in a few months. In fact Realm Grinder has remained one of the top 5 games on Kongregate for years. Believe it or not, the game got its current lovely looks because the old interface no longer could expand as it needed to. Yes the great overhaul visually was to allow it to become greater than it was. Lol, but oh boy did we have mixed feelings about the upgrade. However, we dont argue anymore as we knew it was needed. It allowed for new features and growth.
Anyways, the actual review of gameplay haha.
Realm Grinder starts off like every other idler, buy a few buildings and click the screen. Then you make a choice, side with Evil or Good. Evil favors passive gameplay, or true idling. Good favors active gameplay, like rapid spell casting or yes clicking. When you select your alignment you can choose a faction which are further specialized.
Now keep grinding that way til you can dig and find stuff, oh hey you got new factions to play with. Now keep grinding and diggin boys, there must be more to find (fun fact excavations originally required Gems that got refunded when you reset).
Bingo, you found the Dwarves and Drow. Now, keep grinding til you can Reincarnate.
Congrats, now the tutorial is over and the game begins. *Grabs the Merc Banner* Oh, Mercs hehe you get to pick and choose your faction upgrades. *Rides off on a Mutha F***** Dragon*
Ps Dragons are awesome even in an idler.

Despite the thumbs down, this is more of a mixed review (which I wish Steam would allow). Just Cause 3 is like a 6/10 game - it's very possible to have a good time with it, but you have to slog through a lot of repetitious gameplay via clunky controls, and plenty of crashes and technical issues.
BETTER THAN JC2:
-More versatility with the grappling hook, like multiple tethers and reeling enemies off cliffs
-The wingsuit is pretty fun once you get the hang of it
-It's fun to feel like you're leading a resistance army against the island
-The music is very good
WORSE THAN JC2:
-Minimap is gone
-Weapon upgrades are gone, and the game is a lot more boring for it. You'll find your favorite early on and it'll never improve in accuracy, damage, or ammo capacity.
-Gear Mods are collected by doing challenges. Many challenges are frustratingly difficult and farming them slows down the game
-The island is bigger and emptier with little to do and less rewards to find. There's a lot of boring travel time.
-Enemy ragdoll physics from getting shot, tethered, or thrown around are less entertaining. There's less satisfaction combat
-Your most common phrase will be "Who the ♥♥♥♥ is shooting at me"
-Movement feels much clunkier and you'll spend a lot of time overcorrecting, trying to get Rico to jump off ledges, turn around, or let go of a grapple.
-Closing the wingsuit or grappling in from it requires hours of challenges to unlock, and it's a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to land with it until then.
I wish I'd had a better experience with it, maybe it's more fun the better you are at it, and if you know exactly how to pace yourself. Maybe I'll change it to a recommend if I play it a second time. But as I tried to free all the little towns around Medici, it quickly became tedious busywork, and you spend so much time in the air that it's hard to feel like anyone down there matters.
Buy it on sale if you liked JC2 and want some more, but if you're hoping for a markedly better experience, it'll probably disappoint you.

Other than that, I have nothing but praise for Factorio.

This is very much a step down for the Creative Assembly compared to earlier Total War games. The campaign UI really does do a poor job conveying information, often hiding the information you want in metrics that are misleading. The diplomacy system is wretched, as rather than being able to freely specify an amount, you are required to give in incriments of 10% of your treasury. When trying to get AI powers to sign trade treaties, its rather odd to offer them several thousand gold because you can't offer them a few hunderd.
On the battlefield, the combat is more of a grind. Even when flanked or encircled, units will stick around for a disconcerting length of time. Naval combat is not an improvement over Shogun 2, and the tactic seems to be, "Get artillery ships, win." Battle is just not as fun as in past games.
On the campaign map, the province system is rather clunky. Having multiple areas connected to a capital really makes things problematic from a strategic sense, since it makes far more sense to go all or nothing, and take an entire province, than settle for a portion of it. Additionally, the objectives given in the single-player game, while historic, force the player to play the game in a way that might not be fun for them.
In short, Rome II has shaken my faith in the Creative Assembly as a quality development studio.

For those of you who love fps and horror with forboding atmospheres, then this game is worth a play.
This game puts you in the shoes of a mysterious person who has lost his memory with only a single task written on his PDA "Kill Strelok", but he doesn't know who Strelok is or why you are tasked with killing him. So now you must explore "The Zone" around Chernobyl and find out the truth.
If you like, there are plenty of side quests to keep you busy and earn money to buy stuff from traders.
The game is an open world enviroment around the Chernobyl Power Station, where you will find hostile bandit groups, various S.t.a.l.k.e.r factions, dangerous anomalies, man-eating mutants and heavy radiation pockets. To survive, you will need to loot for food, ammo and better weapons which you can get from fallen enemies and stashes found in ruined buildings. The game has a variety of weapons to fight your foes (rifles, sniper rifles, shotguns, etc), but don't carry too much as this will slow you down or even preventing you from moving at all.
There is also a multiplayer mode where there are some interesting game modes to choose from.
The S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series is known to have occational in-game glitches but this isn't a constant problem and I haven't found any game-breaking ones. Something I found a bit disappointing with the game is that there is no after-story, free-roaming mode which you would nomally find in any open-world game. So be sure to save a copy of your game before going to the finale.
Over all, although glitches can happen sometimes, this won't effect your experience. This game will have you engaged in an interesting story-line and keep you busy with side quests and muliplayer modes.

Ok, Im as qualified as it gets to writing a review on this game. "Oh really, you are a big expert on this idle game," you think.
Yes, yes I am. Iv played this game since it was first plopped on Kongregate back in the golden age of idle games. The game you see here is absolutely nothing like what it was those beginning days.
There once was no beautiful scenery of a growing kingdom in pleasent pixelated sprites.
There was once a time where there were no Dragons, a time with no ascentions, no research, no reincartantions, no mercenaries, no Dwarves or Drow, no major Neutral Factions, and not even the excavations. Oh lord, who remember the days before Autocasting.
I was there when this game was just AdCap with even crappier graphics and interface, and the only special gimmick was the RPG like alignment system. Just Good and Evil. Just Angels, Demons, Fairies, Goblins, Undead, and Elves.
But slowly over the years it took the foundation it laid and expanded adding more faction play styles. Reincarnations, the more potent form of a soft reset was added because of growing pains. Mercs were added for customized powerhouse play styles (wanna increase your reset currency by factors of 1 million percent in 15 minutes, you can). The Devs are as passionate about this game as its players. When rumors of the neutral prestige faction started we all decided it must be a faction starting with the letter 'D' just like the Drow and Dwarves. There are strategy guides and well crafted builds for late game progression.
The game grew so fast that it dwarfed AdCap, which occured in a few months. In fact Realm Grinder has remained one of the top 5 games on Kongregate for years. Believe it or not, the game got its current lovely looks because the old interface no longer could expand as it needed to. Yes the great overhaul visually was to allow it to become greater than it was. Lol, but oh boy did we have mixed feelings about the upgrade. However, we dont argue anymore as we knew it was needed. It allowed for new features and growth.
Anyways, the actual review of gameplay haha.
Realm Grinder starts off like every other idler, buy a few buildings and click the screen. Then you make a choice, side with Evil or Good. Evil favors passive gameplay, or true idling. Good favors active gameplay, like rapid spell casting or yes clicking. When you select your alignment you can choose a faction which are further specialized.
Now keep grinding that way til you can dig and find stuff, oh hey you got new factions to play with. Now keep grinding and diggin boys, there must be more to find (fun fact excavations originally required Gems that got refunded when you reset).
Bingo, you found the Dwarves and Drow. Now, keep grinding til you can Reincarnate.
Congrats, now the tutorial is over and the game begins. *Grabs the Merc Banner* Oh, Mercs hehe you get to pick and choose your faction upgrades. *Rides off on a Mutha F***** Dragon*
Ps Dragons are awesome even in an idler.
