Mini Transistor review (spoiler free):
I'll start out by saying a lot of love went into that game. The music, sound design, voice acting, and overall art direction are top notch, which is all the more impressive when you find out that a team of twelve built this game from the ground up. The painted world feels just as beautiful as Bastion's, even though you won't be visiting locations that are as varied.
The combat can be a little confusing at first do to the sheer number of ability combinations and the amount of planning that's involved, but you definitely get the hang of it with some experimentation. You will feel kind of limited initially since you won't have enough "memory" to equip and use all your abilities with passives and upgrades. As a result you will be sitting there with a lot of your ability, upgrade and passive slots empty, even at the end of the game. The difficulty feels like it scales quite nicely. As the game progresses enemies will upgrade in parallel with you, gaining new abilities as you gain tem yourself. And if you feel like the game is still too easy you can equip "limiters" (similar to the shrines in bastion) to make the enemies more difficult, which allows you to get a bonus to experience. I did wish there was an easier way to see some of your stats. You will have to do a bit of digging in order to find out what exactly what your health, damage, ability cost, and turn() values are.
I clocked the game in at around 10 hours, though I spent a lot of time tinkering and trying to figure out the best combinations of abilities, upgrades and passives, and I did all the challenges you can unlock initially. I thought the story was a little weaker than bastions in that you have to do a lot more investigating to figure out exactly what's going on and the world doesn't feel as integrated with the gameplay. After beating the game I felt like I knew the broad strokes of  what was going on, but I felt like there are definitely some gaps to fill. Hopefully with new game+  I will uncover some new information. With all that being said, its still a great bittersweet tale to experience.
TLDR: Great game, decent  story, good blend of action and strategy, and awesome art direction. 8.5/10
Awesome combat, gorgeous artwork and quality soundtrack make this a must have!
Great atmosphere, complimented by a very original soundtrack and combat style. I'm still getting the feel for this game, but so far it has been a very unique and satisfying experience.

Before anything, I will preface this and say if you have any interest in ARPG's and are looking for a wonderful and short experience, you SHOULD pick this game up. Well worth the $20 in my opinion.  If you want a detailed explanation, feel free to read and a TLDR is at the bottom.
PROS:
◘Visually pleasing to the eyes, absolutly gorgeous presentation in both animation and the enviornment.
◘Sound design is top notch.
◘Narration done throughout the game is fun to listen to.
◘Can play with either mouse or keyboard.
◘Fairly intriguing theme and story get you interested
◘Should run fairly well on most machines.
◘Fairly challenging as you can easily be "killed" multiple times during any battle.
○When you "die" in combat, 2 things can happen: The first is on the brink of death you engage a emergency Turn mode (Turn is explained later below) and can fight to kill a few more enemies. The second possibility is that you "break" a function from combat for a while, and after visiting 2 (or more) Function Kiosks you can reactive them. If you break them, you are then forced to play around with your kit to experiment with new loadouts.
◘Variety of combat with many different enemies with various different upgrade versions of them.
◘Absolutely STELLAR combat system along with the configurations along with it (Which are detalied below)
○As you play the game, you obtain various skills and upgrades through leveling up or finding them around the world and they are called Functions.
○You can use these Functions in 3 ways: The first is the Active Function which you use for combat that does its base effect. The second is the Upgrade Function, where you take one of your Functions and use it to augment another Active Function, giving it special or different effect. And lastly is the Passive Function, in which you take a Function and put it into a passive state where it will always give a effect, or activate at specific under different conditions. EVERY Function in the game connects together in one way or another.
○As you play the game, you are allowed to fight in either real time where you cast your abilities against the enemies movements and actions with no cooldown penalty, engage the Turn system to pause the game and tactically decide how you want to approach the situation. In Turn you can move almost instantly anywhere and manually aim your shots and action which are limited by a action bar. You then execute the procedure and watch your plan unfold rapidly. However, the downside to this is that once you are done with your Turn actions, you cannot use your abilities until your Turn meter has recharged. Because of these 2 systems you have a choice as to how you want to fight your battles.
◘You can use "limiters" to further increase the difficulty of the game and gain a small amount of bonus EXP for leveling.
◘New game plus mode with all of your stuff you unlocked.
CONS:
◘The UI can be just a little bit wonky with assigning Functions to various roles.
◘Because the story is not made apparently clear at first, you can easily get lost.
◘Turn actions that detail the effects may not always be accurate, as enemies may dodge and it doesn't tell you that information.
◘May be just a bit short for some, as I and other have managed to beat the game at around 6 hours.
◘Because there is new game plus and not much more, some people may not find a lot of replayability from this, resulting a 6 hour experience for $20 dollars.
◘The only real set of graphics options are just resolutions.
TLDR: Great combat, visuals and fun for ARPG fans. Can be beaten in about 6 hours, and depending on the user the new game plus can offer replayability.Can be of a bumpy ride for the first hour for people to get used to, but you get over it quickly.
Overall, I feel that just about everyone should buy this beauty. The devs that made this deserve every dollar they earn and then some for the amount of effort and love that was poured into this game.

Despite the thumbs down, this is more of a mixed review (which I wish Steam would allow). Just Cause 3 is like a 6/10 game - it's very possible to have a good time with it, but you have to slog through a lot of repetitious gameplay via clunky controls, and plenty of crashes and technical issues.
BETTER THAN JC2:
-More versatility with the grappling hook, like multiple tethers and reeling enemies off cliffs
-The wingsuit is pretty fun once you get the hang of it
-It's fun to feel like you're leading a resistance army against the island
-The music is very good
WORSE THAN JC2:
-Minimap is gone
-Weapon upgrades are gone, and the game is a lot more boring for it. You'll find your favorite early on and it'll never improve in accuracy, damage, or ammo capacity.
-Gear Mods are collected by doing challenges. Many challenges are frustratingly difficult and farming them slows down the game
-The island is bigger and emptier with little to do and less rewards to find. There's a lot of boring travel time.
-Enemy ragdoll physics from getting shot, tethered, or thrown around are less entertaining. There's less satisfaction combat
-Your most common phrase will be "Who the ♥♥♥♥ is shooting at me"
-Movement feels much clunkier and you'll spend a lot of time overcorrecting, trying to get Rico to jump off ledges, turn around, or let go of a grapple.

A logistics game at its core, Factorio manages to make factory management fun. It follows the tried and true MMO strategy of getting stuff so that you can get more stuff faster. Start off by hand. Upgrade to automated mining. Transport system to get ore from mine to forge. Another transport system to send processed materials to automated fabrication to help produce materials needed to research better mines, better forges, better weapons, and better automated fabrication. Soon the natives start taking offense at your exploitation of their world, so you ramp up production. Build walls. Automated sentries. Research avails faster better weaponry and the means to expand your territory to attain more resources needed to continue research and weapons production.
A delightful cycle of resource acquisition and base development.

Before even jumping into the Alien: Isolation campaign, I could tell it was something special and unique. The first thing I would like to point out about Alien: Isolation, is the sound design; it is top notch and feels truly authentic to the Alien Universe. The Universe we came to love from the first film.

This is a game that needs to be played with a good sound system, or even better, a good pair of headphones. As I snuck through the tight hallways and corridors, I felt truly emmersed in the world. Never have I played a game before where my heart rate would stay in a heightened state for such a long period of time. I remember staying hidden in a locker, waiting to see if I could figure out the Aliens pattern, only to realize he didn't have one.
The A.I. of the Alien as well as the sounds he makes as he is hunting you down is truly unsettling. The footsteps clunk and thud as he walks around giving the idea that he is a formiddable, heavy beast that you really don't want to mess with.

Alien: Isolation is a love letter to fans of the original film. If you ever wanted to scratch that itch, and feel what its like to be hunted down by an Alien on a spaceship, this is your game.  It is a very unique experience. I loved playing every minute of it.

I don't know what it is, but playing Transistor feels like a chore. While the game looks and sounds extremely nice, just like Bastion, I had to force myself to keep playing it. It took me three years and 5 restarts to finally be able to plow through Bastion, and after 1.5 hours I'm already at the verge of quitting with Transistor.
The gameplay simply isn't fun. Mixing turn-based elements to an already sluggish "action" RPG framework feels misguided, and actually brings the shortcomings of the system (like targeting) into the limelight. Realtime mode basically consists of waiting for cooldowns before the next pause, and the flow of combat is constantly disrupted.
The ultimate annoyance is frequently taking already earned skills away from the player to promote experimentation with different combos. Well guess what, I like to find a working thing and roll with it; stop making me have to spend time in skill trees and menus and just let me play without constant interruptions, damn it!
Transistor also has network problems and lag, with frequent 2-3 second hitches. In a game marketed as a single player experience, this simply should not happen.
Maybe one day I will finish Transistor. I really like Supergiant Games' sense of style and their stories, but their gameplay design is a constant source of disappointment. Props for attempting to innovate in the action RPG genre, but this felt like a severe de-evolution to me.

As I've expected, Supergiant Games has done it again: A beautifully crafted masterpiece of an indie game. Good soundtrack? Check. Logan Cunningham providing yet another good voice for a character? Check. Story and combat to keep you glued to your screen? Check. My only gripe? The short, yet sweet storyline. Lasting for only around 4-6 hours, it's quite an enjoyable experience albeit short and slightly expensive (although I consider that $20 paid for itself). I suggest getting it on sale for a lower price, but even with a high pricetag it's well worth it on its own. If you want to support the devs even more, grab the soundtrack. It's amazing.
Final Verdict: Solid 8.5/10. It has its rough edges and it's obviously not a perfect game. It, however, is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing so grab it anyway.

This is a devilish little game that hides surprises under its retro exterior. The premise is simple: you're an immigration official in Arkana in 1983, which feels a lot like Eastern Germany and the Soviet Union. Your biggest asset is your wits: visually inspect as many people's credentials as possible each day in order to earn money to maintain you and your family in your Class 8 dwelling in Arkana. Each day, a new rule is added to the ones already in effect, which often complicates matters and your ability to be as efficient as possible.
This game is a wonderful little morality play: some people will beg you to let them through anyways (and you are allowed two errors each day before being fined for subsequent errors), and it really exemplifies the paranoia that existed during the Cold War, while also showing the difficulties that real-life immigration officers deal with on a daily basis.
Aside from your mental agility, you're given (in)efficient tools here and there to help you, such as access to limited databases, a full-body scanner, and the ability to detain suspicious individuals, for instance.
The only criticisms of this game that I have are:
1. The people that you see each day are in the same order and have the same credentials, so one could circumvent the system by keeping a list of the people and whether or not to approve them for entry in order to maximise your paycheque. If this was randomised, it'd be even better.
2. It's not always clear how exactly one uses the tools at one's disposal. The pictures are helpful, but some text explicitly noting what one needs to do in order to access new tools would be helpful.
3. Since each day ends at 6 pm, it would be helpful to have a better-looking clock in the booth so it's easier to tell how much time is left in the day, especially if you're hoping to squeeze one last applicant in before you're finished for the day.
This is a great little game to play here and there when you don't feel like firing up a fullblown game, particularly if you like logic puzzles and having to make snap decisions based on often incomplete information and hoping that you didn't just let a terorrist into Arkana (which I have done!).

So I've been playing this game for about 12 hours straight since I bought it, when compared to Just Cause 2, it feels much more alive, unlike the island nation of Panau, places you liberate, stay nice and populated and there are always cars on the road, so it feels more like a real place.
I've had a lot of fun blowing things up as the devs really tried this time to make you care about the story just a little bit, but when you get a game that has a huge focus on blowing♥♥♥♥♥♥up, you can't really expect me to follow the plot and remember who any of the characters are, I barely remember the protagonists' name, and that's only because they keep calling you by name, that's the reason I know his name at all, but it's so painfully irreverent, that you forget it instantly.
Some of the design choices are questionable, I'm talking about the controls that take some getting used to, since the space bar is used to open the parachute on foot and inside cars, the handbrake is Shift, so naturally when you want to use the handbrake, you're going to find yourself jumping out of the car and opening the parachute, and you can change the open parachute in car to shift and handbrake to spacebar, but holding down spacebar will still open the parachute in the car, you have to change both on foot and in car settings if you want anything to work, so that's probobly due to the fact that this game was clearly developed for the consoles, and then poorly ported to PC, another evidence to that is how much of a resource hog this game is! I heard people with 980Ti and 1080 having problems with it, so me with my 780Ti had my work cut out for me, but when I started playing, it didn't seem bad, on ultra I got 30 fps, after some fine tuning, I got to 60... but they it started to rain! This game has one of the cheapest looking rain effects in recent years, but it just eats away at your GPU! From a good and stable 60fps, I got 5-10 when the rain started! After turning the water effects off, I got normal frame rate again. They are slowly fixing the issues with the game, so it's getting better.
My final advice is: Do not spend full price on this, a developer that does a lazy job on a port, is one that does not deserve the 60$ price he asks for, if the game is above 20$, do not pay for it, I got it on sale for 15$, that's around the price it's worth

The Just Cause franchise is kinda like junk food: deep inside you know it's terrible, but you're enjoying yourself so much that you don't really care.

The devs also made some weird decisions, like dropping the minimap and health mechanics from JC2, and I do miss them.
The black market and fast travel mechanics are also different: every item is free, but unlocking them is pretty tedious. Plus you can only call upon the services via one use items of which you can carry few at a time, though they are pretty easy to come by.
If you read other reviews you'll have noticed that the optimisation of the game isn't good. Personally I haven't encountered many glitches (2-5 in the first 10 hours), and all of them were minor/visual. Booting it up takes too long though, and the DRM is annoying.
All in all though the game is hella fun. What you see in the trailers is exactly what you get; Michael Bay: the Video Game. Take advantage of it during the Steam sales, it's definately worth the reduced price.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
Fun culinary fact of the day: it's better to measure ingredients by weight than volume as it's more accurate!
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

I've discovered S.T.A.L.K.E.R. years after its release, and it took quite a time to figure out how to play it properly.
I won't mention the almost permanent "dying" due to gunshots, radiations, and various anomalies - that's part of the experience : wandering inside the Zone, a perimeter around the nuclear plant of Tchernobyl, full of mutants, factions and hazards. So S.T.A.L.K.E.R. is a "quicksave/quickload" game in old-school fashion (even in easy mode).
I liked the design of the wasted lands, and the warring factions, but not loved it. Trying to find your way to Strelok isn't picnic.
So far, I've understood that the main strategy is to :
- find a serie of guns (pistols, machineguns, rifles, shotguns...) for which you can gather enough ammo ; and upgrade the most efficient ones
- always keep a nice amount of bandages (bleeding), syringes (radioactivity), medikit (heal) and food (eat) otherwise
- gather artefacts to keep the best ones in your belt and resell the other ones. The best I've found (for me) were the ones reducing radioactivity & bleeding ; and boosting endurance.
- never pack more than 50 kg of stuff otherwise you'll lose stamina too quickly (because you'll have to go back and forth alot of time in this game - no teleport).
The game lacks some clear information about what is important to play properly, you're basically left alone. But since it takes about 30 min / 1h to die stupidly, it takes time to figure out the whole thing.
Another dissapointing aspect of the game is the dialog window and the inventory window, two modes not that exciting. Plus, the game still run while you use your inventory, so sometimes you die without knowing why.
Despite these negatives elements (and the fact I wasn't able to go farther than a "locked" checkpoint), the first instalment of the serie was quite engaging and pleasing in its punishing ways ;)

TL;DR version
ToS looks pretty,
lots of customizing skills, stats, and classes
fun to play (on controller)
but, it is very crowded, (harder to do certain quests)
unforgiving with mistakes in builds, (plan ahead on tosbase)
trading is unavailable for free players, (and limited for premium)
and lacks a means to play with friends comfortably.
Real review below.
This is the game I was waiting for. I've been looking for a nice Ragnarok-esque experience since my teenage years.
As soon as I saw a screenshot of this game I had to know what it was and lo and behold. It's being directed from the same man who did Ragnarok Online. I'll get to the point though and focus on major aspects only while being fair.
PROS
- Beautiful game, stunning really. The class costumes are very detailed.
- Extremely in-depth class, stat, and skill system. You can take the same path as another player and still end up with different strengths. you don't even have to take the same class advancement's to reach the same class. It is completely up to you how you want to build.
- Gameplay is amazing. I recommend a controller. Combat just feels right with it. (button combinations are weird however, could use more controller support instead of weird keybinds like R2+start to use items.) Mouse and keyboard will probably result in less fun and is just a strange way to play an action-oriented game.
CONS
- Game is absolutely swamped, at least on the Klaipeda server. This results in quests relying on a rarer mob to appear be an absolute nightmare. You will find players lose all manners at this stage and killsteal you like it's no one's business. They will also killsteal you at grinding locations or anywhere with dense mob packs. It seems to me like the larger, rarer mob spawns have been reduced further since beta, meaning some quests, if not required for story, are better off skipped in the interest of saving your sanity.
-Stats and Skills are Permanent. I recommend planning your builds ahead of time on sites like tosbase. You can reset Skills with a premium cash item, but there is no option for stats. (with exception of the single one-time stat reset potion for $50 supporters) If you mistakenly confirm a bad stat or skill placement or even a class advancement, it is set in stone. This is a very outdated mechanic that should disappear. I can understand paying cash for a skill reset is fine (they have to make money to support this game somehow) but not having one for stats is damning. You would be forced to recreate your character if you are not satisfied. There are however 500+ levels or so I'm told, so maybe your build is salvageable, but this also means you have no freedom to experiment which results in cookie-cutter builds, which is an atrocity to such an in-depth class and skill system.
- Trading and playing with friends in this game is a trial at least. There are no ways to comfortable play with low level friends. You have to stay within 20 levels of each other just to not mess with each other's xp. Manageable at low levels, sure, but when you are in the 200+ range and you happen to play more than your friends, you will run into issues. A syncing option or mentoring program would do wonders here. Trading is a whole other problem. If you and your friend are not Token users, you can't trade. simple as that. You both have to be "Premium" players to trade. If only premium players can initiate trades, this would be more forgiving, but you are also limited to 30 trades a month per 30day token. This means playing together and grinding out materials that your friend needs but isn't premium is pointless. If you aren't premium, you better be satisfied with being a solo player or not relying on friends for any mats or gear. It is just a frustrating system and it needs to be fixed.
OTHER
- Just a nit-pick, but a full character reset option (class, skills and stats) would be sooooo very welcome. I don't care if it costs a lot, but without the option to do this, it will lead to boring, safe, standard (cookie-cutter) builds and slow growth and variety due to lack of experimentation and general fear of ending up with a gimp character.
I can go on with the pros and cons of this game but I would like to keep this brief as I have a tendency to prattle on with details.
I do want to clear up a few misconceptions I've come across however.
These skills that people seem to complain that you have to pay to get, are attributes. They are basically enhancements to your skills which cost silver and time to train. Admittedly, it is a weird system to wait an amount of time to level a skill, which is what the problem should be, not that they can only level 1 at a time and token players can do 2. The problem here being I shouldn't have to teleport back to town to upgrade a level of my attribute again. If it were able to be done anytime I wanted, this would be less aggravating.
While it is artistically pleasing to me, some people still think that unless your game is at Crisis level graphics, it's♥♥♥♥♥♥ Very disappointing and spoiled age of gamers around.
Sadly, this game is receiving a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥reviews but it's mostly from whiny players that grew up with a very entitled gamer mindset. (they want things to be much easier) Those of us with more experience in playing older games actually appreciate a lot of what ToS offers. It ended up more as a review and suggestion (for IMC games) instead, apologies. :D

I don't know what it is, but playing Transistor feels like a chore. While the game looks and sounds extremely nice, just like Bastion, I had to force myself to keep playing it. It took me three years and 5 restarts to finally be able to plow through Bastion, and after 1.5 hours I'm already at the verge of quitting with Transistor.
The gameplay simply isn't fun. Mixing turn-based elements to an already sluggish "action" RPG framework feels misguided, and actually brings the shortcomings of the system (like targeting) into the limelight. Realtime mode basically consists of waiting for cooldowns before the next pause, and the flow of combat is constantly disrupted.
The ultimate annoyance is frequently taking already earned skills away from the player to promote experimentation with different combos. Well guess what, I like to find a working thing and roll with it; stop making me have to spend time in skill trees and menus and just let me play without constant interruptions, damn it!
Transistor also has network problems and lag, with frequent 2-3 second hitches. In a game marketed as a single player experience, this simply should not happen.
Maybe one day I will finish Transistor. I really like Supergiant Games' sense of style and their stories, but their gameplay design is a constant source of disappointment. Props for attempting to innovate in the action RPG genre, but this felt like a severe de-evolution to me.

As I've expected, Supergiant Games has done it again: A beautifully crafted masterpiece of an indie game. Good soundtrack? Check. Logan Cunningham providing yet another good voice for a character? Check. Story and combat to keep you glued to your screen? Check. My only gripe? The short, yet sweet storyline. Lasting for only around 4-6 hours, it's quite an enjoyable experience albeit short and slightly expensive (although I consider that $20 paid for itself). I suggest getting it on sale for a lower price, but even with a high pricetag it's well worth it on its own. If you want to support the devs even more, grab the soundtrack. It's amazing.
Final Verdict: Solid 8.5/10. It has its rough edges and it's obviously not a perfect game. It, however, is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing so grab it anyway.

Papers, Please is an amazing game given the fact that you are doing similar tasks everyday. The style is simple but it still feels real enough that you feel emotion toward some of the people passing through. There are so many different endings and most of the time you do not realize untill after the ending that one certain event caused your demise. That or you ran out of money, your family died, or a terrorist killed you after you failed to shoot him.
The deeper parts of the game are the moral choices you have to make throughout your time at work. Do you join the order? Do you stay loyal to your country? Do you take money that appears to save your dying family or burn it knowing the sender is unknown? Do you cure your sick wife or give the family heat? Or do you skrew everyone and upgrade your booth instead. One slip up, one missed weight or invalid seal, can be the difference between a suicide bomber getting into the country and you saving yourself and the guards.
This game is very entertaining and quite dark which makes it hard to stop playing because you want to know what comes next. I highly recommend Papers, Please.

If you're looking for a positive review, then you're in the wrong place, HOWEVER, if you're here for a tremendous chicken Stir Fry recipe, THEN LOOK NO FURTHER!
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
Fun culinary fact of the day: it's better to measure ingredients by weight than volume as it's more accurate!
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan and heat through. Serve with noodles.

Before even jumping into the Alien: Isolation campaign, I could tell it was something special and unique. The first thing I would like to point out about Alien: Isolation, is the sound design; it is top notch and feels truly authentic to the Alien Universe. The Universe we came to love from the first film.

This is a game that needs to be played with a good sound system, or even better, a good pair of headphones. As I snuck through the tight hallways and corridors, I felt truly emmersed in the world. Never have I played a game before where my heart rate would stay in a heightened state for such a long period of time. I remember staying hidden in a locker, waiting to see if I could figure out the Aliens pattern, only to realize he didn't have one.
The A.I. of the Alien as well as the sounds he makes as he is hunting you down is truly unsettling. The footsteps clunk and thud as he walks around giving the idea that he is a formiddable, heavy beast that you really don't want to mess with.

Alien: Isolation is a love letter to fans of the original film. If you ever wanted to scratch that itch, and feel what its like to be hunted down by an Alien on a spaceship, this is your game.  It is a very unique experience. I loved playing every minute of it.

Tree of Savior (TOS) is a nice game with many areas to explore, complimented by an unique art style. Although this game require quite a while invested in to grind at some point in your journey, it is quite fun to play solo or with your friends.
Sure, there are a ton of gold spammers, as per any other, if not most of all the other MMOs in existence. Server is laggy, especially in the North American's server, but if you wait till it passes over, it's completely tolerable.
The community within this game is mostly friendly and encouraging (except for those sarcastic ones, you know who you are), I've even met a handful of nice players along the way. Most of the time, disregard for the gold spammers, there would be a lot of newbie questions filling up the chat, which is what the game's shout should be there for. While there are individuals who would respond with a "Just Google it!" kind of unhelpful reponse, there are still those willing to help no matter how many times the same questions has been asked by different players who were troubled. It's nice to know that someone is always out there trying to help others.
Regardless how I'm enjoying my time in TOS thus far, it is quite difficult to enter dungeons in this game. Most of the time we would get kicked out of the server while attempting to enter a specific dungeon. The game would then greet you with its server queue message with a rather long line up until you're able to connect back into the game again, which kinda sucks.
And then there's the market's silver retrieve time right after you've sold something (the market taxes you about 30% off of your item each time, that also sucks), sometimes it takes about 2 days, sometimes around 3 days, that is quite absurd, imo. It might be hard to make silver for newbies as a result of this, but depends on your class, it gets better (unless you're a priest with your buff skills costing 20/30 silvers each usage time, which would happen every 10 seconds or so in dungeons).
If you look past all those problems, including not being able to trade with someone unless you've purchased a subscription token via the TP store, the game is indeed quite fun. Especially how the game is free to play, ready to launched on April 28th that doesn't have as much pay to play features like other MMOs.
P.S. Before you buy a token, it's wise to know that you cannot trade tokens or silvers, you can only put it up on the market.
As most mmos it has latency problems at launch.  But when everything is working properly its super fun.

A fun ride with a lot of replayability, action packed with many cool set pieces. Finally a Sonic game with some actual story, instead of some "meta commentary" excuse. Some dialogues ended up being funny rather than serious, but all the better. Wish there'd be a bit more "meat" to the game design regarding the whole "war" idea, maybe separate pro-Sonic and pro-Robotnik campaigns, but whatever. The platforming is kinda junky, with the double jump weaker than the one in Generations, making challenge missions with heavy platforming a headache for the super fast Sonic. Nevertheless, I can recommed it as an excellent time waster, full of energy and spectacle.

I look at the bad reviews and in some cases It feels like people are just trying to find something to complain about. This game and Sonic Generations are some of the strongest 3D Sonic games made in my opinion. I feel like judging them against the classic 2D sonic games is unfair, bringing Sonic to 3D is inherently going to make it diffrent gameplay wise to a degree.
Sonic doesn't have time for complainers, not when there is so much fun to be had. Quality criticism is valid sure, but some people are putting down this game for some very silly reasons here.
Sonic would be very dissapointed in all of them and say lighten up and to stop being a stick in the mud.
Joking aside, In the end, you have to ask yourself what you want from a Sonic game. Me, all I want from a sonic game are levels that are a blast to run through with replay value, fun characters, great music, fun bosses and robot designs, and a simple yet engadging story that doesn't take itself too seriously. This game knows exactly what 3D Sonic games should be and zeros in on that with all it can muster. In addition, it feels like the devlopers cared about the experence. The game doesn't feel like it was desgined in a boardroom of bean counters.
The only con I can agree with is that the Bosses aren't as strong and inventive as some of the other games in the series, but do I let that kill the experence for me? No.
Now kick back, have a chilly dog and let yourself have fun. If you aren't careful, you might enjoy youself by accident. :)

Sonic Forces is a massive dissapointment. And that should not be excused just because its a sonic game. tl;dr: Avoid like the plague.
If i had payed £5 for this game i would still feel ripped off. There is no excuse for releasing a £35 game with 3 hours of playtime. SEGA should have payed me to sit through this soulless mess of a game. I also believe there was borderline false advertising, as you only get to fight 2 out of the 4 'returning villains' advertised in the E3 trailer.
The controls and physics:
Remember that level in Unleashed / Unleashed project where it was icy and modern sonic slid all over while boosting? Yep, thats him now.
The avatar is just modern sonic but he has to go slow (which is better imo).
The only way i can describe Classic Sonic's physics is: Imagine if the classic Sonic from Generations was having a stoke. Thats how it is.
At least that is when you are allowed to control your characters, 50% of the time you aren't.
The levels:
They are not designed with the characters abilities in mind. Modern sonic will often boost to his death, especially on his last level where the stage takes a sharp tun after encouraging you to boost. I should not be punished for playing the game as intended.  The avatar levels are glorified cutscenes (Half of Space Port's completion time is waiting for a cutscene). And classic sonic's stages punish exploration, by disguising bottomless pits as small drops with secrets in.
Also, Classic sonic's final level has an automated section that kills you if you run through it normally. You will die at least once to it.
Difficulty:
The difficulty comes from the characters' sloppy barely working controls, but other than that there is none. Even on hard mode the final boss was easy as pish. I don't dare look at what normal was like, Robotnik probably just seppuku'd on the spot.
Story:
The story is hideously undeveloped, the story could be good but it is never properly explored.

Finished the first playtrough in 5 hours, didn't feel like messing around the the challenges yet since the story drew me in. The combat system is a little bit more 'calm' then that of Bastion but stands fully right on it's own terms, adding small, Fire Emblem esque vibes to the Turn system. Do you burn out your turn with attacks and be unable to attack for a few seconds, or do you keep attacking manually.
In short, Good story, Amazing artstyle, Fun and challenging gameplay, naration and music fantastic. Consider this one of my contenders for GOTY 2014
Edit 1: I forgot to mention how much I liked the completely optional 'Press TAB to hum' button.

Gotta say I didn't play for long on my first time seeing it. I was looking for an idle game with a ton of features, and at first glance I didn't think this game had it and was kinda annoyed I didn't get to build cities/realms like the pictures made me think I would be doing. Boy I was wrong once I finally gave it a chance.
Some awesome things this game has that isn't immediately obvious (Spoilers I guess but not really, they are obvious main features for anyone whos played long enough)
3 levels of prestige (Abdicate, Reincarinate and Ascending)
Many more factions than the original 6 you start with as options, and eventually you get to mix and match faction abilities
Large number name system doesn't break as with many other games that only go up to "Decillion"
When you start approaching numbers that would break the game to calculate (After a few weeks/months prolly), you switch into using an entirely new currency called "Diamond Coins"
Bascially I'd be hard pressed to find an idle game with more "progression" content than this one, in terms of a game focusing sheerly on clicking/idling this idle-game is the most content packed I've seen so far.
If you feel overwhelmed by the sheer amount of options in this game, google "R0 realmgrinder guide" and read that guy's thread for advice on advancing.

Papers, Please is an amazing game given the fact that you are doing similar tasks everyday. The style is simple but it still feels real enough that you feel emotion toward some of the people passing through. There are so many different endings and most of the time you do not realize untill after the ending that one certain event caused your demise. That or you ran out of money, your family died, or a terrorist killed you after you failed to shoot him.
The deeper parts of the game are the moral choices you have to make throughout your time at work. Do you join the order? Do you stay loyal to your country? Do you take money that appears to save your dying family or burn it knowing the sender is unknown? Do you cure your sick wife or give the family heat? Or do you skrew everyone and upgrade your booth instead. One slip up, one missed weight or invalid seal, can be the difference between a suicide bomber getting into the country and you saving yourself and the guards.
This game is very entertaining and quite dark which makes it hard to stop playing because you want to know what comes next. I highly recommend Papers, Please.

Buy it and play it. If for some remarkable reason you end up not enjoying it, at least you supported the notion that some ideas begin as merely an enjoyable game, and yet are singular enough to transcend into the realm of art.

Firstly, I've just beaten the game so I still have a little bit of that "wow" factor in my eyes, so bear with me if I am a little blinded to some of the flaws, this will be updated after a "Recurse" runthrough as a more detailed review; however, this, like Bastion, is more of a "first impressions" kind of game, so, without further adeu, the show. Oh, and no spoilers. TL;DR list at the bottom. Oh, and the beauty of the graphical goes without saying, so there's no real exposition on that below.
I gave a glimpse through the negative reviews and saw one that spoke of a con of the story being that you had to "read between the lines" to get the full picture. For one, a story SHOULD make one think. To take the pieces of the puzzle and put them together before they're all wrapped up together. Now if you blazed through the story, equipped only one combo, found it best for you, didn't read any terminals and ignored the mysterious man in the mechanical sword then you will be hopelessly lost by the story's end. All you'll know is that there was this guy. He's in a sword now. Things happen. Ending happens (no spoilers!) It's a game you can do that in. But if you take your time, explore, read the terminals, stop moving when the sword speaks so you can listen, try out all the different possible ways you can slot the transistors abilities, read all the files, save the cheerleader and save the world? You'll know EXACTLY what's going on any you'll be sucked right into this graphic, interactive novel of a game. Just like with a graphic novel though, you can't black out all the words and hope to get a story out of the pictures alone. I will say that, to some gamers who aren't usually completionists (I'm far from it!) this may seem daunting and tedious and you may lose interest on the firet playthrough, and that's okay! This game's made to play again, just like Bastion was. This, as was Bastion, is a game created almost entirely to tell a story. As I related it, a graphic novel except you're burning baddies rather than flipping a page.
This might just be me, but I never found a combo I just
with. I was constantly trying new things, shuffling things around. Always looking to see how I could best tackle a situation. Now once I got a certain later-game power, I will admit that I ended up with a bit of a god-complex going around and smashing everything in sight. Then one group of enemies out-numbered and out-smarted me. That said I needed  to change my strategy once again. You basically have three ways to play. Head-long like Bastion, which is technically doable... full strategy by utiliszing movement-enhancing abilities while out of "Turn()" mode and relying completely on "Turn()" for your attacks, or a fusion of both as I did, utilizing Turn() for big damage combos and then mopping up in normal combat while my Turn() was on cooldown. All in all, the gameplay is very engaging and, while repetitive (and what game isn't, at it's core, a little repetitive?), offers enough variety in strategy and personal gameplay choices that I think most gamers would be satisfied. Just keep in mind that this game IS heavy on the strategy aspect. If you don't like strategy games, you may not like this game. There's also one thing that's been bugging me as well. Sure they're nice to have and neat little character pieces to have in the game but there ARE two seemingly useless controls in the game. The first is (with KB+M mind) holding the tab key to hum. it creates a beautiful accompaniment to the beautiful music in the game, but it serves no gameplay purpose. As with using the "Q" key out of battle to perform a "flourish" in which Red tosses the transistor up, leaps up to it, then lands a few inches away. Completely pointless, can't even do it in combat as some flavor thing. It's just there. I'll forgive it since I have a (not so) secret love affair with the fact that SG Games seems to focus entirely on story and these abilities lend toward character quirks of both Red and the Transistor, but it still would have been nice to have had some serious implementation into the game's function. (and if there is, it's not apparent, so if I am mistaken feel free to disregard. There is
level where the humming does something, but it's another bit of story flavor.)
While you don't get to see much of these characters, save for Red, the game sure paints a pretty picture about every single one you "encounter." I'll focus on the characters you see the most of. Red and The Transistor. Red is, from the start, porteayed as a very independant woman. There is one thing I love about her though. While she's strong and independant, she's still a woman. Beyond that, she's human. Too often female heroines are made to be either dainty yet defiant or so hulk-like they'd even put a man to shame. She has this wonderful balance of being a strong, independant woman that does get scared and does act a little irrational at times; yet, she knows what she has to do and she perserveres through it. She casts aside her gown, dons the jacket worn by the man that saved her life, and just kinda gets to it. She acts
and I think that's the first thing that got me about her. They don't play up her being strong and shove it in your face, nor do they assume that just because she's a woman she must be frail of emotion. Both sides of the emotional / strong coin are done in such a beautifully subtle way that it just comes out right. This is no different for the Transistor. (Minor spoler, sorry!) The Transistor is not just the sword, the voice is that of the man that saved Red's life. Now I won't get too much into that, but his personality just works well. The game managed to make me feel bad
Now I will say there's one problem with Red. A lot of what you get is second-hand. You get a feel for Red through the speech of the Transistor and that's where the Transistor comes in so well. He paints a wonderful picture that's supplimented by little return comments on terminals and expressions in cutscenes and little subtle things she does in her actions. Read into all of that and you'll see that these are two very real characters. To harken back to the graphic novel analogy, you wouldn't get a complete story if all you did was read the words either. It takes both the images and the words to make the story complete. So too with this game, and the characters are what tie things together.
The music in this game is spectacular. There's not too much more to say. While there's nothing really "catchy" that you might find yourself humming as you go about your business, it's still beautiful nonetheless. Oh, and when you're in the sandbox (you'll know what I mean eventually, only a minor spoiler, I promise!) give the record a kick and hum along with a few songs. It's really interesting and fairly haunting to hear them with that hummed accompaniment. It makes you realize that all of the songs are technically songs by Red. Makes you wonder if she hears them in her head while she's out and about.
And so, in trying to avoid the character limit and to add in points that really are just bullets, here's the TL;DR list.
Personal Pros:
Compelling story
Active, strategic gameplay
Engaging characters
Beautiful, Artistic graphics
Possible Cons:
Story isn't thrown at you, takes some seeking out
As with most strategy, some may find it repetitive
Due to the "active storytelling" syle, some might find the Transistor a bit
chatty
All in all, I dodn't find much wrong with the game at its core. It's something I think more games should strive for, and that's to be a vehicle for a story with some fun gameplay and great graphical artwork along the way.
If you're apprehensive, don't be. Even as a poor man, I can say that it was well worth the twenty bucks.

New to this game is also a really nice flexible ability system, where you can decide to use your new weapons as weapons, additions to old weapons or as passive abilities. This makes it so that you have seemingly endless options when it comes to your playstyle.
In my opinion no characters aside from the main character were noteworthy, which is kind of a shame, since that contributed a lot to Bastion's atmosphere.
I shouldn't really be comparing it this much to Bastion, as they aren't directly related to each other, but I think a lot of people wanting to buy this is because they want it to be a similar experience.
As a conclusion I'd recommend this game to everyone who liked Bastion, but it doesn't quite live up to the expectations (storywise) I had after playing the first one.

S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl was the very first game of the S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series I played. The game takes place in an alternate reality, with the Chernobyl Exclusion Zone being the setting. The Chernobyl Exclusion Zone is a 30 square Kilometer area surrounding the Cernobyl Nuclear Power Plant which suffered a catastrophic explosion and subsequent meltdown in the 1980's. This "Zone" in the game is home to mutant creatures such as Dogs, Boars, Birds, and Humanoid Creatures, as well as S.T.A.L.K.E.R's who are treasure and artifact hunters, guides, and mercenaries paid to work in and around the Zone. The game takes place over 20 years after the initial disaster, when a second disaster occurs creating pockets of radioactivity and producing anomalies. This is where the main character comes in. You play in First Person as an amnesiac S.T.A.L.K.E.R, nicknamed The Marked One. You are rescued by one of the locals and in exchange you perform tasks and go on missions, while trying to figure out who you are and why you lost your memory.
As far as First Person Shooters go, S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl is one of the more fun ones; However, there are a few bugs. Enemy soldiers respawn way to quickly in some areas, NPC's even Quest NPC's are mortal and will stay dead if killed, making some NPC's difficult to contact or keep alive for long, on the harder difficulty settings. The Game AI is very adaptable, making the NPC's react differently depending on the tactics you choose to use. The environment is also errie, and when played at night, in the dark with headphones really makes you feel immersed in the game. The story is interesting, though told a piece at a time through missions and meeting new contacts. Better than Bastion?  Maybe.  Like the previous offering from Supergiant Games, Transistor delivers on multiple fronts:
1. Visuals: Transistor is aesthetically beautiful in a way that few other games are and if Supergiant continues down this particular road, all of its games will be instantly recognizable.
2. Sound: The same awesome narration with a new voice follows us into Transistor.  It's topped off by another beautiful soundtrack from the Supergiant team that you'll want to listen to many times after completing the game.
3. Gameplay: Where some might have found the gameplay in Bastion a little simplified, Transistor kicks it up with a hybrid turn-based/real-time combat system, numerous weapon combinations and enemies with unique abilities that make battlefield strategizing more of a priority.
4. Story: Perhaps the only place where I could knock this game, Transistor follows in the footsteps of Bastion with a couple interesting twists and a really solid story backed up by bits of in-game lore, but leaves some of the world-building up to player theorizing.  This can be a positive or negative depending on what you're looking for in a game.  Regardless, Transistor still manages to craft a compelling narrative that outstrips a lot of games on the market today.
In short: I can't think of any remotely good reason not to buy or recommend this game.  It's a great example of what happens when a group of developers and artists come together with a solid and unique vision and pull it off.

I have a hard time explaining how deeply in love I am with this game. It's a masterpiece.
(Spoiler Free)
The first thing that hits you is the world, and the art, and throughout my entire thirteen hours (on my first playthrough) the environments never get stale or old. Everything is gorgeous and feels handpainted.
The story and the characters are incredible and deeply engaging, but I won't say anything more than that all the voice actors involved are phenomenal.
Battles are fun, fluid, and tactical. The mixture between the strategy and turn-based combat and something more real-time never gets old. Bastion this is not, Transistor is more methodical, and much slower. You're allowed to take your time to plan out what you'd like to do and put it into action. The skills and abilities system keeps the variety up. Usually I'd find my niche and stick to what I liked, but Transistor had me switching up my abilities at every single checkpoint, and not just for all of the files that I was addicted to collecting to get every single tidbit I could out of the writing.
This noir wouldn't be complete without the jazzy cyberpunk soundtrack, which I could listen to forever and never get bored of. Not only is it good on it's own, but it sinks itself deep into the game and plays dynamically and reactively depending on what is happening at the moment.
But, above all else, what makes Transistor a masterpiece is the atmosphere. The absolute dedication the game has to it's world and how much it sucks you in at every opportunity. Optional environments and points of interest litter every single map just to get another line or two out of the Voice. The way the music works itself in, the way enemies interact with you and all your abilities, the way the environments twist and change, the terminals you find, the files you can read, and the small interactions and character moments out of Red herself are unlike anything I have ever played before. If I were making a "Videogames as art" list, this would top it off.
I will never forget this game.

I decided I would write a review specifically about Transistor's similarities to Bastion and what it does better and worse.
Combat: Both games feature incredibly customizable combat. Bastion has around 10 different weapon, which can all be upgraded, and you can have two with you at a time for combos such as all melee, all range, mix, all fast, all slow, etc etc. Transistor gives you four slots for attacks, starting you off with a weak fast attack, a slow strong attack, a dash, and area of effect. However, it quickly becomes more than that. The amount of combat customization is staggering, you get a hefty amount of moves. BUT then very single move can be used as one of up to four passive abilities AND can be used to modify your current active moves. The customization takes it a step up above Bastions already impressive amount.
As far as the systems go. Bastion was very much action oriented, The Kid has a dedicated Roll and Block button and the combat is that of an action game. However, it's much harder to draw similarities to transistors gameplay. It's much more tactical, you have the ability to go into a "planning" mode where time stops, and you can take as long as you want to choreograph a set of actions for the protagonist, Red, which she will then execute very quickly while the enemies must sit there and take it. After planning mode is finished and your moves executed, the meter must recharge before Red can do this again, leaving her vulnerable. She has no dedicated block or dodge, anything resembling these abilities must be achieved through the loadout you pick, leaving her vulnerable and her only option to find cover behind the protruding blocks on the ground, which can be destroyed by either you or enemy fire (they will regenerate.) However, while planning mode leaves you vulnerable, the ability to quickly execute moves makes it a must, activating abilities in real time alone isn't going to cut it. It's tough to get the hang of it, but once you find a build that works for you, and get a full grasp on how to best utilize the mechanics, that combat can be incredibly fun. Some may prefer the action combat of Bastion, some may prefer Transistors strategic approach, this will come down to personal tastes, however, Transistors combat mechanics are structurally in-depth and interesting, if they click with you I believe you will have loads of fun.
Death in Bastion also has less long term affects. You run out of potions? Back to The Bastion with you. Transistor is interesting because what happens is when you run out of health your active more that uses the most power breaks, and remains broken for two savepoints. This is quite a bit more interesting as the penalty for running out of health is that you have to temporarily change up your strategy. Which is quite a bit more interesting than a game over. I do not know what happens once all four of your powers are gone. I assume once that happens you do experience a game over situation.
Enemy variety is a bit down from Bastion. However the actually variety in function of the enemies is up. This is likely because of the more tactical aspect of the game. The enemies can come together in a perfect harmony that will make you really need to think about how you are going to approach a situation, and they can really keep the pressure on. Another thing worth noting is the enemies level up with you, so as you progress enemies you've been seeing since your first encounter in the game will continue to stay as threatening as ever.
Fans of Bastion also might remember praying to the gods to impose more challenge on the game in return for rewards. This happens as well in Transistor, however, it is mandatory. Occasionally when you level up, you are essentially given a choice as to how the game will get harder for you, with each option also having a corresponding reward. This system is very cool, however this does mean you cannot pile all of these challenges on at will like you can in Bastion, which some may not like. Overall though there almost two different uses of a similar system. Bastion is essentially turning on hardcore mode within the worlds lore for some rewards. Where Transistor is essentially saying "Ok, the game is gonna get harder now, but you get a choice in how that happens." Another nice thing is the rewards are all just unlock slots for your customizable build, and the none of the challenges are expressly harder so which choice is the most desrable all comes down to you. Causing you run into interesting situation where there slot you want might make the game harder in a way you find especially difficult.
Overall, the combat's level of customization is staggering, from a technical standpoint Transistor is quite a bit more in-depth.
The hub world: This is probably the only area where Transistor falls flat. They decided to include a hub world. In Bastion, The Bastion is where you deal with a lot of your upgrades, as well as getting little tidbits of the worlds lore, and selecting which level you would like to go to (including challenge levels). In Transistor all of those things, including the lore tidbits, are dealt with via leveling up, and the terminals you run into throughout the game which also work as save points (there is no level system). From a gameplay standpoint, the only reason this hub exists is for the challenge courses. You also cannot visit it whenever you'd like, doors to this, as I recall, unnamed place appear throughout your game, you will not know when. Because of this going there essentially becomes a pain. Where as in Bastion it just happened. Making any of the content there less appealing. I would rather have accesed the challenge courses from the terminal I access everything else in. There is also seemingly some things to do, a hammock to lie in, a ball to bounce, I ended up with a tamed version of one of the enemies. But I don't really know for certain because by half way through the game I stopped even going in when I saw a door open for it. Short and simple, it was a neat little area, it didn't need to exist, or it should have been easier to access. However, this is the only time where the design of the game feels anything short of well thought out and smart. The game would have lasted longer for me if it wasn't a chore to get to the bonus content. This also brings me to my next point.
Game length: I beat the game at around 3.8-3.9 hours of playtime, a bit under what seems to be the average of 5. Don't get me wrong, it was a damn good 3.8 hours I don't regret. But there was easily the possibility for two other bosses, two at the least maybe even three, that would not have detracted from the experience if they existed the game even sort of lead me to believe I would encounter. Bastion's playtime was also longer because it invited me to experience it's extra content, whereas Transistor made me go out of my way to find it. Which is why I ended up skipping it largely.
Artistic design stuff: This is largely subjective so I'll be brief and just mention some changes people might want to be aware of.
The voice of Rucks, Logan Cunningham, returns. This had me worried that Transistor would be "Bastion but different" but he is not a narrator this time, and he is actually using a (somewhat) different voice. His role feels different enough from his role as Rucks that the game doesn't feel like "Bastion but this time x is different". Some may also find him less "intrusive" this time  although I doubt anyone who liked the amount he appeared in Bastion will find him particularly "absent" comparatively. Artstyle is kinda similar but different enough, it's nice seeing a cohesive world in this style and I'm sure plenty of people will be glad to find you cannot fall off the edge of the world this time. The dev's website

It is, quite simply, brilliant. You should buy it, you will not regret it.

One of the most original games I have played. The theme of of a run-down, war torn, corrupted communist country and its disillusioned inhabitants permeates every aspect of the game, from dialog, dirty grey palette pixel scenery, music and storyline. It is really well carried out.
Papers, Please is proof that a good concept will go even longer than AAA-funding in creating a memorable gaming experience. I love that it is still possible for one clever game designer to build a success on his own like this. I hope to see more games from him in the future.

This is how you do a game about choices. Not that lame good/bad decision making mechanic that ultimately just unlocks 2 different endings. The consequences of your choices in this game determine what story you experience and defines your character. You essentially experience the game differently each playthrough based on choice.

If you are a fan of games like Phoenix Wright and you want more discrepency finding action, then give Papers, Please a shot.

I’m not here to suggest you into buying it. After browsing many reviews both there and on the Metacritic, I see STALKER as a moving train. You’re either hopped on it, or not.
STALKER is not your usual big entertaining AAA-title, like Crysis or Call of Duty. It is more like living Monument. For my point of view, it is even bigger than Halo franchise.  Maybe bigger than Moby♥♥♥♥♥♥(the Whale). And with strong Russian accent. I’m not saying that only Russian-speakers can understand this scenery, but you really have to have somewhat specific system of values and behavioural pattern, to get in tune with that game. And what pattern it could be?
Let me tell you where this game takes roots. It will be much better, than usual pro/contra stuff.
Okay, first, there was a book. It was written by Strugatsky brothers and called “Roadside Picnic”. In there was painted our world after a brief impact with extraterrestrial civilization. Those aliens weren't contacted with people, they just used our planet as a campsite, and then disappeared in the space, while left some garbage at their leisure. The book’s story tells about some scientist who is researching that impact by studying strange alien artifacts, which can be recovered from abnormal zones aliens left behind. Due to its completely alien nature, the most of those “campsite” zones are extremely dangerous. Just like an oil puddle for ants.
After filming that scenario, directed by Andrei Tarkovsky, it turns out that the most natural and the most alive-looking character is not a day-dreaming scientist, wishing to make the world a better place. No, the main character of the movie was a simple guy, who dwelled the Zone by his instincts, intuition and luck, just for make a living for another day. The Stalker.
No, that’s not the end of the history lesson. After that movie, Chernobyl catastrophe happened. It was really far from the resemblance with the “Roadside Picnic” events, but, after all impersonal cruelty that striked the territory around Chernobyl area, a big circle of the deadland was created, which fitted to the anomaly zone by its size and tragic background.
And after that tragedy, there was a Soviet Union crush, which created so-called “roaming 90’s”. Ex-Soviet people, left in the dark age with squashed moral principles, which kept them together all soviet years, started a struggle of survival on the ruins of former life. It was then when bandits were ruled every activity, promising some outcome, preferably the fastest and dirtiest way possible.
Finally, in the new millennia the governments of the former Union finally take some power back in their hands, so there was a time of peace in the 00’s in the Ukraine. Some talented people gather there and created a very powerful (yet not too stable) engine, and they blended Strugatsky, Tarkovsky, roaming 90’s under the shadow of Chernobyl zone…
So, here you are: a simple man, who tries to get by and live another day, yet must adapt and survive in the hostile terrain. You hunt vile creatures, explore and getting used to the location, where every 10 straight steps leading you to another death trap. You collect some strange artifacts, survive encounters with bandits and hostile military forces, you helping some random and generic friendly stalkers (and even getting some help in return). And after some time, you feel yourself like at home there…
Just like a soldier in his beloved trenches. Or a hunter in the wilderness, alone among wolves and bears. That’s a pattern of behaviour I was talking before. You’re not a hero in the shining armor, saving the world there. You just a survivalist, who’s getting stronger the harder fate trying to bend him. Without hope in government, in global order and justice, in helping hand from the Heaven… just to live another day.
I know what not everybody could be like this. But Stalker game is giving so alive, so thrilling modus operandi that I know many people who played only in this videogame in the whole life.
Inexpressible in words, unforgettable experience. Suspense. To kill or to be killed?
Okay, enough with pathos. As a game, STALKER obviously has flaws. Frequent engine crushes, questionable features like constant respawn of enemies, narrow ravine between locations…
But all this pales, when I remember how many time (even before Steam) I’ve spent there.
So that game takes a mark 10/10 from me, for being like no other. A quintessence of a part of my life.

I love the character customization, I love the class customization. While there may be only four classes, there are hundreds of possibilities. Many moons ago in 2003 I stumbled upon a trailer for a game called S.T.A.L.K.E.R. Oblivion Lost
Needless to say after watching that I quickly became obsessed with this game. Searching high and low for every bit of info I could get my eyes on, The GSC forums became my 2nd home while I awaited its arrival.
I remember at the time I was playing Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, With it I fell in love with non-linear open world 1st/3rd person games with RPG elements and how much I could get immersed in virtual worlds. I am all for fantasy settings don't get me wrong, but there is nothing more terrifying than reality. (With a spin of fiction of course, alternate reality if you will) The abandoned urban/industrial locations in S.T.A.L.K.E.R. were more my cup of tea. That in itself made me very excited to play it. I couldn't wait to get lost in its world.
While I waited though I researched about the Nuclear disaster at Chernobyl in April 1986, it was mixed emotions for me. I was sad/amazed/intrigued. Sad for all of those people who lost their lives because of this. Nothing but respect for the liquidators and anyone involved in the initial cleanup. Those people are heroes and deserve nothing less. Amazed that this game had some real history in its background story. Even if it is incredibly embellished (mutants, anomalies, artifacts etc etc.), you have to admit it makes for an interesting premise to a story. Finally, Intrigued on what these game developers had in store for the players to experience, without making a mockery of those who had lost their lives in this tragedy. The game also borrows elements from "Roadside Picnic" by Boris and Arkady Strugatsky and the 1979  Andrei Tarkovsky film "Stalker". If you haven't heard or checked them out yet, they are most definitely worth it. Masterpieces in their own right.
Well turns out it was a long wait lol, game finally arrived in March 2007. It was no longer Oblivion Lost, it was now called Shadow of Chernobyl. Which was a welcomed change imo, what was not a welcomed change was the amount of content/features that were removed from the game. Vehicles, locations/maps made smaller and simpler, monsters/mutants, superior lighting from old alpha builds among many other things had been removed it was rather disappointing to say the least. The survival aspect of the game took a huge hit, leaving many in the community confused as to what happened during development. GSC Game World regardless of all the missing features still delivered a good game and it was well received by critics as well.
The game at release had performance issues and bugs that required some patching. Once that happened it was clear that S.T.A.L.K.E.R. - Shadow of Chernobyl was a game ahead of its time. In a league all its own and a true gem in the PC gaming world. The atmosphere takes front row seat in this game it is almost like another character in the game. Such believable atmosphere it is downright amazing, it keeps you on the edge of your chair as you play.
:
- Incredible atmosphere!
- Impressive use of lighting and shadows,
- Cloud shadows that shift as day/night cycles progress.
- None stylized (photo based) textures (adds to the realism), Replicating the rust and decay feel.
- Great cut-scenes that hold up even by today's standards.
- Plenty of side quests
- Exploring is encouraged to find secret stashes scattered throughout the world to find loot, weapons, ammo, suits and artifacts. Artifacts can be placed on your belt to grant the player abilities like resistance to radiation, increase weight limit etc. Some interesting combinations that can be made with the multitude of artifacts available in the game.
- The games AI can be quite challenging because they adapt/react/flank/take cover depending on your approach. This adds to the games replayability immensely, if its one thing I have learned playing this game is that when it comes to killing the AI is that no playthrough is ever the same. Never. They are very unpredictable lets put it that way.
- Trading system with merchants and other friendly AI characters
- "The Zone" is alive even when you are not in the same vicinity, AI will be fighting mutants and/or other factions (Bandits, Duty, Freedom, Loners, Military, Mercs, Ecologists & Monolith) All fight among themselves.
Besides all the bells and whistles the story is incredibly engaging and keeps you interested throughout. Without too many spoilers (I am sure most people reading this have already played this but still) You play as "Marked One" an amnesiac trying to retrace his steps, he is then set on a mission to the heart of "The Zone" (term used to refer to the 30 kilometer Chernobyl Exclusion Zone, established after the accident.) to find a target and their whereabouts. Game also has multiple endings depending on the choices made by the player, 7 in total.
:
- Lots of "fetch" side quests (Surprise? lol)
- AI that can sometimes see you from "miles" away (vanilla)
- Some quest giving characters can die. (vanilla)
Just a heads up. Nothing game breaking but worth noting. Just like all games, it is not perfect. :)

When your done with vanilla (though not necessary, I would recommend the community fixes of ZRP goes well in a first playthrough to have the best bug-free experience with the game). Shadow of Chernobyl has some amazing mods worth playing, especially if you are looking for new storyline or another playthrough with better visuals, more weapons, new side quests, improved enemy AI, realistic weapon damage & accuracy etc. Some I can recommend are:

- Priboi Story
- L.U.R.K.
- OGSE (Old Good Stalker Evolution)
- AMK v1.4
- Secret Trails 2
- ABC Inferno (if you are a masochist)

- Autumn Aurora
- STALKER Soup
- Oblivion Lost
- AMK: Autumn Edition
- Lost Alpha (standalone)
Some of these mods add in the cut content (mutants, weapons, vehicles etc.)

The list goes on really, just my humble recommendations on the ones I have tried.
Clear Sky and Call of Pripyat are awesome games as well, worth checking out at least once. They also have great mods which I will not mention in this review. But I will say that there is something about Shadow of Chernobyl's allure and atmosphere that didn't carry over as well to the other two games. Out of all three games, Shadow of Chernobyl is by far still my favorite.
I don't claim to know everything about these games, because honestly I don't. I still discover new things about them every time I play them. They are gifts that just keep on giving. Thank goodness for Eastern European  game developers!
