I was and still am a fan of Skyrim, so I'm excited to get to know this game.  So far so good, I'm into it.  I spend over 10 hours playing in 2 days.  I'd call that a win for the game developers.  But only time will tell if I log 600 hours like I did in Skyrim when it became a Steam game, prior to that if I had to guess I'd say I have 1200 hours in game.
That said, the game is completely different.  Combat is mostly the same, with only a few changes.
Cons:
Riften is nothing like I remember, there is no Ratway, instead there are two enterances I found in Riften to make it to the round room with all the unsavory criminals you sell stolen stuff to.  From what I've read none of the zones Skyrim or older Elder Scrolls players remember are the same, they've all be redesigned, but I can live with that as I'm sure most gamers can too.
Earning Gold is very hard comparted to Skyrim.  It's easiest to be a theif and steal expensive stuff then sell it to a fence to get your bankroll started.
Fences (NPS's who buy stolen items have a cap) not sure what that cap is, but I can tell you I can steal a lot more stuff than the sell limit in a game session.
Crafting, Enchanting and Alchemy have changed.  This is a good thing.  I made a habit of exploiting enchangments and potions to make weapons and armor that made my character invincible.  At times that was a good thing, like if I was stuck on an enemy, however it takes the difficulty out of the game so I'm ruling that as a bad thing.  Cheating is bad M'kay.
This game isn't exactly a pay to win game, but it kind of is.  You can earn what you need to get through, but if you choose to pay for Crowns you can advance much faster.  My level 8 character is still wearing cloth wraps to protect his feet and none of his gear is his level.  Armor and weapons are expensive, so either you pay to win or play hundreds of hours to earn what you could pay for.
I haven't spent any time blacksmithing, leatherworking, enchanting or any of the 'productive member of society' skills.  I'm sure you could sell your stuff and make money that way.
Money is hard to come by, not all loot you find is worth money, some of it is just a waste of space in your now limited storage.  Storage is no longer measured by weight, it's now measured by the amount of items you carry.  Your character starts off with a backpack with 60 slots.  You can fill it with 60 flowers and need to see a merchant to unload your stuff.
Pros
Just to continue the storage thing, you can buy bank and backpack upgrades, but early on they're expensive and don't add much to storage.  400 gold got me from 60 items to 70 items.  At level 4, $400 gold is a lot of money. .
The world is gigantic.  It takes all the worlds from every Elder Scrolls game and puts them together so you won't get bored exploring this place.
As I mentioned before combat is different, this is a pro not a con.  Not only can you melee, shoot arrows from a distance or use magic, but now you also have special attacks and abilities to enhance the combat experience.
Crimes go away over time.  Say for example you're low on funds and decide to murder an innocent player and take all the stuff he has at his camp.  You run from the law and escape into what we used to call the ratway.   Sell your stolen loot, then log out.  By the time you log back in, the guards forget about your crimes.  I'm not sure how long you need to log out or hide for but it's not that long.  I got into trouble stealing stuff, logged for a few hours then came back with a clean slate.
I'm sure there are many pros and cons I'm not privy to at this point, I'll update my review later when I know more about game play.
So far, I'd rate this game an 7/10 because pay to win is lame and no gamer wants to grind.  You guys had it mostly right with Skyrim.

Just beat Transistor, and I think it's safe to say that yes, it does live up to Bastion in every way.
But that's not to say it's just a reskin of bastion as the trailers would have you believe at first glance, because it isn't. It plays very differently; while Bastion tested your reflexes, Transistor will test your pre-planning ability.
Transistor has a V.A.T.S.-like core gameplay element that allows you to plan your attacks ahead, but unlike V.A.T.S. from Fallout, using this will leave you very open to attack. Using this function will disallow any offensive action until it recharges; so you must use it effectively because the enemies are much faster than you are.
The soundtrack is very different to bastion. I wouldn't say it doesn't live up to Bastion's, it's just very different in it's genres presented, and that is totally okay because it's still as great as you would expect from Supergiant Games and fits the cyberpunk setting very well.
Speaking of the setting, it's beautiful. I love how you get the sense that the creators had this whole other rich, lore filled world planned out in their head but could only make "Just a video game" about it. It's not expositioned to you as most games would do, it's just there, which is exactly what the secret to making a setting like this is supposed to be like, because it means that you get the feeling that even without the main character and their plight, it would still exist.
I give this game a "Buy this right now"/10, even despite it's minor hiccups, which I will now list.
Every now and again, the game locks up for a few seconds. This is guesswork at best so take it with a grain of salt, but I believe it may be caused by an unoptimized sound cache reset because the dynamic soundtrack is played in chunks of audio that change and layer as you do certain things. It could also be an enemy spawning issue, but again, I don't know for sure. It's so minor and infrequent that it's just worth noting, although not really a bother, since it seems like something that can be patched out.
This has only happened in the challenge rooms so far, but some of the enemy capabilities are at odds with good gameplay design when their strengths are combined together. This one time, I accidentally knocked a "Cheerleader" (Basically a radar that makes enemies invincible) next to a vine, which heals other enemies. So the vine was healing the cheerleader, the cheerleader was shielding the vine, and the remaining fetch would go back to the vine to heal itself and be shielded every time I got it's health really low, and transistor time or whatever it's called wouldn't load fast enough to let me finish off the fetch before it did so. I'd show a screenshot of what happened, but there's currently an error with steam that won't let me upload it. Anyway, I had to restart the challenge map, but it never happened again thoughout the entire game.
Another thing is that this game, while very enjoyable, should be played in short bursts. I beat it in one 9 hour sitting, and it began to feel repetitive by the end, as any game would. Just when it started to change the enemy variety up by adding in the "Men" which are basically these enemies with special abilities that throw pretty much tracking explosives at you, the game ends. They're fun to fight, but they show up so late game that you barely have time to enjoy their presence, though I'm sure I'll see more of them on my New Game+ playthrough.
This one is a nitpick and not really necessary so disregard it if you wish, but: At the end there is a part where you fight an enemy who also has transistor time and can preplan attacks against you. The multiplayer potential for that is amazing, because the fight was actually very enjoyable. I would have loved a 2 player mode for that sequence that you unlock after beating the game, even if it was just local pvp on one PC/Console instead of over the internet, but I understand that there are probably engine limitations and whatnot so it's just a fleeting pipe dream.
The story, while very gripping and entertaining, didn't have any characters I could personally relate to or connect with, so when certain things happen throughout the game, I found it hard to really, truly care. But that's probably just because I'm a cynical♥♥♥♥♥hole, the writers told the story they wanted to and they did it effectively, even if some of the characters didn't really get much development outside of the biographies that add to themselves by the end of the game.
Aside from these issues though, I fully and wholeheartedly recommend this game. At $19.99 as a brand new price for this memorable experience of a game, you can't go wrong.

Better than Bastion?  Maybe.  Like the previous offering from Supergiant Games, Transistor delivers on multiple fronts:
1. Visuals: Transistor is aesthetically beautiful in a way that few other games are and if Supergiant continues down this particular road, all of its games will be instantly recognizable.
2. Sound: The same awesome narration with a new voice follows us into Transistor.  It's topped off by another beautiful soundtrack from the Supergiant team that you'll want to listen to many times after completing the game.
3. Gameplay: Where some might have found the gameplay in Bastion a little simplified, Transistor kicks it up with a hybrid turn-based/real-time combat system, numerous weapon combinations and enemies with unique abilities that make battlefield strategizing more of a priority.
4. Story: Perhaps the only place where I could knock this game, Transistor follows in the footsteps of Bastion with a couple interesting twists and a really solid story backed up by bits of in-game lore, but leaves some of the world-building up to player theorizing.  This can be a positive or negative depending on what you're looking for in a game.  Regardless, Transistor still manages to craft a compelling narrative that outstrips a lot of games on the market today.
In short: I can't think of any remotely good reason not to buy or recommend this game.  It's a great example of what happens when a group of developers and artists come together with a solid and unique vision and pull it off.

I have a hard time explaining how deeply in love I am with this game. It's a masterpiece.
(Spoiler Free)
The first thing that hits you is the world, and the art, and throughout my entire thirteen hours (on my first playthrough) the environments never get stale or old. Everything is gorgeous and feels handpainted.
The story and the characters are incredible and deeply engaging, but I won't say anything more than that all the voice actors involved are phenomenal.
Battles are fun, fluid, and tactical. The mixture between the strategy and turn-based combat and something more real-time never gets old. Bastion this is not, Transistor is more methodical, and much slower. You're allowed to take your time to plan out what you'd like to do and put it into action. The skills and abilities system keeps the variety up. Usually I'd find my niche and stick to what I liked, but Transistor had me switching up my abilities at every single checkpoint, and not just for all of the files that I was addicted to collecting to get every single tidbit I could out of the writing.
This noir wouldn't be complete without the jazzy cyberpunk soundtrack, which I could listen to forever and never get bored of. Not only is it good on it's own, but it sinks itself deep into the game and plays dynamically and reactively depending on what is happening at the moment.
But, above all else, what makes Transistor a masterpiece is the atmosphere. The absolute dedication the game has to it's world and how much it sucks you in at every opportunity. Optional environments and points of interest litter every single map just to get another line or two out of the Voice. The way the music works itself in, the way enemies interact with you and all your abilities, the way the environments twist and change, the terminals you find, the files you can read, and the small interactions and character moments out of Red herself are unlike anything I have ever played before. If I were making a "Videogames as art" list, this would top it off.
I will never forget this game.

I've had this game less than 2 weeks and have played over 120 hours on this game. The game itself is fantastic. I love the combat system, and I adore the building aspect. However, there are two major flaws in the game right now.
1. Hackers. You've no doubt read other reviews complaining about this problem. If you use an official server, you're more than likely to come across a hacker or two. Flight, infinite health, the ability to wipe your inventory clean and teleporting are just a few examples of what you commonly see. Furthermore there are ways for players to duplicate items and in 5 minutes they can have resources that would have taken 20+ hours to farm. This makes the game extremely frustrating.
2. Lag? Okay, the games in 'pre-alpha', of course there's going to be lag. I can appreciate that, but I would just like to point out that this is a huge issue within the game, often making combat impossible, (freezes, characters floating and freezing etc). On top of that, servers very regularly crash without warning, and when this does happen, you could be playing for an hour before realising you've actually disconnected. (Your progress is then lost).
There are, however, ways to combat these issues. A lot of the community servers have active admins, who take care of hackers instantly, and have rules against exploits. Community servers also tend to have very low ping, so any lag related issues do not occur.
Unless you have a lot of patience with potential hackers and lag issues, I would WAIT to buy this game. (For now). In the recent news of this game, the developers have explained that they are next "Working To Combat Exploits/Hacks". Hopefully it won't be long before these hackers are at least a rare occurence. The developers have been frequently updating the game, with updates only days apart. To me, this is promising that the game will be constantly developed and improved.
In short, if you buy this game play on a community server with low ping and good admins.

Fortunately though, I did play it a bit on my old Windows 8 computer, so the small amount of refresher time was enough to at least feel able to leave a fair review.
As far as the gameplay goes: it is a time management game. Unfortunately, it does it in the worst way. That is, while this is marketed as a veterinary game, the gameplay is literally just rapidly clicking as fast as you possibly can. You basically click the animal once to evaluate them, and then go to the medicine cabinet to get a syringe, then click the animal again to give them the shot. Sometimes there's a contagious disease that requires hand-washing or the need to go grab the x-ray machine to use on some patients, but even then, it's all just rapid clicking. This is a game that would have gained so much from the inclusion of mini-games or even just different diagnosis/treatment possibilities, or something. Plus, the "upgrades" are insufficient. You quickly get up to having six beds to make use of, spread across the room, but you can't move that far quickly enough to not make it seem more like a chore rather than fun in trying to reach the goal score.
Educational value-wise, I'd say there's really none, though it tries in some ways in-game to pretend otherwise. Granted, it isn't marketed as such in the store, so I can't fault it much for that. Though I would suggest that adding some real educational value would have helped the game a LOT - even if only by making it be a great game for kids.
The graphics and such are pretty much what one expects from such games, so I don't fault those. The main problem, really, is that it just doesn't take advantage of what it could have been.
Daisy > Barbie
You don't really do anything to help the pets. Your goal is just click in order as fast as you can to get the most pets through before your timer runs out.

I was and still am a fan of Skyrim, so I'm excited to get to know this game.  So far so good, I'm into it.  I spend over 10 hours playing in 2 days.  I'd call that a win for the game developers.  But only time will tell if I log 600 hours like I did in Skyrim when it became a Steam game, prior to that if I had to guess I'd say I have 1200 hours in game.
That said, the game is completely different.  Combat is mostly the same, with only a few changes.
Cons:
Riften is nothing like I remember, there is no Ratway, instead there are two enterances I found in Riften to make it to the round room with all the unsavory criminals you sell stolen stuff to.  From what I've read none of the zones Skyrim or older Elder Scrolls players remember are the same, they've all be redesigned, but I can live with that as I'm sure most gamers can too.
Earning Gold is very hard comparted to Skyrim.  It's easiest to be a theif and steal expensive stuff then sell it to a fence to get your bankroll started.
Fences (NPS's who buy stolen items have a cap) not sure what that cap is, but I can tell you I can steal a lot more stuff than the sell limit in a game session.
Crafting, Enchanting and Alchemy have changed.  This is a good thing.  I made a habit of exploiting enchangments and potions to make weapons and armor that made my character invincible.  At times that was a good thing, like if I was stuck on an enemy, however it takes the difficulty out of the game so I'm ruling that as a bad thing.  Cheating is bad M'kay.
This game isn't exactly a pay to win game, but it kind of is.  You can earn what you need to get through, but if you choose to pay for Crowns you can advance much faster.  My level 8 character is still wearing cloth wraps to protect his feet and none of his gear is his level.  Armor and weapons are expensive, so either you pay to win or play hundreds of hours to earn what you could pay for.
I haven't spent any time blacksmithing, leatherworking, enchanting or any of the 'productive member of society' skills.  I'm sure you could sell your stuff and make money that way.
Money is hard to come by, not all loot you find is worth money, some of it is just a waste of space in your now limited storage.  Storage is no longer measured by weight, it's now measured by the amount of items you carry.  Your character starts off with a backpack with 60 slots.  You can fill it with 60 flowers and need to see a merchant to unload your stuff.
Pros
Just to continue the storage thing, you can buy bank and backpack upgrades, but early on they're expensive and don't add much to storage.  400 gold got me from 60 items to 70 items.  At level 4, $400 gold is a lot of money. .
The world is gigantic.  It takes all the worlds from every Elder Scrolls game and puts them together so you won't get bored exploring this place.
As I mentioned before combat is different, this is a pro not a con.  Not only can you melee, shoot arrows from a distance or use magic, but now you also have special attacks and abilities to enhance the combat experience.
Crimes go away over time.  Say for example you're low on funds and decide to murder an innocent player and take all the stuff he has at his camp.  You run from the law and escape into what we used to call the ratway.   Sell your stolen loot, then log out.  By the time you log back in, the guards forget about your crimes.  I'm not sure how long you need to log out or hide for but it's not that long.  I got into trouble stealing stuff, logged for a few hours then came back with a clean slate.
I'm sure there are many pros and cons I'm not privy to at this point, I'll update my review later when I know more about game play.
So far, I'd rate this game an 7/10 because pay to win is lame and no gamer wants to grind.  You guys had it mostly right with Skyrim.

Ships!  Aliens!  Space Stations!
You get the idea - if you've watched the original Alien...then seen the second movie, it felt like there was something missing...  fifty seven years to be exact.  With all the bad video game adaptions of the Alien franchise, Sega and Creative Assembly decided if they were gonna make this puppy - they were gonna go all in.  Getting the cast to reprise their voice rolls was brilliant, the add-on scenerios to play out the desperate escape from the Nostromo and the search for the alien by the Nostromo crew was wonderful to say the least.  That's not even talking about the main game yet...

The alien seems to be more interested in ruining YOUR day than the androids and other station inhabitants - but give it enough incentive, the trash will take the trash out...  and leave you a clean area to loot valuable survival items (assuming the alien leaves and doesn't trash you next, that is...).
My only complaints is that the headlamp uses batteries like a flashlight from the 1920s and it can be frustrating when the alien gets fixated on your location, trapping you in a place with no escape.  Besides that, its a game definitely worth the retail price - so on sale, it would be a no brainer.  Two bear thumbs up!

I bought this for the storyline/campaign mode, in the wake of the super-hype that EA put out about the sequel to what was actually an excellent game (COD4), unfortunately this one was a full blown console port with poorly thought out multiplayer maps, idiotic weapon balancing and downright ridiculous features to appease the 8-14 year old audience.
Major faults:
1. lobby gameplay, not server support.
2. tiny maps, tiny teams, limited gameplay options.
3. Nuclear weapons.    enough said.
4. cheaters.  This game has valve-anti cheat, which means it does not have anti-cheat.
If you enjoy owning n00bs, this is your game -.-

What I liked about Forces:
•There's plenty of multiple paths and exploration value, even in boost levels. My favorite level is Mortar Canyon. It's well built 3D stage.
•All 3 types of gameplay are on point. None of them goes off the Sonic style of gameplay like werehog or treasure hunt did.
•Avatar gameplay and routes can vary depend on the wispon you take with, giving it more replay value
•Levels don't overstay more than its welcome, and its short length encourages all S rank and Red star rings challenge. It's fun to replay it many times.
•Airboost is fun and helpful, this is coming from someone who didn't like the boost before this game
•Cool cinematics and setpieces
•Pretty aesthetics
•Character dialogues are in character
•Story has energetic tone and light goofy mood in general, sometimes hilariously "serious"
•Endless continue
•Character customization is actually really cool
What I didn't like:
•Poor control
•Really poor physics
•Classic sonic's levels are not bad, it just suffers badly from poor control and physics.
•The later the level goes on, bottomless pit comes off as challenge instead of actual skill based courses. Then again this is the issue that every modern sonic has.
•Almost all levels are similar to each other in gameplay. The only unique level gimmicks I can think of are water slide in Aqua Road and a brief gravity flip in Capital City.
Overall, it's 7/10 for me. It's flawed but charming enough to make me really enjoy it.

If you're the type of person who plays the main story of a game and gets to the credits, and then considers the game finished so you stop playing it, Sonic Forces will be a very short, insanely easy game that is not worth your money.
If you like to 100% games, especially Modern Sonic games, including doing all the red rings and various other collectables, S-ranks and such, this is a solid, full length game with a mission system that will keep things fresh as you replay the games ~40 stages.
It was clear Sega dumbed down the main story mode to make sure even the youngest gamers could complete the story, but there is more than enough content in the mission system to make up for the super-easy campaign mode.
But it seems most people reviewing here are judging the game based simply on the story mode. Which I guess is how most people play games. Just note that if you actually like completeing games, it's not short or easy like everyone is claiming. You will breeze through the story mode, and then the actual game will begin.

Only thumbing this up to counterbalance the poor score, my actual stance on this game is neutral.
You can read about finer points in other reviews. All I'm adding is that this is not a bad game, just a letdown. One will find the immense potential for this game to be at least somewhat fascinating. I got the feeling that they are heading towards the right direction for future Sonic games, they just need to fine-tune and flesh out. Here's to wishing them not repeating their mistakes and having the correct mindset moving forward. This game is a great blueprint, Sonic Team, don't waste it.

So honestly, at first I had my reservations about this game.....
But when I got more into the game I had a change of heart!
I think this game has some good elements and some not so good.
For one, I love the idea of the Avatar! I found the Avatar gameplay the most interesting honestly! The incorporation of Wispons also helps!! Second, Modern Sonic plays pretty well too! I like the modified boost feature and the levels for the most part! The music throughout the game is also well-made and diverse! From rock, to techno, to classic 8 bit  sounding music! I also enjoyed the more serious tone of the story!
Now I know I said I liked the level design, which I do, but I also think the levels, mainly Modern Sonic's, could be longer! I love the detail in the envrionments and it would've been nice to immerse in it more through longer levels! I also feel like at a lot of times the game played itself, mostly during turning and steering segments. Not a big deal, but still kind of threw me off at first. I also think Classic Sonic's physics could be tweaked. I felt like he didn't bounce off of enemies after he jumped on them.
I think the game overall is good! I certainly don't label it The Best Sonic Game, but it has potential. I think it's definitely a better attempt at a Sonic game than Lost World or 06 from a critical standpoint. I recommend the game to any Sonic fan just to give it a spin, I enjoy playing this as well as Mania and I think they're both good additions to the Sonic series!

This game is one of the dopest games I've ever played. It is something fresh, sure it has some things from other games, crafting, farming, etc. But this game just smashes the mold with PvP and the player driven story. What I mean by that is, a new king is crowned, he is a noble king, helping his kingdom and roping the marauders plaguing his land, then out of nowhere he turns corrupt, sets the tax at 20% and all guilds and families band together to take him and his knights down. It's so fun to be a part of those kinds of things. Just cause the community on each server is so diverse. I recommend this game to anyone that's looking for a good old fun time.
With that being said, the only problem with it is the hacking and exploits. Today, for example. My friends and I were working hard building a home and collecting resources. We've maybe put 3-4 hours into this magnificent building. Then out of nowhere some other guild starts launching rocks at us with a trebuchet (that was way awesome). Then we returned the favor. We had previously attacked another guild and taken 80+ trebuchet stones (which are annoying to make because they take so much stone) and started to destroy these guy's castle. I had no idea what I was getting into with this game. From what I'd heard you just sit at a border checkpoint and decide if people are allowed to enter the country or not. And that's exactly what I got, but Papers, Please is so much more than that. It's not just a job simulation, it's a story of moral choices and corrupt government. It's not just about a border guard, it's about a man who struggles to provide for his family, who must work for the smallest of wages to make some of the toughest choices. You sit in your little checkpoint booth. A man comes up and hands you his passport. You skim over the information and stamp a big green "APPROVED" for him. He thanks you and starts to walk away, but before he does he says, "my wife is right behind me, please be nice to her." Sure enough, up steps a nice young woman. There's her passport. You look down and see an expiration date of last month. "This document is expired" you say. She stares at you, eyes wide and pleading: "Please, if I go back to my country they will kill me. Please let me in." What do you do? Do you risk losing your paycheck and therefore leave yourself unable to buy medicine for your sick son? Or do you abandon all morality and turn the woman away?
Papers, Please is not an easy game, nor is it free of consequences. Not only does it become insanely difficult to reivew piles of papers and make sure every little details is accrate and correct, but every choice you make determines who you are and the path you take. Will you work tirelessly for the glory of Arstotzka, or will you join the Order and be a part of the uprising against the tyrannical, corrupt government?

Dark Souls 2 and it's prequel Dark Souls  are some of the most challeging games I have ever played. Sometimes parts of the game may seem impossible and extremely frustrating but once you beat it there is no feeling like it I have yet to find elsewhere in gaming. The game itself from an aesthetic standpoint is beautiful and runs great all the environments are unique and really immerse you in the souls world which is filled to the brim with history and lore. Every skeleton has a story every destroyed castle or abandoned cave has history and you can tell when you walk around. Its really easy to get lost in such a well built world and you will see minutes turn to hours easily. In comparison to the first game DS2 has some pluses as well as some minuses gameplay wise.
+'s:
-Matchmaking is a lot more smoother
-Teleport between bonfires makes traveling about easier.
-No more areas like blight town that have crazy grapchis issues
-PC is pretty well polished have witnessed very little to 0 bugs(so far)
-Even more challenging bosses
-Beautiful environments
-Even better overworld or home base brings a lot of the NPC's together for you
-DLC is really good
-'s:
-Fastraveling kinda destroys the cohesivness of some environments with each other
-Have to travel back to overworld and speak with NPC to level up
-Some "shortcuts" in DS2 feel sloppily made or not really helpful and there are a lot less due to fast travel(Im looking at you Last Bastille).
-Some Enemies and bosses attacks have insane "homing"/"lock on" making them really frustrating to fight
-with some boss fights difficulty is added with adding more enemies overall(kinda cheating i feel like).
Mixed:
Some enemies/bosses copy pasted from first game can be cool at times but not at others.
Overall the game is great and some of the cons I listed are really nitpicky things to look at if you loves Souls games than this one is a great addition to the bunch and really brings a lot to the table. I would recommend this to anyone that is looking for a challenge or just a good game to sink some serious time into.

I'm stuck in the Communications floor with the Alien, a bunch of bloodthirsty synthetics and a few hostile humans.
The door that leads to the exit is offline so I need to backtrack a bit to reboot some systems and restore power.
I see a save station so I save my game.
I check my motion tracker. It blanks out for a few moments but it eventually reveals nothing on the scanner.
I walk confidently into a dining area. There is damage: some fire and lots of debris everywhere. I need to watch my step.
I see the generator at the far end of the room and a terminal. My objective. That's when I hear a blip from the motion tracker.
I panic as I hear something large slump down from the vents with a large THUD. I hide behind a couch and peek from the side of it. Amidst the flashing red emergency lights and all the smoke I can see the outline of an elongated head and a tail whipping from side to side.
The
is here, in the room with me.
It starts walking about, searching for any kind of movement. If it spots me I'm dead. I sneak in the opposite direction and hide in a locker.
Through the narrow slits of the locker I see the creature checking every nook and cranny of the room. Then it turns and takes a good look at the locker I'm in. It starts walking slowly towards me.
I have to hold my breath as it inspects the locker closely. It feels like an eternity has gone by until it leaves to search another room. It's gone for now.
I exit the locker and check my motion tracker again: There's movement far behind me but its far enough to give me time to restart the generator.
I walk to the generator and I restart it. It makes a loud whirring noise as some of the lights in the room come back on. The sound makes me panic as I hurry to the computer terminal to reboot systems. I heard a loud hiss somewhere in the distance.
I navigate to the utility folder and do what I need to in a jiffy.
With the power now on I turn around to make my way to the door.
The alien is right behind me.
I SCREAM as it grabs me and proceeds to make a whole in my skull.
Game over.

I jump out of a vent and land in a sort of security desk. There's a guard there that is long dead. A magazine has been forcefully shoved down his throat. It's an unsettling sight. WHo killed him and why? Was he making too much noice? I hear a metal clank around the corner. Immediatly I duck under the desk and check the motion tracker for enemies. My heart is pounding.
This game is an incredible environmental suspence and horror piece of art. The horror genre is a hard sell for me as I am turned off by needless gore and jump scares. If however the envirnment and atmosphere overwhelm the feeling of unease I have at facing off with an Alien I am more than happy to finish the game. This is what Alien Isolation brought to the table.
I've only ever watched Alien and Prometheus and they've taken quite a bit from the aesthetics of both movies. It's so refreshing to see an older style of technology and architecture. To compare, try to think back on Mass Effect's ship. Vast open areas that are filled with holographic screens everywhere. The porodominant color is a sort of LED blue on everything. There's an elevator that takes you between decks. Overall it's just boring and played out. In this game they've done the complete opposite. A simple corridor is absolutely packed with tubes, symbols, subsystems and real depth indicating an absurd amount of work on the artist's part. The result is a living environment that help create the mood way more that the Alien ever does.
Sound is so important in this game as players will realize quickly and i' has not gone to the wayside in this game. The ship creaks and groans. The Alien clamers in the vents and human NPC's provide their nervous and aggresive dialogue to heighten the suspense. (as a sidenote I finished the game without killing a single human and found it more enjoyable that way, try it it's fun)
The plot is tight, fitting and plays like the original movie did back in the day. Tense, well written with believable characters.
I love how despite having great weapons ion the game you'll almost never want to use them unless forced into a corner. A wonderful way to encourage different playstyles and show off all sorts of Half Life remniscent encounters and will leave you in awe of this fictional ship and characters they've created.

Length of playthrough is perfect in my opinion. I may end up revisiting it some day. All in all this is by far my favorite horror game and possibly one of my favorite single player FPS's. It will not disapoint. Get used to dying. Learn from dying. Then enjoy the game.

I'm twentyish hours in and I feel like I've barely scratched the surface.  Every time I restart a factory I feel like I've learned something about layouts and space/resource management.  There are many Eureka! moments in this game and they all feel great.  Theres just something really satisfying about staring at my screen trying to puzzle something out and wondering how I'm going to make things work and then having an idea pop in my head (which may or may not be correct) and trying it out.  When things do go as planned I feel like a genius and when they don't I feel like its very easy to understand why things weren't working the way I had hoped.  Because its easy to understand what you did wrong and learn from it, every time I restart my game I feel like my new factory is significantly better than the previous one.  They only real criticisms that I have is   I really like the art style as well.  Reminds me of watching my uncle play PC games when I was younger.  The only real criticisms that I have for the game is that it takes a long time to get a new factory up and running.  It can take awhile to get to a point where your factory can start automating red science (where I feel like the goes from being a grind to being more engaging) and that their is no planning mode initially (Like in Prison Architect).  You have to pre-plan so much when you start a new factory that it would have been nice if there was a way you could start marking down where you're going to put things while you're waiting for your resources to build up.  There's a blueprint mode that comes later as research, but I really wish it was something that you got initially.  Beyond those two complaints, however, I'm having an absolute blast playing it and could see it being something I stay with for a long time.

Another fantastic piece of work by Supergiant, the spiritual sucessor to Bastion does its predecessor justice. While the story is slightly more simple than the story in Bastion, the art direction, sound, music, and gameplay are all just as good, if not better. The game's core mechanic is the turn() function (ability) that you posess. Turn() allows you to freeze time and plan out your next move. It may not be the most original mechanic, but it works very well in this game.
In addition, each of your attacks and abilities (called functions) can be used either as a primary attack, an upgrade to a primary attack, or a passive boost. For example, one ability, bounce(), when used as a main attack, fires a shot that ricochets between enemies. However, when applied as a boost to another ability, it causes that attack to have a possibility of ricocheting between enemies. Or it might reduce that attack's cooldown time, depending on the attack. Of course, it can also be used as a passive bonus, in this case granting the player a regenerating shield that reflects a single shot. As you can immagine, the number of possible combinations is enormous.
Also, do yourself a quick favor. See the button that says "Transistor + soundtrack"? Yeah? Good. Click that one. Because this game has some incredible music. I mean, the main character is a singer. It's like Darren Korb is rubbing how amazing of a composer he is in our faces. Don't believe me?
.
And that's not even touching on how beautiful this game is.
This game will not disappoint you.

Well, that was playthrough #1. After doing all challenges, listening to and reading everything I possibly could and only once having to use the "Retry" function, Steam tells me I have 7 hours under my belt.
The following is my critique of the game, ignoring the New Game+ mode (for now). While I do reference Supergiant Games' first title, Bastion, quite heavily, the points I make should also be accessible to players who have yet to play Bastion (seriously, get that game). While I try to be objective, some sections of this review are highly subjective; the game suffers from virtually no technical (and thus "objectively objective") faults and what I point out as bad may appear as "creative" or "challenging" or just "different" to others.
Please refer to additional reviews and critiques before you decide whether or not you want to buy Transistor.
If you want to avoid even those, skip to the conclusion section at the end.
Transistor is an isometric tactical Action-RPG with a linear story.
First of all, the things I was happy with -
:
-
, obviously. Darren Korb and Ashley Barret did an amazing job and the music leaves little to be desired. It's a different style than Bastion's soundtrack, so, of course, whether you like it more or less than Bastion's is a matter of taste, but it is very atmospheric and carries the game together with
-
. No surprises there. The music may be the soul of the game but the expert narration (and fantastic voice acting) are its heart.
-
. The world of Transistor is original and colorful; the "feel" is the same as in Bastion but it has a distinctly different theme; the result is stellar.
-
. The ability to collect a variety of skills, all of them with different effects, depending on whether they are active, passive or modifying an active skill, makes for some interesting (and tough) choices as to how you want to play. Not everything works well but you can try everything.
Now to the things that I was less impressed with -
:
-
. Sadly, it is nowhere near as great as (I) expected. Precision is not its strong point and those who were hoping for Frozen Synapse levels of refined tactical combat will be disappointed, as will be those that expected a slick Hack&Slash. Some sections are almost impossible to beat with only one of the modes but intelligent use of both does not help in all situations and more often than not (especially later on), you can find yourself cheesing the game in less-than-fun ways when you encounter fights that are frustrating enough that you'd like to skip them, due to issues with
-
. Few enemies are balls-to-the-wall hard, but many are insanely annoying. Having to deal with enemies who have the ability to cloak themselves (which, somehow, also makes them invulnerable) without the player having any way to disrupt this cloak (other than waiting for them to deal damage to you) or to damage them in cloak makes several mid- and endgame sections downright infuriating. Especially if said enemies are rapidly regenerating health. Several enemy attacks cannot be avoided and the player's ability to heal himself is extremely limited, making the whole combat system less a matter of skill and more one of a proper choice of abilities (which is where the combat system is at odds with its RPG elements); due to this, some fights (especially boss fights) and victories are anything but satisfying and can leave a bitter aftertaste.
-
. While Bastion had only a few characters with little depth but strong-enough features to make them relatable and carry the story, Transistor has almost none. "The voice" is the strongest one by far but remains a lot more blank than Bastion's narrator. The female lead, Red, has even less than that (or Bastion's Kid). The human antagonists are hardly characterized at all and what remains is a faceless menace that changes the world around you and attacks you constantly... and yet fails to really make you feel threatened.
-
. Where Bastion's story was about a simple goal for most of the game (restoring the Bastion), Transistor lacks direction. You feel like a tourist who is being guided from one landmark to the other without any drive or ultimate goal behind it, which becomes even more apparent at the game's conclusion. The plot works with local tension only (i.e. short-term obstacles and goals). The lack of strong characters makes it hard to build-up a bad guy and the pace at which the city changes and the threat swallows it leaves no time to make you care about it or its inhabitants. Unlike the Bastion, you didn't build it with your own two hands and, despite being in a city, you never get a chance to interact with anybody. This leaves the romance as its only redeeming factor... except it isn't either, because the main characters' interaction is very one-sided. The sad truth is: Transistor's story is forgetable.
And finally -
:
-
. While the design is great, you hardly see anything of the city (or the rest of the world). Vistas are few and far between and the game doesn't feature any maps or background information that allows you to see the "big picture". Sadly, this devaluates most of the ingame biographies and what lore there is because it becomes that much harder to relate to for their lack of context.
-
. It certainly isn't Mass Effect 3 levels of terrible but, frankly, it makes no sense. The game's conclusion renders pretty much the entire hero's journey pointless and I have to ask what motivation Red had in the first place. That isn't to say that it isn't beautiful in several ways but nonetheless highly disappointing if you were hoping for a well-written story.
-
. From what I have heard from several people, 7 hours is not a good time. It is quite possible to beat the game in under 5 hours. New Game+ may add replay value here, if you truly enjoyed the combat system and don't share my gripes with it, but if you don't, it leaves the question of value for your money. And, regardless of New Game+, my impression is that the game tries to do too much in too little time - Introducing you to a world, threatening this world and making you its involuntary savior has worked before... but it doesn't work for Transistor.
(Or: tl;dr)
Transistor is a good attempt to solve a task that was almost unsolvable - To create the next "Bastion". Design-wise, it is every bit as strong and a true treat for the eyes and ears, with some great ideas on how to keep progression interesting and your game experience unique.
But a closer look reveals a system that tries to combine real-time and tactical combat and, as a result, is the master of neither. The beautiful world that seems so full and interesting is a facade, a mere stage decoration with too little behind it to keep it from falling over when leaned on, leaving a lot of the ingame lore without sufficient context. And while music and narration are great, they cannot hide the fact that the play itself is boring and the characters forgotten as soon as they leave the stage.
Supergiant Games gave their game and its world too little time to introduce themselves and captivate you and the result is all the more disappointing for it.
Nevertheless, I recommend Transistor for the interesting experience it is; you may find the combat system and story, despite their flaws, more satisfying than I did and, either way, you do not want to miss out on the soundtrack and Logan Cunningham's sexy voice. Supergiant Games deserves the money for a brave attempt, even if this attempt falls short.
If you aren't dying to play Transistor right now, pick it up once it goes on sale.

Listen, it's not as bad everyone is making it out to be.
The music is one of the best parts about the game, no doubt. Gameplay-wise, it feels okay. Classic Sonic ruined this game for me honestly; he's pretty down-graded from Generations and plays worse than Sonic and your Avatar. The Episode Shadow content is SIGNIFICANTLY short as balls, but it helps explain a little bit behind Infinite's backstory.. but only a LITTLE.
The Avatar customization is incredible as you progress through the game, get missions completed and get S-Ranks. But at the start, it's very minimal and pretty poor. I'd hope there was more in-depth customization going on, but its pretty mediocre at the start. The 'Wispons' are pretty neat, some work better than others for certain stages, but overall you can unlock more weapons as you progress; eventually will get some with secondary abilities to make the levels play better. For example: I got a Drill Wispon that pretty much completely stops you in your tracks when you try to stop moving, rather than the normal gameplay where you practically 'float,' a noticable problem I've seen with lots of people with this game.
Story overall is incredibly short and can be beat within 4 hours, a common problem with the Sonic games since Colors. Sonic Team has definitely made a solid story here compared to the previous games, although the dialog is pretty damn cringy in the beginning and felt completely rushed to "get to the point." I personally enjoyed Unleashed because it was lengthy (approximately 9-10 hours to complete) and had a good story behind it; lots of side quests to do and both gameplay styles were fun. That's where this game lacks entirely. Sega needs to go back this the Unleashed formula and add more content to their games, rather than just making stages with no collectables (red rings dont count for me, they're a nuisance personally).
HOWEVER, despite all that, I recommend this game for any Sonic fan that wants to play this on their sexy af PC because Nintendo has had them exclusives for the past couple years. Plus, if you've ever wanted to create your own Sonic character, then this is a great way to finally do so (officially in a sanic game lol). I've also had 0 technical issues as well; no crashes or texture glitches or anything of the sort. This is a solid PC port and I really enjoyed playing this. I would probably get this when it's on sale though, $40 is a decent price, but considering how short the game is, it's hard to defend that price entirely. I would hope Sega can update this game with more Story DLC perhaps and more missions to play, this game definitely needs/deserves more content than what it actually has.

I played this game on my gaming PC which has a gtx 1080 so I was able to play it at 4K unlocked FPS with all the settings maxed out so YMMV.
Like any Sonic game, need I say more?
About 40 levels if you count the boss fights and bonus DLC levels.
The level themes have had a decent amount of variety. You have your GreenHill clone, industrial level, space level, a bit of desert, casino, and water here and there, forest level, city level, and Eggman’s base level. But I wish the game could have included a fire and ice level.
For a Sonic game I thought the length was fine others who’ve never played a Sonic game may think otherwise but a platforming game can only be so long when you have a character that moves so fast, besides I’d rather take quality levels over a large quantity of bland levels. It took me 6-hours to complete the story but there’s plenty of post-game stuff to do such as collecting all the red-rings and getting all S-ranks, completing all the side missions, and collecting all the avatar gear. The main game is longer than Generations so that’s a step forward at-least. And may I just ask for all the people complaining that the game is too short, would you like Sonic Team to bring back the werehog? Honestly just think for a second. The reason why we got the werehog in Sonic Unleashed was because Sonic Team feared that the game would be criticized for being too short with the boost gameplay alone. So I just want to say, please be careful what you wish for, or in this case, please be careful what you complain about.
Most levels will probably average you 2-3 minutes on a good run. To some however this may seem short but people have to keep in mind that this is a Boost-Sonic game. Sonic moves so fast that the levels can only last for so long. Not to mention that being able to take multiple routes to get to the goal is a staple in the Sonic franchise which understandably cuts from the length of the levels. So whatever floats your boat. If you prefer long and linear levels then Forces will disappoint you, but if you prefer shorter levels with multiple routes then you’ll enjoy the levels Forces has to offer)
The major selling point of this game that is supposed to set it apart from previous Sonic games is the fact that instead of fighting against Eggman to protect the world, Eggman in this game has already won. He’s already taken over the planet, Sonic is captured, and Sonic friends are desperately trying to salvage the 99.9% of the world that they’ve lost. But the problem is that we don’t see Eggman conquer the world, we are just told that he did. After the cutscene when Sonic is defeated by Infinite, we are told through text that 6-months have passed and Eggman has taken over the planet and are later told through dialogue between Knuckles and Silver that Sonic was captured and taken prisoner by Eggman. This was a really disappointing transition for me, it's almost as if the animation team wasn’t given enough time to animate scenes of Eggman’s robots taking control of the planet, the rise of the Eggman empire, and the capture of Sonic which should have been the focus of the game story-wise.
However despite my complaints about the story, at the end of the day, Sonic Forces is a cartoony platformer game. A Story with animated cutscenes and voiced dialogue isn’t needed or expected, it’s really just icing on the cake and I respect Sonic Team for taking a risk and trying to have Sonic deal with a serious plot again, so I do not count story nitpicks as a real con against this game. If we can have games like Mario Odyssey with no plot at all get 10/10s then Sonic should be criticised for plot either.)
I found this very disappointing and felt that the game gave off a bit of false advertisement.
All of Modern Sonic’s bosses feel the same. Classic Sonic and the Avatar character each only get one boss aside from the final boss.
Nowhere near as bad as Sonic 4 but I thought that Classic Sonic felt too heavy in comparison to Mania. And occasionally when I would create sharp movements or land from a jump, it felt as if the character would continue moving in a specific direction when I want him or hear to move in another direction making platforming and dodging attacks more difficult than it should be at times.
Unless you already have momentum going prior to jumping, your character won’t be able to move much in the air. This reminded me of the Sonic 06 jumping physics except now you have to be facing your target for the homing attack lock-on icon to appear which resulted in me falling to my death or leaving me unable to attack an enemy making me vulnerable for attack a few times, where if this was a game like Sonic Heroes, I would have been able to execute my homing attack just fine.
Overall, I’d give the game an 8/10, Sonic Forces has it’s problems but I definitely believe that it is a good game

This game... where do I start? Well my first Total war game was Empire, I only played the online battles with my friend... than came Shogun 2 were I tried my hand at the main campaign but didn't get very far... now enter Rome 2 (Which I bought when it was Emperor Edition) and now I'm playing it more than the others. Why? It's a good, fun game.
Now I'm seeing a lot of people complain about bugs and how it's still extremely buggy... I'd like to know what they really are playing as I've only see a few bugs in my play time and nothing that actually made me me angry... things like during a siege I had 1 ladder unit kinda do what it wanted... I still won the battle with no issues so it didn't bother me... I've not seen any crashes and the online works just fine... Anyways, to the pro's and con's list!
Pros:
-It's quite beautiful. On my laptop I can run it at ultra and it looks really nice both in the campaign and during battle.
-The setting is my favorite time period so I'm instantly enthralled in the campaings
-The town building is simple yet allow for some important decisions. It's also nice to see your city get bigger when improving.
-Sound design is great, some people say the soundtrack sucks but whatever, I really like it.
-The map is really quite massive streaching from Britania all the way to places I don't quite know... but it's big.
-Multiplayer Campaign... This is my favorite feature as it allows me to work with friend who will help me actually beat the game... I have ADD so get bored quickly...
-Many campains to play through with just the base game alone
con's
-Yes... blood is a DLC even though it was in Shogun 2... but I found that I rarely am close enough to notice it... I'm busy actually giving orders to my units...
-The fighting is a bit bugyy and looks bad sometimes, more of a mosh pit soldiers actually fighting
-Community sucks... yeah at least from my stance it does, I've asked for some help and they often reply with "Go play Rome 1 instead of this garbage"... so that's a black mark
-Diplomacy is a bit... off. Having someone call war against you who has 1 city against you (3 cities) an ally (2 cities) and another ally (2 cities) is a bit dumb...
-Tehcnology could have been fleshed out quite a bit I think
-Lacks some of the historical insight that were in games like medieval 2 (Only played a few minutes of it but loved it for it's history!!)
TL;DR: Overall this game is really good if you like Total War games and love Roman History. As for the DLC they have... it's not a big deal as the women of mars things is a lot like the blood DLC... if you look close enough you see it, but it doesn't really make a difference normally... There's enough people to play as in the base game that paying 8 bucks for a bunch of new places isn't that bad... in my opinion... This game is fun espeically when playing online campaign with a friend. The theme and setting is great and feels great to play.

Broforce is an intense side scrolling shoot'em up game.
The game starts off with a terrorist threat, but that’s only one part of the evil enemies you will encounter in the game.
To fight of the evil in the game you use different characters that are called bro’s. Each bro is influenced and inspired by film characters. Every bro has a unique set of attacks and sometimes a special ability.
Every mission you start off with a random bro and every bro you save during missions are randomly generated. This variety keeps things interesting during this hectic shooter.
The game features a campaign mode which you can run solo or with others in co-op or multiplayer.
The mission maps are fully destructible with gaps, explosives, falling stones and other threats. So you need to keep an eye out on the environment.
For a challenge you can try the other difficulty, community created levels or your own level if you like to make them.
All in all the game is a lot of fun to play solo or with friends.

Lots of people are comparing this game to Ragnarok Online (RO), but Tree of Savior is actually more similar to another famous IMC game, Granado Espada (GE). The same group of people worked on all three games, and it shows.
While its art and class design is meant to invoke RO, the teams system, item shop, megaphones, EXP cards, map design, audio, and even costumes are basically copied from GE.
As with RO and GE, Tree of Savior was created by a talented team with big ambitions, powerful artistic vision, but poor quality control. These are the type of creative folks who have great ideas, but don't know how to package or deliver their product professionally. This has resulted in rough launches and patchwork gameplay (especially questing) during the early days of all three games.
That being said, RO and GE both went on to be very successful MMOs. If there is one thing that could doom ToS, it's the excessive restrictions for non-premium players.
Despite its shortcomings, the game is clearly a labor of love with much content to explore. If out of nothing but nostalgia, I would still recommend giving Tree of Savior a try.

The game is more or less described on the steam page. You play as a Junior Officer in a cavalry regiment in a fictional world resembling ours in the early to mid 1800's, but where Germany has apparantly been replaced by an Elven Nation, and the rest of Europe appears united against, what I deduce to be Slavic nations.
There even appears to be some reference to Colonial America in some of the provinces held by the European-Equavialent nation.
The technological is prior to the invention of revolvers and proper artillery platforms.
The game features minor magic - all nobility in the game are referred to as "bane blooded" who have the innate ability that they are sensitive to magic. Some can even cast spells through runes, used for healing and killing on the battle field, as well as forging magical weapons and armor.
Banecrafted armor and weapons are very rare in the world though - reserved for particularly elite soldiers and Knights of the Red order.
Banecasters are also fairly rare - only on few occasions do they become relevant in the actual game.

Whoever praises Fallout 3 and New Vegas, should have firstly played this game.
I'm not saying this game is better than Fallout 3, I'm just saying that this title is the real post-apocalyptic FPS experience.
So many years have passed and now I've played this game also on Steam, and I must say that even if time passes by, this game never gets old.
Let's start with the main point of this game: gameplay.
Not considering the RPG style inventory and quest system, the ballistic of weapons is something you don't see often so well made in an FPS.
After handling well a weapon, you acquire the skill to use it right, and every weapon feels different.
Enemy's AI is another great point in favor: they always know how to catch you the right way, disregarding of the place, and their movements are always smart and unpredictable.
I think this AI is smartest than F.E.A.R.'s one, and probably the best I've ever seen in an FPS.
Graphics are very good, even if a bit dated. The entire zones are fully explorable and they are wonderfully designed.
Sounds of weapons feel like having a gun in your hand and when you get hit, you can feel it on your skin.
The overall experience is something very unique considering standard FPS games on the market.
For the bad part: the game lack most of the fundamental tweaks, like fast travelling (yeah, this is pretty boring, especially because enemies respawn), the possibility to repair your equipment, time limited side quests and a fixed and low limit for carriage (I know it's "realistic" that your character can carry just 50 Kg, but it's a videogame and it's boring).
The very bad of this game is the plot [SPOILER ALLERT]:
Yeah, there may be some cool moments and twists, but the story is pretty stupid (go there, then there, then I need you to take that and carry it on there...) and the only narrative value is the way it let you know the story behind the catastrophe, but as a character based story, it's not so interesting.
I think this is one of these games that should be definitely be played by every FPS lover, after Half-Life and F.E.A.R.

Another fantastic piece of work by Supergiant, the spiritual sucessor to Bastion does its predecessor justice. While the story is slightly more simple than the story in Bastion, the art direction, sound, music, and gameplay are all just as good, if not better. The game's core mechanic is the turn() function (ability) that you posess. Turn() allows you to freeze time and plan out your next move. It may not be the most original mechanic, but it works very well in this game.
In addition, each of your attacks and abilities (called functions) can be used either as a primary attack, an upgrade to a primary attack, or a passive boost. For example, one ability, bounce(), when used as a main attack, fires a shot that ricochets between enemies. However, when applied as a boost to another ability, it causes that attack to have a possibility of ricocheting between enemies. Or it might reduce that attack's cooldown time, depending on the attack. Of course, it can also be used as a passive bonus, in this case granting the player a regenerating shield that reflects a single shot. As you can immagine, the number of possible combinations is enormous.
Also, do yourself a quick favor. See the button that says "Transistor + soundtrack"? Yeah? Good. Click that one. Because this game has some incredible music. I mean, the main character is a singer. It's like Darren Korb is rubbing how amazing of a composer he is in our faces. Don't believe me?
.

Well, that was playthrough #1. After doing all challenges, listening to and reading everything I possibly could and only once having to use the "Retry" function, Steam tells me I have 7 hours under my belt.
The following is my critique of the game, ignoring the New Game+ mode (for now). While I do reference Supergiant Games' first title, Bastion, quite heavily, the points I make should also be accessible to players who have yet to play Bastion (seriously, get that game). While I try to be objective, some sections of this review are highly subjective; the game suffers from virtually no technical (and thus "objectively objective") faults and what I point out as bad may appear as "creative" or "challenging" or just "different" to others.
Please refer to additional reviews and critiques before you decide whether or not you want to buy Transistor.
If you want to avoid even those, skip to the conclusion section at the end.
Transistor is an isometric tactical Action-RPG with a linear story.
First of all, the things I was happy with -
:
-
, obviously. Darren Korb and Ashley Barret did an amazing job and the music leaves little to be desired. It's a different style than Bastion's soundtrack, so, of course, whether you like it more or less than Bastion's is a matter of taste, but it is very atmospheric and carries the game together with
-
. No surprises there. The music may be the soul of the game but the expert narration (and fantastic voice acting) are its heart.
-
. The world of Transistor is original and colorful; the "feel" is the same as in Bastion but it has a distinctly different theme; the result is stellar.
-
. The ability to collect a variety of skills, all of them with different effects, depending on whether they are active, passive or modifying an active skill, makes for some interesting (and tough) choices as to how you want to play. Not everything works well but you can try everything.
Now to the things that I was less impressed with -
:
-
. Sadly, it is nowhere near as great as (I) expected. Precision is not its strong point and those who were hoping for Frozen Synapse levels of refined tactical combat will be disappointed, as will be those that expected a slick Hack&Slash. Some sections are almost impossible to beat with only one of the modes but intelligent use of both does not help in all situations and more often than not (especially later on), you can find yourself cheesing the game in less-than-fun ways when you encounter fights that are frustrating enough that you'd like to skip them, due to issues with
-
. Few enemies are balls-to-the-wall hard, but many are insanely annoying. Having to deal with enemies who have the ability to cloak themselves (which, somehow, also makes them invulnerable) without the player having any way to disrupt this cloak (other than waiting for them to deal damage to you) or to damage them in cloak makes several mid- and endgame sections downright infuriating. Especially if said enemies are rapidly regenerating health. Several enemy attacks cannot be avoided and the player's ability to heal himself is extremely limited, making the whole combat system less a matter of skill and more one of a proper choice of abilities (which is where the combat system is at odds with its RPG elements); due to this, some fights (especially boss fights) and victories are anything but satisfying and can leave a bitter aftertaste.
-
. While Bastion had only a few characters with little depth but strong-enough features to make them relatable and carry the story, Transistor has almost none. "The voice" is the strongest one by far but remains a lot more blank than Bastion's narrator. The female lead, Red, has even less than that (or Bastion's Kid). The human antagonists are hardly characterized at all and what remains is a faceless menace that changes the world around you and attacks you constantly... and yet fails to really make you feel threatened.
-
. Where Bastion's story was about a simple goal for most of the game (restoring the Bastion), Transistor lacks direction. You feel like a tourist who is being guided from one landmark to the other without any drive or ultimate goal behind it, which becomes even more apparent at the game's conclusion. The plot works with local tension only (i.e. short-term obstacles and goals). The lack of strong characters makes it hard to build-up a bad guy and the pace at which the city changes and the threat swallows it leaves no time to make you care about it or its inhabitants. Unlike the Bastion, you didn't build it with your own two hands and, despite being in a city, you never get a chance to interact with anybody. This leaves the romance as its only redeeming factor... except it isn't either, because the main characters' interaction is very one-sided. The sad truth is: Transistor's story is forgetable.
And finally -
:
-
. While the design is great, you hardly see anything of the city (or the rest of the world). Vistas are few and far between and the game doesn't feature any maps or background information that allows you to see the "big picture". Sadly, this devaluates most of the ingame biographies and what lore there is because it becomes that much harder to relate to for their lack of context.
-
. It certainly isn't Mass Effect 3 levels of terrible but, frankly, it makes no sense. The game's conclusion renders pretty much the entire hero's journey pointless and I have to ask what motivation Red had in the first place. That isn't to say that it isn't beautiful in several ways but nonetheless highly disappointing if you were hoping for a well-written story.
-
. From what I have heard from several people, 7 hours is not a good time. It is quite possible to beat the game in under 5 hours. New Game+ may add replay value here, if you truly enjoyed the combat system and don't share my gripes with it, but if you don't, it leaves the question of value for your money. And, regardless of New Game+, my impression is that the game tries to do too much in too little time - Introducing you to a world, threatening this world and making you its involuntary savior has worked before... but it doesn't work for Transistor.
(Or: tl;dr)
Transistor is a good attempt to solve a task that was almost unsolvable - To create the next "Bastion". Design-wise, it is every bit as strong and a true treat for the eyes and ears, with some great ideas on how to keep progression interesting and your game experience unique.
But a closer look reveals a system that tries to combine real-time and tactical combat and, as a result, is the master of neither. The beautiful world that seems so full and interesting is a facade, a mere stage decoration with too little behind it to keep it from falling over when leaned on, leaving a lot of the ingame lore without sufficient context. And while music and narration are great, they cannot hide the fact that the play itself is boring and the characters forgotten as soon as they leave the stage.
Supergiant Games gave their game and its world too little time to introduce themselves and captivate you and the result is all the more disappointing for it.
Nevertheless, I recommend Transistor for the interesting experience it is; you may find the combat system and story, despite their flaws, more satisfying than I did and, either way, you do not want to miss out on the soundtrack and Logan Cunningham's sexy voice. Supergiant Games deserves the money for a brave attempt, even if this attempt falls short.
If you aren't dying to play Transistor right now, pick it up once it goes on sale.

3 hours into the game and this is my review:
It is a very difficult game to play, just like it's predecessor, Bastion, and can be confusing at first as you are placed in a situation that makes players ponder what had just occurred to make this situation happen.
But as you travel, you will realize how beautiful this game is: the soundtracks, the voices, the art work, the city, the combat, the playstyle, and much much more.
I most of the time enjoyed the difficult combat, giving me hard times and times to even stop and think how to get past a sticky situation using the "turn()" ability. The challenges in this game also excites me as there are ways to make your playtrough much easier and masterful at each battle. This game, just like Bastion, is a great game.
There are some parts that slightly frusterates me in this game which is the short random lags (but I will blame my computer for that since it isn't really a gaming computer), and sometimes, the "jaunt()" ability can't cut corners, but it's an opinion.
Overall, this is a great game and if you can get past the difficult battles, you will really enjoy the story of this game as I have.

It's got a neat concept. You are building a village, and when you buy objects to generate currency it builds buildings for you on the screen. When you reach a point you can ally yourself with a certain faction featuring your favorite fantasy character (orcs, demons, etc). The idea is that in idle games you often want to reset and start over the entire process of collection money and buildings from scratch, but the restart process has more variety as you can now get different buildings and ally with a different faction. There's also a mana system for the powerups rather than having cooldowns, and thematically that is a really cool change to see.
Other than that the little nitpicks i made it's a perfectly acceptable idle game. Definately give it a go.

So I grew up on Rome: Total War and I can say that this whole game, without a doubt, is a massive improvement from that.
Some would say the building system for the campaign maps is awful, but I find it adds a new area of strategy. In Rome Total War, the original, you could build anything anywhere. The new version of this requires you to plan it out more as there is limited space. Religious buildings, public order buildings, military camps, and so on. Whatever you add changes the way you treat the region.
Combat got a massive vamp in quality since the days of RTW. It still keeps the same feel, but adds unique animations for combat. Then there's the new battle types. In RTW you could only do land battles such as sieges, open field combat, river crossings, and ambushes. In Rome II, you can not only do these with improved quality, but you can also use naval units! Added to the list of battle types, naval control really spices up the strategy. If there's a city that's undefended, you can raid it with a fleet, shoot them from the sea and land ships of melee troops to attack the town. If you have a sieging army advancing on your city, your ship mounted artillery can wreak havoc on the enemy before they start to assault your walls. Of course, there are the usual naval battles where a fleet clashes against another fleet!
Keep in mind there are some glitches that happen from time to time. I once saw a ship land next to another and the second one circled it entirely (cutting through land) before beaching itself as well. There was also the occasional until that couldn't function when it was placed on a wall and told to move somewhere else. Sometimes your artillery shoots at an enemy that's so spread out that it shoots at an empty space.
Overall tho, I would reccomend this game if you're a huge fan of strategy games, realtime and turn based.
