I haven't spent the most time on this game yet (yes. YET) but I can say this will be a very time consuming purchase I've made.
To start of I'd like to touch the ongoing discussion about things like "Do not think of this as Skyrim" or "This is SO different from Skyrim" ... it's really not.
[Stay for the end, there's a contra-argument for the game xD]
I mean - you have the typical MMO elements like people everywhere and interaction with them. You have dungeons for groups, you probably have PvP (haven't gotten into that yet), you have guilds and you can level in groups with your friends. But other than that it feels very much like a typical Elder Scrolls game. You have quests (ye, also an MMO feature but not mainly), the gathering is similar, the crafting is somewhat similar, the way you can just ... run around on the Map and explore, loot caves, just derp around and do your thing; rob a whole city, kill NPCs all day long, noone's gonna stop you except the law and soldiers who'll be on your butt for the rest of your game.
The differences for me are the combat + ability stuff and the way you interact with NPCs. You don't have as many interaction options because sure - it's an MMO, you don't have all day to read through 500 topics the NPC has to offer (speaking from Morrowind-experience there). But all in all it doesn't feel much different. So in general I'd agree with "This isn't Skyrim" ... but not with "It's totally different from Skyrim/Oblivion/Morrowind".
... alright let's begin the actual review not that that's out of the way.
I love the graphical design. It's a trip down nostalgia lane for me wherever I go because I remember little things from Morrowind or Oblivion like Urnes, Monsters, Landscapes, Armor pieces, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ordinates heck even the booktitles. Oh and the game is not short of lore, really not. Books everywhere, lore everywhere and a main story I am almost following reading-wise (I'm a bit lazy in that regard with MMO's)
The game seems very well optimized for computers. I am basically playing on a potato right now but except for some crashes because my graphic card just can't take it I have barely any issues with the game, it runs very smooth. The sound design is great, recording the dialogues with NPCs must have taken years because there's just SO.MANY.
I have yet to test dungeons and get further than level 15 but all I can say for now is that I really, reaaaaally enjoy the game.
There is one downside to the game though and it's one that might be important to you if you are thinking about buying this game - it's the group-function for leveling and questing.
The game feels a bit like it's more for heavy solo-MMO-fans because the quest system is a bit messy at the moment. I like that you can share quests with your group but actually doing quests with the group ain't that much fun if your playstyles differ. Because everyone in the group has to do everything in the quest on their own. You are basically just soloing the quest ... together. If you finish one part of the quest, your group still has to do it themselves, nothing counts for both of you and it's kind of hurting grouping a lot because you basically either have to be very in synch or just ... split up for a lot of times to follow your own style of playing and speed. If your friend is a heavy lore fan, reading every dialogue and you just want to get the quest done you're in for a long wait.
It's a thing that definitely needs improving. But on the other hand, just aimlessly running around with a friend, stealing stuff, looting and exploring, it's really, REALLY great. Just quests are ... meh.

Like many others, I loved Just Cause 2 and eagerly anticipated Just Cause 3 but was disappointed by what we got. Not that it's a bad game, the core Just Cause gameplay is intact and it's mostly fun, but other than shiny graphics and a few other improvements it's by and large a step backwards from Just Cause 2.
First off, the improvements.
Graphics
Audio
Physics
Multi Tethers
Retractable Tethers
Wingsuit
Rebel Drop - Can order any vehicle (including civilian ones) and don't have to spend money
Epic cave systems and underground bases
Chaos objects on map
New vehicle types, especially the cargo vehicles with working doors
Vehicle controls are significantly improved, especially with a keyboard
Unfortunately, there are also a lot of things JC3 didn't do as well.
Story missions lack interesting set pieces and have some incredibly annoying escort/protect missions
Progression system involving challenges is annoying rather than fun
Many challenges are outright bugged or broken
Random side missions are a waste of time and often incredibly annoying due to the poor AI
AI is atrocious. They switch between clueless idiots and ruthless aimbots that aggresively spawn out of thin air depending on the heat status.
No minimap, health bar, or sprint
Poor movement and aiming controls when on foot
Guns are not balanced and most of them are useless
No weapon/vehicle damage/health upgrades to keep them relevant as the game progresses
Smaller, less interesting world map with a huge amount of empty space on the main island
Significantly less vehicles, and agency style vehicles are only available as overpriced DLC
Leaderboards system adds nothing to the game, but has a mandatory forced login when the game starts up that wastes my time, in addition to an obnoxiously long intro video
Major, potentially gamebreaking bugs still present in the game over a year after release
Overall, this game doesn't really offer anything compelling over JC2. This game is still fun, but the parts that make it fun were done in JC2, and in many cases done better. Given how cheap JC2 is, how well it's held up over the years, and how it's actually more fun than JC3 most of the time, my recommendation is to only get this game if you can get it on sale with a really good discount.

Soooo, Transistor, just finished it first time minutes ago.
Had to write a review for it!
Why?
Because it's good and I want people to know, my thanks to the developpers if you want :)
Didn't played Bastion, but I read it was quite good so i decided to give Transistor a go...
Results:
Graphism are great. I mean, I started gaming on a gameboy... So I remember when photorealism wasn't a thing. Ambiance is important, and here: you can feel the love of the studio for their work. +1
Music is just fan-ta-stic! I'm gonna buy the OST and put it in my MP3 'cos it's just THAT good for me.
Gameplay: the combat system is great and you'll jump from just bashing ennemies to carefully planning your moves in a blink of a eye. Played with a gamepad and it just felt great.
Difficulty: want a good challenge? Yeahhh... That's not a challenge at all, you're not here for that. BUT! The game has his difficulty arranged by steps. Let's say I played 3/4 of the game without dying once and the last 1/4 had some challenge, had to search for the good combo and all... Let's say I'm ok with the softcore ways here, BUT there is a newgame+ which I didn't tested yet, so: I suppose this part has more struggle :)
Story: won't say a thing here, but totaly liked it. The kind of mindf***k story that you travel with and still think about after, plus, it give you urges to redo the game and fully understand what you missed first time. Totally my case here.
Lenght: didn't rushed it, finished it in one sit ==> 6 hours strait. So, yeah, not that long... But will come back for the NG+ as the story and the gameplay are cool and I want to see how they pushed it, I bet the NG+ is a good challenge :)
Plus, it's a 20$ game, not a AAA. Totally ok with that.
Conclusion: yeah, I recommand it. But, why?
Because it's was a great ADVENTURE, developpers made a great work, you can tell, playing it, that they consider gaming like an art, not just like an industry. And that's the kind of game I want to see more of.

Everything I wanted from another Supergiant Games masterpiece. Beautiful art, fun gamplay, captivating soundtrack and narration, and all of it laced with combat that is deep and keeps me coming back for more.
Yes.

I loved Bastion and I love this game even more.
The narrative style is different but still present. The sound track is just as excellent as Bastion's if not more so. The art style is different but just as good. Everything you liked about Bastion is there and just as good, but different.
Except the combat. The actual combat itself is brilliant and rewarding, with thousands of possible ability permutations and lacking the feeling that any one combination beats out the others. All the abilities are useful, all of them fun, and all of them let you tackle each fight in a variety of interesting ways.
Some people have complained about the combat in this game, but their complaints are quite bluntly bewildering to me. While it does get increasingly challenging, and dying can be frustrating, I never had to redo any one fight more than twice, and the game autosaves often.
I have not enjoyed a game this much in a very long time. It is exciting to even talk about. This is Game of the Year - or at the very least the Indie Game of the Year.
For $20 you get around 9 hours of singleplayer content that is brilliantly designed, written, and narrated.
For $10 you get a soundtrack that is around 1 hour, 9 minutes of excellent videogame soundtrack.
In my opinion you do yourself a disservice not purchasing this game.

Alien: Isolation is a genuinely amazing game with an interesting take on the 'Survival Horror' genre.
The game itself is beautiful, and is pretty well optimised, on top of this you can get the modified settings to make the game look even better.
Most of the models and textures are also amazing, I can't think of any specific examples but some smaller unimportant textures can be a crappy resolution but overall the graphics are fantastic.
As all horror games should have, Alien: Isolation has an amazing atmosphere, you have the classic pitch black rooms with a flickering light as the only source of light and well lit rooms. You can often see out of a window and see the true size of Sevastopol station. You can be a fairly dark area and have your motion sensor bleeping to inform you of the incoming Alien or the cold narration of the Working Joe's as you murder them and they just keep coming towards you. The game is very immersive with a fairly minimal HUD on the most difficulties. Overall an amazing aspect of the game.
The difficulties are..
For the most part they're self explanatory, novice is very easy and from there they get slightly harder with reduced items, harder hitting enemies and a smarter deadlier Alien. The only significant step up is Nightmare mode.. Nightmare mode is extremely difficult, here are the changes:
- The motion tracker is broken
--Distorted Signal (goes offline for a few seconds every 2 seconds)
--Gives unreliable information
- Authentic Flamethrower
--Fuel burns faster (so you run out bloody fast)
--Fuel is rare
- Reduced Resources
--No ammo drops from enemies
--Fewer items to scavenge
- Less game feedback
--No health bar
--No ammo counter
--No flashlight indicator
- More Dangerous Enemies
--Androids are ~1 hit = RIP
--Survivors will detect you easier and will often 1 hit you
- More hostile environment
--Map system offline
--Harder hacking
- Ultimate alien
--More aggressive
--Adapts faster
--NO SECOND CHANCES
In nightmare mode you actually find yourself struggling to do an easy area on another difficulty eg. facehugger sections, since you have such little ammo. You also have to rely much more on stealth abilities and using the environment to your advantage. Getting caught by an android means certain death - which in the synthetic area where your weapons are removed is extremely difficult since you can't use the EMP bomb to stun them. During my playthrough I only ever had one stun baton so use that sparingly.
You play as Amanda Ripley-McClaren, daughter of Ellen Ripley from the Alien film franchise. (Watch the first Alien film, for one it's a bloody good film and secondly, it's a little bit relevant to this game.. If you haven't seen it then prepare for a
..) Amanda was just ten years old when her mother disappeared following the loss of the Nostromo in deep space.
Now for a quick refresher of what happened in the Alien film.. In 2122 the US Commercial starship
was summoned to LV-426, a desolate planetoid, where an unknown warning signal was being broadcast from The Derelict (The port prong on The Derelict measure 161.6 meters in length and the starboard prong 174.3 meters. The craft is 116.6 meters wide and 61.0 meters wide between the starboard and port prongs. Not essential to known, but a fun little fact.) - The company behind sending the USCSS Nostromo was Weyland-Yutani. The Nostromo's crew, including Ellen Ripley, investigate LV-426 to discover the remains of the ships pilot (An Engineer or 'Space Jockey' - which is a whole other topic, look into that for yourself) and also a large chamber filled with hundreds of egg like objects. One of the eggs open and a Face Hugger latches onto the face of a member of the crew, rendering him unconscious - the other members of the crew then proceed to break quarantine to bring him back aboard the Nostromo. The Facehugger cannot be removed once it has attached itself to its victim as it has acidic blood, preventing it from being cut off and any attempt to remove it with force causes it to tighten its grip around the victims neck. The facehugger supplies the victim with oxygen to keep them alive as it implants an egg, hence the victim becomes the host of a perfect killing machine. Once the egg is implanted the facehugger detaches and runs away, dying off. The crewman wakes up, seemingly fine, shortly after the Alien bursts out of his chest (chestburster phase) and runs off, it rapidly grows to ~8ft and begins murdering the crew. Ripley activates the self destruct sequence on the Nostromo and escapes to be put in hypersleep for 57 years, here Aliens begins.
In 2137 the flight recorder unit of the USCSS Nostromo was recovered and taken to Sevastopol Station, Ripley was informed of this by a
called Samuels, who is under the employ of Weyland-Yutani, Ripley is employed as an Engineer in the sector where the Nostromo was lost as she wanted answered to what had happened to her Mother. Ripley joined Samuels and the small Weyland-Yutani team being sent to recover the recorder from Sevastopol Station. Ripley and the team travel to Sevastopol on board Captain Verlaine's privately owned ship, The
. When the arrived they discovered that communications with the station where scrambled and hence needed to board the station, with the docking facilities damaged Ripley, Samuels and Taylor, the Weyland-Yutani lawyer, attempted a spacewalk to the station but following an explosion and some falling space debris this failed and Ripley was separated from the other two.
After some exploring you'll find the Maintenance Jack and then you'll meet a very friendly man called Axel, who is here as a tutorial as sorts - teaching you what a vent is, what a flash light is, what getting shot at is and what getting stabbed in the chest by an Alien looks like in a very beautiful cut scene looks like. When you eventually reach the Lorenz SysTech Spire you gain the .375 Revolver and the Security Access Tuner - the hacking tool of the game. Emily is Away is a unique game in many ways. The aesthetics and visual style are immediately captivating and familiar by way of utilizing Windows XP + AIM (R.I.P) to capture a simplistic art style. It immediately grabs your attention where a lot of other games wouldn't. The fact that you get to pick your own screenname and a new icon for each year is a nice touch as well. And depending on the different screennames you pick for yourself, you can get even more icons! It's very cute and nice, even if it's weird to be giving myself a Binding of Isaac avatar for a game that starts out in 2002. And you can customize your text color and background, though so far I haven't found any unique dialog from it like the screenshots promise.
There are two central characters in the game: yourself (who you can name whoever you want, yay ambiguity and self-inserting!) and Emily, the titular character. The game explores the relationship (of sorts) that you two have over the years, from senior year in high school to the end of college. As you two talk, you explore the friendship you have and some of the unsaid feelings between the two of you. It's nothing new or revolutionary, but the way it's presented certainly would hit close to home for a decent number of people.
A really nice thing that the game does right is showing you the thought process of your character. They typo and make some mistakes, going back and deleting various words or phrases, or even whole messages that get deleted due to their intimacy and emotions. It shows how your character wants to present themselves best for Emily and show off their best side. The different choices you can make that decide different things your character does (like the music they like or the school they go to) let you form a (sort-of) idealized character of your own as you talk to Emily. It's a very neat concept... if it mattered.
Ultimately, nothing you do in this game matters. All those choices you're given lead to the same outcome eventually. The game promises "A dialogue decision-based branching narrative.", but when all of the dialog ultimately leads to an ending that just... happens, it just feels like a waste of time. While I have no problems with the story itself and the way it gets presented, it doesn't help the fact that the story, the choices, and even the character development feels so bare and... so dull. And the absolute worst thing an emotionally-driven game like this could be is dull. I don't ever feel like I'm in this world I'm building, and Emily is a close friend of mine; it just feels like I'm chatting with an AI once every so often.
The game is also short. For free games that can be a good thing, and a game like this also can benefit from short playthroughs. The downside is that, due to the fact that this game has no real choices of sorts, there's hardly any replay value. You can choose different paths to go. You can play one certain part and have Emily be annoyed at you, then play that part another way and have her be indifferent. But it just really doesn't make a difference. There's no diversity, nothing to make the game exciting, and because of that, the game feels like it plods and drags itself along in its roughly hour-long playthrough. One thing that'd probably help is talking to all of those other friends in your friends list. There's no incentive to look at their profiles or see how they change because, well, why would you? You can only talk to Emily. It feels like fluff to make the game a bit more full.
Was I affected? Ultimately not. I've been in this situation before (though it didn't last over a number of years), and a couple points in the game did sting me a bit, being out of a relationship now. But they're fleeting moments in a game that almost feels like it doesn't want you to keep playing, Certainly, the fact that so many people have felt so strongly and receptive towards the game makes me think I'm in the minority. And it's free, so you can't go wrong with the price! Give it a shot yourself. You don't really have much to lose. However, given what the game has, what it promises, and how its execution handles, I can't recommend it.

Total War Rome 2, one of the many games in the Total War series. Shall we have a look and see if it’s any good?
First of all, the gameplay, seeing as that is what you're buying it for. The gameplay is solid. You can have a lot of units doing a lot of different things at once and, so long as your PC fits in with the specs, it will run fine. That is, unless you are online, but we will come back to that later. Units are well balanced in the sense of a sword unit vs a sword unit will fight head on for a long time if left alone, which one wins will depend on the quality of the unit (essentially the cost in the select unit panel) and how many battles that unit has fought in and become experienced. For example, a Gold experience Roman legion will lay waste to most of anything, unless it is up against a unit which specialises in killing them (For example, Pike's are best for killing horse units and spear are best for the front line to form a shield wall).
The online however, which is what many people have bought this for, is awful. You will almost always end up playing against someone halfway across the world with a ping as high as the Empire State and it will look like a slow-mo Michael Bay film. This is cool to look at, but becomes soul destroying after the first couple of games putting many people off permanently. As for me, I have both Rome 2 and Attila and they both suffer from this so much me and my friends haven't touched the games in ages (In fact I think we may have in fact uninstalled them).
As for the DLC, it is simply daylight robbery. They charge you money for factions that should’ve been in the game in the first place. Attila does this too. One of the most anticipated factions, the Spartans, are DLC so prepare to have to fork out more money for something that should’ve been included anyway. If any of you reading this are familiar with Fallout 3 and its DLC, this is not like that, this is simply stuff that has been ripped from the game and they attempt to sell it to you in pieces. It is a disgusting practice that should not be tolerated by anyone and, if you do get this game, please for the love of future gaming DO NOT BUY THE DLC!
Overall, the game is good. The campaign is fun and will keep you busy for hours. The online is broken and buggy but if you’re willing to deal with this then it can be fun when everything works right and clicks into place. Would I say it’s worth £30? ABSOLUTELY NOT! I got this game ages ago on sale for £8. Look elsewhere or wait for the sale. Apart from that, I hope you enjoy it.

If you're looking for the greatest Sonic game of all time, this isn't it. That doesn't, however, make it a bad game.
Playing this game, I get the feeling SEGA is actually trying this time, adding a new gameplay style (The Avatar) that, on it's own merit, is pretty fun!
Modern Sonic plays as you would expect, there's not much new going on there, a boost-heavy Temple Runner, and Classic Sonic plays like he did in Generations, but the camera feels better and his new Dropdash move helps make it feel less clunky making him surprisingly fun to play.
The Avatar stands out, as you can completely change the path and strategy you take depending on your wispon, but, as with any sonic game, you quickly learn what the best routes are through repeated playthroughs of specific levels, which you'll be doing a lot of if you want to unlock every avatar clothing item. Challenges like 'Get S Rank in Level 8' and 'Beat Level 6 in x seconds' incentivize you to keep playing and get better, as well as the Daily missions and SOS challenges, where you either play with a rental Avatar or have to find them in the stage.
Finally, the Duo Stages, where you play as both Modern Sonic and the Avatar, could be the best part of the game, as you essentially have both movesets at your disposal, allowing for more paths and more options.
The only major gripe I have with this game is that Modern Sonic, when not running at 90 mph in a straight line like he's supposed to, controls like a rolling bag of bricks making it hard to jump up even simple staircases, noticable most in Egg Gate where there are staircases in both 2D and 3D segments. It'd work best if he controlled like he did in Adventure 1 until he hits a certain speed.
Not an AMAZING Sonic game, certainly doesn't compare to Mania, but not the bad one that everyone's making it out to be. It's an alright Sonic game, and I can see myself continuing to play this, at least for a little while.

I haven't spent the most time on this game yet (yes. YET) but I can say this will be a very time consuming purchase I've made.
To start of I'd like to touch the ongoing discussion about things like "Do not think of this as Skyrim" or "This is SO different from Skyrim" ... it's really not.
[Stay for the end, there's a contra-argument for the game xD]
I mean - you have the typical MMO elements like people everywhere and interaction with them. You have dungeons for groups, you probably have PvP (haven't gotten into that yet), you have guilds and you can level in groups with your friends. But other than that it feels very much like a typical Elder Scrolls game. You have quests (ye, also an MMO feature but not mainly), the gathering is similar, the crafting is somewhat similar, the way you can just ... run around on the Map and explore, loot caves, just derp around and do your thing; rob a whole city, kill NPCs all day long, noone's gonna stop you except the law and soldiers who'll be on your butt for the rest of your game.
The differences for me are the combat + ability stuff and the way you interact with NPCs. You don't have as many interaction options because sure - it's an MMO, you don't have all day to read through 500 topics the NPC has to offer (speaking from Morrowind-experience there). But all in all it doesn't feel much different. So in general I'd agree with "This isn't Skyrim" ... but not with "It's totally different from Skyrim/Oblivion/Morrowind".
... alright let's begin the actual review not that that's out of the way.
I love the graphical design. It's a trip down nostalgia lane for me wherever I go because I remember little things from Morrowind or Oblivion like Urnes, Monsters, Landscapes, Armor pieces, the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ordinates heck even the booktitles. Oh and the game is not short of lore, really not. Books everywhere, lore everywhere and a main story I am almost following reading-wise (I'm a bit lazy in that regard with MMO's)
The game seems very well optimized for computers. I am basically playing on a potato right now but except for some crashes because my graphic card just can't take it I have barely any issues with the game, it runs very smooth. The sound design is great, recording the dialogues with NPCs must have taken years because there's just SO.MANY.
I have yet to test dungeons and get further than level 15 but all I can say for now is that I really, reaaaaally enjoy the game.
There is one downside to the game though and it's one that might be important to you if you are thinking about buying this game - it's the group-function for leveling and questing.
The game feels a bit like it's more for heavy solo-MMO-fans because the quest system is a bit messy at the moment. I like that you can share quests with your group but actually doing quests with the group ain't that much fun if your playstyles differ. Because everyone in the group has to do everything in the quest on their own. You are basically just soloing the quest ... together. If you finish one part of the quest, your group still has to do it themselves, nothing counts for both of you and it's kind of hurting grouping a lot because you basically either have to be very in synch or just ... split up for a lot of times to follow your own style of playing and speed. If your friend is a heavy lore fan, reading every dialogue and you just want to get the quest done you're in for a long wait.
It's a thing that definitely needs improving. But on the other hand, just aimlessly running around with a friend, stealing stuff, looting and exploring, it's really, REALLY great. Just quests are ... meh.

I like building and crafting games. I like Factorio just for that. The fact that you can build your own factory on an alien planet to prepare it for human life is fun.
This game is in early access and I bought it before it was available on steam. This has a lot of stuff to figure out when you start playing and there is a lot of things happening at the same time.
You start as usual by gathering resources to set up your first production line. You also need to start to plan ahead. Think about defenses and research. This game knows enemies which will attack you at some point and can be overwhelmingly powerful if you lack the proper defenses. It could result in starting over from scratch.
The game has a fun learning curve. I started out by building my production lines. When the first resources were automated, I felt content with the results. But then the next automation issue rises. The next production line, which needs more resources and more stuff to be automated as well. And the defense needs to be managed. How to get sufficient power? How to put your production lines in order so you have room to expand? How to get that one or two resources from place A to B without the need of tons and tons of conveyor belts? How do you organize your logistics, defenses and layout of your factory? It’s all that and much more. Start small and expand your factory empire. Keep on building and in search of new resource locations.
It’s a fun game if you’re into automation, building, crafting and base defense games. Who knows what future content is coming to Factorio. There are lots of ideas and I hope the devs will keep on adding stuff and ways to make a hell of an end game.

This game is honestly incredible. It is easy to work out, but works so well with the main mechanic not being the game's difficulty, but your efficiency. Without an efficient layout, the game becomes a lot more difficult,as you have to make workarounds around problems that you, as a player, created for yourself. It is so satisfying to work out the solution to a problem, and to get to see your new conveyor belt start to move items into your crafting system.
For this reason, I would reccomend you go in blind, and dont use any high efficiency templates you find on the internet. This will remove part of the games challenge for you, because as said before, this games difficulty comes from you, not the games overall design. For example, a little bit of thinking early on can make tasks in the distant future much more pleasant to complete. Giving yourself space in this game is key.
It's worth mentioning that I have always liked these "high focus on automation" type games. This is why I have sunk way more time than I would like to admit into Modded Minecraft versions such as Feed the Beast and Tekkit, which both offer high amounts of automation. This meant that the appeal of the game was obvious to me, and I bought it pretty quickly after seeing it for the first time.
All in all, if you like doing things manually, this game isn't for you. But for any of you who like seeing a huge factory of things working together in tandem, I'd reccomend this game highly.

So, first review for Transistor:
The game is pretty, both to the eyes and the ears. Music is solid (beyond solid, it's ♥♥♥♥ing amazing), the art style is gorgeous (sort of what would happen if you took the cel-shaded style of Bastion and crossed it with Art Deco), and the detail is good, but not overdone or too busy.
The gameplay certainly won't be for everyone, but I like it. It's an interesting take on a "tactical" style, and the sheer variety of moves and ways to go about doing solving a fight are pretty keen. Lots of abilities to use, and multiple ways to tweak each ability, not to mention passive buffs. All of this while trying to maximize a cap on how much "boom" you can wade into a fight with at once.
Only problem I have so far: some bugs definitely made it out of their QA department. Hard-crash bugs. This is a bad thing. It's not hitting everyone, and apparently it's better if you play it in Offline Mode on Steam. I'm guessing Supergiant Games is driving for a fix at the moment, because no studio likes handing out game crashes.
So, yeah: I definitely recommend it. It's on the shorter side (haven't beat it yet, but I have a feeling), but beautiful, fun, and has a refreshing take on the mechanics of a platformer. Might just wanna wait a few days for the bugs to get squashed.

I'll start by saying: If you didn't like Bastion, you won't like this at all. The storytelling is very similar. The game is also pretty short, I finished clocking in at 5 hours (did not 100% obviously, you need NG+ to unlock all the different powers and such). But during NG+, I don't see the story changing much. It will be something for only completionists.
But, outside of that I found Transistor to be a great experience. Supergiant delivers again with a chillingly beautiful soundtrack, Darren Korb proving his skills at composing. As a person who loved the art style of Bastion, Transistor does not differ a lot from it with the exception of having more "3d" models as compared to the mostly 2D Bastion, this is most easily seen on your protagonist. The voice acting in the game is top notch, Logan Cunningham giving another near perfect preformance on his character and as the narrator. The enviroments are always beautiful to look at, if a little confusing to navigate at times. The story kept me hooked all the way through the game, with the characters being fleshed out along the way, never feeling generic and always very enthralling.
The combat in the game was a very interesting idea executed well, but not to perfection. It can feel tedious at times and frustrating at others when something just doesn't lineup perfectly. Endgame, you will probably have a combo that will be able to instagib the strongest enemies, you only obstacle being the cooldown bar on your Turn(), which is the main form of combat in Transistor. It's a strategic pause that allows you to set up a bunch of moves that enemies can not react to for the most part. With the backstab mechaninc and the variety of Functions (moves), it has more uses than just being a "VATS" like way of fighting ala Fallout. While recharging, its a game of dodging attacks before you can go back in on the enemies.
Where the combat really shines is how varried you can make your moveset. Each unlockable function is very different than the last, and aren't just moves: they can be infused to combine with other functions (Example: combine the knockup and the pull functions to create an AOE pull) or can be used as passive traits, all taking up some of your power bar, limiting how many functions you can have going.The stories included with each function are a very nice touch that fit the asthetic very well, but unlocking all 3 pieces can be a pain sometimes, since each one will need to occupy each of the 3 uses (passive, upgrade or move) to unlock the full story. Luckily, you only need one battle in each use to unlock each part and with an upgrade station seemingly after every battle you should unlock them all quickly and be able to go back to a more comfortable moveset.
There was only a few spots in the game I would consider "hard", for the most part your average player should be able to blow through their first NG with relative ease. The enemies aren't the brightest, not to say that they are bad, but sometimes they will just stare at you as you recharge behind a wall, not even bothering to try and pressure you to move.
Death is also really hard to achieve, after reaching 0 HP you will get a "free turn()" where you can try and save yourself or win the fight with your what you have left. If you fail and get hit again, you will lose one of your functions socketed. But, since you will usually have 4, chances are you will most likely never lose them all. I have never lost one, so I could not say if they are gone forever, but seeing the difficulty of the game I assume you recover them at the next station. The only time dying will really matter is in the training & challenge areas, where if you die once or twice you may just restart a challenge.
Is it worth playing through?
Is it worth the current $20? That's a bit more debatable, due to it's shorter length. I wouldn't say not to buy it, but the second it goes on sale it is a must grab.

Alien: Isolation is a genuinely amazing game with an interesting take on the 'Survival Horror' genre.
The game itself is beautiful, and is pretty well optimised, on top of this you can get the modified settings to make the game look even better.
Most of the models and textures are also amazing, I can't think of any specific examples but some smaller unimportant textures can be a crappy resolution but overall the graphics are fantastic.
As all horror games should have, Alien: Isolation has an amazing atmosphere, you have the classic pitch black rooms with a flickering light as the only source of light and well lit rooms. You can often see out of a window and see the true size of Sevastopol station. You can be a fairly dark area and have your motion sensor bleeping to inform you of the incoming Alien or the cold narration of the Working Joe's as you murder them and they just keep coming towards you. The game is very immersive with a fairly minimal HUD on the most difficulties. Overall an amazing aspect of the game.
The difficulties are..
For the most part they're self explanatory, novice is very easy and from there they get slightly harder with reduced items, harder hitting enemies and a smarter deadlier Alien. The only significant step up is Nightmare mode.. Nightmare mode is extremely difficult, here are the changes:
- The motion tracker is broken
--Distorted Signal (goes offline for a few seconds every 2 seconds)
--Gives unreliable information
- Authentic Flamethrower
--Fuel burns faster (so you run out bloody fast)
--Fuel is rare
- Reduced Resources
--No ammo drops from enemies
--Fewer items to scavenge
- Less game feedback
--No health bar
--No ammo counter
--No flashlight indicator
- More Dangerous Enemies
--Androids are ~1 hit = RIP
--Survivors will detect you easier and will often 1 hit you
- More hostile environment
--Map system offline
--Harder hacking
- Ultimate alien
--More aggressive
--Adapts faster
--NO SECOND CHANCES
In nightmare mode you actually find yourself struggling to do an easy area on another difficulty eg. facehugger sections, since you have such little ammo. You also have to rely much more on stealth abilities and using the environment to your advantage. Getting caught by an android means certain death - which in the synthetic area where your weapons are removed is extremely difficult since you can't use the EMP bomb to stun them. During my playthrough I only ever had one stun baton so use that sparingly.
You play as Amanda Ripley-McClaren, daughter of Ellen Ripley from the Alien film franchise. (Watch the first Alien film, for one it's a bloody good film and secondly, it's a little bit relevant to this game.. If you haven't seen it then prepare for a
..) Amanda was just ten years old when her mother disappeared following the loss of the Nostromo in deep space.
Now for a quick refresher of what happened in the Alien film.. In 2122 the US Commercial starship
was summoned to LV-426, a desolate planetoid, where an unknown warning signal was being broadcast from The Derelict (The port prong on The Derelict measure 161.6 meters in length and the starboard prong 174.3 meters. The craft is 116.6 meters wide and 61.0 meters wide between the starboard and port prongs. Not essential to known, but a fun little fact.) - The company behind sending the USCSS Nostromo was Weyland-Yutani. The Nostromo's crew, including Ellen Ripley, investigate LV-426 to discover the remains of the ships pilot (An Engineer or 'Space Jockey' - which is a whole other topic, look into that for yourself) and also a large chamber filled with hundreds of egg like objects. One of the eggs open and a Face Hugger latches onto the face of a member of the crew, rendering him unconscious - the other members of the crew then proceed to break quarantine to bring him back aboard the Nostromo. The Facehugger cannot be removed once it has attached itself to its victim as it has acidic blood, preventing it from being cut off and any attempt to remove it with force causes it to tighten its grip around the victims neck. The facehugger supplies the victim with oxygen to keep them alive as it implants an egg, hence the victim becomes the host of a perfect killing machine. Once the egg is implanted the facehugger detaches and runs away, dying off. The crewman wakes up, seemingly fine, shortly after the Alien bursts out of his chest (chestburster phase) and runs off, it rapidly grows to ~8ft and begins murdering the crew. Ripley activates the self destruct sequence on the Nostromo and escapes to be put in hypersleep for 57 years, here Aliens begins.
In 2137 the flight recorder unit of the USCSS Nostromo was recovered and taken to Sevastopol Station, Ripley was informed of this by a
called Samuels, who is under the employ of Weyland-Yutani, Ripley is employed as an Engineer in the sector where the Nostromo was lost as she wanted answered to what had happened to her Mother. Ripley joined Samuels and the small Weyland-Yutani team being sent to recover the recorder from Sevastopol Station. Ripley and the team travel to Sevastopol on board Captain Verlaine's privately owned ship, The
. When the arrived they discovered that communications with the station where scrambled and hence needed to board the station, with the docking facilities damaged Ripley, Samuels and Taylor, the Weyland-Yutani lawyer, attempted a spacewalk to the station but following an explosion and some falling space debris this failed and Ripley was separated from the other two.
After some exploring you'll find the Maintenance Jack and then you'll meet a very friendly man called Axel, who is here as a tutorial as sorts - teaching you what a vent is, what a flash light is, what getting shot at is and what getting stabbed in the chest by an Alien looks like in a very beautiful cut scene looks like. When you eventually reach the Lorenz SysTech Spire you gain the .375 Revolver and the Security Access Tuner - the hacking tool of the game. From here the real game starts with frequent Alien attacks and various attacks by people and synthetics -you'll know when the Working Joe's become a hostile threat following the scene where it brutally murders another survivor called Hughes. However, not all Working Joe's are hostile, so be careful with which ones you attack.
What separates Alien Isolation from the other various Survival Horror games is the way it handles weapons(/items), generally the way these games work is they make you powerless so that hiding is the only option, but in Alien: Isolation you are given a vast array of weapons with a variety of different uses.

Alien Isolation is a solid game. Keeping in mind you have to have a decent computer to run the game as it  requires entry level builds to run without any hitches. When I first saw a product demo played at E3 via on a You Tube re-broadcast, I took into accound the graphic detail,audio clearity and solid mechanics... I knew this was a game I must own. This is not a Call Of Duty game!! Alien Isolation contains F.P.S or (First Person Shooter) elements but is first and foremost is  a "Servivor Horror" game and not a "Run And Gun" title.
317 hours is what I have logged into this game and the high replay value ensures I keep playing. The unpredictable nature of this game keeps it from becomming stale and morphs into a "Grind" in the worst sence of the word. There is 1 thing I would like to see from a future titile release and reads as follows. First after beating the game the upgrades and invitory blueprint slots remain unlocked and open.

Many games tout having choices that effect the story line and even you the player in a profound way. Rarely do they have it so well integrated into the actual gameplay itself; as many have it thrown in a dialogue tree (usually after killing a small country's worth of populace).
has raised the bar on how to combine story and gameplay in a simple to learn manner, while cranking up the tasks and making even the toughest border patrol agent slip-up here and there. It's hard to talk about the mechanics without giving away the story, that is how intertwined they are.
There are many endings as well but I really feel this game shows what games really do well: creating the story through gameplay. If you would have told me in my teenage years that I would fall in love with a game about playing a checkpoint agent at the border of a somewhat Eastern European country where my family depended on my job performance but so did the possible outcome of my country, I wouldn't believe you.
There has never been (and probably won't be again) a game where I have felt some much power and joy pressing a stamp.

80% of my time with playing this game so far: creating my character.
I picked this game up because it was on sale for only 15 dollars at the time. While I may have little time on the pc version, I have 500+ on the consoles, and I can assure you that the game obviously looks better ( and runs better ) on pc.
This game at core is an unforgiving but learnable hack and slash game that does give the player some sense of accomplishment and reward after each important segment of the game, like beating a boss or finally completing your gear set, but later on when all of that becomes common achievements for almost all players, you come across something most players of this game like to call "Fashion Souls." This game certainly does have beauty, in character models and the areas of the game.
I mostly focused on the characters though, because thats what you're going to look at for most of the game, obviously. Fashion in character models can go either way, actually looking good or going out of your way to make your character look as horrendous as possible, but before all that you want your game to look good first. If your computer can handle the highest setting in this game ( which nowadays most people's can ), then look find some mods that improve that further, the graphical ones that I use currently are G.E.M., GeDoSaTo, and ENB (you need GeDoSaTo before ENB). To make getting those mods easier I made a Nexus account at
, which after the graphical enchancers you can get retextures for armor that otherwise does not suit you. If your computer really cant handle this then you can just skip this entirely.
The only important part is actually making your characters face, which if you dont like when your done making it, you have to make a new character entirely. Obviously most of the time you're going to spend your time in the advanced settings, but the basic setting make the base of your character, so you definitely need to editing that first.
When I'm finally at the advanced settings, I have only 1 rule of thumb after I finish with skin color: At the settings that physically change your character, move the dot 5 spaces to the left, then go back to the original spot and move 5 spaces to the right. If I think the changes are too drastic, only move 3, or stop at 2 spaces max. Follow that rule and you will have a good looking character in about... 30 minutes to and hour. Fashion takes dedication, ok?
Ugly characters are far simpler to make. Simply move the dot to the left or right as far as you can, then leave it at the setting you think is the ugliest. When you're done with the advanced settings, you actually want to go back to the basic settings and mess with the random characters alot. Go to random, choose the ugliest character, repeat. With this method i have gotten the mouths and the chin to clip into eachother.
After your done with the character, all you need to do now is get the equipment and armor that suits you and now you are a creation of beauty! ( or miasma ) Now get into multiplayer and show characters with the default faces how superior you are!
If you see a character that looks like a god of fashion with the name Adol Christin or someone from Bravely Default, thats most likely me.
Tl;dr?
I like making my character more than playing the game.   Facial Features/10
I did it! I finally made a character! Took me over a hundred hours to makes a character, but it was totally worth it. 10/10, would recommend.

Great Game!
It's like playing a better version of Generations. The gameplay is very fun and engaging, keeping the basics of the modren Sonic games of being able to blend 3D and 2D platforming together seemlessly. I can't comment much on the gameplay cause they didn't really change much just improved it so it's like generation's game play but better.
The tag team stages are fun, and the Avatar itself is also great. I like the fact you can switch out weapons and take multiple diffrent paths in each stage depending on which weapon you have, and they each have your own ability. You miss your boost when playing as the Avatar, but you can quickly get used to the new gameplay that comes with them. They have also added quick time events to the stages, which normally happen during in game cutscenes, which I felt was a nice touch and gives the player some more interactivity instead of just watching it happen.
It's also a game to cater to fanservice but that's not  exactly a bad thing, I can't express how much joy it brings me as an adult to have the option to make my own Sonic character and bring them to life in game. When I was first seeing trailers and content for this game I just figured you could only play as your character in stages, but imagine my surprise when I booted up the game and it loads your character into the theater cutscenes! Like my character its standing there, talking with the other characters! He's giving Sonic a high five! This is great! the inner 10 year old in me is crying with joy at the fact I can see my own Sonic character in this game, interacting with the others, something I've only ever dreamed of and thought I'd have to learn how to 3D model and mod in order to see. If you told me 8 years ago I could see my Sonic Character in game, I wouldn't believe you... I hope Sega continues this for future games cause it's fun.
Spolier, but the main story is basically revolving around your character too, which is understandable since you're the new guy and stuff so everything is really up to you this time, I mean Sonic helps you of course but the really important stuff is all you, which I also like. It may seem like it's making your character a bit over powered, but other games I also enjoyed gave your character everything too. Reminds me of the Saints Row Series in that regard, a game series I really love, mind you. In future games perhaps your character will shift to a side character a bit or take equal part with Sonic instead of being the main star, which I think would be fair cause the characters would be used to your character by then.
Alright time to talk about some negative things. But first, I see a lot of reviews complaining about crashing, framerate, and other bugs. I think they are judging the game too quickly since it only just came out, and I also think there's a lot of stigma around it just because it's a Sonic game and some people are just itching to have something else to slap the Sonic '06 label on. The crashing problem was fixed within 2 hours by SEGA and they said they are also working on other small bugs, so I think that's a good sign.
Me however had no problems with crashing, or framerate. The most I would get with framerate drops was very busy momments in the game but it wasn't unplayable it just dropped a bit from 60, and my PC isn't THAT great anymore since its older now, and I have everything on max so I did expect minor frame drops, hell I loose frames from 60 to 40-50 in Overwatch all the time. People forget that you need good PCs for top performance, so I think you should check your specs first before you complain about FPS drops, maybe you need to knock your graphics down a bit, buddy.
I only found 2 issues in the game. 1. The audio was /slightly/ off in the 2nd Cutscene where sonic got his butt handed to him, but it wasn't enough to take away from the action of it all, and 2. one of the boss battles, the one againts the gaint bee, the floor tends to cut in and out sometimes depending on how and where you move, but it is still playable and beatable.
People are also complaining about the story being too short, but the story is at least 2 and a half hours long, that's like standard for a game these days. IF you rush in and just do everything as quickly as you can yeah you're gonna have it done in 2 and a half hours. However, there is lots of collectables to pick up, and if you if you do the Avatar stages you have like at least 3 diffrent paths you can take at any given time depending your wepon of choice, giving good replay value. Also if you're not used to Sonic, it may take you a few tries to get S ranks, which should also keep you busy. I got a few S ranks on my stages as I played but I had to go back to some and re do them because I didn't get an S rank, and I'm a veteran player. You also have SoS missions which reward you every so often with new stuff, adding to replayablity, and daily missions as well. There's also in stage missions such as using a certain weapon or boosting at a certain time. Ontop of that Shadow can be switched out for any of Sonic's stages, so you can replay them as Shadow, and Shadow also has some stand alone DLC. I don't see the 2 hour story as a problem.
One thing I will complain about is the character creator is lacking a bit. Now believe me I didn't expect to get my oc exactly as he's drawn on paper, but I was expecting a bit more options than what they gave us. I haven't checked out the other species but if the Hedgehog is anything to go by there's not many customization options aside from diffrent colors, seems to only be 3 head shapes, 6 eyes, etc. I honestly was expecting the character creator to be like a mixture of the main cast's body parts and then a few new shapes ontop of that, but you can't even choose hair peices like Amy or Tails have, they have to be unlocked as "headgear" and are already precoloured so you can't even get it to match your character's fur.
That brings me to another point and another reason why you're gonna be replaying the game with mission and ranks, you have to UNLOCK all the cosmetic items for your character. Everything is preset colors and such and only have about 2-3 alternate versions. A color picker for cosmetics would of been great and is entirely possible, as well as an item shop to buy cosmetics from, since right now Rings are nothing but points, and I was kinda expecting a shop you could buy items from with your Rings.
Also, the momentum is a bit off, but that also just takes some getting used to, know if you do a dead stop, you will not clear that large gap if you try to jump over it, etc. Just some adjustments. Also I play with a controller so no idea how it works with PC controls. I reccomend a controller.
Overall the game is very good and better than I expected and I'm looking forward to three things:
- > The modding community picking this up now and going to town on it with Avatar options and levels like they did with Generations, or possibly Sega considering opening up the Steam Workshop
- > This game to prove to SEGA it went over well, and we get another game like it in the future with our custom characters added into the mix.
- > Now that they got the custom characters out of the way PLEASE give us back the Chao Garden in the next game.

You know those games that become your new ''thing''? Like you play them for hours and days and weeks maybe a few years. For some of you maybe it's WoW, maybe Counter Strike, maybe Runescape. For me it was ESO. As you all can probably see I've played this game for quite a bit. And I loved it. I just fell in love with Elder Scrolls Online. Maybe it's because I love the lore of this universe, Maybe it's because the huge open world, Maybe it's because how addictive the game is. As you can tell, This game gives everything it should give. It's nearly perfect for an MMO. ''But why, fonidol, why are you giving this game a negative review?'' Well, let me explain that to you.
I think it was around early 2015. They introduced a new in-game store called ''Crown Store'' where you basically have to pay real money in order to get these crowns to buy some of this Crown store's contents. It seemed very innocent at the beginning. There was only a few cool mounts which you can get in game with no problem, a few costumes which did nothing but made you look fab, and a few♥♥♥♥♥♥potions which were completely useless. It seemed very cool. But as the game developed and made progress, they naturally added some new content to the crown store. Like new costumes new mounts and DLC's which you had to pay money to acquire. I believe the first DLC was ''Imperial City'' where you go to a abandoned city filled with daedra and get cool loot from 2 new dungeons which you can only have access to them if you have the DLC. That made me a little bit worried because I loved the game and didn't want it to become like an♥♥♥♥♥♥p2w game filled with microtransactions. The time passed and they added a new DLC. And then another one, another one, another one. With every DLC, comes new gear and weapons which are needed for specific builds. Now that's where they crossed the line. Because as you know, this game has a huge PvP which you actually have to have a decent build in order to be successfull. But in order to have these 'decent' builds, you have to have these new gear sets came with the DLC's. That made me a little bit angry. Because the last thing I wanted to do was pay money in order to get something that will make me a better Dragonknight, a sorcerer, a nightblade and so on.
Another thing is at the current stage of the game, everything you can get from Crown Store with just a credit card and fingers, is available in the currency of the game, golds. But oh my god isn't it difficult to acquire. A horse is 10000 gold, a house is more than a ♥♥♥♥ing million golds and some potions are worth more than my life.
I'm not cool with the game's current stage and I don't think it's going any better.
Buy at your own risk.

So, first review for Transistor:
The game is pretty, both to the eyes and the ears. Music is solid (beyond solid, it's ♥♥♥♥ing amazing), the art style is gorgeous (sort of what would happen if you took the cel-shaded style of Bastion and crossed it with Art Deco), and the detail is good, but not overdone or too busy.
The gameplay certainly won't be for everyone, but I like it. It's an interesting take on a "tactical" style, and the sheer variety of moves and ways to go about doing solving a fight are pretty keen. Lots of abilities to use, and multiple ways to tweak each ability, not to mention passive buffs. All of this while trying to maximize a cap on how much "boom" you can wade into a fight with at once.
Only problem I have so far: some bugs definitely made it out of their QA department. Hard-crash bugs. This is a bad thing. It's not hitting everyone, and apparently it's better if you play it in Offline Mode on Steam. I'm guessing Supergiant Games is driving for a fix at the moment, because no studio likes handing out game crashes.
So, yeah: I definitely recommend it. It's on the shorter side (haven't beat it yet, but I have a feeling), but beautiful, fun, and has a refreshing take on the mechanics of a platformer. Might just wanna wait a few days for the bugs to get squashed.

I'll start by saying: If you didn't like Bastion, you won't like this at all. The storytelling is very similar. The game is also pretty short, I finished clocking in at 5 hours (did not 100% obviously, you need NG+ to unlock all the different powers and such). But during NG+, I don't see the story changing much. It will be something for only completionists.
But, outside of that I found Transistor to be a great experience. Supergiant delivers again with a chillingly beautiful soundtrack, Darren Korb proving his skills at composing. As a person who loved the art style of Bastion, Transistor does not differ a lot from it with the exception of having more "3d" models as compared to the mostly 2D Bastion, this is most easily seen on your protagonist. The voice acting in the game is top notch, Logan Cunningham giving another near perfect preformance on his character and as the narrator. The enviroments are always beautiful to look at, if a little confusing to navigate at times. The story kept me hooked all the way through the game, with the characters being fleshed out along the way, never feeling generic and always very enthralling.
The combat in the game was a very interesting idea executed well, but not to perfection. It can feel tedious at times and frustrating at others when something just doesn't lineup perfectly. Endgame, you will probably have a combo that will be able to instagib the strongest enemies, you only obstacle being the cooldown bar on your Turn(), which is the main form of combat in Transistor. It's a strategic pause that allows you to set up a bunch of moves that enemies can not react to for the most part. With the backstab mechaninc and the variety of Functions (moves), it has more uses than just being a "VATS" like way of fighting ala Fallout. While recharging, its a game of dodging attacks before you can go back in on the enemies.
Where the combat really shines is how varried you can make your moveset. Each unlockable function is very different than the last, and aren't just moves: they can be infused to combine with other functions (Example: combine the knockup and the pull functions to create an AOE pull) or can be used as passive traits, all taking up some of your power bar, limiting how many functions you can have going.The stories included with each function are a very nice touch that fit the asthetic very well, but unlocking all 3 pieces can be a pain sometimes, since each one will need to occupy each of the 3 uses (passive, upgrade or move) to unlock the full story. Luckily, you only need one battle in each use to unlock each part and with an upgrade station seemingly after every battle you should unlock them all quickly and be able to go back to a more comfortable moveset.
There was only a few spots in the game I would consider "hard", for the most part your average player should be able to blow through their first NG with relative ease. The enemies aren't the brightest, not to say that they are bad, but sometimes they will just stare at you as you recharge behind a wall, not even bothering to try and pressure you to move.
Death is also really hard to achieve, after reaching 0 HP you will get a "free turn()" where you can try and save yourself or win the fight with your what you have left. If you fail and get hit again, you will lose one of your functions socketed. But, since you will usually have 4, chances are you will most likely never lose them all. I have never lost one, so I could not say if they are gone forever, but seeing the difficulty of the game I assume you recover them at the next station. The only time dying will really matter is in the training & challenge areas, where if you die once or twice you may just restart a challenge.
Is it worth playing through?
Is it worth the current $20? That's a bit more debatable, due to it's shorter length. I wouldn't say not to buy it, but the second it goes on sale it is a must grab.

Alien: Isolation is the story of Baby Ripley going in search of the presumed dead Mama Ripley.
While Alien: Isolation has some good things going for it, the gameplay itself drags it down and ultimately makes for a highly repetitive and frustrating experience. Alien: Isolation is NOT a shooter. It is a survival horror which plays heavily on stealth elements. Yes there are guns - but they are not a focal point.
The Good:
- The ambiance is simply fantastic. Everything from the lighting (swirling fans and fog effects) to the clanging of unknown noises in the vents. You feel like you are being hunted. It's awesome.
The Bad
- Simply put the gameplay itself is rather frustrating. In most scenarios your goal is to sneak past enemies without them detecting you. You have ways to execute this by using tactics such as hiding under tables, in closets, behind furniture, and finding alternative routes such as hidden vents. This becomes frustrating because some enemies (ahem, Alien) have close to zero patterns of movement. They seem to move as they please. When the Alien kills you twenty times due to its erratic pathing the game is no longer fun and just becomes obnoxiously tedious.
- The game feels dragged out - far beyond what is necessary. You finish one mission simply to find you now must do something else; the game just keeps putting barriers in your way. This is fine to some degree but at a certain point it no longer feels natural - it simply feels like the designers wanted to make the game longer by forcing you to complete irrelevent things over and over. If I wanted some chores to do I would call my mom.
Overall, Alien: Isolation's environment is beautiful. Unfortunately, the gameplay is not. It is boring, reptitive, and drags on and on with no clear direction or rhyme and reason.
Alien: Isolation takes about 15 hours to complete.
5/10

ESC: The Video Game
Nah, but the game is scary as hell. It perfectly captures the mood of the original Alien film from 1979. It has this dark and forbodding kind of atmosphere that can't be replicated anywhere but the Alien universe. The graphics... are stunning. No, check that, they're ♥♥♥♥♥♥-inducing. These are are some of the best video game graphics to date besides EA's Battlefront by DICE. Everything is detailed to an upmost extreme, which can extend your gameplay hours a ton. You'll just wander around the ship looking at signs and listening to recording tapes, that is, when you're not being hunted by the lone Xenomorph. Unlike the previous Aliens: Colonial Marines, which isn't half bad in my opinion, this game goes for the chilling survival experience, like what Amnesia did. The alien is an unstoppable threat, so your only chance of survival is to avoid it and not get caught by it. When you do, you get the biggest jumpscare you've ever had in a video game. Be sure to try to avoid it. It's hard to though, so you're always tense whenever just walking the ship by your lonesome, listening to creaks in the vents and hearing the ship fall apart. This is definately an auditory game. You need good sound to get the best out of this experience. My advice? Turn off all the lights, put on some surround headphones, turn the settings in-game to maximum, and make it fullscreen. You will♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants. So, yes, I absolutely highly recommend the game. It's a frightening experience with a large campaign that will keep you tense all the way to the end. One minor note though: AVOID THE DLC.

I have played it for quite a while now. I've S ranked pretty much every level of the game except maybe 2 of them, those are actually pretty damn hard. But, if I were to say something, objectively, it isn't half bad of a game.
-It might look kinda streamlined at first, but you'll soon realize after replaying the levels you'll encounter many different pathways. I can understand people don't like this kind of levels, but I think that is quite the improvement from colors, but I admit it isn't as good as Generations, as objectively speaking as I can. I still, to this day, am replaying the game!
-Controls don't suck at all. Modern Sonic controls better than Generations. He feels more precise, keeps speed when jumping and has double jumping for even a more methodical and precise approach to the 2D platforming sections. Classic Sonic controls better, with the awesome addition of the drop dash. It isn't Sonic Mania and I don't understand why Classic Sonic had to be brought back, but at least it improved from Generations. Lastly, Avatar controls perfectly fine. Similar control scheme as Modern Sonic, he simply has no boost.
-Then we've got the people that say it is buggy. Besides the first 2 hours in which the game was literally unplayable because Denuvo crashed it, I've found no glitches or bugs in my entire playthrough. Add 3-4 hours to my playtime because I played it offline. Physics, or the lack of them, as you wish to refer to them, work perfectly fine for this type of game and they are not broken. I could use a safe wall here and there, but if they are not there maybe we shouldn't just recklessly boost constantly, as they want us to use it better maybe?
- Story is ok. Not best story, but at least this time they tried something else. Cannot say much more without spoiling, but I hope we all can agree that we don't want something as brainless as Generations or as complicated and over-dramatic as previous entries. Just a nice written story is what is needed, kinda like Unleashed?
- Gameplay is nice. I tell you this, if you enjoyed Generations you'll also find lots of enjoyment here. But of course, if you didn't like Generations, do not bother. It is as simple as that, we do not need to begin yet another war, people.
- Music is pretty much what you would expect from a Sonic game. Amazing remixes of previous songs, new techno tunes and lots of vocal. It is alright, quite impressive that after so much time they still lead the competition with their music, yet it isn't as amazing as before. But still, pretty much enjoyable.
I think I haven't forgot anything with this review but my point is, just enjoy the game for yourself. Go get into the game, have fun, or dislike it, that's fine. But simply enjoy the game for what it is, not for what you want it to be. This game is good, of course not perfect. Hopefully you'll enjoy it.

You know those games that become your new ''thing''? Like you play them for hours and days and weeks maybe a few years. For some of you maybe it's WoW, maybe Counter Strike, maybe Runescape. For me it was ESO. As you all can probably see I've played this game for quite a bit. And I loved it. I just fell in love with Elder Scrolls Online. Maybe it's because I love the lore of this universe, Maybe it's because the huge open world, Maybe it's because how addictive the game is. As you can tell, This game gives everything it should give. It's nearly perfect for an MMO. ''But why, fonidol, why are you giving this game a negative review?'' Well, let me explain that to you.
I think it was around early 2015. They introduced a new in-game store called ''Crown Store'' where you basically have to pay real money in order to get these crowns to buy some of this Crown store's contents. It seemed very innocent at the beginning. There was only a few cool mounts which you can get in game with no problem, a few costumes which did nothing but made you look fab, and a few♥♥♥♥♥♥potions which were completely useless. It seemed very cool. But as the game developed and made progress, they naturally added some new content to the crown store. Like new costumes new mounts and DLC's which you had to pay money to acquire. I believe the first DLC was ''Imperial City'' where you go to a abandoned city filled with daedra and get cool loot from 2 new dungeons which you can only have access to them if you have the DLC. That made me a little bit worried because I loved the game and didn't want it to become like an♥♥♥♥♥♥p2w game filled with microtransactions. The time passed and they added a new DLC. And then another one, another one, another one. With every DLC, comes new gear and weapons which are needed for specific builds. Now that's where they crossed the line. Because as you know, this game has a huge PvP which you actually have to have a decent build in order to be successfull. But in order to have these 'decent' builds, you have to have these new gear sets came with the DLC's. That made me a little bit angry. Because the last thing I wanted to do was pay money in order to get something that will make me a better Dragonknight, a sorcerer, a nightblade and so on.
Another thing is at the current stage of the game, everything you can get from Crown Store with just a credit card and fingers, is available in the currency of the game, golds. But oh my god isn't it difficult to acquire. A horse is 10000 gold, a house is more than a ♥♥♥♥ing million golds and some potions are worth more than my life.
I'm not cool with the game's current stage and I don't think it's going any better.
Buy at your own risk.

Long story short... this game is designed to punish the players for almost everything they do.
PROS:
- graphic
- soundtrack
CONS:
- class system:
the class system seems like a PRO when you start playing... but you'll find out it is not soon enough. the game offer no class reset and it's extremly easy to mess up a character even at lvl 220 by picking the wrong class change at high rank forcing you to delete and start over from lvl 1 or quit. Skills are purposedly designed not to scale with either level and stats... so you'll have to choose if you want to be competitive at low lvl using low lvl skills and useless at high lvls... be useless at low lvls picking only base low lvl skills and competitive at high lvls... or put money into the game by making a good low lvl build, buyint the reskill potion in the cash shop, and rebuilding for high lvl gameplay... way to go!
- grinding:
the grinding in the game is aweful. At low lvls might seem fun but when you reach high lvls you'll soon find out that the monster density and respawn rate is just too low. You'll find yourself fighting with tones of other people for the very few grinding spots in the game or walking in almost totally empty maps for 5-10 minutus barely finding anything to kill.
Add the fact that this means that lots of players will be competing over a very small amounth of enemies and you will understand why you NEED to aspect to see a lot of kill steal and if you're a support class you're screwed.
- dungeons and missions:
korean gets 5 runs, we get 2.. 3 with a token. Consider the fact that if you are going to play a full support class dungeons and missions are the only things in the game your character will be useful for before level 200.If this wasn't enough both missions and dungeons are very badly designed.. they are maps with overpowered enemies in it and that's all.. add the fact that dungeon enemies DO NOT drop any kind of item... only the bosses drop a cube that randomly gives you either something nice (rarely) or completely useless crap.
- trade, market, team storage:
all these aspects suck bad.. if you're a free to play player you'll be punished hard by not beeing able to trade, having only 1 item in the market at a time and have absolutly no team storage. If you pay for the toekn then you'll be punished bad by having only 30 trades a month, still limited slots for the marketplace, a team storage with ONE slot... and in both cases you'll not be able to trade silver to your other characters.
- crafting classes:
the game has specific crafting classes that can be AFK with a shop open while you play with another player, and sell services like weapon repairing and stuff. GREAT idea very bad implementd into the game! You'll find out that craftring classes are taxed 50% every time they have an income and, in order to offer their services they hae to buy items. This means you'll be forced to price services 5x-6x times more then NPCs... so the number of customers you're going to have will be extremly small. Even if you manage to earn something you can't pass your earnings to your alts beause the game doesn't allow silver transfer in between the same account... way to make crafting classes completely useless.
- playing with friends:
can be a painful experience! you have a lvl range you need to be in order to keep earning experience and there're so many lvls in the game that at some points you'll most likely outlevel your friends or be outleveled by them thus making it impossible to play togheter... and seems like the devs are against a tutoring system. you can't trade anything you drop and can't use to your friend unless you BOTH are token users.. if you are a token user and your friend is not.. you can't trade him. you can't enter the matchmaking tool for dungeons if you're already in party with someone else so no "i'm with my 2 friends and we complete our party with the matchmaking tool" kind of talk... if you have a friend made party you get less experience in dugeon that if you play with total strangers using the matchmaking tool.
CONCLUSIONS:
I initially gave a positive review of the game because i hoped it would get better since it has the right features to succeed.. the problem is that all these feature are implemented in the most aweful way i've ever seen in an mmo even comparing it to 10 years older mmos.
A game should be fun, people should want to spend money on a game because they find the game fun.
ToS punish the players every step of the way in a way that only masochists can enjoy in the long run, and instead of having an healthy business model were they give you something to enjoy so you're willing to pay for it... they decided for a business model when they stress you so much with restriction an stupid designs that the reason to spend money in it is "not to get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥of every second of the experience"... and at times, like with the build issue i pointed my finger at during the review, it will feel like they're tricking you into giving them money.
So no... thanks but no... not going to play this game anymore than i already have as long as things stays ike this, not going to spend any more money into it (i did buy the founder pack because i had high hopes and wanted to support the devs)... and i can't do otherwise then give it a negatie review and suggest you don't even get into it: your time will be much better playing something else.

Overall, I quite like the game. There seems to be nice variety as far as enemies/areas and such are concerned, and the art style is great. There are plenty of positive reviews out there detailing all the things the game gets right, and I tend to agree with most of it.
Unfortunately, the game has a few issues that have me unable to recommend it. These are:
- Difficulty: The game, so far (I'm around level 25 atm), is incredibly easy. I rarely lose any health during fights, and don't remember ever having gone below 50% during the few hours that I played.
- Controller usage: I haven't bothered checking forums for others' experiences when playing the game with a controller, but mine wasn't great. When using my Steam controller with the basic gamepad layout, the game generally plays alright, but it's a pain dealing with the interface (inventory and such) as you can't scroll through menus using the controller's arrows. Instead, you need to use the analog stick as some weird kind of mouse, which isn't very functional.
- FPS issues: This is the main problem I have with the game, and the reason I haven't played a lot more. The game regularly freezes, with FPS dropping tremendously. It happens like once a minute or so, and really makes the game close to unplayable to me. Having looked around, I couldn't find a fix yet.
- Pay to win: This gets mentioned a lot, and defenitely seems to be the case. XP boosts and such are fine, but things like movement speed boosts make me fear more premium items will be added to the store over time, further increasing the gap between paying and non-paying gamers.
As I mentioned at the beginning, the game seems pretty cool asides from these points. Hopefully things will improve over time, as the game's still in an early stage.
