Alien: Isolation is the story of Baby Ripley going in search of the presumed dead Mama Ripley.
While Alien: Isolation has some good things going for it, the gameplay itself drags it down and ultimately makes for a highly repetitive and frustrating experience. Alien: Isolation is NOT a shooter. It is a survival horror which plays heavily on stealth elements. Yes there are guns - but they are not a focal point.
The Good:
- The ambiance is simply fantastic. Everything from the lighting (swirling fans and fog effects) to the clanging of unknown noises in the vents. You feel like you are being hunted. It's awesome.
The Bad
- Simply put the gameplay itself is rather frustrating. In most scenarios your goal is to sneak past enemies without them detecting you. You have ways to execute this by using tactics such as hiding under tables, in closets, behind furniture, and finding alternative routes such as hidden vents. This becomes frustrating because some enemies (ahem, Alien) have close to zero patterns of movement. They seem to move as they please. When the Alien kills you twenty times due to its erratic pathing the game is no longer fun and just becomes obnoxiously tedious.
- The game feels dragged out - far beyond what is necessary. You finish one mission simply to find you now must do something else; the game just keeps putting barriers in your way. This is fine to some degree but at a certain point it no longer feels natural - it simply feels like the designers wanted to make the game longer by forcing you to complete irrelevent things over and over. If I wanted some chores to do I would call my mom.
Overall, Alien: Isolation's environment is beautiful. Unfortunately, the gameplay is not. It is boring, reptitive, and drags on and on with no clear direction or rhyme and reason.
Alien: Isolation takes about 15 hours to complete.
5/10

ESC: The Video Game
Nah, but the game is scary as hell. It perfectly captures the mood of the original Alien film from 1979. It has this dark and forbodding kind of atmosphere that can't be replicated anywhere but the Alien universe. The graphics... are stunning. No, check that, they're ♥♥♥♥♥♥-inducing. These are are some of the best video game graphics to date besides EA's Battlefront by DICE. Everything is detailed to an upmost extreme, which can extend your gameplay hours a ton. You'll just wander around the ship looking at signs and listening to recording tapes, that is, when you're not being hunted by the lone Xenomorph. Unlike the previous Aliens: Colonial Marines, which isn't half bad in my opinion, this game goes for the chilling survival experience, like what Amnesia did. The alien is an unstoppable threat, so your only chance of survival is to avoid it and not get caught by it. When you do, you get the biggest jumpscare you've ever had in a video game. Be sure to try to avoid it. It's hard to though, so you're always tense whenever just walking the ship by your lonesome, listening to creaks in the vents and hearing the ship fall apart. This is definately an auditory game. You need good sound to get the best out of this experience. My advice? Turn off all the lights, put on some surround headphones, turn the settings in-game to maximum, and make it fullscreen. You will♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants. So, yes, I absolutely highly recommend the game. It's a frightening experience with a large campaign that will keep you tense all the way to the end. One minor note though: AVOID THE DLC.

The presentation is bold but not overwrought. The music is fantastic and a mix of ambient songs with five vocal tracks that call back to the plot of the game itself. “Red” is a character of unfortunate circumstances who must piece together what happened to the city she inhabits.
Combat is done in pseudo turn-based mode, or all in real time. The mechanics of combat remain very fresh due to the skill system. Each skill can be used in its own right, or slotted into another skill to serve as an enhancement to the base skill. Therein lays the dilemma, do you use this skill as a main skill or a passive skill? There are certainly rewards for changing up your build as well.
There is a sizable amount of optional content. Lore is tucked nicely in with combat skills you unlock as you progress through the game. The tutorial is there but it isn’t patronizing, in fact it’s one of the best I’ve seen in years. Controller support is in the game as well as a native support of keyboard and mouse. The controls are responsive for the most part, some skills can require a bit more precision than Red sometimes wants to give.

TL;DR > DO NOT GET INVOLVED WITH ANY HI-REZ GAME.
The gameplay is good, graphics are good, playing with friends is fun and all, but.
Matchmaking problems. Server problems on a daily basis. Broken maps, deserter bans and much more. And to make it short: NOT WORTH YOUR TIME.
1. Servers lagging out, kicking you out of the match lobby and you get a deserter ban for 30 minutes. It's happened over 20 times now. It's nerve breaking because you didn't do anything wrong and got banned, and it counts like you left the game.
I live in a big city, never have internet or power outages, my internet speed is over 70 mbps, and have a decent pc - I can run Smite max graphics on 1920x1200. THESE THINGS SHOULDN'T HAPPEN.
2. Servers lagging in game, usually Clash mode, and we are talking people teleporting every two seconds. Servers dropping players and not letting them connect back - this bug has been here for over a year.
3. Matchmaking. I'm level 120, and often times get matched with players below level 30, against a team of players that are around my level. Sometimes the enemy team gets unlucky. The new players get massively reported for feeding even though it's not their fault - they are new, and that's why if you haven't started playing - you shouldn't. If you don't learn very fast you will get banned because of player reports.
4. No balance in game. After the 80th god released in the game, things just started getting very bad. A guardian shouldn't be able to do as much damage as a ADC. He's a Guardian, not a Tiger tank. Newer mages all have ridiculous kits. For example, newest mage Discordia, has insane damage early and late game. She has one damaging ability, one cc and damage ability, an escape ability that: gives her cooldown on her first two abilities, lets her walk trough ANY object and makes her invisible, and an ultimate that deals alot of damage and spreads on two enemies that are near. Somebody who has a good kit is Zeus, but he is VERY slow and doesn't have any escapes to compensate for that damage output.
If you look and directly compare newer to older gods, newer gods all have some forms of invisibility or escape, an ability that does a ridiculous amount of damage no matter the class, and an insane ultimate that doesn't need any skill to use.
5. My siege map has been broken for a ridiculous ammount of time, submitted a ticket and got a c/p response. When you enter the map, screen just splits in half or everything gets black. No textures, no models. And there are parts of the map where I get epilepsy from the textures trying to exist. Unplayable.
6. Smite takes a ridiculous amount of time to start up. I run it from an SSD and it takes 3 mintues and 15 seconds to just START. And at least one more minute for the game to load to the main menu. It might seem trivial to complain about this, but no other game has ever loaded that long for me. I can start any other game at least 10 times by the time Smite loads.
God, I loved playing this game. I really did. I had countless hours of fun with my friends. I loved playing Loki, and many other assassins, mages and warriors. I owned over 400 skins on my account. I said owned because I won't bother with Hi-Rez ever again. I don't regret a thing, but for you, if you are looking for a new game to have fun with - golden days of Smite have long passed.

This will be my 1st review of any game I have ever plasyed.
I have played both DS games on PC and XBOX 360. IMHO the 360 doesnt do these games justice! I much prefer the PC version pf both. Ok review time....
+Pros: It's a Dark Souls game!
-Cons: It's a Dark Souls game! You will die....many times!
- The AI of some mobds isn't that great - use it to your advantage!
Graphics are great, ambiance is great, story line not much there, but the lore and trying to decipher it is a challenge and fun too. Battles are challenging and fun and anything can easliy kill you, boss or otherwise. This game, albeit simple, its very tough.
Advice: Create a character that can use some kind of ranged attack early on even if its a simple bow and arrow, this will help you progress very well. Ranged is good for killing at a distance and with a bow you can zoom in on an area and do some recon.
Get a shield and use it often, practice parry as much as you can. When entering a newly discoverd area take your time, 9/10 you will be ambushed, die and lose those precious souls!
Speaking of souls, do not be afraid to spend them, if you are greedy and are trying to save too many the game will find a way to kill you...trust me!
Take advantage of the terrain, you can find ways to pull enemies to a spot for and easier battle or find a choke point if there are many enemies on your tail. Again, ranged battle is good!
If possible try to stay human because you can summon NPC's and other players to help in difficult spots or boss battles the only disadvantage of being human is other players invading your world...but that is fun too! . Youtube and Dark Souls Wiki pages are your friend. Read messages other players leav on the ground some are very helpful and will warn you of whats ahead. Also, leave messages for your fellow players too!
Overall, great graphics, gamplay, music, ambiance, battles and so on! Good luck and don't break your PC or game controllers due to anger and frustration!

Game started, clicked play, computer burst into flames because game was so hard 20/10
Real Review:
At time of writing this reveiw, I haven't beaten the game yet. Let me tell you, if you think that Dark Souls was hard, 2 is nothing compared to that. It took me
tries to beat this boss. It took me 2 hours to just get to him, and part of that time was just respawning to grab my souls. Now I'm not very good at this game, so it does take me a bit longer than most to get throught the game. But when you die five times on the FIRST boss, there is nothing like that I have ever seen. It took me one to two tries to get the Tarus Demon in 1, but this is just not even funny. Now I have thrown my controller at my moniter, even threw it on the ground, that is usally when I quit. So far, I'm not really seeing any clear path or story, which is really what I think Dark Souls it about. You don't know what you are supposed to be doing or why you are doing it. You just do it. And this is probably one of the only games that can get away with it. You are so busy trying to do one of three things: Get your souls back from your last death, fight the next boss, or soul farming. You don't have time to worry about what section of the quest or story you are on, you are to busy already doing something else to worry about that. Now this is a JRPG, so yes, there is no way to know where you are supposed to go next. But this is also an open-world game, so do whatever you want. Now know that, you will die if you go to far. But I have gone to areas I should not have gone to and still fought and survived (I put survived because it was a survival). Here is a very good tip, if you are at a stop where you just abosolutly cannot get a boss or a group of enemies, take a break and chill for a bit, go watch TV or some YouTube (DON'T WATCH DARK SOULS!) Then after a couple of hours or so, come back with a clear mind and try again. Also just remember that your not even in NG+ yet, so you don't know what pain is like just yet.
Update 1:
Well, not much to say here. The game ended like anygood Open-World RPG... It made you do it again. I love Dark Souls, it has one of those unmatched gameplay styles, but if you make me go through all that again, EVEN HARDER. Congrats. You have taken my time and my life and crushed it like a Lifegem. This game is harder first time around, with going from everything being pretty much instant in Dark Soul, to everything taking time in Dark Souls II and the new Agility stat, I say this game will be very worth your while, plus, you will get your $60 - $50 bucks out of it.

I have played it for quite a while now. I've S ranked pretty much every level of the game except maybe 2 of them, those are actually pretty damn hard. But, if I were to say something, objectively, it isn't half bad of a game.
-It might look kinda streamlined at first, but you'll soon realize after replaying the levels you'll encounter many different pathways. I can understand people don't like this kind of levels, but I think that is quite the improvement from colors, but I admit it isn't as good as Generations, as objectively speaking as I can. I still, to this day, am replaying the game!
-Controls don't suck at all. Modern Sonic controls better than Generations. He feels more precise, keeps speed when jumping and has double jumping for even a more methodical and precise approach to the 2D platforming sections. Classic Sonic controls better, with the awesome addition of the drop dash. It isn't Sonic Mania and I don't understand why Classic Sonic had to be brought back, but at least it improved from Generations. Lastly, Avatar controls perfectly fine. Similar control scheme as Modern Sonic, he simply has no boost.
-Then we've got the people that say it is buggy. Besides the first 2 hours in which the game was literally unplayable because Denuvo crashed it, I've found no glitches or bugs in my entire playthrough. Add 3-4 hours to my playtime because I played it offline. Physics, or the lack of them, as you wish to refer to them, work perfectly fine for this type of game and they are not broken. I could use a safe wall here and there, but if they are not there maybe we shouldn't just recklessly boost constantly, as they want us to use it better maybe?
- Story is ok. Not best story, but at least this time they tried something else. Cannot say much more without spoiling, but I hope we all can agree that we don't want something as brainless as Generations or as complicated and over-dramatic as previous entries. Just a nice written story is what is needed, kinda like Unleashed?
- Gameplay is nice. I tell you this, if you enjoyed Generations you'll also find lots of enjoyment here. But of course, if you didn't like Generations, do not bother. It is as simple as that, we do not need to begin yet another war, people.
- Music is pretty much what you would expect from a Sonic game. Amazing remixes of previous songs, new techno tunes and lots of vocal. It is alright, quite impressive that after so much time they still lead the competition with their music, yet it isn't as amazing as before. But still, pretty much enjoyable.
I think I haven't forgot anything with this review but my point is, just enjoy the game for yourself. Go get into the game, have fun, or dislike it, that's fine. But simply enjoy the game for what it is, not for what you want it to be. This game is good, of course not perfect. Hopefully you'll enjoy it.

I really am scratching my head to what happened behind the scenes with this game. Despite allegedly having a longer development cycle than any other mainline Sonic game of the past decade, everything about Forces feels incredibly half-baked. I know people love to say “CUZ SONIC TEAM’S AN INCOMPETENT DEVELOPER” but that doesn’t seem accurate since these ARE the people who made Colors and Generations. But since Forces turned out to not be great people are probably gonna be calling for the “boost” gameplay to be scrapped entirely, but is that really a good idea? I think we can agree the last thing the the series needs is right now is yet ANOTHER shake-up. The answer isn’t “get rid everything and replace it with the a totally different gameplay formula,” it’s “stick with what works, and make it better.” That’s why Mario’s been so successful. But it looks like Forces only did half of this. It brought back the gameplay style that’s been proven to work, but it just feels like lesser version of what came before. The core mechanics of the Unleashed/Colors/Generations/Forces gameplay are fine. That’s not the problem here. But those mechanics need to be complimented by strong level design, which means several alternate pathways to give levels replayability and enough actual platorming to keep it from feeling like you’re doing nothing but running in a straight line. All this is what made Unleashed (the daytime levels that is), Colors, and Generations work. Sonic Forces only had three level designers. The previous Sonic games (Sonic Colors, Sonic Generations, Sonic Unleashed) had seven or eight level designers. If that wasn't worrying enough, two of the three level designers had never worked on a Sonic game before Forces, and the other level designer only worked on Sonic Lost World.
That may explain why the level design is ... mediocre to say the least.﻿
Don't come off telling me I'm just one of those people that hate 3D Boost games. There's reasons why a portion of these games are bad. Sega NEEDS to get new developers

STALKER Shadow of Chernobyl is my favorite game of all time. There's no way to properly express how fantastic it is. But I'll try I suppose.
The game takes place in Chernobyl, as the title suggests, though this Chernobyl is a much more mysterious one. After scientists went and messed around in Chernobyl after the disaster, weird crap started happening. Blowouts, anomalies, artifacts, and nasty warped mutants craving human flesh. The game is a mix between the real life place Chernobyl, obviously, mixed in with world and plot elements from the novel Roadside Picnic (which is my favorite book ever) and the film based on the book, Stalker (which is a great film too). I will never know why they picked that book, Chernobyl, and mutants in one game but one can only think it must've been some divine force that made it happen. The game is a lot like a realistic, Slavic, and overall more terrifying version of Fallout. Not saying that Fallout is bad though.
Gameplay is top-notch, the shooting is pretty great and going and finding artifacts can be really tricky. Depending on your alliances, you'll go up against either bandits, different factions, loners, or everyone. The fights are intense and may require many reloads before you figure out how to stump your enemies. This is not an easy game at all, even on the easier difficulties. It's hard as balls and will mess you up hard, you can't go without quicksaving. I'm not good at videogames, so it was a struggle to finish this one, but it was worth it.
I can't go talking about a game without talking about it's faults though, no matter how much I adore it. The AI is weird in this one.... it goes from Vash the Stampede level of accuracy to the level of skill you'd expect from a drunk man. The graphics aren't exactly triple-A material either but the atmosphere and the overall visual design makes up for it.
STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is an interesting and unique title; there really isn't anything like it. It has its bugs and technical isssues, yes, but that won't stop me from loving truly awesome, scary, intense game. In the words of Number 6™, "There's nothing quite like Russian post-apocalyptic fiction, comrade!"

There's a lot written already, so I'm going to try to not say what's been said.  This revew could be a million words longer, and I've only had the game for a month and a half (and over 200 hours invested).
This game is not perfect; reviews saying as much are delusional.  It is not horrible; reviews saying this are from angry people who expect too much.  This plays not like an MMO with a Skyrim skin, but more like Skyrim with mandatory MMO elements.  If you loved Skryim, it's worth trying out.  If you love MMOs, it's worth trying out.  But the mix may or may not be good enough, depending on what you want in the game.  i recommend this, but...  There is a lot of but in my recommendation.
- The voice acting is very well done, and there's a ton of spoken dialogue, but... there's also a ton of reading books, which means there's a lot of backstory that I'm clicking through and telling myself "one day I'll read all those lorebooks".
- The game mechanics are a lot of fun, but... most are generally not as fleshed out as they could be.  Like pickpocketing, which is good wholesome evil fun, except that you're basically stealing one of three types of treasure with random names from every NPC, so that beggar will be carrying the same sort of treasure items that the noble will, not like food or a coin or something.  You're not stealing people's armor and weapons, like you did in Skyrim.  Intimidation and Persuasion exist as skills that unlock dialogue options, but the implementaiton is painfully linearly embedded and you can't just try being persuasive/intimidating to see how it affects things, so much as you get to click the option if you have the skill, and maybe it saves you from paying gold to complete a quest.
- You don't have to pay a subscription fee, but...  you're hamstringed by your carrying/bank capacity if you're not an ESO+ member, and you get 'free' crowns (ingame currency purchased with real money) and then there's the experience bonuses.  Subscription isn't required to play, but the game is a lot smoother when you pay it, and when you break it down you get $15 in 'free' crowns when you pay for a month at $15.  It becomes a 'good' deal, but know that it's annoying to try and play for free, even if the subscription is not necessary.
- It plays like Skyrim, in that you go on quests and experience a grand story where you're influencing the world (that you see) and most of the time you can bring friends with you on your quests, but...  It's full of grindy MMO game mechanics, daily quests, gathering for hours and hours to sell materials to other players so you can get things, farming the same monsters repeatedly to get the right pieces of armor/weapons, etc.  If you love MMO, it's certainly got the MMO mechanics.  If not, it can be daunting.
- The zone chats are for the most part friendly and full of people who (with sarcastic wit) will provide assistance to new players, but...  There are the occasional trolls throwing out offensive buzzwords that you find in online game chats.  Well, at least it's not full of bots and hackers, tho there's sure to be a few of those running around.
- Character development feels pretty involved, with a level cap of 50 and individual skill trees for all your weapons, class and race, and then you can venture out and find "skyshards" to get more skill points to spend, and the champion system lets you continue building on your character after you've reached max level, but...  There are only 4 classes to pick from, and that makes everything feel kindof simplified, and the skill abilities only have a single branch so it's not like there's real depth there.  Plus, after you've allocated all your points, and re-rolled a few times (at an increasing cost of gold), then you get things roughly where you think you want them and they change the character mechanics (it's called nerfing, and you can pretty much expect it in an MMO).
Bottom line, if you want the single-player gameplay, get Skyrim.  If you want to play through an Elder Scrolls story with some friends (or your wife, in my case), and you don't mind the MMO experience, this is well worth getting.  Just don't charge in with expectations that it's perfect, or even smoothed over for the most part.  It runs, it doesn't crash much on our mid-level laptops, and it looks really really pretty.  And I've managed to sink more hours per week into this than I have my full-time job since I've purchased it.  With that in mind, I recommend this.

I used to like ESO. Sadly, I've seen it patched to appeal to the kind of people who play League of Legends and WoW (over competitive, toxic people, you know the sort) because that's where ZOS thinks they'll make their money. Good luck to them with that.
Let me give you a rundown:
Crafting used to make the best gear in the game, it was a level higher than anything that dropped. Since crafting isn't grindy enough though and the end-game PvE players complained no end, crafting has been nerfed into the ground and it's no longer a level higher, the stats are objectively worse, and there's just no point in it any more.
This is after they swore up and down that crafted gear would always be better than what drops. The case now? You have to grind for your gear in dungeons, the best gear being in group dungeons of course. This spites their casual audience to appeal to a more WoW-minded crowd that they believe will bring in more money.
They changed dungeon scaling so that instead of it scaling to the level of the party leader, it scales up to CP160. The problem with this is that low level people won't have the skills and passives unlocked to do well, here. Group dungeon has been effectively locked away from casuals, it's meant for the PvE Master Race, now. By which I mean the people who love mindless, repetitive grind.
Why do this? ZOS believes that they can make money from Skinner box models, similar to WoW. It's an unethical thing, but their management has been terrible of late. They don't realise that casuals tend to have altitits and they'll spend loads of time just roleplaying in a game. These casuals are also the ones who'll buy outfits from their cash shop. It's amusing that they think that an end-game PvE person or a PvP player will have any interest in housing or a chef costume... It's delusional.
They're locking the upcoming housing system behind grinding. You have to have a massive amount of achievements unlocked and a huge amount of money ready to even have a house. So you either have to spend your life grinding away, or you have to buy it from the store for frankly ridiculous prices. This isn't going to work well for them.
Up until Tamriel Unlimited, the balancing team had been pretty great. However, with Tamriel Unlimited, their creative director left and everything went downhill. Undocumented stealth nerfs to drops and skills, and balancing refocused away from keeping casual play viable to appealing to the toxic, competitive players (both PvP players and end-game PvE players alike). They've been alienating casuals no end.
In fact, there was a recent thread about how the Radiant Destruction nerf will screw up the kind of fun concept builds that casuals use. The only people who've complained about the skill are toxic PvP players and elitist end-game PvE players. This escalated so quickly that their community team had to step in, reducing a thread from seven pages to three, leaving behind only smarmy L2P posts. Good going. Way to alienate your casual players.
Goodbye roleplaying! Goodbye peaceful crafting/bank times! I know from third party forums that a lot of roleplayers left when they added duelling. That's right, ESO has duelling now. What do you think that toxic, crappy people are going to do with a tool like that? They're going to grief people. The same thing happened in Champions Online, and that lead to duel-free zones.
ESO doesn't have duel free zones and the developers have told us in no uncertain terms that it never will. They don't care about roleplayers. They don't see them as a viable demographic. No money to be made off of roleplayers, right? Except... Who buys the fancy clothing from the crown store? Who do they think is going to buy the player housing? End-game PvE players or PvP players? Hahaha.
Don't make me laugh.
If this evidence wasn't enough, as I mentioned above, there's been a lot of forum favouritism. The moderators have been deleting the posts of casuals who've complained about this, along with locking/deleting threads. I've been watching it happen and the whole thing is a train wreck. Essentially, the community team knows how the majority of their demographic feels about these changes, but they're just shutting them down because that's what management wants.
ESO is going out of its way to alienate their casual players. They don't want us or our money. And to that I say: Fine. That's actually fine. If you don't want my money, I'm okay with that. The problem is? Champions Online and Battleborn made similar choices, appealing to the "hardcore" PvE crowd and toxic PvP players. What's happened to those games? They're dead. They have anywhere between 50 and 300 concurrent players on a good day.
The management team at ZOS could look at these numbers to realise where those games went wrong with alienating their casual audience to see what they shouldn't be doing. Instead, they're just repeating the same old mistakes.
So I'm afraid I have to say... ESO is a toxic wasteland filled with annoyances, frustration, disappointment, and crappy people. If you're a casual player and/or a roleplayer, just avoid it. You'll only end up feeling depressed. Just be thankful you won't have to feel as defeated and betrayed by the whole affair as I do. I liked ESO.
ESO is quickly becoming as bad for casual players as any other MMO. When casuals aren't even allowed to have a voice on the forums, you know it's past the point of no return. I wonder if they'll delete my review, too?

Her Elder Scrolls oyunu evrene yeni parçalar, olaylar ve karakterler katmıştır. Ve bu genelde eskilerinin üstüne eklenmiştir. Yani çağlar kaldığı yerden devam etmiş, yeni olaylar meydana gelmiştir. Fakat ilk kez Elder Scrolls Online’da bu gelenek terk edildi.
Morrowind, Oblivion ve Skyrim gibi serinin son üç oyunu yeni çağlar ve olaylar eklerken, ESO, Skyrim’den sonra değil, tam 1000 yıl öncesinde geçiyor. Yani geçmişe dönüyoruz. Peki hikayeyi nasıl bağladılar diye sorarsak, ESO’nun geçtiği dönemdeki olaylar fazla net değil, karakterler hakkında bilgi yok, lafın kısası tam bir muamma söz konusu.
Elder Scrolls evreni toplamda 6 çağdan oluşuyor: Şafak Çağı, Elf Çağı, 1. Çağ, 2. Çağ, 3. Çağ ve 4. Çağ. Skyrim 4. Çağ’da geçiyordu, Oblivion ve Morrowind 3. Çağ’da, son olarak yeni oyunumuz ESO ise 2. Çağ’ın 583. yılında başlıyor. Bakalım neleri oyunda göreceğiz, neler olmayacak.
Birkaç olayda daha adından bahsedeceğim bu kişiyi ilk ele almak doğru olur diye düşünüyorum. Tiber Septim 2. Çağ’ın 828. yılında doğduğuna inanılmakta. Oyunun geçtiği tarihten 3 asır sonrasında olduğu içi haliyle oyunda göremeyeceğimiz kişiler arasında. Dolayısıyla Tamriel’da bir birlik yok, Amulet of Kings bulunmamış. Elder Scrolls Online’da görevlerin birinde bu kadim kolyeyi bulma görevi de alacağız.
Ejderhalar
Ejderha meselesi Elder Scrolls evreninde hep bir merak unsuru olmuştur. Ejderhaların Elder Scrolls oyunları içinde ilk kez Skyrim’de geldiği bilgisi maalesef yanlış bir bilgi. Nasıl mı? Geçmişe dönelim.
Elf Çağında Tamriel’a Ejderhalar hükmetmekteydi. İnsanoğluna kan kusturan ve istediğini yapan bu yaratıklar Kadim Parşömenlerin kullanılmasıyla ve elbette Kynareth’in Paarthurnax’a olan emriyle yenildiler. Alduin önderliğinde Tamriel’ı terk ettiler. Neden Ejderha savaşı çıktı sorusunun cevabı ise insanların ayaklanıp isyan çıkarmasıdır.
Alduin tüm ejderhaların başı olarak kabul edilir. Onun önderliğinde diğer Ejderhalar insanlara saldırdı. Fakat insanoğlu anlamıştı ki Ejderhalar da kendileri gibi etten kandan bir canlı, ölüm onlar için de geçerliydi (tam olarak değil). Bu savaşta mağlup olan Ejderhalara karşı büyük bir av başlar. Tüm ejderhalar katledilir ve sağ kalanlar Alduin önderliğinde zamanda kaybolur. Bu olay Elf Çağında gerçekleşir. Peki ortalıkta hiç ejderha kalmamış mıydı? Kesinlikle vardı. Nafaalilargus
Elder Scrolls Travels: Redguard oyununda Nafaalilargus adında kırmızı bir ejderha bulunuyor. Bu ejderha Tiber Septim’e hizmet etmiştir. Tiber Septim ESO’nun geçtiği dönemden 300 yıl sonrasında bulunmakta. Ejderhalar bir nevi ölümsüzdür, tekrar canlandırılabilirler. Eğer olur da Elder Scrolls Online’da ejderha görürsek şaşırmak doğru olmaz. Çünkü Nafaalilargus adındaki bu Ejderha, ESO’nun geçtiği dönemde hayatta.
Bir diğer Ejderha ise Skakmat adındaki yeşil ejderha. Kendisi Betony Savaşı’nda bulunmuştur (Savaş 3. Çağ 402’de yaşandı). Savaşın tarihine baktığımızda ESO’dan sonra olduğunu görüyoruz ve demek ki Skakmat’ın da bu dönemde yaşıyor olma ihtimali var. Fakat ejderhaları görecek miyiz, orası yapımcıların insafına kalmış…
İkinci İmparatorluk
ESO, fetret devrinde geçiyor. Hemen Osmanlı aklınıza gelmesin, Elder Scrolls’ta Interregnum adında geçiyor. Reman’ın kurmuş olduğu İkinci İmparatorluk, Üçüncü Reman’ın Morag Tong tarafından öldürülmesiyle taht Akaviri kökenli yöneticilere geçmiştir. Versidue-Shaie sonrasında Savirien-Chorak başa geçmiştir.
İmparatorluğa musallat olan Morag Tong örgütü, Savirien Chorak’ı ve tüm sülalesini 2. Çağ 430 yılında katletmiştir. Böylece tahtın varisi kalmamış ve tüm bölgeler bağımsızlıklarını ilan etmiştir. Tamriel tam bir kargaşa alanına döndü özetle.
Akavir İstilası
Akavir’deki topluluklar birden fazla kez Tamriel’ı istila etti. Oyunun geçtiği zamanın öncesinde Ada’Soom Dir-Kamal adında bir Akavir generalinin ordusuyla yaptığı istilayı ele alacağım. Skyrim İç Savaşı.
Bu şahıs ordusuyla beraber 2. Çağın 572. yılında Skyrim’in kuzey sahillerine yani Windhelm’e saldırıyor ve burayı yağmalıyor. İleride kurulacak olan Ebonheart Pact’ın kralı Jorunn the Skald-King’in annesi ise Skyrim’in kraliçesi ve tahtın varisi olan ablası yağma sırasında şehirde bulunmaktaydı. Akavirili askerler şehri yağmalar ve herkesi öldürür. Ölenler arasında Jorunn’un annesi ve ablası da bulunmaktadır.
Kendi ordusunu toplayan Jorunn, Morrowind’den gelen Almalexia’nın ordusuyla ve Black Marsh’tan gelen Argonian mızraklı birliği ile birleşip Ada’Soom Dir-Kamal’ın ordusunu bozguna uğratır. Düşman ordusu denize dökülür. Fakat bu yetmez, Vivec Dunmer birliklerine suyun altında nasıl nefes alınacağını öğretir. Yüzerek kaçmaya çalışan Akavir askerlerini yakalayan Dark Elfler bunları boğarak öldürür. Ada’Soom Dir-Kamal’ın ordusundan geriye hiçbir şey kalmaz.
Argonian, Dark Elf ve Nordlar bu tehdide karşı birleşmiştir ve üçlünün arasında asırlardır süren düşmanlık yerini zoraki bir birlikteliğe bırakmıştır. Daggerfall Covenant’tan sonra kurulan ikinci ittifak Ebonheart’ın kuruluşu bu şekilde gerçekleşir.
Mannimarco
Daha önce Daggerfall ve Oblivion oyunlarında gördüğümüz Solucan Kral Mannimarco, Elder Scrolls Online’da baş kötüler arasında yer alıyor. Sahip olduğu mistik güçlerle ölüleri diriltip onları yöneten bu büyücü, Abnur Tharn’ın komutasında bir ölüler ordusu kuruyor. Aynı zamanda Tamriel’ı Coldharbour’a çekmesi için Molag Bal ile de iş birliği içinde. Önce geçmişine biraz göz atalım.
Mannimarco bir High Elf ve Psijic Order’da yetişir. Burada iyi bir eğitim alır ve örgütün diğer gözbebeği Vanus Galerion ile sıkı fıkı olur. Lakin bu başarı onu kör eder ve Mannimarco kara büyüye merak salar. Ruhlarla uğraşır, ölüleri diriltir. Bu durumdan haberdar olan Vanus sert bir dille arkadaşını uyarır. Karanlık işlerle uğraşan Mannimarco, dostunu kaale almaz. Psijic Order’da bu gidişattan memnun olmaz ki, kuvvetle ihtimal Mannimarco’yu buradan uzaklaştırmak amacıyla Tamriel’a göreve gönderir.
Vanus bu durumun daha kötü olacağını tahmin eder, çünkü o zamanlar Tamriel’de, yani ana kıtada adam akıllı bir büyücü okulu yoktur. Mannimarco’nun burada elini kolunu sallaya sallaya kara büyüyle uğraşacağını düşünen Vanus okuldan ayrılıp Mages Guild’i kurar. Mannimarco, Tamriel’da çok sayıda takipçi ve hizmetkar toplar, tam bir ölüler ordusu kurmuştur artık. Aynı zamanda Vanus da bir büyücü ordusu kurmuştur ve “Mannimarco’yu ben yarattım, durdurmak benim sorumluluğumda” felsefesi ile yaşamaktadır.
Mannimarco sonunda ininden büyük ordusuyla çıkar ve büyük savaşın yapılacağı yere gelir. Mannimarco’nun ordusu çok sayıda Golem çağırır fakat Vanus’un ekibi çok tecrübelidir, Mannimarco’nun ordusu mağlup olur. Vanus önemli bir şey keşfeder: Mannimarco kendisini bir lich’e dönüştürmüştür. Keşfetmesine keşfetti ama, Vanus savaşta hayatını kaybeder lakin kazanan taraf olmuştur.
İttifakların Kurulması
2. Çağ 541 tarihinde Reach bölgesinin yerlileri olan Breton halkı High Rock’ı işgal eder. Daggerfall, Camlorn, Shornhelm, Evermore ve Wayrest kendi arasında ittifak yapar ve Daggerfall Covenant kurulur.
563 yılında ise Wayrest Kralı olan Emeric ittifakın başına geçer. Ebonheart cephesinde ise Akavir istilasına karşı birleşen Dark Elf, Nord ve Argonianlar ittifaklarını bozmaz ve Ebonheart Pakt kurulur. Aldmeri Dominion’da ise, Emeric taç giydiği sene ortadan kaybolan tahtın varisi Ayrenn tam 17 yıl sonra vatan topraklarına geri döner.
Rahmetli kral Hidellith’in yerine tahta geçmeye hazırlanan Naemon’un heyecanı kursağında kalır ve asıl taht sahibi Ayrenn 580 yılında tacı giyer. Böylece Aldmeri Dominion’da kendi birliğini sağlamış olur. Ayrenn’in başa geçmesinden üç yıl sonrasında ise ittifaklar arasındaki savaş başlar.
Elder Scrolls Online’a hoş geldiniz…

Alien: Isolation is the story of Baby Ripley going in search of the presumed dead Mama Ripley.
While Alien: Isolation has some good things going for it, the gameplay itself drags it down and ultimately makes for a highly repetitive and frustrating experience. Alien: Isolation is NOT a shooter. It is a survival horror which plays heavily on stealth elements. Yes there are guns - but they are not a focal point.
The Good:
- The ambiance is simply fantastic. Everything from the lighting (swirling fans and fog effects) to the clanging of unknown noises in the vents. You feel like you are being hunted. It's awesome.
The Bad
- Simply put the gameplay itself is rather frustrating. In most scenarios your goal is to sneak past enemies without them detecting you. You have ways to execute this by using tactics such as hiding under tables, in closets, behind furniture, and finding alternative routes such as hidden vents. This becomes frustrating because some enemies (ahem, Alien) have close to zero patterns of movement. They seem to move as they please. When the Alien kills you twenty times due to its erratic pathing the game is no longer fun and just becomes obnoxiously tedious.
- The game feels dragged out - far beyond what is necessary. You finish one mission simply to find you now must do something else; the game just keeps putting barriers in your way. This is fine to some degree but at a certain point it no longer feels natural - it simply feels like the designers wanted to make the game longer by forcing you to complete irrelevent things over and over. If I wanted some chores to do I would call my mom.
Overall, Alien: Isolation's environment is beautiful. Unfortunately, the gameplay is not. It is boring, reptitive, and drags on and on with no clear direction or rhyme and reason.
Alien: Isolation takes about 15 hours to complete.

ESC: The Video Game
Nah, but the game is scary as hell. It perfectly captures the mood of the original Alien film from 1979. It has this dark and forbodding kind of atmosphere that can't be replicated anywhere but the Alien universe. The graphics... are stunning. No, check that, they're ♥♥♥♥♥♥-inducing. These are are some of the best video game graphics to date besides EA's Battlefront by DICE. Everything is detailed to an upmost extreme, which can extend your gameplay hours a ton. You'll just wander around the ship looking at signs and listening to recording tapes, that is, when you're not being hunted by the lone Xenomorph. Unlike the previous Aliens: Colonial Marines, which isn't half bad in my opinion, this game goes for the chilling survival experience, like what Amnesia did. The alien is an unstoppable threat, so your only chance of survival is to avoid it and not get caught by it. When you do, you get the biggest jumpscare you've ever had in a video game. Be sure to try to avoid it. It's hard to though, so you're always tense whenever just walking the ship by your lonesome, listening to creaks in the vents and hearing the ship fall apart. This is definately an auditory game. You need good sound to get the best out of this experience. My advice? Turn off all the lights, put on some surround headphones, turn the settings in-game to maximum, and make it fullscreen. You will♥♥♥♥♥♥your pants. So, yes, I absolutely highly recommend the game. It's a frightening experience with a large campaign that will keep you tense all the way to the end. One minor note though: AVOID THE DLC.

I'm a huge fan of the Alien movie, and I have to say I might like this even more than the movie. It has a gripping and terrifying story, with what's in my opinion excellently executed gameplay. It has genuinely frightening environments even in areas without any bodies or enemies, and my favorite thing about the environment is that they kept the design language exactly the same as the Alien movie. The technology in Alien is such an interesting mix of old and new, and I think they nailed it in the game between the sound effects, the hardware design, and the software design. Also, Being that there's really not any large open environments, that gives the game a huge performance benefit (my overclocked GTX 860m can run it on ultra with hardly ever dropping below 60fps at 1080p). If you're a fan of the original Alien movie, I'd definitely pick up this game.

Whether or not you like Transistor depends on whether or not you're immediately charmed by the graphics. Those are definitely the games strongest point, if you're into them. They're quite nice, but there are plenty of other games with great graphics.
The narration undoubtedly takes a page (or the entire book) from Bastion with the talking sword, but it's pretty sparse, and doesn't really deliver too much, especially in terms of story. Undoubtedly, its weakest point, the story confuses minimilism with sparseness. There's incredibly little motivation, information about what is happening, or really much of anything. It's really disappointing. Minimalism should highlight the best parts of game by cutting the worst parts out, rather than leaving out the core of what a story needs to have.
The combat is pretty iffy. Not really terrible, but around the third wave of enemy upgrades, the game decides to frustrate you, throwing away its own mechanics in a desperate attempt to keep the game fresh. Otherwise, it's quite easy, even with keeping all of the handicaps on. There's no other gameplay besides the combat.
The interface (especially the access point screen) is clunky, at best. If you wanted to build your build from scratch, it'll take 20 or so screen switches by mid game. By end game, it might go as high as 32 screen switches. Very slow, and while the game treats you with story to reward switching up your build, it punishes you big time with the sheer amount of effort it takes to do so.
Personally, I liked the graphics, but I don't believe they can carry a game, and nothing else about Transistor was particularly enticing.

As you're likely aware, most of the hype for Transistor is due to the success of a little game called Bastion. Bastion was released on Steam in 2011, where it met acclaim due to its art-style, musical direction, and use of a running Narrator revealing the tragic story behind the Great Calamity. With Transistor being recently released, Super-giant has created a different but still engaging successor to Bastion.
My current playtime of 4 and a half hours is how long it took me to hit the end credits. I've thoroughly enjoyed those last four hours, more enjoyment than I've had in most games released in the last few years. I was glued to my seat the entire time and forsook a bath-room break to see the entire story to conclusion.
Playing as Red, you travel the surreal world of Cloudbank using a device referred to as the Transistor. Unlike Bastion, the combat is a blend between Planning and Real-time. This combat is augmented by the use of Functions (skills acquired by leveling-up and exploration). The greatest strength of the gameplay can be seen in the complexity of these functions. I switched through about 20-odd loadouts through the game and felt a total change in how the combat played out. With each set having its own strengths and weaknesses. Comparing it to Bastion, you only have the Transistor, but you have more unique skills, upgrades, and control than Bastion. My biggest criticism of this combat is that some abilities are imbalanced. Cull + Void can one-shot just about anything with a quick downtime, and Jaunt + Spark allows you to perform constant damage at minimal risk. I found myself using the Planning side of the combat more (queuing abilities using Action points) because of just how chaotic the latter sections of the game are. Since most of the enemies fire bullets and beams, there's a lot of action on screen, and when you throw it certain enemies (like the Snapshots) real-time combat can be a chore at times.
Something quite unnecessary to comment on is the game's art and sound direction. It's different, but it's as well-executed and memorable as Bastion. There is little more to say- colors pop, musical talent bleeds through every pore, and heart and soul can be found at every avenue.
The story however is an odd duckling. As Super-giant's take on Sci-fi, the game explores futuristic concepts and plot points. The characters are all well-grounded and believable, though unfortunately you interact with most of them only through text screens. The Transistor is somewhat of a highlight (voiced by the Narrator from Bastion). He lacks that immediate cool factor and due to Red being mute most of the exchanges are one-sided. There are great moments to be had between the two, one of which is when she has to use a computer terminal to speak with him. Yet I doubt he'll become as well-loved as Logan Cunningham's Narrator performance in Bastion.
Speaking of terminals, Cloudbank is littered with them, and unlike Bastion, text is the primary method of communicating the world's history and events. It's all interesting to read but unfortunately puts a disconnect between the player and the world. You experience the changing state of the world, but it's hard to care about the people as the game goes along. Their stories occur outside Red's viewpoint. You don't have the sad, omnipresent musings of the Bastion Narrator here, but the comments of the Transistor. He is equally as melancholy but much less in the know...
Which is a bit of a problem because Cloudbank is MC-Escher-odd to put it bluntly. It's a city where the landscape changes by popular poll, the people speak of the 'Country' like it's heaven, people and things can be processed into the data. The nature and history of Cloudbank were nowhere to be found on my first play-through. Which makes the environments and story seem dreamlike and difficult to connect with as things steadily start to be become ungrounded and head into sci-fi territory. Characters are unnecessarily vague and seem to be in a trance. Some pieces of dialogue are delivered as if they're a profound founding, but these dialogues are little more than platitudes. The villains are... well their motivations were easy to understand, but it seems like a lot of plot points go unanswered.
Which is how the story is for me, the big parts are delivered with ease. You understand the motivations, what the Transistor is, what the Process is. But the little details, the ones that make plot-holes and seem to be buried underneath layers of text somewhere, aren't well handled. It's almost like they went for an approach popularized in the Demon/Dark Souls series, where fan-theory will be the only answers available. As cool an approach as that can be, I'd liked for the plot here to be more concrete, for the author to intrigue me with amazing dialogue, world-design, and characters. I prefer that to having to find my own answers to all the questions because characters are too vague.
I want to say that the story was a simple but well-told and thematic tale. But the theming of Transistor does feels weaker than Bastion and it's much too complicated for how short the game is. The characters also feel less charismatic and likeable, but this is just my personal tastes showing.
So, why am I recommending it?
Well, the gameplay is without the faintest doubt in my mind unique, solid, customizable, and engaging. Exploring the early part of Cloudbank felt like exploring the Caelondia the Narrator always talked about in Bastion. The world-design is dynamic, ever-changing, and the effect the Process has on Cloudbank is saddening and is a more effective motivation for stopping them than what the plot implies. Speaking of that plot, the Transistor and Red's relationship are simple, human, which helps ground the setting better and provides a point where the audience understands that humans actually live in Cloudbank. The whole plot however is a bit esoteric. The villains while nicely voice-acted lacked development. For what the game's plot was trying to be, it needed more time to flourish. Yet the time I spent with Transistor I have no qualms in saying I enjoyed it deeply and don't regret dropping $20 for it. If that quantity of time bothers you, it'll go on sale eventually.
And for those that are interested, yes there's a new-game plus where both you and the Process return to duke it out in Cloudbank. There are also optional side-challenges that unlock music tracks and mostly inconsequential dialogue  (which I didn't care about, because that's just how I roll)  and extra lore to unlock by maxing out each Functions' File.
If I must lament anything however, it's the lack of more human characters in Transistor to go along with the more complicated story. I feel more viewpoints would have built the world in such way to equal what the Stranger and the Kid did together in Bastion. Or that Transistor was longer, so less of the main plot had to be bum-rushed and more time was spent discovering, exploring, and learning. The game didn't outstay it's welcome, but I will say that I'd hope we'd gotten to desserts before it decided to pay the tip and head out.
***As a side note currently users have been experiencing stuttering and frame-drops. I had it so bad after three hours I had to restart my computer. It worked perfectly fine for me after that, but be advised that you may encounter performance issues if you buy at launch.

Personally I think it's fine, it's not the best Sonic game in the world but it was still very entertaining. The graphics were amazing, the story was okay, could've been better, the voice acting for me personally was okay, but some lines felt a bit forced. Now the gameplay was the best part for me, the modern stages felt fast, not Unleashed or Generations fast but fast, the 2D sections were a bit weird, sometimes you'd jump really high, sometimes you didn't, sometimes you would run really quick randomly and other times slower which made the 2D platforming hell for me. The same can go for all the 2D sections including Classic and the Custom character. Like I said Classic didn't control very well for me so I liked his stages the least. And last the Custom Character, his/her stages were personally the best of them all, they were fun to traverse through and the Wispon ability made the stages easier to complete. However, despite how good the stages were, they were just way too short, if the stages controlled easier and were longer I'd give this game a better score. Then there's the bosses, Zavok, Shadow, Chaos and Metal Sonic were hyped up a lot, only to be used once and some even not used as bosses but rather background characters. The infinite bosses were way too easy and not challenging at all. The death egg robot was a bit harder than the others but still felt easy. Like always, Sonic games always give us the best music, I loved all the music in this game, and I loved that they brought vocal songs back. Overall I'll give it a 7.5/10. However I think that £50 is a bit too much for how short it is.

Only played the opening stage, and I can say that this by far is the most clunky, slow, and overall boring Sonic game I've ever played. Refunding immediately. The difficulty, even on "hard" mode is essentially a child's game. If anyone finds this game even remotely interesting, I will be shocked.
Edit:
This is coming from a long time fan of Sonic, both good and bad I've managed to play my way through every single game that's released. I wasn't even able to get through 2 levels before I decided to put this down.

I, at least, had fun with it. It was engaging enough in its story and atmosphere to keep me invested enough to finish the game, something that I haven't done with a Sonic game in a very long time. The character creation was nice, though admittedly the custom characters kinda look like weird Sonic-Toontown hybrids to me. The gameplay, especially some of the platforming, was kinda iffy, but tolerable enough. Combat was pretty fun though. That said, Classic Sonic felt kinda forced to me, an element only added because Generations was successful, and I think Tails could easily have fulfilled his role in the story. The visuals, music, and even the voice acting were all fantastic, and I did genuinely enjoy myself.
In terms of performance, I ran into some issue with my system (which is near the minimum specs, just a touch above), particularly with the cutscenes, which ran at about 20-22 fps even when the rest of the game ran fine. However, putting Steam into big picture mode fixed the issue. Otherwise, the only significant slowdown I encountered was because of particle effects, and was tolerable and short lived.
All together, I'd say that this is a good game, but maybe wait until a sale if you're unsure of whether you want to buy it.

I reccomend the game, but there are issues.
The good :
Fun combat system, different swings for different angles and situations in melee, bows crossbows and spears to the basic ranged fighting.
The throne. Very fun to have the throne to fight over and a tax rate that you can choose, should you become king.
Building system is very easy to use and you can make some really awesome stuff. I guess it's like minecraft building but I have never played minecraft.
Good amount of stuff to do. Raiding, farming items, farming materials, crafting weapons and armor, crafting torture devices, capturing other players, building, becoming king. And more.
The bad:
Hackers are all over the busy non-passworded servers. The servers without hackers usually don't  have a very active player base so I find that I spend alot of time alone or raiding people that I have never actually seen online.
Glitchy as hell inventory on most servers. I have had many characters not be able to use their starter gear and have either been forced to leave the server or run around collecting sticks to make a club and then finally be on the same footing as other fresh spawns.  I have been told to relog to fix this... relogging usually makes my entire inventory disappear and I cannot do anything with the character any more.
Today, 3/28/15, I managed to make a character without glitched starter gear / inventory, and after about 5 minutes of farming I made a Stone axe for cutting wood, the axe did not work, much like my starter items on the other characters I have made, but my club did, and suddenly my bandages stopped working also.
To clarify, when I say my items "stopped working" I mean that the item is in my inventory, assigned to my action keys (1-6) and when I select the item it appears to be selected on my action keys hud but my character is not holding it and will not swing the item or use it (banadge myself, eat, drink etc)
I have been told that server owners can delete my characters file stored in the server files but I have only found 1 admin who knew how to do it.
And I have only made 1 character who was able to claim the throne. All of my characters have the option to "Claim Throne" by pressing E or Q or whatever the default key is, but nothing happens. Much like my inventory issue, the interface to use it lights up green like it is working but nothing ever happens.
My advice is this, get the game and give it a try, it's worth the $20, but be prepared for issues, like 90% of the steam games I play, it is still in "early access" beta/alpha stages. I am glad I bought it but I will limit my play time until these issues are fixed. It's far too frustrating to even try to play at this point.

STALKER Shadow of Chernobyl is my favorite game of all time. There's no way to properly express how fantastic it is. But I'll try I suppose.
The game takes place in Chernobyl, as the title suggests, though this Chernobyl is a much more mysterious one. After scientists went and messed around in Chernobyl after the disaster, weird crap started happening. Blowouts, anomalies, artifacts, and nasty warped mutants craving human flesh. The game is a mix between the real life place Chernobyl, obviously, mixed in with world and plot elements from the novel Roadside Picnic (which is my favorite book ever) and the film based on the book, Stalker (which is a great film too). I will never know why they picked that book, Chernobyl, and mutants in one game but one can only think it must've been some divine force that made it happen. The game is a lot like a realistic, Slavic, and overall more terrifying version of Fallout. Not saying that Fallout is bad though.
Gameplay is top-notch, the shooting is pretty great and going and finding artifacts can be really tricky. Depending on your alliances, you'll go up against either bandits, different factions, loners, or everyone. The fights are intense and may require many reloads before you figure out how to stump your enemies. This is not an easy game at all, even on the easier difficulties. It's hard as balls and will mess you up hard, you can't go without quicksaving. I'm not good at videogames, so it was a struggle to finish this one, but it was worth it.
I can't go talking about a game without talking about it's faults though, no matter how much I adore it. The AI is weird in this one.... it goes from Vash the Stampede level of accuracy to the level of skill you'd expect from a drunk man. The graphics aren't exactly triple-A material either but the atmosphere and the overall visual design makes up for it.
STALKER: Shadow of Chernobyl is an interesting and unique title; there really isn't anything like it. It has its bugs and technical isssues, yes, but that won't stop me from loving truly awesome, scary, intense game. In the words of Number 6™, "There's nothing quite like Russian post-apocalyptic fiction, comrade!"

Alien Isolation is a survival horror game set after the events of Alien. You play as Amanda Ripley, Daughter of Eleanor Ripley, who is searching for answers as too the whereabouts of her Mother.
It plays similar to the style of Amnesia, where you can't kill the main enemy, the Xenomorph. Like the first film, there is only one Xenomorph, which is a nice touch. This adds to one of the problems that this game has which is constant throwbacks and references to the films. If you
have seen any of the films, you can guess where the story is going to go and what is going to happen to characters. I understand them wanting to please the fans but it becomes too much at points and just copy and paste parts of the films. I think it would of been better to just have little references like props and locations that are similar and make a story that stands alone.
The gameplay is odd. The main idea of the game is to hide because you cannot kill many enemies. In theory it sounds good but eventually you realize that objectives would take about 2 minutes if it wasn't for people or the Xenomorph being in the way. It just makes the game feel dragged out instead of tense. The combat feels clunky and moving about feels very sluggish. Hiding also has this problem where enemy's will instanly come near your hiding spot after you are in a locker or storage area no matter where they are. It doesn't make it tense or scary, it just means it takes longer to move.
The Story is quite weak aswell. For a 15 hour campaign you spend a lot of time walking to rooms and looking at a computer or flicking a switch.  There are lots of little side story's that don't really matter too much and repeat the same thing of "We are trying to escape and this Person/Alien/Power Outtage/Computer has stopped us". It's not really all that compelling after doing this for 10 hours.
It's annoying as I am a fan of the Alien franchise and After the "game" that was Colonial Marines, I was looking forward to this game. The great reviews did seal the deal with my excitement and I was ready for Thee Alien game. But I was just left bored and dissapointed.
I can understand why people liked this game. It does a pretty good job at creating atmosphere and having tense set pieces for you to survive. The flashback scene was incredible and exploring The Delerict was easily the best part of the game. But it just has too many flaws that I couldn't get invested in it. Back tracking through the whole game, bad AI, disjointed story, and all the other problems were just too much to actually enjoy.
I would say to play this for yourself and make up your on opinion. I personally didn't enjoy this game but I know others will. If you have seen the films and you are an Alien fan, you will probably like this game. This is the only reason I will still recommend it.

This is the first review I've written in a very long time, if ever. This game is so deserving of it.
Factorio is of a genre that many many games have attempted. Crashed on an alien infested planet, you must now use the resources around you to craft bigger and better stuff and survive. Only Factorio has ever pulled this off to my content, and at an immense level. Factorio is a game you could sit down and play for hours upon hours. A friend and I meant to stay up for 2 or 3 hours playing our multiplayer world. We wound up playing for nearly 14 hours straight.
Pros:
- Solid Multiplayer
- Good campaign
- Excellent tutorial and tips
- Research is challenging, but achievable
- Late game tech is insanely expensive and not world endingly OP
- Pre-requisite auto-build; I.e. Items that require an intermediate craft product, will automatically craft the intermediate in inventory. Crafting a steam boiler requires a stone furnace. Alright after a year of this being released I have to change my review...
I played a couple hundred hours of the closed beta and then I played some time after the release. Initially I was really happy that IMC added European servers etc. to the release after enough people complained. I thought it was mental that they were going to release worldwide with just 2 US servers.
It was all downhill from that.
1. The game is so, so full of bots. I find myself reporting so many bots per day and when bots can actually whisper you back and laugh at you even though you caught them red handed. You know that they have just been doing this for months and don't care at all.
2. There's absolutely nothing 'social' about this game at all. You can join a guild but unless you join one that is so super active there's really no one to talk to. Most of the people online are just afk vendors that are trying to make a bit of money charging for repairs. Also you can't really find a decent guild into up around level 200.
3. There's just no pvp at all in this game, and you can't really get into Pvp until level 100 which is just mental. If you're new to the game chances are you aren't going to hit level 100 all that easy. Well when you finally get there the Pvp starts but it's just so unbalanced and there's very little content for Pvp at that stage.
4. Instances are few and they're quite boring. There's no rare drops or anything. You just smash minions and trash and then hit the boss hoping that you get something decent out of your reward cube like a card to make a bit of silver. Instances take a while to complete and if a party member leaves you can't get anyone else to come in. Also you have to constantly go to the instance entrance map and queue there which sucks because some of them are in the middle of nowhere and that means less people do the instance. Finally you can also just insta-clear the dungeons if you are bored by using a clear card and I mean really. This is just the dumbest thing I've ever seen in my life. It literally means you can just buy exp boosts, insta-clear cards and as long as you get a group of 5 you can insta-finish your daily 3 dungeons immediately. The levelling system is totally bs, and the fact that you are capped at 2 or 3 instances a day in order to space out the levelling is just such a stupid design mechanic.
5. Making money is impossible without a token and well so is anything else. You get 30% extra exp with a Token and you get to list 9 more items on the market. You absolutely have to have one to make any money or to be able to level efficiently. I know this is to force people to buy a token so IMC gets money but I regret my first token purchase because I don't feel like IMC deserves it.

This is the first game from supergiant done completely on their own (Warner Bros. published Bastion) and it is a testament to what indie studios can accomplish when they aren't fettered by a large studio. I wasn't exactly sure what to expect with Transistor and while it is the spiritual successor to Bastion a lot of it is very different and everything that it borrows from Bastion is improved.
The art style, music, and narration are all in the same vein as Bastion, which is to say they are a masterpiece. The artwork is very beautiful especially during cutscenes and found myself taking screen shots constantly for desktop backgrounds, etc. The music is a big part of the experience as well, and just as in Bastion, both the music and the artwork set the scene. I would not say they improved on Bastion because that would be saying Bastion was flawed in those aspects. And Bastion is more of a western feel while Transistor is very much a cyber-punk game. However, the artwork is more detailed, rich, and beautiful, probably due to the fact that this is a newer game. I also feel that the music is a bit more developed and varied. The narration is also wonderful.
The gameplay has changed significantly from Bastion, so if you're expecting the fun but rather simple gameplay of Bastion, you will be pleasantly surprised. In Transistor, you only have one weapon, if you can call it that. Your weapon looks like a sword, but it is more like a computer that you can upload programs to. Those programs are your powers and you pick them up as you progress through the game. The awesome thing about these programs is that they have three different uses. You can use them as active powers, passive powers, or you can use them to alter other active powers. For example, you have an area of effect attack, and an attack that gets enemies to fight for you. You can alter the AOE attack with the conversion attack and you have an AOE attack that converts enemies. This obviously gives you an immense amount of flexibility in combat and very different gameplay styles and approaches to defeating your enemies.
These programs/abilities are then socketed onto your sword, which is the Transistor of the games title. In keeping with the cyberpunk theme, your Transistor has a limited amount of RAM...each program uses different levels of RAM...some only take up one space of RAM, others take up more. Another cool thing about your Transistor is that it is the narrator for your game...I don't want to say too much because I don't want to give away the story, but it all makes sense a little while into the game.
Another thing that makes the gameplay very fun is that you can pause time on the battlefield. While paused, you can move around the battlefield, and choose which powers you want to use and which enemies you want to target. This allows you to escape when surrounded, or flank your enemies (since attacks from behind do more damage). This gives the game a turn-based feel to it. It does not really feel like a hack and slash at all...you can use your powers in real-time as well, but when facing very powerful enemies, you will die very quickly when using that tactic.
I have not actually died yet while playing but I have discovered another thing about the gameplay in almost doing so. When you're health bar gets to zero, you don't immediately die, you simply lose one of the programs you have socketed into your Transistor. My assumption is that you will die after you lose all four programs. This also requires you to carefully plan which programs you use and how you have them modified, etc. Just another thing that makes this game awesome.
Finally, the story is very intriguing. You play as Red who is a famous artist and singer. Apparently, there's a group called the Camerati (sounds kind of Mafia-ish) who is angry at you for some reason and they try to kill you. They have also killed the other important people in the city you live in (called Cloudbank). That is all I can say since I haven't played it completely yet, and I don't want to give anything important away. But I can say that the story is very intriguing and every aspect of the game helps tell it.

Five hours in so far and I must say I'm loving it. Similar art style to bastion but with a digital and art nouveau coat of paint. The story is interesting and has some rather deep themes of self determination and a p[erson's place in a near utopian world.
The world itself is a beautiful depiction of the ultimate ideal of a democratic free market utopia with hints of a plot worthy of John Galt's madness. It's nice to see the idea of people trying to make a utopia better, it is an over looked plot idea.
On top of that the game is a wonder to play. The combat is deep and layered, with a lot of the choices firmly under player control. The game encourages actively varying one's play style as it is the only way to learn more about the world and the people in it. The turn mechanics is interesting and does require thought and preparation, as things don't always work out the way you expect them to, esspecially later when enemies begin to passively inteact with you when the time stop is enabled.
So far my only qualms are with the default mouse and keyboard controls, they just seem a bit awkward, if you're determined to play on mouse and keyboard I would advise binding the abilities to buttons on the mouse, or just using a controller, the controls are very tight and most of the time precision is only required when using Turn, and those mistakes can be undone easily.
$20 may seem a bit steep but this game is worth it. If you can't aford it then I would highly adivse putting it on your wishlist and grabbing it as soon as it goes on sale, or watch the Humble Bundle page like a hawk. Suffice to say, Super Giant Games has done it again and created another game that I will hold up with a "Games are Art" sign.

The art direction and style is the only thing top notch here.
The music was ok... The main theme was over used and abused too much, and the lyrics were pretty bad. If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.
Eat. [2]

I'm changing my original review, although not changing the fact I do not reccommend this particular S.T.A.L.K.E.R.
Pros:
1) A pretty epic story
2) Fun battle encounters
3) Entertaining throughout the game.
Cons:
1) The constant rocking when walking takes serious getting used to & will most likely make you dizzy at first.
2) Broken English and inaccurate subtitles are sometimes a minor hinderance.
3) There's a serious issue with glitches. Mission glitches, Secret Stash glitches, enemy spawning glitches, & every now and them you'll get environmental glitches like getting permanantly stuck behind or inside and objector even falling through the ground entiriely.
4) The moster AI leaves something to be desired (they are stupid).
5) The saving, although relatively simple (Press ESC, click save, select save spot, confirm, then click return), it does ruin the fluidity of game-play when you have to save every 5-10min or risk losing all your progress. A simple quicksave key would have fixed this issue.
6) Compared to other S.T.A.L.K.E.R games, there's a serious lack of weapons & modifications. In fact, the only mods you can do is add & remove scopes on a select few weapons & an undermount grenade launcher on even fewer weapons. There's also a supressor you can change onto any handgun.
7) Death, you die, a lot! Specifically as you get closer to the end of the game, which frankly, just becomes irritating.
Altogether this game is a conundrum to me, I did like playing the game, but I don't think I would reccomend this game anyways, simply because all of the  "Con"  factors & the fact that you have two better choices in the S.T.A.L.K.E.R series.

Don't let my Steam gametime stats fool you - I've been around the Zone for quite some time...
The first STALKER game I played was - funnily enough - the last one released in the series: Call of Pripyat. But eventually, I  got around to GSC's debut entry in the franchise.  And boy, was I glad that I did. About five years, three playthroughs and one
PC upgrade later, I've come to understand and appreciate ShoC for what it was meant to be, buried beneath all those bugs: one truly tense and atmospheric game. ShoC is a distinctive game (indeed, STALKER is a distinctive franchise): if you like fairly open-world gameplay that combines FPS, RPG and OMG HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥elements, this is one cheeki breeki game for you.
Thanks to the fine people who worked on the Zone Reclamation Project patch, ShoC was basically transformed from a glitchy, bug-fest (at least upon release) into a cult classic. ZRP, unlike other mods such as the oft-lauded Complete, gives you something really special: a leaner, meaner Zone to chew on, compared to Complete. It's basically vanilla ShoC 2.0 - an ESSENTIAL mod if ever there was one. Complete is pretty good for what it is: a 'complete' overhaul that, despite its claims, really DOES change the gameplay. Quite simply, it's much easier than ZRP/vanilla ShoC (even on Master difficulty) and those epic gunfights where you trade bullets with bandits is compressed. For a game where combat is so important, Complete totally streamlines it. Yet it's still one worth checking out on subsequent playthroughs, as it does introduce a whole host of pretty neat features and spiffy new textures (among bug fixes and the like) but ultimately, you'll end up playing ShoC Lite. It's a really pretty and fairly deep ShoC Lite, though, which is totally fine for those who want that kind of experience. I started with Complete all those years and playthroughs ago on my gimped laptop and while I totally dug STALKER the game, I really am glad that I got to play through what I consider the authentic STALKER experience with ZRP - the changes Complete makes are glaringly obvious if you play Complete then ZRP/vanilla. Complete's good - hell, pretty great in some respects - but it's not really STALKER. Though I am looking forward to trying out mods like Oblivion Lost and AMK for ShoC. There are tons of mods out there for ALL the STALKER games.
For your maiden voyage into the Zone, though, the ZRP and Shaders MAX mods (which improve FPS rates and can even introduce major graphical improvements while retaining a vanilla feel) are trustier allies than all the perfect condition AK-47's in the world combined.
Now get out of here, STALKER!
