Great game (even in Alpha), yes it has its issues as does every game when in Alpha... thats the point of being in Alpha, to sort out the bugs and hackers and what not.
If games didn't have an alpha or beta release then the gaming industry would die in a fire due to no one buying games becuase their to buggy. Any one complaining about a game thats in alpha or beta needs a head check...
The game itself is alot of fun, even with hackers storming through servers. At the moment there isn't alot of content again due to it being a alpha release but there is still plenty to keep you busy. This game has a huge amount of potential and will hopefully go far. I have been playing this game for about a week now and have enjoyed every second of it. Yes the hackers and griefers do get annoying but once development is further progressed I dont think they will be an issue.
A tip for people trying to play this game solo... Don't, it's not a single player game, get some friends into it or make friends in game and create or join a guild, the game becomes alot more fun when your playing with multiple people.
Combat is alot of fun, an example of this is from my own experience, I had just made a set of leather armor and iron tools and sword and was running around gathering more resources when I was attacked by 2 fresh players, they killed me as they were able to run faster then me since i was wearing armor and they weren't. They completely looted everything I had and split my items between themselves, I respawned on the beach and ran right back to my corpse to find nothing, I then spotted the two of in the distance sorting out who got what from my loot. I ran over to them drift wood club in hand and started another 1v2 fight but this time I got the jump on them, after a 3-4 minute battle I had killed both of them and taken my items back.
The combat system isnt just about who has the best gear in a fight, tactics are needed to win battles. After I finished collecting my gear, I went off to start building my base / castle / house what ever, this is a proccess and to be able to build something when other people are on the server you have to watch your back (as well as everywhere else), as I was putting up the walls of my house I spotted someone standing on my outter wall, he had built up some steps to get over it. I had made the mistake of building the wall to close to my area limits (an area that has been captured using a guild crest, the better quality the crest the more land captured) so he was able to build just outside the captured land limits and jump onto my wall. He did this a few times before I was able to rebuild the wall and stole quite a lot of my resources.
I was annoyed at first but then realised that this is what makes the game unique.
The ability to tresspass on others plot of land and steal from them. There are a number of ways to do this, lockpicking cam be used on many of the doors and gates in the game, being able to pick a lock and sneak in to someones house to steal from them whithout them knowing is a fun and unique aspect of the game, there's also the ability to break through walls and gates/doors using seige weapons such as the trebuchet (which is alot of fun and not that easy to use), or you can break down walls and such by hand using an assortment of weapons currently in the game (this takes far to long though). Not to mention you can capture other players, drag them around in chains and keep then locked up or take a whip to them which is very unique.
Then there's the throne, another unique concept that in my opinion is a lot of fun, being able to claim the throne and take the land and place taxes on the resources. Those who want the throne need to take it by force and like any power struggle there will be tyrants and heroes. Tax can be put at a maximum of 20% or it can be as low as 0%. At 20% you will notice a big difference when your gathering resources. I found this system to be a lot of fun.
Overall I give this game an 8/10.

I've never played a clicker/incremental game as fleshed out as Realm Grinder. It's got the usual staples, but it stands out in the crowd due to its depth and different styles of gameplay thanks to the multiple factions you can choose to play as. There's even one that lets you tweak gameplay to fit your own playing style (or to get certain trophies) where you can pick your own spells and perks.
By far, the best thing about Realm Grinder is that patience and progress are greatly rewarded. While abdications act like the usual revive/rebirth/time travel/whatever that every single clicker game seems to have, reincarnation will bestow many additions that will help you get even further such as more assistants, greater building bonuses, higher chances to find faction coins, and a bigger offline production bonus.
Trophies aren't just for show either; they actually provide upgrades and additional options like auto-casting magic.
The bottom line is anyone giving up on this game early is missing out on most of what the game has to offer. The developer isn't kidding when they say that there's tons of content.
It's almost tempting to say that other companies should learn from Divine Games, but I think most of the clicker fan base probably just wants the mindless kind of gameplay.
Edit: Forgot to mention that I've played this game for a few months now on iOS and currently on Reincarnation 8. Also, for beginners: don't listen to whiners stating that you need an auto-clicker program to get anywhere. Good alignment more or less requires active gameplay but evil alignment is for those that want to progress through idling. If lots of clicking is♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off, just choose evil.

Alien Isolation is a survival horror game set after the events of Alien. You play as Amanda Ripley, Daughter of Eleanor Ripley, who is searching for answers as too the whereabouts of her Mother.
It plays similar to the style of Amnesia, where you can't kill the main enemy, the Xenomorph. Like the first film, there is only one Xenomorph, which is a nice touch. This adds to one of the problems that this game has which is constant throwbacks and references to the films. If you
have seen any of the films, you can guess where the story is going to go and what is going to happen to characters. I understand them wanting to please the fans but it becomes too much at points and just copy and paste parts of the films. I think it would of been better to just have little references like props and locations that are similar and make a story that stands alone.
The gameplay is odd. The main idea of the game is to hide because you cannot kill many enemies. In theory it sounds good but eventually you realize that objectives would take about 2 minutes if it wasn't for people or the Xenomorph being in the way. It just makes the game feel dragged out instead of tense. The combat feels clunky and moving about feels very sluggish. Hiding also has this problem where enemy's will instanly come near your hiding spot after you are in a locker or storage area no matter where they are. It doesn't make it tense or scary, it just means it takes longer to move.
The Story is quite weak aswell. For a 15 hour campaign you spend a lot of time walking to rooms and looking at a computer or flicking a switch.  There are lots of little side story's that don't really matter too much and repeat the same thing of "We are trying to escape and this Person/Alien/Power Outtage/Computer has stopped us". It's not really all that compelling after doing this for 10 hours.
It's annoying as I am a fan of the Alien franchise and After the "game" that was Colonial Marines, I was looking forward to this game. The great reviews did seal the deal with my excitement and I was ready for Thee Alien game. But I was just left bored and dissapointed.
I can understand why people liked this game. It does a pretty good job at creating atmosphere and having tense set pieces for you to survive. The flashback scene was incredible and exploring The Delerict was easily the best part of the game. But it just has too many flaws that I couldn't get invested in it. Back tracking through the whole game, bad AI, disjointed story, and all the other problems were just too much to actually enjoy.
I would say to play this for yourself and make up your on opinion. I personally didn't enjoy this game but I know others will. If you have seen the films and you are an Alien fan, you will probably like this game. This is the only reason I will still recommend it.

I’ve been playing before it arrived on Steam. I’ve had 40 or so hours of absolute fun.  It’s one of the best prices per hour of fun of anything I own.  I’ve only “won” once, so that number will continue to improve; having played once, I learned so much, I’m sure I can do better! The core gameplay is exactly what it sounds like: build an automated factory. At first you’ll be manually mining ore and building tools, but as you want increasingly complex things, or increasingly many things, you’ll automate more and more.  Eventually you’ll have a massive factory that would make Henry Ford proud.  There isn’t alot of “challenge” here; losing isn’t really a possibility using the default settings.  There are aliens, and they do grow more powerful and they do attack more often as your pollution increases, but they’re more of a spice to the gameplay than a core challenge.  The real challenge is closer to a puzzle: how do you optimize your factory, how do you juggle the dozens of different lines of products and materials? As of the early access, some of the UI is really rough. It’s entirely functional, but sometimes what a button does is quite cryptic, and laying rail lines in a pain in the butt.  But they know about and are working on those of these issues (check out their blog!). The game is solid; it hasn’t crashed once in 40 hours of play.

Don't let my Steam gametime stats fool you - I've been around the Zone for quite some time...
The first STALKER game I played was - funnily enough - the last one released in the series: Call of Pripyat. But eventually, I  got around to GSC's debut entry in the franchise.  And boy, was I glad that I did. About five years, three playthroughs and one
PC upgrade later, I've come to understand and appreciate ShoC for what it was meant to be, buried beneath all those bugs: one truly tense and atmospheric game. ShoC is a distinctive game (indeed, STALKER is a distinctive franchise): if you like fairly open-world gameplay that combines FPS, RPG and OMG HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥elements, this is one cheeki breeki game for you.
Thanks to the fine people who worked on the Zone Reclamation Project patch, ShoC was basically transformed from a glitchy, bug-fest (at least upon release) into a cult classic. ZRP, unlike other mods such as the oft-lauded Complete, gives you something really special: a leaner, meaner Zone to chew on, compared to Complete. It's basically vanilla ShoC 2.0 - an ESSENTIAL mod if ever there was one. Complete is pretty good for what it is: a 'complete' overhaul that, despite its claims, really DOES change the gameplay. Quite simply, it's much easier than ZRP/vanilla ShoC (even on Master difficulty) and those epic gunfights where you trade bullets with bandits is compressed. For a game where combat is so important, Complete totally streamlines it. Yet it's still one worth checking out on subsequent playthroughs, as it does introduce a whole host of pretty neat features and spiffy new textures (among bug fixes and the like) but ultimately, you'll end up playing ShoC Lite. It's a really pretty and fairly deep ShoC Lite, though, which is totally fine for those who want that kind of experience. I started with Complete all those years and playthroughs ago on my gimped laptop and while I totally dug STALKER the game, I really am glad that I got to play through what I consider the authentic STALKER experience with ZRP - the changes Complete makes are glaringly obvious if you play Complete then ZRP/vanilla. Complete's good - hell, pretty great in some respects - but it's not really STALKER. Though I am looking forward to trying out mods like Oblivion Lost and AMK for ShoC. There are tons of mods out there for ALL the STALKER games.
For your maiden voyage into the Zone, though, the ZRP and Shaders MAX mods (which improve FPS rates and can even introduce major graphical improvements while retaining a vanilla feel) are trustier allies than all the perfect condition AK-47's in the world combined.
Now get out of here, STALKER!

First impression: fantastic sound and art direction, just as expected. Seriously, if you decide to buy this (and you probably should), make sure to crank up your volume, put on your best headset and maybe slap some glue on its speakers so you can never take 'em off again. Trust me, you're not gonna want to.
So what do we have here? Let me just sum things up:
: check. The voice behind Rucks from Bastion is back, do I need to say more?
: check. This is done in almost the same manner as before, with one minor difference I won't mention for those who'd rather find out on their own.
: check, check and check. Jen is one of my favorite artists and she no doubt has outdone herself yet again.
: no comment. If you're still not sold by words alone, check out the soundtrack on
and draw your own conclusions.
What's different from Bastion?
: confusing at first as you'd probably be expecting action-packed hack n' slash, but in the end it boils down to being a curious hybrid of Frozen Synapse's tactical gameplay and some of Bastion's core mechanics, all mashed together into something I find difficult to describe. Personally, it also reminds me of The Bureau's "Battle Focus", just minus all the slo-mo. Powers and combos are there: as before in Bastion, you'll probably spend some time looking for a perfect skill combination to cater your own playstyle, which is a fun experience in its own right as there are quite a few options to pick from.
: I finished it in under 7 hours with most of the challenges completed. While it IS a lot shorter than Bastion, you still get access to New Game+ upon completion so you can blast your way through it again. I still find game's length disappointing however, so if you're really concerned about that, I'd strongly advise you to wait for sale.
In general, Transistor is still as charming, well-paced and beautiful as its predecessor: you can absolutely tell they're both cut from the same cloth. But, while Bastion was somewhat more experimental in terms of narration, Transistor takes a bold step forward and puts even more information at your disposal than before. Which is probably a good thing. That is, if you like reading. Well, you've come this far, so I'll just assume you do.
Issues I ran into so far:
- My only and the main gripe with this game: abnormal, seemingly random freezing. I'm not talking "locking up at checkpoint saves" kind of freezes, either. I had to ctrl+alt+del at least 6 times due to it completely freezing up on me, "hl2.exe has stopped working"-style, with looping sound and everything. AFAIK this is a common problem at the moment of writing, so you've been warned.
P.S. Hold TAB while you're in game. Don't ask, just do it. :)

- Do not have friends who you want to play multiplayer with who use different platforms (Eg. Mac and Windows) (NOT LIKE ME)
Rome II has been great so far. However, my main issue with this game is that I spent tons of cash to buy it, expecting to be able to play with my Windows-using friends like I can with basic games like Europa Universalis 4, a game more than 1/10th of the size of this game. But... SEGA seems to have other plans. You see, with this game, you can only play with your buddies on Mac, if you own a Mac, or your buddy on Windows if you own a Windows. So if you want to play with your mates and you own a different OS, tough luck. I wouldn't even mind buying a DLC (as long as it is reasonably priced) at this moment in time. I have to play battles, campaigns, and other gamemodes by myself now. It's not really the multiplayer environment I was envisioning when I spent my cash on it. At least I got it on sale on Humble Bundle...
Honestly, that was the most disapointed I have been for a game since Elder Scrolls: Online first came out. And it's not only this game, either. EVERY TOTAL WAR TITLE THAT HAS MULTIPLAYER (so far) has been like this. Rome 1? Nope, Shogun? Nope, no "cross-platform" multiplayer support. I shouldn't have "cross-platform" incompatibilities unless he's using a goddamn PS4 and I'm using a MacBook Air or something. Then, I'd understand.
Ranting aside, the game is still very solid. It's very strategic and the campaigns are awesome. I'd recommend it to people who do not use a different OS from their buddies who they wish to play multiplayer with. Otherwise....

Long time player of the Total War series, Rome II is one my top three favorites in the franchise along with original Shogun and Medieval II.
Picked it up soon after launch, IMHO the game has improved in performance and bug fixing, sure, there are occasional issues, but the game overall runs well.
I have been happy to recieve additional content in the form of campaign modes, playable factions and upgrades/patches as well as a good selection of opt in DLC.
The Workshop support is great. Access to community created content helps with replayability and if I want a more 'custom' campaign this is where I go.
For fans of strategy games or the Total War series this is worth having.

Countless times I've simply driven through the ground and into an endless ocean underneath the map for some reason. Comparing the game to Just Cause 2, I'd say I'd probably prefer the the previous version. It didn't really feel like there were many major upgrades, and I felt like there were just more things to do in JC2. The challenges system in this game is wonky and makes it extra annoying when you realize how many driving and flying challenges there are that need to be completed with this games terrible driving.
The game looks fantastic but has a buttload of problems. If you enjoyed JC2 you still might enjoy this. I wouldn't recommend purchasing at full price, but if you get a chance to try the game, it's definetely worth a shot, even if there are so many things that could be done to improve the game.

This is a just close to passable game. This is like any other MOBA except that the combat is 3rd person and mostly in a single lane with a very boring back and forth gameplay. There are 2 fields of battle in this game, Joust and Arena.
In Joust, it is 3v3 and you try to kill the enemy team's Titan after destroying 2 of their lane towers. In this mode, respawning has a cooldown.
In Arena, each team has a set number of tickets and you try to bring down the enemy team's number of tickets to 0. You bring the tickets down by killing heroes and escorting bombs/soldiers into the enemy portal. In this mode, respawning is immediate upon death. Each of the modes have their own pros and cons.
Sadly, the gameplay just isn't compelling/addictive enough for me, you get reminded of World of Warcraf PvP.

Been playing ESO for nearly 2 years now nonstop. And here's what I have to say about it. To clear up any confuson, NO this isn't skyrim the MMORPG, that's what many assume about this game then leave dissapointed because of it. It's an MMORPG that takes place in the past, thousands of years before any of the maingame Elder Scrolls Games began.
The Main quest is simple, you're the vestige a soulless person out to fight against Molag Bal, the daedric prince of♥♥♥♥♥♥and corruption to get your soul back. you meet some interesting characters who will aid you in that quest.  But like all TES games, the strength isn't in the campaign or the main storyline, but with the freedom it gives to the player. Now with One Tamriel out you're free to visit any available location on Tamriel given that you discovered the wayshrines for fast travel. if not you're free to explore and literally walk throughout the land. Enemy npcs are scaled to your level so you won't have to worry about stumbling upon Overpowered enemies...that is unless you're in craglorn or cyrodil which is designed for more skilled players.
The crafting is amazing, from the begining you'll be able to teach yourself the basic skills in tailoring, smithing, provisioning, woodworking, enchanting, and alchemy. as for how skilled you get in one or all of those crafting skills, is entirely up to you and how much time you dedicate to it. but the payoff is worth it when you're in a higher level or in a guild. Need to craft an epic level hallowjack or stalhrim armor that makes you regenerate stamina for your super OP PVE Nightblade build? you can do it given the time researching traits, style motifs, and getting the necessary materials all available to you. Need to craft an xp boost because you don't want to spend 100 crowns for an xp scroll? get a psijic ambriosa recipe, max out your provisioning skill, and get the needed ingredients. the list goes one from there.
you'll also have in game guilds to join such as the fighters or mages guild. Each with their own unique storyline and rewards, to progress through the ranks you either hunt certain enemies or go out and search for lorebooks.
you're also able to fully customize your character and dye armor and shields given that you unlocked some dyes by unlocking the required achievements. which will keep you playing the game many times on multiple characters to get.
The game also has one of my favorite things, a roleplaying community which is something I never got to experience in the single player Elder Scrolls Games. you can have your character interact with other player's characters, go into political debates of Cyrodil, or go grave robbing, mercenary missions, mage school lessons, missionary work, give sermons, fight against other players, the list goes on.
Lastly to top it all off ESO is now introducing the playerhouse feature which can be earned through in game gold or crowns, meaning everyone can get it if you have the money IRL or not to own it. which i'm sure will add for even more hours into the game for those who have been playing it for a while now.
The strength of the game is from the player's freedom of choice to do whatever they want in this open world MMORPG based on the already crazy and amazing Elder Scrolls Universe, and the amazing community and support surrounding this game. So grab a copy, make your character, and go out into this very unique fantasy world.

I was strongly tempted to not recommend this game considering Fallout 3, another post-apocaltypic FPS-rpg title was released only a year after this game and has aged very well in comparison but I'm being a little more fair since I consider this more of an "indie" release. I do recommend this game for die-hard FPS-RPG fans who still crave a russian spin on a post-apocalyptic setting after playing the METRO games. To like this game though you'll have to look past numerous glitches, no fast-travel, a wonky interface (have fun trying to zoom in on the map with the mouse) dated graphics (sometimes it feels like you're fighting an army of clones),  clunky combat mechanics (I'll get into that more) and reading text in lieu of voice clips. I found the combat particularly annoying as notihng shouts "fun" as having a perfectly tuned rifle constantly jam a bullet or two into a clip at point blank range forcing you to helplessly watch your enemy shoot the crap out of you as you reload. Better still is the lack of damage recognition you get from your opponents. There is only one animation for when you've wounded your foe no matter where you've shot them, causing them to look like they've simply eaten some ice cream too fast and then miraculously shooting at you again liike nothing happenned, no limp, blood, gore or any indication of damage whatsoever after a shotgun blast right to the face. The grenade launcher actually does kill things though, at least until the last level anyways.  I'd have to say the most dissapointing thing about this game for me though is that I thought there'd be a little more attention to detail regarding Pripyat and the Chernobyl Reactor itself, but alas Pripyat is just a generic street-war area with just that famous ferris wheel in it and you don't even get to see the nuclear facility and the massive sarcophagus covering it anyways outside of cutscenes. :-/

From 8-5 (and sometimes longer) I work as a Visa Officer in a U.S. Embassy. The fact that it can do this, and that it can so thoroughly tap into the same part of my brain I use all day at work, makes it a marvel.  It's a marvel I hate playing, and one I can be paid for.  I recommend it to everyone who does not do what I do.

Rome II is a turnbased strategy that you will love if you can tick at least one of the following:
- Have a great interest in history, Roman or Greek (like me)
- Enjoy commanding troops and using strategic thinking (like me)
- Like having the option to play a variety of interesting and varying factions (like me)
- Generally enjoy a good game (like me)
- Do not have friends who you want to play multiplayer with who use different platforms (Eg. Mac and Windows) (NOT LIKE ME)
Rome II has been great so far. However, my main issue with this game is that I spent tons of cash to buy it, expecting to be able to play with my Windows-using friends like I can with basic games like Europa Universalis 4, a game more than 1/10th of the size of this game. But... SEGA seems to have other plans. You see, with this game, you can only play with your buddies on Mac, if you own a Mac, or your buddy on Windows if you own a Windows. So if you want to play with your mates and you own a different OS, tough luck. I wouldn't even mind buying a DLC (as long as it is reasonably priced) at this moment in time. I have to play battles, campaigns, and other gamemodes by myself now. It's not really the multiplayer environment I was envisioning when I spent my cash on it. At least I got it on sale on Humble Bundle...
Honestly, that was the most disapointed I have been for a game since Elder Scrolls: Online first came out. And it's not only this game, either. EVERY TOTAL WAR TITLE THAT HAS MULTIPLAYER (so far) has been like this. Rome 1? Nope, Shogun? Nope, no "cross-platform" multiplayer support. I shouldn't have "cross-platform" incompatibilities unless he's using a goddamn PS4 and I'm using a MacBook Air or something. Then, I'd understand.
Ranting aside, the game is still very solid. It's very strategic and the campaigns are awesome. I'd recommend it to people who do not use a different OS from their buddies who they wish to play multiplayer with. Otherwise....

This game isn't perfect, but if you like Sonic Generations you will probably enjoy this one. If you don't like 3D/Modern Sonic at all this game will not change your mind.
The story is a more than a bit cheesy at times, but it's a lot of fun. Your custom Avatar character gets a decent amount of spotlight. Anyone who has ever wanted to star in their own self-insert Sonic fanfic, this is the game for you. Also a lot of previous characters show up, which is neat if you like that kind of thing.
The Avatar has a lot of options for species and a decent amount of face types and color choices. In the beginning you don't start with a lot of custom clothing parts for the Avatar, but very quickly you'll start earning tons of them.  There are a lot of different parts and a decent amount of variety.  Also, the different Wispons really let the Avatar stand out as a character with their own playstyle and not feel like "Not-as-good Sonic". Each different type of Wispon gives the Avatar a different attack and special skill, so you can choose the one best suited to your playstyle or to the level.  Honestly, the Avatar stages were probably my favorite.
Modern Sonic and Classic Sonic play much like they did in Generations.  Their levels play to their gameplay types well, and are genrally well designed. Modern Sonic has fast paced 3D levels with fun setpeices while Classic Sonic has 2D levels with more emphasis on platforming.
That being said, there were a couple times near the end where the level design was a bit frustrating, or where a automated boost part did not line up quite right and I went flying off the stage instead of where the game seemed to be trying to send me.
Overall there are definitely more fun parts than frustrating ones.  If you like 3D Sonic games, give this one a try.

Sonic Forces does not deserve the hate it's been getting, in my opinion.
It's not a very fun game, nor is it a good one, either. However, it's not as bad as people make it out to be. It could be WAY worse (like Sonic '06 or Boom).
The worst thing in the game, for me at least, is the story. It's pretty incoherent and I don't feel like my character really did anything to progress or impact the story. All you really get when you finish a level is characters exchanging a few words before going into another (what feels like) irrelevent level. And the way the cast treats your character feels like a 12 year old's Sonic fanfiction. You're Sonic's new best friend in the whole world, even though you've only spent like 5 seconds together. Not Good. Not bad. Mediocre. That's the short of this review.
Sonic Forces has renewed public opinion that Sega isn't really sure how their Sonic games even work anymore. With the positive reception of Generations, one would think they would continue to refine the formula. Boost gameplay is controversial, but certianly works. Ideally one would hope that their next game would be split in some way between Boopst Gameplay and something more akin to Adventure style gameplay in order to appease their divided fanbase.
Sonic Lost World was their answer the praise bestowed upon Generations. A rebooted gameplay formula altogether that received mixed reception and did not appeal to fans. Since there was a negative backlash over straying form the proven gameplay, Sega decided to stray yet further with Boom. Boom received all around negativity from general and fan audiences.
With Forces, I was hopeful they would at least bring back a refined version of boost. Generations had shown cleanly what the strengths of the gameplay could be in learning the courses, discovering the faster shortcuts and managing meter and prepping you reflexes were paramount to getting those extra few seconds faster.  Sonic Forces feels like a completely separate dev team of a completely separate company tried copying the gameplay formula by watching the game being played.
Watching Modern Sonic's gameplay in trailers or seeing someone else play makes it look like the gameplay style seen in Generations, but it feels anything but. The controls feel stiffer than ever. Sonic doesn't respond well to inputs. Time and time again movements like the quickstep or homing attack don't seem consistent in execution. You might be boosting down a ramp, dodging spike grinders with quickstep, only for a random quickstep to take one or two seconds to come out, by then it's too late.  I checked multiple controllers and even different input methods and this occurred semi-frequently. Even having someone else play yielded similar results. Sometimes Sonic doesn't do the thing you want, as if there's some degree of input lag that spontaneously rears its ugly head. My system maintained its FPS throughout the game, with only one instance of slowdown in an unrelated section.
Combined with this is the floaty nature of Sonic's platforming. Unlike Generations large, oversized platforms are mostly gone, with smaller platforms instead, that require more precision that Sonic's near weightlessness doesn't really afford. It feels overwhelmingly common that a jump you performed with perfect timing doesn't work because Sonic careeens in midair into a pit at the slightest touch of the movement stick. Other times it's like he's a stubborn brick and doesn't respond to your input at all unless you push the stick all the way (This may be the aforementioned potential input lag)
Classic Sonic has this je ne sais qoui to how awkward it's platforming can feel. It exists as a some kind of weird hybrid of Generations and Mania. They have some kind of momentum based mechanic I can't seem to figure out that throws all of your predicitons for a loop, but they didn't commit to it like Mania does, making the entire set of stages feel inconsistent.
Avatar stages suffer from inconsistent character speed, sometimes slow and speeding up, sometimes 0-100mph in a second. The cinematic grapple sequences sometimes broke causing it to just drop me off a ledge during the swing. Wispons either slow syou down to an absurd degree (Hammer), Obscure the playing screen, making it difficult to make out projectiles through the effects (Busrton), or completely rocket you off ledges with their attack animations (Drill, Whip).
Partnered stages bring about both the issues fo modern Sonic's gameplay with the Avatars. Inconsistent speeds and and overabundance of screen clutter. In addition, actions for both characters are mapped to different buttons on your input device as opposed to having a dedicated switching mechanic. If you're boosting and try to do a homing attack, to hit a higher platform route, you will instead find the Avatar coming out with his hook to swing himself under the route using a grapple-point you didn't even see. By the time you figure out the controls for these stages, they'll be over. There are only 4 in the game.
Level Design is wholesale cut and pasted across characters. Find a video and compare Modern Sonic's City stage to Avatar's City Stage to Partnered City Stage to even Shadow's City stage and find them all traversing the same expanse of level with some minor twist at the very end.
In terms of setpiece, Stage 16/30 is the most interesting setpiece I think I've seen in a Sonic game so far. I was really interested in what was going on around me, even as I struggled to ge the Avatar to cooperate. It even far outweighs anything offered in the final "climactic" stages.
I'll take a moment to point out that the visuals are overly complex. It can be difficult to make out exactly what obstacles are even ahead of you at times (mainly in 2d sections) because they blend in so well with the background. Metroplosi is offensively white. Making out walls, ramps, curves, etc. is sometimes infuriating when the sky is white, the background is white, the walls are white, the ramps are white, the curves are white, hell, even the shining enemies can be a pain to pick out sometimes.
Boss fights were mostly forgetable. Modern Sonic's issues almost dissolved during his boss fights, which is a definite plus. Classic Sonic, all I did was drop dash back and forth acros the arena and was basically never hit. Avatar, I literally did the same using the drill. Partner boss fights were functionally identical to Modern Sonic's.
Story was honestly pretty bland. It starts off pretty serious, like it's actually intending to go somewhere interesting, but once you hit Stage 4 it's just going thorugh the motions. Even the characters seem to sotp caring about what's really happening and just start saying generic "Let's do it!" line delivery. Even Sonic is lampshading in the story that there's no actual stakes "We always win. We just don't know yet how we're going to do it yet".
Music was largely forgettable. I think Ohtani is running out of steam here. The vocal tracks were pretty catchy in their own right, but those compose just 10 of the apparent 87 tracks in the game, Those other 73 of those remaining just sound like generick synth-guitar beats without much feeling. Just background noise. This may be because Sonic games now basically focus exclusively around just Sonic instead of the varied beats you got form games like Adventure 2 that could style themselves differently to suit the personalities fo the character.
Overall, the game just took me a couple hours. Something I wans't expecting with 4 gameplay styles present in the game. I figured one or two of them (Avatar and Partner) might be used for significant padding in some way, but those two stylesa are essentially frankensteined versions of Modern Sonic. It's not really worth your $40 value, and with the cut and paste level design and how all of them are only about a minute anyways with few interesting shortcuts, there's no reason to go back and replay them. This includes going back to get a higher rank because the game aggressively distributes S-ranks even if you do poorly and die several times.
What's most infuriating about this game is that every so often while playing, I could almost feel like I was about to enjoy myself, but the issues and blandness of delivery caused me to disengage form the experience, creating an overall mediocre experience.

There are about 6 levels in the game with alternate versions used as "new episodes". The characters have a delay on every action, the jumps feel floaty, and some levels are impossible if you have "speed up after landing" due to all the pitfalls. Speaking of pitfalls, there are an absolute ton, this is your main enemy in this game. In the end I can't say I recommend this game to anyone who isn't a foolish fan who'll buy any game Sonic Team makes, or someone who has the money to toss around. Can't wait for mods to fix the... everything.

You know how most early access games, and games that flop always start with: "Well man this has so much potential, the devs just havn't realized it yet"?
This game has realized that potential. In it's current state, RoK is an extremely good time. It is a medieval simulation with fun chivalryesque combat, rust style building and sandbox with full loot and added systems like capturing people to enact justice etc. This game could be released with all of the systems that  are currently in place and be a complete experience, as far as I'm concerned and it would be a great game.
That being said, this game is far from done in it's current state. The code is easy to hack and the game is riddled with hackers, every server... every few minutes someone is doing something rude with their cheats to ruin the progress of everyone else. It's very reminiscent of the early months of DayZ mod with the amount of cheaters present; and it kills the experience.
The resources are not spread out very well, which makes for an interesting battle for resources adding the desperation the game needs, but some just don't make sense... like stone only being able to be mined from a few select rocks when the map is covered in rocks. The mobs are thin, the player caps are low and the servers crash often. The building system is broken in that people can place and pickup blocks very quickly if they own the land, making raiding someone's base laughably bad when they have a stack of blocks and can trap you in a corner. The movement can be glitchy and extremely laggy on alot of servers making the pvp intolerable.
On top of all of those problems this game is incredible. The scenery is good, the animations and character customization is fun the crafting is enjoyable, not too complicated as to need a spreadsheet to play but not too simple as to have nothing to work toward as in DayZ or rust. All in all I give this game a 7/10 in it's current state, with quite the potential to become a solid 9-10/10.

One of the most challenging games I've played in a long time. The best thing I like, you don't have your hand hold.
Now first off, Dark Souls as a franchise has this reputation for being impossibly difficult and makes you die every couple minutes, and that's true. Here's the thing though, the challenge is extremely indicative of how hard I used to find video games. I remember getting stuck and dieing dozens of time trying to get a star in Super Mario 64. I got older, and games became less difficult. Dark Souls seems to scale up and provides that same challenge I used to love in video games.
Yes, you will die. A lot. You will be a zombie, and you will get invaded, but this is hands-down the most rewarding game I've played. There's a legitimate sense of discovery of "well I'm not sure what to do, but I think I can go here now. Let's find out."
Quick note about the combat, if you like the Monster Hunter series' combat, Dark Souls is very similar. Fast paced and dodge-centered (unless you just build straight tank).
Overall, Dark Souls 2 is a complete RPG experience, filled with a sense of discovery and pioneering your own character and class. The story requires discovery as well.
TLDR: Great game. Great RPG. Great online. 10/10 will die again.

This game is awesome!! It is like a mature, more serious version of Fallout (though admittedly not as intricate, it's not really an RPG at all). The biggest point in this games favour is the immersion. After an hour I really got wrapped up in the whole world here. It really makes you feel like a loner in a desolate land where everyone is struggling by against bizarre and mysterious forces. Even little things like... hearing the distant cries of animals, the sounds of gun fights somewhere far off, a group of survivors just sitting around the campfire, chatting and playing guitar. It really adds to the immersion!
The missions are somewhat varied. You don't feel bored really. Some missions (in the labs) are really some of the best ever, giving a feeling of survival horror or like the Shalebridge Crade from Thief 3. The locations are all memorable and no two are comparable. The gun play is decent enough though you can get killed pretty easily so this requires much more caution. There's some good chances to customize your load out (though not to Fallout levels).
As for negatives... it could use a fast travel system like Skyrim. The map is huge and some missions mean travelling one side to the other regularly. Also, in a game where immersion is so evident I'd have expected to do more reading/listening to reports and notes left by other survivors. Some people hate that but I think in this game, if well done, really would've added to it.
NOTE: there is also a big modding community for this game. Search for the Stalker Complete series. There is a "Complete" mod for each Stalker game. I am currently playing the vanilla version and it plays fine but have a look at the mod.

An hour in this game is simply amazing, the art and music is overwhelmingly good and the gameplay is sound and original. Interesting and unique game mechanics and an unraveling story make me not want to stop playing.

Where Bastion scored with simplicity and threw you right in an involving albeit abstract story where you had fun with the narrator, the spark in Transistor just doesn't ignite.
The story is even more abstract, and what gave you some familiarity in bastion (like talking about the inhabitants, telling you where they lived and what they used to do) you play a singer in Transistor, who was kinda attacked...and pulled a speaking electronical sword out of a dead guy which...eats souls which are actually programs...let's say it's very abstract or "artsy" and does not provide much familiarity. You don't really know/ understand what is happening and what you are doing.
It's about the same with the combat. In Bastion you run around having fun beating on stuff, testing out weapons, destroying objects in the game world. In Transistor there are no objects in the game world which can be destroyed (besides of white blocks) the enemies (evil programs) aren't as plastic as in Bastion and the combat doesn't feel really like one big working mechanism. You hit "turn", can plan for the next couple of seconds, and then hit "turn" again where all the actions are executed. However the planning doesnt feel very good, as it's inexact and you need to issue some orders multiple times "to get them right". It requires some fiddling with the controls and the "planning tool" (holding attack button) might show that it hits enemies, which it actually isn't. And after you executed one turn...you need to either fight in unprecise, hectical action combat or flee and run like a little girl and wait till the "turn" button is ready again. This just doesn't feel fun.
And there is the skill system. The skills are souls/programs which you can combine with each other which gives a lot of options and sounds nice on paper. But it doesn't really feel like "I need to try this out!" and rather "ok...now how do I built something with it which is at least somewhat useful?" Also the overview and Interface of the skills isn't really well done and explained well.
The game is actually doing not a great job in explaining several of the mechanics and what is happening in the game. t throws you into the game, gives a hint now and then but you don't feel like you know what you are doing. Something which simply could not happen in Bastion.
Bastion scored with simplicity. You got a bow, shot with it, tweaked it, and it just felt "right".BEsides of that Transistor is also a really short game with it's 5-7h though it has an additional mode with random enemies to bring replayability if this is really what you want.
Therefore I do not recommend this game. If you don't mind the whacky combat and find the abstract story involving, you might be interested. And if you didn't play Bastion yet - get that one instead.
I am aware that some people won't like it if I write a negative review about a game which "must be good, because these guys made bastion" (and who might not even read these lines and downrate it right away) but I think I am intitled to say that Transistor does not live up to the expectations and just doesn't feel right. Switching to a more tactical combat isn't bad. I am a big tactics fan on my own. But it's not well implemented and doesn't feel good and fun.

You're probably like me and went in with the mindset of "There's no way it can be better than Bastion."
Folks, they did it.
Let me get the negatives out of the way: It's as short as Bastion, especially if you skip the challenge mode stuff. Also I ran into a handful of areas with very significant framerate drops.
But here are the reasons you should get this game:
-Incredible story from beginning to end. There are still questions left after the (amazing) ending, but they're not significant enough to detract from the overall narrative.
-Interesting combat system. I wasn't sold on the combat after seeing the initial trailer, but after getting a few abilities I discovered just how well designed the combat is. It's fun, it's challenging, it can vary wildly from playstyle to playstyle, and it just works.
-Really neat upgrade system. You only have 4 "active" abilities, however you very quickly obtain more than that. The abilities that are not being used can be put into the upgrade slots of the active abilities. As an example, One ability has the power to generate explosives. When putting that ability into your default "swing" ability, your swing now does AoE damage. Also, much of the lore and backstory is hidden behind unlocks in these abilities. By using these abilities in battle, either as an "active" ability or an upgrade, you unlock a tiny bit more lore. It's a fantastic way to both immerse the player further into the world and also encourage them to try out all of the abilities.
-The music. Get the soundtrack. No question about it. If you played Bastion, you know exactly how amazing the soundtrack is.

Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings

As a long time Sonic fan I am willing to say that Sonic Forces took some major steps in the wrong direction. First off I'd have to say the level design does not flow as smoothly when compared to Generations in both the "Classic" and "Modern" levels plus the level designers seem to have a major hard-on for bottomless pits and cheap enemy placements. Next I'll have to say the sountrack relies far too much on a synthesizer and not quite as memorable as the last sucessful 3D game (i.e. Generations). Another thing is the floaty controls and Sweet Zombie Jesus riding a rocket powered pogo stick I've died far too many times due to that which again compared to Generations were well done. One of the few good things that came out of the game was the character creation but with the issues mentioned earlier it is hampered. For the sake of your wallet wait until a sale during the holidays, buy one of the good Sonic games such as Generations (if you do not own it already), Mania (see previous answer), or another good platformer if you know where to look.

A step forward for Modern Sonic. 8.6/10
Gameplay: 8/10
Music: 10/10
Level Design:7/10
Story: 9/10
Graphics: 9/10
Pros;
+Extremely Fast Paced, mostly what you guys expect from Sonic and his speed.
+New and Improved boost mechanic.
+Easy to remember controls.
+Precise movement.
+NON LINEAR LEVELS (For the most part.)
+Outstanding Soundtrack (as usual.)
+Custom Hero does a great job at giving the player a break from Sonic's overwhelming speedy levels.
+Ability to remove Dialouge, Hints, etc.
Cons:
-Too precise, you stop on a dime which defeats the purpose of Classic Sonic's momentum based gameplay.
-They made it sure you weren't boosting to win so boosting a little too much may make you end up in a bottomless pit or two (just a small nitpick.)
-The Story skips over some small details I'd like to know a little more about and doesn't go that deep into the story. (nitpick)
-Too short, they dissmissed Act 1 and Act 2 giving us only 30 stages (Which is not alot, trust me.)
-Platforming.
-No color optimization for Custom Hero's clothing. (nitpick)
-Classic Sonic's inclusion. (nitpick)
-Sometimes hard to focus on one thing with everything going on in the background.
Also, I haven't experienced a crash once during my playthrough even though my graphics card is pretty dated BUT there were framerate drops eventually causing the death of me mutiple times. In addition, the Denuvo has ZERO effect on the game as people think it does, you wouldn't even notice it would be there had they not made a disclamer. Although many people might think Sonic is still struggling, the Boost formula is the most reliable and best go to for Sonic. Looking at the game alone and not comparing it to others, it's pretty stellar and well worth the $39.99.

It certainly is a thrilling game, the atmosphere is top notch and it is definitely a true homage to the original film. The story is interesting, the characters for the most part quite engaging and of course the "creature of unknown origin" is terrifying.
Gameplay mostly consists of "Fix the thing" which then breaks so it becomes "fix the other thing" which also breaks so it becomes "fix the third thing", from which you hop from vent to vent or cupboard to cupboard. The pacing therefore was a little slower than I prefer, but it absolutely works regardless and it does help build and deliver tension. Cowering in a crawl space with an alien snorting right in front of you as it searches for you is un-nerving!
I got the game on considerable discount (75% off) and it was more than worth the price I paid for it. It's a good stealth game whether you like Alien or not (I'm no huge fan of the films but I like them). Sevastopol (the space station you are on) is a pile of junk but its a nice place to explore. Once you get the hang of constructing items and using them (ie distractions) the gameplay is good fun. It takes a while before you get any of the interesting weapons but they certainly add a bit of flavour in the later stages of the game.
There are plenty of surprises, nothing is "on rails" and the sound effects are wonderfully mixed in. A few missions away from the space station provide a nice change of pace. I wasn't so satisfied with the ending, but that doesn't  taint the overall experience.
Recommended, especially if it's on sale. I'm yet to try survivor mode as I can't see much replay value in the story mode, but am glad I bought it and played it.

Some of the issues that I have with this game is the way the shop works, the p2w aspects, the lack of difficulty due to bots, and the prices for the cash shop.
The way the shop works is that you have 4 random items that spawn and refresh every 12 hours. You have no choice but to wait, watching until you find what you're looking for and this can take months for a single piece of gear.
The game is p2w but only if you want to play in the tourney, or if you're up against older players. In random battles you almost always go up against bots who's armor, health, and weapons scale with your own. This means you don't need gear at all to win most of the time.
There is no difficulty, and no need for strategy thanks to the poorly coded bots. And for the most part whichever side uses the most grenades will always win as bots don't use them.
And then there is the prices of the cash shop, which lets you buy wulong, gold, or premium time. It is expensive to buy the gold which is needed for the top gear in-game. $100 will buy you 3k gold. The best weapons in the game for each of the 5 toons cost about 1.5k-1.8k gold + 500 - 1k gold to fully upgrade. The top armor costs about 700 - 1.5k gold a piece + w/e is needed for upgrades. (or so i been told) To give you a better idea, this means it costs about $300 to fully equip 1 toon and an extra $100 is needed for each extra toon as the armor can be swapped between them.
In the past the older players where actually able to get the top gear much easier and cheaper, so a lot of the older players already have the full set of top notch gear. For the new player however, its much harder because the gold that is needed is just part of the problem, you will also have to wait for the item to show up in the shop. This can take months or even years for a full set regardless of how much gold you buy. Because you don't need gear at all to play and win against bots there is really no reason to buy gold at all.
Note: To clear up a few things I read in other reviews, there is no longer an energy mechianic it's done away with. Also a few people have played for a few hours and said you need money to unlock all the toons, this too is incorrect. While it's true that you start with 2 of 5 toons and you need 150 gold to unlock each of the other 3, you also earn free gold by playing the game and leveling up the toons you have, as well as free gold from the daily logins. You make 125 gold every time you take a toon to level 10 and you have 10 generations as well. So a f2p player can earn 1250 gold from each toon x 5 different toons for free. No real money is needed.

Where Bastion scored with simplicity and threw you right in an involving albeit abstract story where you had fun with the narrator, the spark in Transistor just doesn't ignite.
The story is even more abstract, and what gave you some familiarity in bastion (like talking about the inhabitants, telling you where they lived and what they used to do) you play a singer in Transistor, who was kinda attacked...and pulled a speaking electronical sword out of a dead guy which...eats souls which are actually programs...let's say it's very abstract or "artsy" and does not provide much familiarity. You don't really know/ understand what is happening and what you are doing.
It's about the same with the combat. In Bastion you run around having fun beating on stuff, testing out weapons, destroying objects in the game world. In Transistor there are no objects in the game world which can be destroyed (besides of white blocks) the enemies (evil programs) aren't as plastic as in Bastion and the combat doesn't feel really like one big working mechanism. You hit "turn", can plan for the next couple of seconds, and then hit "turn" again where all the actions are executed. However the planning doesnt feel very good, as it's inexact and you need to issue some orders multiple times "to get them right". It requires some fiddling with the controls and the "planning tool" (holding attack button) might show that it hits enemies, which it actually isn't. And after you executed one turn...you need to either fight in unprecise, hectical action combat or flee and run like a little girl and wait till the "turn" button is ready again. This just doesn't feel fun.
And there is the skill system. The skills are souls/programs which you can combine with each other which gives a lot of options and sounds nice on paper. But it doesn't really feel like "I need to try this out!" and rather "ok...now how do I built something with it which is at least somewhat useful?" Also the overview and Interface of the skills isn't really well done and explained well.
The game is actually doing not a great job in explaining several of the mechanics and what is happening in the game. t throws you into the game, gives a hint now and then but you don't feel like you know what you are doing. Something which simply could not happen in Bastion.
Bastion scored with simplicity. You got a bow, shot with it, tweaked it, and it just felt "right".BEsides of that Transistor is also a really short game with it's 5-7h though it has an additional mode with random enemies to bring replayability if this is really what you want.
Therefore I do not recommend this game. If you don't mind the whacky combat and find the abstract story involving, you might be interested. And if you didn't play Bastion yet - get that one instead.
I am aware that some people won't like it if I write a negative review about a game which "must be good, because these guys made bastion" (and who might not even read these lines and downrate it right away) but I think I am intitled to say that Transistor does not live up to the expectations and just doesn't feel right. Switching to a more tactical combat isn't bad. I am a big tactics fan on my own. But it's not well implemented and doesn't feel good and fun.

I'm not particularly good at micro management, and this game seemed super daunting at first glance.  But after playing a few hours solo and with a friend, I've found that it isn't as collosal as it seems. If you're considering buying it, don't be turned off by how overwhelming it looks.

You're probably like me and went in with the mindset of "There's no way it can be better than Bastion."
Folks, they did it.
Let me get the negatives out of the way: It's as short as Bastion, especially if you skip the challenge mode stuff. Also I ran into a handful of areas with very significant framerate drops.
But here are the reasons you should get this game:
-Incredible story from beginning to end. There are still questions left after the (amazing) ending, but they're not significant enough to detract from the overall narrative.
-Interesting combat system. I wasn't sold on the combat after seeing the initial trailer, but after getting a few abilities I discovered just how well designed the combat is. It's fun, it's challenging, it can vary wildly from playstyle to playstyle, and it just works.
-Really neat upgrade system. You only have 4 "active" abilities, however you very quickly obtain more than that. The abilities that are not being used can be put into the upgrade slots of the active abilities. As an example, One ability has the power to generate explosives. When putting that ability into your default "swing" ability, your swing now does AoE damage. Also, much of the lore and backstory is hidden behind unlocks in these abilities. By using these abilities in battle, either as an "active" ability or an upgrade, you unlock a tiny bit more lore. It's a fantastic way to both immerse the player further into the world and also encourage them to try out all of the abilities.
-The music. Get the soundtrack. No question about it. If you played Bastion, you know exactly how amazing the soundtrack is.

Stalker shadow of Chernobyl is a free roaming fps game.
Stalker takes place in what’s known as the zone after the nuclear incident in Chernobyl which has ruined a lot of the landscape, turned most animals into monsters, and poisoned a lot of areas with radiation and has created what are called anomalies which are murderous whether effects in one small spot, you play as a stalker (which stands for scavenger, trespasser, adventurer, loner, killer, explorer and robber) known as the marked one, you have amnesia and you are left with a PDA saying to kill some guy named Strelok, the story is almost non-existent but that doesn’t matter because a lot of games I play the story takes a huge backseat and doesn’t really matter that much.
Stalker’s gameplay revolves around exploration, combat and completing quests and side quests which will give you rewards given to you by various people you’ll come across which will be marked on your PDA. In stalker you have an inventory system very similar to resident evil 4 where it’s a grid and each item will appear as a diagram and will take up space on the grid only you can stack all items, there’s weight limit with the inventory system: once you’re above the weight limit your stamina will drop extremely quickly if it will let you sprint. You have various suits and artefacts that you can find which all have different effects on the player such as resistance to radiation, reduction to how much you’ll bleed out when you are shot, an increase in stamina etc. You have a hunger and thirst system which you’ll need to use drinks and food when an icon appears on the right side of the screen, you’ll have to drink vodka or use certain medical equipment for when you have radiation poising and you’ll have to use bandages and med kits to stop you from bleeding out which both of these are notified by an icon that will appear on the right side of the screen. You can also trade items with various NPCs. There are also various enemy factions which you’ll come across in this game.
It’s extremely difficult to say what’s to like about this game but one thing I can say is that this game is strangely compelling but it comes with a few glaring issues and problems.
Stalker has some of the worst gunplay I’ve ever seen in any shooting game, most of the time you can’t hit what you’re aiming at, regardless of the distance between you and what you’re shooting at, regardless of whether you’re stood still or moving, regardless of your posture, regardless of whether you’re spraying or using burst fire or single shots and for the most part regardless of what weapon you’re using. However if you turn on the crosshair, unless the gun has a scope, hip firing is significantly more accurate than using iron sights,well when you put it on paper you are more accurate firing at a wall using iron sights from a distance but this magically disappears when shooting at an enemy, and hip firing is generally more effective against enemies and it also doesn’t help that the iron sights are horrible in this game and seriously get in the way. Even if you are going for the “realistic” way: DON’T, because iron sights are useless in this game (they’re better in the two sequels though)
The combat is just far too inconsistent in this game. In most games the enemies can hit you most if not every single time and the damage output is consistent and varies game to game, in Stalker the enemies have a completely random chance of hitting you, they also have a random damage output, so sometimes you’ll get just a scratch but others you’ll die instantly. A perfect examples of this is where I had to defend an area from a bandit raid, I was about 50 feet away from the enemies, they seemed to be unable to hit me until one of them suddenly and randomly did and I died instantly. You can go from an enemy noticing you and killing you instantly in one shot, then reload a save but this time that enemy might not be able to hit anything even when you are banzai charging towards them with the knife, which I have done before. Your success all comes down to retrying until you succeed because you got lucky, it doesn’t ever feel like skills matter in this game, and it’s, not like reaction time matters or anything in this it’s just ridiculous. There is the argument of “it’s trying to be realistic” no game is properly realistic, none, not even something such as Arma 3. I guess quite a fair bit in reality with wars can be down to luck but nothing like in this game.
when you reload a save, the enemies go back to their starting positions and sometimes their starting positions are behind you and you’ll get killed right away when you’ve loaded a save.
The movement in this game is almost headache inducing it does this really sickening head bobbing when you move, it sways to the bottom left and right really quickly.
I’ve had an extremely difficult time deciding whether to recommend this game or not, I guess it all comes down to whether you think you can put up with these problems and I’m only recommending this game because I don’t hate it enough to not recommend it. Though after several playthroughs I like it significantly more than the first time I played this game.

Good game? Yes.
Well performing game? Eh not really, quite demanding of resources so frames will be low throughout, putting graphics on medium and turning of V-sync slightly helps, and going offline also seems to give some performance boost, but the poor performance is most noticeable when you are in the heat of a battle.
Ok so a bit more in depth now:
Driving mechanics- for quite a few reviewers there seems to be issues with controlling vehicles. Personally I use keyboard and mouse and it works fine, though I did need to remap some controls to suit me I got used to it pretty quick.
Flying (vehicle) mechanics- by far better than driving, maybe because there is less that you can crash into, until you get onto planes. The boost gear mod makes you crash into the runway whenever I try to take off.
Vehicles in general: Planes are annoying, you can hijack pretty much any vehicle instantly, military vehicles are overpowered as all heck but I'm down with that.
Flying (wingsuit) mechanics- Ok so the vehicles aren't great but the character certainly is
. Personally the wingsuit is my favourite method of travel, the feeling of seeing Rico (your character) glide so close to the ground, grappling along elegantly is absolutely brilliant, one of the most satisying feats I have personally done in probably all my time gaming came from my first few hours playing this game when I managed to fly over a bridge alongside some cars.
Ragdoll mechanics- These are annoying pretty much every time you fail anything and get sent sprawling across the floor, especially when you get into combat, it is all just a bit too long and slow.
Combat mechanics- Pretty much the same as any other third person shooter, with a few differences such as the grapple hooks and no melee at all, save a kick/shove. Tanks shoot things, helicopters/choppers fly and shoot things, lots of explosions etc.
Territory system/map control- Not particularly exciting, you can just keep flying into a certain base, shoot one target, die, come back, shoot another over and over until you get everything should you so wish. Dying results in no penalties, leaving enemy territory half broken doesnt result in the enemy rebuilding it and liberating territories as a whole is a bit too easy, but this game really isnt meant to be taken too seriously.
Civilians- Generic talk, generic player play foddle, but this time you can tie them together, attatch them to a car and drive them off a cliff.
Action vs Wandering about- the map is big, you can teleport places and call in vehicles but these require flares and such which are quite difficult to find so you will do a lot of running or flying or driving or, Leonardo Da Vinci forbid, swimming, but even so there is plenty to do, and you wont have to travel far to find a place to liberate, unless you find yourself going back on yourself.
DLC- they seem worthit, though short. They do provide some content but the Sky Fortress dlc took me about an hour tops to complete. Eden so they are fun.
Collectibles- There are a lot, dont go crazy trying to get them all because it will ruin the experience. Just take yer time I'd say.
Overall: It is a good game, possibly get it when on sale though, and be prepared to face some (pretty major) lag and fps drops. Even so it is still a good game, and I recommend.

UPDATE: Found out that the game is actually better playable on Keyboard rather than with the X360 Controller.. Characters are a little more controlable, but still face some of the issues described above.
But due to this, I decided to change my rating to 51% Good, 49% Bad, so I changed my recommendation.
Also, found out that Double Boost on Keyboard only works on the first Pyramid stage. The other stages that use double boost, like Metal Sonic or Null Space, for some reason, the game does not detect the keyboard mash input to start the boost properly...
-
I really didn't want to give this game a bad review... I really didn't... But unfortunatelly, there's not a "Meh" choice here... It's either Yes or No.. And.. For what I've played... It's 51% No, 49% Yes, so...
Going on with this... If you LOVED Sonic Mania, and ENJOYED Sonic Generations... Sonic Forces is gonna be "Meh" to you...
Then again... I can't for the sake of anything figure HOW they broke this game... It's just... It's just... *affff*
So, these are the most important points I have to review:
Gameplay wise, physics all around, either in Classic/Modern/Custom are "messy", to say the least...
Messy in a way that... If you are trying to get through a part that has you do multiple platform jumping... You're either gonna have too much momentum.. Or almost none... And you either miss the platform by passing it, or by not reaching it... And this is one of the most important points I just can't understand.. I mean.. I don't remember having these issues on Generations, hell, not even on Colors playing in an emulator on my PC! So, I must ask myself... Why?
Sonic Classic does NOT perform like in Sonic Mania, so you can forget about that. And unfortunatelly, it also performs worse than in Generations.
Modern Sonic, for me, out of the 3, is the best controllable one, ONLY if you are not boosting like hell. If you are unlucky enough to find a turn... You're out. That's it. No drift, no side-step will save you, nothing... You just go over. And then again, there are parts that, if you boost, you go over, but if you don't, the game kinda controlls the turn for you? I mean.. How is this possible? Is this supposed to happen? Is this a bug, where the game is supposed to grab you, but since you are boosting, it doesn't?.. I can't understand this...
Custom Mode... Well.. One things good! If you use the eletric whip, as long as you are attacking non-stop you are invincible! Except for bottomless pits... Oh! And one thing good here: You get a little out of control when whipping all over the place, but FORTUNATELLY, you won't go over the edges... Unless you stop wipping... If you stop, and are unlucky to still be pressing a direction... It's down the edge... Remember when Sonic used to stop at the edges and almost fall, and did that animation of losing it's balance? That does not exist here.. But, keep whipping, and you won't fall off! And Invincibility! Prety awesome, right?
Anyway, control-wise it has the same momentum issues... But other than that... It's pretty much almost Classic mode with gimmicks...
Level design: some parts, specially in Custom mode, will make you not be able to see what's coming ahead of time, so sometimes you just bump into enemies before even having enough time to react. Sonic Modern stages could be longer... Since you almost BOOST BOOST BOOST (DxD reference here) all the time, levels are short... Really short....
Graphics: Game looks beautiful. Bright colors. Great graphics and animation.
Sound and BGM: Hmmm... I find it good for the Custom mode to have voices in music... Altough a little sketchy sometimes, but it's still enjoyable. Modem mode still has great BGM... Classic mode... I gotta say, I hate it the BGMs.... I mean... For me, unfortunatelly, it seems that they tried to grab that Mega Drive feeling, but failed misarably, and the BGMs of Classic levels sound more like a mash between 8-bit NES and SNES somehow, rather than MegaDrive / Genesis. I mean... Not even 8-bit Master System compares to this... I just... I really don't know any other way to describe it, they tried, and failed miserably. The way I love the Mega Drive BGMs of Sonic games, these do not even reach 40% of that quality for me...
To finish this long text wall, bugwise, I really didn't see any bugs worth mentioning, loadings are also not that long, aside from the Video FPS issues for those that do not use Big Picture mode, and some other performance issues sometimes in mid-levels, that dropped a few FPS, but not enough to make the game unplayable, I really don't see anything more worth it to detail here.
I bought the game on pre-order, full price, but for those that read this, if you aren't that eager to play this game, my opinion, is to wait for price drop and/or sale. Otherwise, feel free to buy it at full price.

I've finished Sonic Forces and I can finally write a proper review.
PROS:
- The best graphics in a Sonic game so far
- Game runs smoothly at 60fps
- Easy to learn how to play
- Great option for beginners or young players
CONS:
- Very easy game. Even on "Hard" difficulty I didn't have any trouble at all with all stages, except for the last one where I did die one or two times
- Extremely linear and short levels. Most of them you just hold the boost button and 30s later the level is over. Most of them when you think something interesting will happen the level ends
-  Way too many story elements placed together that fail on actually becoming part of the plot
Overall this feels like a very casual game for players that never played a Sonic game before and have no idea about what to expect. You'd better off playing Generations or Mania if you are looking for a good experience.

In this game, you stamp passports.  EXCITING!  But don't let the mundane description fool you: the game is a masterpiece in it's own right.
Papers, Please is a testament to how dated graphics and a simplistic core element can be used as a vehicle for a rich experience by implementing the power of choice.  Each person, every randomly generated life you come across, awaits your stamp of Approval or Denial.  Their minor reactions feed the player's psyche to continue the grind, checking papers and comparing photos, cross-referencing lists for potential criminals or fraudulent seals, churning out dozens of people to feed his or her faceless, nameless "Family".
Abusing your power or neglecting your duties don't result in an immediate game over, instead you receive citations in increasing severity based on how problematic the offense was.  Decorated the applicant side of your immigration booth with nonsense?  If your boss sees it, you get fined, but you can always hide the drawings of "Son" underneath official papers during inspections, then put them back up later.
The game rapidly escalates in difficulty, but decreases in reward and intrigue, allowing the player to merge seamlessly from a "game" with a clear carrot-and-stick bait, to an experience where I actually questioned whether or not this was designed as gameification of the career to attract, immerse and train border agents in the process, and exemplify the tribulations and  consequences of those choices.

flying across the top of my screen. WHY AM I NOT ABLE TO DISABLE THIS?
The framerate drops, the constant slows, this game was not ready for release.   I hope that IMC gets their stuff together before this game makes it's full free to play release, otherwise a beautiful game, full of potential, will have gone to waste.  I love the gameplay mechanics, the class system and the friends Ive made in game.  My friends and I have enjoyed our experiences, but the servers need fixed and a maintenance to sort out all of the bugs. All in all, I give the game for strict gameplay, a 8.5/10.  This is because the quests are your typical MMO quests. It cuts down on running all over the place when you could be getting the next quest to carry on.  I also like that the game rewards you for playing and exploring their game.  You can get collection boxes from treasure chests in just about every area, there are world bosses that randomly spawn, and the job quests seemed fairly different between each advancement.
All in all, I've really had a good time while the game has worked for me, but the fact that NPCs can just straight out break on you, and the fact that you cannot disable the horrible banner at the top of the screen makes me cringe.
If IMC somehow does manage to fix their stability issues, and ward off the RMT bots, this game will be worth it.
However, there is no player trading and I feel the game lacks soul because this feature is missing.  As a person who strives to help anyone I can, this really limits me to helping people through hoping they get a drop they want, or helping them level up. TL;DR - No player trades, massive lag, and horrible service is going to ruin this game.  If they address these issues, fix the bugs and take care of stability problems, the game would most definitely be one to spend hours on, having a great time.
