I bought the $50 early adopter package.
This game runs on 1 core.  People complain about optimization but it will never get better.  It's why the game craps out when more than 10 units are on the screen and why PvP is limited to 5v5.  It will never get over this hump because of the garbage engine the game is designed on.
Having said that, the the gameplay is good enough to have kept me entertained for some time.  But the biggest problem with the game is the Devs and community.  IMC really couldn't care less about this game; they probably have already started working on their next game as this game's population is dwindling by the day.  There are game-breaking bugs that have been in existence since day 1 (and from what I've read, from old betas even).  I cringed everytime I had to use an elevator or something similar to move from one place to another because it usually meant I'd be crashing.  The servers would go down for 24 hours at a time on some days.
The XP wall was absolutely insane for certain classes and is why so many people probably used bots to begin with.  Some classes it would probably take 500+ hours to grind to max level.  I played a Cleric-type class and it was an absolutely atrocious grind.  I found myself in areas that were more than 10 levels above mine because I ran out of ways to gain XP.  There needs to be more balance when it comes to XP from monsters vs Cards and Dungeons because the former takes up about 80% of the playing time and gives you about 2% of your XP, save for the first 20 or so lvls of the game.  I was also a token user (at all times) and had plenty of XP tomes to use, but it didn't seem to do anything at all.  XP from monsters is absolute crap when playing solo.
The straw that broke my back was the game-breaking Panda pet for PvP and just how terrible PvP was in general.  I have 5k+ hours in WoW and played over 1k hours in Star Wars Galaxies as a bounty hunter pre-combat update; I love PvP.  I was so excited about the PvP potential in this game with the Guild vs. Guild stuff.  I was thinking it'd be the closest thing to Star Wars Galaxies with the griefing.  But terrible party systems, connections, bugs, and guild restrictions ruined it.  Plenty of classes, but only a handful are viable in PvP.  Others are clearly better for PvE.  To have a guild, you have to have a Templar.  Meaning you either have to main a Templar or grind up an alt just to have a guild and do GvG PvP.  PvP (not sure if this has changed) was a complete crap shoot; the lvl ranges were ridiculous, and you couldn't que with your party members.  Every team was randomly selected, which made it easily the worst PvP I've ever experienced in any game. And the Panda would take a steady year or more of grinding to obtain, after which it would become the Meta as not having it would mean you were at a huge disadvantage.
Overall, the game had great potential.  But as many have said, the Devs are trash and ignore the community, reinstate botters, and ignore game-breaking bugs like the cinematic bug.

Private server is the only way to play this game. A server with defined rules and a decent admin are a must. Whether they use cheats or not, you'll absolutely hate this game on public servers. Friends of mine couldn't even play on them. They'd spawn in and instantly die. Roving death squads on beaches or if they'd survive a bit, they'd be hunted down and dragged to death eventually anyways.
When it comes down to it, there is no reason to feed the immature troll players which this type of game brings in. Just make a private server, invite some friends on, enjoy. Much better experience.
That said, this is alpha. The game is clearly in early stages. A very playable early stage but early nonetheless. A lot of potential can be seen. However, they have to get to the point where you don't have to wipe the servers after every update. When that happens, then it is time to join in. Currently you can keep playing without server wipes but the devs don't recommend it.
Much of this game seems to revolve around forcing people into conflict. The supply nodes for some key items are rare. On a packed server, you won't be crafting huge castles. It will be all about fighting or killing others off then becoming king and demanding tribute so then you don't have to fight over nodes. It is a unique but also problematic approach. One which some people will either love or hate.
Still, as soon as the game is more stable and doesn't require wiping all the time, or till you host your own server, just hold off on this.

This is the first game i've sat and researched in 7 years and this is why...
Usually when I play games I switch off, hit keys/buttons and just zone out the day, s.t.a.l.k.e.r shadow of chernobyl does the absolute opposite. I have learned in my limited amount of playing that complacency equals death, there is no relaxing, there is no zoning out there is only concentration.
The atmosphere of the game, sound engineering, tonality of the setting and the ambience really give off that feeling that you aren't in a playground, you are in a world where one wrong corner and one stray bullet can stop you dead.
The best way the developers could get that message across to the player is when you first step out of sids bunker, there's a random series of beeps, the wind blows and sometimes a cat wails in what is probably its last moments.
The wind blows emptily through the tree's in the distance you can hear the droning about the zone being a deathtrap and a first time player can feel extremely out of their depth, confused and lost. That feeling of dread and confusion will stick to you throughout the game, that feeling is your survival instincts, a gut feeling you never really understood until now.
The first thing many players including myself learn is that you aren't  a walking death machine, you are frail and the zone let's you know that with a swift death, a death you will repeatedly see until the game crushes your precogniscent mindset on how you play shooters. You will reach a point where you will be angry and the game feels too hard and unfair but deep down, you know it was your own error that killed you so many times.
Learn the mantra: "The zone gives with one hand and can take with the other."
Next comes your rebirth, you become cautious of everything, every noise, every voice, bang, scream, growl and even your own footsteps. You learn the cordon like the back of your hand, you study where the dogs go and how the boars attack, you watch the military patrol, you'll probably get brave and after earning enough seeking artifacts you'll bribe the guard to let you through the railway bridge. You memorize every stash you find, you break every box, you loot everything and you drag yourself, heavy footed to the newbie village, down into sids bunker and you unload your winnings.
Then, your second lesson begins; you aren't a mule, you cannot carry every gun in the eventuality you will need it, you don't need 30 cans of meat or 50 medkits, you will never need to carry every AK47 you find. Yes I know i've played fallout and yes it kills me to leave stacks of guns on the roadside. But you need to train that out of yourself, if not, you will die and lose it all and it's that crushing choice between leaving a nice heavy suit at the bottom of a ladder or suffer a grim death at the jaws of a pack of dogs that will be your making.
Learn the mantra: "Greed Kills"
The third lesson is one that takes time to practice and patience. The zone does not work to your advantage, you are a guest in the zone and everything there is designed to kill, you will become aware that even the air itself can kill you. One thing that terrified me was anomalies, I initially thought after studying the cordon that anomalies were a semi-visible entity that could be easily avoided, how wrong was I when I walked straight into an electro anomaly, and a burner, and vortex anomalies. The third lesson took time and plenty of error to get right, bolts are key in passing through new areas safely pay attention to the beeping you hear that's your only way of knowing they're nearby, that and always staying mindful of the other noises around you.
Learn the mantra: "My ears precede my eyes"
The forth lesson in one that you should have been practising since day one in the zone and that's foreplanning; ensuring you have the ample equipment for the job. The landscape of each mission can vary massivley so preplan your travel. Read about the areas online, ask the stalkers about the surrounding areas, learn all you can, because even with that knowledge you can still be taken by suprise.
Learn the mantra: "the enemy of my enemy will also kill me...unless I know they both will already"
The fifth and final lesson is discipline, knowing your environs is all well and good but understanding that the previous four lessons are not merely one time tips but a collective of constants is key. Repeating the same processes over and over becomes almost habit the act of stop, look, listen, wait becomes second nature, this is when you begin to fully understand the game you play with the zone. The game isn't to win and kill everything, it isn't even to be the best, it's about being the one who knows when to pick their moments, the right equipment, the right time of day, the right moment to move from building to building.
S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Chernobyl isn't your average game, it's a lesson in life in a way, it's a mantra in itself that if you give up, you'll only feel sour about doing so, if you fail repeatedly then the way you're doing it is wrong and most of all if you relax for just one second you could get your face inverted by a bandit with a sawnoff.

The force of Bros, the whirlwind of bullets and freedom, the completely-over-the-top real life simulator against worldwide terrorism in the name of America. There is more, but if I were continue the reader would actually perish in red, white and blue colored fireworks, out of a sheer excitement and patriotism.
The game is a 2D platformer shoot’em up, not to different from the likes of Metal Slug, where all the characters are old action hero movie protagonist, and the only thing left to shoot is terrible, terrible, terrorists. You wanted to play Arnie as he was in "Commando" well here ya go, totally in there, Rocket launcher in tow and pain-a-plenty.
The game features a lengthy campaign filled with a large variety of environments for you to stretch your creativity and bullet dispensing skills. and you're probably thinking, "creativity? I thought I was going to blow everything up!" and YOU mysterious reader, isn’t wrong, but the game's chaotic nature permits to go through stages through different ways, “OH man is it like one of those random genera-“ NO IT ISN’T, but you can create different paths yourself. Be it by shooting the environment, creating holes and passages for you to sneak way past enemies or you can bomb everything and watch as all them fear-inducing, gun-wielding, ski-mask wearing jerks fall into their demise, or punch their face, in the face. best part of this glorious mess, it can be done with up to 4 players, online and/or locally.
the list of characters is pretty extensive  and it is cool to recognize the majority of them. sadly most of these freedom fueled fighters of justice, come from around the era of the early 90s and 80s, and as a result the game works better on older audiences, which may spot better the references.

All characters have a "shoot" a "grenade" and a "melee." of course each of these is completely different for each champion of steel and lead, and to add to the mix, you don’t get to choose your freedom fighters, instead they are selected at random (once they are unlocked). while not exactly amazing, the concept of losing your favorite for some lesser god of liberty, is an interesting way to spike the difficulty or force change in strategy, trough variety. and if you dont like, well tough luck, cus then you ain't got the force of the bros in you.
The game is tough, it is fun, filled to the brim with characters from a glorious era and a myriad of explosions. so how about pick up your dream of Americanizing the world and make it true, With or Without friends!

Quickly became one of my favorite games ever..
I have played Cabellas games for a long time, mostly on the console and with gun controllers even. I have always loved hunting games since good ol duck hunt but this game has taken it to a new level for me.
Multiplayer is better than any other altho as a F2P user you rely on finding a game hosted by a subscriber so you and whoever your playing with can join in.
The F2P is fairly limited but improved a lot. The game gives F2P members an ability to enjoy subscriber perks by completing missions or competitions to earn gm$ which can be used to purchase licenses for different game and some other store items. You can also earn free em$ instead of paying which is done by completing offers from their website. I have earned a bit of em$ allowing me to buy new gear like calls, camo, weapons and sights as well as a 1 day hog license when I was starting out.
I was able to obtain a couple retail liceneces of the game from a few websites which gave me a 6mo subscription each time and a some gear too which has enhanced my gameplay and quickened my process of getting to hunt other animals which has made things more enjoyable. When I started as a F2P I was stuck on Loggers Point any really only able to hunt Mule Deer until I could get a shotgun and ammo with gm$ that I earned by completing missions which let me hunt cottontail rabbits too. Now F2P can hunt a few more things and 2 animals are changed out weekly so things are much better than they were when you don't have an active membership.
The game is alot more realistic than most too which is GREAT because I wanted more of a simulation myself and not many games do this so much. I was a little irritated at first with this as I had to figure out which ammo and weapons I could use but after realizing and starting to read everything more I figured it out quickly.
I'm not usually a "Tutorial Guy" but I did find the provided tutorials useful especially after starting on a map I couldn't do anything on then talking to people who tried to help me figure out a little before being a "rager" and just quitting before I got started.
I originally rated the game 9/10 because I thought they needed to provide a little more to start out or a few public F2P hunts and such to make it seem less like a P2W type game as you had to figure out how to really play free unless you enjoyed hunting strictly mule deer on Loggers Point. Since the updates during 2015 into 2016 I would now rate the game 10/10. I can't wait for more updates as new weapons, camo, features, animals and maps get added from time to time.
I'd also like to add that I would appreciate it more if they made it a cross-platform game as I run Mac and Linux. I also think they should sell memberships and the in-game currency "em$" on the steam store as I'd like to keep my purchases here for tracking purposes.. Then they could also add steam trading cards which could be earned like other games by spending so much per card drop to encourage sales of extra game items and memberships... (Memberships were added but only the more expensive versions that include extras which people like me don't need since we have the itmes that they come with. I'd like to be able to buy just game time or game time + em$ instead but atleast they added some things to the steam store and they even go on sale sometimes.)

This game is still great. I wish that this game continues to grow and thrive, and that more people will come to know it. This is a wonderfully unique game with so much class customization, unique gameplay between classes and sub-classes, as well as a living player run economy of all kinds of crafted weapons, recipes, items, armor sets, monster cards, gems, hats, and more!
I am on Klaipeda (NA) and though the population has declined since launch, as all MMO's do, there are still plenty of people in town and you bump into people while out leveling all the time. Some sub-classes are able to sell class specific buffs that normally other people couldn't use, but you get to rent them for coin. Others repair your armor and weapons over the typically limit so you have to take less trips to town, and there are others as well who provide services to other players when they aren't out adventuring.
There are just too many things that are great about this game. I wish that you would give it a chance and learn to love it like I do. Whether you want to have a few minutes soloing and grinding for "zen" feelings, or you want to get into a group to farm experience or items or run dungeons this game can accomodate many different feelings.
If you need friends or are looking for a guild, please check out the
forums as well as Tree of Savior Fanbase which is also a great website for mapping out your Class builds and all your skill points. There is also an item search database on that website for when you are having trouble finding something or someone.
This game has been touted as the "spiritual succesor of Ragnarok Online" and it holds true to that, but It's also so much more including much more varied class choice, customization and an incredibly more fluid movement and combat system.
Good luck, and may the Goddess watch over you!

I enjoyed Sonic Generations a lot; keep that in mind because this game was essentially developed and marketed as a successor to that game. Colours was good too. I even enjoyed Lost World and the maybe 20% of Unleashed that defined the boost games.
I'll start with the positives. Graphically the game has some stunning environments, in particular the Metropolis level (not THAT Metropolis) and Modern Sonic's Death Egg level. All of the levels look fine but there is a serious deficit of variety, with too many samey industrial environments and only seven different zones.
As for the PC port, the performance that I experienced was generally better than expected, but the game suffers from some dropped frames. This is curious because raising the resolution by a whopping 2.25x (from 1080p to 1620p) doesn't tank the framerate as you would expect if GPU performance was the issue, whereas raising my refresh rate to 72Hz in borderless mode exacerbated the issue greatly, suggesting CPU performance issues. This console port shouldn't naturally tax the CPU, so the cynic in me wants to blame poorly-implemented Denuvo, but I honestly haven't got a clue.
Note that many people have had more severe issues, but I can't comment because otherwise I'm happy with the port. I'm playing this with a Ryzen 1600, GTX 1060, 8GB DDR4-3200 system, for reference.
Finally, there are good levels here! I had fun with most of the Modern Sonic levels and a few of the Avatar levels.
To segue into the bad things about Sonic Forces (and there are a lot) let's look at what they got wrong with the Classic Sonic levels.
- Sonic actually feels heavier and less responsive than Generations. You can cancel momentum in a jump almost immediately by pushing back, but he struggles to actually move backwards past that point. It feels as if there is no 'curve' to movement speed, only extremes; "gotta go fast" or not at all. Avatar and Modern Sonic controls are similarly poor but it's most egregious during Classic's stages which focus on platforming.
- There was clearly an effort in this game to give Classic Sonic control parity with Mania Sonic, to the extent that they gave him the drop dash and took away the spindash button from Generations. This only really serves to highlight the physics differences and the gulf in level design quality between the two games, and is made an especially poor decision by the fact that YOU CAN'T USE THE D-PAD. This was a feature in Sonic Generations, and surely consciously so, as it was in Mania, because controlling a 2D Sonic game using analogue sticks is obviously ludicrous. How was this not flagged up at any point up to release?
- The music sounds like it was put together in the week before the game shipped. No, I'm dead serious. The quality ranges from 'bad Mega Drive game' to Sonic 4. Just the most basic, unimaginative rubbish possible. One level (maybe Classic, maybe Modern) had music that seemed to be looping every few seconds, in a lazy attempt to convey urgency (if we're being charitable). Many sound as if they didn't finish making all of the separate instrumental tracks before shipping, that's how basic they are.
- The levels in general lack the depth and polish of the levels from Generations. Having finished the game, I immediately replayed Green Hill in both games, and the difference was incredible.
This applies to all of the levels, actually. Generations was a tightly designed game, offering you many options for moving through levels at your own pace, from understanding the structure of each level through trial-and-error, to the different movement options and technical nuance in performing them. The game had very dense levels, in gameplay terms, and encouraged speed and style as an optional gameplay challenge above simply finishing the level, allowing players of low and high skill level to enjoy their own 'version' of the game.
Sonic Forces forgoes this, and the levels are generally not heavily layered or challenging. Attaining S ranks is simple, and why wouldn't it be? The levels are simple.
Sonic is missing a few abilities in this game, but the most annoying to me is the little hop he'd do on a light jump. Why? It didn't detract anything and contributed to the valuable 'style' aspect of Generations. Traversing short gaps using it felt very cool and was optimal since it preserved forward momentum. Drifting was a fairly simple mechanic but it was fun and broke up the action while requiring some skill and feeling pretty cool to pull off.
The avatar adds a grappling hook, a slower homing attack, and one of several weapons (or 'wispons'), plus wisp abilities. I didn't actually care that much for wisps the first time, I felt like they slowed the game too much while having little value beyond being situational side-route accessors. I didn't enjoy the avatar stages at all but apparently others thought they were the best in the game so YMMV. That said, the avatar has some really great music for it's levels (and for the record, Modern Sonic's music is hit-or-miss, but generally pretty good!)
Okay, the story is boring. The villain's motivation is beyond meagre, and the initially dark tone of the story gives way to the light, humdrum Sonic house style ala Lost World and Colours. Let's face it, we all wanted a trainwreck self-serious story somewhere between Shadow and Sonic '06, and that's what the marketing made this look like.
This is getting stupidly long, so to conclude, I don't hate myself for buying this game because I'm a huge Sonic fan but if I was a professional reviewer attempting to make an objective quality judgement I don't think I could rate this higher than a 5 or 6. By comparison I guess I'd give Lost World a 7. Generations would be an easy 9.

People wanted actual Ragnarok Online 2, but instead got laggy Torchlight 2 made into mmo and got mad. It's understandable. RO was a game you could succesfully sink a decade of your life into.
The game itself, however, is quite enjoyable. It would be really good if certain severely cancerous elements would be removed, like no 1 to 1 trade without premium or certain quests being impossible to complete because there's 200 other hobos hunting for this one specific mob at the moment. And, of course, tremendous lags while servers are filled with gold trader bots.
Game has wonderful aestetics, aside from dialogue sprites that are creepy af, it's either majestically bearded knights with tumblr noses and babyfaces, or creepily faced ladies with breats on full display. Actual ingame models and locations look very crisp, design of mobs is pretty much wierd as usual, even more cartoonish than in RO. I'm yet to see actually spooky creatures that RO had, like Amdarais or Evil Druid. Music is too *le anime*, on some bosses i swear to god it seems like they hired Kalafina or something. Character customisation is pretty much lacking, can we get at least different clothing colors or something?
Questing is linear and may seem mandatory, but there are other ways of leveling it seems, i'm too lazy to look into that (some peeps reported seeing lvl 150 chars at first day). Quest story is... well. If you played Diablo 3 you will manage through, it seems. Quests are as follows: collect this, activate that, kill those mobs. Sometimes it becomes a bit more interesting, like for instance in one quest you have to turn into mob and then speak to other mobs to lure them into a shrine to blow them up. Felt sorry for poor mofos, actually.
Fighting actually feels pretty good if you enable mouse controls, but once again, right now everything just lags, so you will miss all your spells. You can also activate your joypad and crash the game, nice feature indeed. There's major complaints that bosses have same patters with spawning minions/totems, but they actually have differend attacks and kind of spells. Anyway, it's not like bosses in RO were anything to write home about.
Another major complaint people have is about classes not mixing very well with each other, people  keep screwing up their builds. Again, so far it seems pretty fun. I don't understand how most of abilities scale because there's no actual formula displayed, but i can live with that. To advance to other class you usually have to perform some fast quest like kill 12 dudes or something.
Aside from learning abilities, you can "research" attributes for silver and sometimes real time. They power certain abilites up, like add more scaling percent, debuffs, or toggle-remove certain effects. You can either take different sub class each time you advance, or can choose to keep the class to get more powerful class related abilites.
Yeah, it's easy to screw up, but considering you have game wiki and common sense not to take spear oriented class after you leveled something that works with two handed swords, you should manage. Anyway, it's WAY more sensible than RO where you have to keep in mind that with top possible equipment you can get, your stat should be dividable by 5 or 2 or something, one wrong attribute point and YOU DUN GUFD.
On technical side right now - rubbish. If you want to buy early access special snowflake ticket - wait till whine about lag stops, if it ever will. RIght now i would call it "sometimes playable." Not gonna point the fingers, but someone could've launched more servers at the launch. Some quests are bugged, but you can usually work that around by switching channels or switching control mode. At least random game crashes stopped.
Anyway, i give this game 100 female highlander butts out of 100 and award with nostalgia medal with engraved scene of porings gang-rаping a high priest.

After Sonic Generations and Sonic Mania, you'd think Sega would have a solid idea of how to make the next game and what the fans would want out of a Sonic game. Upon finishing this game, I can safely say Sonic's developers have not learned the lesson of all the failed Sonic titles. Yet.
Sonic Forces is not a good game. Well, it's mediocre. The mixed review scores on this site and on Metacritic is exactly what such a lazy effort deserves. There's no heart in this mess of a game. The conrols are worse than Generations. I can't even wrap my mind on how that could be. Generations wasn't perfect, but it had very precise ccontrols. Here? Not even close!
Too many times you'll fly off the edge, with you trying to stop! You can't sidestep in midair like you could in Generations or Colors. (Author's note: this may have been a memory laspe.) You can't slide around corners, meaning if you hit a sudden curve too quickly, chances are you are going right off the edge. The avatar's controls are imprecise as well! It feels slippery for lack of a better word. You think you could easily make a platform, but then you realize you hit the jump button too lightly and either under or over shoot the platform, falling to your death. At least Generations added the orange sign that shows a fall coming up that the camera may not show. That's not even here! So that's a step BACKWARDS! This is like playing the older Sonic games and having to deal with clunky controls! Yes folks, we've gone BACK to having bad controls and camera issues in a Sonic game after Generations and Colors fixed that! Even Sonic Lost World handled better than Forces!
Story is important in games. The developers of Forces think so too. So the story actually takes center stage here. You'll be playing a stage and are CONSTANTLY interrupted with Sonic and  friends talking to you. It can actually distract you! And it CAN lead to you dying! Why is the story so serious here? The tone is like that of the Archie comics! Very serious! I mean, we're told that Eggman TORTURED Sonic for six months while he was in captivity! I don't even know what to say to that. It's funny, yet disturbing at the same time. But don't worry, Sonic didn't seem to mind! He's cracking jokes about chili dogs right after being freed.
Some weirdo fan fiction character named Infinite is the focus in the story. Most of the game centers on trying to unravel the mystery of Infinite and his Phantom Stone powers. Ultimately he's defeated and he leaves no impact. Aside from him, it's the same old Sonic versus Eggman tale. But previous stories, while hammy, have actually been done better than this. It makes me yearn for Sonic Adventure 2's campy mammal melodrama! That's how bad this game's story is!
The extra Shadow episode is three stages. When I finished the main story and played Shadow I literally could not believe that was the end. You're shown the beginning scene from the trailers where Sonic first meets Infinite. He gets his♥♥♥♥♥handed to him, then it ends. So does the Shadow Episode. I literally sat there, waiting for another stage, in total disbelief that was the end!
Speaking of the shortness of the Shadow campaign......
The main story is very brief. You could finish it in less than four hours if you tried. FOUR HOURS! There are only a few stage designs: Green Hill, Chemical Plant, Destroyed City, Death Egg, Mystic Forest and Eggman's Fortress. That's it. You'll be playing through the exact same stages multiple times. Chemical Plant is replayed more than any other stage. Why? That's not even going into the bosses. All you do is boost to get close, jump up and ram them with the spin attack. Each and every one. Some require more strategy.....not really. All you have to do is wait for them to leave themselves open when they are NOT on an auto-run platform like Metal Sonic or the first and last phase of Infinite! The avatar's shortcomings really shine here, as you'll clumsily get hit by easily avoidable projectiles, OVER AND OVER AGAIN! The final boss, Death Egg Robot, is the hardest in the game, yet most predictable. How can that be? You've guess it! THE CONTROLS! You'll slam into rockets, lasers and flying debris all the time. Then you'll fall off the platform and die. It's unbearable! Not in a fun way either! You can make a challenging boss WITHOUT it being a drag to fight against!
No effort was put into refining this game at all and it shows! They finished it, made sure it looked good enough, ironed out the biggest bugs, then shipped it out for sale. No time was spent going back over the finished product to change fundamental elements of the game to improve the overall quality. This really feels like a game that's in the pre-release stage of development: it's almost done but a few more months or years could have been invested in it to really make it sparkle with brillance!
Guys, I say with so much affection, save your money. Buy Sonic Mania. It's way more fun and is cheaper. I regret wasting $40 on this crap!
Sonic Team, you HAVE to do better. This is unacceptable at this point! Whenever glorified FAN GAMES are beating your games in terms of quality content, you have some serious problems! As Sonic himself said in earlier games
"HEY! STEP IT UP!!!!!"
4/10

Ok... lets get this out of the way. This game has some very very cut and dry similarities to another game called Fortresscraft. And from what I understand there's a bit of bad blood between these two... but make no mistake each game is great in their own respects and past their similarities the two divide very quickly in terms of style, not just visually but gameplay wise as well.
The Factory-
You remember that Bugs Bunny Looney Toons factory scene, where there's conveyor belts and machines working and its loud and Powerhouse (you're welcome btw) is playing in the background? That's this game incarnate. vast lines of conveyors, robotic arms, and automated assembly lines. You can literally make a car manufacturing plant if ya wanted to. Its that in depth. The only thing you don't need to do is assemble the individual components (Doors, windows, drive shaft ETC)
The War-
You're not alone. You will periodically come under attack by aliens that are almost sprite thefts of Starcraft 1 zerg. That's fine, I actually think that's a plus. They're FAST and they're mean. So you must construct additional turrets in order to defend yourself...but sometimes that's not enough. SO BUILD A MOTHER ♥♥♥♥ING TANK!!!!
The Science-
there's a pretty in depth research system that adds new equipment and passive buffs to your machines. Not much to say there other than its pretty good and very smooth.
The End-
Not a clue. Can't wait.
The Result-
A visually naseutating Rube Goldberg machine of conveyors and assemblies. Vast fields of ore stripped and left baren. Pollution and slaughtered local wild life all to feed your needy machine.... Can't wait to see what else they add.

One of the most challenging games I've played in a long time. The best thing I like, you don't have your hand hold.
Now first off, Dark Souls as a franchise has this reputation for being impossibly difficult and makes you die every couple minutes, and that's true. Here's the thing though, the challenge is extremely indicative of how hard I used to find video games. I remember getting stuck and dieing dozens of time trying to get a star in Super Mario 64. I got older, and games became less difficult. Dark Souls seems to scale up and provides that same challenge I used to love in video games.
Yes, you will die. A lot. You will be a zombie, and you will get invaded, but this is hands-down the most rewarding game I've played. There's a legitimate sense of discovery of "well I'm not sure what to do, but I think I can go here now. Let's find out."
Quick note about the combat, if you like the Monster Hunter series' combat, Dark Souls is very similar. Fast paced and dodge-centered (unless you just build straight tank).
Overall, Dark Souls 2 is a complete RPG experience, filled with a sense of discovery and pioneering your own character and class. The story requires discovery as well.
TLDR: Great game. Great RPG. Great online. 10/10 will die again.

(WARNING: LONG COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW, READ EDIT 4 FOR OVERALL SUMMARY)
This game is created by the same makers as Bastion, which is one of my favorite games ever. Upon loading, Transistor is visually appealing, and Logan Cunningham (Rucks in Bastion) makes a reappearance which is exciting. Controls are fluid, music is amazing--I'm very excited to play through this game!
EDIT 1: After playing for about an hour, I must say that I think all the expectations I have had for this game are met. Unlike Bastion, which was more of a go-get-em game, Transistor really makes you think and analyze your tactics in battle, especially with the new "time stop" system where you can plan out your actions (each move you make will cost part of your "energy bar"). There are plentiful save points, and a nice level-up system to improve your skillset. The game is mysterious so far, and I think it really fits into the mood. However, some people might dislike how the story isn't really clear, and you're just following the path without much reason until (supposedly) later on in the game when things will be made more clear.
My only qualms with the gameplay itself are the somewhat repetitive nature of the fights (although each fight calls for new tactics), and the somewhat tricky level-up system which seems a bit arbitrary. The upgrades arn't clearly defined as to what exactly they do. Overall, some parts of the game feel like I'm not sure what's going on or what I'm supposed to do to upgrade the Transistor with, but that just adds to the mysterious nature of the game at the beginning.
EDIT 2: Having come across the first "boss" now, I really think that I can speak for all people when I say--wow. The way in which the "characters" speak is amazing. The fight had me on my toes, really making me consider the best way to defeat it without losing too much health. I was blown away at how the screen colors changed and blurred as I started to lose more and more health.
EDIT 3: After tinkering for a while at an Access Point (checkpoints basically), I think I figured out exactly how the upgrades work. The Transistor has four slots which hold a primary ability. Each primary ability has two secondary "upgrade" slots. In addition, you have four passive slots. You will collect "cores" which you can slot and re-slot at any Access point. For instance, I could socket Crash() into Ability 1, with Break() as its "upgrade" to have a medium-damaging medium-range attack that mini-stuns (opposed to the regular melee-ranged attack without the Break() upgrade). Or, (normally), you could leave Crash() as Primary Ability 1 (melee-range attack) and Break() as Primary Ability 2 (Long-Ranged attack). Or, you could put one into your passive once you get more cores. There are also "Limiters" which increase the power of the enemies you face (similar to Idols in Bastion), but reward you with more EXP. Indeed, the customization is insane in this game--I can foresee myself spending quite a bit of time customizing once I obtain more cores. Play how you want to play--fighter, stealth, assassin, long-range--just customize your cores to fit your playstyle! Extremely well done, albeit a little confusing at first to figure out the customizations. Only qualm might be (if any)...there are TOO MANY choices!
EDIT 4: Finished the game, Steam says it took me ~5 hours overall, but this doesn't include the second playthrough (Recursion Mode) which I think I will be playing soon. Overall, I think this game is a worthy successor to Bastion. However, I still prefer Bastion. Why? Bastion was a bit more clear-cut and easier to process. The Calamity happened, fix it. In this game, it took until halfway through the game for me to actually realize most of the protagonist/antagonist/story arc. There were also quite a few "did not expect that" moments, which can be both seen as positive and negative overall. I personally was confused at the ending--in a way, for me, not much closure, but I accepted it. I could see it going over poorly with lots of people however. This game feels a lot darker than Bastion for sure, and I really thought that the narration in some parts was quite hefty and really tugged at my conscience. It definitely leaves you with a lot to think about and has more going on beneath the surface--you will want to play this game with a very open and sharp mind. Great to discuss as well.
Also, remember to check out all the OVC Terminals--you definitely don't want to skip those as a fair portion of the story and development relies on you reading and filling in the blanks from the information given at them (Thanks to Dragonfire973 for reminding me!). Also, when you have time, make sure you socket all the functions into every slot (Primary/Secondary/Passive) and read up on all the information unlocked.
Pros:
Amazing Artwork, Beautiful Soundtrack, Superb Narration. I expected nothing less.
Lots of customization for how you want to play the game.
Story-arc similar to Bastion, so this story will feel somewhat similar.
Cons:
Somewhat repetitive battles, but interesting nonetheless.
Often confused as to what really was going on story-wise (not much explanation of what was going on), but this could be intended.
Not much closure for the ending, but definitely lots to think about. Really made me think about the whole story after the credits had rolled.
Score: 9/10
A very nice game overall. The aesthetics of the game are unmatched. However, some people might feel like the game is a bit confusing to wrap your head around. I preferred Bastion's ending to Transistor's, because Bastion was more clear and provided some closure. However, it did leave me with a lot to think about, and I want to go through the game again to see if I pick up anything I missed the first time through.
If you have any doubts on buying this game, your doubts should be dispelled--this game is worthy of your $20; a beautiful second game released by Supergiant Games.

Sonic the Positive Reinforcement Hedgehog: The Game
I didn't go into this expecting ground-breaking stuff that'll change the sonic universe forever (SEGA kind of has a problem keeping things into perspective in that regard anyways), but I didn't go out of it disappointed either.
It's essentially a mix of the color/generations formula, with some QTE in the mix (I believe that was unleashed's sthick?).  The game isn't the longest, but I find the $40 dollar price tag comes into place when you are collecting stuff like the customization options and the wispons.  Blazing through it will take you like 3-6 hours, it follows a story any standard E rated game would be privy to, so if you are in it to consume the levels in a one and done fashion, this game isn't for you.  It also has SOS missions which give more cosmetics if you complete them under the conditions provided (sometimes being forced to use the avatar of someone else), as well as daily missions which can reward you with a score multiplier.  Those daily missions seem crucial for getting S rank in a few missions, such as green hill zone or the first custom level, you'd have to go about them perfectly or find the right path otherwise.
Game ran very smoothly for me, no hiccups or anything.  I heard others weren't so lucky, I'm guessing it's a video card or processor thing.  Though if it's the latter, I'm rocking an i5 and this game still ran like a dream.  Controls can be a bit funky thanks to the difference in gravity between Modern Sonic and Classic Sonic.  If I had to guess it was to make Classic Sonic's spin more controllable due to his lack of homing spin, so he is more feathery as a result.  The custom character doesn't go as fast but is a bit more focused on gadget and wisp usage, most levels have usage for most wisps.  Seems the most useful is the lightning whip which gives you the wisp that lets you dash into ring trails and even enemies like a gimped boost.
Customization is pretty nice, though I'd of preferred they just give us the ability to dye clothes as we see fit...but I suppose they needed to pad out the mission rewards somehow.  When it comes to the characters, you get cat/dog/wolf/rabbit/hedgehog/bird/bear with each race having a unique ability (most of them have to do with getting hit though).  Gender differences are cosmetic in race, but also in victory pose (for whatever reason male get the only clapping animation, I guess only gentlemen clap).  They pretty much share clothing options, so both a male and female can rock the blue Amy dress.  Speaking of, one of the hilarious things about that is that males can rock the dresses better than the chicks, due in part to the ladies being stuck with a body suit they can't take off unlike men who are completely nakad by default.  They'll need to wait until they get the two piece bathing suit, which pretty much makes it into a bra...and even then they still have their bottom set sticking out of the lolita dress and often contrasting with the style.
All in all, game is pretty good if you don't go into it expecting a new golden age of sonic games.  I'd say it would fall short of Generations due most in part to it's shorter levels, but it also provides more levels that have more branching paths if you know where to look.

Most disappointing game of the year for me.
I really wanted to love this game. Sonic Generations is one of my favorite games of all time so when Sega announced this game, I was thrilled. I knew I wasn't gonna enjoy the story but if Sonic Team could provide a boost formula Sonic game with the same quality as Sonic Generations, I knew I would love it.
However the more they showed off the game the more skeptical I became, though I couldn't put my finger on what was putting me off. None the less I purchased the game hoping to be proven wrong and unfortunately it seems my expectations were correct.
I just wanted a boost formula Sonic game that could live up to and improve upon Sonic Generations, but instead we got the exact opposite of that. The levels, the enemy designs and even the soundtrack look and feel boring and uninspired. With mediocre level design, poorly placed enemies that only exist for you to slaughter, an embarrassingly bad story and a shameful pc port, I can't recommend this even to a sonic fan. It's an incredibly short and forgettable experience that doesn't have anything to warrent it's price tag.
I disliked it so much I actually refunded it, though the horrible pc port heavily contributed to that. It required me to use big picture mode or the sound wouldn't work in cutscenes, [though with how the story turned out silent cutscenes probably would have been a blessing in disguise] the framerate was unstable and the game had a game breaking bug that made the game crash when you got to the third level, though the crash was fixed quickly. The game also softlocked on me during one of the dialog sequences though I'm not sure if it is a pc exclusive issue or not.
After I refunded it I watched someone else suffer though the rest of the game and I'm confident that refunding it was the right choice as the game only seemed to get worse from the point I refunded it.
Take my advice and purchase Sonic Mania, [though if you're reading this, you probably already have] Mario Odyssey, A Hat in Time or Sonic Generations. These games will give you a significantly better experience and are 100% worth their price tags.

An overwhelming amoutn of cautious and safe rehashes and that i knew it owuld have been better if they went all in on originality. This game is a step forward as far as originality goes, but i hope they get the message that it's working and get even braver. For example, I'd like to see the create a character feature become a main feature of the series and make your character available for the whole game, not just some stages. Heck, i'd support a Sonic game where you do not control Sonic and instead encourage this new feature. In addition, new locales would be good. I say there was less rehash, but it was there. Chemical plant and Death Egg were beautiful, but i feel like we've visited them enoguh, haven't we? Take it to another planet and let your team make some new and exciting locations. Trust yourselves a little more and remove the crutches.
Lets talk gameplay and difficulty. So we have forward moving and 2D segments again, just like generations. Again, i want to see more courage here. It was smart to create SOnic Mania for the 2D fans, but you need to commit to it. There shouldn't have been 2D sections in this as we had that game. Let these things co exist in the world as seperate entities. You've shown us you can make good 3D, so own it. The 2D controls felt janky unfortunately and there was an over reliance on bottomless pits and spacing out checkpoints towards the end. This just makes the game more frustrating. So the 3D stuff was better and threw some multi route stuff at you. Too much hand holding, invisible wall corridors and boost to win stuff. Also, please try to remember that you aren't an endless runner, so don't reduce the controls down to resemble one at parts. Bosses were occasionally interesting, mostly annoying and were button mash spam fests when it came to doing optimum damage. There were multipel times where i did poor damage to a boss because i was not using the meta strategy of "at the right time mash A repeatedly to auto lock multiple homing attacks" and felt like you know employing strategy. Deeper boss fights please.
Back on the character creation stuff i also want to see some more races as well as more options with the nose style, because yes, theres alot of sausage nose action that forces my characters to weak masks to not look like goofy.
So, final thoughts, it's another step in the right direction. I recommend it and hope to see mroe of this kind of boldness in the next entries with less reliance on well tread areas and 2D shoe horning.

Notes:
- Lives are outright gone, the game tallies your deaths on the stage result screens.

- Original Character content is the biggest draw on display here, with tons of customization and having some of the most unique stages, especially when controller your character and Modern Sonic at the same time.
- Classic Sonic is easily the weakest link of the game, with the worst on-average level design, and reliance on 'Blast Processing' music (This is the same Sonic from Sonic Mania, where the OST is legendary without sounding 16-bit).
- Stage 28 is by far the worst stage in the entire game. It is a Original Character stage that is purely in 2D segments, and expects percise platforming. Think of the skills needed in surgery, but they give you a chainsaw instead of a scalpel.
I also recommend playing this game on Hard, as Hard is not that difficult.
Overall, this game warrants a solid 7/10. It had something special brewing here, but they focused too hard to past glories to let the new concepts reach their true potiential. What is on offer though, its pretty alright, its just not gonna blow you away.

I've spent a few hours playing this game and I have to say it actually not a bad game. It could be better in some places, while others can just be improved by just a little bit. It's close to Fallout 1 and 2, very similar to Planatary Conflict. I understand that I'm playing this in Early Access so keep that in mind if your read this.
Characters: There are currently a total of 5 playable characters, with their own special classes, Sniper, Scout, Medic, Robot (tank), and Infantry (assault rifle). Every character plays "TRUE" to their class, however there really isn't much in class improvments other than 8 skills in each class. Sure you can upgrade those skills and become amazing, but players don't have freedom to customize their characters. Yes you have the 8 skills you can level up. but when you max out your scout or whatever, every scout is that damn same.
+ Solid Class with strong builds, but lacks customization
-  Unffortunatly there are only 1 male and 1 female character model in the game that is reused for everyone (+1 robot)
* This can be fixed by giving the classes like maybe 12 skills instead, but your character can't have all the skills when they max out. The player will have to choose what they want to build. That way i'm not using the same tactics over and over again to deal with the same type of class everytime.
Equipment: Weapons can be unlocked by getting kills with your weapon. The more you kill the faster you and unlock it. The same goes for grenades and first-aid. Using the two will unlock better grenades and health-kits. Weapons and armor can be upgraded and improved, this is great and all but, once you finish upgrading an item, you can't progress farther with them anymore. You'll have to acquire the next teir of items. Also you can't choose the type of upgrdes you want to put on the item. The item has a set list and thats it.
* MORE WEAPONS (you can never have enought weapons)
- Weapons are unbalanced - (sure I'm still in the beginning of the game and what not, but I've been watching the game and the damage going around and i've noticed that damage on a weapon don't really mean much in the end) most of the time it's the class and it's specail skills that determine the effectivness of a weapon. Yes the weapon does have it's own stats and power that gives you that edge. However, my scout has been murdering "EVERYTHING" with only the second sub-MG in the game. I'm able to crit for 300+ DAM normal and 600+ DAM skill at lv.3. (normal damage around 150 avg) Meaning at this level, I can 1 shot kill, or take out 90% of their health, not to mention I get to attack twice as a scout. On my turn, someone is probably going to die... I feel great when I'm doing this, but I rather pvp in a balanced world where the player's mental ability is the key to victory and not the math you do to max out your damage.
Gameplay: The game is actually pretty straight-forward. Move behind cover, shoot the enemy, and sometime capture a point. It's a top-down grid locked tactics pvp is what it boils down too. With smart plays and a good team, you can really do alot of crazy thing even though the classes are somewhat limited. Reguardless, the gameplay is solid. I understand the this game is still in early access, but i really hope to see the following...
+ Moveable Objects
+ Destructable Enviornment and Cover
+ Ammo and Reloading
+ Mines and Traps
+ Go Prone
+ Higher and Lower elevations
+ Smoke and Fog to reduce visibility
+ Difficult Terraine and Damaging Terraine
+ Capture the Flag (game mode)
(damn if anything, just one of these will do)

Edit, 07.01.2016: In short: So the energy system is gone, since there were many negative reviews stating precisely that this kind of mechanic does not belong on steam. (Good work people. Speak out that we do not want steam to become a semi-Facebook.) Hence, I edited parts of my review. But in sum, I still find the game to be too repetetive, shallow and cannot overlook the fact that you can only craft a tiny amount of free stuff, while there is a p2w marketsystem in place aswell. Again: I'd rather pay for customization, knowing that we all have the same chances, than paying for superiority.
+ Fallout-esque artwork. The maps look alot like a polished Fallout 1 or 2. Or a apocalpse-themed Jagged Alliance 2.
+ Turn-based combat. Every team has 20 seconds for its actions. Thats more than enough, keeps the game at a great pace and opens various strategy options.
+ Lots of skills already. You can upgrade your merc with exp and ingame currency. So you do not have to spend any dime to advance. You can freely choose how to spent the exp. Also, when your merc levels up, you can spend 3 points per level on his abilities to upgrade him or her even more.
+ 5 different classes. Sniper, tank, scout, medic/tank and grunt.
+ Tactical gameplay on different maps. You will probably see some of the maps but currently their are not too many gamemodes.
+ Short loading times. There is barely no loading time. You can hop in and out without having to wait a longer period of time.
+ Nice soundtrack. Even if I do not understand a word, I can still feel that the soundtrack fits into the game and compliments it.
- Ingame cash for superior items. Cash items do have better stats and give great advantages over regular items. Like better evasion, higher damage output, more health, you name it. Sort of "pay 2 win" or "pay 4 advantages".
- Low playerbase. I know this game just launched, but with the current playerbase its hardly fun. Most of the times, each team has one real player and the rest is filled up with bots. Yes, bots. There is no way around them unless you want to wait 4 hours for the matchmaking. But the A.I. is really annoying since they will constantly run into their deaths and feed the enemy team. So, after all is does not make a huge difference if you play in any tactical way.
- Capture mode is a pain in the bottom and has nothing to do with strategy. Its basically spamming spawns, rushing to the capture point and standing next to each other spamming AOE damage. Thats not fun. Not at all.
- Grindy. Very grindy. That would not be a problem if the matches were engaging and exciting. But since you basically shoot bots all the time it quickly becomes a mind-numbing process.
In sum: While there is a great game that could be alot of fun, there are various mechanics that do not feel right at all. Instead of paying for customization, like in LoL or other games where the items are strictly only cosmetics, you can buy better items with real money. You could also get those items by playing the game and logging in daily, but it would probably take a year and you would always be the "worse equipped" merc in your rated game.
I'd rather pay to customize my merc in a non-p2w way than have to pay to keep up and to keep playing. So, I cannot really recommend this game, even if it looks so gorgeous and could be so much fun.

A step above Colonial Marines, but still a buggy mess.
Pros:
-Actually scary at times, better atmosphere than a lot of horror games.
-Alien AI is well programmed
-A pretty long game and not just a bunch of cheap copy paste jump scares
Cons:
Buggy mess. Where to start. Ive gotten stuck in terminals where the game camera stays locked on the computer even after I've hacked it and left, forcing a reload. Backtracking in the later missions causes weird sound issues. Climbing into vents can sometimes be impossible because the button prompt refuses to show. Paths that are supposed to be opened by scripted events sometimes have invisible walls, forcing a reload. Enemies can clip through objects that you're hiding in, which since they have their head inside the locker you're hiding in, the game thinks there's no actual wall there and they detect you. Human enemies will sometimes do no damage when shooting at you even if there's nothing between you.
Aside from bugs:
-Human AI is dumb as rocks, either that or everyone in the future can't see more than 3 feet in front of them
-The android enemies must have super senses because if you get detected and run from them, they will follow you no matter where you run. So even if you run down every hallway, then hide in a locker, they will still track you to that locker, meaning that if you don't stay there for several minutes while they follow your path, you end up getting caught anyway.
-Difficulty is a joke. It's easier to murder everyone you meet then hide from the alien than to actually use any form of stealth.
- Hacking mini games are stupidly easy and feel like its just there to delay you. May as well be a single button push to open anything
-Game puts a lot of effort into atmosphere then makes it all pointless once the Alien shows up. Seriously, there's serious effort put into it, but there's no time to explore or take it in because you have to deal with an insta death walking around.
Seriously, they put effort into this game, its just sad it turned out like this. Once you learn the motions, its less scary and super predictable. Remember the necromorphs in dead space that played dead? That's basically what this game does, it has several tricks it likes to use, which are good, but then does them 10 times each making it pointless.

I really wish I could say that this is the return to form we've all been waiting for when it comes to Sonic.
Unfortunately it isn't.
I feel like this game was made by a bunch of developers who've never played a game before. Over-simplified levels and mechanics, clunky controls and tutorial hints which are borderline insulting to anyone who has played a game before. Seriously, putting in "Press A to Jump" is assuming that your audience is a bunch of bricks. I don't care that the hints are removable (thank f*** for that,) just the mindset of the people who made that riles me up!
Seriously, I haven't even played through half the game yet, and I'm already tired of it! I've heard that some people have managed to complete the game in under three hours, a little less than I've spent on it. Granted those people were likely just completing the game and not fulfilling all the achievements and trials sprinkled in, but for a 40$ game that's still unacceptable.
Granted, it's not a complete waste of time. The characters and story are passable, the graphics are lovely, the soundtrack is awesome and as stale as the gameplay feels it's at least bug-free as far as I can tell, which is sadly an achievement for Sonic games today.
And there are some good ideas here, with the custom character's Wispon (weapon) being a highlight in my eyes. But as for the CC themself... I think the game could do without them. I don't mind the idea of having your own OC in a Sonic-game, but it needs to serve a purpose other than "self-insert." I personally think adding them in Forces was a waste of time and effort, which could've instead been given to the rest of the game. And if you had to play as someone other than Sonic or... other Sonic, then why not his friends? Heck, the mere idea of using technology to zoom around the city and beat up eggbots sounds exactly like Tails! Why not get to play as him instead of OC number 73654? They gave Knuckles a big role in the story, and yet we can't rough up badniks with him? The CC's just a gimmick to lure people in with the potential to play as your own character, or simply play dress-up...
In the end, this game is basically just a giant cash-grab. It looks good on the surface, has a famous name attached to it and has been hyped up like crazy within the community, but it fails to deliver on its promises. I wanted this game to be good, heck I wanted it to be the best game of all time! But wishing does not make it so...

I am on board with all of the YouTube reviews I’ve seen, who all feel pretty neutral about Forces, and even some of the critic site reviews, who don’t necessarily hate it but acknowledge that it’s a letdown.
Forces is in this weird limbo where it’s not bad, but not good either. The visuals are beautiful; the music objectively is okay, so some people hate it or love it; the avatar customization is fun; the base mechanics are good; and the story is a nice comeback for making Sonic’s world feel like it has more life in it. But while all of these good things are present, the actual use of them/the execution is what isn’t good.
Level design: way too linear (for Modern, Classic, and Avatar), not enough challenge, and no variety. Don’t need to beat a dead horse with this; just go back and look at all of the past Sonic games. They asked more of your skill as a player that Forces does not. Forces had too many short stages instead of a balanced number of stages with enough depth of challenge and fun.
Avatar elements: they invested a lot into this, and clearly it was too much. They meant for the avatar features to be the ‘meat’ of this game, so it feels like they neglected many other things in lieu of that. And the different Wispons that you get are pointless since level replayability and collecting/doing everything doesn’t mean much.
Classic Sonic: there was absolutely no need for him to be there—story and gameplay wise. They didn’t hit the nail on the head with his physics in Generations, but did a good enough job. For some reason though, they made his physics worse in Forces; he feels like I’m playing a superspeed ball of lead. And his presence does nothing for me: I don’t feel more excited to get some old school 2D platforming because “muh nostalgia”, I just feel like I’m completing a chore when playing him. I’m not a 90’s Sonic junkie like most of his modern critics, but I still like playing 2D Sonic, and I enjoyed Classic in Generations, but not at all in this game. He is pure fanservice.
Payoff: not at all does the game make you feel like your skill has improved, that you are working your way up to even more fun, or that you’ve earned anything worth having. As one reviewer said, it feels like one big interactive cutscene.
Story: some people thing it’s cringey, cheesey, or trying to hard to be edgy, but that’s not what I want to point out. I cite the story’s flaw of offloading some of its weight off on Episode Shadow and the prequel comics. On top of that, Sonic Team still sorta halfassed the story by not showing much and leaving a lot of dialogue and development in those popup window conversations or to our imagination.
I don’t like doing number ratings for things, but if I had to, I’d give Forces somewhere between 5 - 6/10, out of personal opinion; but in regards to the critics’ perspective, definitely between 4 - 5/10. I prefer to say whether a game is great to own, worth a play, or should be skipped; in the end, I personally feel Forces is worth a play, at least for a little, tiny, unbelievably small bit of fun/time-killing, but think in the long run is totally skippable.
TL;DR: Sonic Forces has me feeling the most neutral I have ever felt about anything. It isn’t terrible, but most of it’s worth is to kill some time rather than have a great time.

This, ladies and gentlemen, is how to release an early-access title.
Now, looking at the early access description, it says that "We have been working on Factorio for over 4 years. The game is very stable and is highly optimised for prolonged gameplay and creating huge factories. We have sold over 110,000 copies on our website, and we feel now is the right time to release to a wider audience." and well, they are right. Being very well-optimized and well balanced the game features unlimited playground for your own factory.
Now - it may sound boring to build up your factory, but you can rather think of this as a strategy game relying more on economy than on military aspects - while military is still important. There are spawn camps which will attack you frequently and you have to defend yourself against them. As your factory gets bigger, everything gets more and more automatized and faster and you need to really think of a good design, otherwise you will run into problems.
This game is challenging, interesting and you can have a lot of fun with it. It runs well, there are basically no bugs / glitches and everything just seems... correctly done.

I have bought Demons Souls, Dark Souls 1, and then Dark Souls 2.
I had never gotten anywhere in the first two games, and was still a total noob when it came to Dark Souls 2. I am not one to use guides in any way until i have at least tried it myself first. I persisted with DS2 and it was oh so worth it.
I found the beginning realy difficult, and it certainly took me alot of time to work out how I wanted to play. Particularly how the stats and gear affected how effective i was at that style. I eventually settled on a full mage, and probably did alot of things the hard way. But step by step, boss by boss, I got better. I have not had such pleasure in progress before, and it kept me coming back.
DS2 seemed to progressively teach me without really holding my hand on how to play better, and I really appreciated that with this iteration. I have progressed from a player that would abosolutely **** myself over a boss, to one who had a tried and proven skill set and strategies who might even get the boss on the firstish go.
The graphics are nice but by no way amazing. The next HD version in the works however should look pretty great. I found the lore of the game to be teasingly interesting and soothing, I found the early game very difficult and then end game quite straight forward but rewarding. I have not tried the DLC.
The combat mechanics seem solid, but I'm sure there is debate on this subject between the different DS games.
I highly recommend DS2 to anyone who has not played these games before, then once finished, perhaps try the earlier versions.

Also known as "When was the last time I saved" and "Cheeki Breeki Simulator", S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Shadow of Acronym is not a game that pulls its punches. A great point? Don't play the game on Novice, because a good percentage of your bullets won't render, meaning you'll click, but the gun won't shoot. It is a game best played on Master edition or not at all, which is fine by me, because all of my bullets do as much damage to my enemies as my enemies do damage to me. This is not a game to play if you fear failure. This is not a game to play if you think you're good at videogames. This is not a game to play if you freighten easy, because this game, though old, will find new ways to terrorize you. Enemy monster-types are not scary because they look the part, they're scary because of what they can do, and they're VERY good at it. Everything matters, not getting to a point in time can cause a man in charge of advancing your quests to die. Not helping out your fellow STALKER may mean that bandits will be there instead of friendly faces. This is a game of choices, and not all of the ones you make are going to be good ones. It's up to you to make the best out of a bad situation, and if that means taking a break by the campfire to chug vodka in an attempt to cure radiation poisioning, in a small encampment, with a few fellows gathered around to talk in a language you likely don't know, well. That just means you're playing the game the right way.

It's neither open-world (or maybe it is, if you call the ability to roam the countryside with nothing to do in it "open-world"), nor survival (oh jeez, my hunger metter is low. I'll eat one of those canned whatevers that every enemy drops), and judging by the inability of my char to hit anything smaller than a truck from more than 10 meters away, I'm seriously in doubt about considering it an FPS.
Not to mention the stupid fixation with making the enemies soak damage like if they were made of steel, most of the time shrugging off bullets while melting your face in a salvo.
I hear that, if you manage to not get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off by random encounters against tons of enemies (to make up for the horrid AI) that depend more on your luck to hit and not be hit by enemies and your patience than on your skill, or by suddenly being shoot in the back of the head rigth while entering a new area, then you probably can find the classic choice between factions and whatnot. From what I've seen this far it's "this guys are neutral. Those guys are mad at you for no reason. Oh and those ones too. Go shoot them or something".
The weapons found so far are boring, amounting to 3 types of samey pistols, a double-barreled shotgun, and 3 or 4 types of automatic rifles, which I call "mister spready", "spready junior" and "the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of spreadyfell", in honor to his lesser spreadiness. Seriously, it's more ammo efficient to just charge headfirst guns blazing than it is to carefully shoot at a distance. And you'll save time even if you have to reload the save once or twice.
To summarize, I find this game barely enjoyable, and even if it turns out to have some hidden beauty later in the game, it does not convince me at all to keep playing and see for myself.

I am on board with all of the YouTube reviews I’ve seen, who all feel pretty neutral about Forces, and even some of the critic site reviews, who don’t necessarily hate it but acknowledge that it’s a letdown.
Forces is in this weird limbo where it’s not bad, but not good either. The visuals are beautiful; the music objectively is okay, so some people hate it or love it; the avatar customization is fun; the base mechanics are good; and the story is a nice comeback for making Sonic’s world feel like it has more life in it. But while all of these good things are present, the actual use of them/the execution is what isn’t good.
Level design: way too linear (for Modern, Classic, and Avatar), not enough challenge, and no variety. Don’t need to beat a dead horse with this; just go back and look at all of the past Sonic games. They asked more of your skill as a player that Forces does not. Forces had too many short stages instead of a balanced number of stages with enough depth of challenge and fun.
Avatar elements: they invested a lot into this, and clearly it was too much. They meant for the avatar features to be the ‘meat’ of this game, so it feels like they neglected many other things in lieu of that. And the different Wispons that you get are pointless since level replayability and collecting/doing everything doesn’t mean much.
Classic Sonic: there was absolutely no need for him to be there—story and gameplay wise. They didn’t hit the nail on the head with his physics in Generations, but did a good enough job. For some reason though, they made his physics worse in Forces; he feels like I’m playing a superspeed ball of lead. And his presence does nothing for me: I don’t feel more excited to get some old school 2D platforming because “muh nostalgia”, I just feel like I’m completing a chore when playing him. I’m not a 90’s Sonic junkie like most of his modern critics, but I still like playing 2D Sonic, and I enjoyed Classic in Generations, but not at all in this game. He is pure fanservice.
Payoff: not at all does the game make you feel like your skill has improved, that you are working your way up to even more fun, or that you’ve earned anything worth having. As one reviewer said, it feels like one big interactive cutscene.
Story: some people thing it’s cringey, cheesey, or trying to hard to be edgy, but that’s not what I want to point out. I cite the story’s flaw of offloading some of its weight off on Episode Shadow and the prequel comics. On top of that, Sonic Team still sorta halfassed the story by not showing much and leaving a lot of dialogue and development in those popup window conversations or to our imagination.
I don’t like doing number ratings for things, but if I had to, I’d give Forces somewhere between 5 - 6/10, out of personal opinion; but in regards to the critics’ perspective, definitely between 4 - 5/10. I prefer to say whether a game is great to own, worth a play, or should be skipped; in the end, I personally feel Forces is worth a play, at least for a little, tiny, unbelievably small bit of fun/time-killing, but think in the long run is totally skippable.
TL;DR: Sonic Forces has me feeling the most neutral I have ever felt about anything. It isn’t terrible, but most of it’s worth is to kill some time rather than have a great time.

Finally getting around to playing this one. Got it on sale, it sat in my library for a good few months, cooling down from the hype. Now I'm digging into it to see what all the fuss is about.
This game is likely the only game in the licensed Alien game lineup that accurately portrays the vision of the film; the first (and best) film, released in 1979. Some parts of the game are reminding me a bit of Bioshock in outerspace, which is not a bad thing, but just a vibe I'm getting at this stage in the game.
Overall a really solid experience. Not as tense as Outlast or Amnesia, which is a nice change of pace. Things are still startling and jumpy at poitns but I'm not whiteknuckled throughout the entire game, which gives me ample time to explore the very detailed environments that pay homage to the original film.

Hopefully they will add anti-cheat soon and that will make the game actually playable, but right now it just feels like a very frustrating waste of time.

This game was fantastic.
You wouldn't really expect visually inspecting the customs papers of artistically low-res nobodies to be so engaging, but Papers, Please makes you stop and think, feel, emphasize, with the people passing through a fictional customs checkpoint in a fictional totalitarian state almost as casually as it has you also put them through full body scans to verify sex or check for drugs. It's truly a unique experience.
I haven't yet played through to every end yet-- a lot of the decisions you make on your 30 day journey have a big impacts you can't fully see. It's a beautiful, emotionally involved game, but even transcending that is the pure joy of being an efficient cog in the Arstotskan bureaucracy. The joy of this game is basically inexplicable, I can only ask that you give it a shot.

is a fast-paced game that will put your brain to work. You become your own worst nightmare as you are immediately informed of your failures. What starts out as a simple click of a button soon becomes in-depth research as you fight against the clock to make enough money to keep your family alive.

Glory to Arstotzka!

Papers, Please forced me to do some serious, introspective thinking about my values as a human being. Pleasure rushed through my veins with every passport I denied. I force a husband to abandon his wife at the border. I look down. My loins are stirring. I look up. I detain an innocent person for a minor infraction. I look down. I have a raging erection. I look up. I take a man's bribe and deny him anyways. I start to look down, but it's too late. My monitor is being splattered with sweet, lawful, justice juice for the glory of Arstotzka.
Sweet God, what have I become?

Also it has a pretty decent story, though one you can easily ignore due to the massive amounts of side-quests there are.
In short... it's kinda like a Russian Fallout, though set in Ukraine. It's quite similar to Metro 2033 in its atmosphere, though this game is an FPSRPG rather than just a straight shooter like that game is. This is the first in a series of three games (sadly there won't likely be anymore since the devs are dead), so if this series interests you at all, then this would be the likely starting point.
Have fun! :D

This and Fallout: New Vegas are my favorite singleplayer sandbox shooters. Unlike Fallout, this one's combat is purely real-time, and time keeps ticking when you're in your inventory. You'll be rummaging through your gear and get capped by a merc or gored by some terrifying mutant if you're not quick enough. The gunfights are a good mix of slower methodical long-distance encounters, and close combat with shotguns etc when in a bunker or building. The atmosphere is amazing and only slighted by some bugs here and there that break the immersion (mainly when NPCs get stuck or their animation loops). The story is pretty tough to follow and the ending isn't very rewarding, but the journey getting to that end is well worth it.
